At the age of five, he took leave of his parents to shave his head; he sought out renowned masters everywhere and extensively explored the multitude of scriptures, becoming proficient in both Buddhist and secular learning and broadly mastering the wisdom of both ancient and modern times.
At the age of fifteen, he first conceived this aspiration, desiring to travel to the Western Regions; he admired the noble conduct of Faxian and yearned for the lofty character of Xuanzang.

Furthermore, he was diligent without wasting a moment and never set a book down from his hands; having received full ordination upon reaching the age of twenty, his steadfast resolve became even firmer.
In the second year of the Xianheng era, at the age of thirty-seven, he finally set out on his journey.
Upon first arriving in Panyu, he gathered several dozen like-minded companions; however, as they were about to board the ship, all but a few withdrew and desisted.
Jingfengli traveled alone, enduring every hardship and peril.
In every land he reached, he was fluent in the local languages.
Whenever he encountered tribal chieftains, they all treated him with great courtesy and respect.
Gṛdhrakūṭa and Kukkuṭapāda were both visited in succession;
Mṛgadāva and Jetavana were all beheld.
Every sacred site was fully sought out.

After twenty-five years, having traveled through more than thirty countries, he returned to the region of the Yellow River and the Luo in the middle summer of the year Yiwu (665), the first year of the Zhengsheng era of Empress Wu.

He obtained nearly four hundred volumes of Sanskrit texts comprising the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras, totaling five hundred thousand verses; he also brought back one set of the true image of the Vajrāsana and three hundred grains of śarīra.

The Empress Dowager personally went out to meet her at the East Gate; the monastics from various temples led the procession with banners, canopies, songs, and music, and by imperial decree, she was installed at Fo-shou-ji Temple.
At first, he translated the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* together with the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda from Khotan;
after the Jǔshì era, he undertook the translations independently.

From the year of Gengzi until the year of Gui-mao in Chang’an, at Fuxian Monastery and Ximing Monastery in the capital of Yongjing, he translated twenty works in total, including the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Maitreya-buddhābhisaṃbodhi-sūtra*, the *Ekākṣara-vidyārāja-mantra*, the *Vyūharāja-dhāraṇī*, and the *Dīrghanakha-parivrājaka-sūtra*; the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, the *Nidāna-mātṛkā*, the *Ekottarakarmaśataka*, and the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā*; the treatises *Hastavāla*, *Upādāyaprajñapti*, and *Ṣaṭprabheda-upadeśa*; and the *Nāgārjuna-pañcaśatika-stotra*.

The Śramaṇa Aṅgaja from North India verified the meaning of the Sanskrit text; the Śramaṇas Bolun, Fuli, Hui-biao, Zhiji, and others transcribed and verified the wording; the Śramaṇas Fabao, Fazang, Degan, Shengzhuang, Shenyi, Renliang, Dayi, Cixun, and others verified the meaning; and Xu Guan, Assistant Professor at the Imperial University (Jingdun Taixue), supervised the transcription and presented it for imperial inspection.
Empress Wu composed the "Preface to the Holy Teachings" (*Śāsanaprasthāna*) and ordered it to be placed at the beginning of the scriptures.

Subsequently, in the first year of the Shénlóng era (the year Yǐsī), during the reign of Emperor Zhōngzōng, he translated the *Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra* at the Inner Sanctuary in Eastern Luò. Furthermore, at Dàfúxiān Temple, he produced four works: the *Jaya-sūtra*, the *Gandharvarāja-bodhisattva-dhāraṇī*, and the *Sarvālaṃkāra-rāja-sūtra*. Śramaṇa Pándù read the Sanskrit texts; Śramaṇa Xuánsǎn received them by pen; Śramaṇa Dàyí verified the text; and Śramaṇas Shèngzhuāng and Lìzhēn verified the meaning. Cui Tí, Vice Minister of the Ministry of War, and Lu Càn, Palace Secretary, polished the prose and corrected the characters, while Yang Shènjiāo, Director of the Imperial Library and Prince Consort, supervised the project.

The Emperor deeply revered the Buddhist scriptures and, drawing upon his exceptional sagely insight, composed the "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripitaka of the Great Tang’s Dragon-Rising Era.
Furthermore, he went to the western gate of Luoyang to proclaim the newly translated sutras to the assembled officials.
In the second year, Jing accompanied the imperial entourage back to the capital of Yongjing; a Translation Institute was established at Dajianfu Monastery, where he resided.
In the third year, an edict summoned him into the palace to spend the ninety-day summer retreat with nine other śramaṇas engaged in translation.

The Emperor, reflecting that in his former life he dwelt among the Fang clan, where he was beset by obscurity and distress with no refuge, prayed to the Medicine Master Buddha; he subsequently received divine blessings and, bearing this past grace, has once again expounded the Great Way.
Thereupon, he commanded his disciples to retranslate it once more in the Dafoguang Hall; the resulting two-fascicle text was titled the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabhāsa-pūrvapraṇidhāna-guṇa-sūtra*.
The Emperor presided over the Dharma assembly and personally transcribed the texts by hand.

In the first year of the Tanglong era (Gengxu) of Emperor Ruizong, at the Great Jianfu Monastery, he brought forth twenty works, including the *Bathing Image Merit Sūtra*, the *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* for the two assemblies, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-ratnodbhava*, and the *Ālambana-parīkṣā-ṭīkā*.
The Śramaṇa Dharmamitra of Tukhāra verified the Sanskrit meaning; the Śramaṇa Balananda of Central India verified the Sanskrit sense;
the Śramaṇa Dharmānanda of Kaśmīra verified the Sanskrit text; the layman Īśvara, chief of Eastern India, verified the Sanskrit original;
and the Śramaṇa Huìjī and the layman Li Shìjiā of Central India [assisted].
Having read many Sanskrit manuscripts, the śramaṇas Wénghāng, Huìzhǎo, Lìzhēn, Shèngzhuāng, Àitóng, and Sīhé verified the meaning; Xuánsǎn and Zhìjī transcribed the text;
and the layman Gōtama Vajra from Eastern India and Prince Āshùn of Kaśmīr verified the translation.
More than twenty officials, including Li Jiao, Grand Master of the Hall for Cultivating Literature; Wei Sili, Minister of the Ministry of War;
Zhao Yanzhao, Vice Director of the Chancellery; Lu Zangyong, Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel; Zhang Yue, Vice Director of the Ministry of War;
and Li Yi, Secretary of the Chancellery, successively refined the text with literary polish, while Wei Jushi, Left Vice President of the Department of State Affairs, [supervised the project].

Yuan was supervised by Su Gui, Right Vice President of the Department of State Affairs, and by Yi, Prince of Guo (posthumously titled Sizi), Grand Master of the Secretariat; both served as joint supervisors.

In the second year of the Jingyun era (the *xinhai* year), he again translated the *Sutra of the Divine Incantation Praising the Merits of the Tathāgata* and other scriptures at Dajianfu Monastery, with Xue Chongsu, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, serving as supervisor.
From the Jiushi era of Empress Wu to the Jingyun era of Emperor Ruizong, he translated a total of fifty-six works comprising two hundred and thirty fascicles.

Furthermore, he separately compiled five works totaling nine fascicles: the *Biographies of Eminent Monks Seeking the Dharma in the Western Regions of the Great Tang*, the *Record of Inner Dharma Sent from the South Seas*, the *Essential Rituals for Confessing Sins*, the *Essential Rituals for Using the Threefold Water*, and the *Ritual Procedures for Protecting Life through Releasing Creatures*.

Furthermore, there was produced the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vaibhāṣika* (or *Sarvāstivāda-bhadra-stūpa*), which consists of the *khandakas*, *vagga*s, and similar sections found within the various Vinayas; these are merely differences in the pronunciation of the Sanskrit, such as "Chu" and "Xia," and it comprises approximately seventy-eight fascicles.
Although Jing translated across all three collections of the Tripiṭaka, he specialized in the Vinaya; in the intervals between his translation work, he gave detailed instruction to his disciples.
In all his actions, he prioritized diligent protection [of the precepts].
This water-strainer for purifying impurities is truly exceptional among its kind.
Its practice has been transmitted by fellow students throughout the capitals of Chang’an and Luoyang.
How magnificent!
This was also a great event for the Bequeathed Dharma.
He passed away in the second year of the Xiāntiān era at the age of seventy-nine and with fifty-nine years of ordination seniority; his funeral expenses were provided by the government.
Of the works produced by Baosidu, only the original texts remain; I have not yet had the leisure to provide a detailed commentary, as the day of my departure has already approached.
Nevertheless, his transmission of the sūtras and vinaya stands on equal footing with that of Master Xuanzang.

Regarding his writings, they are mostly characterized by literary elegance; in transmitting the secret mantras, he reached the very pinnacle of their subtlety, such that it was only then that the nuances of the two- and three-syllable combined sounds were fully understood.
The stupa now stands on a high ridge to the north of Longmen in the capital of Luoyang.
The postscript states:
"The term 'yì' (translation) is synonymous with 'yì' (exchange); it means to exchange that which one possesses for that which one lacks."
It is like the various species of *karka* and *juzu*: when transplanted from their native soil, the *juzu* transforms into *karka*.
Although the names "karka" and "juzu" differ, there is no difference between them in terms of their pungency, fragrance, or the texture of their leaves.
Furthermore, just as the nyagrodha tree in the Western Regions is the willow in the Eastern Land (China)— though their names differ, the substance of the tree is one—
so too have there been many translators from the Han dynasty down to the present Song dynasty.
During the transition between the Jin and Wei dynasties, when people from Western India arrived, they referred to it only as "nyagrodha.
It was only when the local translators were pointed toward the willow trees by the Western monks that they finally grasped the meaning of the term.
Subsequently, an Eastern monk went there and recognized that the nyagrodha was the willow of the Eastern Land (China).
Thus, the dialects of both lands were simultaneously and thoroughly understood.
Yet, those of the two classes—exclusively Westerners and exclusively Easterners—cannot be considered entirely proficient.
When a monk from the East travels to the West, he may be deemed truly excellent only when he has mastered the Sanskrit script and fully comprehended the Buddha’s intent.

Regarding those who transmitted and translated [the scriptures], from the Song and Qi dynasties onward, there were indeed those who went there and returned; however, as for those who entered the territory to observe its customs and inevitably heard of its governance, Xuanzang and Yijing were those who attained the true reality of this matter.
These two masters were both fully proficient; they were like one who, seeing the seal script, knows it to be the writing of the Son of Heaven and can thus trust it.

According to the *Rites of Zhou*, the Office of the Xi-xu was charged with communicating with the languages of the barbarians; could Jing’s talent and wisdom not be called the Xi-xu of the Buddhist gate?
The Biography of Vajrabodhi of Guangfu Monastery in Luoyang, Tang China. Vajrabodhi; in the language of China, "Vajra Wisdom."
He was a native of the country of Mālaya in South India, which in the language of China means "Radiance"; the borders of that country are near Mount Potalaka, the palace of Avalokiteśvara.
His father, a Brahmin well-versed in the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), served as the preceptor to King Kaniska.
When Jñānagupta was several years old, he could recite ten thousand words daily; having perceived them with his eyes and transmitted them to his mind, he never forgot anything throughout his life.

At the age of sixteen, she attained awakening to the principles of the Buddha and took no pleasure in studying the various treatises of the Nirgranthas; she subsequently shaved her head and donned the dyed robes of a nun, which was due to the power of roots of merit planted in past lives.
Later, he followed his teacher to Nālandā Monastery in Central India, where he studied the Sūtras, Abhidharma, and other texts.
Upon receiving full ordination, he audited the Vinaya of all eighteen schools.
He then traveled to Western India to study the various treatises of the Hīnayāna, as well as the Yogācāra, the Three Mysteries, and the gateways of dhāraṇī.
For over ten years, he attained complete mastery of the Tripiṭaka.

Next, he traveled to the Kingdom of Siṃhala and ascended Mount Laṅkā; from there, he journeyed eastward through more than twenty countries, including those of the Buddha-vow-holders and the naked people.
Hearing that the Buddha-dharma was flourishing in Zhina (China), he boarded a ship and set sail, arriving only after several years due to numerous hardships encountered along the way.
In the Jiwu year of the Kaiyuan era, he arrived at Guangzhou; by imperial decree, he was invited to reside at Cien Monastery, and subsequently moved to Jianfu Monastery.
At whichever monastery he stayed, he invariably established a great maṇḍala initiation hall to ordain members of the fourfold assembly.
The two Chan masters Dazhi and Dahuì, as well as the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra, all performed the rites of disciples toward him.

Later, he accompanied the imperial entourage to Luoyang; from the first month until the fifth month of that year, there was no rain. Despite prayers offered at the sacred shrines of mountains and rivers, there was no response.
Thereupon, he issued an edict for Fazhi to establish an altar and offer prayers.

Accordingly, using the *Amoghapāśa* (Unfailing Hook) and relying on the Bodhisattva rites, an altar was constructed at his residence with a depth of four cubits; he personally painted images of seventy million bodhisattvas and set a time for the consecration ceremony (*pratiṣṭhā*), decreeing that it would surely rain the following day.
The Emperor dispatched Chan Master Yixing to observe him closely and discreetly.
On the seventh day, a scorching heat prevailed and the sky was cloudless. After midday, he finally opened his eyes;
at that very moment, a northwest wind arose, blowing tiles off roofs and uprooting trees, while clouds collapsed and rain poured down, striking terror into those near and far.
Furthermore, at the site where the altar was established, a hole was pierced through the roof, and water poured down profusely upon the ritual ground.
At dawn, the officials and commoners of the capital all said:
"Zhi has captured a dragon, which has flown away after piercing the roof."
When they sought to observe the site, there were tens of millions of people; this was indeed a divine manifestation of the ritual altar’s efficacy.

At that time, the Emperor was preoccupied with the mysteries of the *xuanpin* (the metaphysical source) and had not yet placed high value on the Gate of Emptiness (*kongmen*). The relevant authorities, seeking his favor, memorialized that the foreign monks from the frontier regions should be sent back to their own country, and the day for their departure was set.
When the attendant heard of this, he informed the Emperor.
The Master said, "I am a monk from India and not a barbarian from the frontier; I have no business with Your Majesty's imperial edicts, and I shall certainly not leave.

After several days, he suddenly boarded an imperial carriage and was taken to Yanmen. Upon offering his formal farewell, the Emperor was greatly astonished and issued a hand-written decree ordering him to remain.

Initially, the Emperor’s twenty-fifth princess was the object of his deepest affection; having been afflicted by a chronic illness for some time that could not be cured, she moved to the Xianyi Outer Residence. There she remained with her eyes closed and silent for over ten days.
An imperial decree was issued ordering Zhì to bestow the precepts upon her; this command was given because it was foreseen that she would certainly die.

Zhì went there and selected two seven-year-old girls from among the palace women, wrapped their faces with crimson silk, and laid them on the ground. He then had Niù Xiántóng transcribe a copy of the decree on a single sheet of paper, which was burned elsewhere, while Zhì performed esoteric incantations over them.
The two daughters recited it from memory with perfect clarity, not omitting a single word.
His wisdom entered samādhi, and by means of inconceivable power, he caused the two girls to carry his decree to King Yama.

After the interval of a meal, the King ordered his deceased foster-mother, Lady Liu, to escort the Princess’s soul to follow the two daughters; thereupon, the Princess sat up, opened her eyes, and spoke as she had before.
When the Emperor heard this, he did not wait for his guards or attendants but galloped on horseback to the outer residence.
The Princess reported, "The workings of destiny are difficult to alter;
now that Your Majesty has sent me back, I shall merely pay my respects to Your Sacred Countenance."
"May he pass away after only half a day," she said;
and from then on, the Emperor began to revere her with deep devotion.

Empress Wu was uniquely favored among the six palaces, and she frequently presented him with precious playthings. Zhi urged the Empress to urgently commission a golden image of the Bodhisattva Amitāyus (Kongō Juryō Bosatsu), and further exhorted the Prince of Hedong to have an image painted within the Vairocana Pagoda.
He said to his disciples, "The lifespans of these two men will not be long.
After several months, it happened exactly as he had said; indeed, many instances of such prior awareness occurred.

There was no principle his wisdom did not penetrate, and no matter he did not verify through practice; whether it concerned the sūtras, śāstras, vinaya, secret mantras, or other texts, he would analyze and explain them according to any inquiry, like a bell suspended from its stand.
Should anyone enter his gate, Zhì would look upon their face once and never forget it.

Whether in speech or silence, rising or sitting, he remained steadfastly unchanged; whether encountering joy or anger, opposition or favor, he showed no different countenance. Those who gazed upon him in worship could find no limit to his depth, and they naturally submitted to his influence.

Since arriving in Panyu in the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era, he gradually made his way to the Divine Realm (China), where he extensively propagated the *Guhyagarbha Tantra* (*Mizang*). He constructed maṇḍalas and performed rituals according to the Dharma, all of which were accompanied by auspicious and miraculous responses.
The śramaṇa Yixing held this teaching in high esteem and frequently sought instruction from him; [Amoghavajra] guided him one by one with his wisdom, never withholding anything in secret.

Having established an altar for himself and received the empowerment according to this dharma, Yixing, recognizing its capacity to benefit sentient beings, requested that it be translated and circulated.

In the eleventh year, by imperial decree, he translated at Zisheng Monastery the *Yogācāra-japa-vidhi* in two fascicles and the *Saptakoṭi-dhāraṇī* in two fascicles. Eśvara, a chief Brahmin from Eastern India serving as a direct secretary, acted as the oral translator, while the śramaṇa Wengu of Mount Song served as the scribe for the transcription.

In the eighteenth year, at Dajianfu Monastery, he further produced the *Mañjuśrī Five-Syllable Heart Dhāraṇī* and the *Essentials of the Yoga Method of Avalokiteśvara*, each in one fascicle. The śramaṇa Zhizang acted as the oral translator, while Xingyi transcribed the words and edited them into a finished text.
Furthermore, he observed that there were missing passages in the older versions of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-hṛdaya-mantra* (Suikyu), which he supplemented to make them complete.
Regarding the dhāraṇīs and mudrās translated by Zhi, they all proved efficacious upon their application; as for their secret circulation, these were the most excellent among them.
Having received instruction at the two capitals, those he saved were exceedingly numerous; whether lay or ordained, his lineage was transmitted in succession.
On the full moon of the eighth month in the twentieth year, the Ren-shen year, at Guangfu Temple in Luoyang, he addressed his disciples, saying:
"When the white moon is full, I shall depart."

He then paid homage to Vairocana Buddha, circumambulated him seven times, and withdrew to his own quarters. There, he burned incense and made a vow; having placed the Sanskrit manuscripts and the newly translated teachings upon his head and entrusted them [to his successors], he passed away in profound stillness.
He was seventy-one years of age and fifty-one years of seniority in the monastic order.
On the seventh day of the eleventh month of that year, he was buried to the right of the Yi River at Longmen, where a stupa was erected to commemorate him.
Fukū, a disciple of Saichō, submitted a memorial recommending [the posthumous honor], and by imperial decree, he was granted the title of National Teacher (Kokushi).

Duhongjian, a Grand Secretary of the Secretariat and a disciple who had received the *guanding* initiation, was one who had long been devoted to his service; he composed an inscription to record the Master’s virtues.
The commentary states:

Regarding the manḍala rites of the five families, for the purpose of capturing spirits and demons, it is exceedingly easy to effect the removal of maladies and the expulsion of malevolent influences by causing them to manifest through a young boy or a young girl.

People of recent times employ these [practices] to seek profit for their bodies and mouths; consequently, they rarely produce verifiable results and are generally held in contempt by their contemporaries.
Alas! The True Dharma has become so diluted and weakened as to reach this state!

The Biography of Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery in Jingzhao, Tang China. Regarding the monk Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery in Jingzhao, Tang China: his Sanskrit name was Amoghavajra; in the language of Han, it means "Amogha-vajra" (Non-empty Vajra). The two characters "Zhi" and "Xing" (Cessation and Practice) are an abbreviation [of his full name].
Originally from a Brahmin clan in Northern India, he lost his father while still young and followed his uncle to travel and observe the eastern lands.

At the age of fifteen, he became a disciple of the Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi; initially instructed in the *Siddhaṃ* script and the treatises on grammar (*śabdavidyā*) based on Sanskrit manuscripts, he mastered them thoroughly within ten days.

The Master was greatly impressed by him, conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon him, and initiated him into the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu. By means of the ritual of casting flowers, he discerned that the disciple would later cause the teachings to flourish extensively.
Upon receiving full ordination, he became proficient in the Sarvāstivāda school and mastered the scripts and languages of foreign lands.
Whenever his master translated scriptures, he was always commissioned to assist in the translation work.
Regarding the study of the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* (grammar), where others required twelve years of effort, he completed it in six months.
He recited the *Mañjuśrī-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna* for the duration of one year, completing it in just two evenings.
His quick-wittedness and sharp faculties were all of this nature.
When he sought to study the New Yoga, the Five Families, and the Three Secrets, three years passed before his teacher would grant him instruction.

When Huikong intended to return to India, his master dreamed that the images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in all the temples of the capital were traveling eastward; upon waking, he realized that Huikong was truly a vessel for the Dharma, and thus granted his request.

He bestowed upon him the empowerments of the five families, the homa rites, the methods of the ācārya, as well as the *Vairocanābhisambodhi Sūtra*, the *Susiddhikara-vidhi*, and so forth, transmitting them all in their entirety.
Thereafter, the Master traveled to Luoyang. While attending upon him there, he encountered the Master’s passing, which occurred in the twentieth year of the Kaiyuan era.

Once the portrait hall was completed and the posthumous title had been conferred, [the Emperor] respectfully received a bequeathed decree ordering him to travel to the Five Indias and the Kingdom of Siṃhala; thus, they deliberated on the long journey.

Upon first arriving at Nanhai Commandery, the Inspector Liu Julin earnestly requested initiation; thereupon, at Faxing Monastery, he conferred the precepts upon successive waves of hundreds of thousands, even millions of people.
Xuankong prayed to his tutelary deity for ten days, and Mañjuśrī appeared before him in person.
When he was about to board the ship, the Imperial Inspector summoned and admonished the leading foreign merchants in the territory of Panyu, including Yixibin, saying:

"The Tripiṭaka Master is now proceeding to Siṃhala in South India; you must strictly instruct the ship's captain to ensure that the Master, along with his disciples Han Guang, Hui Long, and twenty-seven others, as well as the state credentials, reach their destination safely without any negligence or loss."

In the twelfth month of the twenty-ninth year, they boarded a *kūṇala* vessel and departed from the South Sea. Upon reaching the borders of the kingdom of Ho-ling, they encountered a great black wind.

The merchants were struck with terror; each performed the rituals of his own country to avert the calamity, but to no avail. They all prostrated themselves, entreating for mercy and praying for protection, while Huìxī and the others wept bitterly.
Kong said, "I now possess a dharma; you need not worry.

He then took a five-pronged bodhicitta vajra in his right hand and held a case containing the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra in his left. Performing the ritual, he recited the *Mahāpratisarā* once, whereupon the wind subsided and the sea became calm.
Furthermore, they encountered a great whale emerging from the water, its spouting waves like mountains, which was even more distressing than their previous calamity.
The merchants resigned themselves to their fate and, as before, performed the ritual together, instructing Huìxiàn to recite the *Sāgara-nāgarāja-sūtra*. After a short while, all the perils subsided.
Having arrived in the Kingdom of Siṃhala, the King sent an envoy to welcome him.
As he was entering the city, his infantry and cavalry guards lined the streets in dense ranks.
When the King saw that [the Master] was empty-handed, he prostrated at his feet and invited him to reside within the palace, providing him with offerings for seven days.

Every day, a golden *hu* measure was filled with scented water; the King personally bathed for the sake of the Void, followed by the Crown Prince, the Queen Consort, and the ministers, according to the royal rites.

Kongshi first met the Acharya Samantabhadra, whereupon he presented offerings of gold, jewels, brocades, and other valuables, requesting that the eighteen assemblies of the *Vajraśekhara* Yoga teachings be revealed, as well as the mandala rites of the Great Compassionate Womb (*Mahākaruṇā-garbha*) of Vairocana. He also requested permission for Han Guang, Huiji, and others to receive the consecrations of the five families.

Kūkai himself studied without a fixed teacher; he extensively sought out more than five hundred sections of the Secret Treasury, as well as various sūtras and śāstras. Regarding the original samayas, the secret mudrās of the various deities, ritual forms and images, altar methods and insignia, and the textual meanings and natures and characteristics, there was nothing whose source he did not exhaustively investigate.
One day, the king held a performance featuring the taming of elephants; everyone climbed to high vantage points to watch, and none dared to approach.

[The monk] recited mantras with his mouth and performed mudrās with his hands, abiding in the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) as he stood in the middle of the road. Several headstrong elephants suddenly stumbled and fell to the ground, leaving the entire kingdom in wonder.
Subsequently, he traveled through the regions of the five Indias, where auspicious omens frequently manifested.

In the fifth year of the Tiānbǎo era, he returned to the capital and presented the memorial from King Śīlamitra of Siṃhala, along with golden and jeweled necklaces, Sanskrit manuscripts of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, various pearls, and white cotton cloth; by imperial decree, these were temporarily lodged at the Court of State Ceremonial (Hónglù).
A subsequent imperial decree ordered him to enter the palace to establish an altar and confer the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) upon the Emperor.
Later, he moved his residence to Jingying Monastery.
That year, during the summer retreat, there was a lack of rain; the Emperor issued a decree ordering him to pray for rain.
The Emperor decreed:
"One must not delay when the time comes, nor act with violence when it rains.
He then established an altar for the Peacock King in the open air; before three days had passed, the rain had already fallen in abundant, soaking showers.

The Emperor was greatly pleased; he personally presented a precious casket containing a set of purple *kāṣāya* robes, which he himself donned upon [the Master], and further bestowed two hundred rolls of silk.

Later, when a great wind suddenly arose one day, the Emperor issued an edict for Kōng to perform a rite to suppress it. He requested a silver flask for the performance of ritual empowerments (*adhitiṣṭhana*), and in a mere moment, the storm subsided.

Suddenly, because a goose in the pond accidentally bumped a jar and it tipped over, the wind rose again, even more violent than before. The Emperor ordered him to stop it once more; it ceased immediately, and the effect was as before.
The Emperor thereupon bestowed upon him the title Zhizang (Treasury of Wisdom).

In the eighth year of the Tiānbǎo era, he was granted permission to return to his native country; he traveled by means of five state courier horses as far as Nánhǎi Commandery, where he received an imperial edict ordering him to remain.
In the twelfth year, by imperial decree, he was ordered to proceed at the request of Gēshū Hàn, the Regional Commander (Jiédùshǐ) of Hé and Lǒng.

In the thirteenth year, he arrived at Wuwei and stayed at Kaiyuan Temple; the military governor, along with his retinue, all wished to receive the empowerment (abhiṣeka), and several thousand officials and commoners ascended the ritual platform together, while his disciples, including Hanguang, also received the teachings of the five families.
He specially conferred the Dharma upon Li Yuanzong, the Marquis Who Opens the Court, and bestowed upon him the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu.
On that day, the earth shook within the ritual arena, and the sky proclaimed:
"This is the ultimate sincerity of the multitude's hearts."
After fifteen years, an imperial edict summoned him back to the capital, where he resided at Daxingshan Temple.

At the beginning of the Zhide era, while the imperial carriage was stationed in Lingwu and Fengxiang, Fazhong constantly submitted secret memorials concerning his well-being; Emperor Suzong likewise secretly dispatched messengers to seek the secret teachings.
When the capital was recovered and the rightful succession restored, events unfolded exactly as he had foreseen.

During the Qiannian era, the Emperor invited him into the palace to establish a *dharmadhātu* and perform the *homā* ritual, whereby he conferred upon the Emperor the consecration of the seven treasures of a *cakravartin* king.

At the end of the Upper Yuan period, the Emperor fell ill; Kōng performed purificatory rites using the *Dàsuìzhēn* mantra seven times, and on the following day the Emperor recovered, whereupon he accorded him even greater marks of extraordinary honor.
Kong invited him to enter the mountains, and Li Fuguo issued an imperial decree ordering him to cultivate merit at Zhiju Monastery on Mount Zhongnan.

On the evening of his recitation, he was moved by the appearance of Mahāsukha-sattva, who extended his brow-hair to emit light as a sign of verification; Kong’s spiritual rank thus bordered upon *siddhi*.
Kong said, "If sentient beings have not yet been delivered, how can I deliver myself?"
When Emperor Suzong passed away and Emperor Daizong ascended the throne, his gracious favor became even more profound.
Once the two sutras, the *Ghanavyūha* and the *Benevolent Kings*, had been translated, the Emperor composed a preface for them.
On the day the decree was promulgated, auspicious clouds suddenly appeared, and the entire court presented congratulations.

On the first day of the eleventh month of the first year of the Yongtai era, an imperial edict appointed him as Special Advance (Tejin) and Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Qing), and conferred upon him the title of Great Master of Vast Wisdom (Dayangzhi Sanzang).

In the third year of the Dali era, a meditation hall was established at Xingshan Temple. By imperial decree, twelve sets of brocade cushions and thirty-two embroidered silk banners were bestowed, and furthermore, provisions for a twenty-one-day vegetarian fast were granted to the monks of the meditation hall.
The Emperor commanded his close attendants, the high ministers, and the various commanders of the imperial guards to all enter the consecration ceremony.

In the winter of the fourth year, Kong memorialized that a Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva should be established as the presiding elder (upādhyāya) in all communal dining halls throughout the empire; the decree granted this permission, likely because [Kong] was dissatisfied with the fact that Kauṇḍinya was merely the first to be converted within the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
In the summer of the fifth year, an imperial edict was issued requesting that Kōng go to Mount Wutai to cultivate merit; at that time, a comet appeared.
When the religious rites were concluded, the star likewise vanished.

In the autumn, Bukong arrived from Wutai Mountain; the Emperor sent a palace eunuch with the horse Lion-Chestnut (Shizi Cong), along with its saddle and bridle, to welcome him outside the city and provide him with tents and supplies along the road.
On the second day of the tenth month in the sixth year, the Emperor’s birthday, he presented a memorial regarding the scriptures he had translated, stating:
"Since my youth, I have served my former teacher, the Tripiṭaka Master, for fourteen years, receiving and studying the Yoga system of the Dharma."

He traveled again through the five regions of India to seek out those teachings not yet transmitted to him, as well as various sutras and śāstras, totaling more than five hundred works; in the fifth year of the Tiānbǎo era, he returned to the Capital.
The Retired Emperor issued an edict for him to enter the palace and establish a consecration (abhiṣeka) maṇḍala, granting permission to translate all the Sanskrit scriptures he had brought with him.
Within the palace, Suzong established the homa and consecration rites.

Successively, we have received the commands of two sagely sovereigns to collect the Sanskrit texts of former generations from foreign lands, to repair those with frayed cords or missing pages, and to translate those not yet translated.
Your Majesty has reverently followed these bequeathed instructions, once again commissioning their transmission so as to benefit and deliver all classes of beings.

From its inception during the Tiānbǎo era until the sixth year of the Dàlì era, there are a total of one hundred twenty-odd fascicles comprising seventy-seven works, along with the catalog and the names of the monastics and laypersons who acted as scribes and recipients; these are supplemented by a brief extraction of the liturgical manuals for recitation. Having completed the transcription, on the occasion of the Emperor’s birthday, I respectfully present this for Your Majesty’s perusal.
The imperial decree was disseminated throughout the central and provincial regions, and [the work] was included in the *Catalogue of All Scriptures* (*Yiqiejing mulu*).
Li Xiancheng proclaimed the edict granting eight hundred bolts of empty-patterned brocade and silk; each of the ten virtuous masters who participated in the translation was also granted thirty bolts.
The śramaṇa Qianzhen submitted a memorial of thanks.
Monastic and lay disciples were granted gifts according to their respective ranks.

Furthermore, as the capital had not seen rain during the spring and summer, an imperial decree ordered him to offer prayers; it was stipulated that if it rained within three days, this would be due to the Master’s spiritual power.
That it poured down copiously after three days had passed was not due to the power of the Dharma.
Having received the imperial decree to establish the altar, it rained heavily by the second day, which sufficed.

The Emperor bestowed upon him a purple silk robe and one hundred rolls of various colored silks, along with seven sets of robes for his disciples, and provided a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks to repay his services.
Kong Jin submitted a memorial requesting the construction of a Mañjuśrī Pavilion; the imperial decree granted his petition.
The Consort, Prince Han, and Princess Huayang jointly completed it, contributing approximately thirty million coins from the Inner Treasury.
He further translated the *Nyalutawang Jing* (The Sutra of King Nyalutawa), with successive imperial edicts bestowing rewards that lined the roads in both directions.
By the ninth year, from spring through summer, he proclaimed the sublime Dharma and exhorted his disciples.
Whenever he spoke of the *Samantabhadra’s Vows and Practices* or the *Sutra on the Emergence of Boundless Dharma Gates*, he would urge them to recite and uphold these texts, sighing repeatedly.

Those who first receive the Dharma are specifically instructed to focus their attention on contemplating the Bodhicitta and the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) of the Honored One; by directly interpreting the letter *A* to realize the non-arising of all phenomena, they shall realize the body of Great Enlightenment as clearly as pointing at something in the palm of one's hand—thus he repeatedly entrusts them with this teaching.
One night, he commanded his disciple Zhao Qian:

"Bring me brush and inkstone; I shall briefly set forth the ritual procedures for the *nirvāṇa* and cremation to bequeath to future generations, so that they may follow these in conducting funeral rites."
Śāriputra bowed his head and requested three times: "I beg you, out of compassion, to remain for a long time.
Otherwise, on what shall sentient beings rely?
Ākāśagarbha merely smiled.
Shortly thereafter, he manifested illness and submitted a memorial to take his leave.

An imperial envoy was dispatched to inquire after his health and bestow medical provisions; he was further granted the rank of Kai-fu-yi-tong-san-si and enfeoffed as Duke of Su with a fief of three thousand households, yet he firmly declined these honors, which were not ultimately accepted.
Kongshen was deeply displeased and said, "The noble assembly stands solemnly as if extending hands in consolation; the white moon is full, and I am about to depart.
How can I, at the very moment of death, still covet fame and position?"

He then specially retained the five-pronged vajra bell and ritual scepter (ghaṇṭā-vajra) transmitted by his former master, along with a silver plate and rosaries made of bodhi seeds and crystal, and sent them for presentation via the imperial messenger Li Xiancheng.

On the fifteenth day of the sixth month, having bathed with fragrant water, he lay down with his head toward the east; facing north, he gazed toward the imperial palace and entered the stillness within the Great Seal Body Samādhi. He was seventy years of age, and his years as a monk (śrāmaṇera-śrāmaṇerī) were fifty.
The disciple Huilang succeeded him in the position of consecration.
There were several other practitioners who understood the Dharma.

When the Emperor heard this, he suspended the court audience for three days, bestowed upon them silk, cloth, and various goods, as well as four hundred thousand coins, and provided over two million coins for the construction of a stupa.
An imperial edict appointed Li Yuanzong, the Commissioner of Merit, to oversee the funeral arrangements.
Before his passing, various monks dreamed that a jeweled terrace a thousand fathoms high collapsed, the new pavilion of Mañjuśrī crumbled, and a vajra flew up into the heavens.
Furthermore, the rear pond of Xingshan Temple suddenly dried up without cause; the bamboo in the grove produced fruit, and the flowers in the courtyard withered and changed.

On the sixth day of the seventh month, his body was cremated. The Emperor issued an edict for the high-ranking official Liu Xianhe to perform a sacrificial rite at the temple and posthumously conferred upon him the title of Minister of Works (Sikong), with the honorary name (shì) Dàbiànzhèng Guǎngzhì Sānzàng (Great Eloquence and Rectitude, Vast Wisdom Tripiṭaka Master).
When the fire was extinguished, several hundred grains of *śarīra* were collected;
eighty grains were presented to the Imperial Court.
His cranial bone did not burn, and within it there was one grain of *śarīra*, half-hidden and half-visible; by imperial decree, a separate stupa was erected for it within the monastery.

Master Kong’s practice of transformation benefited sentient beings extensively; he was most preeminent in the gateway of *dhāraṇī*, and his level on the stages of patience (*kṣānti*) could not be determined as high or low.
From the beginning, the Imperial Court held him in especially high esteem; once, during a drought, an imperial edict was issued for Kong to pray for rain.
Kong said, "On a certain day, you may offer prayers to him; perhaps you might force him to appear, for his violence is truly strange.

An imperial decree was issued to invite the Master’s own teacher, Vajrabodhi, to establish a ritual altar. Indeed, the wind and rain did not cease; people in the marketplaces were swept away and drowned, and trees were uprooted and toppled.
The Emperor immediately issued an edict to stop it.

Xuangong fashioned five or six clay female figures in the courtyard of the monastery and poured water over them while chanting in the Sanskrit language and cursing them; after a short while, the sky cleared.
The Emperor of the Xuanzong era summoned the master of arts Luo Gongyuan to compete in magical feats with Kong in the private audience hall.
While there, Kong repeatedly scratched his back with his hands turned backward.
Luo said:
"I borrow the Venerable Master’s *cintāmaṇi*.

At that time, there was a flower-patterned stone in the hall; he brandished the *cintāmaṇi* in the air and struck it before the stone, shattering it to pieces. Although Lu took up the *cintāmaṇi* repeatedly, he could not grasp it. The Emperor wished to rise to retrieve it.
Kong said, "Third Brother, do not rise; this is merely a shadow.
He then raised his hand to show Luo, and the *ruyi* was once again perfectly intact in his grasp.
Furthermore, on Mount Beimang there was a giant serpent that woodcutters frequently encountered; its raised head resembled a small hill, and at night it would often draw in the moisture of the dew.
Seeing a monk in the air, it spoke in human speech, saying:
"I am a disciple suffering the retribution of my evil deeds; how may you, O Monk, deliver me?"
"Every time I wish to overturn the Yellow River and submerge the city of Luoyang to satisfy my resentment," he said.
Hui-kong accepted his refuge precepts for him and explained the law of cause and effect, saying,
"Since you have received your present retribution because of your own anger, why do you still harbor hatred and resentment?"
"What can my strength achieve?
You should heed my words; this body must surely be abandoned.
Later, the woodcutter saw the snake dead at the bottom of the stream, its stench wafting for several li.

When Kūṅfán was summoned by imperial decree to pray for rain, he had no other ritual procedure; he simply prepared a single embroidered seat, took a wooden spirit-child about three inches high, recited mantras while tossing it with his hand, and then cast it away.
Once he had taken his seat, when the corners of his mouth twitched, his teeth bared, and his eyes blinked, the rain would arrive.

Furthermore, during the Tianbao era, when the leaders of the three kingdoms of Western Tibet, Dashi, and Kang led their armies to besiege Xiliangfu, the Emperor summoned Amoghavajra (Kong) to enter; the Emperor himself presided over the ritual at the Daochang.

Xuankong held the incense burner and recited the secret mantras of the *Renwang jing* twenty-eight times. The Emperor saw five hundred divine soldiers in the palace courtyard and, startled, questioned Xuankong.
The Emperor said, "The Prince of King Vaiśravaṇa is leading his army to rescue Anxi; please prepare a meal immediately and dispatch him.
On the twentieth day of the fourth month, a report was indeed received stating:

"On the eleventh day of the second month, about thirty *li* to the northeast of the city, a divine army was seen amidst clouds and mist; their stature was tall and majestic, and as drums and horns resounded, the mountains and earth shook and collapsed, causing the barbarian tribes to flee in terror."
Within that camp there was a golden-colored rat that gnawed through the strings of all the bows and crossbows.
At the tower of the northern city gate, the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa glared in wrath, causing the barbarian commander to flee in great haste.

The Emperor read the memorial and thanked Daoxuan; he subsequently issued an edict to place images of the Heavenly Kings upon the watchtowers of all provincial cities, which was the beginning of this practice.
After Daoxuan passed away, the imperial decrees bestowed upon him by three successive reigns were all submitted for his enshrinement.
To flourish in life and to be mourned at death—among the Dharma-transmitting monks who came from the Western Regions, few have been like him in antiquity or in the present.
His successor to the dharma-seat was Master Huilang.
Yan Ying, the Grand Minister of the Censorate, composed the inscription, and Xu Hao calligraphed it; it was erected within this very monastery.
The Epilogue states:

Regarding the transmission of the Dharma and the turning of the wheel, in the Eastern Land (China), Vajrabodhi is the First Patriarch, Amoghavajra is the Second Patriarch, and Huilang is the Third Patriarch; the variations in the doctrines inherited by their successors can be understood from this point onward.
Thereafter, the school branched out into various lineages, all of whom said:
"The transmission of the Great Yoga Teachings has been extensive indeed; yet why is it that there are so few who achieve realization?"
It is just as Yu-jia gave birth to Ying-long, Ying-long gave birth to the Fenghuang, and once the Fenghuang had descended, it gave birth to the various birds.
How could one wish for there to be no transformation or change? That would be impossible!

The descendant of Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s paternal uncle, King Amṛtodana, was named Śubhakarasiṃha in Sanskrit, which in the language of China means "Pure Lion" (Jìngshīzǐ); its meaning is translated as "Virtuous Fearlessness" (Shànwúwèi).
Another name is Śūbhakara, which means "Fearless" (Wúwèi), also a translation based on its meaning.
His ancestors originally came from Central India; due to national turmoil, they divided the kingdom and established a separate rule in Oḍra.
His father was King Buddhahasta, who, possessing a divine countenance born of awe-inspiring virtue and having long cultivated merit and artistry, was thus tested through successive trials.
At ten years of age he commanded the army, and at thirteen he succeeded to the throne, winning the hearts of both soldiers and civilians.
His brothers, jealous of his ability, raised troops and incited rebellion; their internal strife was extreme.
When I led my forces to wage war, a stray arrow struck my person and a wheel slipped, wounding my head.

Although my own kinsman has been defeated and, according to military law, ought to be executed, I have suppressed my personal feelings for the sake of the Great Cause and granted him a general amnesty.
He then wiped away his tears and informed his mother, as well as addressing the ministers, saying:
"In my previous military expedition, my filial duty was already severed.
Now I wish to abdicate the throne in order to fulfill my sense of righteousness."
Consequently, he yielded his position to his elder brother and earnestly sought entry into the Way.
His mother, moved by compassion, granted him permission; she secretly entrusted him with the state-transmitting jewel, just as feudal lords divide their ritual vessels.
Traveling south to the seacoast, he encountered an exceptionally sublime monastery where he attained the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
He gathered sand to construct stupas, numbering nearly ten thousand.
Although a black snake bit his finger, he never wavered or ceased his efforts.
He again boarded a merchant vessel to travel through various countries; while secretly practicing meditation and recitation, white light emanated from his mouth.
For three days without wind, the ship traveled ten thousand *li*.
While traveling with a merchant caravan, he encountered bandits, and his life was as precarious as if his very breath were being snatched away.
Out of compassion for his fellow travelers, he silently recited the mantra.
Thereupon, the forms of the seventy million deities fully manifested before him, and the bandits were subsequently slaughtered by an enemy force.
The invader then confessed his crimes and sought refuge, pointing out the path through both the level and the perilous terrain.
They subsequently traversed remote wildernesses and crossed further poisonous waters; upon reaching the borders of Central India, they immediately encountered its king.
The King’s consort was the elder sister of Wei; she inquired into the reasons for his abdication and praised him beyond measure.
On that day, they returned home hand in hand, and as the clouds of compassion spread their shade, the entire realm underwent a profound transformation.

Wei Fengyi was brilliant and outstanding in demeanor; his intelligence surpassed that of his peers. He thoroughly investigated and mastered the Five Vehicles, and his realization encompassed the Three Studies. He attained a profound understanding of the sources of *dhāraṇī* and meditative contemplation.
He became thoroughly proficient in all artistic skills and techniques.
He first visited Nālandā Monastery—here called Shiwuyen (Sudāna), the fountainhead of the Semblance Dharma and the assembly hall of the multitude of sages.
Out of fear, he surrendered the state-protecting jewel, which was polished upon the forehead of the Great Image; by day it resembles the crescent moon, and by night it is like the orb of the sun.

In the temple there was one named Dharmagupta, who held the secret key to the gate of Samādhi and bore the esoteric seal of the Tathāgata; though his appearance was that of a man about forty years of age, he was actually eight hundred years old—Tripitaka Master Xuanzang once met him in the past.
Fearing [to offend], he prostrated himself to touch the Master’s feet and served him as his primary teacher.

One day, while attending to him during a meal, there was a monk by his side who was a native of Zhendan (China). Fearing observed the contents of his bowl and saw that the oil cakes were still warm and the millet rice was still hot.
Startled, he sighed and said, "The Eastern Land is more than one hundred thousand li from here; could it be that you have already returned after being matured there?
Guputa replied:
"You are able to remain silent; you are truly one who can learn from this.

Thereafter, he was granted the *Bhairava-dhāraṇī*, Yoga, and the teachings of the Three Mysteries (*triguhyavidyā*). With nāgas and devas surrounding him, as if a dense forest were before his eyes, he received all the various mudrās and mantras instantaneously and all at once.
On that very day he was conferred the empowerment and became a teacher of gods and humans, being titled "Tripiṭaka.

As for the meaning of "Tripiṭaka," internally it consists of precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom; externally it consists of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Śāstra, all of which are encompassed by dhāraṇī.

The dhāraṇī is the swift wheel of bodhi, the ocean of liberation and auspiciousness; all Buddhas of the three periods of time are born from this gateway. It is the transmission of illuminating wisdom, a single lamp alone.
The faculties differ in their specific natures, and thus the lamps are likewise infinite.

Consequently, there are as many samādhis as there are atoms in ten billion Śākyamunis; by means of these, the Bodhisattva takes them as a comprehensive framework to encompass all meditative concentrations, ascending instantaneously through the stages and drawing near to Great Enlightenment—this is the essential meaning.
At that time, fearing [the dangers] yet traveling through the vast wilderness, he paid homage to all sacred sites without shrinking from hardships.
Every place he visited, he returned to three times.
He also entered Mount Kukkuṭapāda to have his head shaved for Kāśyapa and received the touch of Avalokiteśvara’s hand upon his crown.
Once, while observing the summer retreat at Vulture Peak, he was led by a fierce beast deep into a mountain cave.
The cave was as bright as day, and there he beheld an image of the Muni, with his attendants on either side appearing as if alive.
At that time, Central India suffered a great drought, so they requested Baoyi to pray for rain.
Suddenly, he saw Avalokiteśvara within the solar disc, holding a *kamaṇḍalu* in his hand and pouring water onto the ground.
At that time, the assembly was filled with joy and moved by a sense of wonder, experiencing what they had never known before.
Furthermore, they forged gold into the shape of palm leaves and transcribed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
They also melted gold to cast a stūpa, making it equal in size to the body of the Buddha.

Because her mother had feared that she had been traveling abroad for so long, she believed she had already passed away; she wept morning and night until she lost her sight. When the letter arrived with inquiries after her well-being, [her vision] was suddenly restored as it was before.
In the realm of the Five Indias, since the passing of the Buddha, ninety-six heterodox schools have flourished, each adhering to its own views.

[I] fear that all may follow their respective attachments, thereby becoming obstructed and harboring doubts; thus, I shall untie the bonds of error at the gateway of the mind and abandon the lost ferry on the path to awakening.

The Dharma-clouds bestow their moisture equally upon both the great and the small; the waters of meditative concentration fill both square and round vessels according to their capacity. They topple the banners and drums of heterodox schools and raise the victorious standard of the Mind-King, causing those practitioners to restrain their madness through mindfulness and perceive the Buddha within their very bodies.
Kumārajīva said, "Son of good family, you have a karmic affinity with China; you may go now.
Fawei then bowed his head in farewell and departed.
Upon arriving in the kingdom of Kaśmīra, he reached a river at dusk;
as there was no bridge, he feared having to cross by floating through the air.
One day, while he was receiving an invitation at the home of an elder, a *arhat* suddenly descended and said:
"I am a follower of the Hīnayāna, while you, Great Virtue, are a Bodhisattva who has attained the stages," he said, yielding his seat and deferring to him out of respect.
Fearing that [the Master] would bestow upon him a robe of fine cloth, he ascended into the air and departed.
He feared that [the King] might again go to the kingdom of Udyāna, where white mice would circle him in submission, daily offering gold coins.
He preached the *Vairocana-sūtra* in the courtyard of the Turks and practiced dhyāna-concentration beneath the tree of the Khatun; the Dharma appeared as golden characters, arrayed in the sky.
At that time, a palace attendant of the Turks pressed her breast with her hand, and milk flowed forth in three streams into Wei’s mouth.
Wei then joined his palms and maintained a reverent expression, saying,
"She was my mother in a previous life."

Furthermore, while on the road he encountered bandits; though they raised their blades and struck him three times, his limbs remained unhurt, and the wielders of the swords heard only the sound of metal.
Later, as he ascended the Great Lake of the Snow Mountains, he feared he would not survive.
Kubjottarā arrived from mid-air and said, "The body of a Bodhisattva is identical to that of the world; he does not abandon birth and death.
You have long since been free from signs—how could you possibly be ill?"
Having finished speaking, he ascended into the sky; Wei Xian was struck with awe and his illness was instantly cured.

Traveling through the territory of Tibet, he stayed together with a caravan of merchants. The Hu people, greedy for goods, led their hosts to surround them. Wei Mi applied the mind-seal (*cittamudrā*), and the Tibetan chieftains requested forgiveness.
Upon reaching the western frontier of the Great Tang, a divine being appeared at night and said:
"This eastern region is not within my domain; Mañjuśrī truly protects the Divine Land."
Having prostrated at his feet, he vanished; this was much like the god Kapila escorting the joined-eyebrowed [Śākyamuni].
Fearing that the scriptures might be damaged by being carried on a camel, he reached the Western Region and crossed the river.
The dragon submerged the camel’s feet, causing it to sink beneath the spring; out of fear, the monk also entered the spring.
He stayed in the dragon palace for three days, proclaiming the Dharma and transforming beings, bringing enlightenment to a great many people.
When the camels were led out onto the shore, they passed through without becoming even slightly damp.

Previously, while traveling along perilous paths through the territory of North India, his reputation had already reached China; consequently, Emperor Ruizong issued an edict for Śīlāditya and General Shi Xian to go beyond the Yumen Pass to await his arrival.

At the beginning of the Kaiyuan era, Emperor Xuanzong dreamed that he met a true monk of extraordinary appearance; the Emperor personally used pigments and brushes to paint his likeness upon the walls of the palace hall.

When Wei arrived here, he matched the vision of the dream exactly. Delighted by this auspicious affinity, the Emperor adorned the inner Daochang and honored him as the Head Teacher; from the Princes of Ning and Xue downward, all knelt upon their mats and held offering vessels before him.

The Great Being received his audience in the celestial palace, joining the Brahma assembly at the imperial throne; he honored the National Preceptor with the Way of Guangcheng and led the sovereign toward the Vehicle of the Tathāgata—thus, the majesty of the Dharma-gate reached its peak here.

At that time, there was a master of arts who held the talismans of ghosts and spirits and participated in the power of transformations; he was summoned before the Emperor to compete in their supernatural wonders.
Wei remained serene and unmoving, so that the practitioner found his hands and feet had no place to apply their skill.

In the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era (the Bingchen year), he arrived in Chang’an carrying Sanskrit manuscripts, which were ordered by imperial decree to be housed in the Southern Courtyard of Xingfu Temple.
Subsequently, he was summoned to reside at Ximing Temple, where he received repeated inquiries after his well-being and extraordinary gifts.
In the fifth year, the Ding-si year, he received an imperial decree to perform translations at the Bodhi Monastery.

Fearing that he might not be able to achieve success on his own, he requested permission to invite eminent monks to collaborate on the Chinese and Sanskrit texts. First, he opened the session with the translation of one fascicle of the *Ākāśagarbha-śravaṇadhāraṇī-dharmaparyāya*. The śramaṇa Siddha served as the oral interpreter (*yǔshì*), Wuzhuo transcribed the text (*bishòu*) and composed the literary style, and the manuscript was then copied and presented to the palace.
The Emperor deeply praised him with admiration and issued an edict that all the Sanskrit manuscripts Wei had brought with him were to be presented to the throne.
Formerly, there was a śramaṇa named Wuxing who traveled west to India; having completed his studies, he intended to return home, but upon reaching Northern India, he unfortunately passed away.

The palm-leaf manuscripts he obtained were all kept at Huayan Monastery in the capital; fearing that they might be lost, he and Master Xingyong selected several copies from among them—texts containing sublime gateways of total retention (dhāraṇī) that had not been translated previously.
In the twelfth year, he accompanied the imperial entourage to Luoyang and was again commissioned by imperial decree to translate the *Mahāvairocana Sūtra* at Fuxian Monastery.
This sūtra exists in its complete Sanskrit form with one hundred thousand stanzas;

what he produced was a distillation of its essentials, titled the *Mahāvairocana Tathāgata-buddhābhisaṃbodhi-vikurvāṇa-adhiṣṭhāna Sūtra* in seven fascicles. The śramaṇa Baoyue served as the oral translator, while Yi Xing received the dictation and refined the phrasing and logic. The resulting text balanced the literary and the vernacular, perfectly harmonizing with the profound intent, conforming to the Buddha’s meaning above and acceding to the capacities of sentient beings below. As a gateway to benefit and aid, this work is the most supreme.

Furthermore, he translated the *Subāhuparipṛcchā-tantra* in three fascicles and the *Susiddhikara-sūtra* in three fascicles; these two sūtras fully encompass the mantra-vinaya, which is to say, the secret precepts.
If one has never entered a maṇḍala, it is improper to read or recite [this scripture] at will, just as it is improper for one who has not yet received full ordination to eavesdrop upon the precepts.

This single fascicle, titled *The Method for Seeking the Retention of What is Heard: The Dhāraṇī of the Supreme Mind of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha Capable of Fulfilling All Wishes*, is merely a brief partial translation of the *Sarvārthasiddhi-maṇḍala* from the Sanskrit original of the *Vajraśekhara*.

By nature he feared worldly passions and delighted in tranquility and simplicity; he cultivated meditative contemplation to soothe his spirit and occasionally opened up sessions for Chan observation to encourage beginners.

For those who followed his exemplary conduct, the lotus flower blossomed within the field of their vision; for those who received his spoken teachings, the nectar of immortality moistened the soil of their minds. Thus, there were people every day who attained a state of transcendent awakening and clarity.
Among his fellow practitioners who came to visit him, he honored only the Elder Tripitaka Master Ratnamati as his preceptor; all others were treated with the etiquette due to disciples.

As for Master Yi Xing, he was held in high esteem by the Emperor and served as a refuge for the wise of the age. Beyond his mastery of meditative concentration and wisdom, even when matters concerning the subtleties of Yin-Yang divination remained unresolved, Yi Xing would consult him before proceeding.
Wèi once cast a copper pagoda at this very monastery; he personally fashioned the molds, and their exquisite craftsmanship surpassed that of both humans and devas.

Because the amount of metal melted and refined was so vast, the courtyard became extremely cramped; fearing that a wind might cause the flames to intensify and the disaster to spread to the sacred precincts, [he was concerned].
Wei Xiao said, "There is no cause for concern; you shall know it for yourself.

On the day the casting was completed, indeed a great snowfall covered the sky; when the sacred stupa emerged from the furnace, auspicious flowers drifted onto the mats, and the multitude all offered words of praise.
Furthermore, during a period of scorching heat and drought, the Emperor dispatched the eunuch Gao Lishi to urgently summon Daoxue to pray for rain.

Daoxue said, "The current drought is simply a matter of natural course. If you insist on forcing the dragons to bring down rain, it will surely be violent; this would only result in further damage and is something that cannot be done."
The Emperor pressed him insistently, saying, "People suffer from the heat; even wind and thunder would be enough to bring them relief.
Having no choice but to comply, the officials prepared the implements for requesting rain—banners, canopies, conch shells, and gongs were all in place. Wei Xian remarked with a smile:
"This will not suffice to bring rain.
He immediately removed it.
Then he filled a bowl with water, stirred it with a small knife, and recited several hundred mantras in Sanskrit over it.

In a moment, there appeared a creature like a dragon, as large as a finger, crimson in color with its head raised, peering down at the surface of the water before submerging again into the bottom of the bowl.
Filled with fear, he stirred the water and recited incantations; after a short while, white vapor rose from the bowl, ascending several feet before gradually drifting away.
Wei said to the strongman, "Go quickly; the rain is coming.
The strongman galloped away and looked back, seeing white vapors swirling rapidly from the lecture hall toward the west, like a bolt of silk unfurling upward through the sky.

Shortly thereafter, the sky grew dark and murky as a great wind arose with thunder and lightning. When the strongman had just reached Tianjin Bridge, the wind and rain began to lash down violently upon his horse, and many large trees in the street were uprooted.
When the strongman entered to report this, his robes were completely soaked.
The Emperor bowed his head in reverent welcome and offered repeated thanks.
Furthermore, there was a giant serpent on Mount Mang; when Wei saw it, he sighed and said:
"Are you wishing to drain the reservoirs of the city of Luoyang?
He then recited incantations in the language of India several hundred times, and within days the snake died.
This was an omen of An Lushan’s subsequent siege and capture of Luoyang.
It is said that once Fawei stayed in the quarters of Vinaya Master Daoxuan at Ximing Monastery. He manifested a coarse physical appearance, which Daoxuan found quite distasteful and contemptible.
At midnight, as Daoxuan was rubbing a louse off his body and throwing it to the ground, Fawei cried out repeatedly, "The Vinaya Master has killed a son of the Buddha!"
Only after Xuān had proclaimed this did he realize he was a great bodhisattva; at dawn the following day, he adjusted his robes and paid him homage.

Judging from this account, only about fifty years elapsed between Xuān’s death and the beginning of the Kaiyuan era. As for [the Master’s] appearing and disappearing according to no fixed rule, it is something beyond human measurement.
In the twentieth year, he requested to return to the Western Regions, but was not permitted by an imperial edict of favor.

On the seventh day of the tenth month of the twenty-third year, the year Yihai, he passed away while reclining on his right side with his feet stacked, having reached an age of ninety-nine and a monastic seniority of eighty years.
The dharma-fellows were filled with sorrow, and the Emperor’s heart was struck with grief; he bestowed upon him the posthumous title of "Minister of State for Ceremonials" (Honglu Qing).
He dispatched Li Xian, Director of the Bureau of State Ceremonials, to arrange the solemn rites, and Vinaya Master Bin to oversee the funeral proceedings.
On the third day of the tenth month in the twenty-eighth year, he was interred in the courtyard of Guanghua Temple on the western mountains of Longmen.
Perfumed by his settled wisdom, his entire body remained incorruptible.

On the day of the funeral, the entire city wept and wailed; the colors of the mountains and rivers were transformed. Among the monastic and lay disciples, Master Baowei and Master Mingwei—of the Zheng clan of Xingyang and the Wang clan of Langya, respectively—grieved for him with such deep devotion as if they had lost their own parents.

At the beginning of the Qianyuan era, the traditions of the Tang dynasty were once again revitalized; the two Chan masters carved their gāthās, and various lay believers constructed stūpas for them. Their disciples established dwellings nearby, evoking a sense of longing similar to that felt at the tomb of Confucius.
Observing the remains of Wei today, they have gradually shrunk; the black skin is faintly visible, and the bones are exposed.
For successive reigns, during both droughts and floods, people have come to pray here; the responses have appeared accordingly, and offerings of alms have been frequent.
A brocade headcloth and napkin were used to cover him as if he were reclining at rest.
Whenever he was brought out of his niche, he was placed upon a low couch and bathed with scented water.
The wealthy and influential families of Luoyang vied with one another to offer meditation cloths, pure towels, and cleansing beans to support the bathing rites.
Nowadays, when the Emperor performs rites for averting calamities, he frequently dispatches envoys to offer additional gifts and alms, which invariably fulfill his heart's wishes.
The Biography of Shi Zhihui of Luoyang, Tang China: Shi Zhihui’s Sanskrit name was Prajñā; his clan name was Gautama, and he was a native of Kapiśī in Northern India.
Possessing innate intelligence and insight, he developed the aspiration for enlightenment at the age of seven. Departing from his parents' service, he took refuge in the Triple Gem.
At that time, under the guidance of the Venerable Vinayavasu, he memorized the *Catuṣāgama* in one hundred thousand stanzas and the *Abhidharma* in thirty thousand stanzas.
When he reached the age required by the Dharma, he followed his teacher to another country to receive full ordination.

He recited approximately forty thousand stanzas of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, twenty-eight thousand stanzas of the *Abhidharmakośa*, and also recited the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, mastering both its text and its meaning.
For seven years, he specialized in the study of the Hīnayāna there.

Subsequently, he traveled to Nālandā Monastery in Central India, where he studied Mahāyāna treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, and the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra*, as well as the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, *Hetuvidyā* (Logic), *Śabdavidyā* (Grammar), *Cikitsāvidyā* (Medicine), and the Vinaya treatises. He received instruction from the three great masters Śīlabhadra, Sthiramati, and Jinamitra.
He traveled again to the Twin Śāla Trees and visited eight stupas.
He came and went, paying homage for eighteen years.
Hearing that the practice of *vidyā-dhara* (incantation) was highly esteemed in South India, he eventually went there to seek instruction.

There was an abhiṣeka master named Dharmayaśas, who saw that [Wuxing] was diligent and capable of being taught; he instructed him in the Yoga methods, the entry into maṇḍalas, the three mysteries, the protection of the body, the five families, and the sūtras on mudrās. Within one year, he thoroughly mastered more than three thousand five hundred verses.
I have often heard that in the great nation of China, Mañjuśrī resides; thus, pointing his staff toward the East, he vowed to transmit the Buddha-dharma there.
Consequently, I sailed across the sea to the east, but when I was about to reach Guangzhou, a wind blew me back, and I arrived at the eastern coast of the kingdom of Śrīvijaya.

Furthermore, having gathered provisions and repaired a large ship, he traveled extensively through the various kingdoms of the South Sea for twenty-two years before returning once more to Fanyu. Suddenly, a violent storm arose, the ship was wrecked, and everyone perished; only Hui remained alive.
By the fifth watch of the night, the wind finally ceased, yet the scriptures and treatises he had brought with him were nowhere to be found.

When he reached the seashore, the bound volumes were already there on the beach; he recovered them from within a large bamboo cylinder in the white sand, as if they had been supported and delivered there by some ghostly being.
He then sighed and said, "I believe the roots of the people of China have now matured!
He subsequently traveled northeast for half a month and arrived at Guangzhou; this was at the beginning of the Jianzhong era of Emperor Dezong.
During the reign of Emperor Dezong, while serving the mandate of Heaven amidst difficulties, he first arrived at the capital in the second year of the Zhenyuan era.
There he met his fellow villager Luo Haoxin, a regular general of the Shen-ce Army and the son of his maternal uncle Hui; they consoled one another with a mixture of grief and joy.
Upon arriving at his home, [the Emperor] invited him to stay and provided offerings for eight years.

In the eighth year, he submitted a memorial recommending Huìfǎn to transmit the translation, and by imperial decree, eminent monks of exceptional reputation from the various temples in the capital were ordered to participate in the translation. Kapiśī Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā provided the exegesis based on the Sanskrit manuscript; Śramaṇa Lìyán of Guǎngzhái Temple, serving as a court attendant (Hànlin dàizhào), acted as the oral interpreter; and Śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xīmíng Temple served as the scribe. Śramaṇas Dàoyè of Zīshèng Temple, Liángxiù of Xīmíng Temple, Yìngzhēn of Zhuāngyán Temple, Cháowù of Lǐquán Temple, Dà'àn, and Biànkōng all served as proofreaders of the meaning.

On the eighth day of the sixth month, intending to compose titles for the scriptures, an imperial edict was issued directing Wang Xiqian, Commissioner of Merit for the Right Street, along with Wang Mengshe, General of the Right Shen-ce Army, Ma Youlin, General of the Household Cavalry, and others, to escort the Sanskrit scriptures out from within the palace.

The monastic community and the musical troupes, each maintaining their respective dignified deportment, proceeded in alternating formation. Men and women gathered to watch, and carriages and cavalry lined up side by side as they were welcomed into Ximing Monastery for the purpose of translation.
On that very day, he was granted one thousand strings of cash, thirty bundles of tea, and one large casket of incense to serve as offerings and alms.
He titled it the *Mahāyāna-nyāya-ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra* in ten fascicles.

Furthermore, the *Avadāna-sūtra on the Nārāyaṇa Power Asked by the Elder of the Avataṃsaka* and the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, each in one fascicle, were all translated in the eighth year of the Zhenyuan era.
In the tenth month of that year, the transcription was completed.

On the twenty-eighth day, a decorated carriage was prepared with full ceremonial regalia, and the work was brought in through the Guangshun Gate; when the Emperor examined it, he was delighted and bestowed his congratulations with great warmth.

An imperial edict was issued to grant vegetarian meals at the Shen-ce Army, along with five hundred rolls of "hui" silk and a set of winter garments; the other recipients were each granted gifts according to their respective ranks.
Hui-biao submitted a letter of thanks, for which he received an imperial rescript praising his merits.

On the same day, Luo Haoxin—Translator of Scriptures, Meritorious Minister for Stabilizing the State under Imperial Favor, Grand Master with the Rank of Kai-fu Yi-tong San-si, Acting Director of the Household of the Crown Prince—submitted a memorial, stating:

“Your humble subject’s cousin, the śramaṇa Prajña, previously presented the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Mahāyāna-arthāvatāra-ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*. On the nineteenth day of the fourth month of this year, I humbly received an imperial edict ordering Wang Xiqian to select monks of exemplary conduct and realization at Ximing Monastery to translate it.”
"Now that the collection of scriptures has been completed, let us go together to Guangshun Gate to present them.
The imperial response stated:
"Your cousin long ago awakened to the Mahāyāna; from afar in the Western Regions, he sought to travel to this superior land."
He proclaimed the profound mysteries of the six sense faculties and expounded the subtle words of the twin trees.
Considering that these teachings should be revered with utmost sincerity, he commissioned this translation so that they might circulate widely.

"You have long admired loyalty and diligence, and you hold the office of commander of the imperial guard. Having examined your memorials, I fully perceive your intentions; I acknowledge your gratitude.
[The Emperor] treated him with favor because he had achieved considerable merit in battle during the siege by Zhu Ci and was included among the inner guards, earning the Emperor’s special esteem.
Hui received excellent guidance from his master, and his work in translation was rendered illustrious; the Emperor composed a "Preface to the Scripture" for him.
Later, Hui passed away in Luoyang and was buried on the western ridge of Longmen, where his stupa remains to this day.
Biography of Xuánjué of Yúhuā Monastery in the Táng Dynasty. Śramaṇa Xuánjué was a native of the Kingdom of Gaochang; his lineage in the western regions remains unknown.
As a student who aspired to the Mahāyāna, he studied and scrutinized the sūtras and śāstras under the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang and also participated in the translation work at Yuhua Palace.
When the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* was nearly completed, he requested that the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* be translated together with him; however, Xuanzang declined, being physically exhausted.
Upon waking, he saw that a stupa, magnificent and towering, had suddenly collapsed in his dream; he rose in alarm and informed Xuanzang.
Xuanzang said, "This is not a matter concerning your person."
"This is merely a sign of my impending death," he said.
Daojue was moved by grief for Dao'an and urged his fellow practitioners to compete in seeking medical treatment and medicine.
