As for the words and characters of India, they were composed by Brahmā; originally consisting of forty-seven syllables, they were subsequently expanded and elaborated upon, becoming known as the *Tsaṅ-pei* (the "Expanded" or "Detailed" collection).

It consists of twelve chapters that instruct the young and ignorant, forming the "Treatise on the Five Sciences" (Pañcavidyāsthāna-śāstra); for the most part, it differs from the Hu [Chinese] tradition.
Since the territory of the five Indias is so vast and far-reaching, how could there not be some minor variations?

Furthermore, from the time this method was first translated during the Eastern Han dynasty until the Sui dynasty, all [translators] referred to the Western Heavens as the "Hu" country; thus, having lost the true lineage of the Brahmā realm, they spoke of the scriptures of the Hu lands.
Only Dharma Master Yancong clearly understood this principle; he alone compiled the *Zaolu* (Record of Fabrications) to severely rebuke [the errors] that fill the heavens.

To accord with the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* while harmonizing it with the *Āgamas*, the merit lies within ourselves. If we lose our way by using foreign names to obscure the Indian terminology, whom shall we blame for the failure?
In the Tang dynasty, there was Master Xuan who likewise joined in this proclamation.

From that time on, whenever anyone heard the clicking of the tongue or beheld a dark-complexioned countenance, they would categorically identify him as an Indian monk and unanimously assume it to be Sanskrit.
Master Cong may indeed be said to be so busy wielding his axe to catch the cicada in the white dew before him, that he is oblivious to the yellow-clad sparrow reflecting light behind him.
Since it is said that in the Western lands there are both Brahmans and Hu, why not likewise distinguish between the South and the North?
Failure to properly discern and evaluate these matters leads to three errors:
first, to alter the foreign (Hū) into the Indian (Brahman), without analyzing how the foreign is opened up so that the foreign returns to become the Indian—this is an error;
second, not being proficient in the two phonetic systems of Hū and Brahman, thereby allowing the foreign to be treated as the Indian—this is an error.
It was an error not to know that there were multiple translations;
at first, they were all called "Hu," just as from the Sui dynasty onwards they were all collectively called "Fan"—a case of what is known as "excess being no better than deficiency."
If one speaks according to the fundamental source, Brahman is taken as primary;
yet if one speaks from the perspective of its derivative branches, the term "Hu" (Hūṇa) may also be retained. Why is this so?

From the Five Indias to the north of the mountain ranges, translations have been produced in succession; I suspect that Master Daozong left this work here specifically to await this very day, and thus I dare not decline it.
Third, it is both in the vernacular and in Sanskrit.

For example, when the Indian sūtras and vinayas were transmitted to Kucha, the people of Kucha did not understand the Indian language; thus, they referred to India as the country of Yinteqia (Indika) and translated [the texts] accordingly.
If it is easily understood, one may retain the Sanskrit term; this refers to cases where both the Hu (Chinese) and the Sanskrit versions exist.
Fourth, there are "neither" phrases;
these consist solely of Chinese words.
Third, regarding retranslations and literal translations:
first, literal translations.
These are, for example, those translated in this land of the East directly from the five Indic scripts.
Second, retranslation.

For instance, when scriptures were transmitted north of the passes through Loulan and Yanqi, the local inhabitants did not understand Indic languages; thus, they were translated into the "Hu" (barbarian) languages. For example, what is called *upādhyāya* in Sanskrit is rendered as *hūsà* in Shule and *héshàng* in Khotan.
Furthermore, "Heavenly King" (Tianwang) is *Kauṇḍinya* in Sanskrit and *Vaiśravaṇa* in the vernacular (Hu).
Third, it is both direct and repetitive.
For instance, when the Tripitaka Master came directly bearing the sealed documents, his route passed through the lands of the Hu (Central Asians), so he may have retained some Hu language.
This is evidenced by the fact that Jue Ming recited from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* words such as "upādhyāya" (和尚).
Fourth, the two non-sentences:
these refer to those who, although they brought the Tripitaka along with it in the Hu language, did not translate them upon arriving here.
Fourth, coarse speech and refined speech.
In the field of *śabda-vidyā* (grammar), there are two types: first, *sāmānya*, which refers to ordinary, colloquial speech;
second, *vaidika*, which refers to formal, canonical speech.

The Buddha’s teaching mostly relies upon the *sāmānya* (common) [language], wherein the meaning resides in the sense rather than the literal expression; furthermore, because it is for the sake of all beings, the *vyañjana* (particular) [language] cannot be understood by all classes of people.
Thus, that which is called "complete sound" (*kṛtsna-śabda*) refers to speech where the phonemes are distinct, clear, and standard; this is subtle speech (*sūkṣma-vāk*).
That which is "half-sound" (*ardha-śabda*) refers to speech where the phonemes are indistinct, corrupted, and deviant; this is coarse speech (*audārika-vāk*).
First, that which is coarse and not subtle,
such as the vernacular languages of the five regions of India.
Second, that which is exclusively subtle and not coarse.

Those such as Dharmapāla, Ratnamegha, Master Xuanzang, and Yijing—who thoroughly understood phonology and prosody and translated using the refined language and classical diction of Central India—are the ones referred to here.
3. Both coarse and subtle.
This refers to cases where the language in the Sanskrit original involves both coarse and subtle elements.
Alternatively, it is annotated as follows:
"The sound of this is corrupt and deviant," which refers to coarse speech.
Fourth, the two non-sentences are missing.
Fifth, regarding elegant and vulgar expressions in the Chinese language:
It is also said that sounds are common to both the Chu and Xia regions.
Furthermore, regarding these dialects, "elegant" refers to the texts of the scriptures, while "vulgar" refers to the speech of the streets and alleys.
This is roughly the same as in the Western Regions: "refined" (*sūkṣma*) refers to that which is canonical and correct, while "coarse" (*audārika*) refers to that which is corrupt and deviant.
First, that which is elegant rather than vulgar, such as the use of formal literary language found in the sūtras.
Second, there are those that are colloquial rather than elegant, such as the expressions "begging for a head" (*qītóu*) and "bargaining for the cheeks" (*bójiá*) found in the sūtras.

Third, there are those that are both elegant and colloquial; these are not refined compositions by scholars, but were recorded by the hands of monks who faithfully transcribed them, wherein pure gold and uncut jade are intermingled and harmonized.
Fourth, the two non-phrase [categories] are missing.
Regarding the sixth, direct speech and esoteric speech:
there are two types of phrasing; that which engages with the conventional is direct, while that which engages with the ultimate is esoteric, such as "Bālāśva."
First, this is explicit but not esoteric: "Varuṣa" is translated as "dwelling in harsh speech," because due to their harsh speech, people do not draw near to them.

Second, this is esoteric and not explicit; "Bhāṣita" is translated as "the other shore known by Bodhisattvas. This is because, having thoroughly realized the principle of the three natures of non-existence, it is not something to which ordinary sentient beings can easily approach.
Third, the "both" category refers to the identity of good and evil, as well as the ultimate and conventional truths, all of which are equally unfit for proximity.
Fourth, the "neither" category refers to the exclusion of the aforementioned characteristics.

Furthermore, "Abhihagalu" means "frequently attaining meditative concentration"; "Uppāda" means "arising, uprooting, and turning away from [defilements]"; and "Sāra" means "truly free from distraction."
These various names within the sūtras and śāstras serve as examples to clarify the meanings of both explicit and esoteric language.
Furthermore, there are other words in the Hu (Chinese) and Fan (Sanskrit) scripts, which can be easily understood through these four lines.
In all such categories and precedents that encompass the expositions of those scriptures, commentators have not yet seen the "whole ox," while practitioners merely follow the "old horse.

Tong replied:

"If the words do not relate to the classics and are not the words of the *Zi* or the *Shi*, yet you employ them for translation and correspondence, how can one allow such talk from the back streets to be intermingled with the midst [of the canon]?"
Therefore, Dao’an said:
"To wish to transmit the subtle words of a thousand years past to the vulgar customs of the hundred kings' present age—
this is no easy task."

'What is recorded by the Fótú (Buddha) accords with and intermingles with the Chinese *Lǎozi jīng* (Scripture of Laozi).'"

This [statement] arises from seeing that certain translators used phrases from the two chapters of the *Daode jing* and immediately concluded that they corresponded with the contents of the *Laozi jing*.

One knows that if one were to employ external texts, such slander would inevitably be invited.
For instance, Kumārajīva’s translation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* may be called a perfect synthesis; it possesses the natural linguistic flavor of the Western Regions.
Now, observing Fang Rong’s polishing of the text for the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* and Sengzhao’s composition of his *Treatise* by citing [Buddhist sources], they are surely subject to this reproach.
If one were to incorporate vulgar and colloquial language, how would it differ from the records of butchers and wine-sellers?
Thus, it would be better to have a composite text than no text at all; between a formal classic and a vernacular work, the latter is preferable.
However, if one becomes deeply immersed in the vernacular, the fault is not slight;
yet, if one strikes a balance appropriate for the times while preserving the dharma-language, this is what is called grasping the essential purpose of translating the scriptures.
Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma largely relies upon the *sāmānya* (common) [mode].
Furthermore, regarding the rise of translation and the intent behind its practice, if the original origins are not clarified, how can they be shown to future generations?
Now, in investigating its propagation, I shall briefly set forth the general outline.
As for the teachings, they are not uniform and comprise three categories:

first, the *vyakta-śāsana* (explicit teachings). These consist of the various sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras of the various vehicles; as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, "the explicit teachings are, for the most part, the teachings of the Mahāyāna Piṭaka."

"Second, the Secret Teachings consist of the Yoga, Empowerment (Abhiṣeka), Five Families, Homa, Three Mysteries, and Maṇḍala methods. Regarding the *Yoga*, it is said: 'The Esoteric Teachings are for the most part the teachings of the Śrāvaka Piṭaka.'"
As for the "Teaching of the Three Minds," it is the Chan method that points directly to the human mind, realizing one's nature to attain Buddhahood.
The next, the "First Wheel of the Dharma," refers to the Exoteric Teachings, of which Kāśyapa Mātanga is considered the founding patriarch.
Next, the second is the Wheel of Precepts, which is Esoteric Buddhism (Mikkyō), taking Vajrabodhi as its founding patriarch;
next is the third, the Wheel of Mind, which adds the meaning of this wheel, namely the Dharma of Chan (Zen), taking Bodhidharma as its founding patriarch.
Therefore, those who transmit the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra) transmit the sound of the Dharma with the sound of the Dharma;
those who transmit the Wheel of Precepts (śīlacakra) transmit the secret with the secret;

and those who transmit the Wheel of Mind (cittacakra) transmit mind with mind. These three teachings, three wheels, and three patriarchs traveled from West to East, transforming the mundane into the sacred. They have flowed through fifteen dynasties—Han, Wei, Jin, Song, Qi, Liang, Chen, Sui, Tang, Zhu Liang, Later Tang, Shi Jin, Liu Han, Guo Zhou, and now the Great Song. This legacy of the Dharma-gate for future generations spans twelve thousand two hundred years, ensuring that the True Teaching has flourished for posterity.
Someone asked:
"Regarding the translation halls and scriptural libraries, where officials are established and duties divided, may I hear about this?
He replied:

"This office is first governed by the 'Chief Translator'—that is, a Tripitaka Master who has brought the palm-leaf manuscripts—who must be one thoroughly versed in both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings."

Next, as for the "scribe" (bishou), he must be one who is proficient in both Chinese and Sanskrit and whose learning encompasses both the *saṃsāra* (existence) and *śūnyatā* (emptiness); only after thorough questioning and full understanding does he set pen to paper.
Those who established this circular diagram since the Western Jin and the Later Qin dynasties were the śramaṇas Daohan, Xuanzé, Yao Song, and the father and son Nie Chengyuan.
As for emperors and kings, such as Yao Xing, Emperor Wu of Liang, Empress Wu, and Zhongzong, some personally took up the brush, and this was also referred to as "composing literature" (*zhùwén*).
Next, as for "transmitting the words" (*duyu*), it is correctly termed "translating the words" (*yiyu*).

To transmit and convey [the meaning] so that understanding may arise is also called "transmitting the words," such as when the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (The Treatise on Manifesting Consciousness) was translated by the śramaṇa Zhantuo acting as the translator of the words.

Next, regarding those who "verify the Sanskrit original," they seek its authoritative measure and are able to verify it through secret knowledge; thus, the expressive terminology is unerring and that which is revealed is free from error.
This is the *Vinaya* Sanskrit manuscript translated by the layman (upāsaka) Īśvara.

As for the appointment of one official titled "Verifier of Sanskrit Meanings" (*zhèngfànyì*), this was intended to clarify the strengths and weaknesses of the Western [Sanskrit] terminology, ensuring that the Chinese language would not fall short of the original Sanskrit meaning.
Furthermore, one position titled "Certifier of the Meaning of Dhyāna" was established, filled by the śramaṇa Datong.

Next was the position of "Editor of Texts," for which there was no fixed number of members; scholars proficient in both Buddhist (internal) and non-Buddhist (external) learning were appointed to fill it.

Since the scribe’s transcription rests upon the silk and paper, how could the phrasing be entirely free of colloquialisms? Provided that the original intent of the Buddha is not lost, what harm is there in editing and correcting them?
Therefore, at Yi Jing’s translation center, more than twenty individuals, including Li Qiao, Wei Sili, and Lu Zangyong, were responsible for the subsequent refinement and polishing of the text.
Following this was the "Certification of Meaning" (*Zhengyi*), which served to verify the meanings expounded within the already translated text.

For instance, when translating the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, three hundred people including Huìsōng and Dàolǎng examined and corrected the textual meaning, while Fùlǐ of the Táng served as the scribe for successive sessions.

Next is the "Brahma Chant" (*brahmā-gīta*). When the Dharma assembly first commences, the Brahma chant is performed beforehand to serve as a preliminary introduction, inspiring sentient beings toward goodness; it was only during the Yongtai era of the Tang dynasty that this position [in the ritual order] was first heard of.

Next was the "Collation," in which the already translated texts were compared and verified; during the Sui dynasty, Yancong further commented upon the meaning of the texts, demonstrating the utmost degree of careful scrutiny.

Next was the "Supervisor Ambassador" (*jianhu daishi*); during the Later Zhou, Duke Pinggao Hou Shou served as the General Supervisor and Inspector, while under the Tang, Lord Liang Fang served as the supervisor for Master Xuanzang, followed in succession by Xu Guan, Yang Shenjiao, Du Xingyi, and others who were appointed to this office.

Alternatively, monastic personnel were employed; for instance, during the Sui dynasty, ten individuals including Mingmu and Tanqian supervised and managed the translation work, determining the essential doctrines.
Their locations included Qin’s Xiaoyao Garden, Liang’s Shouguang Hall, Zhanyun Pavilion, and the residence of Prince Runan of the Wei dynasty.
Furthermore, during the Sui dynasty, Emperor Yang established the Institute for Translating Scriptures (*fanjing guan*), wherein certain monks held the title of *xueshi* (scholar).
During the Tang dynasty, such institutions were established in Guangfu Temple and other locations, or within imperial gardens, as their sites were not fixed.

Furthermore, setting aside the offices of "Director of Orthography" (*zhèngzì*) and "Master of Characterology" (*zìxué*), Xuánying once held such a post; subsequently, these positions were sometimes established and sometimes abolished.
From the fifth year of the Yuánhé era of Emperor Xiànzōng of the Táng dynasty until the Zhou dynasty—spanning approximately one hundred and fifty years—the transmission of this path remained silent.

"In the fifth year of our Emperor’s reign over the Great Treasure, there was the śramaṇa Fajin of the Huazhou Prefecture, a transmitter of the Esoteric and Exoteric teachings, who requested that the Tripitaka Master Dharmadeva from the Western Regions translate scriptures at Putin. The provincial and prefectural officials submitted a memorial for his advancement; upon the Emperor’s perusal, he was greatly pleased and bestowed purple robes upon each of them. Consequently, an imperial edict was issued to construct a Translation Institute to the west of Taiping Xingguo Temple."

A subsequent imperial edict was issued to search for and purchase Buddhist scriptures throughout the empire; the Indian monks Dharmapāla and Dānapāla were appointed to collaborate on this task, with the Master Huiwen, the Director of Monks of the Left Street, serving as the verifier of the meanings.

Furthermore, an imperial edict was issued for the Tripiṭaka Master Daoyuan of Cangzhou to verify the Sanskrit characters, while Zhixian— a śramaṇa of the Two Streets renowned for his mastery of the meanings of the scriptures—
was carefully selected to compose the Chinese text. Zun, Fading, and Qingzhao were ordered to serve as scribes,
and Shouluan, Daozhen, Zhixun, Fayun, Huichao, Huida, Ke'gui, and Shanyou [were appointed as assistants].
To corroborate the meaning and arrange the sequence of the text, the subject Liu Su and the high-ranking official Wang Wenshou were appointed as supervisors;
Zhang Ji, Director of the Ministry of Rites, and Tang Yue, Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, were assigned to refine and polish the prose.
[The following works were] presented: the *Jiaoliang shouming jing*, the *Shane baoying jing*, and the *Shanjian*...
Regarding such scriptures as the *Nirmāṇa*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-kumāra*, and the *Amṛtabherī*,
he conferred upon the Tripiṭaka masters Tian Xizai, Fata, and Shihu the title of "Teacher," granted them the external office of Junior Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial,
bestowed upon them horses from the imperial stables, and so forth.
The scribes and the śramaṇas who verified the meaning were each granted purple robes and varying amounts of silk.
An imperial preface to the newly translated scriptures was composed and placed at the beginning of the canon.

Beholding how the Buddha-sun shines once more and the Wheel of Dharma has set forth its course—unveiling secrets from within a casket of red jade and opening the fragrance of blue lotus blossoms—the sacred resonance is such that who among previous generations could compare with it?
"Furthermore, those who translated and propagated [the scriptures] favored either brevity or prolixity.
Prior to the Sui dynasty, the titles of the sutras were concise;
from the time of Yijing onwards, the names of the scriptures became notably lengthy."
In ancient times, names were taken at random and applied by force; later, my own intentions became overly complex and exhaustive.
Furthermore, in the old translations of secret mantras (*dhāraṇī*), there were few annotations regarding the correct pronunciation.
In the Tang translations, the words are clearly stated and the phonetic transcriptions are detailed; that these recitations yield efficacy is superior to the traces of the past.
The Master Jing translated various scriptures, specializing particularly in the *Vinaya* section; his literary style was lofty and highly admirable.

Vajrabodhi was a patriarch who guarded the secret treasury, while Amoghavajra was a master craftsman of many translations; as teacher and disciple succeeded one another, their spiritual resonance was mutually manifest.
Wuweiyanci’s prose is both abundant and plain;
when he invokes the verses of the *Buddhōṣṇīṣa* for awakening and salvation, no one finds fault with him.
Rìzhào’s composition on the *Xiǎnshí* (Manifestation of Consciousness) leaves ample room for his sharp intellect to flourish.
Contemplating the *Sūtra of the Lion’s Roar*, he studied with delight the *Avataṃsaka*; its esoteric language severed all conceptual chapters, a realm for great beings.
Translating the *Ratnakūṭa*, he [clarified] the *Bodhicitta-mañjuśrī*;
the principles of the "Flower Dwelling" (*Huaxu*) were harmoniously luminous, while the "Consecration" (*Guanding*) stood as a secret and profound model of style.
Dí diligently served as the scribe, and the *Prajñāpāramitā* was completed at the translation site.
As for the other gentlemen, they all translated using "interleaved tablets" (*jiādié*); if one wishes to know their specific characteristics, I shall briefly offer an analogy.
It is like the case of human beings: all people are humans, yet how is it that their physical builds and features each resemble those they emulate, specifically their fathers?
If this is so, then they are identical in their greatness, differing only in minor details.
This is truly because the translation of the scriptures is the foundation of the Buddha-dharma; when the foundation is established, the Way arises.
That which the Way produces gives birth only to the sons of Śākya, and for this reason, this chapter is placed at the beginning.

Therefore it is said: "When the former kings were about to perform the *prāyaścitta* (expiatory rite) for the sea, they would first have a ritual at the River; this was to show that they did not forget their origin.

Section Two: Exegesis (Yijie), Part One. Section Two: Exegesis, Part One. Twenty-one Main Biographies; Seven Supplementary Entries. Biography of Kuiji of Daci’en Temple in Jingzhao, Tang Dynasty. Biography of Śramaṇa Kuiji: His courtesy name was Hongdao, his secular surname was Wei-chi, and he was a native of Chang’an in Jingzhao.

The ancestors of the Wei-chi rose together with the Later Wei and were known as the "Wei-chi Tribe," much like the feudal states of China; upon entering China, they took their tribal name as their surname.

Mengdu, the sixth-generation descendant of Wei Pingdong Jiangjun, fathered Luojia, who served as the Western Garrison Commander of Dazhou during the Sui dynasty; he was thus the progenitor of the clan.
His father’s name was Zong, who held the titles of Left General of the Imperial Guard, Governor-General of Songzhou, and Duke of Kai’guo County of Jiangyou under the Tang dynasty.
As for the Duke of Eguo, his virtue was that of an elder brother; there is a biography of him in the *Jiu Tang Shu*.
Ji’s mother, Lady Pei, dreamed that she swallowed the lunar disc with her palm, and upon waking, she became pregnant.
When the months had been fulfilled and the child was born, he was unlike other children; as he recited and practiced his studies, his spirit was alert and his faculties were keen.
Master Xuanzang, having previously seen him on the road—his eyebrows elegant, his eyes bright, and his demeanor free from affectation—remarked:
"He is truly of noble lineage; this is no mistake."
"If we can escape by means of some karmic coincidence and he is ordained as my disciple, then my Dharma will have a place to rest.
He further reflected that while in India, when it was time to return home, he had consulted the divination of a Nirgrantha and received an extremely auspicious omen:
"Master, simply return eastward; a person of wisdom shall be born."
He then went to the General of the North Gate and subtly exhorted him to leave the household life.
His father said, "He is of a coarse and violent nature; how could he be won over by instruction?"
Xuanzang said,
"This capacity and magnanimity would not have arisen except in a general, nor would it have been recognized except by me.
Although the father agreed, Xuanzang nevertheless firmly refused.
After being exhorted repeatedly, he bowed to comply with the command, but then resolutely raised his voice and said:
"Listen to my three conditions, and only then shall I vow to leave the household life:
I shall not sever my attachments to sensual desires, nor to meat and strong-smelling foods, nor shall I abstain from eating after midday."
"Xuanzang first used worldly desires as a lure, and later led them into the Buddha’s wisdom; he feigned agreement with what they previously desired.
Because he fulfilled their long-standing wishes over many years of travel, those in the Guanzhong region called him 'The Monk of the Three Chariots.'"
This was precisely the twenty-second year of the Zhenguan era.
Yiji’s own preface states:
"At the age of nine, I encountered the hardship of my parents' death, whereby I gradually distanced myself from worldly customs."
"If that were so, the discourse on the three vehicles would be a profound misrepresentation.
At the age of seventeen, he entered the monastic community (the "dark forest").
Upon entering the Dharma, by imperial decree he became a disciple of Master Xuanzang and first resided at Guangfu Temple.
Subsequently, I received a separate imperial decree selecting those of sharp intelligence and outstanding talent to enter Da Ci’en Monastery.
There, I personally attended upon Master Xuanzang to study the languages of the five regions of India; I resolved complexities, untied knots, and mastered the subject matter with systematic clarity.
All who heard and saw him were filled with admiration and submission.
He could survey all the *Khandakas* and *Vargyas* at a single glance without error; how could he have needed to labor over them again in memory?
At the age of twenty-five, he responded to an imperial decree to translate scriptures, lecturing upon and mastering more than thirty texts from both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions.
He applied his creative mind with diligence to his writings; for by inquiring earnestly and reflecting on what is near at hand, the Way is not far off.
He composed approximately one hundred commentaries (*shu*).

Regarding the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* translated by Xuanzang, at the outset he received it together with four others—Fang, Shang, and Guang—who were responsible for refining the language, taking down the dictation, verifying the text, and compiling the meanings.
After several mornings had passed, Xuanji requested to retire.
Xuanzang questioned him, and he replied:

"Last night I dreamed of the Golden Countenance, and this morning I hastened toward the White Horse. Although I have obtained the dregs of the Dharma-gate, I have lost the pure essence of the profound source; I do not wish to labor at the task of blending and synthesizing."
"If we consolidate everything into one person, then when we receive reprimands, there will be someone to whom they can be attributed.
Xuanzang then consented.
He resolved the affairs of the Three Worthies through principle and entrusted them solely to Kuiji; this was truly the delegation of responsibilities according to individual talent.
At that time, he recorded what he heard as it occurred and completed his comprehensive commentary on the lectures.

Not long after, the Dharma Master Ce of Ximing Temple—also a man of brilliant talent—managed to gain access to the lecture hall for the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* through a gatekeeper to whom he had offered gold. Concealing his form, he listened and synthesized the teachings, thereby penetrating the essential meaning of the treatise.
Just as the counting of seats was being completed, Daoci convened the assembly at Ximing Monastery by striking the wooden mallet and announced that he would lecture on this treatise.
When Jizang heard this, he felt ashamed for having been left behind and could not overcome his deep sense of regret.
Xuanzang encouraged him, saying, "Although Master Cè has composed commentaries, he has not yet mastered *Hetuvidyā* (Logic).

He then lectured on Dignāga’s treatises for him; Kuiji became exceptionally proficient in the "Three Members" (*trirūpa*), and his mastery in establishing arguments and refuting opponents, as well as his exegesis of the chapters on the "Assignment of Meaning," was without peer.
It is further said that when Master Xuanzang requested him to lecture on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* for his own sake alone, he was again overheard by Master Cè as before;
however, this time Xuanzang spoke first.
Xuanzang remarked, "The doctrine of the five natures (pañca-gotra) is to be propagated by you alone; others shall not possess it."

Later, he traveled in person to Mount Wutai and ascended Mount Taihang; arriving at an ancient Buddhist temple by the West River, he stayed overnight there. In a dream, he found himself halfway up the mountain, where beneath a cliff immeasurable people were crying out in agony. Amidst the darkness and confusion, he could not bear to hear it at first.
He proceeded on foot up those tiered peaks, all of which were the color of lapis lazuli, and from them he could see all the various lands.
Looking upward at a city, a voice issued from within it, saying:
"Stop! Stop! Ho! Master Ji, it is not fitting for you to come here."
After a short while, two celestial youths emerged from the city and asked,
"Did you see the sentient beings suffering in the hells beneath the mountain?
He replied:
"I have heard your voice but do not see your form.
The youth then threw him a sword hilt and said,
"If you cut open my belly, you shall see."
Ji himself cut it open; his belly split apart, two streams of light shone forth, illuminating the foot of the mountain, where he saw countless people undergoing extreme suffering.
At that time, the youth entered the city, took two scrolls of paper and a brush, threw them [into the fire], and received them as they were offered to him, departing with them.
When dawn arrived, his sense of wonder and amazement had not yet subsided.
As the night drew on, a light appeared within the monastery that did not extinguish for a long time.
Upon investigating it, he found several scrolls emitting light; when he examined them closely, he discovered the *Maitreya-sūtra on the Rebirth Above*.
He then recalled his previous dream, thinking, "It must be that Maitreya has commanded me to compose this commentary to clarify its principles.
As he took up the brush to write, two sets of seven śarīra relics fell from the tip of the pen; they were as large as Wu-style cherries and a lovely red color.
Next, regarding those who descended as ordinary people (*pingdang ren*): their appearance was like that of millet or sorghum grains.

One account states that when he traveled to Taiyuan to transmit the Dharma, three carriages followed him: the front carriage carried cases and boxes of sutras and treatises; the middle carriage was for his own use; and the rear carriage carried his female attendants, servants, and provisions.
Along the way, he encountered an old man who asked whom he was carrying.
He replied,
"My family."
The father said,
"Your understanding of the Dharma is indeed profound, but I fear that taking your family along would not be in accordance with the teachings.
Upon hearing this, Daokai immediately regretted his former errors and departed alone, his spirit serene and detached.
To say that the old man was Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva is merely a fragmentary statement.
When Xuanzang was at the Yuhua Palace engaged in translation, where would the three carts have been placed?
Daoci converted disciples wherever he went, and those who benefited from his teachings were numerous.
He traveled east to Boling, where he was requested to lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; he subsequently composed the *Great Commentary* (*Dàshù*) upon it.
Upon returning to his home temple, he constantly maintained correspondence with former colleagues from the translation bureau.
He visited Vinaya Master Xuan repeatedly;
Master Xuan was frequently attended by messengers of various heavenly kings who would either perform administrative duties or provide secret notifications regarding miscellaneous matters.
On that day, when Daoji was about to leave, Daoshuan remarked on his late arrival.
Daoji replied, "The Mahayana Bodhisattva was here just now; he was accompanied by many benevolent deities, and it was because our supernatural powers were suppressed by them that we were delayed."

In the first year of the Yongchun era (Renwu), he manifested illness; on the thirteenth day of the eleventh month, he passed away at the Translation Hall of Ci’en Monastery. He was fifty-one years of age, and his years of ordination (dharma-lakṣa) were not recorded.
He was buried in the northern canal of Fancun, enshrined alongside the tomb mound of the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang.
His disciples were overcome with grief; those who followed the funeral procession and gathered for the burial filled the valleys and mountains, comprising a multitude of both monastics and laypeople.

Jishi was always diligent and courageous; he fashioned an image of Maitreya and recited the Bodhisattva Precepts once every day before it, vowing to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven, thus seeking to fulfill his aspiration.
Thereupon, auspicious light emanated from his entire body, brilliant and magnificent to behold.

Furthermore, after he had fashioned a statue of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva out of jade and stone at Mount Wutai and completed the transcription of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in golden characters, it too emitted a divine radiance.
The disciples took Xuanzhi as their standard in succession, regarding him as if Xuanzang were still present.

On the day of Guiyou in the seventh month of the fourth year of Taihe (the gengxu year), the stupa was moved to Pingyuan. The śramaṇa Lingjian of Dajian Guosi supervised the stupa pavilion and the relocation of the coffin; upon opening it, he saw that forty of Xuanzhi’s teeth remained unbroken, as white as jade.
The multitude snapped their fingers, saying, "This is one of the marks of a Buddha.
Today, the images depicted in Buddhist temples throughout the world are titled "The True Image of the Founder of the Hundred Commentaries," for which Emperor Gaozong composed a hymn of praise.
One version says his secular surname was Xuanzong.

However, his physical presence was imposing and dignified, possessing the martial vigor of a Huan Qiu; yet his compassionate mind and tireless dedication to instructing others were entirely natural to him.
As for its iconographic features, it bears a jade pillow upon its neck, its facial features are majestic, and its ten fingers are joined together like a mudrā.

Regarding the variations in the characters used for his name and title, they differ because the *Ci'en Zhuan* states that when Master Xuanzang finished transcribing the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* at the Yuhua Palace in the third year of the Longshuo era,
on the twenty-second day of the eleventh month of that same year, he ordered Da Chengji to submit a memorial requesting the Emperor to compose a preface.
On the seventh day of the twelfth month, the attendant-delegate (tongshishi) Feng Yixuan arrived.
From this point on, he was called "Lingji"; the *Kaiyuan lu* records him as "Kuiji," or sometimes as "Chengji," but these are incorrect.

He [Xuanzang] called it the "Foundation of the Mahāyāna" (*Mahāyānāśraya*); since Huili and Yancong did not entirely reject this title, they referred to it as the "Foundation of the Mahāyāna," much like saying one does not listen to Tai. It was for this reason that they carefully sent Da Chengguang to present the memorial along with him.
Nowadays, those within the realm call him the Dharma Master Cien.
The concluding verse says:
"The doctrinal gateways of 'Nature' (Xing) and 'Characteristics' (Xiang) reached their full perfection only during the Tang dynasty."
Master Xuanzang is the progenitor who founded the Yogācāra and Vijñaptimātra traditions, while Master Ji is the patriarch who preserved the texts and composed commentaries.
These "progenitors" and "patriarchs" are ancestral rites that shall not be extinguished for a hundred generations.
Truly, the merit of benefiting all beings is vast and great.
If I, Xuanzang, were to lack this foundation, how could I serve as the patriarch to propagate this teaching?
How could I open the eyes of the people of the world?
The two masters established meritorious deeds that match their words; both shall endure imperishably.
Thus, while Ji was the adopted son of Duke Bo, Master Xuanzang was his disciple—truly a case of a general’s lineage coming to serve as a general of the Dharma, a peerless figure in a thousand years.
Therefore, the *Book of Documents* says: "When the father has cleared the land of weeds, the son will be willing to sow; how much more so when he can be willing to reap!
Is this not a reference to the hundred species of plants and trees?

The Biography of Shi Daoshi of Ximing Monastery in the Capital of the Tang Dynasty, as Transmitted by Daoshi of Ximing Monastery in the Capital of the Tang Dynasty. Shi Daoshi, courtesy name Xuanyun, was surnamed Han; his ancestors were from Yique.
His ancestors had served as officials and were therefore of the capital city of Jingzhao.
From birth he was robust and well-favored; gradually he became sharp and intelligent. Soon, weary of the multitude of worldly sands, he sought to join those who rescue even the smallest ants.
His two parents doted on him and repeatedly forbade his request, but after a long time, they finally granted his wish.

At the age of twelve, he left the household life at Qinglong Temple, following Master Zhideping and residing under the guidance of Master Linxinjian. He investigated the Vinaya school with rigorous scrutiny and delved deeply into its scriptures; he was particularly devoted to the Supreme Vehicle (Mahāyāna) and attained a profound and lucid understanding of the true nature of reality. At that time, his reputation was widespread, and those in the Three Prefectures looked up to him with reverence.

During the Xianqing era, the Great Emperor, noting that the sutras and treatises translated by Master Xuanzang had not yet been sufficiently propagated, soon issued an edict for him to enter the palace. Furthermore, he commanded that the virtuous monks (dade) of Ci'en Monastery take turns performing their religious duties there without interruption; the world was also included in this selection.
Furthermore, when the Western Ming Monastery was established for the Crown Prince, he was summoned to enter this monastery due to his brilliance and erudition.

At that time, Vinaya Master Daoxuan was implementing the Vinaya regulations in the region, and his influence was spreading widely; they were like two chariots of the five divisions of the Dharma driving together, jointly guiding the tracks of the three vehicles. No one could equal him, and his reputation for the Way was fragrant and far-reaching.
Furthermore, during the intervals between my lectures and studies, I continued to peruse the profound Tripitaka.

I reflected that throughout the vast succession of ages from antiquity to the present, many have composed works; yet, despite their elegant sentiments and refined phrasing, they fall short as historical records.

Thus, having plucked the essence from the garden of literature and inhaled the fragrance of the *campaka* flowers of the Great Meaning, I have compiled these materials by category and titled them the *Fayuan zhulin* (Pearl Forest in the Garden of the Dharma). It consists of one hundred chapters, bound into ten volumes.
Beginning from the "Chapter on the Measure of Kalpas" and ending with the "Miscellaneous Records," a separate preface is provided for each section.
This enables students and readers to consult the work according to its gates and divisions, thereby summarizing all that they know as easily as pulling a main rope or grasping a collar.

The world’s attention was focused upon it for ten years until its completion in the first year of the Zongzhang era; Li Yan, a Gentleman of the Lan Tai, composed a preface for it, and this text circulated throughout the realm.

Furthermore, he authored *The Retribution of Good and Evil Karma* and *The Treatise on Faith and Merit*, totaling twenty-three fascicles; *The Meditation Manuals for the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna* and *Mahāyāna Contemplation*, totaling eleven fascicles; *The Ritual for Receiving Precepts* and *The Ritual for Paying Homage to the Buddha*, totaling six fascicles; *An Essential Discussion of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* in five fascicles; *An Abstract of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya for Nuns* in five fascicles; and *A Collected Commentary on the Diamond Sūtra* in three fascicles. These ten works comprise one hundred and fifty-three fascicles in total.
He produced many writings throughout his life, though their ultimate extent remains unknown.
He avoided the imperial taboo name of Emperor Taizong by frequently using alternative characters; thus, he was commonly referred to as Xuanshun.
Biography of Shì Pǔguāng of Dàcí'ēn Monastery in Jǐngzhào, Táng Dynasty. Shì Pǔguāng was a person of unknown origins.
By nature intelligent and quick-witted, he selected his own timber and requested to serve under the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang.
His diligent and reverent heart was such that none among his peers could equal it.
As for his intellectual understanding, it may be likened to a revolving wheel; having heard little, he realized much, and Master Xuanzang silently gave him his approval.
In the final stages of the translation project, Prajñāvarman’s erudition stood preeminent among his colleagues; his excellence as a Tripiṭaka master contributed significantly to its brilliance.

Initially, Xuanzang had found that the ancient translations of the *Abhidharmakośa* were deficient in meaning, so he personally obtained a Sanskrit manuscript and retranslated the authentic text. He then secretly transmitted it to Prajñāvarman, who had largely memorized the oral exegesis of a Sautrāntika master from Western India.
Guang composed commentaries and treatises on the scriptures.
One account states that his commentary was so comprehensive that Yuanhui abridged it into ten fascicles, much like the *Tuo* [abridgment] of the Han dynasty.

Furthermore, he once accompanied Xuanzang to Yuhua Palace to translate the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*; his contributions were such that they surpassed even those of Huizhao, for which reason he was then known as "Dacheng Guang" (Light of the Mahāyāna).

Observe that from the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, when Xuanzang first began his translations at Yuhua Palace until the first year of the Linde era—a period spanning twenty years—he produced a total of seventy-five works comprising one thousand three hundred and thirty-five fascicles, consisting of Mahayana and Hinayana sutras, vinayas, and shastras. Approximately seven-eighths of these were transcribed by direct dictation from his own hand; some identify this person as Jiaguang, while others call him Puguang.
If one examines the records, since he participated in the translation work alongside Bianji, he is indeed Fuguang.

Regarding the *Biography of Fabao of Great Ci’en Monastery in Jingzhao, Tang*, by Shengzhuang: Fabao was also a spiritual disciple (*śrāvaka*) who studied the Dharma under the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang.
His nature was exceptionally sharp and keen, which was foremost among his qualities.

When Xuanzang first finished translating the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Bao had lingering doubts regarding the "delusions of view within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and requested further instruction on this matter.
Xuanzang separately inserted sixteen characters into the treatise as words of rebuttal.
Baoming said to Xuanzang,
"Do these two lines and four lines exist in the Sanskrit original?"
Xuanzang said,
"I have composed this based on the meaning of the principles and according to my own sentiments. Baoyun said:
"Master, how could you possibly augment the authoritative word of the Sage with ordinary speech?
Xuanzang replied,
"I already knew that such words would not be put into practice."

"From this point on, they have acted with arrogance and defiance at Xuanzang’s gate; even regarding the meaning of the 'six types of analysis and synthesis' (*ṣaḍ-vibhāṣā*), the Sarvāstivāda school takes the *Abhidharmakośa* as its definitive authority."
Master Guang often shared [the views] with other masters from Kaśmīra; "ji" (recorded) is a redundant character in the text.
At that time, the two Dharma Masters Guang and Bao were like Daorong and Daoyi among the disciples of Kumārajīva.
Later, he further refined his mastery of profound meanings, causing his reputation to rival that of Confucius and Mencius.

In the third year of the Chang’an era, he participated in the translation bureau of Yi Jing at Fuxian Temple and Jing Ximing Temple; there, he served as a *zhengyi* (certifier of meaning) alongside Baozang, Shengzhuang, and others. At that time, he was already showing great promise, and none could match him!

Biography of Yuan Ce of Ximing Monastery in the Capital of the Tang Dynasty. Regarding Yuan Ce of Ximing Monastery in the Capital of the Tang Dynasty, whose courtesy names were Bocen and Lingbian: his clan and lineage are not clearly known.
From childhood, he was exceptionally bright and possessed profound, versatile insight.

When Master Xuanzang, the Tripitaka Master, expounded the newly translated *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* for Master Ci'en Ji, Fa-cè bribed the gatekeeper to listen in secret; upon returning home, he compiled the essential points of the teachings into a treatise.
As he was about to conclude his lecture, Yuance rang the bells at Ximing Monastery to summon the assembly, announcing that he would lecture on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Xuánzàng was displeased by what he perceived as Yuance’s intent to attract followers away from him, and thus yielded the instruction of the lecture to Yuance.
When Xuanzang lectured on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, [Wen]bei again eavesdropped on him as before to receive its teachings, yet he did not lag behind Ji.
By the end of Gaozong’s reign and the beginning of Empress Wu’s, he was selected for his proficiency in exegesis and entered the Translation Institute, where everyone held him in high esteem.

He also translated such scriptures as the *Mahāyāna-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (The Manifestation of Consciousness in the Mahāyāna), for which he provided comprehensive commentaries on their meanings; in this regard, he was a peer to Bochen, Lingbian, and Jia Shang.
His authored *Commentary on the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* provides a detailed exposition of the sūtras and śāstras, which has been widely practiced throughout the land.
Yuan Kang of An Guo Monastery in the Tang capital: Yuan Kang of An Guo Monastery in the Tang capital; the monk Yuan Kang’s family name and clan are unknown.
During the Zhenguan era, he traveled to the capital to pursue his studies, earning a reputation for his robust and expansive learning.
Although his physique was stout and short, his temperament was bold and courageous; he understood much upon hearing little, and was highly esteemed by his peers.

Formerly dwelling in the mountains and wilds, he constantly devoted himself to the recitation of the *Avalokiteśvara* [Sūtra], seeking an increase in wisdom and understanding; he subsequently moved the spirits of the deer, so that one head produced eight-pronged antlers, its form being utterly extraordinary.
When Kang saw him, he stroked him until he became tame and submissive; he subsequently raised him as a pet and rode him for long distances, yet the horse never showed a sign of weariness.
Kang placed the texts of the *Three Treatises* upon its back and tied small scrolls to its tail, intending to drag it into the capital as a joke:
"The followers who preach existence do not comprehend the nature of emptiness; I shall crush them with this lightly-loaded axle and cause them to realize the True Principle."
Furthermore, he wore coarse cloth garments and trailed a hemp sash; he donned a bamboo hat, the brim of which was one zhang and two chi wide.
His attire was so strange and bizarre that all who saw him were struck with awe.
Having entered the capital city, he saw a Dharma Master presiding over a grand assembly to lecture on a sutra and guide the people.

Kang joined the gathering and approached the master’s seat; he immediately posed questions regarding the points being expounded, engaging in an exchange of several hundred words. Everyone was astonished by Kang’s such eloquence and quick-wittedness.
He further teased the Dharma Master, saying:
"The sweet peach bears no fruit; the bitter plum bends its branches low.
The lecturer replied:
"A Wheel-Turning King has a thousand sons; a eunuch has no grandsons.
This was a satire on Kang’s lack of disciples.
Kang said:

"The lacquer used for caskets is red, and the varnish used for caskets is black; yet that which you follow as 'red' is not merely vermilion or crimson, and that which you enter as 'black' is not merely lead or ink."
The entire assembly said, "His words and reasoning are so clear and lucid; could he be anyone other than a Great Being who has manifested his traces here?
When the Emperor heard this, he said with joy:
"Since no such person has appeared for generations," [the Emperor] issued an edict for him to enter An Guo Temple to lecture on this *Sanlun*.
He subsequently composed a commentary to explain the principles of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.
He separately compiled the *Xuánshū* (The Mysterious Pivot) in two fascicles, which comprehensively elucidates the fundamental tenets of the *Zhōnglùn*, the *Bǎilùn*, and the *Ménlùn*.
His ultimate end was later unknown.

It is worn on the left side with a sash fastened on the right, and it contains much cotton wool.
However, as this is a garment for warding off the cold, it is not used in hot countries; its use there is nonetheless permitted by the Sage.

When it flowed to the Eastern Land, it was transformed into colored silk; its borders were trimmed and attached to the left and right sleeves, hanging down in trailing folds to signify that I have mastered the sūtras and śāstras.

This is the biography of Shi Jingmai of Fojusi Temple in Jianzhou, Tang China. Shi Jingmai was a native of Zitrong.
In his youth, he was self-restrained; as he grew older, his aspirations and conduct became lofty. He was particularly adept at investigating the subtle depths of the sutras and treatises.
Possessing a grave and profound temperament, he did not engage in frivolous associations; he traveled only after carefully choosing his destination, eventually arriving at the capital region.

During the Zhenguan era, coinciding with Xuanzang’s return from the West, an imperial decree was issued to establish Guangfu Monastery in the capital on behalf of Empress Dowager Taimu for the purpose of translating scriptures.
Regarding all necessary administrative labor, matters were to be deliberated with Xiao Yu (Xuanling), ensuring that they were provided with ample support.

He then summoned eleven virtuous monks (*bhadanta*) who were masters of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras, highly esteemed by their contemporaries; Xuanzang was selected among this elite group and immediately took up residence at Ci'en Monastery.

Together with Xi Xuan of Puguang Temple, Mingzhen of Guangfu Temple, Bianji of Huichang Temple, and Daoxuan of Fengde Temple on Mount Zhongnan, they took up their pens to compile the text and translated the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (The Scripture on Past Events) in seven fascicles.

Later, when [Xuanzang] was at the Yuhua Palace and the Translation Institute of Cien Monastery, he received the dictation from Shenfang and Mi; both were praised for their adaptability, and thus they were able to grasp the essence of the scriptures.

Later, he authored the four-fascicle *Yijing tuji* (Illustrated Record of Translated Scriptures), which systematically catalogues and orders the titles of scriptures from ancient and modern times, the ranks and names of translators, works translated individually, those translated multiple times, and those of doubtful or spurious origin; all of this is now included in the Buddhist canon.
During the Kaiyuan era, Zhisheng further appended titles to these works.

Regarding the Biography of Shunjing of Silla, China: Shunjing was a native of Lelang Commandery; as he belonged to a local clan and a lineage of the Eastern Barbarians, his history is difficult to detail with precision.

He received from Master Xuanzang the "Inference of True Consciousness-Only" (*tattva-vijñaptimātra-anumāna*) and thereby established the "Inconclusive Reason of Contradictory Determination" (*viruddhāvyabhicāri-hetu*).
It was sent during the Qiánfēng era, conveyed by an envoy on his way to present tribute.

"As for the Dharma Master Sunyeong of Silla, his reputation resounded throughout Tang and Tubo, and his learning encompassed both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
He revered the legacy of Kāśyapa, practicing the dhūta austerities alone;
he was intent on the virtues of Bakula, constantly renowned for his few desires."

Subsequently, he refined his arts in the Western Xia and spread his illumination to the Eastern Barbarians; as his reputation for the Way grew ever new, both monastics and laypeople paid him respectful homage.

Although there were not a few "dragons and elephants" (great masters) among them, he was frequently acclaimed abroad as being peerless; it was in this context that he composed the *Niyatavirodha* (The Determination of Contradiction).

Master Ji thought to himself: "This man from a distant land possesses such sharp intelligence that he has boldly challenged Master Xuanzang; his latent capacities have been activated in secret, and he has skillfully mastered the meaning of the Tripiṭaka. What a pity!"
In his own country, Xing had composed numerous treatises, some of which were transmitted to the Central Plains; the doctrine he followed was the "Definitive Teaching of the Dharma-lakṣaṇa Mahāyāna."
Having seen in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* that one attains Buddhahood from the very moment of generating the bodhicitta, he gave rise to slander and disbelief.
Some said:
"When he was about to lift his hands and feet, he commanded his disciples to support him down to the ground; then the earth slowly split open, and Master Jing’s body suddenly fell into it."
At that time, Yansheng’s body sank into the earth.
To this day there is a pit, over ten feet in length and breadth, truly deep and cavernous, which is called "Shunjing Naraka."

Therefore, those who prefer white regard black as defilement, while those who prefer black regard white as defilement."
Jing’s angry mind was even more severe; his fierce and sharp karma increased like a shot arrow, and in an instant he fell into hell.
In ranking the order of eminent monks, would you place one who gives rise to filth and makes himself stink?
Tong said:
"A teaching difficult to believe is easily met with swift slander and derision; how could such slander come from only one person?
Only by causing those known to the public to fall directly into the three miserable realms can it be known that Wonseon and Gyeongbo were truly manifest Bodhisattvas of the Exoteric Teachings."
How much more so when Zhao Dun accepted evil for the sake of the Dharma, while a Bodhisattva sacrifices his very body for the sake of the Dharma—how could this be considered strange?

Have you not seen how the non-Buddhist Nirgranthas each slandered the Buddha, yet it was specifically Devadatta who was cast into prison alive; later, however, he received the prediction of Buddhahood at the assembly of the Lotus Sutra? Reflect on this quietly.
Biography of Jia Shang of Da Cien Monastery in Jingzhao, Tang Dynasty. As for the monk Jia Shang, it is unknown where he was from.

Possessing an innate wisdom and a magnificent, extraordinary temperament, he steadfastly adhered to the *Piṭaka* collections; he investigated both the nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena, applying himself diligently to spiritual cultivation and devoting himself to the work of translation.
From afar, he directed his mind toward the gate of the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang; having beheld the richness of the ancestral temple, he also caught sight of the elegance of the household.
For a long time, he examined the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the purport of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*, and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, gaining a profound mastery of their essential meanings.

Accompanying Xuanzang at the Yuhua Palace while the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* was being translated, he served as the proofreader for the meaning and the editor of the text, excelling in many capacities.
When the Tripiṭaka Master fell ill, he commanded Shang to record all the sūtras and śāstras translated, totaling seventy-five works comprising one thousand three hundred and thirty-five fascicles.

Furthermore, he recorded one thousand scrolls of painted images and commissioned ten koṭis of statues; he had scriptures transcribed, released living beings, and lit lamps, and commanded Shang to recite them aloud.
Xuanzang joined his palms with joy and said, "This was my heart's desire;
that you should guide me through it, so that I may pass away without regret.
After Xuanzang passed away, he composed commentaries and sub-commentaries, producing various anthologies whose categories of meaning were numerous.
During the reign of Empress Wu, he joined Bochen, Lingbian, and others at the translation assembly to verify the meanings of the texts, his meritorious contributions becoming increasingly extensive.

Previously, while serving Master Xuanzang at Yuhua Palace during the translation of the scriptures, they reached the first chapter, the "Chapter on Adorning and Purifying the Buddha-lands. This section describes how all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, through their supernatural powers and vows, bring forth the most magnificent treasures, exquisite incense and flowers, and the five sensory objects produced by the power of intention to adorn and offer to the place where the Dharma is preached. On one night, the Abbot Huidé beheld within the precincts of Yuhua Monastery a vast, pure, and majestic scene, filled with music and celestial instruments.
Furthermore, I heard that the three halls were lecturing on the Dharma;
when I informed Xuanzang the following day, our joy was in perfect accord.
Yet, I still do not know how it all ended.

Biography of Huizhao of Zhi Prefecture during the Tang Dynasty. Regarding Huizhao of Zhi Prefecture during the Tang Dynasty: the monk Huizhao of Great Vows Beyond the World was a man of unknown origins.
From his youth, he was alert and wise; having first donned the blue scholar’s robe, he relied upon the local schools, where his recitation and study were comprehensive and thorough.
Entering the Dharma to cultivate his person, he did not violate the precepts; thus, he was popularly known at the time as "Ācārya Zhao.
Subsequently, he mastered the profound depths of the sūtras and śāstras, becoming highly proficient in translation and transmission.
Ever since Tripitaka Master Xuanzang arrived in the capital, [Wuzhuo] constantly peered into its innermost depths.
Later, he personally studied under the master Dasheng Ji, becoming even more refined and erudite.

When Bodhiruci was translating the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra* at Chongfu Monastery, Wuzhuo was selected for the position of *zhengyi* (verifier of meaning). The Silla Dharma Master Shengzhuang took up the brush, while the śramaṇas Dayuan and Chenwai were both contemporaries of outstanding brilliance—true elephants and dragons of their era.
At that time, Wu Pingyi was serving as an envoy, while Lu Zangyong and Lu Jingchu were both present at the assembly.
When Cui Ti, the Vice Director of the Secretariat, arrived at the Translation Hall for the incense offering, he sighed and said:
"All those of pure character are gathered here; how could they be kept apart?"
Consequently, he submitted a memorial requesting permission to collaborate in the editorial refinement of the new translations.

Initially, when Yuanzhao served as the *arthaviniścaya* (verifier of meaning) at Yijing’s translation bureau, he corrected many errors; wherever there were corrupt words or erroneous interpretations, they all followed his designations, and none dared to overstep his regulations.
Later, he composed various commentaries on the meanings [of the scriptures] and was styled Zhao of Zizhou.
The Biography of Yancong of Da Cien Monastery in Jingzhao, Tang China. Regarding the monk Yancong: it is unknown where he was from.
At the end of the Zhenguan era, he traveled to the capital to observe its splendors and sought the Dharma at the gate of the Tripiṭaka Master.
However, his talent did not equal that of Wenguang or Xuanzang; he merely engaged in extensive and continuous study.
In the fields of both Buddhism and Confucianism, he had attained a profound mastery of their subtlest principles.
His skill in composition and calligraphy far surpassed that of his contemporaries.

There was a śramaṇa named Huili of Xisi Monastery in the Wei kingdom, whose temperament was fierce and impetuous; taking the protection of the Dharma as his personal mission, he authored a five-fascicle biography dedicated to recording the flourishing propagation of the Tripiṭaka Master from the Zhenguan era onward, as well as the various hardships and perils encountered during his travels through the Western Regions. This work is titled the *Ci'en Zhuan*, a name derived from the title of the monastery where he resided.
When he had finished carving the *śāla* wood, fearing that some of its beauty might have been lost, he buried it in an earthen pit.
When his illness became critical, he commanded his disciples to dig up the earth and retrieve it, after which he passed away.

Biography of Yixiang of Silla, China: Shi Yixiang’s secular surname was Park, and he was a native of Gyeongrim-bu in Silla.
He was brilliant and extraordinary from birth, and as he grew up, he renounced the world; he entered the Way with ease, his nature being naturally so disposed.

Upon reaching the age of twenty, hearing that the Buddhist schools in the land of Tang were flourishing, he joined forces with the Dharma Master Wonhyo to travel westward. When they reached the border between Haimen and Tangzhou in their own country, they sought out a large ship, intending to cross the vast waves of the sea.
Suddenly, while on the road, he encountered a heavy rain; he consequently took shelter within a clay niche by the roadside to avoid the wind and dampness.
When they looked at one another the following morning, they found themselves beside the skeletal remains of an ancient tomb.
The heavens rained down fine drizzle, and the earth became a mire; unable to advance even a foot or an inch, they lingered and failed to proceed.
Furthermore, while they were lodged within the hollows of the kiln-bricks, before the night had ended, there suddenly appeared a ghostly apparition as a specter.
Master Xiao sighed and said:
"In my previous lodging, I stayed in an earthen grotto and found it peaceful;
yet this night, as I remain here, I am entrusted to a realm of ghosts where calamities abound."
Thus one knows that because the mind arises, the various phenomena arise; because the mind ceases, the tomb and the grave are non-dual.
Furthermore, the three realms are mind-only, and the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only.
Since there is no dharma outside the mind, why seek elsewhere?
"I shall not enter Tang," he declared, and departed with his bag for his own country. Xiang, however, traveled alone and solitary, vowing never to retreat even unto death.

In the second year of the Zongzhang era, he reached the shores of Dengzhou by means of a merchant vessel. While wandering for alms, he arrived at the home of a lay devotee; seeing that Xiang’s countenance was upright and noble, the host detained him at his gate for a long time. There was a young girl there, elegantly dressed and finely adorned, named Shanmiao, who sought to seduce him with artful charms, yet the stone-heart of Xiang could not be turned.
Nütiōu received no answer, yet she immediately gave rise to the aspiration for the Way and made a solemn vow before him, saying:

Xiang then proceeded directly to the Venerable Master Zhinan at Mount Zhongnan in Chang’an to study the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* intensively.
At that time, National Teacher Kangzang was his fellow student.

He then went to the home of an old patron in Wéndēng to thank him for his offerings and support over many years; he immediately hired a merchant vessel and, after a brief delay, cast off the moorings.
His daughter, Shànmìào, had already prepared a set of Dharma robes and various ritual implements, filling several boxes, which were transported to the seashore.
The boat from Xiang had already departed far away, so his daughter chanted a spell over it, saying:

Thereupon, she rolled up her sleeves and threw herself into the sea. After Xiang entered the country, he traveled extensively across mountains and rivers; even in the lands of Goguryeo and Baekje, where the wind and cattle do not meet, he remarked:

Biography of Shen Kai of Chongfu Monastery in Jingzhao, Zhou: Shen Kai, whose secular surname was Guo, was a native of Taiyuan and a descendant of Linzong from the end of the Han dynasty. His religious name was Mingxun. He was a man of Taiyuan. He was a descendant of Linzong from the end of the Han dynasty.
Inheriting his family’s official robes and cap, he later followed his father to serve in the Qin court, becoming a native of Jingzhao.
He had six brothers, and Kai was the youngest. From childhood, he was intelligent and quick-witted;

his aspirations were beyond the ordinary, and he took no pleasure in fleeting glory, vowing instead to shave his head and don the monastic robes. He took the Dharma Master Ming as his teacher, serving as his disciple—this Ming being the same as Da-xun.

By the time he reached the age for full ordination, he had mastered the principles of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras; his ears heard and his mouth recited them as easily as fine cotton cloth takes dye.
He subsequently lectured on treatises such as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Abhidharmakośa*; his brilliance and insight were such that among his contemporaries, few could rival him.
Later, while lecturing on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, he observed the interpretations of the ancient masters and sighed deeply, saying:
"While these are indeed elegant, they do not yet reach the ultimate excellence."
He then composed his commentary at Baizhao Mountain in Anlu; one source states that he wrote it at Shicheng Temple in Shan County, Yuezhou.
Possessing a natural talent for artistry, he fashioned a clay image beneath the southern cliff of Shan Creek, reflecting its form in the water.
Now there is a pond that has already dried up.
Beneath a cliff, within the dark crevices of the rocks, there is a wooden coffin; it is said that this is where Kai was encoffined.
Passersby looking down from above could see everything clearly.
It is further said that because of Kai, the temples of Cien, Ximing, and others ordained princes and nobles.

When the sutras and śāstras were being translated, an imperial decree was issued for all monks of eminent conduct and scholarly talent from various regions to proceed to the capital; Kai accordingly responded to the summons and entered, where he was assigned a residence at Chongye Temple.
It was not until the reign of Empress Wu that his memorial was finally put into practice.

Biography of Huiyin of Guangfu Monastery in Jingzhao, Zhou: The monk Huiyin was a man of unknown origins.
His spirit of brilliance was abundant and overflowing; standing among his peers, he was like a crane seen amidst a flock of chickens.
During the reign of the Emperor Tenno, those of high learning and renowned virtue were carefully selected, and he was secretly chosen for this office.

In the second year of the Linde era, an imperial edict was issued for the Bureau for the Compilation of Writings at the Western Dragon Gate of the Northern Gate to collaborate with ten individuals, including Xuánzé of Xìmíng Monastery, to extract the essential meanings and profound texts from among all the scriptures, totaling thirty fascicles titled the *Essential Abstracts of the Chan Forest* (*Chánlín yàochǎo*). Biography of the Monk Sengyuan of Huqiu Mountain Temple, Zhou Dynasty. The monk Sengyuan, whose courtesy name was Biankong, was surnamed Yu and was a native of Changyi in Gaoping.

His practice of humble courtesy was innate to his natural wisdom, and his capacity for eloquence and discernment was renowned as preeminent.
In the second year of the Longshuo era, he received an imperial decree to undergo tonsure; in accordance with a profound spiritual resonance, he returned to be affiliated with this mountain.

After Master Yan had passed away, he received the full precepts from Chan Master Huixu and studied the Three Treatises under Dharma Master Ceng of Changle Temple. The profound and signless nature of these teachings cleared away his doubts and obstructions; through skillful means, he attained liberation and realized awakening with serene composure.
Because he realized wisdom through the mind, he subsequently went to Chan Master Rong of Jiangning to seek instruction in the Dharma of the mind.
By concentrating his thoughts and practicing seated meditation, the various demons were subdued;
through diligent and energetic cultivation, even fierce beasts became constantly docile.

Consequently, his fame spread everywhere, and his reputation and brilliance were peerless throughout the eight directions; even those who frequent taverns for profit ceased their tracks and no longer trod there.

When praised and admired, his countenance remained serene;

He often sheltered himself beneath tall pines, his thoughts directed toward lofty and far-reaching ideals.

The Biography of Master Yinzong of Miaoxi Temple on Mount Kuaiji during the Tang Dynasty. Master Yinzong, whose secular surname was Yin, was a native of Wu Commandery.
When his mother, Lady Liu, was first pregnant, all the neighbors saw a dignified and elegant śramaṇa slowly enter their house;

His calligraphy was exceptionally refined, and his writings were widely disseminated.

On the twenty-first day of the second month in the second year of the Xiāntiān era, he manifested his passing, leaving instructions that he be buried according to the rites of a Cakravartin King; he was eighty-seven years old.
The Master of the Prince of Kuaiji, Qian, erected a stele inscription for him.
Biography of Shi Zongzhe of Chongfu Monastery in Taiyuan Prefecture, Tang Dynasty: Shi Zongzhe was a native of Pingyao in Xihe.
