When Śikṣānanda arrived bringing the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Avataṃsaka*, he worked together with Yijing and Fuli to translate the new scriptures.
Furthermore, at the translation bureau of Yi Jing, he served as a verifier of the meaning alongside Shengzhuang and Dayi.
Formerly, Du Shun of Dunhuang transmitted the *Huayan fajie guan* to his disciple Zhiyan, who lectured and taught this version translated during the Jin dynasty.
Zhiyan entrusted the teachings to Fazang, who was lecturing on the new *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* for Empress Wu Zetian.

When they reached the sections on the "Celestial Net" (Indra’s Net), the "Ten Profound Gates," the "Ocean-Seal Samādhi Gate," the "Gate of the Meaning of the Sixfold Synthesis," and the "Gate of the Universal Eye Realm"—all of which are comprehensive and specific networks of meaning within the *Avataṃsaka*—the Empress was utterly bewildered and could not resolve her doubts.

The "Treasury" (Zang) refers to the golden lion that serves as the guardian of the hall; because he composed this work on the gates of meaning (*yimen*) so that it would be direct, swift, and easy to understand, it was titled the *Jinsi zi zhang* (Chapter on the Golden Lion). It sets forth ten gates detailing the characteristics of the general and the specific, whereby the Emperor subsequently attained awakening to its essential meaning.

Furthermore, for those who have not yet mastered the practice, he devised a skillful means: he took ten mirrors and arranged them in the eight directions, with one each above and below, each separated by more than a zhang. The mirrors faced one another, and in their center he placed a single Buddha image and lit a torch to illuminate it, so that their reflections intersected and their lights mingled.
Scholars have thereby come to understand the meaning of the infinite interpenetration of the ocean of lands (*kṣetrasamudra*).
The skillful means of the Tripitaka in its transformative guidance are all of this nature.

As for the mandate to propagate and translate [the scriptures], it likewise cannot yet be abandoned; this is because the Emperor places his faith in them, and they are what the monastic community relies upon.

When the various Indian monks had finished their translation work, on the eighth day of the tenth month of the year Yi-hai, the second year of the Shengli era, the Emperor issued an edict that the scripture be enshrined at Foshouji Monastery for the purpose of lecturing upon the Great Sūtra. When the lecture reached the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World," the lecture hall and the grounds of the monastery all shook. The Chief Administrative Monk Seng Hengjing submitted a formal memorial to report this event to the throne.
The Imperial Edict stated:
"Yesterday, you were requested to expound upon subtle words and elucidate profound mysteries.
On the day the initial translation began, a dream of nectar presented auspicious omens;..."
At the moment the lecture began, the earth shook as a sign of its extraordinary nature.
This was surely the Tathāgata manifesting his traces to accord with the texts of the nine assemblies;
how could my own meager and humble self dare to claim credit for these sixfold earthquakes?
"Having perused your letter, joy and trepidation arise within my breast.
Thus it was said.
That he was held in such high esteem by emperors and sovereigns is truly no empty praise; for this reason, the Huayan school was entrusted to Chengguan, who is ranked as the third patriarch.
He authored the *Commentary on the Heart Sūtra of Prajñā*, which was esteemed by his contemporaries and circulated throughout the world.
Is it not he who was also titled the National Preceptor Kangzang?
Biography of Shi Hengjing of Yuyuan Monastery in Jingzhou, Tang China. Shi Hengjing’s secular surname was Wen, and he was a native of Dangyang.

In the twenty-second year of the Zhenguan era, he received imperial edict to enter the monastic order and was permitted to study the Tripitaka. Upon hearing it once, he could recite it; he practiced exactly as he taught.

Initially, he followed Vinaya Master Wengang to train in the *Vinaya*, and later entered Yiquan Temple on Mount Fuzhou to pursue the teachings of Zhiyi (Zhizhe Chanshi) regarding the gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Ten *li* to the south of the monastery, a separate vihāra was established, known as Longxing (Dragon Rising).
From the reigns of Empress Wu Zetian and Emperor Zhongzong, he was summoned three times to enter the palace to provide offerings and serve as a preceptor for the conferral of ordination.
In the third year of the Jinglong era, he submitted a petition requesting to return to the mountains, and the imperial decree granted his request.
An edict was issued for the Secretariat, the Chancellery, and the Academicians to establish a vegetarian feast at the Inner Daochang of the Lingguang Palace.

Previously, he had summoned more than twenty eminent monks from throughout the empire who were also practitioners of the Way to regularly cultivate merit within the inner palace; now that the ritual fasting was concluded, he sent Jing, Daojun, and Xuanzang back to their respective hometowns.

The Emperor personally composed a poem, and the scholars responded with verses; these included several individuals such as Li Qiao, the Minister of the Secretariat, and Li Yi, the Secretary of the Secretariat.
At that time, Jing and his companions carried the poems and walked with their mendicant staffs, and the whole world esteemed them for this honor.

Jing compiled the *Treatise on Accordance with the Definitive Meaning* in two fascicles, the *Treatise on the Compendium of the True Dharma* in seven fascicles, and the *Treatise on Buddha-nature* in two fascicles.
Those who studied his school were like those who receive a refreshing drink when parched with thirst.
On the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month in the first year of the Xiāntiān era, he passed away at the monastery where he resided; he was seventy-nine years of age.
His disciples enshrined his remains in a burial mound on the western plain of the monastery.
The commentary states:
Xuanzang of Jiangling and the Tripitaka Master were like a form and its shadow, their proximity being but slight.

Yet, while their names are identical, their actual substance differs; they are much like Lin Xiangru, who attained what the powerful Qin feared, and Ma Xiangru, whom Yang Xiong came to admire and emulate.
Thus, it can be seen that each has its own strengths and weaknesses.

The Biography of Master Yi Xing of Songyang Temple on Mount Song, the Central Peak of Tang: Shi Yi Xing, whose secular surname was Zhang, was a native of Julu. His original name was Su, and he was a descendant of Zhang Gongjin, the Duke of Tan, who served as a founding minister at the beginning of the Tang dynasty.
From his youth, he did not associate with his peers; he was intelligent, quick-witted, and possessed the maturity of an elder.
He would recite a text from memory after reading it only once.

Having encountered Chan Master Pujì’s extensive propagation of the essentials of Chan, many turned their hearts toward him; thus, [the youth] realized the world is an illusion, took Pujì as his teacher, and left the household life to receive the tonsure.
Regarding the sūtras and dharmas he recited, there were none that he did not master with precise intonation.
Once, when Master Ji convened a great assembly, śramaṇas from near and far arrived as scheduled, numbering more than a thousand.

At that time, there was the retired scholar Lu Hong, who lived in seclusion on a separate peak; his Way was lofty and his learning vast, yet despite the imperial court repeatedly sending for him with the "rush-mat carriage," he ultimately declined and did not rise to serve.
The presiding official of the great assembly first requested Master Hong to compose a preface and eulogy for the lay community.
On that day, Hong produced the text from his sleeve and placed it upon the table.
Once the ritual chanting had begun, Hong said to Master Ji, "I have composed several thousand words;

moreover, the characters are obscure and the style is archaic. I request that you, who are eloquent and refined, proclaim them. You must certainly explain and point out the meanings as you teach them."
Master Ji called for Huixing; Xing unrolled the paper, read it, and smiled before placing it back upon the desk.
Daohong marveled at his casual ease.
When the monks gathered in the hall, Xing stepped forward with his sleeves rolled up, delivering his speech in a resonant voice with elegant phrasing, without a single error.
Hong stared in astonishment for a long time; sighing deeply and unable to stop himself, he spoke again to Master Ji, saying:
"This is not something you can instruct him in; you should allow him to travel abroad to study."
From then on, he regarded these three as his teachers, rarely proceeding without consulting them for guidance.
While traveling to Dangyang, he encountered Sengzhen, who had compiled the "Preface to the Vinaya Piṭaka" and possessed a profound mastery of the *vinaya*.

Nevertheless, there were books concerning the *yin-yang* and *chan-wei* systems, all of which he investigated in detail; he traveled more than several thousand li in search of experts in calculation, consulting those renowned for their skill.
When I finally arrived at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai, I saw a courtyard with ancient pines spanning several dozen paces; its gate rested against a flowing stream, serene and profoundly still.
Standing at the screen of the gate, I heard the sound of calculations being laid out within the courtyard, a rustling noise like *sū sū*.
The Master said to his attendant:
"Today there shall be a disciple coming from afar seeking my methods of calculation; by the reckoning, he should have arrived at the gate. Is it not possible that no one has come to guide him here?"
He immediately removed one counting-stick and said to his attendant,
"The waters before the gate have turned back to flow westward; my disciple shall arrive."

Xing followed these words and entered, prostrating himself to request the Dharma; [the Master] bestowed upon him the full transmission of the decision. Thereupon, the water in front of the gate flowed eastward once more.
From this time on, his fame resounded both far and near, and high officials and ministers spoke of him with great acclaim.
When the Emperor Xuanzong heard of this, he issued an edict for him to enter the palace and asked Huixing,
"What abilities do you possess?
Huixing replied:
"He is merely able to recall and review [the texts], having no other particular talent.

The Emperor then ordered an official of the inner court to fetch the palace registers to show him; after he had finished perusing them from beginning to end, he covered the original text, yet his memory remained so precise and fluent that it was as if he had practiced it all his life.
After he had chanted for several sheets of paper, the Emperor unconsciously descended from his couch and prostrated himself, saying,
"The Master is truly a sage.
He sighed in admiration for a long while.

Soon thereafter, he was summoned for audiences where he would respond without hesitation; his prognostications regarding calamities and blessings were as clear as looking at one's own palm, and his words were frequently beneficial.
At that time, there was a man of spiritual arts named Xing Hepu, whose depths no one could fathom; he once said to Yin Yin:
"The Monk Yixing is truly a sage."
Han Luo Xia Hong, while constructing the calendar, said:

Who other than a sage could have foreseen this!
Furthermore, he studied the secret mudrās of dhāraṇīs under Vajra Tripiṭaka and ascended the aforementioned Buddha altar to receive the treasure of the Dharma King;

In transmitting the *Mizang* (Secret Treasury), he was certain to reach the profound depths of the treasury.
Both Emperor Ruizong and Emperor Xuanzong invited him to the Inner Jixian Academy; shortly thereafter, an imperial edict ordered him to reside at Xingtang Monastery.

He subsequently composed a commentary in seven fascicles on the translated sutras, as well as the *Vinayapiṭakasaṃgraha* in sixty fascicles, the *Śākyavaṃśāvalī* in one fascicle, and the *Kaiyuan Daoyan Calendar* in fifty-two fascicles.
This calendar was incorporated into the "Treatise on Calendars and Music" (*Liyu zhi*) of the *Jiu Tangshu*, where it was regarded as an unalterable standard.
He also constructed a celestial globe (*youyi*), with the ecliptic and equatorial circles fashioned from iron, which were produced within the observatory.

Next, there was an old palace lady who was an elderly woman living in the neighborhood; in the past, she had frequently provided for the poor when they were traveling, and now that they had attained prominence, she constantly thought of repaying her kindness.
One day he went to pay his respects and said:
"My son has committed murder and is about to be executed. Furthermore, Your Majesty is noble and refined;
I beg you to petition for a reduction of his sentence to death, so that he may serve out the remaining years of his mother's life!"
After he had wept thus several times, Xing said,
"Regarding the laws and punishments of the state, how could one possibly obtain exemption through pleading?
He then ordered his attendant monk to provide him with some money and goods, telling him to leave as he pleased to seek other means.
The nurse, brandishing her elbow, cursed him roundly, saying:
"I lived as a neighbor to you, providing for you in turn; from swaddling clothes to being held in my arms, I nursed you at my breast.
Now that you have grown up, how can you forget this kindness!"
His mind moved with compassion, and he found no joy throughout the entire night.
Thereupon, having completed his calculations, he summoned his attendants and instructed them, saying:
"All of you, take cloth bags to a secluded spot in such-and-such a ward and sit there at noon to wait. As soon as you see any living creature fall into a bag, return quickly."
The next day, as expected, a sow led seven piglets; the attendants drove them from different directions, and the sow mother fled, allowing them to capture the piglets and return.
Having prepared a large jar, he placed them inside one by one, closed the lid, sealed the opening with "six-yi" clay, and recited several incantations in a foreign tongue before ceasing.
At dawn, an imperial eunuch arrived with an edict to enter and inquire, saying:
"The Office of Astronomy has reported:"
"Last night, none of the seven stars of the Big Dipper were visible;
why is this? He replied, "In the past, the Later Wei once lost the planet Mars (Venus), and until now, the Imperial Chariot has remained invisible."
This is Heaven’s great warning to Your Majesty.
Even when a single man or woman does not find their proper place, it brings about frost or drought; yet when moved by profound virtue, such calamities can be withdrawn.
What could evoke such profound compassion as the burial of exposed bones?
To subdue all demons, the Buddhist community employs a heart of loving-kindness; yet for my humble and biased views, nothing is more fitting than a general amnesty for the empire.
The Emperor followed his instructions.
That night, he reported that one star of the Big Dipper had become visible; after seven nights, it returned to its original state. His arts were unfathomable.
Furthermore, during the Kaiyuan era, when a severe drought occurred, the Emperor ordered him to pray for rain, to which he replied:
"It must be a vessel upon which the form of a dragon appears; only then can rain be brought forth.
An imperial edict was issued for an inner palace official to search throughout the inner treasury together with [the Master], but all reported that none were suitable.
A few days later, he pointed to an ancient mirror with a dragon coiled upon its handle and said joyfully,
"This is a true dragon.
He then brought it into the ritual arena, and on that very day, it rained.
Such was the efficacy of his extraordinary arts in communicating with the unseen.

When Emperor Xuanzong was at Daming Palace, he casually and privately questioned him regarding the fortune or misfortune of the state, as well as matters concerning the end of his reign’s mandate; Xing responded instead with other talk.
The Emperor questioned him incessantly, whereupon he finally said:
"Your Majesty shall have a journey of 'ten thousand li'.
He further said:
"The state and the altars shall ultimately attain good fortune.
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
He further sent the Emperor a golden casket, shaped like a pellet, which contained something inside; when shaken, it always made a sound, yet upon opening it, nothing could be found. It said:
"If there is an emergency, open it.

When the Emperor fled to Shu, he was so flustered that he completely forgot this matter; however, upon arriving in Chengdu, he suddenly remembered opening it, and found that among the medicinal ingredients was *angui* (Chinese angelica).
The Emperor said, "This medicine was produced here; you, Master, know that when I encounter difficulties, I shall return to Shu.
He then saw Wanli Bridge and said:
“The words of Yi Xing were proven divine.
The Emperor ordered an official to burn incense and offer prayers on his behalf; this was to express gratitude.

At the beginning of the reign of Emperor Zhaozong, Yi was enfeoffed as the Prince of Ji, later becoming the Crown Prince, the Prince of De. When the Tang dynasty was extinguished by the Liang, it fulfilled Yi Xing’s prediction that “the state would ultimately end with ‘Ji’ (auspiciousness).”

In the ninth month of the fifteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, his illness became critical at Huayan Temple. He intended to enter the palace in a sedan chair to take his leave, but he stopped after a brief interval.

That night, Emperor Xuanzong dreamed that he was looking down upon a Chan residence, where he saw a rope bed, paper screens, and an open fan. At dawn, when he inquired and verified the details, they were exactly as he had seen them in his dream.

Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued for the eminent virtuous ones of the capital to establish a Great Dharma Assembly (Dàodǎochǎng) to pray for his recovery; his critical illness slightly improved.
Such was the extent of his imperial favor.

On the eighth day of the tenth month, while accompanying the Emperor on a tour to Xīnfēng, he was free from all ailments and had uttered not a single word; suddenly, having bathed in scented water and changed his robes, he sat cross-legged in right mindfulness and, with a serene expression, manifested his passing.
One account states that after delivering his farewell message to the Emperor, he personally traveled eastward to Mount Song to pay his respects to his original teacher, Jì.
At that time, Pí Kuān, the Governor of Hénán, was visiting Jì;
Jì said, "I have some minor matters to attend to and cannot yet grant the Great Governor the leisure for a detailed conversation."
"Furthermore, please pause and rest.
Kuān then dismissed his attendants and stayed in an adjacent room to observe what Hè was doing.
He saw that Hè had entered the pure main hall, where he sat in silence burning incense, as if waiting for someone.
After a short while, there was a knocking at the door, and voices called out repeatedly:
"The Master of Heaven, Monk Yixing, has arrived. His monastic title was "Master of Heaven" (Tiānshī), which was first seen here; he spoke of being the teacher of the Son of Heaven.
He entered with a hurried and anxious air, prostrated at the feet of Master Ji, and whispered into his ear; his demeanor was even more reverent.
Master Ji merely nodded and said, "There is nothing that cannot be done."
Having finished speaking, he bowed again; he repeated this speech three times, and the Silent One replied only, "So it is, so it is; there is nothing that cannot be.
When the discourse was concluded, he descended the steps and entered the southern chamber, closing the door behind him.
Ji then slowly summoned his attendant and said, "Sound the bell quickly; Xing has already entered parinirvāṇa.
His attendants ran to see him; he sat with eyes closed, his hands covering his nostrils, and his breath had already ceased.
The fourfold assembly of disciples wailed and lamented so fervently that it shook the mountains and valleys; consequently, he rested his spirit at Wangji Temple.

From the time of his passing until his burial, a period of twenty-one days elapsed, yet his fingernails and toenails did not change, while his beard and hair grew longer; his complexion remained serene and joyful, which caused the multitude to be struck with wonder and amazement.
Upon reading the memorial, the Emperor was filled with sorrow and lamented, saying:
"The Chan Master has abandoned me; my grief and longing for him are profound!
The state provided the funeral expenses, and by imperial decree he was buried at Tongren Yuan, posthumously titled Chan Master Dahui.
The Imperially Composed Epitaph was a source of honor for all the śramaṇas under heaven.
Biography of Zhi Sheng of Xichongfu Monastery in Jingzhao, Tang Dynasty. Regarding the biography of the Śramaṇa Zhi Sheng: it is not known where he was from.
His mastery of doctrinal principles was profound and far-reaching, and he studied both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles; yet, regarding the *Vinaya*, he was particularly adept in its essential tenets.

Furthermore, his literary nature was increasingly refined, and he possessed broad knowledge of both ancient and modern matters. He often expressed dissatisfaction with the records of Nie Daozhen and Dao’an, as well as those of Mingquan and Vinaya Master Xuán, who each authored catalogs of the *Tripiṭaka* recording the dates and persons involved in the translation and transmission of the scriptures—namely, the Jin-lù, Wei-lù, Han-lù, and others. Consequently, in the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, the cyclical year being Gengwu, he compiled the twenty-fascicle *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*, which is the most precise and essential of all.
Why is this so? Various masters have been greatly confused by the texts regarding cases where the same original was translated differently, or where old titles were given new names;

thus, the authentic and the spurious became intermingled. Sometimes a single scripture appeared as two versions, or a single chapter was translated separately; yet when each such instance was carefully evaluated, few could be found at fault.
In his catalog, he excluded and did not retain the scripture recited by Jiang Mi’s daughter; this may truly be called a refined discernment.
By blocking the source of demonic and spurious teachings, he exercised such independent judgment.
As for the later *Zhenyuan lu* by Yuanzhao, its literary style and doctrinal tenets differ from [the earlier works] by several hundred li.
During the Linde era, Daoxuan produced the ten-fascicle *Neidian lu*, while Jingmai produced the four-fascicle *Tuji*; each of them appended one fascicle of their own.
In the catalogues of the scriptures and teachings, none surpasses that of Daosheng.
Biography of Yuanhui of Dazhong Yunsi Temple, Tang Dynasty; Biography of Yuanhui of Dazhong Yunsi Temple, Tang Dynasty. By Huaiyuan and Chongyi. Shi Yuanhui: it is not known where he was from.

Throughout the region between Guanzhong and Fufeng, his reputation was preeminent; he had investigated the nature and characteristics (dharmalakṣaṇa) with meticulous precision and was adept at mastering all the various schools.
From his youth, he applied himself most intensely to the single gateway of the *Abhidharmakośa*.

At that time, Jia Zeng, the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, had turned his heart toward the teachings of Śākyamuni and took great delight in this literature; he frequently commissioned Huì to discuss the characteristics of this school.

However, the difficult points were the "delusions of view within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," and the complex sections were those concerning "acquisition and non-acquisition."
I have therefore requested Master Huī to provide a brief outline; for Master Guāng’s commentary on the meaning is so extensive that it is extremely difficult to navigate.

Furthermore, Vinaya Master Huǎiyuǎn of Shèngshàn Monastery shared my aspiration, and thus he abridged the ancient commentaries—reiterating and explaining the verses, while providing citations and detailed annotations for the treatises. This version is remarkably direct and concise, making it easy for students to understand.
Later, Chong Yi composed the ten-fascicle *Jinhua Chao* to provide an exposition of it.

Following the two masters Daoguang and Sengbao, Master Hui appeared in the interim; his commentary was widely circulated throughout the two He regions, the two Capitals, the region south of the Yangtze, and the states of Yan, Qi, Chu, and Shu.
Biography of Xuan-yi of Huayan Monastery in Jingzhao, Tang Dynasty. The monk Xuan-yi, surnamed Dou, was the maternal grandfather of Emperor Xuanzong Shenwu.

With flourishing branches and noble leaves, none can rival my family; many of my elder brothers, friends, nephews, and younger siblings have ascended to the ranks of the court, some maintaining themselves with elegant refinement, while others vie with one another for the glory of official rank.

Yi possessed a wind-like spirit and a brilliant, refined demeanor; he was carefree and transcended the mundane. Having realized the traces of form and emptiness, he reached the realm of true stillness; he treated fine delicacies as mere chaff and viewed high office as something trivial.

Soon thereafter, he joined the ranks of the monastic community; his studies surpassed those of his peers, and he delved into the secret treasury of the scriptures, opening and reading them until he mastered their principles.
One day, he sighed deeply and said:

"The days since the Sage departed have grown distant, and the written records have become disordered and inverted. Sometimes only the character for 'five' remains where 'summer' should be, and at other times errors like 'ox' and 'fish' have proliferated. Furthermore, scribes have committed thefts of characters, and proofreaders have lost entire phrases."

If the fascicles of a *khandhaka* are lost, it is like the disordered sequence of the *Liji*, where daily errors and corruptions lead to confusion from which there is no recovery; if even one of these occurs, the fundamental social order (*yilun*) will suffer ruin!

Consequently, he consulted the catalogs compiled by scholars of antiquity and the present day, and examined various scriptures; the texts spread across his desk in profusion, and the accumulated scrolls overflowed the halls.
Where characters were erroneous, he clarified their meanings and organized them; where categories were disordered, he investigated their principles and systematized them.
As the years passed through cycles of stars and frost, his achievements became manifest.
Were it not for one whose resolve was as firm as metal and stone, and whose will as steadfast as ice and bitter herbs, how could such a feat have been attained?

Having synthesized and organized its categories, it is indeed systematic and free from confusion; it comprises thirty fascicles in total and is titled *Shijiao guangpin lizhang* (The Comprehensive Chronological Chapters on the Extensive Categories of Śāsanā).

I have examined the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras, as well as the collections of the worthies and sages from both the eastern and western lands, totaling one thousand and eighty works. These were transcribed on paper produced in the two districts of Puzhou and Gongcheng; their quantities were verified, and their sequence and chapters were fixed, so that future generations may not suffer from uncertainty.
The chapters therein are quite systematic and essential; "to prepare for unforeseen events was an excellent practice of antiquity.
Yu Lingchen of Leiling wrote a preface for it.
After his escape, nothing further is known of his end.
The Biography of Shi Daoyin of Qinglong Monastery in Chang’an during the Tang Dynasty. Shi Daoyin’s secular surname was Changsun, and he was a native of Gaoling in Chang’an.
His father was Rong, a Palace Attendant Censor.
His mother, née Ma, dreamed that five-colored clouds covered her head, and she subsequently conceived.
Her mother often listened to lectures on Mahāyāna sutras, never ceasing by day or night; this was intended as the practice of Tai Ren’s prenatal education.
Upon reaching full term, a rare fragrance wafted abroad; from childhood, he possessed a refined spirit and an elegant disposition, and his learning was thorough and clear.

He entered the jinshi examination and was ranked among the successful candidates on his first attempt. His fame resounded throughout the capital; his literary talent was pure and extraordinary, bringing glory to his kin and neighbors.
Later, a monk from India knocked at the door to beg for alms; after the meal was finished, he requested to stay overnight.
When Yan received him and engaged in conversation, his words were all grounded in principle, and the Indian monk praised him in admiration.
Having mastered the nuances of rhetoric, as he was about to step out the door, he suddenly vanished from sight.
From this point on, Yin no longer had any desire for official selection and requested permission to leave the household life.

One should know that when a fine pearl is but an inch in size, even water a hundred fathoms deep cannot conceal its radiance; how then could father or kin obstruct such a fierce and sharp resolve for entering the Way?
He then took Vinaya Master Shenyan of Jingzhao Fu Temple as his teacher, seeking instruction from him without ceasing.

Upon receiving full ordination, he immediately studied the Vinaya texts and subsequently applied himself to the Sūtras and Śāstras; in this way, he became proficient in both the internal (Buddhist doctrine) and external (secular learning) fields.
At that time, there was the Dharma Master Fuli of Xingshan Temple, who was skilled in composing literature.
He said to Huīyìn, "I rely on your youthful brilliance; you may compose for me a single copy of the *Western Paradise Praise*."
He then folded the paper and took up his brush, composing without a single pause.

In a brief moment, it was complete; its diction was elegant and refined, and the pure Buddha-land, with its majestic surroundings and objects, appeared as if manifest before one’s eyes upon reading the text.
After the Master had finished reading the ritual text, he looked toward his attendants and said, "As for these rare talents and exquisite verses, none of us can fathom them.

Thereafter, he devoted himself to study at his desk, exerting himself with diligence day and night; he became eloquent and difficult to best in debate, excelling in both establishing arguments and refuting others.
Master Lishi (Li Yi) admired his exemplary conduct and once declared in the midst of a vast assembly:
"The flow of Huiyin’s arguments is like a spring gushing forth.
From that time on, he was heard by the Emperor and served at the imperial court.
When the Emperor Xuanzong visited Luoyang, he issued an imperial decree for [Huai]yin to accompany the imperial entourage along with [Dao]liangxiu and [Fǎ]xiū.
The Censor Li Jing also requested that Huaiyin lecture on the *Jingye zhang jing* at Tiangong Temple; the commentary (*shu*) was likewise a work authored by Huaiyin.
At that time, Master Xiying was the preeminent teacher of the realm. Concerned about the future of the Buddha-dharma— wondering who would be capable of defending it and who could propagate it—

he submitted a memorial to summon the most outstanding scholars from throughout the empire, both those versed in internal Buddhist teachings and external secular learning, to assemble at Fuxian Temple in Luoyang to establish a great forum for debate.

Huiyin was highly esteemed by the assembly, who elected him to take the foremost seat. Regarding treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Hetuvidyā*, and the *Śata-dharma-prakāśamukha-śāstra*, he established six major categories of great meaning, leaving his opponents utterly bewildered and humbled.
Xingyi was struck with wonder and said, "The great Dharma requires a pillar and a beam; this person is surely the one for it.
My mind now has a foundation upon which to rely; even death would be sufficient."
When the imperial carriage returned to the west, he was ordered to accompany the entourage.
He then fell slightly ill and submitted a memorial; the Emperor sent a palace messenger with medicine and a prescription, issuing an edict that said:

Biography of Zhizang of Mount Wu in Hang, Jiyang, Yuezhou, Tang Dynasty: The monk Zhizang was surnamed Pi; he was of Indian descent. His grandfather had followed [the Chinese] to the Middle Kingdom, and his family had lived in official service for generations before later settling as immigrants in Luling.

When he was young, he entered a monastery and, observing the profusion of ritual images and offerings, realized that the common practice of seeking the truth through outward forms was superficial. Consequently, he applied his mind to each of the three trainings, yet it was in the *Vinaya Piṭaka* that he excelled with the greatest precision and acumen.

In the third year of the Dali era, he traveled to Yuzhang and registered his name at Tiangong Temple; as the assembly earnestly requested that he preside over the ordination platform, he was then revered for his formidable prowess and styled the "Tiger of the Vinaya."
Whenever he ascended the Dharma seat to proclaim the Vinaya, the hall was filled to capacity and the seats were full; those who listened and received his teaching never grew weary.
He elucidated names and principles and analyzed subtle words with such clarity that even the most complex chains of reasoning could be unraveled.
During the Zhenyuan era, he met Chan Master Daji and was deeply enlightened regarding the essentials of the mind.
Later, while traveling to Kuaiji, he built a small chamber atop Mount Wu in Hangzhou to practice seated meditation.
He then composed the *Miaoyi* (Profound Meaning) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
His expositions were continuous and profound, and students flocked to him.
In the second month of the fourteenth year of the Yuanhe era, he passed away without illness at the age of seventy-nine.
Regarding the collection of the cremated relics by Yuanjing, he erected a stupa on the northern peak of the monastery grounds.

As for "Hang-usan," it is a corruption of the local dialect; it should be pronounced "Hang-sai. This refers to the ancient practice of using bamboo rafts (*hang*) to cross the Zhejiang River, where the rafts were stored upon reaching the shore; hence it is called "sai."

Biography of Shenqing of Huiyi Monastery in Zizhou, Tang Dynasty. Regarding Shenqing of Huiyi Monastery in Zizhou, Tang Dynasty: his religious name was Shenqing, his courtesy name was Lingyu, his secular surname was Zhang, and he was a native of Changming in Mianzhou.
He was born at the foot of Mount Dà'ān; three brothers followed one after another into the monastic life, all of whom possessed great renown, though Qīngjū was the middle one.
At the time of his conception, his mother suddenly developed a distaste for pungent and fatty foods.
Even as a child, although he was engaged in play, whenever he encountered a Buddhist image he would prostrate at its feet, and whenever he met a monk he would bow his head to the ground.
At the age of thirteen, he began his studies under Dharma Master Bianzhi of Kaiyuan Temple in Mianzhou.

At that time, the imperial decrees were strict and severe; those wishing to leave the household life were required to limit their recitation of scriptures to one thousand sheets before being permitted to have their heads shaved.
Huiqing then recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Vimalakīrti*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, and *Śūraṅgama* sūtras, as if he were restoring them for the second time.

At that time, the former Chancellor Qiao Lin was serving as the Governor of Mian Commandery; struck by the boy’s precocious brilliance, he personally descended from his station to offer him the rites of invitation to renounce the world, which occurred during the Dali era.
By the age of seventeen, he had mastered the fundamentals of his studies and immediately began lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

In summer he practiced the *śīla* (precepts), relying on the study of new commentaries.
Having thoroughly mastered the great principles, he then proceeded to the capital.
Later, due to his excellent literary talent and extensive learning, he entered the inner court to serve as an attendant.

In his later years, he was afflicted by profound sorrow; he returned to Huìyì Monastery, where he devoted himself to lecturing, guiding disciples, and composing works, leaving him scarcely a moment of leisure.
He passed away at Fēngdǐng on the grounds of his home monastery during the Yuánhé era and was interred at the Bái mén Ārāma, located outside the northern gate of Qī City.
In his youth, Qingping was fond of composing writings and delighted in compiling anthologies; he possessed immense talent and had plumbed the depths of learning.

This is because it comprehensively explains the essential nature and functional activities of all phenomena categorized within the five positions (pañca-vastu) as conceived by the Hīnayāna—namely, matter (rūpa), mind (citta), mental factors (caitta), non-associated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra), and unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta); thus, it is called the "Source of Dharmas" (dharmāmbudhi).

The *Shixin lun* (Treatise on the Mind of Consciousness), the *Chengguan lun* (Treatise on Clarifying Contemplation), several fascicles of the *Jusheli yichao* (Excerpts on the Meaning of the Abhidharmakośa), and ten fascicles of the *Beishan canxuan yulu* (Recorded Sayings on Penetrating the Mysteries at Beishan) comprise over one hundred fascicles in total, all of which have been circulated throughout the ages.

Among these, the *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) encompasses the three teachings most extensively; it is that which has been most cherished by the great scholars, renowned monks, and eminent gentlemen of both the North and South.

As the temple is situated north of Qicheng City at the foot of Mount Changping, it is called "Beishan" (Northern Mountain). Because it systematically records the profound principles of the three teachings, it is truly titled the *Cane Xuan* (Investigating the Profundities).

Fubo’s eloquence was transcendent, his phrasing and reasoning swift and resonant; in responding to the Emperor’s intentions, he always accorded with the True Vehicle (*samyak-yāna*). Even in moments of haste, he never failed to make the propagation of the Dharma his primary concern.
From this, the Son of Heaven came to know all the more that the Buddha was a Great Sage and that his teachings contained matters of great inconceivability.

At that time, the court was in the midst of pacifying the realm; having bound Wu and subdued Shu, and having drained Cai and swept away Yun, the Son of Heaven sat with folded hands, free from affairs.

The Emperor personally led the assembly of monastics to welcome the sacred relics from Mount Ling and established a Dharma assembly within the Secret Palace; for the sake of the people, he requested blessings and personally attended to the incense and lamps.

Subsequently, punishments were not cruel and weapons were not used wantonly; the young children raised no cries of sorrow, and the blue seas were free of turbulent waves. This was clearly the manifest efficacy of employing the True Doctrine in support of the great administration.
Now, in wishing to manifest the Great and Inconceivable Way and to assist a sovereign of great transformative action, must there not necessarily be a profound resonance and a mysterious covenant?
For ten years, he presided over the ritual protocols of the inner palace and recorded the affairs of the clergy in the Left Ward, serving as a model for the pure assembly.

He lectured on the *Nirvāṇa* and *Vijñaptimātratā* sūtras and śāstras; acting as a master who took responsibility for the transmission of the teachings, he guided both monastics and laypeople through no fewer than one hundred and sixty lecture series.

He operated the three mysteries within yoga and attained non-arising through siddhi; he maintained the recitations of the various families more than one hundred thousand times daily, regarding the Pure Land as the place to rest his shoulders and venerating the golden sutras as a way to repay the grace of the Dharma.
Throughout his life, he offered and bestowed tens of millions of items, all of which were used to honor and adorn temple buildings with the most exquisite carvings and paintings;
yet in his own quarters, he slept on a single bed, finding self-realization through silent meditation.

Noble ministers and eminent clans all looked up to him with admiration; the wealthy, the martial, and the merchants alike gazed toward him in reverence. They presented gold and jewels to express their sincerity and prostrated themselves before his dignified countenance; those who came daily numbered in the thousands, beyond the power of words to fully record.

He regarded all sentient beings as if they were the Buddha; he cultivated goodness by remaining free from the four marks of selfhood. His mind was as level as the earth, smooth and without hills or mounds, treating kings, dukes, commoners, and servants alike with sincerity.

On the first day of the sixth month in the first year of the Kaicheng era, he passed away reclining on his right side facing west; though it was the height of summer, his venerable countenance appeared as if alive, and throughout the night, a wondrous fragrance remained richly pervasive.

In accordance with his final instructions, he was cremated; more than three hundred śarīras were obtained. While the fire raged, a divine light shone as bright as the moon; once the embers were spent, the sacred bones remained as perfect as round pearls.
He was posthumously granted the title of "Great Attainment" (Dàdá), and his stupa was named "Mysterious Secrecy" (Xuánbì).
His secular age was sixty-seven, and his years as a monk could be calculated accordingly.

Among his disciples, both monks and nuns, there were approximately one thousand; some lectured on profound doctrines, while others governed great monasteries. Devoting themselves to meditation and upholding the Vinaya, they became teachers of men, and fifty of their followers all attained realization.

Biography of Chan Master Zongmi of Guifeng Caotang Monastery, Tang Dynasty: Chan Master Zongmi, surnamed He, was a native of Xichong in Guozhou. His secular name was Yuan. He was a disciple of Chan Master Zhao. Chan Master Zongmi’s lineage is as follows: he was born into the He clan and was a native of Xichong in Guozhou.

His family had long been prosperous and powerful; from his youth, he was well-versed in Confucian classics and sought to serve the world to sustain the lives of living beings, carrying his exceptional talent as an official on the civil service examinations.

In the second year of the Yuanhe era, he happened to pay a visit to Chan Master Yuan of Suizhou. Before Master Yuan had even spoken with him, [Dongshan] inwardly felt great joy and admiration for him, and thus followed him to shave his head, don the dyed robes, and receive instruction.
In this year, he received full ordination from Vinaya Master Zheng.
He subsequently traveled to Jingnan to visit Zhang, who said to him:
"You are a transmitter of the teachings; you ought to propagate them in the imperial capital."
He further met Master Zhao of Luoyang, who said, "This is a person of the Bodhisattva stage; who could recognize him?
Finally, he met Master Guan of Huayan on the Capital Plain, who said:
"Vairocana’s Flower Treasury—can anyone follow me on its journey except you alone?

Initially, while in Shu, he received the sutra during a vegetarian feast and obtained twelve chapters of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* (here referred to as the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra*). Having deeply penetrated its meaning and intent, he vowed to propagate this scripture.
While staying at Hanshang, he received the textual meanings of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* from a sick monk; though he had never previously studied them, he began lecturing on them immediately.

Consequently, he composed commentaries and sub-commentaries (*śāstra-ṭīkā*) on the *Awakening of Faith*, the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Nirvāṇa*, the *Vajracchedikā*, the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Ullambana-puṣpa Sūtra*, the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*, and the *Pratideśanā-praṇidhāna Sūtra*, as well as the *Categorization of Doctrinal Meanings*, the *Ritual Liturgies*, the *Methods of Cultivation and Realization*, the *Illustrated Biographies*, and the *Compendium of Essentials*.

Furthermore, he compiled the various Chan teachings of the different schools into the *Chan-zang* (Chan Canon), providing a general preface for it, along with his "Responses," "Letters and Verses," and "Discussions."

Furthermore, there are five fascicles of the *Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya* (*Sifen lü shu*) and two fascicles of the *General Discourse on the Sub-commentary* (*Chao xuantan*), totaling approximately two hundred fascicles and six illustrated panels.

All of these take the single mind as their foundation to unify all phenomena, manifesting the true essence to harmonize principle and phenomenon; they transcend all dualistic existence and operate in solitary autonomy by merging the distinction between things and the self.
Mitsu was repeatedly summoned into the inner palace to inquire about the essentials of the Dharma.
On the anniversary of the Emperor’s birthday in the second year of the Taika era, he was granted a purple robe and the title of Daide (Virtuous One).

On the sixth day of the first month in the first year of the Huichang era, he passed away while seated in the Xingfu Pagoda Courtyard; his appearance remained as dignified as on ordinary days, and his countenance appeared even more serene.
On the seventh day, he was placed in his coffin; by this, one may know the power of his self-realization.

On the twenty-second day of that month, the clergy and laity enshrined his whole body at Mount Guifeng; on the thirteenth day of the second month, he was cremated, yielding several dozen śarīra relics, which were brilliant, lustrous, and large.

Later, his disciples wept as they searched for the remains among the ashes; they certainly found them and returned with them, enshrining them all within a stone chamber. From this, one can perceive the depth of his compassion for those who lacked the karmic affinity to meet him in person.
His secular age was sixty-two, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇerī-vaṣa) was thirty-four.
His final injunctions were:
