At first, as the fragrance of the secret path was already pervasive and its fame most brilliant, the inner assembly’s longing for its scent was like that, and the response of the court nobles was likewise so.

Since the Changqing and Yuanhe eras, eunuchs who had established merit and held office became as numerous as fireflies; suspicion prevailed between the inner and outer courts, leaving the sovereign in peril.

At that time, the Prime Minister Li Xun treated the eunuchs with excessive intimacy. When the false "Ganlu Incident" broke out during the Kaicheng era, the eunuchs led five hundred imperial guards out from the palace gates, slaughtering everyone they encountered.
At that time, Wang Ya, Jia Su, and Shu Yuanyu were in the Zhongshu (Secretariat) having a meal when they heard the rebellion had broken out; they fled toward Zhongnan Mountain to seek refuge with Mi.
Only Li Xun wished to shave his hair and hide there, but his attendants dissuaded him, and he changed his course to head for Fengxiang.

At that time, Qiu Shilang became aware of this and dispatched men to capture Mi and bring him into the left army. There, he confronted Mi face-to-face and enumerated his crime of failing to report [the rebellion], intending to execute him.

Mi remained composed and said, "I have known Master Xun for many years and was also aware of his rebellion; however, according to the teachings of my original master, one must rescue those who suffer without regard for one's own life or limb. To die under such circumstances is truly what I am willing to accept."
The Commandant Yu Hengzhi praised him for this and memorialized the throne to pardon his crimes.
When the court officials heard of this, they wrung their hands and shed tears.
Some said:
"If the Master of Esoteric Teachings [practices] Chan, Vinaya, or the Sūtras and Śāstras?
To this he replied:
"The Esoteric Way is like a state surrounded by four enemies; no one can give it a name. It may be called 'the Great Bodhisattva of Perfectly Round Wisdom who Self-Realizes and Benefits Others.'"
Therefore, Pei Xiu’s commentary states:
"Critics claim that the Master did not adhere to the practice of Chan, but instead extensively lectured on the sutras and śāstras;
he traveled to famous cities and great capitals, making the promotion of Buddhist establishments his primary concern."
Is he then merely a servant of much learning? Could it be that he has not yet forgotten fame and profit? Alas!
How can those who debate this know the direction in which the Great Way tends?

Now, the single mind is the synthesis of all dharmas; when divided, it becomes precept, concentration, and wisdom; when expanded, it becomes the six perfections; and when dispersed, it becomes the myriad practices.
The myriad practices have never been anything other than the one mind, and the one mind has never contravened the myriad practices.
Zen is but one of the six perfections; how could it alone encompass all dharmas?
Furthermore, the Tathāgata entrusted the Dharma-eye to Kāśyapa, but not his dharma-practice.
Thus, that which is realized through one's own mind is the Dharma, while that which arises in accordance with vows is practice; these two are not necessarily always identical.
Thus, the single mind is that from which all phenomena arise, yet it does not belong to those phenomena.
One who attains it gains mastery over all dharmas; one who perceives it encounters no obstruction regarding the teachings.

The fundamental Dharma cannot be explained through conventional laws, and the fundamental teaching cannot be transmitted through formal doctrines; how, then, can it be sought by following mere traces?
From Kāśyapa to Puṇyayaśas, there were ten patriarchs in all, all of whom were arhats, and those they saved were likewise arhats.

Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, and Vasubandhu first opened the way for the Mahāyāna; they composed treatises to explain the sūtras, crushed the heretics, and served as the foremost leaders of the bodhisattvas.

Yet Venerable Śāṇakavāsin alone took the power of the precepts as his spiritual majesty; Venerable Māluṅkyaputta alone took ascetic practice as the path to the goal. As for the other patriarchs, some extensively propagated the Dharma teachings, some devoted themselves exclusively to meditative stillness, some departed like a cicada shedding its shell, some were extinguished by cremation, some ended their lives by clinging to a tree, and some suffered harm to repay their karmic debts. This shows that while the Dharma is necessarily the same, the practices are not necessarily identical.

Furthermore, those who merely follow tracks do not practice wholesome conduct; those who strictly adhere to the compass and the墨 (mo) line lack skillful means. Without swiftness, one cannot be considered a great ox; without transcending, one cannot be considered a Great Being (Mahāsattva).

Therefore, the Way of the Teacher takes knowledge and vision as its wondrous gate, tranquility and purity as its true flavor, compassion and patience as its armor and shield, and wisdom and severance as its sword and spear.
He breaks down the high fortifications of internal demons and penetrates the solid ranks of external thieves; he pacifies the heterodox and the mixed, and releases those bound in captivity.
When encountering a destitute son, he rebukes him to lead him back to his home; when seeing a poor woman, he scolds her to cause her to illuminate her chamber.
That the impoverished son does not return home and the destitute woman does not become wealthy—this is a source of shame for our Master.
That the Three Vehicles do not flourish and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (*Sifen lü*) is not upheld—this is a source of shame for our Master.
Loyalty and filial piety cannot be cultivated simultaneously; that one is unable to bear the burden is a source of shame for my teacher.
To avoid fame while remaining mired in appearances, or to hide oneself and increase arrogance, is a source of shame for my teacher.

Therefore, he was restless in seeking to rescue others and urgent in opening the way for their guidance; he did not exalt himself on account of a single practice, nor did he tower above others because of a single virtue.
When someone sought his refuge, he would go to them without waiting for a request;
when someone sought to increase their understanding, he would reveal it to them without waiting for their frustration.
Though he was but a youth, he did not disdain receiving visitors; though he was haughty and stubborn, he never grew weary of being exhorted and encouraged.
Such was his manner of expounding the teachings and saving sentient beings, thereby assisting the transformation of the state.

Therefore, one who follows the method of honoring the teacher shall give when others are greedy, restrain when they are violent, comply when they are rigid, be submissive when they are perverse, enlighten when they are ignorant, and rouse them when they are indolent; he shall satisfy those who seek self-glorification, transform those who are obstinate, make public those who pursue private interests, and instill righteousness in those who are immersed in their passions.

Among the common people, there are those who abandon their homes and families to enter the Dharma together, dividing into monasteries to dwell; those who transform their livelihoods, sever the consumption of meat, uphold the precepts, and establish households as lay practitioners (*upāsaka*); those who emerge from seclusion to cultivate governance and take the salvation of the suffering as their path; and those who withdraw to serve their parents, making offerings abundant as their practice.

As for the rest who came with eager intent and departed with joyful hearts, arriving with sleeves fluttering and returning with full bellies, they were so numerous in every place that they could not be recorded.
Is he the Bodhisattva entrusted by the True Tathāgata? Is he the good friend who does not wait to be requested by sentient beings?
Is he one of the four reliances?
Or is he one of those on the ten stages?
"I do not know the extent of its realm, nor the breadth, depth, or shallowness of its courtyards and halls.
How could those who debate know where the Great Way leads?
Such was the understanding and insight of the great man, and his comprehension of the mind was like this.
"Those who have intimately known the mind are many, yet none were as profound as Prime Minister Shengping; this was surely because those of like nature seek one another.

Emperor Xuanzong further expounded the True Vehicle and brought all virtues into orderly arrangement; he posthumously conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Dinghui, and his stupa was named Qinglian (Blue Lotus).
He maintained his mourning attire and observed the rites of a disciple; the fourfold assembly numbered several thousand people.
The postscript states:
"The commentaries and compositions of the Minister of State of Hedong truly represent the ultimate mastery of the literary brush."
However, it is not that this lady alone has reached the pinnacle of her art; how could others possibly fail to reach their own pinnacle?
Observe that shadow and echo follow one another, never having begun as anything different.
A shadow awaits the arising of a form; an echo follows the coming of a sound.
There was Master Zongmi; to him there was Prime Minister Pei.
Were it not for the Prime Minister, how could he have known Master Mi? Their succession is like a circle, never reaching an end; such is the way of these two masters.
Thus we know that by truthfully contemplating both the Dharma and the royal law, Master Mi’s conduct was most perfect;
and since he should have manifested in the body of a high official, the words of Prime Minister Pei may serve as a means to measure him.
Now, regarding those in the Chan school who, failing to understand this, criticize the Esoteric tradition for being unsuitable for lecturing on the various scriptural teachings, I reply to them:
"Does not Bodhidharma himself say, 'My Dharma accords with the definitive (nītārtha) teachings'?"

"Furthermore, those with little learning and scant wisdom are incapable of this themselves; since they are moreover associated with afflictions and delusions, can one not feel indignation toward them?
If someone were to mock me for being unsuitable to associate with high officials, yet repeatedly visiting kings and rulers, I would reply:
"The transmission of the Dharma rests upon kings and ministers; if I do not associate with kings and ministers, how could I possibly propagate and manifest the religious teachings?"
The Buddha said, "Is it not the case that the ministers of a King of the Wheel of Power (Cakravartin) are like this?
In the sentiments of people today, those who associate closely with the king's ministers are disparaged.
Yet they fail to realize that if the hearts of those close to the king's ministers are merely seeking to align themselves with profit and fame, they deserve the reproach of 'refusing the sovereign.'"
"Or perhaps he merely associates with religion out of personal devotion—is this not truly great?
How can one avoid minor suspicion? Those who harbor such suspicion are themselves envious.
If one understands this meaning, there is neither 'can' nor 'cannot. Alas!"
Biography of Shi Cheng’en of Ximing Monastery in the Capital of Tang. Shi Cheng’en was a man of unknown origins.
From the time he first resolved to pursue learning, Daosheng knew that he must seek out teachers everywhere; whenever he entered a school, he invariably exhausted the paths of meaning.
He often instructed his disciples, saying:
"A love of learning approaches wisdom; the diligent practice of virtue approaches benevolence."
"Once benevolence and wisdom have gradually been perfected, these distinct names share the same reality; advancing toward the stage of a Bodhisattva is like a ball rolling down a slope.
He delighted in encouraging others to study and never forgot to provide instruction and guidance.
Furthermore, at the end of the Tiānbǎo era, when Guāngzhōng was in turmoil, he sought refuge in Gūzāng.

While staying there as a traveler, he lamented that although the territory bordering the Qiang and Lu tribes was extremely close by, its inhabitants placed the highest value on the study of the Sūtras and Śāstras.

He transformed those within his community through his benevolence and encouraged them toward their ultimate success; they were deeply imbued with the refined culture of China and all ascended to the treasury of righteousness.

From that time on, he extensively revised the *Commentary on the Treatise of a Hundred Dharmas* (*Śata-dharma-śāstra-vyākhyā*) along with its sub-commentary (*piṇḍārtha*), which circulated throughout the Western lands.

This commentary takes Ci’en as its ancestral authority and the Lu-fu [commentary] as its primary tenet; for the most part they are identical, with few instances of divergence, and were subsequently transmitted and disseminated by his disciples.

In the third month of the fourth year of the Xiántōng era, the monk Fǎxìn of Xīliáng meticulously studied this path and submitted to the Prefectural Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) Zhāng Yìcháo a memorial regarding the works of Huì'ēn, requesting that the Great Virtuous Ones (Dàdé) of the Two Streets and Three Schools be commissioned to examine and finalize them, as they were truly fit for practical application.
By imperial decree, the monk was granted a purple robe and appointed as the Great Virtuous One (*Mahāsattva*) of that province.
Biography of Zhi Xuan of Mount Danjing in Pengzhou, Tang China: The monk Zhi Xuan, whose courtesy name was Houjue, was surnamed Chen and was a native of Hongya in Meizhou.
His great-great-grandfather was Tu Nan, who served as the Magistrate of Shehong County in Zizhou.
His grandfather was Xian, and his father was Miao; none of them achieved success in the imperial examinations.

His mother, Lady Wei, dreamed that the moon entered her bosom, and from this he was born. Although he could not yet speak while being nursed, whenever he saw the form of a Buddha or a monk, his face would invariably brighten with joy.
At the age of five, his grandfather ordered him to compose a poem on flowers; before he had taken even a few steps, he completed it, saying:
"Flowers bloom in full red upon the trees, Then fall until ten thousand branches are empty. Only one remains, Which tomorrow will surely follow the wind."

The Patriarch sighed in lamentation and said with dissatisfaction, "I raised this grandson, hoping he would attain the highest rank in the civil service examinations and wipe away the shame of two generations.
Now I see the child's resolve; it is not that I have failed to provide for his future, but he will surely follow the Empty Gate (Buddhism), which contradicts my original hopes."
At the age of seven, he indeed encountered Dharma Master Fatai lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Ningyi Temple.
As the temple was adjacent to his residence, Xuan went to the assembly where the lecture was being held; upon hearing the Dharma discourse but once, it was as if he were beholding his past causes.
That evening, he dreamed that the Buddha’s hand was stroking his crown.
Upon waking, he informed his grandfather and requested to become a *śrāmaṇera*. His relatives observed that he was determined and could not be dissuaded, so they granted him permission.
At the age of eleven, he underwent tonsure.

He then followed his teacher to Sian Temple in Tangxing County, where he was instructed in forty-two fascicles of Mahāyāna sūtras, including Master Huiyuan’s *Yishu* and Master Biankong’s *Yuanzhi*, totaling one million two hundred and fifty thousand words.
They all encompassed the profound mysteries.
At the age of thirteen, he pointed out errors among the monastic community, manifesting the air of a mature master.
At that time, Prime Minister Du Gong Yuan-ying was stationed as governor in Western Shu; having heard of Xuan’s reputation, he ordered him to ascend the hall.
He gave a lecture at the Puxian Pavilion of Daci Temple.

The assembly, both monastic and lay, numbered about ten thousand people daily; they listened with rapt attention and hearts fully inclined toward him, their expressions of awe and admiration never ceasing.
From this time on, the people of Shu no longer called him by his name, but referred to him simply as "Chan Pusa.
According to tradition:
"In a previous life, Xuan’s name was Zhixuan; while lecturing on the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* at Sanxue Mountain in Hanzhou, he moved heaven and earth such that the ground transformed into lapis lazuli."

Xuán received full ordination from Vinaya Master Bianzhen at Jingzhong Temple; having barely begun his studies of the *Vinaya*, he subsequently mastered the *Abhidharmakośa*, thereby continuing the lineage of instruction established by Vinaya Master Shangu of Chang’an.
Again, following his original teacher, he descended through the Three Gorges, passed through Jingzhou and Xiangyang, and arrived at Ziseng Temple in the Divine Capital (Chang’an).

This temple was a central gathering place for those of the three vehicles from all quarters; there, the profound sutras and śāstras were expounded, and both monastics and laypeople looked up to him in admiration, so that the shoes left outside his door increased day by day.
When Emperor Wenzong heard of this, he summoned him for an audience and consultation, which greatly pleased the Emperor.
Later, he studied the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Weishi lun) under Master Xian of Anguo Monastery.
Furthermore, he studied non-Buddhist classics and the works of the hundred schools of thought, mastering them all without exception.

Daoyuan often lamented that his native accent was unfit for lecturing; consequently, while reciting the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī* at Mount Xiang’er, he dreamed of a divine monk who cut off his tongue and replaced it with another.
The next day, he suddenly began to speak in the Qin dialect.

There was a man named Yang Maoxiao, a great scholar who had come to Xuan to investigate the inner scriptures (Buddhist texts), desiring to emulate Xie Lingyun by annotating the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. He frequently held up his scrolls to pose questions, which Xuan analyzed and resolved for him on the spot.
He sent a letter saying:
"In these times, who other than you could be considered a dragon or an elephant among men within the realm?
Subsequently, Yang Rushi of the Ministry of Justice, Gao Yuanyu of the Left Vice-Chancellor, and Yang Rushi of Chang’an all came to his door, intending to form a Lotus Society.
Once, while Sengxuan was sitting in deep meditation, he saw Meng Maoxiao wearing purple robes and a green cap; after performing three prostrations, Maoxiao ascended into the air and departed.
Xuan sent someone to investigate and inquire about him. That evening, Maoxiao instructed his son, saying:
"I have long wished to shave my head and don the black robes, carrying my water jar and sandals to serve Master Xuan; what hinders me is this official headgear."
"When I am laid to rest, I shall be enshrouded in a purple *kāṣāya* and wear a crown of blue lotuses.
At this point, his prior vision was finally realized.

When Emperor Wuzong ascended the throne, he initially held Buddhism in high esteem; later, however, influenced by the counsel of those who were deluded, he sought to worship Mount Penglai and constructed a lofty terrace in hopes of attaining immortality through transcendence.
Although the censors submitted memorials and the ministers spoke repeatedly, the Emperor’s mind was ultimately not turned.

On the occasion of the Dayang Festival, when monks and nuns gathered at the Linqide Palace, the Emperor alone summoned Xuan to debate with the Daoist representatives, asking whether the state of transcendence could or could not be attained through cultivation.
The Emperor folded his hands and referred to the teaching of Laozi, “Governing a great state is like cooking small fish,” engaging in a dialogue with the Daoist priest.

Xuancheng expounded upon the principles of imperial governance and the foundation of moral transformation, stating that the arts of the immortals are merely the lofty pursuits of solitary commoners in the mountains and forests; furthermore, these require past karmic causes and are not suitable for a sovereign.
The river of his eloquence flowed downward and the ocean of his辩 (discernment) poured out crosswise for several thousand words.
Those who heard him were struck with trembling in their thighs; he greatly offended the Emperor’s will, and among those around him, there was none whose countenance did not lose its color.

Chou Shiliang, the Left Commandant of the Imperial Guard, and Yang Qinji, the Inner Secretary of the Privy Council, valued his talent and eloquence; fearing that he might soon receive an order of dismissal, they secretly urged him to compose a "Poem of Blessing for the Emperor."
Xuánlì composed five chapters, the final of which states:
"Birth in heaven fundamentally depends on the karma for birth in heaven; one does not necessarily attain immortality simply by seeking it.
The back of the crane is precarious and the back of the dragon is slippery; O Sovereign, please remain here for a thousand years."
Upon reading the poem, the Emperor gained a slight understanding.
Although the Emperor did not accept his loyal admonitions, he praised his insight and eloquence.

Xuán immediately returned to his old mountain in Bāmén; there, while maintaining the use of a cap and comb as was customary, he became even more distinguished in his observance of monastic discipline.
Just as he was entering the regions of Lake Dongting and the Xiang River in a small boat, Yang Geshi Han, who was then serving as the Intendant of Guilin, invited him to stay at Kaiyuan Temple.

Coinciding with the ascension of Emperor Xuanzong to the throne, Yang Gong took charge of the Left Imperial Guard from his position in the inner palace. Having achieved great merit in establishing the imperial succession, he requested the revival of the Indian (Tianzhu) teachings and submitted a memorial seeking to trace the traces of the mysterious sounds [of the Buddha].
Xuán again hung up his tattered robes and returned to Bāoyìng Monastery in the capital.
Coinciding with the lectures and praises held for the Longevity Festival, he was granted a purple *kāṣāya* and appointed as the Head Seat (*śīzuò*) of the Three Teachings.
The Emperor constructed Fagan Temple at his former princely residence and issued an imperial decree for Xuanchang to reside in the Yuxu Pavilion there.

On the anniversary of his birth in the third year of the Dazhong era, he summoned the Censor-in-Chief Li Yisun and the Palace Attendant Yang Han-gong; monks and Daoists were arrayed like a mountain peak to debate the principles of their doctrines, which greatly pleased the Emperor’s heart.

He memorialized the throne that the foundations of all the abandoned temples throughout the realm should each be rebuilt by imperial decree; thus, Buddhist monasteries flourished once more, and Xuan played a significant role in this.
An imperial edict ordered an artist to paint his portrait within the palace precincts; such was the degree of esteem and honor bestowed upon him.
He was a close friend of the Chancellor, Lord Pei Xiu, and together they vigorously promoted the restoration of the Buddhist teachings.
In the eighth year, he submitted a memorial requesting to return to his native mountains; there he extensively practiced acts of benefit and salvation, and many were those who received his grace.

In the spring of the second year of the Guangming era, Emperor Xizong fled the capital for Western Shu. Later, he dispatched Guo Zuntao bearing an imperial letter, ordering [the Master] to travel by palanquin to the imperial encampment.
Upon meeting, the Emperor engaged him in conversation, and [the Master’s] explanations greatly relieved the Emperor's mind.
Zuo Junrong, the Palace Attendant Tian Lingzi, and various high-ranking officials consulted on the matter with great earnestness.
The Emperor, wishing to honor his excellence, ordered the various scholars to compose a posthumous title for the Master Xuan; however, none of them satisfied His Majesty’s wishes.
He then took up his brush and wrote:
"I take 'opening, showing, awakening, and entering' to be the essential principle of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
'Awakening' means enlightenment and clarity; it is to awaken to and reach the Great Way, and to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."
It is further said:

"To awaken is but a single kṣaṇa; not to awaken is for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Therefore, for one who awakens, the meaning of attaining Buddhahood through the true vehicle (bhūta-yāna) is clearly realized."
"I now bestow upon you the title 'National Preceptor Wuda.
Although this is but a forced designation, it serves to express my imperial intent.
Xuan declined the honor repeatedly but was unsuccessful; he then requested permission to return to his old residence at Jiulong.
On the twenty-first day of the first month, while lying in bed, he saw all the sacred sites and famous traces from his past travels appearing before him.
On the seventh day of the second month, he heard a voice in the air saying:
"You shall certainly be reborn in the Pure Land."
He then questioned him, saying,
"Who spoke those words?
Xingkong again replied:

"Buddha! In the seventh month, he heard the sound of a struggle outside his door; after hesitating for a moment, a bodhisattva descended into the courtyard, and the matter was extinguished. As the apparition gradually withdrew until only a dark form remained, it earnestly praised and exhorted him:
"Do not let this suffering weigh upon you."
Having finished speaking, he vanished.

Furthermore, one night, a pearl flowed out from beneath his left foot, causing him myriad forms of agony; when he gazed closely at the pearl, the two characters "Chao Chuo" were clearly visible within it.

He then realized that Xuan was indeed Yuan Ang; it was because Ang had once petitioned for the execution of Xiao Cao during the Rebellion of the Seven Kingdoms to appease the kings of Wu and Chu that he was merely feigning confusion before Ying.

He summoned his disciple Cideng to deliver a posthumous memorial by word of mouth, entrusting him with the instruction to abandon his corpse, feeding half to the bellies of fish and half to the maws of birds and beasts.
"For a long time," he said, "I have maintained such an expectation for the Western Pure Land."
Having finished his final entrustment, he passed away reclining on his right side facing west at the age of seventy-three, with fifty-four years of monastic seniority (*saṃghavarṣa*).

During the Xuánzhōng era of the Táng dynasty, Xuán had traveled to Zézhōu and inquired after the Dharma Master Xiǎoyuǎn; they were born in the same year and likewise passed away on the same day and month.
Xuán strictly maintained the prohibitions and precepts, possessing few desires; he did not eat fruits or vegetables after midday, wore only coarse cloth and hemp, and slept upon straw.
He practiced the Way during the six periods of the day, sleeping for only one watch at night, while spending the remainder in seated meditation.
He regarded all sentient beings with equality, making no distinction between noble and base, young and old, and treating them all as one.
Among those with whom he had long cultivated deep bonds of affection was the State Councilor Pei Xiu.
Initially, when Pei was stationed at Jingmen, [Daoyuan] traveled to Mount Wutai; on his way, he passed through Zhugong, yet he accepted no gifts or offerings whatsoever.
Knowing his frugality and restraint, Pei secretly dispatched people along the route to provide for him, much like how Su Qin sent his attendants to secretly supply Zhang Yi with provisions.

Once, while passing through Zhenfu County in Luogu Valley, he stayed at the home of the Ongshi family, which overlooked a deep pool. In the pool lived a large fish resembling a dragon, possessing four feet and sharp, pointed teeth; the family had been feeding it daily for four generations.
Whenever he intended to cast his net or hook, clouds and mist would suddenly darken the sky.
Xuan struck the boat and stroked the fish’s head; it would stare with wide eyes and leap about, whereupon Xuan would grant it the Three Refuges.
Before long, she appeared in a dream to Lady Ong and said:
"I thank you for your protection and mindfulness over successive generations; having now received my refuge, I have been reborn in heaven and bid you a final farewell."
Next, he bestowed the precepts upon the deity of the Niliang Mountain Temple at Jiangyao, Li Bing, and the dragon-god of Beiguo Longmen in Yichang; he then abolished their offerings of animal blood.

There was one named Li Shangyin, a paragon of letters for his generation whose peerless talent had no rival in his time. He had long served as an official in the retinue of Lord Liu of Hedong at Zizhong and had long admired the Way of Xuan. Later, he attended upon Xuan with the etiquette due to a disciple; at that time, Xuan resided at Xingshan Monastery while Li lived in Yongchong Ward.
Yishan suffered from severe eye disease and, fearing he would become blind, gazed toward the Zen monastery from afar, offering silent prayers for deliverance.
On the following morning, Xuanming sent him three stanzas of the "Verses on the Celestial Eye" (*Tiānyǎn jì*). Upon finishing his reading, his illness was cured.
When Yi-shan was bedridden with illness, he said to the monk-recorder Sengche:
"My aspiration is to shave my head and dye my robes to become a disciple of the Mysterious One (Buddhism). I am sending this letter and verse as a parting farewell at the end of my life."

It is said that Xuansheng constantly composed the two-fascicle *Commentary on the Collated Explanation of the Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, and commissioned Sengche to compose the *Fajian* (Mirror of the Dharma) to illuminate its imagery, much like the *Ten Wings* [of the Book of Changes].
The *Commentary on the Great Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* in two fascicles was written by Sengche;
his *Fadeng* classifies and points to its chapters.
The *Commentary on the Śrīmālā-sūtra* in four fascicles was written by Sengche; his *Fayuan* interweaves them like warp and woof, much like a book of supplementary commentaries.
Furthermore, there are commentaries on both the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

In addition, between the regions of Qin and Shu, he composed various Buddhist writings, including essays, external treatises, admonitions, discourses, inscriptions, and songs and poems, totaling more than twenty volumes; together with six volumes of liturgical texts for repentance, they comprise approximately three hundred thousand words in all.
Later, the stupa was moved to Fuseng Temple on Mount Chalung.

In the second year of the Zhonghe era, his disciple Jingguang Dashi Sengche, the Supervisor of Monks of the Left Ward, composed this biography. His dharma-grandson Juehui, the Supervisor of Monks of the Right Ward; Juehui’s disciple Chongzunsun Guangye, the Supervisor of Monks and State Preceptor Yousheng of Wushu; and their descendants—like the continuous succession of melons and gourds—are all renowned public figures.
At Fengxiang Prefecture, Xuanzhen was transcribing [the scripture], while Li Yishan stood in attendance holding a fly-whisk.
The postscript says:
"Why did Master Xuan claim that Yuan Ang and Zhixhuan were his two successive incarnations?"
Tong said:

"Human life spans a hundred years; from the Han to the Tang dynasties, how many times could the profound mysteries have appeared and vanished amidst mountains of bones and seas of tears? This can be known by simple calculation."

"Thus, Master Xuán possessed many talents and practiced the Way; such a person has been rarely heard of since antiquity. That his Dharma heirs have flourished and multiplied is something no one else can rival.
Biography of the Monk Chè of Dà'ān Guó Temple in Jīngzhào, Táng: The monk Śramaṇa Chè of Dà'ān Guó Temple in Jīngzhào, Táng, was a man of unknown origins.

Minli possessed a naturally gifted and transcendent character that far surpassed his peers; from his youth, he was sharp-witted and keenly intelligent, and he admired National Teacher Wudao as if he were an incarnation of him, just as Yan Hui resembled Zhongni.
Subsequently, as he frequently attended the master’s presence, he came to perceive its profound subtleties; he served and followed him with unwavering devotion, never growing weary for even a moment.
Gazing upon the gateway of his teachings, he was perhaps close to attaining a mastery of them.
Whenever Wuda encountered a new meaning or a distinct chapter, he would invariably entrust it to Chechang to elaborate upon it.

He authored the *Fajian* (Mirror of the Dharma) in four fascicles as a commentary on the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, the *Fadeng* (Lamp of the Dharma) in two fascicles as a commentary on the *Mahā-amitāyur-dhyāna-sūtra*, and the *Fayuan* (Garden of the Dharma) in ten fascicles as a commentary on the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*.
Observing that Wudao’s work serves as a commentary, it is like the *Zhuo* of Zuo Qiuming;
and that Che’s work describes the *Sanfa chao*, is it not like the collective exegesis of Du Yu and Fu Yan?

The Biography of Zhìyuǎn of Huáyán Monastery on Mount Wútaishān in the Tang Dynasty. Zhìyuǎn, whose secular surname was Sòng, was a native of Rǔnán. His family had resided there for generations. He was a monk of the Yuan period who attained mastery in the interpretation of the scriptures. His lay name was Sòng, and his family was based in Rǔnán.

His father passed away early, leaving him an orphan to attend to his widowed mother; he was so preoccupied with the ritual of serving her countenance that he found no leisure for either morning or evening.
His mother constantly recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and had mastered its five fascicles.
Possessing far-reaching insight and brilliant acumen, he stood out with solitary distinction.

At the age of twenty-eight, he took leave of his parents to follow a teacher, taking refuge in the tradition of the Heze school; there he realized its profound principles and managed monastic affairs for six consecutive autumns.
In all matters of sustenance, he never allowed for confusion or intermingling.

From that time until he took his leave of his teacher to seek further rites, another eight years passed; although he had extensively mastered both schools, his mind remained still bound and obstructed.
I have heard that the single branch of Tiantai encompasses the wondrous principle, wherein concentration and wisdom are fused as one, and understanding surpasses practice.
The ten vehicles of objective realms and contemplation originated from this single school.
He cultivated the three virtues of nature and practice, expounding them with refreshing clarity.

He then charged his peers to pursue their studies at Mount Wufeng, where they dwelt in seclusion among the forests and springs, following in the footsteps of those who came before. There, they mastered the principles of the six mundane realms and the four stages of holiness, fully comprehending the gates of opening, showing, awakening, and entering; thus they encompassed the ten realms and the thousand suchnesses, integrating both essence and appearance.
Obstructing and illuminating simultaneously, negation and affirmation occur at once.
The primary and the secondary are perfectly interfused; ordinary beings and sages are equal. The mind’s eye is opened wide, such that both object and self vanish together.
In just forty years, he propagated [the Dharma] with unparalleled mastery.

His far-reaching legacy was refined through the Way; his resolve was arduous yet his spirit remained harmonious. He never removed his robes while lying down, and would not accept special invitations for meals.
At that time, the harvest was poor and firewood for cooking was frequently lacking; he would often scoop up water to rinse his mouth, intending to pass his days in this manner.

His body suffered from sores and scabs, yet he did not apply ointments or rub them with his hands. He strictly observed the precepts and cultivated his conduct, remaining vigilant over both mind and speech.
He constantly refined his body and mind through the four kinds of samādhi.
As for calligraphy and epigraphy, he was quite proficient in the beauty of cursive scripts and seal characters.

Whenever there were monastics or laymen of talent and learning who marveled at his eloquence, they would sometimes search out obscure and hidden points, seeking to blunt his sharpness or find flaws in his argument to determine victory or defeat.

In his outward demeanor he sat upon his mat with an air of haughty aloofness, yet in his private conduct he was humble and reverent; he came to exalt my mountain, and his departure followed the four *siddhāntas*.

By the fourth year of the Huichang era, at the age of seventy-seven and forty-eight years since his ordination, he suddenly ceased eating for several days, yet he continued to preach the Dharma without weariness.
On the seventeenth day of the second month, he admonished his disciples, saying:
"Throughout my life, I have cultivated spiritual progress without deceiving my own mind or speech; now I have obtained two kinds of karmic retribution."

Its one and many are mutually identical. Biography of Xuan Yue of the Wooden Pagoda Hall at Longxing Temple in Jangzhou, Tang Dynasty. The monk Xuan Yue, surnamed Zhang, was a native of Zhengping.

His character and temperament were firm and pure; from childhood, he harbored a heart that sought transcendence from the mundane world. Having fulfilled his long-cherished aspiration, he entered the Longxing Monastery in the prefecture, where he recited a thousand words daily and never again received further instruction.

After shaving his hair, he fulfilled the monastic discipline; he examined his own mind and followed the models of the precepts, diligently maintaining both the prohibitions and the prescribed practices without ever violating them.
From this point on, his reputation and integrity rose sharply, and his contemporaries looked up to him with admiration.
Within a few years, he had mastered both the Vinaya and the Abhidharma; he sought out teachers everywhere to investigate the profound mysteries of the scriptures.

He arrived at Chongsheng Temple in Chang’an and, being selected for his preeminent virtue in the precepts, was appointed to preside over the ordination platform. He lectured on the Vinaya and the *Abhidharmakośa* some forty times; his nature was profound and tranquil, and his scholarly investigations were thorough and flawless.
He composed the *Jùshè lùn jīnhuā chāo* (A Golden Flower Commentary on the Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya) in twenty fascicles, which was highly esteemed by his contemporaries.
When he ascended the lecture platform for his two expositions, there were over three hundred people present, all of whom sat facing north to receive his instruction.
He had transmitted his teachings to about one hundred disciples who traveled between the Fen and Qin regions to study under him until he grew old.
He lived out his final years in a small room at this monastery; his secular age was seventy-six, and his dharma age was fifty-six.
The disciples of the Dharma, both monastics and laypeople, collected several hundred grains of śarīra from the cremation pit and constructed a brick stūpa to the west of the prefectural city.
Biography of Yanhui of Mingfu Temple in Huazhou during the Liang Dynasty: Śramaṇa Yanhui, surnamed Sun, was a native of Yangwu County in present-day Dongjing.

Among them were men of great learning and talent; thus, they were divided into two groups of ten "Evils" (the Ten Evils).
These "Ten Evils" may be likened to the titles of the Eight Hundred Masters.

As for the Ten Superior Evils, they were thoroughly proficient in both *dharmatā* (nature) and *dharma-lakṣaṇa* (characteristics); they loftily erected the banner of the Dharma, and in the three means of proof—thesis, reason, and example—as well as in establishing and refuting arguments, they were unimpeded.

At the lower level, those who commit the ten evils study both internal and external doctrines, composing poetry in the style of the *Feng* and *Sao*, engaging in debates and discussions on the scriptures, possessing clear voices and eloquent tongues, chanting Buddhist hymns (*fanbai*), and serving as ritual masters (*biaobai*) to guide and proclaim the teachings.

Biography of Shi Guiyu of the Present-day Tongjing Xiangguosi Temple during the Liang Dynasty: Shi Guiyu, surnamed Mei, was a native of Shouchun.
His father, Yuanxu, recognizing his son’s sharp intelligence, instructed him in the *Shijing* and the *Shujing*; in his recitation, study, and memorization, he surpassed all others by far.

Before even a year had passed, his understanding of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Araṇyavyākaraṇa-sūtra* (Renwang jing) was thorough.

By the time he reached the age of twenty, he had fully observed the precepts; he maintained the three modes of conduct with dignity and never neglected the four modes of deportment. He studied and listened to new chapters of scripture, and soon mastered their exposition and teaching.
Later, hearing that the *sūtras* and *śāstras* were flourishing in the capital of Luoyang and the Three Commanderies (Sanfu), he joined companions to seek out teachers.

After barely ten years, he had mastered the natures (*dharmasvabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), refined his understanding of both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and achieved profound mastery—as if his vast knowledge were as empty as space—in the specialized categories of the *Abhidharmakośa*, the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*), and the treatises on the *Abhidharmakośa*, *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha*.

He then traveled south to Yan to attend upon Master Huī, where he once again reviewed his studies; refining them like vermilion made even more brilliant by cinnabar, he nevertheless lamented that Yi-zhang’s commentaries were not yet entirely perfect.

He subsequently went to Xiangguo Temple in the present-day Eastern Capital, where he compiled the *Xin-chao* (New Excerpts); through his diligent lecturing and instruction, his disciples attained deep understanding.
At that time, the Later Ruler of the Zhu Liang dynasty and [Zhang] Yu had studied together since their youth in the school, sharing a close and intimate friendship over many years.

The ceremonial processions of both streets escorted him to the monastery; furthermore, by imperial decree, the Imperial Portrait Hall at the East Pagoda was established as a center for long-term lectures.

Biography of Yin, Magistrate of Changshui in Luoyang during the Later Tang Dynasty. Shi Yin, whose secular surname was Yang, was a native of Wenxiang in Shanfu.
From his youth, he practiced virtuous conduct and sought to leave the secular world; he received the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* from a master in his native district.
Once he had reached the appropriate age according to the Dharma, he received the precepts and studied both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings concurrently.
Regarding the dharma-gates of names and numbers, he refined them into a state of pure essence.
His mastery of the *Amitābha Sūtra* and the *Mādhyamaka* reached their very marrow and fat; his fame and brilliance resounded far and wide, such that none could rival him.

While traveling through Changshui in Luonan, he encountered lay devotees who had turned their hearts toward the Dharma and were constructing a monastery; he stayed there to lecture and expound the teachings.
Over the course of thirty years, he propagated the Dharma by teaching one treatise and one sutra each time, totaling more than fifty recitations of each respectively.
Every day he recited the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha* as his regular practice.

He maintained his conduct with such integrity that his mind was free from all blemish; those who looked up to him from near and far took him as their spiritual guide, like those who, longing for plums, were finally able to drink the juice.

From his youth, he knew how to transcend the mundane world; as he grew older, he vowed to pursue his studies. His nature was one of such rigorous asceticism that others could not endure his hardships.
