Because he felt that the commentaries on the *Chongfu Sūtra* by masters such as Fengxian and Zhizheng were neither sufficiently detailed nor concise—much like adding water to water, which ultimately fails to provide relief—he subsequently composed the fourteen-fascicle *Yiping Chao*.
In the same year, the binding of the scrolls was finally completed.

Furthermore, while lecturing on the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, there were the prefaces by Minister Jia Zeng and the monk Yuanhui; he annotated both with his own sub-commentaries (*chaojie*). These writings are rich and abundant, and I have previously had the opportunity to "dip my fingers" into them to gain some understanding.

Regarding the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, his exegesis was analytical rather than abbreviated; he further composed many critical commentaries on the *Xiaoyuan* [of Sengzhao] to spare it from being stained by the "blue flies" of detractors.
As for other works, such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*, and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, each has its own distinct treatises on their meaning.

His temperament was moreover narrow and impetuous, differing from that of others; among his disciples, not a single one met with his approval. He once personally attended to the hearth while preparing food for a vegetarian feast; when the fire died out as he kindled the wood, and it flared up again as he blew on it, his anger flared, and he doused it with water. He did not eat all day, yet continued to lecture.
In his later years, his eyesight became so dim that when he ascended the lion throne, he would wear a bamboo hat while lecturing, merely to prevent his pupils from blinking.
Some criticized him for showing disrespect to the assembly, but he did not take such remarks to heart.

When the Prince of Wusu, the Qian clan, was touring the provinces and arrived at Yue, [the Master] went out to pay his respects. The Prince had long admired his reputation and accorded him exceptional courtesy, commending him repeatedly for his labors.

During the Qianhua era, he received full ordination at Kaiyuan Temple in Kuaiji; the Emperor then appointed him to oversee the selection and training of candidates for the ordination platform. He was the first among those in the regions of Wu and Kuaiji to hold this office.
The King presented him at court and recommended that he be granted the purple robe.
Emperor Zhuangzong issued the decree, and an official carried it to Yingqiu.
At that time, while studying the *Preface to the Commentary on the Sūtra of the Upper Birth*, he reached the passage: "Like a great bell, it receives all in emptiness."
Taking up the handle of the fly-whisk, he said:
"I have received this name without any basis in reality; from now on, I shall receive it in vain. Let the youth take note of this.
When he reported these words to the King, the King said:
"This monk surely has no portion of an imperial edict; how can he be said to receive it in vain?

In the year of Tongguang Yiyou (925 CE), he reached the end of his life. When the sea vessel carrying the official decree arrived, calculating the date of his passing, it was found that it coincided exactly with the day he was at Qingshe; thus, it truly accorded with Wukuo’s words.
There exist several volumes of his *Collected Works* (*Wenji*) and over thirty volumes of his *Exegesis on the Meaning of Chapters* (*Shuyizhang*), which have been circulated through the ages.

Regarding Shi Kezhou of Longxing Temple in Hangzhou during the Later Tang: his secular surname was Fu, and he was a native of Jinling. He was the successor to [the tradition of] Kezhou of Longxing Temple in Hangzhou during the Later Tang.
He left the household life at Jianyuan Temple in his home region.
His nature was upright and virtuous, and he pursued learning with diligent inquiry.
A friend encouraged him, saying:
"If it is not the proper ground, trees will not grow there.
Now, the *Yuzhang jing* calls this place a river, while the *Lun* calls it a sea; why do you not go there to request instruction?"

Zhou was deeply moved by his guidance; carrying his bag, he reached that place and encountered the great assembly of Dharma Master Yunbiao. There he studied the *Fahua* and the Great Commentary of Ci'en to the utmost, and as the days passed and the months rolled on, he mastered its profound meanings.
At the beginning of Emperor Zhaozong’s reign, while returning from Jiangxi to the regions of Tai and Yue, [the Emperor] commanded him to initiate [his teaching].

In the second year of the Qiandehua era of the Liang dynasty, he received an invitation to preach at Longxing Temple in Hangzhou, where the assembly of both monastics and laypeople constantly numbered five hundred.

The Wukusong King Qian of Liangzhe ordered that sutras be preached for the netherworld at night within the Tianbao Hall; ghosts and spirits would manifest their forms to serve as guards, often seen by people.
Once, during a sacrifice at the shrine of the Copper Official, the shamaness remained for a long time without descending. Later, she spoke through the medium, saying:
"I have followed the Great Deity to the Tianbao Hall in the West Gate to listen to the Dharma, and am only now returning."

Upon hearing this, King Wusuku treated him with great solemnity, bestowing upon him a golden *ruyi* scepter and a bowl from the Zhou dynasty, a set of purple robes, and the honorary title "Zhengzhi Tongming" (Pure Resolve and Penetrating Clarity).
In the first year of the Tiānchéng era, he passed away at his own quarters in Guānyīnyuàn.

Initially, during the fourth year of Qiánníng of the Zhōu dynasty, while lecturing on commentaries at Sōngshān Temple in Tàizhōu, he found that the annotated notes (cǎo) were missing; he subsequently condensed the essential points of the commentary into five fascicles, titled the *Píngjīng Cǎo* (Annotated Commentary with Critical Evaluations), along with five scrolls of *Yīnxùn* (Phonetic Readings and Explanations), and a single scroll of a commentary on Xuánlǜshī’s *Fǎhuá Xù Cǎo* (Commentary on the Preface to the Lotus Sutra). These works circulated throughout the regions of Zhèjiāng.
His disciples followed one after another in an unbroken succession.

Later, during the Later Tang dynasty, Zhenhui of the present-day Phagmo Drupa (Xiangguosi) Monastery in the Eastern Capital transmitted [the lineage]. Regarding the monk Zhenhui: his secular surname was Bao, and he was a native of Changshu in Wu Commandery.
At the age of thirteen, he entered the monastic order at Ryūkeiji Temple in his native province.
By nature he was grave and serene, yet he vied with himself over even the smallest fraction of time.
Not long after his first year had passed, he had completely recited the *Lotus Sutra*; thus, as a constant practice, he recited two sections daily.
At the age of nineteen, he sought out renowned masters in Yangzhou to receive the full precepts (*upasampadā*).

Thereafter, traveling west to the Yi and Luo regions and north to the borders of Jin, wherever there were lecture assemblies, he attended to seek further benefit. He scrutinized the sutras and treatises and exhausted the depths of both the nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena; among his contemporaries, few could rival his diligent pursuit of these studies.
As for those who were not his friends or weak allies, he abandoned and turned his back on them as if they were strangers.

In the first year of the Tianyou era of the Tang dynasty, he took up residence at the Xiangguo Temple in present-day Dongjing and lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* some ten times; yet, as people did not yet accord him with respect, one can see that even the sale of rare treasures depends upon the right timing.
When the Liang dynasty established its capital in this metropolis, people from all quarters flocked there.
In the second year of the Zhenming era, [the Master] encountered the Governor of Songzhou, Duke Kong Yanghui, and came to recognize his virtuous conduct through his exemplary character.

He then set forth the rites for teachers and friends, relinquished his stipend and wealth to establish a hall for the long-term lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* within the West Pagoda Courtyard; from that time on, the assembly flourished and gathered in great numbers.
Hui read the texts of the Great Canon (Tripitaka) by his side and practiced the Way during the two periods of the day, persevering without weariness.
As for the worldly arts and the teachings of the hundred schools, he excluded them from his discourse; he admonished his disciples, saying:
"The doctrines of heterodox paths muddle and disorder the true mind. Since they are indeterminate and do not perfume the consciousness, why must one practice such worldly customs?"
"I only wish to let out the lion's roar; I shall not make the cry of a wild jackal.
Thus, he devoted himself solely to incense, candles, and sweeping, taking the inner courtyard as his place of rest.

On the tenth day of the second month in the second year of the Qingtai era of the Later Tang dynasty, he summoned more than fifty disciples. He personally prepared scented water for a ritual bath and ordered them to chant the *Sūtra on the Rebirth Above* while performing prostrations before the Buddha. He completely relinquished his clothing and assets as an untimely offering, providing half of the alms for the monks to be used for a communal meal.
On the eleventh day, he faced the sky with palms joined and said, "I trouble the multitude of sages to descend from the void to welcome me.

His full assembly of one hundred disciples all heard the sound of celestial music on that day; he passed away shortly thereafter at the age of seventy-three, having spent fifty-four years in the monastic order.

He spent more than thirty years lecturing at the monastery, delivering a total of thirty-seven lecture series on the sutras, perusing the Tripitaka twice, and cultivating the practices for rebirth in Maitreya’s Inner Court.

On the eighteenth day of the second month of that year, he was buried at the site of the East Temple Estate in Junqiao; more than a thousand monastics and lay disciples gathered to escort him, accompanied by banners, canopies, and solemn ritual observances.
The Biography of Shi Kezhi of Changshou Monastery in Luojing during the Later Tang Dynasty. Shi Kezhi, whose secular surname was Ma, was a native of Gaoqiu on Mount Dafang in Fanyang.
At the mere age of twelve, he possessed a profound aspiration to transcend the mundane world and relied upon Vinaya Master Fazei of Minzhong Temple.
At fifteen, he received the *śrāmaṇera* vows; taking leave of his teacher, he went to Zhending to study the sūtras and śāstras.

At that time, Dharma Master Renchu was lecturing on the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* at the Great Huayan Monastery. [He] mastered the text after reading it only three times; his grasp of its profound meanings reached the divine, and the assembly recognized him as exceptionally talented and outstanding.
There was an elderly and venerable master named Vimalakīrti, a remarkable figure of the Śākya gate, who asked the Master of Chu:
"Among your disciples, who is the most outstanding and preeminent?"
He replied, "There is a śrāmaṇera from Youzhou who reviews the old to know the new and exerts himself with untiring diligence.

Thereupon, he requested an audience and proceeded to question him on the *vītarāga* (Sengjun) syllogism; as the śrāmaṇera responded to each difficulty with flexibility, his arguments could not be refuted.
Vimalākṣa said, "Those who come later are to be feared; as the sūtras state, 'though small, they must not be deceived.
He then exerted his influence to request that [the lectures] be halted in Hengyang, and among both the monastics and the laity, there was none who did not admire him.

Upon reaching the age of nineteen, he traveled to Mount Wutai to seek the precepts; during the preparatory rites prior to their conferral, he was moved by a spiritual radiance from Mañjuśrī that illuminated his body.
Thereafter, he returned home to visit his parents and his teacher, where he expounded the teachings at the monastery.
At twenty-three, he went to Bingzhou to study the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Śataśāstra*.
During the Jingfu era, he arrived at Hechi, where he was invited to lecture on "Hetuvidyā" (Logic).
Later, at Dazhuangyan Temple in Chang’an, he instructed his disciples for several years.
In the third year of the Qianning era, he presented poems to the throne; Emperor Zhaozong bestowed upon him a purple *kāṣāya* and had him compose verses within the inner palace.

Liu Ren-gong, the Governor of this province, who held the northern gate and commanded both the barbarians and the Han, heard of Daozhi’s reputation and sent a letter summoning him to return to his native land.
Daozhi’s father and teacher had passed away one after the other, yet his mother still lived at home; Daozhi therefore went out begging with an alms bowl to provide her with fine delicacies.
After he had been reciting the *Qinglong shu* for three years, Wenche suddenly saw a giant python appear in his room; it raised its head and looked at him, as if having something to report.
At that time, there was a fellow monk of the same monastery named Ju Xiao, a learned Buddhist scholar, who remarked:
"A snake does not blink its eyes; yet this creature is moving.
Could it not be a dragon?"
He halted the burning incense and prayed, saying:
"I, this poor monk, am reciting the *Qinglong Shu* and preparing a vegetarian feast to support my mother. If indeed the dragon deities take pity on me, I hope to encounter a single donor."
After several days had passed, Yan Shijiazi said, "The Minister of War has summoned me to provide offerings.
At that time, Zhuangzong dispatched troops out through Feihu to besiege him; as years went by, Bai Gu’s valor and nobility caused the siege to cease and his anxieties to be dispelled.

Before long, Yan fell, and the Liu father and son were taken captive and brought back to Jinyang; they settled in Zhongshan to escape the chaos. Wang Chuzhi, the Regional Commander, who had long admired their reputation, requested that they be accommodated at Kaiyuan Temple and provided them with a monthly stipend.
He composed one fascicle of the *Dunjian jiaoyi chao* (A Commentary on the Meaning of Sudden and Gradual Teachings), which remains in circulation today.
In the third year of the Tiānchéng era, the year Wŭzǐ, the imperial army came to punish [the rebels], and Dingzhou fell.
Wang Yanxiu, the Commander-in-Chief for the Suppression of Rebellions, received a letter from Prince Ying, Feng Dao, instructing him to seek out [the monk] and stop his journey.

Upon meeting him, Wang escorted him to Luoyang by carriage and horse; there, Prince Qin, Congrong, the Governor of Henan, treated him with great courtesy and memorialized the throne to appoint him as a Grand Master, bestowing upon him the title Wenzhi.

While serving as the abbot of the Jōju-nyo-in (Pure Land Cloister), on the twenty-second day of the first month of the first year of the Enjun era (the Jia-wu year), he was suddenly stricken by a slight illness. He summoned his disciples, saying, "Assist me in my rebirth," and while reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha, he passed away peacefully.
He was seventy-five years of secular age and fifty-six years of monastic seniority (*bhikṣu-kaṭhina*).
On the second day of the intercalary first month, he was cremated, and his remains were collected.
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Qingtai era, a stupa was erected at the southeastern corner of Guanghua Temple on Longmen Mountain.

Zhi Feng was sharp and outstanding in character, with a solitary loftiness in his observance of the precepts. Among the hundred schools of thought, the histories, and the various records, nothing escaped his notice once it passed before his eyes.
Beyond his vast erudition, that for which he was particularly renowned was his mastery of regulated verse and prosodic laws.
There is a poem titled "Presented to the Elder of Fanchuan" that has been passed down by word of mouth.

During his time in Dingzhou, Zhongshan and Taiyuan were in a state of mutual suspicion and hostility, while the feudal lords were engaged in annexation. Wang Ling, wishing to restore friendly relations and bring peace to the people, consequently ordered a monk to preside over a vegetarian feast at Qingyun Temple.
Someone presented a white magpie to the King, who said,
"Let the poet-guest from Yan try to compose a verse on this subject.
He completed it on the spot, with the final couplet reading:
"Who knows who it is that mutters these words? He must surely come before the King to report that all is well.
The King was delighted.
As for the poet Li Dong, his character was eccentric; he admired the style of Jia Langxian and met him at Hechi during the Jingfu era, presenting him with only three poems.

At that time, the Chancellor Lord Sun Wo, Lord Zhao Feng, Lord Ma Yisun, Academician Dou Mengzheng, Vice Minister Fu Meng, and Vice Minister Li Xiang all sang their verses for one another, their voices harmonizing like the resonance of the *xuan* and *chi* flutes.

Recently, after concluding my lectures in Chang’an, I visited the Xiaoyao Garden on Mount Zhongnan; this was the site where Dharma Master Shi of the Yao Qin dynasty translated the scriptures. As the years have passed, it has fallen into ruin and become overgrown with thick grass.
He further said, "I am a disciple of Śākyamuni; how can I endure this and not take action?
He submitted a memorial to Emperor Zhaozong requesting that the temple be renovated. The Emperor granted his permission and reaffirmed the bestowal of the plaque "Cao Tang Si" (Grass-Hall Temple).
Later, he invited the Chan master Jingxiu of Fanchuan to gather disciples and discuss the profound mysteries.
While residing in Luoyang, he lectured extensively on external teachings and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* incessantly, without knowing any limit.

In the past, he resided mostly on Mount Zhongnan and Mount Kongtong; thus, there exists the *Three Mountains Collection* (*Sanshan ji*), consisting of three hundred and fifty poems, which was widely circulated during his time.
The disciples cultivate literature, wisdom, and practice, thereby gaining a faint glimpse of their teacher’s Way.
Biography of Ju Min of Chongfu Monastery in Taiyuan, Han Commandery: Shi Ju Min, surnamed Ren, was a native of Xihe.
His father traveled among the arts and brought splendor to the secluded hills and gardens;

his mother, née Wang, observed the eight precepts and took refuge in the Triple Gem. From the time she conceived him in Min, she further delighted in virtuous causes and sought blessings and merit, thereby giving birth to this worthy son.
Upon his birth, at the tender age of seven, his will and character were earnest and sincere; upon seeing a Buddhist image even for a moment, he gazed up with joyful devotion.
His parents, recognizing that this was due to a karmic affinity from past lives, would sometimes take him into the temple, where he would find such delight that he wished to forget his way home.
Arriving at Jingxin Monastery in his native commandery, he met the Master of Śāstra Xuanyuan; longing for that master's quarters, he wept as he begged for his guidance.
His parents, knowing they could not thwart his aspiration, both gave their consent.

At the age of ten, he had completed the recitation of the two sutras, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*; he would daily maintain ten scrolls of them without interruption, as if holding a vessel of lapis lazuli.
His movements were slow and deliberate, and his self-restraint was like that of a mature elder.

Upon reaching full maturity, he diligently practiced the *śīla* (precepts), thoroughly mastering the categories of what is permitted and what is prohibited, and constantly reflecting upon the mirror of joy and sorrow.

From that time forth, he thoroughly investigated the principles of the Mahāyāna through its sūtras and śāstras; having found his master’s lineage, he devoted himself exclusively to the three studies of the various schools.
Day and night, he attended to his desk by the window, finding no leisure for anything else.

Aside from the *Yanxi yizhang* (Chapter on the Meaning of Study), he cultivated these two causes through six practices; regarding the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*, his efforts became increasingly earnest in his later years.

Furthermore, he transmitted the *Suvarṇasaptati-śāstra*, eliminating all other distractions; each of them lectured on it ten times. He continued to seek out those who could assist and illuminate his understanding, and having extensively read various books, he attained the most refined grasp of its meaning and eloquently expounded its full excellence.

Soon thereafter, having received the imperial decree, he resided at the Tenwangyuan within the city walls; together with his disciples, they provided for all needs without deficiency, maintaining the lineage without interruption.

In the first year of the Qianguo era, the Han Founder—on account of [the Master’s] reputation, which had been admired since the days when he was still a hidden dragon in the territory of Jin—specially bestowed upon him a court robe and conferred the purple cassock, granting him the title of Great Master Yuanzhi.
Subsequently, an imperial edict was issued summoning him to reside in the Lecture Hall of Chongfu Temple, where he was further appointed as the *Sengzheng* (Director of Monks) for the jurisdiction.
After a year, the Dharma was transformed in Jin; he inspected and disciplined the monastic community with the same ease as the wind bending the grass.
On the fifth day of the eleventh month in the second year of the Qianguo era, he passed away without illness.
At that time, the fourfold assembly was filled with grief and the entire city mourned his virtue.
He was ninety-three years of secular age and fifty-four years of monastic seniority (*dharma-varṣa*).

Thereupon, following the funeral rites of *caitya-vibāpa* from the Western Regions, they offered abundant perfumed water; some held banners and flowers, while the assembly of both clergy and laity filled the outskirts of the city. Dark, somber clouds obscured the sun, and before the flames could be extinguished, everyone held precious vases, awaiting the emergence of the form of a grain of rice from the beam, so as to behold together the body refined through cultivation.
At that time, those who obtained śarīra relics received them in varying quantities, more or less, according to their individual karmic conditions.
Having separately acquired these bone remains, he presented a detailed memorial to the throne.
The Han Emperor decreed that they be interred at Tianlong Temple on the Western Hills, with all matters provided by the government and a stone stupa erected.
An imperial edict conferred upon him the posthumous title of Dashi (達識).
Biography of Hengchao of Kaiyuan Temple in Deyou Prefecture, Han: Shi Hengchao, surnamed Feng, was a native of Fanyang.
His grandfather did not hold office; for generations they had cultivated the Way of Confucianism, and the family was worth tens of millions.
From birth, Chao was intelligent and wise; even among a group of children, he did not crave playthings.

At the age of fifteen, he mastered the Six Classics at an early age; he was particularly adept at the *Feng* and *Sao* styles, and his novel diction and tonal rhythms spread through the mouths of the people.
One day, while reading Buddhist scriptures, he suddenly attained a clear and profound awakening.
He then sighed and said:
"Human life, with its wealth and honor, is like a phantom or a bubble; only the True Vehicle can provide transport across the sea of existence.
He subsequently entered the monastic order at Zhubi Temple.

Before three years had passed since his ordination, he was just beginning to deliberate on further advancement in his studies; yet, without tiring day or night, he encountered the death of his teacher, for which he observed the funeral rites of the Śākya tradition, maintaining the ritual protocols without negligence.
The virtues of filial piety and fraternal respect are what the people of Yan prize.

In the third year of the Qiandehua era of the Liang dynasty, he went to Mount Wutai to receive the *mokṣa* (prātimokṣa) precepts; from this point on, he traveled from the near to the far, earnestly inquiring and reflecting upon that which is close at hand.

Soon after, he was summoned to recite the chapter on "Cutting Wood" (*Famu*). Furthermore, being familiar with his adult friends, they entered into an agreement to seek out a master craftsman from afar.
However, as the two rivers lay between them and the war had not yet ceased, the roads remained impassable.
To the south was the Patriarch Liang, and to the north was Emperor Zhuang; they vied for preeminence in a contest of weight, like deer chasing one another at the moment of survival or extinction.

At that time, Hui-chao remained confined within his home province, amidst Wei, Bo, Bing, and Fen, studying seven versions of Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras. He had mastered their doctrines through contemplation, yet he was utterly cut off from the renowned masters of Yong, Luo, Liang, and Song.
Nevertheless, although their travels were not extensive, their mastery was exceptionally profound; their knowledge was as full as a vase, and their reputations spread far and wide.

Thus, Xi Chen of the Bing region and Zhenbian of Zhongshan—these two men reached the pinnacle of both conduct and speech, and had attained significant stages in their realization and cultivation. Upon seeing them, Yao Yi was moved to praise them, saying:
"The horns and head of the Dragon of Meaning are fully complete; they shall wait for their flight and exertion to bring forth the great rain!"
His reputation as a man of great virtue was established in many such ways.
In the second year of the Longde era, he hung his monk’s staff at Wudi, where Chao remarked:
"This is the ancient territory of the entire state of Qi, with the lands of Zou and Lu as its good neighbors."

He then stayed at the Kaiyuan Monastery, establishing a cloister in its northeastern corner; there he lectured on various sutras and treatises for over twenty years, expounding them each more than thirty times.
His integrity was lofty and transcendent, and his conduct was calm and deliberate; whenever monastics or laypeople beheld him, there were none who did not feel awestruck and fearful.

His voice never raised a shout of command, and his speech was free from boastfulness or extravagance; these qualities arose spontaneously, and were not something obtained through the intimidation of power or authority.

Successive provincial governors and incoming and outgoing envoys, having heard his reputation and admired his character, would present their credentials and seek an audience; yet those who were treated with such formal courtesy were merely dismissed by the boy, who would decline them on the grounds of being occupied with his studies, for [the Master] rarely granted audiences.

At first they harbored some reservations, but in the end they were subdued by his lofty virtue; throughout the regions of Qi and Lu, those of outstanding talent did not travel more than a few hundred li to seek him out at his gate to engage in debate and challenge his views.

When the gentlemen first beheld Sengchao’s countenance and listened to his discourses, they found them to be grounded in the *Analects* and the *Records of the Historian*, while being further corroborated by the scriptural traditions.
When some questioned him on "Hetuvidyā" (Logic), Chao replied with a poem whose diction was novel and its principles profound; everyone sighed in admiration and submission.
At that time, the Prefect, Lord Li, highly esteemed his lofty character and wished to present a memorial to recommend him for the gift of purple robes.
When Hui-chao heard of this, he was startled and composed a poem with his brush, saying:
"In vain I wear these coarse brown robes, growing old; Floating in my bowl, the Way remains unfulfilled."
I vow that in death I shall transmit the sutras and śāstras, and in life remain untainted by profit or fame.
I weary of the mountain colors hidden by trees; I cherish the window facing the moonlight.
In time, following Fan Li and Lü Shang, may I sail alone upon the clarity of the Five Lakes.
Li Junfu sent someone to exhort him, wishing to establish a karmic connection with him.
Sengchao remained firm and unshakable, saying:
"If you do so again, then I shall be beyond the Lulong Pass."
Upon hearing this, the Commandant of the Commandery desisted.

Furthermore, Feng Dao, the Chancellor and Prince of Ying, having heard of his reputation and knowing him to be a kinsman from their shared homeland, first sent him a letter expressing his intent to seek his guidance.
Chao said, "I am but a humble recluse who abandoned my parents early to devote myself to the practice of cultivation.
My original aspiration was to become known to Maitreya; I did not expect my name to be casually passed on to the ears of a high minister."
"What benefit would this bring me?

His disciples urged him earnestly; having no choice, he composed a reply in writing, explaining in detail that how could a person who has left the household life allow his mind to dwell upon empty fame or meager profit?
The Prince of Ying treated him with even greater reverence and memorialized Emperor Gaozu of the Later Han, whereupon he was granted the purple robe.

From that time on, however, he became increasingly melancholy; on the third day of the second month in the second year of Qianguo, he fell slightly ill and passed away at his residence within the monastery after several days.
The members of the monastery all heard celestial music resounding through the air; this was clear proof that he had ascended to Tuṣita Heaven.
He was seventy-three years of age and had thirty-five years of monastic seniority.

The disciple Dongzheng, along with more than a hundred students, observed the period of mourning for the heart (xin-sang). The officials and commoners of the city, as well as monks and nuns, gathered by the hundreds to escort him outside the city walls. They performed the full rites of cremation and collected over two hundred śarīra relics, which were distributed among the faithful.
Fifty pearls were bound externally; a pagoda was erected at this monastery to bury them.

King Yeong did not learn of this until later, when he submitted a separate memorial requesting that the master be posthumously granted the title Dejeong (Virtuous Rectitude), whereupon the imperial edict was engraved upon the stone pagoda.
Biography of the Monk Sengzhao of Falin Monastery in Luojing, Han China. The monk Sengzhao, surnamed Zhang, was a native of Fanyang.
At the age of fourteen, he left home to enter the monastic life at Minzhong Temple. He was exceptionally intelligent beyond his peers, and his physical appearance was noble and distinguished.
When he first began receiving the sūtras and gāthās, he could recite several thousand words daily; what his eyes encountered surpassed even his prior mastery.
His discourses on doctrine and insight possessed the air of seasoned maturity.
He was subsequently ordained as a śrāmaṇera;

since receiving full ordination, two intercalary months have passed, during which time he has memorized more than six major divisions of the scriptures, namely the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the *Mahākaruṇā*, the *Vimalakīrti*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and others.

He further applied himself to listening to and investigating the sūtras and śāstras; over the course of more than ten years, his profound mastery of the texts and their underlying meanings surpassed even the most eminent scholars.
During the Tiānyòu era, he traveled southward and arrived at Zhōngshān, where the regional commander Wáng Chùzhí invited him to reside at Fǎhuá Temple.

Successive governors requested him for office; the Grand Tutor, Duke of Longxi, submitted consecutive memorials recommending him, whereby he was granted a purple robe and the title of Great Master Zhen.
Subsequently, Lord Ma of Fufeng invited him to serve as the Chief Monk (Sengzheng), but this was not to his liking.
Upon arriving in Luoyang, he received an imperial decree to expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and resided at the Falin Monastery.

Given that the capital was vast and teeming, with people from all quarters converging like the spokes of a wheel, when Huizhao led the introductory invocation, they all bowed in submission beneath his influence as if by a single gust of wind.
On the twenty-sixth day of the third month in the first year of the Qianguo era, he passed away at the lecture hall at the age of seventy and with fifty years of monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera*).

The fourfold assembly mourned him with deep longing; Minister Li of Yiding, who had previously served as his patron (*upāsaka*) and later protected his residence in Luoyang, provided all the necessary funds for the funeral rites and the observance of mourning.

On the third day of the fourth month, his spirit was transferred to the south of the city, where the *caitya-vibhāga* (cremation) rite was performed and the *śarīra* were collected; they were red and lustrous, numbering several hundred grains.
Lord Ding of Jiyang, serving as an assistant official in charge of the region, erected a stupa on the southern ridge of Guanghua Temple for him.
Throughout his life, he presided over more than seventy lecture assemblies, diligently serving the Dharma.
His disciples were numerous.
The Minister of State, Marquis Sun, held him in the highest esteem; the dozens of poems he composed for him, both before and after, became a celebrated topic of conversation throughout Luoyang.
The Biography of Shi Congyin of Jiang, Transmitted by Congyin of Tiangong Monastery in Luoyang during the Han Dynasty. Shi Congyin, surnamed Liu, was a native of Sanxiang in Luoyang.

In his childhood, he was quick-witted and intelligent, vowing to transcend the mundane world. Once his parents gave their consent, he entered the Zhuge Monastery in his native district, where he relied upon a teacher to recite and study the scriptures, refining his spiritual mind.

Shortly thereafter, having completed his full ordination at Songyang, he went to Changshui to study under masters; within just a few years, he mastered the three treatises: the *Śata-dharma-prakāśamukha-śāstra*, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*.
Master Yin was advanced in years, yet he highly praised Yinyi’s profound mastery of both the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* (Characteristics) and *Dharmatā* (Nature) teachings.
Later, at the invitation of the Bujin Monastery in Luoyang, Yin went there to expound the Dharma.
During the Qingtai era of the Later Tang dynasty, Yin entrusted the lecture seat to him, and he ascended the Dharma throne three times daily for the assembly.
During the long days of summer, he would read through one fascicle of the Tripitaka; his diligent and austere discipline was beyond compare.
In the first month of the second year of the Qianyou era, he manifested illness and passed away at the age of fifty-three in lay years, with thirty-two years of monastic seniority.
Thereupon, following the Indian custom of cremation, his remains were collected; they were perfectly pure and worthy of veneration. His disciples erected a stupa, which remains to this day.
Next, there was the monk Mengjiang of Countyquan Monastery in Changshui County, surnamed Yang, a native of that same district.

His divine spirit was radiant and transcended all mundane states; he subsequently fulfilled his vow to leave the household life and constantly recited the *Benevolent Kings* and *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras.
After receiving full ordination, he lectured on the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*.

During the Qingtai era, he was invited by Guanghua Temple at Longmen to expound the Dharma for the assembly. When the Emperor visited the temple, he questioned him; [the Master’s] wondrous eloquence was celestial and transcendent, delighting the Sovereign’s heart. At that time, the Emperor bestowed upon him a purple *kāṣāya* before the throne, but he resolutely refused to accept it.
He served as an instructor for over twenty years; after his lectures, he would practice the Way and pay homage to the Buddha, taking only one meal per day.
He was compassionate and patient toward all beings, and it was rare to see him show a single expression of anger.
In the third year of the Xiande era of the Zhou dynasty, he passed away from illness. Monastics and laypeople alike mourned him with deep sorrow, and they erected a stupa for him.
Biography of Shi Zongji of Longxing Monastery in Hangzhou during the Han Dynasty. Shi Zongji, whose secular surname was Yu, was a native of Lin’an.
From childhood, he was outstandingly gifted, and his will was firm and upright.

Once, when a thunderbolt struck a tree next door, Huiji fell prostrate along with it; his elder sister, a nun, took him onto her lap and looked at him, saying, "He has not died from the strike; he shall yet live."
Waiting until the night was far from over, he revived and began his work again.
He then urged [the master] to leave the household life and serve as a monk at Xingping Temple.

Later, he went to Quzhou to seek out the Master of Treatises Juxin, where he studied the *Abhidharmakośa* (Treatise on Names and Numbers). His mastery of both the text and its meaning was profound and detailed; moreover, he was difficult to refute or subdue, possessing a sharp and piercing brilliance.
Upon his return to Hangzhou, he was summoned to lecture at Longxing Temple.
At that time, the Monastic Rectifier Yunrang was a formidable and versatile debater, a peerless adversary who shared an intimate friendship with Mr. Lüqiu Fangyuan and Luo Yin of Jiangdong.

Having seen him, he questioned him further; Huiji composed two hundred words in response, which Hui Zheng praised with admiration. Consequently, Hui Zheng invited him to give lectures, and over forty years, he produced seven or eight hundred disciples.
In the year Wushen of the Qianguyu era of the Han dynasty, he passed away from illness in his own quarters.

Previously, while Ji was lecturing, he encountered a strange man who spoke a foreign tongue and inquired about sutras and treatises yet to come from the Western Regions; the entire assembly was struck with amazement.

Ji was blind in both eyes; once, while walking at night, he was guided by a divine light. He frequently perused the writings of ancient masters and remarked, "These can be scrutinized by looking down from above."

He subsequently compiled the *Yǒngxīn Chāo* (Eternal New Commentary) to explain the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, the *Huīlǐ Chāo* (Radiant Principle Commentary) to interpret the *Sūtra on the Rebirth Above*, the *Mile Chéngfó Jīng Shùchāo* (Commentary on the Sūtra of Maitreya’s Attainment of Buddhahood), and the *Bǔyóu Chāoquè* (Supplementing the Omissions of the Yòu Commentary), along with several dozen scrolls of various separately circulated treatises on doctrine, all of which circulate in the world today.
Ji Daoxing was eccentric and aloof; his character was upright and he spoke little. His bearing was lofty and transcendent, and he vowed never to visit the homes of worldly people.
Even in his old age, despite earnest invitations, he rarely attended the houses of laypeople.
Though his dwelling was often empty and he lived with carefree self-reliance, he remained diligent, never letting go of his scrolls even for a moment, delighting in the Way until the end of his life.
To this day, followers of this school are numerous in Yue, and the tradition of lecturing and guidance has not ceased.
Biography of Shi Zhiquan of Guanyin Monastery in Weifu, Zhou. Shi Zhiquan’s surname was Zhang; he was a native of Yongji in Tingtai.
At the age of nine, he served his teacher at the Wusha City Temple in Linqing, the capital of Ye.

Upon receiving full ordination, his physical frame stood tall at eight chi, his complexion was as pure as jade, his gait was like that of a swan in flight, and his voice resonated like the striking of a bell.
People regarded him with awe and all said,
"A truly magnificent man.
He constantly recited the various sutras three times by day and three times by night, never failing in his prostrations before the Buddha.
The Master, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, sent him to Huaitai; upon arriving at Mingfu Temple, he attended the lecture hall of Master Hui.
Within one month, he suddenly realized the essence and function of all phenomena, and his joy was beyond measure.
At that time, there were several dozen disciples in Huī’s school, such as Páo Yǒng and Xiāo Gàn, all of whom were inferior to Zhènquán.
He responded to the requests of the people of Xuīyáng to lecture; not long after, he was further invited by the faithful in Dōngjīng to convert their residence into the Wànsuì Bǎiyuàn Monastery.

Consequently, the capitals of Luoyang, Chen, Xu, Xu, Su, Wei, Qing, and Qin Tai all joyfully requested him to expound the Dharma; they gathered offerings and alms together, providing meals for three hundred thousand monastics in total.
The three families of Dai, Zhang, and Guo in Tianxiong Commandery jointly established an Avalokiteśvara Temple and invited him to reside there.
By nature and innate endowment, Quanmin was keenly interested in it; from beginning to end, he lectured on the *Śata-dharma-śāstra* approximately one hundred times.
When ascending the Dharma seat, he rarely relied on the written text, instead expounding with spontaneous eloquence.
On three occasions later, he perused the Tripitaka to supplement his insight and knowledge.
As for his recitation of sutras and dharanis, he once heard a silence outside his door followed by the sound of a finger-snap; was this perhaps the praise of spirits and deities?
The Wei Governor, Chen Junsirang, was deeply devoted to the practice of taking refuge [in the Triple Gem]. He submitted a memorial recommending the Master Ziyi, bestowing upon him the title Guizheng.

Although he was nearly eighty-one years old, he resolved to study the calligraphic styles of Ou-yang Xun and Wang Xianzhi, eventually attaining a level of mastery that entered the ranks of the "Capable" and "Exquisite."
When someone questioned him about this, he replied,
"I have merely been practicing the art of generating life.

In the fifth year of the Xian-de era, at the age of eighty-three, he summoned his disciples Feng Yan and others to entrust them with his final instructions, ordering that a wooden bier be constructed for his funeral and that he be conveyed to the cremation grounds.
On the eleventh day of the eleventh month of that year, he suddenly passed away. A wooden stupa was erected for him, standing over three *zhang* in height.
When it was set ablaze, white cranes wailed mournfully and purple clouds swirled overhead to cover it.
The śarīra were collected and enshrined within a stupa that was sealed shut.
Biography of Shi Haoduan of Lingguang Temple in Xiuzhou during the Song Dynasty: Shi Haoduan, surnamed Zhang, was a native of Jiahe.
At the age of nine, he left home to enter the Lingguang Monastery; his teacher bestowed upon him the scriptures and the Dharma, which he studied as if rehearsing long-practiced lessons.
Upon reaching the age of twenty, he received the *rūpa-samvara* (the form-observance) together with the *avijñapti* (unmanifest karma).

At Ayuwang Temple in Siming, he encountered Vinaya Master Xijue, who vigorously propagated the Nanshan Vinaya; upon hearing him for the first time, [Fazhao’s] conduct became upright and his understanding was immediately clear, such that no obstacles remained in his mastery of the gates of doctrine.
He subsequently went to study the *Ming-shu* (Enumeration of Terms) tradition and the *Lotus Sūtra* under Dharma Master Yun of Jinhua.
Later, he accepted an invitation from the monastic community of Wuxing to lecture and discuss these works.

The Prince of Wuduku of Liangzhe, the Qian family, summoned him to the Luohan Temple of the Prince’s Estate to provide instruction, and subsequently ordered him to propagate the teachings at the Zhenshen Pagoda Temple.

At that time, there was a master of the Tiantai school named Xuanzhu, who was regarded by his own sect as the tenth patriarch; [Zhi]yuan attached himself to him and successfully mastered the "One Mind and Three Contemplations," whereupon he composed the ten-fascicle *Commentary on the Text of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*.
Through these two essential points of doctrine, a single path was opened.
The Prince of Qi, Zhongxian Wang, lent him the purple robe and specially appointed him as a Dade (Great Virtue), bestowing upon him the title Chongfa (Venerable of the Dharma).
Later, he vowed not to step outside the temple gates, emulating Master Yuan’s refusal to cross the Tiger Brook.

He held these matters in high esteem for over twenty years; he wore no extra garments on his person and consumed no rich flavors. His dwelling was never bolted with a lock, and he sat upon nothing but a single mat.
On the eighteenth day of the third month in the second year of the Jiànlóng era, he passed away while seated in his own quarters; his countenance remained as if alive.
Three days later, he was cremated to the west of the city, and śarīra were recovered from the ashes and embers.
He was seventy-two years old by secular reckoning and fifty-two years since his ordination.
He authored approximately seventy scrolls of writings, including commentaries, records, and hymns; those who mastered the gateway of his teachings numbered no more than eighty or so.
His character was upright and resolute, and his speech was never casual or insincere.
During his time seated in meditation, he did not discuss worldly matters; he devoted himself solely to the Buddha-dharma as his primary task. He may truly be called an elephant-king with wings.

Qian Yu, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, once served as the Prefect of Xiuzhou and personally observed Daoxuan’s dignified bearing, subsequently composing the *Xinglu* (Biographical Record) for him.

Biography of Shi Fu Zhang of Tianqing Temple in Dongjing, Song China, by Fu Zhang of Tianqing Temple in Dongjing, Song China. Shi Fu Zhang’s secular surname was Peng; he was a native of Dongming in Kaifeng.

His father, Yin, was a preeminent farmer in the suburban districts; beyond the dust of worldly affairs, his right view remained unswerving, as he constantly read Buddhist scriptures and attained a profound understanding of their essential meanings.
His mother, Lady Xing, once dreamed that she entered a Buddhist temple and reached out her hand to grasp a sacred ritual object; she subsequently became pregnant.
Her father, Zhihuai, sensing that his child was no ordinary person, vowed while they were still joined at the womb that he would renounce the secular world.
At the mere age of eleven, he took Master Mi, a master of *Vijñaptimātratā* from his home district, as his preceptor; upon their first meeting, Mi marveled at him.

He was initially instructed in the three sutras—the *Vimalakīrti*, the *Benevolent Kings*, and the *Lotus Sūtra*—and when he shaved his hair, leaving only the *cūḍā* topknot, he followed Master Mi to Mount Wutai to pay homage at the sites where Mañjuśrī had manifested.
In that year, he received full ordination.
On the day of his *śrāmaṇera* (novice) initiation, he began studying the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* under the guidance of Master Qinglang at Junjiao.

Later, at Suiyang, he further refined his previous studies under Master Daoyaya, and subsequently studied *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* with his original teacher, making significant progress in fathoming the ford of meaning within the waters of the Dharma.
Furthermore, he befriended the Vice Director of the Sangha Tonghui and mastered the *Hetuvidyā* (Inming), reaching its ultimate depths.
He recited three sutras daily alongside two codes of precepts, lecturing and instructing his disciples for nearly twenty years without ever ceasing for even a moment.
During the Guangshun era, the Chief Registrar of the Left Street, Master Guangzhi, recommended him to Emperor Gaozu of the Zhou dynasty, who bestowed upon him a purple cassock.
In the second year of the Qiande era of the Great Song, the Chief Registrar of the Left Street, Daoshen, recommended him to Emperor Taizu Shende, who conferred upon him the honorary title Yiming.
Shortly thereafter, he manifested illness and passed away at this very monastery; he was fifty-five years of age, having completed thirty-six years as a monk.
Before his final breath, he took up his brush to compose a verse to admonish the world and presented it to his friends and associates.

He had fifteen disciples whom he had delivered. On the sixteenth day of the eleventh month of that year, they selected a southern plain in the capital for a cremation according to the *dhāpana* rite. When the wood was exhausted and the fire extinguished, his tongue was found to have remained without being reduced to ash; the assembly marveled at his virtue of the precepts.
His disciples and lay patrons together erected a stupa for him in the fifth year of the Kaibao era.
Previously, his father had constantly devoted himself to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; after his death, when the body was cremated, his tongue likewise remained unburnt.
That father and son were both verified as having attained such realization is truly rare.
The Great Master Qinghui of Xiangguosi Temple, Yibing, composed the "Epitaph for the Stupa.
Biography of Shi Jilun of Foshan Monastery at Chongfu Temple in Bingzhou, Song Dynasty: Shi Jilun, surnamed Cao, was a native of Jinyang. His biography is recorded here.
Though his teeth were not yet fully grown, he was already robust; his will was courageous and his mind resolute, as he sought to leave the household life.
When his preceptor taught him the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he could recite three sheets of paper daily, which astonished everyone regarding his past karmic predispositions.

His wisdom was discerning and surpassed that of others; after receiving the precepts, by the age of twenty-one, he had mastered the profound and subtle principles of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and was able to lecture upon the two treatises of *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and *Hetuvidyā* after a single reading.
Because of these compositions, his commentaries have remained widely prevalent in Hedong to this day.
At each of his three lectures, there were always more than one hundred and fifty disciples who followed his guidance and instructions.
He also compiled the *Fahua Chao* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) in three fascicles.
As a person, he was naturally compassionate and patient, and his adherence to the monastic precepts was steadfast; those who beheld him were moved to heartfelt reverence.

Because the Liu family controlled Bingzhou and Fenzhou, they held his Way in high esteem, appointing him with the title "Fobao" (Dharma-Treasure) and entrusting him with the administrative affairs of the Right Ward of the Sangha. Whether acting with leniency or severity, none dared to disobey or resist him.
In the tenth month of winter in the year Jisi of the spurious Han era, he manifested illness; with his mind praying and his mouth reciting, he expressed his vow to be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
After his passing, the crown of his head remained warm for half a day before cooling, which was the second year of the Kaibao era.

He reached the age of fifty-one. After his cremation was completed, śarīras were recovered from the ashes; people from near and far divided them to take back for veneration. When Chu was seven years old, he came to visit Lixia; the Great Virtue Xiujin presiding at the altar became his preceptor for leaving the household life.
Jin was, in fact, Chu’s paternal uncle.
His younger paternal uncle, Shenglun, resided at Xiangyan Monastery.

Jin also recited the *Avalokiteśvara Pumen Zhijing* nearly one hundred thousand times; he established a practice of prostrating to the *Lotus Sūtra*, bowing for every single character until he had completed the entire text.
Lun was the presiding master of Qingqiu; he lived in seclusion for meditation, reciting the *Mahākaruṇā* and *Uṣṇīṣavijaya* mantras ten million times each.

Chu acted as his mentor, and through their mutual support in spiritual cultivation, Lun attained full ordination (*upasampadā*). He studied diligently without slackening, and his keen intelligence was realized at an early age; regarding the single school of the *Abhidharmakośa*, he penetrated its subtleties to the ultimate limit.
He subsequently lectured on the *Yuanhui shu* (the Commentary by Yuanhui) approximately ten times.

Later, after reading through the Tripitaka three times, he lamented that Confucian scholars had produced many erroneous interpretations of Buddhist texts; since their interpretations were mistaken, their applications of the facts were frequently erroneous.

Modeling it after Bai Juyi’s *Six Categories*, I have compiled the principles, literature, miscellaneous matters, and various categories of the Śākya school, arranging them according to their respective types and establishing topical headings; encompassing the general framework, the work comprises fifty sections in total.

I have categorized and enumerated four hundred and forty sections according to their respective subjects, beginning with the "Section on the Appearance of the Dharma King" and ending with the "Section on the Lion and Animal Classes. Within these, all categories of things have been thoroughly investigated and compiled, ensuring that when you reach for the brush, you shall never lack for material.
For ten years, he applied himself with tireless diligence.

Beginning in the second year of the Kaiyun era of the Jin dynasty and concluding in the first year of the Xiande era, he presented his work for imperial inspection. Emperor Shizong issued an edict to entrust it to the Imperial Archives, bestowed upon him purple robes, and further conferred upon him the title of Mingjiao Dashi (Great Master of Enlightened Teaching).
He passed away at the Longxing Monastery during the Kaibao era.
His secular age was seventy-four, and his dharma seniority was fifty-four.

I, Chu, first conceived the plan for this work and recorded it as I encountered each point; gathering the many and supplementing the few, day after day and month after month, it has gradually formed this compiled record.
Suddenly, upon an ancient stone at the gate of this monastery, the two characters "Liùtiě" (Six-Section Anthology) appeared, naturally and clearly inscribed.
Beholding this divine talisman, I realized my destiny was preordained; thus, I searched through the present and delved into antiquity, composing without ceasing.
At that time, the State Councilor and Minister of State Affairs, Lord Park, composed a preface for Ch’u and placed it at the beginning of the collection; it is now circulated throughout the world.
Initially, Ch’u’s mind had grown weary from his labors in composition, and both his eyes lost their sight; no medical practitioner could cure him.

He then entrusted the dharma robes to Huineng, who received the vestment and went to propagate the teaching in Shaoyang.
Shenxiu transmitted the Dharma to Jingmen and Luoyang; from this point on, the Southern and Northern schools began.
Furthermore, Master Huixin once gazed from afar at Mount Shuangfeng in Jiuyang and saw purple clouds like a canopy, beneath which white vapors spread out in six branches.
Huixin said to Huiri:
"Do you know what this means?"
He said, "The Master's Dharma has branched out into a separate school, which has been passed down through six successive generations.
Xinxin agreed with this most heartily.

Furthermore, when the Dharma flourished at Niu-tou Mountain in Jin-ling, there were six generations from the one who bequeathed the legacy to his descendants down to Hui-chung; these are known as the Six Patriarchs of Niu-tou, marking another branch that split from the lineage of the Fourth Patriarch.
However, as for Daorong, compared to [Daosheng’s] forbearance, he was but a concubine’s son; how could he be matched with the legitimate heir?
During the Kaiyuan era, Lüqiu Jun, a Court Gentleman for Literature, composed a stele inscription for the pagoda.
Emperor Daizong issued an imperial edict posthumously bestowing upon him the title Chan Master Daman, and his stupa was named Fayu.

Since the late Tang dynasty, Qichun had been separated from the central administration and belonged to a peripheral region; yet prior to the year of Kaimao (975), when the Imperial Army pacified the South of the Yangtze, the flesh-body of Huirin fell, shedding tears like blood-drops.
The monastic community did not fathom this, but it was actually a sign of the impending fall of the Li dynasty.

Even now, every year during the first month of winter, people from the prefecture and neighboring districts flock here to perform memorial rites for the anniversary of his death; the assembly remains grand and flourishing.
As his anniversary drew near, there was inevitably rain, mist, and gloom; otherwise, sleet and snow fell in profusion. On the actual day, however, the weather was clear and bright.

The Biography of Huineng of Nanhua Temple in present-day Shaozhou, Guangdong, from the Tang Dynasty: Shi Huineng, whose secular surname was Lu, was a native of Xinxing in Nanhai. His ancestors had originally resided in Fanyang.
His father’s taboo name was Xingtao; during the Wude era, he was exiled as a commoner to Xin Prefecture and passed away at his place of banishment.
I have briefly recounted my family lineage, for fear of being as ignorant as the barbarians of Luting Island.
In the twelfth year of the Zhenguan era, the year Wuxu, Neng was born; he was pure, gentle, and possessed a profound disposition, with wisdom emerging from within his nature.
Although he was steeped in the customs of the barbarians and the uncivilized, such influence did not run deep; yet his eccentric conduct and strange appearance were mottled and difficult to fathom.
His father had passed away when he was young, and his mother lived as a widow; the family was frequently destitute, and their livelihood lacked substantial assets.
He was able to carry firewood, selling it daily by carrying it on a shoulder pole.

Once, while he happened to hear someone reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* at a butcher’s stall, he was able to concentrate his mind as he leaned against the wall, lingering there for a long time without leaving.
He asked, “From whom did you receive instruction in this sutra?”
He replied,
"I was urged to uphold this Dharma by Chan Master Ren of Fengmaoshan in Huangmei, Qizhou, who said that one immediately attains the realization of one's nature and becomes a Buddha.
Huineng heard these words.
Like a thirsty man drinking cold water, he hurried home to prepare what was necessary to support his elderly parents.
During the Xianheng era, he traveled to Shaozhou and met Liu Zhilüe.
Lüyougū possessed an inexhaustible treasury and constantly recited the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
When she was able to listen to [the teachings], she immediately analyzed the meaning of the "Middle" for the nun.
[The nun] marveled that she could do so without knowing any written characters, and said:
"The principles of the Buddhas, if grasped through mere words, do not reflect the Buddha's true intent.
Nishi deeply sighed in admiration and honored him as a "Practitioner" (gyōja).
When others urged him to cultivate the Way at the ancient Bao Lin Temple, he said to himself:
"I originally sought a teacher to pursue the Way; what difference is there between greedily remaining in a monastery and walking backward toward my home?
The next day he set out and reached a stone cave west of Lichang County, where he relied upon the Chan Master Zhiyuan, attending his seat to discuss the profound mysteries.
Yuan said, "The practitioner’s insight is truly extraordinary; I do not understand it, indeed, I do not understand it at all!
I urge you to go to the Fifth Patriarch at Qichun to seek his certification, for I shall ultimately remain in the lower wind to receive instruction."
Before long, he arrived there. Master Ren observed that Sengneng’s bearing and appearance were not particularly outstanding, so he tested him, saying, "From where have you come?
He replied:
A man from south of the Ling Mountains came to pay his respects, saying only, "I seek nothing but to become a Buddha.
Huiren said,
"The people of south of the Ling Mountains have no Buddha-nature."
Neng said,
"People have north and south, but the Buddha-nature has neither north nor south.
He asked:
"What meritorious deed have you performed?
He replied,
"I merely wished to exert all my strength to carry stones and pound them for the sake of providing for the assembly."
Thus, though one may toil at the well and the mortar, leading lay attendants by example;
yet when one fully understands that birth and death are equal to nirvana,
how can the mind distinguish between them, even if patience is cultivated with equal care?
Thus, Xiù sang my praises while Nǚ was able to harmonize with you.
The verses remain upon the walls, yet our interpretations diverge; our exhortations differ, and thus their depth and shallowness are distinct.
Renmi entrusted him with his Dharma robes, saying:
"The successive transmission from my former masters of antiquity—how could it have been for nothing? Alas!"
"In future generations, those who inherit my robe will have their lives hanging by a thread; let the young man take note of this.
Able to calculate the time of his rebirth, he remained hidden between Sihuai and Huaiji, gradually revealing his sharp brilliance.

During a grand assembly on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* presided over by Dharma Master Yinzong of Nanhai, he discussed the dialogue concerning the wind and the banner; Yinzong was defeated in argument and humbled in spirit. Consequently, [Huineng] had his topknot shaved at Faxing Temple and received the full precepts from Vinaya Master Zhiguang. The altar upon which he ascended was the very one constructed during the Southern Song dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman.
Guṇavarman, having already attained the stage of fruition, made a prophetic declaration, saying:
"In the future, there shall be an incarnate Bodhisattva who receives the precepts here.
Furthermore, at the end of the Liang dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha personally planted a Bodhi tree beside the ordination platform and said to the assembly:
"It is prophesied that one hundred and twenty years after this tree is planted, there will be a Bodhisattva who shall preach the Mahāyāna beneath it, delivering immeasurable multitudes.
Now, at this time, he has established his residence here; indeed, beneath the shade of this tree, he opened the Dharma-gate of the Eastern Mountain, which accords perfectly with the former prophecy.
During the Shangyuan era, while he was formally expounding the essential teachings of his school, he appeared somber and displeased.
The assembly asked him,
"Why do you seem so devoid of emotion?"
He said, "The flow of existence is unceasing, and birth and death are impermanent; my teacher has now returned to stillness!
Upon hearing this, the mourners arrived and believed it.
He then moved his residence to Baolin Temple.
At that time, the Regional Inspector Wei Ju ordered him to come out to Dafan Temple; he declined the summons with great persistence and entered Shuangfeng Cao Houxi.
The great dragon suddenly arose, and the flying rain bestowed its moisture with impartiality; all things flourished, and every root and sprout received its benefit.
Guests seeking the five-fold robes crowded at the gate, while the fourfold assembly of disciples surrounded his seat.
At that time, he proclaimed secret gāthās or cited sūtras, universally perfuming all so that everyone heard the Elephant Treasury;
they all attained sudden wealth and every one grasped the serpent’s pearl.
All followed this path and returned entirely to the ultimate perfection; thus, among those in the world who speak of the Way of Chan, Caoxi became the standard by which they were measured.

When the Emperor’s hearing reached down from the ninefold palace and his heart hung in anxiety across ten thousand *li*, he longed to spread the imperial grace to welcome him and desired to take refuge so that his wishes might be fulfilled.
Empress Wu and Emperor Xiaohé both sent down imperial letters, summoning him to the capital; this was due to the recommendation of Meditation Master Shenxiu.
The Emperor again dispatched the palace eunuch Xue Jian with an imperial decree, yet he once more declined on the grounds of illness and did not rise.

His heart, like that of Lord Mou, could not forget the Phoenix Gate; his feet, like those of Master Huiyuan, would not cross the Tiger Brook. He firmly used these reasons for his refusal, not out of a desire to seek honor from the sovereign.

Thereupon, he was granted one set of monastic robes (kāṣāya), one alms bowl, a prayer shawl woven with strung beads, a cotton handkerchief of green material with red floral patterns, and five hundred rolls of silk, to serve as offerings.
Furthermore, he donated his newly built old residence to become Guoen Temple.

In the third year of the Shenlong era, an imperial edict was issued stating that the Buddha hall and the abbot’s quarters of the temple where Huineng resided in Shaoyang Prefecture should be renovated with the utmost magnificence, and the name of the temple was changed to Faquan.
In the seventh month of the first year of the Yanyang era, he commanded his disciples to construct a stupa at Guoen Temple, ordering it to be completed with haste.
On the third day of the eighth month of the second year of the Xiantian era, he suddenly manifested illness; a rare fragrance filled the chamber, and a white rainbow stretched across the earth.
Having finished his meal, he bathed and changed his robes; with the snapping of his fingers never ceasing, his breath grew faint and his eyes closed, as his entire body passed away forever.
At that moment, the mountain rocks collapsed and fell, the streams and springs dried up, birds wailed in continuous lamentation, and monkeys cried out with broken hearts.
Some cried out, saying:
"The Eye of the World has been extinguished; whom shall we rely upon?
He was seventy-six years old when he passed away at Caoxi on the eleventh month of that year.
The disciple Shenhui was like Yanzi among the disciples of Confucius; his diligent devotion and the instructions entrusted to him are recorded in the "Biography of Shenhui.
Shenhui erected a true hall for Huineng at Heze Monastery in Luoyang.
Song Ding, Vice Minister of the Ministry of War, composed the inscription for the stele.

He compiled a genealogy of the patriarchal lineage, and apart from the various patriarchs of the Western Regions descending from the Tathāgata, he depicted the portraits of all six patriarchs of China.
The Grand Marshal Fang Guan composed the "Preface to the Six-Leaf Diagram.
He further noted that because [the image] could maintain its form without dispersing, as if entering a state of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), lacquer and cloth were subsequently added.
Furthermore, the Shu monk Fangbian fashioned a small clay image of the Buddha that was as lifelike as the Master himself had been in his prime.
Nan could say, "After my passing, there will surely be a man of virtuous mind who takes my remains; you all need not be alarmed."
Some recalled these words and bound iron rings around his neck.

In the eleventh year of the Kaiyuan era, it so happened that a man from Ruzhou purchased the head from a Silla traveler; he secretly applied a blade to it, intending to carry it back to the lands east of the sea for veneration.
Someone heard the sound of striking iron and captured him.
Beneath that stupa was stored a *yutrasaṅghāṭī* robe made of *kucchan* cloth; it was dark blue-black in color and lined with greenish-blue silk, a thing not found among humans.
It was stolen several times; each time the thief would become dazed, turn back, and return it stripped of its coverings.
During the Zhide era, Shenhui sent his disciple Jinping to deliver a single toothpick.
In the morning, he was honored by renowned public figures: for instance, Song Zhiwen visited him and composed a long poem;
likewise, Zhang Yanyong sent ten *jin* of incense along with a poem, which was delivered by Wu Pingyi. The poem read:
"The Great Master has departed from this world, leaving behind only his Dharma-body!"
"I pray that this unimpeded incense may be entrusted to you, following my heart as it reaches the South Sea.
Duke Wu, through his disciple Huairang, cast a great bell and commissioned [Wu] Zhiwen to compose an inscription and hymn for it, which was calligraphed by Song Zhiwen.
Next, Song Jing, the Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, came to pay homage at the stupa.
He questioned the disciple Lingtao on the meaning of the "Dharma-patience of Non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Upon hearing the Dharma, Lord Song was filled with joy and prayed before the stupa for a manifestation of auspicious signs.
In a brief moment, a gentle breeze gradually arose, and an extraordinary fragrance permeated the air; a fine drizzle fell, confined only to the precincts of the monastery.
There were many other miraculous occurrences, but I shall omit them here for fear of excessive detail.

Later, Emperor Suzong issued an imperial decree summoning Huineng’s disciple Huitao; however, Huitao cited illness and did not attend. He instead dispatched Mingxiang to present the Dharma robes and alms bowl, which were subsequently returned to him after the presentation was complete.
Emperor Xuanzong posthumously conferred upon him the title Dajian (Great Mirror), and the stupa was named Yuanhe Zhengzhen (Orthodox Truth of the Yuanhe Era).

Later, during the final years of the Tang dynasty, when the Liu family ruled in Panyu, they would regularly welcome the True Body into the city on the occasion of the Lantern Festival during the Shangyuan period to pray for blessings for the people.
After the Great Song dynasty pacified the South Sea, the rebel Zhou Siqiong of Shaoshan set fire to all the temples and pagodas, intending to let the flames spread.
When he attempted to burn the living body [of the saint], several men were required to lift it.
As the smoke and flames drew near, two monks carried him together on a litter; he was as light as a lacquered wooden statue.
In the third year of the Taiping Xingguo era, the present Emperor issued an edict to rebuild the pagoda and renamed it Nanhua Temple.
The commentary asks:
"From what did the Fifth Patriarch recognize this single layman, such that he immediately bestowed the robe upon him?
Tong replied:
"Having understood his mind with a single word, there was no further doubt or hesitation.
Moreover, he could even recall [the contents] from within the cakra of the heart as clearly as the palm of one's hand.
Since Master Ren bestows the Dharma of a single flavor, why would he accept robes and alms bowls while remaining a householder?"
Master Xiu replied, "No.
Tong said, "In this Dharma, does one select between the black-robed and the white-robed? Is it transmitted only to those who attain it?"
When the Zhou enfeoffed the feudal lords, they distributed ritual vessels; those of the same surname and those of different surnames were distinguished.
By means of their ancestral masters, they differentiated between the refined and the coarse, using the robes as tokens of their status.
For example, suppose three strong men shoot at a *kṣāra-śāka* (a hard wood): the first, a *māgadha*, hits it but does not pierce it;
the second, a *prāsādakṣepin*, pierces it but does not pass through;
the third, a *nārāyaṇa*, passes through it and further penetrates other objects.
The *lakṣa* targets are not inherently strong or weak; they differ only according to the varying power of the shot.
In the south, Nena can be said to have received a reward for shooting at the *Nārāyaṇa-lakṣa*.
"If the robe of faith were not transmitted when it reached you, would this not be like the House of Xia Yu receiving the mandate over the world?
Tong said:
'I spoke of "enduring" regarding the transmission of the robe because my life was as precarious as a hanging thread; such was the meaning of my endurance.'"
Furthermore, although Huiye’s reception of the ancestral Dharma was more than sufficient, his practice of transforming others through his conduct was insufficient.

Consequently, it was only later, with the emergence of the "Equal Division" (Junbu) school, that the prior awakening of Master Neng was verified; thus, there is no fault of failing to transmit the teachings out of private stinginess.
Therefore it is said, "He who knows men is wise. Alas!
The Biography of Shenxiu of Dumen Monastery on Mount Dangyang in Jingzhou, Tang China. The monk Shenxiu’s secular surname was Li; he was a native of Weishi in present-day Eastern Capital (Luoyang).
In his youth, he perused the classics and histories, becoming widely learned and well-versed in many subjects.
Subsequently, he resolved to transcend the mundane world, shaving his head and receiving the Dharma.
Later, he encountered Master Wuzu Ren of Dongshan Temple on Shuangfeng Mountain in Qizhou; as the master was dedicated to the practice of seated meditation, [Huineng] sighed in admiration and said:
"This is truly my teacher.
Resolving his mind with austere discipline, he employed himself as a woodcutter and water-carrier to seek the Way.

Formerly, at the end of the Wei dynasty, there was an Indian śramaṇa named Bodhidharma who had attained the sublime Dharma of the Chan school, which had been transmitted from Śākyamuni Buddha through successive generations. Taking the robe and bowl as tokens of transmission, it was handed down from master to disciple until he arrived here by sea.

Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty questioned him regarding matters of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*), whereas Bodhidharma esteemed the transmission of the essential mind of the direct gate (*jìngmén*). Their capacities and teachings were as incompatible as water poured onto stone;
consequently, he went to Wei and lived in seclusion at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song, where he eventually passed away.
In that year, the Wei envoy Song Yun encountered him at the Pamir Mountains (Congling).
When his disciples opened his tomb, there was nothing left but his robes and shoes.
He transmitted the Dharma to Huikě; Huikě transmitted it to Sengcan; Sengcan transmitted it to Daoxin; and Daoxin transmitted it to Huirin.
Because Huirin resided at Mount Dongshan together with Huixiu, his teaching was called the Dongshan Dharma-gate.
Since Huixiu served Huirin, Huirin silently recognized his potential and held him in profound esteem, saying to others:
"I have ordained many people, but none has surpassed you in terms of transcendent liberation and perfect illumination."
Shenru died during the Shangyuan era; Huixiu then went to reside at Mount Dangyang in Jiangling.
Monastics from all quarters bowed before his reputation as if swept by the wind; his fame for the Way was fragrant, universally permeating and transforming all who encountered it.
Upon hearing of this, Empress Wu Zetian summoned him to the capital; she had him carried to the palace on a palanquin and personally performed the ritual of prostration before him.
She provided lavish offerings at the inner chapel and frequently sought his counsel regarding the Way.
By imperial decree, Dumen Temple was established at his former residence on the mountain to commemorate his virtue.

At that time, from the princes and dukes down to the commoners of the capital, all vied with one another to pay their respects; they would prostrate themselves upon seeing even the dust raised by his approach, numbering tens of thousands each day.
When Emperor Zhongzong Xiaohedi ascended the throne, he bestowed even greater favor and honor upon him.
Zhang Yue, the Director of the Secretariat, once inquired about the Dharma and observed the etiquette of a disciple; upon leaving, he remarked to others:
"The Chan Master stands eight feet tall, with thick eyebrows and brilliant eyes; his majestic virtue is towering—he possesses the capacity of a true king or hegemon."
Initially, Master Neng, a fellow student of Xiu, was equal to him in virtue and conduct; they mutually inspired one another, being selfless regarding the Way.
Once, he petitioned Empress Wu to request that Neng be summoned to the capital, but Neng declined with earnest and firm resolve.
Xiu also composed a letter himself, in which he explained the Emperor’s intent in summoning him; yet he ultimately could not rise to go, saying to the messenger:
"My physical form is not imposing; if the people of the Northland see me so short and humble, they may perhaps fail to hold the Dharma in high esteem."
Furthermore, my former master prophesied that I have a karmic affinity with the region south of the Ling Mountains, and I must not go against this.
He passed away before ever crossing the Dayu Ridge.
His Way was subsequently disseminated throughout the world; his lineage is known as the Northern School, while Huineng’s is known as the Southern School.
The names of the two schools, Northern and Southern, originated from this.

Xiu passed away in the second year of the Shenlong era; both officials and commoners came to attend his funeral, and by imperial decree, he was posthumously granted the title of Chan Master Dàtōng (Great Penetration).

Furthermore, he established Ba’en Temple at the former residence of Emperor Xuanzong; Prince Qi Fan, Zhang Yue, Duke of Yan State, and the retired scholar Lu Hong each composed inscriptions and eulogies for it.
Among those who observed the mourning period for their master, titled scholars and high-ranking officials were too numerous to count.
His disciples Pují and Yìfú were both esteemed by both the court and the common people, as they followed the Way of their former teacher.
The commentary states:
Now, sweetness and bitterness counterbalance one another, and their flavors lead to different results.

If sweetness does not overcome bitterness, then pure bitterness prevails; if bitterness does not overcome sweetness, then pure sweetness takes control. Thus, when medicine is used to treat disease, an excessive imbalance must be avoided.

In the past, when Bodhidharma passed away, his subtle words were lost; when the Fifth Patriarch died, the Great Meaning fell into discord. Xiu wiped away the dust to clarify the mind, while Nanquan Hui-neng proclaimed the Way through the realization that both [subject and object] are non-existent.
As for the spread of its transformative influence, the North still maintained the diligent practice of gradual cultivation;
from this point they diverged, and in the Southern regions the teachings of the Sudden Gate (Dunmen) flourished.
It was from this that the teachings of Heze were propagated throughout the Central Lands.
