By using the Sudden Teaching (Dunmen) to distance oneself from the toil of gradual cultivation, one fails to move even a massive boulder;
by attempting to tune the strings of a zither to the sounds of ox-hide and donkey-skin, one merely wastes a restless mind.

This leads to everyone cherishing only their own kin and aligning themselves with their own factions; thus, there arose the impeachment of Lu Yi and the exile of Shen Hui. This is surely the fault of administering medical treatment while adhering exclusively to a single flavor.
Thus, one sees the evidence of how sweetness and bitterness incline toward one another.
If the treatment of illness fails to take effect, it is because contentious rivalry has already taken precedence.
One should simply respect the Dharma for the sake of honoring people; why go so far as to damage the Dharma for the sake of individuals?
Two disciples were washing their master’s feet; before they had even managed to clear away the grime, the master’s shinbone was broken and revealed—could this not serve as a metaphor for this?

The Biography of Huiming of Mount Meng in Yuanzhou, Tang China. Shi Huiming, surnamed Chen, was a native of Poyang. He was originally the grandson of Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty, but after the fall of his state, he became a commoner.
Mingshao left home to become a monk at Yongchang Temple at a young age; his aspiration for the Way was profound, and he sought the Dharma of Shuangfeng.
During the reign of Emperor Gaozong, he relied upon the dharma seat of Master Ren, where he investigated with all his heart, yet initially attained no realization, like a dog that has lost its home.

Suddenly hearing that the Fifth Patriarch had secretly entrusted the robe and bowl to the layman Lu, he led some seventy or so like-minded companions to track him down in haste. Upon reaching Mount Dayu, Ming was the first to see him; the others did not catch up.
Having seen this, Neng cast aside his *kāṣāya* and said clearly, "I have come for the sake of the Dharma, not in hope of robes or alms bowls.
At that time, Master Neng pointed resolutely toward the summit of the ridge; Huiming understood it all through and through. Overwhelmed by both grief and joy, he asked Neng:
"Where should I go? Neng remembered it and said:
"If you encounter Meng, you should reside there; if you meet Yuan, you may stop."
Ming bowed twice and departed, whereupon his name was changed to Dao Ming, as he had previously been called.
Upon descending the ridge, he deceived the monks, saying:
"Just now I climbed a steep peak and looked far into the distance, but there was no trace of him at all."
The Sangha immediately withdrew.
On another occasion, the householder threw his robe and bowl onto a flat rock and said, "This robe is for the sake of faith;
how can it be a matter of forceful contention?"
"I leave it to you to lift it.

Ming then reached out his hand to pull it up; it felt as heavy as a thousand-jin stone, and he had no strength to raise it. He stood with hands clasped in reverence and withdrew from the mat. This was the fourth year of the Xianheng era.
Because Ming had not yet left the household when he previously served in various military commands, he bore the title of "General.
Qin Zhuo, the Governor of Yichun, submitted a memorial proposing his posthumous title.
The Biography of Shenhui of Heze Monastery in the Capital of Luoyang during the Tang Dynasty. The monk Shenhui, surnamed Gao, was a native of Xiangyang.

Still young in years yet of a nature both sincere and intelligent, he followed his teacher to receive the transmission of the Five Classics, through which he was able to penetrate their profound and subtle mysteries.
Subsequently, he sought out the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*, whereby the treasury of his spirit became vast and clear.
Having read the *Book of the Later Han*, he came to understand the teachings of the Buddha.

Thereupon, he applied his mind to the Śākya-dharma and, having no intention of pursuing an official career, took leave of his parents to enter the monastic life under Dharma Master Haoyuan of Guochang Temple in his home province.
In reciting the various sutras, he found them as easy as turning over his palms;
he maintained the great code of discipline (*vinaya*) perfectly, never craving mere scholarly exposition.

Hearing that Master Huineng of Caoxi in Lingbiao was vigorously propagating the Way of the Dharma and that students were flocking there like swift horses, he followed the example of Sudhana’s southern pilgrimage, wrapping his feet in torn garments and regarding a thousand li as no more than a single stride.
Upon seeing him, Neng asked Huì,
"Where have you come from?
He replied:
"It has come from nowhere. Neng said,
"Are you not going back?"
He replied,
"There is nothing to which one returns. Nan said:
"You are far too vague," [the Master] said. He replied,
"My physical presence was on the road."
Neng said, "Is it because you have not yet arrived?
He replied:
"Now that I have arrived, I shall not linger.
He resided at Caoxi for several years before traveling extensively to seek out famous sites.
In the eighth year of the Kaiyuan era, by imperial decree, he was assigned to reside at Longxing Temple in Nanyang.
He subsequently propagated the Chan dharma extensively in Luoyang, and his reputation and brilliance flourished.
Previously, throughout the two capitals, everyone followed Shenxiu, like fish and sturgeons gathering at a pond or dragons attaching themselves to a marsh.
From the time the assembly saw the clarification of the mind, the tradition of the Sixth Patriarch swept away the path of gradual cultivation.
At that time, the distinction between the Northern and Southern schools first emerged; consequently, the gate of Pujì became full and then empty.

During the Tiānbǎo era, the Censor Lú Yì was biased toward Zhìjì and falsely accused him of gathering disciples with suspicious intentions that portended harm to the state. Emperor Xuánzōng summoned him to the capital;

at that time, the imperial entourage was visiting Zháoyìng, where they encountered the hot springs. There, [Zhìjì] was granted an audience, and his arguments were so persuasive and satisfying that an imperial edict was issued to transfer him to the region of Jūn.
In the second year [of the Kaiyuan era], by imperial decree, he was transferred to reside at the Prajñā Hall of Kaiyuan Temple in Jingzhou.
In the fourteenth year, An Lushan of Fanyang raised troops and turned toward the capital; both capitals fell into chaos, and the imperial court took refuge in Ba and Shu.
The Vice Commander-in-Chief Guo Ziyi led his troops to pacify and annihilate [the rebels], yet they were utterly destitute regarding the transport of supplies.

Following the expedient plan of the Right Vice President of the Department of State Affairs, Pei Mian, each great prefecture established a *kaitan* (ordination platform) to ordain monks; the tax levied on these monks in cash was called "incense-water money," which was accumulated to assist the military requirements.

Initially, when the capital city fell first, Huihui was living among the weeds and brush; at that time, Lu Yi had been slain by the rebels, so the assembly proposed that Huihui should preside over the ordination platform.

At that time, the temples and palaces had been reduced to ashes; consequently, a temporary courtyard was established using only thatched coverings, within which a square altar was constructed, and all the wealth and silk obtained were immediately used to support military expenses.
During the reign of Emperor Daizong, when Guo Ziyi recovered the two capitals, Huaiji played a significant role in providing necessary resources.

Emperor Suzong issued an imperial decree for him to enter the palace to provide offerings, and commanded the Grand Master of Works to marshal all available labor and resources to construct a Chan monastery within Heze Temple; this is that very place.
Hui’s extensive expositions revealed and manifested the ancestral style of his master, causing the lineage of Xiu to fall into silence.

In the first year of the Shangyuan era, he took leave of his disciples; rising from his seat, he gazed into the void and prostrated himself, then returned to his quarters, where that very night he passed away.
He passed away at the age of ninety-three, specifically on the thirteenth day of the fifth lunar month.
His stupa was enshrined at Baoying Temple in Luoyang; by imperial decree, the Master was posthumously titled "Zhenzong," and his stupa was named "Prajñā."
The commentary states:
"To cultivate their teachings without altering their customs, and to unify their governance without changing what is appropriate to them—this is because one values gradualism.

If Master Hui would travel from south to north to practice the Dharma of Caoxi, and it were to flourish extensively in Luoyang, such that he did not set himself apart [from local traditions] and external protection was already established, then it would be sufficient.
How much more so when one lacks the wheels of power at their side; since human beings are prone to many deviations, how could one hope not to be cast out?
Someone said:
"If his transgressions are not many, why be so hasty in this?"
Tong said: "When one offends against the taboos of the times, the fault does not lie in the magnitude of the act.
When one loses their proper course, the error does not lie in its depth."
Those who observe this later should urgently take note of the circumstances of the times.
For this reason, although the Buddha studied and transformed practitioners for ten thousand kalpas, he knew that such transformative practice is difficult.
Do not allow stubbornness to harm the Dharma; be cautious!
Biography of Tanchui of Zhulin Monastery in Runzhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Tanchui, whose secular surname was Gu, was a native of Wu Commandery.
The founding of their state and the establishment of their distinguished lineage have long been most illustrious.
The Prime Minister possesses the merit of assisting in the founding of the dynasty; the Minister of State enjoys the reputation for outstanding capability and salvation.
Their noble attire and eminent ancestry are as lofty as the peaks of Mount Tai and Mount Dai.
When we inquire into his illustrious conduct, the Yangtze and Han rivers serve as the guiding principles for the southern realm.

Celestial bodies descended their essence, and the spirits of heaven and earth manifested blessings; his virtue was perfected through prenatal education, as evidenced by the auspicious fragrance and the sign of the dream.
The dark jade tally responded to the auspicious signs of the Supreme Sage; the divine treasure accumulated the vital energy of the Yellow and Fen Rivers.

He was uniquely endowed with extraordinary standards and born no ordinary man; while still in his swaddling clothes, the ignorant came to seek him, and by the time he wore the hairpin-fastener, he had forgotten his own person to devote himself to the Way.
He was harmonious, quick-witted, and pure; gentle, respectful, and capable of great clarity. His divine vessel had long been manifest, and his refined influence gradually spread.

Thereupon, he exerted himself to transcend the mundane world, dwelling his mind beyond all material things. Regarding the secret treasury of the Golden Sūtras, he could recite ten thousand words in a single day; before a year had passed, he had mastered the Great Scriptures with profound thoroughness.
In his later years, he then looked back with longing upon the patriarchal masters and began to serve Great Master Rong of Mount Niutou.
Rong was profound, elegant, magnificent, and heroic—was he not the Bodhidharma of the Eastern Land?
A precious pillar like the Brahma-banner and a bridge across the great ocean, he looked upon them with his superior faculties and instructed them, saying:
"Form and sound are the lethal poison of non-arising; sensation and perception are the pitfall of the perfected person."
"To travel great distances, one must endure much mud; do you not strive for this?

Zui remained silent and reflected upon these words. He straightened his reins and rode on alone, partaking of the flavor of sweet dew and drinking grape nectar—just as the golden-winged garuḍa does not eat other species, and Śakra does not dwell with ghosts.

He then concealed his traces at Mount Zhong, severing the habitual tendencies of outflows, cultivating the adamantine samādhi, and aspiring toward the rank of Great Power; wearing patched robes in the empty forests, he spent many years there.

At that time, Master Juechan of Guangling, a leader of the Daoist school in Huainan, and Master Rufa of Jianye, renowned for his virtue in Jiangzuo, both arrived carrying their staffs. They humbled their minds before the essence of the Dharma; grasping the pearl and harboring the treasure within, they went forth with empty hands and returned with reality.
Thus, the Empress Dowager presided over the court and personally performed Buddhist rites; she held his religious vocation in high esteem and issued frequent edicts urging him to comply.

At that time, Dharma Master Yue of Qixia, a preeminent talent among the gate of Brahma, personally exhorted him with earnest persuasion to attend the imperial court. He submitted a memorial to the sagacious Emperor, fearing that [the current situation] was not yet right.

Cui said: "Zhibo declined the invitation to be the teacher of Emperor Shun; Ganmu refused the decree of Lord Wenhou; Xuanchang opposed the ruler of Song with his eloquent discourse; and Huiyuan did not descend from his mountain yet remained haughty toward the sovereign of Qi. What kind of men were they!"

Thereupon he withdrew northward to Jin, crossing over the eastern ridges; he lived in seclusion amidst the clouds and mist, later settling in the depths of the Bamboo Grove, where he thatched his dwelling with gourds and jars and announced his retirement from the world.

Thereafter, he followed the grand legacy of successive sagely emperors and succeeded to the meritorious deeds of former worthies; he assisted and illuminated the Imperial Dharma and protected and brought peace to both gods and men.
Suddenly, he entered meditative absorption with a composed countenance and passed away after seven days, at the age of sixty-two.
This was the sixth day of the second month in the third year of the Tian-shou era.

On the following day, he was cremated according to the Indian rites; his remains were collected as ashes and a stupa was erected, while the officials and commoners, filled with sorrow, all wailed aloud in lamentation.
The disciples Senggan and Sengyun engraved this inscription on stone to record these events, treating the Master with full reverence.

Zhengyi Dafu, the Commissioner and Regional Inspector of Runzhou, Sheng of Runan, having long admired his reputation from afar, was filled with joy for a long time; he praised virtue and esteemed the worthy, commending and completing the excellence of this work.
Biography of Dharma-dhṛti of Yanzuo Monastery in Jinling, Tang Dynasty. Śramaṇa Dharma-dhṛti’s secular surname was Zhang; he was a native of Jiangning in Runzhou.

His countenance was dignified and solemn, and his physical form was exceedingly supple and radiant. Having renounced worldly life in youth, he served an enlightened master in maturity; the celestial mechanism awakened within him, while the waves of consciousness became tranquil without.

At the age of thirteen, he heard of the Great Master Ren of Huangmei and traveled specifically to pay his respects; having been shown the essentials of the Dharma, he attained an understanding of its profound mysteries.

Later, he returned to Qingshan to serve Chan Master Fang once again, where he further clarified the ultimate source of the school. The Master then commanded him to enter the inner chamber, entrusting him with the transmission of the lamp to continue the illumination and succeed to the legacy of the mountain gate, so that he might widely proclaim the transformative power of the Way.

Once Fang had emerged from the mountains, all the members of the monastic community followed him to inquire about and receive instruction on the essentials of the mind; his reputation soared far and wide until it was known throughout the realm.
Within a few years, followers from the four quarters of the world looked up to him with devotion.
At that time, Xie Yuan of Huangmei passed away and said to his disciple Xuangze:
"There will be ten people who transmit my Dharma hereafter; Fa-chi of Jinling is one of them."
Thus it is known that the Chan lineage of these two houses was transmitted through successive generations.
Later, he entrusted the Dharma-eye to his disciple Zhiwei.
On the fifth day of the ninth month in the second year of the Chang’an era, he passed away at Yanzuo Temple.

In his final testament, he commanded that his remains be left exposed beneath the pine trees to be fed to various birds and beasts, so that those who might consume his flesh and blood would give rise to the bodhicitta.
On that day, several divine banners appeared in the sky from the west, circling the mountain several times.
Everyone witnessed this.
His former residence at Youqi was transformed as the bamboo grove turned white;
his age was reported to be sixty-eight.
Biography of Dao Liang of Yunmen Monastery in Yuezhou during the Tang Dynasty. Shi Dao Liang, surnamed Zhu, was a native of Yuezhou.
In the past, he served as the Prefect of Kuaiji.
When Sengliang was eight years old, he left the household life and became thoroughly proficient in the scriptural teachings.
After receiving full ordination, he studied the "Three Treatises" (Sanlun) of the Hezhong region and further lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

He soon entered deep valleys, wearing tattered robes to cover his body and sustaining his life on vegetarian food; he did not engage in worldly affairs, remaining steadfastly in the state of a perpetual youth.

In the first year of the Shenlong era, Emperor Xiaohé issued an edict summoning Huiliang and ten other masters of the Dharma assembly to enter the inner chambers of the Chánglè Palace for the summer retreat.
At that time, the Emperor commanded him to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
Ruizong, along with the Empress and the consorts, presented him with various brocade quilts and felt mats.
In the second year, an imperial edict invited him to the Western Garden to inquire about the Way; thus, he was held in high esteem by the court.

The Grand Commander Li Xiaoyi, Minister of Works Zhang Xi, Director of Studies at the National Academy Cui Rong, Director of the Imperial Library He Zhizhang, and Prefectural Governor of Muzhou Kang Shen shared a common heart of admiration and veneration; they inquired about the mind of Chan, frequently establishing the relationship of teacher and disciple, and some even transmitted the incense and lamps of the lineage.
He passed away at the age of eighty-two; his disciples Huiyuan and others erected a stupa for him, and Wan Qirong composed an inscription to commemorate his life.
Biography of Shi Daojun of Bijian Temple in Jingzhou, Tang Dynasty: Shi Daojun was a native of Jiangling.

Residing at the Bijian Bijian Hermitage, he cultivated the Dharma-gate of Non-arising of Mount Dongshan; "Faith" and "Patience" are the names of the two patriarchs who taught the Dharma he transformed.
He was diligent and pure in his ascetic practices, never venturing beyond the monastery for over forty years.
His dwelling was nearby, yet people kept their distance, none daring to seek an audience; he remained solely in a state of silent seclusion.

In this way, the śrāvakas were honored by the Empress Dowager and the Emperor during the two reigns of the Tianhou and Zhongzong periods; like Hengjing, they were esteemed for their lofty conduct and entered the palace at imperial command to receive offerings.

During the Jinglong era, he requested to return to his native village; the Emperor bestowed upon him a poem composed by His Majesty, and Fazang and Jing returned together to Zhiyang, where he passed away at his home temple.

Biography of Xuánjué of Longxing Monastery in Wenzhou during the Tang Dynasty The monk Xuánjué, whose courtesy name was Míngdào, was of the secular surname Dài. He was a fifth-generation descendant of the Duke Kǎn of Hàn and a ninth-generation descendant of the Duke Yān. His given name was Liè; having crossed the Yangtze River, he became a native of Yǒngjiā.

Having left home with his hair in twin-tails and shaved his head in his childhood, his mind-source was fundamentally pure; the seal of wisdom encompassed all texts, fathoming the inconceivable and understanding the most profound meanings.
I constantly and firmly know self and non-self;
I fully perceive both emptiness and non-emptiness.
Having departed from the four maladies, I also wear the three robes.
The virtuous waters bathe his body, thereby purifying it;
excellent medicines treat his eyes, thereby making them radiant.
Your elder brother, Master Xuán, is likewise known as a *saṃgha*.
Together with his two younger brothers, they all joined the ranks of the monastic community.

Jueben resided at Longxing Temple; the entire family placed their faith in him, and as they practiced with unceasing diligence, the root of their meditative concentration became firm and unwavering, so that the tree of doubt suddenly collapsed of its own accord.
Having completely relinquished the notion of self, he was not defiled by adventitious dust.
Observing that there was a particularly sublime landscape beside the temple, he subsequently constructed a meditation hut for himself beneath a cliff.
The vast blue sea washed against his chest, and the green mountains bowed in reverence behind his back; as the years passed, he became like an immortal guest of Mount Penglai.
Canopies of flowers and clouds of incense smoke intermingled at dawn and dusk.
When his merit was thus perfected, the Jewel of the Buddha rose majestically;
as the divine bell resounded from afar, the wondrous edifice manifested through transformation.
While he dwells therein, he does not use silk for clothing nor grain for food; how could it be that he wears only coarse cloth like Zhuangzi? He naturally has the nectar of Ānanda as his meal.

Jue, considering himself narrow-minded from solitary study, felt that "three men have a teacher. He thus traveled shoulder-to-shoulder with Chan Master Ce of Dongyang to wander the lands in search of the Way, where he visited Chan Master Neng of Shaoyang and attained his essential instruction.
Some say: "Jue shook his mendicant’s staff and circumambulated the hermitage to engage in dialogue"; these words are recorded in a separate account.
As for Shenxiu’s school, although he traveled far to inquire about the Dharma, it was ultimately at Caoqi that he attained the mind.
Having resolved his doubts, he was able to remain for one night; thus he was called "One-Night Enlightenment" (Yisuo Jue), much like the term "Half-Universal Purity" (Banbian Qing).
On the seventeenth day of the tenth month in the second year of the Xiantian era, he sat upright in meditative absorption at the Longxing Annex Temple, remaining serene and motionless.
The monks wailed in grief and interred him on the thirteenth day of the eleventh month of that year on the southern slope of West Mountain; he was forty-nine years of age.
Previously, before his passing, Ju had confined himself to the western crag and, gazing toward his monastery, sighed deeply, saying:
"People throng together and flower-litters flourish; what use are they!"
Several of his disciples, including Master Xingshi of Wuxing and Master Xuan of Silla, heard this together, yet none could fathom it.
Shortly thereafter, they recorded it as follows:
"Once, while a certain Chan master was traveling with his disciples to enjoy the sights, he gazed afar at a mountain and suddenly exclaimed:"
"The number of people here is vast.
Even his disciples could not fathom this, yet before long, the Master passed away; the place where he was encoffined was a site of great longing.

The Western Hills were more than a day’s journey from the monastery, yet the funeral procession was so densely crowded that the multitude surged like boiling water; such was the depth of their emotion.
Furthermore, before his passing, more than a thousand wild geese flew over the western side of the monastery.
An attendant asked, "Where are these coming from?
A voice from the sky replied:
"It was for the sake of his master’s burial site that he emerged from the sea.
His disciples Huicao, Huite, Dengci, and Xuanji all transmitted their master’s Dharma and were highly esteemed by their contemporaries.

Later, when Li Bei Hai (Li Yong) served as the Governor of Kuozhou, he compiled the *Jue Xing Lu* (Record of the Conduct of Zhi Jue) and erected it as a stele, designating it as a "Divine Way" inscription.

Zhi Jue’s proclamation of the Way was brilliant; through his cultivation and realization, he attained awakening. Wei Jing, the Prefect of Qingzhou, collected and edited these works, which are known as the *Yongjia Ji*.
Initially, Daohui formed a spiritual bond with Master Lang of Zuoxi. Lang sent a letter inviting Daohui to dwell among the mountains.
Thereupon, Daohui reflected that Lang was mired in dogmatic views regarding the mountains and constrained by his attachment to lecturing; he wrote back in response to exhort him to change his ways.
The phrasing is elegant and refined, while the principles are clear and lucid.

It enables the mountain and the world to be as one, and the clamor and the stillness to function interchangeably; the intent of entering the Way is implicitly elucidated therein, a point which those who have attained realization would surely approve.
At his death, an imperial edict conferred upon him the posthumous title of Wuxiang (Signless), and his stupa was named Jingguang (Pure Light).

Biography of Zhiwei of Tianbao Monastery in Jinling, Tang Dynasty: Zhizhiwei, whose secular surname was Chen, was a native of Jiangning. He was originally from the Pure Land school. His lay name was Chen, and he was a person of Jiangning.
Dwelling near the green mountains, his station was imbued with auspicious vapors; he well accorded with ancient portents, as a spirit descended from the sacred peaks.
Thus, even in his childhood, his character surpassed that of ordinary perception; even in his play, he was never tainted by worldly things.
By nature he was frivolous and ornate, so everyone regarded him as strange.

Before long, one morning, he suddenly disappeared; his parents did not know where he had gone, so they traveled to various temples in search of him. Wei had already taken refuge with Master Tong at Tianbao Temple.
He recited Mahāyāna sūtras by the hundreds of sheets even at an early age; his intelligence and acumen surpassed his peers, and all marveled at and admired him.

At the age of twenty, he encountered an imperial favor that allowed him to shave his head and enter the monastic order, being registered at Youyan Temple. Thereupon, he followed Master Chi to inquire about the methods of Chan meditation; he attained a profound mastery of its deep principles and succeeded to the legacy of the former masters.

Having obtained the jewel of the topknot, he became serene and carefree; his appearance was warm and radiant, his face like the full moon, his speech refined and elegant, and his wisdom and virtue as fragrant as orchids.
His reputation was preeminent within his generation, and his fame reached far and near; those in the Jiangzuo region who studied the definitive teachings often visited him.

Among them, Huizhong Chanshi was one who suddenly awakened to the source of the mind, and he was thus appointed as the successor to the mountain gate, widely propagating the transformative influence of the Way.
Daowei retired to Yanzuo Temple, where he preached the Dharma to benefit others and extensively bestowed great advantages.

On the eighteenth day of the second month in the tenth year of the Kaiyuan era, he passed away at the temple where he resided. He left a final instruction to feed birds and beasts in the forest; his disciples, including Xuanting, carried out these words accordingly.
At seventy-seven years of age, Sengwei was practicing *dhūta* austerities while traveling at night. As dawn was approaching, he encountered three tigers.
Wei blocked the path and passed through their midst, showing no sign of fear whatsoever.
The tiger followed him to the mountain gate, looked around in all four directions, and then departed.
Every day, two rabbits and one dog would play together in the courtyard, each entirely free from fear or suspicion.
This was surely because his great compassion was impartial, treating self and others as equal; hence it was so.
Next was Shi Benjing of Siku Mountain; his surname was Zhang, and he was a native of Dongping.
Having entered the Gate of Emptiness in his youth, he held his own integrity and conduct in high esteem.
Traveling to various regions, he met the Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi, where he resolved all his doubts and obstructions.

At the beginning of the Kaiyuan era, he lived in seclusion on Mount Sikong at Nanyue, remaining aloof from the world so that no one recognized him; this was due to his concealment of his true identity.

During the Tianbao era, he encountered Yang Tingguang while the latter was gathering medicinal herbs; they spent the entire day discussing the Way, after which Yang returned to court and petitioned for his summons. By imperial decree, he was invited to the capital and settled at the White Lotus Pavilion.

The Emperor, knowing that the Buddha-dharma was profound and subtle, wondered who was capable of deliberating upon it; he issued an edict to summon Master Yuan of Taiping Temple and the eminent scholars of the Three Studies from the two streets. As questions were posed, they arose like a flurry, much like a hundred arrows pursuing a single rabbit.
Jing’s deportment was composed and dignified as he supported his arguments from all four sides, much like Mo Di’s dismantling of the nine types of siege machinery.
Subsequently, his eloquence flowed like water poured from a high pitcher; following his spirited rebuttals, he cited the teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) as supporting evidence.
He further recited "gāthās" without a single hesitation.
The Emperor’s heart was filled with joy, and those who witnessed it marveled and sighed in admiration.
He entered nirvana on the fifth day of the fifth month in the second year of the Shangyuan era, at the age of ninety-five.
An imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Daxiao; he was also named after his place of residence as Chan Master of Mount Sikong.
Biography of Huilang of Longxing Temple in Luzhou, Tang Dynasty: Shi Huilang, styled Gong, was a native of Suian in Xinping.
At the age of twenty-two, he encountered the leader of the Southern School’s Sudden Teaching at Beishan in Quzhou. Intending to request him as his teacher, the master looked back at him and said:
"You have long accumulated pure karma; I am not your teacher. You should go to Tiantai, where you will surely meet a wise craftsman."

Upon arriving at Shicheng Temple on Mount Shanxi, he encountered a Zen master whose origins were unknown. His hair was white as crane feathers and his skin was as clear as ice; his eyes were like flashing lightning, his voice resonated with the harmony of bells and chimes, and his spirit was in union with the Great Void.
He then asked Lang,
"Where are you going?
Lang replied:
“I wish to go to Mount Tiantai to seek the Great Dharma of the Buddha.
Because they were traveling together for some ten li, they rested beneath the trees of a forest, where [Huiyuan] instructed him, saying:
“The Dharma is eternally quiescent; that [reality] is likewise so.”
"Why must you go so far? You should transform those with whom you have a karmic connection; it is fitting that you return to your place of birth to deliver immeasurable multitudes.

Having finished speaking, [the Master] sought [his destination] by no fixed means, and suddenly his original mind awakened to the Buddha’s insight. Dwelling in forests and drinking from mountain valleys for several years, he finally returned to Huian Temple in his native town.
Vimalakīrti, though a layman, wore the robes of the Dharma;
Cunda, though a craftsman, possessed a mind like that of a Buddha.
Yet the black pearl still lies hidden and the lion has not yet roared; the lost youth’s end remains uncertain, and one who crosses a river remains bewildered by the ford.
One day, the mountain ridges and forest slopes of Qinwang Mountain shook; suddenly, a large tortoise appeared, and everyone said to one another, "What auspicious omen is this?
Shortly thereafter, a Chan monk remarked:

“Huiyong came from Yunmen in Kuaiji; he was eight chi and four cun tall, with a prominent nose and large eyes whose gaze pierced others. He was well-versed in such sutras as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Viśeṣacinti-brahma-paripṛcchā*, and the *Vimalakīrti*, and was furthermore broadly proficient in various śāstras.”
The assembly said, "He is a divine monk;
the great tortoise has responded to him here.
Daolang kept his bodhisattva practices secret and requested him to be his teacher.
Huigong asked Huizheng about the meaning of the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, to which he replied:
"It is like the sun shining upon a firefly; it is like the ocean compared to a cow's footprint.
Master Huigong held him in high esteem, saying:
"Zhenjing is his name.

During the Jinglong era, several dozen households, including Yu Shaoxing, the District Magistrate of Ruchuan County, and Yu Ren, the County Magistrate of Xinchang County—both of whom were from his own clan—all revered him as their master and took turns inviting him to visit them.

One night, he suddenly beheld a divine light emanating from his neck, illuminating the mountains and rivers on all sides for more than ten li; among all sentient beings, there was none who did not take refuge in him.
Master Huiyong treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher; from then on, he returned the bow and requested Huilang to ascend the seat.
He first demonstrated that the Dharma-body is omnipresent and identical to all beings, and subsequently clarified that its pervasive transformation makes all things such as they truly are.
The clergy and the laity were filled with joy and each sighed in admiration, saying:
"In the past, when the mountain shook and the tortoise manifested auspicious signs, it was clearly no other than a response to Master Xuan."
By this time, practitioners of Chan meditation from all four directions had gathered there in great numbers.
In the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era, Li Sichen, the Governor of the province, constructed a monastery on the southern slope of Longshan Mountain and invited [the Master] to reside there.
He then formally established a great ordination platform and widely invited masters of the Vinaya, with Master An of Guangzhou and Master Chao of Kuaiji serving as the leaders.

Subsequently, he conceived the aspiration for the rare Dharma and received full ordination; like a perfect pearl or the full moon, his inner and outer qualities were both luminous. He presided over the platform as an ordination master to all, while simultaneously seeking further instruction as a student; thus the esteem of the assembly increased, and his path became ever more honored.
In the seventh year, Wei Lìqí, the Regional Inspector, turned his heart deeply toward him with devotion.
In the eighth year, Xǔ Sīgōng, the Prefectural Administrator of Shèzhōu, invited him to his seat of government.
When Fǎlǎng ascended the Dharma throne, before long a bear lay prostrate before him; it had come upon hearing the bell and departed when the assembly dispersed.
At that time, everyone was struck with fear and apprehension, fearing he might spring upon them.
Yet, considering his sincere desire to hear the Dharma, such was his way of taming fierce beasts.
On the twenty-first day of the ninth month in the thirteenth year, he addressed his disciples, saying:
"I am about to depart.
I have lived three lifetimes in this region; now is my fourth.
Having finished these words, he passed away in solemn stillness at the age of sixty-four.
In accordance with his final instructions, he was cremated and a stupa was erected for him.

As his disciples were numerous and exceptionally gifted, they transmitted Lang’s Dharma in succession like the spreading vines of a gourd. These included Dao-yin, Hui-you, and Dao-chan of Kaiyuan Temple; Xing-hai of Longxing Temple; Jin-yu of Ningguo Temple; You-pai, Yuan-zheng, and Yi-xing of Baolin Temple in Yuezhou; and Yi-xing of Zhulin Temple in Hangzhou, among others. All of them carried on the lineage of Lang.

In the twelfth year of the Dali era, Xiao Ding, the newly appointed Governor of Taishou, composed the inscription; Liu Changqing, the Imperial Secretary, wrote the calligraphy; and Li Kui, the Regional Inspector, engraved the title. These were all renowned public figures, and thus the monument was widely praised for its perfect excellence.

The Biography of Jufang of Anguo Monastery in Runzhou, Tang Dynasty. Jufang, whose secular surname was Cao, was a native of Anlu. His Dharma name was Zhifeng. He was a person of the Cao clan from Anlu.

In my youth, I established my character and principles; I followed Master Lang of Mingfu Monastery in the provincial seat to receive instruction and pursue my studies, where I listened to and recited the two sutras, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, completing my training before receiving full ordination.
After discussing the *Nanzong lun* for several sessions, he immediately brushed aside his robes and rose to leave.

He subsequently attended the Chan assembly at the monastery of Xiu of the Northern School, where he applied himself with keen diligence to investigation; upon their first meeting, Xiu granted him silent approval.
Xiu asked,
"What is it like where the white clouds disperse?
He replied:
"Not ignorant," [he replied].
He asked again:
"After arriving at this state, what is it like?"
Xuanze said,
"From the single branch of right view, five leaves grow.
Xiu nodded in agreement.
Over the course of several years, he entered the inner chamber to attend upon [the Master] and discuss matters; his understanding of the True Way was nearly peerless.
Thereupon, he took his leave to travel in search of the Way, eventually settling at Hanling in Shangdang.
During the years he spent accumulating [his practice], hundreds of disciples gathered, and his requests for instruction were never hindered.
In all that he taught and proclaimed, the general outline was as follows:
truth and falsehood share the same source; progress is measured by the different "prescriptions" of swift or slow; attaining the mind aids the Way, which depends upon cultivation and refinement.
Wu Wenhuan, the Regional Commander of Yuncheng and Palace Attendant, admired his character and sent an envoy to invite him to return to his residence at Jiananguo Monastery.
There he transmitted the Dharma and transformed his disciples; those who revered his ancestral style did not leave his side, and many attained sudden enlightenment.
The Commander of Yuncheng asked,
"What shall we do from this day forward? He replied:
"The ground was spread with golden sand, and people dwelt in peace within this precious realm.
The regional commander of Wu submitted in faith and submission.
Consequently, the military and civilian population of the entire prefecture all came to revere him.
In the household of the Wu family, everyone from the youngest to the eldest revered her as if she were a divine being, and their offerings and almsgiving were abundant.
She subsequently engaged in the transformation of beings through the Way on Mount Wutai for more than twenty years.
When entering into parinirvāṇa, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"My life has come to an end here.
Having finished speaking, he passed away at the age of eighty-one.
It is said that on the third day of the ninth month in the fifteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, his entire body was enshrined in the stupa.
Next, there was the monk Zhifeng of Anguo Monastery in Hezhong Prefecture; his surname was Wu, and he was a native of Huai’an.

Entering the Way in middle age, he exerted himself in moral discipline and was careful in his personal conduct. He practiced the dhūta austerities, and after the meal at dawn, he would not allow even water or broth to pass his teeth.
At Qingjing Temple in his native province, he received the tonsure and full ordination under Master Heng, where he extensively studied the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
Once, while being cross-examined by someone who rebuked him for being mired in names and forms, he became incensed and abruptly ended his lecture.
He then traveled to Mount Wudang, where, upon seeing Master Xiu’s assembly, his doubts were resolved like ice melting away; he then sought to nurture the "sacred embryo" (the seed of enlightenment).
Suddenly departing, he left for Mount Anfeng at Pujin, where he observed the *śīla* of foot-seclusion for ten years, subsisting on wood and drinking from mountain streams.
At that time, the Prefectural Governor Wei Wensheng requested him to return to the city, where he established the Xin'an Guoyuan for him to reside in.
From this point on, those in coarse woolen robes flourished and became numerous.
The Magistrate asked,
"What will become of me after today?"
He replied, "The sun rises from Mōngfà; when it shines upon a tree, there is no shadow at all.
The Magistrate did not initially understand the meaning of these words, so he bowed with joined palms and withdrew.
After a short while, he was enlightened, and his heart was filled with profound realization.
Feng spent more than twenty years traveling among Mount Zhongyue, living in such frugality that his needs were barely met.
Those who attained the Way under him were beyond counting.
After his entry into parinirvāṇa, his disciples erected a stupa thirty paces north of the prefecture.
This is the biography of Shi Xiangyu of Dafoshan in Yingzhou during the Tang Dynasty. Shi Xiangyu’s secular surname was Li, and he was a native of Jiyin.
His father served as a clerk in Yanzhou.
Sengyu possessed the nature of a man of the Way and constantly studied the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*, his spiritual faculties being exceptionally vigorous.
Soon thereafter, he turned his attention toward the Buddhist scriptures and resolved to cast off worldly ways.
He went to the Zhidian Temple in Cangzhou to seek ordination under Vinaya Master Zhiyuan.
After receiving full ordination, he devoted his energy to the study of the Vinaya, nearly completing his mastery of it.

Once he took leave of his teacher to travel and visit sacred sites, ascending Mount Tiantai and climbing Mount Nanyue; at times he entered mountain ravines and at others he dwelt beneath trees, until finally he reached Mount Wutai.
Later, he participated in Master Xiu’s flourishing propagation of the Dharma; their long-held aspirations were in perfect accord, and they marveled at each other’s subtle, resonant insights.
When Xiu questioned him, Fayu’s responses were as profound as an esoteric scripture, and he provided a complete and illuminating explanation for every point.
Xiu observed his extraordinary demeanor in silence.
After many years among the crowds, once he had thoroughly penetrated the source of the mind, he took his leave of Xiu and departed.
He entered Dafoshan on the Fu River, where he maintained rigorous discipline and practiced seated meditation, eating only one meal before dawn.
The provincial governor, Han Run, deeply revered his Way and earnestly summoned him to emerge from the mountains.
Daoyu, however, merely cited illness as an excuse.

Consequently, the assembly of both monastics and laypeople looked up to him with thirsty devotion and sought his refuge. Governor Han sent successive carriages to transport provisions, and offerings arrived in great abundance; he constructed a Dharma Hall, adorned it with exquisite beauty, and frequently came to inquire about the Way.
Prince Han asked,
"Regarding matters after the Buddha-dharma has passed,
what will it be like? He replied:
"Like the vast void, it rests upon those with power.
Thus did King Han revere and honor him.

His followers often numbered in the thousands, comprising both the worthy and the unworthy living together; frequently, monks of unfathomable character were heard to be among those receiving his teachings.
Once, after delivering a discourse, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"How excellent is this assembly! It is difficult to encounter such a gathering.
You must resolve your doubts; do not let this opportunity pass in vain."
He was commanded to wash his hands and rinse his mouth with water; then, sitting upright, he passed away at the age of seventy-three.
This is the Biography of Master Jiangmo Zang of Dongyue in Yanzhou during the Tang Dynasty. Master Shi Zang, whose secular surname was Wang, was a native of Zhaojun.
His father served as a clerk in Bozhou.
From his youth, he sought out teachers; he naturally admired the Dharma and by temperament preferred solitude.
The region of Qiao was infested with malevolent ghosts who used their charms to possess people.
For seven years in his youth, he dwelt alone in a quiet chamber, his solitary form standing apart in the vast wilderness; he never experienced even the slightest fear.
As he grew older, he became increasingly upright and resolute; thus, was he not named "Dharmakīrti" (Subduer of Māra)?

He requested that a young scholar be presented to Chan Master Mingzan at Guangfu Monastery; the Master, perceiving him to be a vessel of the Dharma, challenged him, whereupon the youth responded with such eloquence and agility that his answers surpassed the questions posed.

He retained him as an attendant, who served him diligently and received the Dharma; he was made to recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, completing the entire work in over a month. He was immediately tonsured, received full ordination, and began studying the Vinaya.
Next, he lectured on the *Nanzong lun* (Treatise on the Southern School), and the great potential for awakening was about to be unleashed.
Suddenly casting aside his fly-whisk (*chūbi*), there were few among the sacred sites of the Nine Provinces that he did not ascend.
Later, encountering the flourishing peak of the Northern School, he vowed to take refuge and dwell there.
Xiu asked, "Your name is 'Subduer of Demons,' yet here there are no mountain sprites or forest monsters; have you instead become a demon?
He replied:
"There is Buddha; there is Māra.
Xiu said, "If you are Māra, you must dwell in the inconceivable realm."
He replied, "Even this Buddha is empty; what inconceivability could there be?
At that time, there was no one in the assembly who was not struck with wonder and filled with admiration for him.
Previously, Master Xiu had made a prophetic prediction:
"You have a karmic affinity with the ruins of Shaohao.

Subsequently, he entered Mount Tai for several years, where students gathered in great numbers and provisions were abundantly supplied; his success as a teacher was second only to that of Master Lang of Jinyu Valley.
One day, he told his disciples:
"I am now old and decrepit; when things reach their limit, they must return to their source—this is precisely that time.
Having finished speaking, he passed away.
He was ninety-one years of age.
*Biographies of Eminent Monks Compiled in the Song Dynasty*, Volume Eight;
*Biographies of Eminent Monks Compiled in the Song Dynasty*, Volume Nine.
Compiled by Imperial Decree by the Śramaṇa Zanning, Master Tonghui, recipient of the purple robe, of Tianshou Temple in the Left Ward of the Song Dynasty, et al.

Part Two of the Third Section: Chapter on the Practice of Chan. The Fourteen Principal Transmissions and the Four Recorded Incidental Cases. Biography of Yifu of Ci’en Monastery in Jingzhao, Tang China. Yifu, whose secular surname was Jiang, was a native of Tongdi in Luzhou. His dharma name was Xingsi; he was given the courtesy name Yifu. He was a man of the Jiang clan from Tongdi, Lüzhou.

From his youth, he aspired to the Gate of Emptiness and cast aside worldly affairs. Initially residing at Huigan Temple in Lantian, he occupied a single *fangzhang* chamber for more than twenty years, never once venturing beyond the confines of his room.
Later, he was assigned to Ci'en Monastery in the capital, where his reputation for the Way stood towering high, captivating the hearts of both humans and spirits.

In the eleventh year of the Kaiyuan era, he accompanied the imperial entourage to the Eastern Capital; as they passed through the two prefectures of Pu and Guo, the regional governors, officials, and the common people—both men and women—all carried banners and flowers to welcome him. The roads at every location were so congested that people prostrated themselves in worship in great numbers, gazing upon him without ever feeling satiated.
He passed away in the twentieth year [of the reign], and by imperial decree was posthumously titled the Great Wisdom Chan Master (Dazhi Chanshi);
he was buried to the north of Ique, where tens of thousands of people attended his funeral procession.
Yan Tingzhi, the Vice Director of the Secretariat, personally observed the mourning rites for him as if he were his own disciple, and furthermore composed the inscription for his stele.

Shenxiu was a preeminent figure of the Chan school; although he possessed profound meditative practice and enjoyed the Emperor’s esteem beyond measure, he never gathered disciples or established a formal dharma lineage.
By the time Pujì had been transmitting the teachings in the capital for over twenty years, everyone looked up to him with reverence.

When Fú first traveled to East Luò, he summoned his disciples and instructed them regarding the date of his passing. On that day, those whom the Vice Minister of War Zhāng Jūn, the Grand Marshal Fáng Guǎn, and the Vice Minister of Rites Wéi Zhé had always held in high esteem all arrived in advance to pay their respects.
Fen was then invited into the hall, where he expounded the teachings for his disciples, saying, "The sun is now setting;
this shall be my final farewell.
After a long while, he said to Zhang Wei: "Come to my room."
"I have been ingesting cinnabar elixirs for many years and have never had occasion to attend a funeral.
Having said this, Zhang suddenly departed in secret.
Fú then suddenly said to Fáng:
"I have been traveling with Master Zhang for many years.
He is about to incur an extraordinary calamity, and both his reputation and integrity will be compromised.
Had he completed this Dharma assembly earlier, he would have been able to avoid disaster."
"How regrettable!
he said, then taking him by the hand, added:
"You shall surely become a renowned minister of restoration; exert yourself!"
Having finished speaking, he passed away.

Later, when Zhang Jun fell into the hands of the rebel court, he accepted their false office; whereas Fang Yi and Dai served two successive dynasties and maintained great integrity throughout—both fulfilled the words of Fu.
Furthermore, Shi Xingxi was surnamed Liu and was a native of Luling.
He nourished his person with gentleness and was upright and sincere by nature.
After leaving the mundane world and receiving the precepts, he sought the round by breaking the square and returned to simplicity by carving away the ornate; such was his natural aspiration.
He traveled to Shaoyang to see Chan Master Dajian, who resolved his doubts with a single word, like striking away ignorance.

Having realized his original mind, the local deities successively informed him that it was time for him to return; he subsequently propagated the teachings in Jizhou, where Zen practitioners from all quarters flocked to his hall in great numbers.

On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month in the twenty-eighth year of the Kaiyuan era, he entered parinirvāṇa at his native place. By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled "Great Master," given the honorific name Hongji, and his stupa was named Guizhen.
That stupa was demolished in accordance with the general policy during the Huichang era; later, his Dharma heirs reconstructed and erected it once more.
Biography of Puji of Xingtang Monastery in the Capital of the Tang Dynasty: Shi Puji, surnamed Feng, was a native of Hedong in Puzhou.
Though still young in years, his natural disposition was lofty and spirited; having left secular life to ascend the altar, he followed the sutras and the vinaya.
When he examined the texts and contemplated their meanings, he stood far apart from the common run of practitioners.
When he first heard that Shenxiu was at Yuquan Temple in Jingzhou, Huizhi went there to serve him as a disciple for six years.
Shenxiu marveled at him and transmitted his entire Way to him.
During the Jiushi era, Empress Wu summoned Shenxiu to the Eastern Capital to discuss the Way; she subsequently recommended Huineng, who was then ordained as a monk.
Upon Shenxiu’s death, all those throughout the realm who were devoted to the teachings of Śākyamuni took him as their teacher.
When the Emperor Zhongzong heard that Puji was advanced in years, he issued a special decree ordering him to succeed his original master in leading the assembly of the Dharma.
In the twenty-third year of the Kaiyuan era, an imperial edict commanded Puji to reside in the capital.

At that time, princes, dukes, and high officials vied with one another to come and pay their respects; yet he remained silent, solemn, and spoke but little, making it difficult for those who came to see his cheerful countenance. Consequently, he was held in even higher esteem by those both near and far.
In the twenty-seventh year [of the reign], he passed away at Xingtang Temple in the Capital at the age of eighty-nine.
At that time, all the officials and commoners of the capital who came to pay their respects donned the mourning attire of disciples.
An edict was issued bestowing upon him the posthumous title of Chan Master Dazhao.
Upon his burial, Pei Kuan, the Governor of Henan, along with his wife and children, all wore mourning garments and took their places in the ranks of the disciples.
The entire city wept as they saw him off, leaving the neighborhoods empty;
such was the reason for the profound respect the Prefect Pai held for Huizhi.

As for Huizhi’s propagation of the teachings, there were many miraculous manifestations, all of which Pai witnessed firsthand; moreover, having received the "seal of the mind" from him, his devotion grew ever deeper, even as many at the time mocked and ridiculed him.
Pei visited him morning and evening, observing the etiquette of a disciple without ever deviating from it.
One day he went to see Jingji, who already knew in advance that his disciple Yixing had passed away.

Upon the passing of Ji, Pei was so stricken with grief that it was as if he had lost a close relative; wearing mourning garments and traveling on foot out of the city, his wife and children did the same, which gave rise to the censure of the gentry.
The commentary states:
In the nature of human beings there are likes and dislikes; those who love someone do not see anything loathsome in them, while those who dislike someone do not see anything lovely in them.
Now, when the myriad things are in chaotic profusion, one may indulge in likes and dislikes; yet the Way of the Mean is that which may be loved but not hated.
Those who love it are gentlemen; those who hate it are petty people. To love it without following the Way, however, is the failing of even a gentleman.

When Minister Pei wears the ceremonial cap and robes while presiding over the court, and his official duties rest upon his person, it was only fitting that he did not avoid private conduct that drew public censure; this was indeed appropriate.
It is like a monk who indulges in worldly affairs—why does he not cast off his *kāṣāya* and don the scholar’s robe?
If one has truly attained the Way, what is so wrong about eventually casting off the shackles of worldly life at the end?
If I do not withdraw my hairpin, how could that be a violation of the rites within the gate of Confucius?
If Kuan were practicing the Way beyond the secular world, what further cause for condemnation would there be?
To those of great attainment who possess the comprehensive vision, nothing is impossible.
The Biography of Huairang of Mount Nanyue at Guanyintai, Tang Dynasty. Shi Huairang’s secular surname was Du; he was a native of Ankang in Jinzhou.

From the age of ten, he had a refined fondness for Buddhist scriptures; his appearance was exceptionally radiant, and he possessed a uniquely spiritual bearing. Those who recognized him predicted that these were the marks of one destined for renunciation, not for the pursuit of worldly status.
The arrival of this jewel among men is an auspicious omen; the national celebration is boundless. Compared to the appearances of the qilin, phoenix, tortoise, and dragon, it is beyond counting.

Heaven and Earth do not possess perfect efficacy, and the cycles of the seasons have their waxing and waning. When the fundamental structures are deficient or ruined, and what is insufficient must be supplemented and restored, all is due to the subtle and secret protection of the unseen. Only those who correspond to the Way can perceive its principles; it is not something known by the mediocre.
In my early twenties, I went to Yùquán Monastery in Jīngnán to serve under Vinaya Master Héngjǐng, whereupon I shaved my head and received full ordination.
He sighed and said:

"Now, one who has left the household life practices the Dharma of non-action; there is nothing superior to this in heaven or among men. This is what the Sūtras mean by 'leaving the four crossroads and sitting in the open air.'"
At that time, Master Tan encouraged Let to go to Mount Song to meet Master An; there, An inspired him, whereupon he entered Cao Hou Xi to visit Master Neng.
Master Neng remained serene; there was neither fragrance nor stench. Was it the vast expanse of the great flood surging forth?
Or was it the harmony of the great music as the *Shao* and *Huo* were performed in concert?
He caused [Huiren] to enter deeply into silent concentration and dwell in the immovable *bodhimaṇḍa*;
such was his treatment of him. Once Master Neng’s great affairs were concluded, Huiren then ascended Mount Heng and settled at Guanyintai.
At that time, there was a monk named Xuan who was brought to the criminal prison; he made a vow, wishing for his teacher Leting to rescue and protect him.
Leting knew of this beforehand and exhorted him. The monk escaped the peril, and it was said that he was "Guanyin Who Saves from Suffering"—it was for this reason that he acquired this title.
When his work for the sake of sentient beings was completed, his dharma-heirs were Daojun and Daoi; both had ascended into the hall and beheld its profound depths.
Subsequently, Master Yi beat the drum of the Dharma in Hongzhou, and his disciples were Weikuan and Huahui.
When Daoyi’s great causal conditions were nearing their end, he said to Huiquan and the others:
"The Way of our Master resides in the wondrous; it is independent yet eternal, reaching its destination without abiding. His work of capability is now complete."
Born from the golden mouth and transformed according to the Dharma, you are my son and he is your grandson; as that which is transmitted by a single lamp, how could it ever come to an end?

Lang was born in the second year of the Yifeng era and passed away on the tenth day of the eighth month in the third year of the Tianbao era at Mount Heng; he was sixty-eight years of age and had forty-eight years of monastic seniority.
The Master built a pagoda on a separate peak.
During the Yuanhe era, Kuan and Hui arrived at the capital, where they propagated their own school; the Dharma gate was greatly opened, and hundreds of thousands of lamps were transmitted.
In the capital during the summer, the grand succession of the Dharma-treasure reached its peak.
In the eighth year, Linghu Quan, the Governor of Hengyang, inquired about the traces of [Hui]rang’s past deeds; Quan then donated his robes and wealth to provide for the memorial vegetarian feast.
From then on, every year in the eighth month, it was observed as the "Anniversary of Guanyin.
During the Baoli era, an imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Dahui, and his stupa was named Zuishenglun.
The inscription composed by the Attendant-in-Ordinary Guī Dēng during the Yuánhé era states:

"Biography of Língzhù of the Lángqiā Courtyard at Dà'ān Guó Temple in the Capital of the Táng. Biography of Língzhù of the Lángqiā Courtyard at Dà'ān Guó Temple in the Capital of the Táng: Śramaṇa Língzhù, surnamed Liú, was a native of Bāxī in Miánzhōu.
When he was nearly of an age to pursue his studies, he finally entered the monastic life; he ascended to receive the precepts and sought out teachers, traveling no less than a thousand li.

At the age of forty, he had mastered the path of the Vinaya and concurrently lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; regarding both the Vinaya and the Sūtra, he was diligent in their transmission and instruction.
In his later years, he sought instruction from Chan Master Dazhao, through which he attained realization of the patriarchal tradition; his resolve became even more steadfast.

Later, he traveled to Chang’an and extensively propagated the Chan teachings. Those who admired the Way and sought a teacher numbered no fewer than a thousand, gathering like fish and dragons at a deep pool.

On the tenth day of the fourth month in the fifth year of the Tiānbǎo era, at the hour of Shēn, he manifested his passing at the Śaila Laṅkā Sūtra Monastery in Ānguó Temple; he had reached the age of fifty-six and had spent thirty-six years as a monk.
As his end approached, many strange and miraculous phenomena occurred within the monastery, signaling the collapse of the very pillars and beams of the Dharma.
He sat upright in the full lotus posture and passed away with a serene countenance.

After twenty-one days, the cremation was performed and a stupa was erected on Longshou Peak, adjacent to the place where Fotudengbolu had enshrined the śarīra and to the right of the tomb of Empress Nüwa; on the tenth day of the tenth month of that year, the remains were transferred into the stupa.
The disciples Langzhi, Daoxun, and Ruyi, in their longing remembrance of the Master’s virtue, have maintained the incense and lamps without interruption.
By order of the Inner Attendant and Grand Marshal Zhao Sikan of Tianshui, the monk Shanyun composed this inscription at the site of the stupa.
There was the monk Dharmavara of Lingzhi Temple in Qiantang; his secular surname was Feng, and he was originally a native of Changle.
Having followed his grandfather to serve in officialdom in Jiangdong, he subsequently became a resident of Qiantang.
Futong, whose courtesy name was Yuanda, inherited the family’s official robes and continued their ancestral vocation.

Nevertheless, he thoroughly investigated the remnants of the hundred schools of thought and, holding fast to his resolve, admired the authentic character of Vimalakīrti. He frequently summoned scholars from the Zen groves for discussion and maintained a separate chamber within his home where he made offerings and performed rites, praying for the birth of a worthy heir.
As time passed, he grew up in his family; his nature was precocious and naturally inclined toward solemnity.
As soon as he was old enough to wear clothes, he requested of his father to leave the secular world, and his father did not refuse or detain him.
Having shaved his head and received full ordination, he investigated the mysteries of the Three Vehicles as if looking at the palm of his hand.

Yet by nature he remained steadfast and upright; in a deep cove of this monastery—situated on the northern bank of the Zhe River—he constructed a separate hermitage far removed from the main temple, where he sat in meditative concentration throughout the day.
At that time, fellow practitioners came to his door to seek instruction; as they engaged with him, he guided them according to their specific needs, and many attained realization.

On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month in the second year of the Tiānbǎo era, as dawn was breaking, he informed his attendant and sat upright before suddenly passing away into *nirvāṇa*. He was sixty-five years of age, and his monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera-vaṣa*) was nineteen years.
At that time, the mountain birds wailed mournfully and the clouds and mist hung thick and gloomy; from far and near, the lay devotees weeping were as dense as a wall.
On the nineteenth day of that month, his coffin was moved for burial on the mountain slope beside the monastery.

There were disciples such as Yu Fajie, along with his son Huaifu and his nephew Xishou, who had long placed their hearts in refuge; they organized the construction of the stupa and provided all the resources from their own households.
The stupa was destroyed during the Huichang era; its foundations remain today.
The stone stele has been effaced and lost—how lamentable!
Biography of Shi Xuansu of Youqi Temple in Runzhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Xuansu, courtesy name Daoqing, whose secular surname was Ma, was a native of Yanling in Runzhou.
Born into a distinguished lineage, he was profoundly compassionate from childhood and lived a life of tranquil virtue.
Even as a youth with hair tied in two tufts, he aspired to the Buddhist path; his parents complied with his wish, and he left home to take refuge in the Pure Realm.
In the year of Ruyi (531), he first received the monastic regulations and registered his name at Changshou Temple in Jiangning.

After his full ordination, the light of his precepts blazed forth like a torch, the water of his concentration was as clear as ripples, his contemplation entered the profound and subtle, and his conduct surpassed that of ordinary men.
Having realized the emptiness of form, he constantly admired the patriarchal masters.

In his later years, he traveled south to enter the seclusion of Qingshan Youqi Temple, where he served Master Wei; for many years he attended him personally, striking the great bell with resounding clarity.
He instructed Wei Hui with the supreme Dharma, enabling him to grasp its immutable essence.

From then on, he concealed his physical form through rigorous asceticism, harmonizing stillness and gentleness; he wore tattered robes as undergarments, remaining unchanged through both cold and heat, and showed neither joy nor resentment toward the noble or the lowly, the hateful or the kin—whereby he was at that time called the "Infant Practitioner of the Bodhisattva Path."
As his spiritual accomplishments were already lofty, few people could hope to behold or pay homage to him.

During the Kaiyuan era, the monk Wang Mi invited him to Jingkou; the regional governor Wei Xian entreated him to reside at Helin Temple, where followers from the four assemblies turned to him with sincerity, filling the temple precincts.
Wearing simple robes and sleeping on an empty bed, he never once stepped outside his door; when kings and lords prostrated themselves before him, he remained unmoved.
He regarded worldly fame and profit as being like a phantom.

Suddenly, one day, a butcher came to pay his respects; he was spontaneously moved to realization, repented of his past transgressions, and requested that [the Master] partake of the midday meal at his home. The Master joyfully accepted and descended to his residence.
The officials and commoners were struck with alarm and all exclaimed, "How extraordinary!
Sō replied, "The Buddha-nature is the same; how could that which is unborn be different?"
"Only those who can be saved shall I save; what difference is there?
At the beginning of the Tianbao era, the people of Wu and Yue looked up to him as if he were about to descend to be born among them.
The monk Xixuan of Yangzhou invited him to the north of the river, but [the Master] secretly fled under the cover of night.
The moonless night made crossing difficult, and the river waves were vast and surging; he steered his boat against the wind.
In a mere instant, a single beam of white light appeared; leading the boat directly across, Tongbo was saved in its entirety.
The people of Chu celebrated, saying that the sun of the Buddha had shone once more.
Crowds from the entire prefecture rushed to the ferry crossing to assemble at the site.
People who rejected the Way had no standing place among them; yet those who offered gifts by shedding their robes accumulated like mountains and hills.
He took no notice of these in his heart, ordering that they all be used to provide for the expenses of the "field of compassion" (for the destitute).
Li Cheng, the Minister of Rites and Governor of Yangzhou, purified his heart with devotion and attended upon him twice daily.

Before long, the monastics and laypeople of Jingkou yearned for the sound of the Dharma; they accordingly sent a formal petition across the river, requesting that he return to the prefecture once more.
The two factions were locked in dispute, unable to decide which side to follow.
Li Shi said to others,
"Our original intention was to serve the Way, yet we have instead given rise to attachment and hatred."
Having complied with his request, he returned to Nanjun; those who encountered him were moved by his presence and admired his virtue, finding few to equal him.
On the eleventh day of the eleventh month in the eleventh year of the Tianbao era, at midnight, he passed away without illness at the age of eighty-five.
His passing moved all within the human realm to grief, and his lamentations reached through the city.
On the twenty-first day of that month, his entire body was enshrined in a stupa at the site where he resided on the west side of Mount Huanghe.

The regional governors and the magistrates of the districts all observed the rites of mourning for the Master, leading the multitude in their expressions of grief until the sound reverberated across the rivers and lakes.

When he previously went to the meditation hall within the temple, the tall pines lay prostrate like canopies; yet when other trees were moved, they returned to their original positions just as before.
Furthermore, on the evening of his passing, the twin paulownia trees in front of his chamber withered of their own accord without cause.
Those who understood this considered it a transformation like that of the Twin Śāla Trees.
Yet, the wondrous principle of the True Vehicle transcends all forms and is difficult to conceive.
Auspicious omens and spiritual blessings will surely manifest in response to such resonance.
As the Sūtra says:
"Responding to conditions and acceding to entreaties"—this is precisely what that refers to.

Among his disciples were the Dharma-mirror (Fajian) and Faching of Wuzhong; these two great beings further illuminated the source of the Way, and their accounts are all contained in separate biographies.

His disciples who received the Bodhisattva precepts included the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel Qi Han, the Governor of Guangzhou Liang Qing, the Regional Inspector of Runzhou Xu Qiao, Wei Zhaoli of Jingzhao, Han Shang of the Secretariat for Palace Memorials, Li Dan, Vice Censor-in-Chief, and Cui Lingqin of the Ministry of Rites. All were eminent figures among the monastic community who shared a profound bond of teacher and disciple; they also once sought instruction at Mount Jing, much as Yue Zhengzichun did with Confucius.
Washing one’s heart in reverent contemplation, the celestial river seems even higher;
as the water-mirror clarifies the mind, those who attain profound awakening are many.

Reaching the Taihe era, [the Emperor] admired his legacy from afar and held his noble virtue in high esteem, posthumously bestowing upon him the title of Grand Vinaya Master and the honorific pagoda name of Taishan Dabao Hangzhi.
Later generations often addressed him by his secular surname, calling him Mazu; others used both his surname and given name together, as in the case of Ma Su.
The commentary states:

Since the "Heaven-Pervading" [Master Huiyuan] established that all monastics must take the Śākya clan as their surname, this perfectly accords with the *Āgama Sūtras* which would later arrive; should we not therefore make this our primary concern?
That Master Su was addressed by his secular surname must surely have had its reason. Alas!

Even among such a flourishing lineage of Dharma heirs, this erroneous appellation could not be suppressed; thus we know that Master Su’s name, Yiyi Fei, was so revered throughout the four seas that he descended into the secular realm.
Now, as we prepare for what is to come, it is appropriate to rectify the titles.
*Biography of Huizhong of Mount Wudang in Junzhou, Tang Dynasty*. Śramaṇa Huizhong, whose secular surname was Ran, was a native of Zhuji in Yue Prefecture.
Who could distinguish his age?
Some say he was in his ninetieth year.
His skin and flesh were as clear as ice and snow, and his spiritual countenance was lofty and refreshing.
Having been fond of learning since his youth, he received the Dharma from Shuangfeng; silently preserving his true nature, his mind inherited the single seal.

His practice was free from the mark of abiding as he traveled to test himself at famous mountains—Wuling, Luofu, Siming, and Tianmu. At White Cliff he leaned against the Emperor’s peak, and at Purple Pavilion he brushed the vault of heaven; sometimes he dwelt peacefully beneath pine trees for ninety days, and sometimes he stilled his thoughts in samādhi while suspended in mid-air.

Having suspended the precept of the bright moon, one also purifies the mind of lapis lazuli; having already crossed the gateway of dhyāna-samādhi, one does not give rise to views concerning non-arising.
Majestic as Mount Sumeru, the eight winds cannot move it;
clear as a polished mirror, what of the myriad phenomena could remain hidden?
If I should remain here, I shall dwell among the thousand peaks of Wudang, becoming as familiar with deer as they are with me;
if I should go forth, I shall follow the single path of Tiger Brook to beg for alms among the people of the world.
I traveled briefly through the regions of Wu and Chu, eventually reaching the Shunyang River.
There I chose to dwell among the groves and springs of Dangzi for over forty years,
deeply entering the holy meditative concentration of the Dharma King and its eighty thousand broad gateways.
The fame of the Way resounds far and wide, and its power is fully manifest!

During the Kaiyuan era, the Prefect, formerly the Palace Secretary and Marquis of Kaiguo Wang Ju, and the Chief Secretary, Vice Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices Zhao Yizhen, were pure in their faith toward the Lake; moved by his reputation, they delighted in the Way, halted their carriage to seek the stillness of the silent realm, and entered a state of profound emptiness.
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and scattered flowers of gold and silver, no different from the Elder Megha;
he grasped the hand of the Buddha and beheld him as a mote of dust, equaling the Rishi Vimala.
He petitioned the imperial court regarding the profound essence [of the Dharma] and was summoned to reside in a fragrant monastery, which was Longxing Temple.
Consequently, former Ministers, Military Commissioners, Princes, Dukes, and high officials all prostrated themselves in homage, following him like the wind to inquire after the Way.
Zhong was profoundly erudite in glossaries and commentaries, extensively mastering the sutras and vinaya; in subduing demons and restraining externalists, who could rival him?

He could not be intimidated by awe nor moved by profit; he consumed his meals at sunrise and purified his mind before the moon. Amidst the clear breeze and flying frost, his steadfast integrity surpassed that of the bamboo. His words were restrained and his principles reached their ultimate depth, thereby breaking the banner of arrogance.
Regarding "sudden" enlightenment, it leaves no trace; regarding "gradual" cultivation, it returns to the ordinary to accord with the Way.
When attained within the mind, even *eranda* (Ilan) becomes a *candana* tree;
when lost at the finger, even nectar becomes a garden of thorns.
The Sublime is ineffable; though flowers abound, fruits are rare. In this world, there are those who grasp at pebbles in the water, believing they have obtained lapis lazuli gems;
or who scoop up bubbles in a jar, claiming to have acquired mani jewels.
This is why Zhong rebuked him and sought to stop him, yet could not bring himself to do so.
Thus, there is the teaching of "transcending Vairocana" to prevent one from seeking the Buddha;
and the discourse on "surpassing the Dharma-body" to ensure that the true nature remains untainted.
How could one transcend Vairocana, or leap beyond the Dharma-body?
Therefore, the mind of emptiness unites with the principle of emptiness; subtle delusions are like clouds and mists, while the penetration of the fundamental source is like the sun and moon.
The court officials arrived with their carriages yoked in pairs, yet he remained unmoved in his meditative concentration as he received their prostrations; his demeanor was solemn and majestic.

This is what is meant by the ancients not rising to welcome those who came within seven paces, bestowing blessings even upon the sovereign of ten thousand chariots—how much more so for the hundred officials!

Emperor Suzong, who had firmly established order throughout the realm, heard of his lofty virtue. On the sixteenth day of the first month of the second year of the Shangyuan era, he issued an imperial edict through the Inner Attendant Sun Chaojin, dispatching a mounted courier to invite him. The handwritten decree read:

"The Emperor sends this inquiry: We have heard that you ride the Supreme Vehicle to bring peace to the Central Land, and that as a Great Being who benefits others, you work together with all to save sentient beings."

The Master, with the mirror of the Dharma held high, expounds the teaching in a single voice; the treasuries open their secrets, and the realm enters perfect clarity. His great compassion never tires of acting as a bridge and raft, and his ultimate goodness surely illuminates universal salvation.
The Venerable Hero’s entrustment truly rests upon my person.
I contemplate joining with Dao’an to proclaim his wondrous efficacy and extensively nourish the flow of blessings and moisture throughout the great trichiliocosm.
To transmit the mysterious pearl of the Ungraspable and to extract the poisonous arrows of those mired in delusion—this is a most auspicious opportunity; do not consider it a labor.
Carrying your monk’s staff, you have come; the capital is not far away.
You have long since purified your mind, answering my humble expectations.
As the spring chill persists, I hope you are well and at peace!
"I send this letter; there is little more to say.
