Zhong, ever mindful that the Dao is omnipresent and that the cultivated fields and the wilds are no different, proceeded to enter the palace with dignified steps and led [the Emperor] up to the main hall.
As the frost-tipped staff first descended, the sun shone upon the dragon-patterned robes; celestial incense burned as the wind drifted through the feathered canopy.
At that time, Zhong raised his head to follow in step, his divine countenance solemn and majestic.
The Son of Heaven held him in high esteem and treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher.
He presented the essentials of governing people and administering the state, and elucidated the spirit of the eras of Yao and Shun.
Upon hearing this, the Emperor sat up straight, his knees drawn forward toward the mat.
The Nine Dragons sprinkled the waters of the lotus, and the Ten-Thousand-Wagons Sovereign tasted the flavor of the *amṛta*.
Thereupon, he was carried upon a palanquin to the hall, where they sat and discussed the Way, setting aside conventional ritual protocols.
Soon thereafter, Zhu Guanghui, the General of the Flying Cavalry, was ordered to proclaim the imperial decree for [the Master] to reside at Qianfu Monastery.
The Chancellor Cui Huan followed him there to seek instruction; their principles resonated within his heart, and he discussed them throughout the court and the commonalty.
Those who truly recognize the truth often find their way there.

When Emperor Baoying ascended the throne and governed the state with filial piety, he did not alter his former regard; he opened up ten thousand *li* of heaven as if beholding the moon over the Three Rivers.

Furthermore, by imperial decree, the inner attendant Yuan Shouhong was ordered to escort him near the palace gates to be stationed at Guangzhai Temple. Incense and rice arrived like clouds, and purple robes descended from heaven.

Although messengers crowded the Chan gate to prevent his advance, and the imperial treasury arrayed jade and silk to fill the courtyard, he regarded them as bubbles and viewed them as dreams; serene and carefree, he delighted in the natural realm of Heaven.
Furthermore, only by not returning from Mount Luofu can one be called "seated in tranquility" (yànzuò);
only by departing forever from the Twin Peaks does one truly accord with the non-arising (wúshēng).
The primordial womb of attaining sainthood lies herein; this is precisely why the myriad practices arise simultaneously and the thousand gateways do not burden the mind.

Thus, the drum of Tuṣita produces sound without form, and the lute of the Asuras resonates without being plucked; incense is transmitted to the Lord of Devas, and flowers rain down upon the King of Emptiness. This was witnessed by Zhong, who constantly recalled the words of the Great Master:
"If you wish to attain the Way, go to Mount Heng or Mount Wudang."

Consequently, he memorialized the throne to establish Taiyi Yanchang Temple on Mount Wudang and Xiangyan Changshou Temple in Dangzi Valley on Mount Baitia, requesting that a copy of the Tripitaka be bestowed upon each temple and that monks be ordained to maintain them.
The portraits of the two sages were enshrined at that Wudang Mountain.
The King’s words were most sincere, and the officials followed his instructions.
Although the Monkey River and the Goose Pagoda have not yet been adorned upon the Central Peak;
With thatch-roofed rafters and a wattle-and-daub door, it was already named a Buddhist temple.

When the Imperial Calligraphy graced its plaque, the characters curled like phoenixes and soared like magpies; the mountains and rivers shone with brilliance, and both monastics and laypeople rejoiced. One could foresee the golden halls soon to be realized, and perceive that the jade terraces were not far off.

In the eighth year of the Dali era, he again memorialized that monks from among those renowned for their mastery of the sutras, the vinaya, and the dhyāna methods should be selected from the monasteries of the famous mountains throughout the empire to fill the quota of twenty-one persons.
The Daoist community, with their feathered robes and black vestments, was without exception filled with joy.
Numbering in the tens of thousands, they were employed to bring blessings to the imperial palace.
When Zhong was in Nanyang and fell within the territory of the rebels, he earnestly requested to avoid the danger, but his pleas were all denied.
Facing the edge of a white blade, his expression remained unshaken; perched upon the azure clouds, he sat calmly without yielding.

When the commander observed that his meditative virtue was as tranquil as still water and his refined demeanor loftily detached, he cast down his sword, prostrated himself, and requested to serve him as a disciple.
At that time, those who encountered bandits while seeking refuge were numerous.
Before long, a group of robbers arrived again and said,
"We cannot follow the example of those before us."
Thereupon, he took up his staff and set out, traveling along the river.
Those who attempted to follow in his footsteps, remaining steadfast and refusing to avoid him, were all put to death.
Thus we know that the clouds, mists, and atmospheric portents were as if foreseen by him; that he preserved them without comment—how profound is the Way!
The Golden Register says, "Prajñā is without knowing, yet there is nothing it does not know"—is this not what is meant?
When inner virtue is fully realized, its external manifestation becomes ever more expansive; though one treasures the jewels within oneself, no one can perceive them.
Alas! When the "Dragon’s Vigorous Display" was discussed, Guṇaprabha did not understand it;
when the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven rained down flowers, Mingche failed to recognize them.
That former sages grew weary of the world and their correct vision subsequently perished—is this not truly tragic!
Suddenly his illness became critical; though the court physicians were of no avail, he knew his time had come. When those around him asked about his final affairs, he said:
"The Buddha has clear teachings; if you follow and practice them, you will be free from all entanglements."
"What more need I say?
On the ninth day of the twelfth month of the tenth year, at the hour of the rat (midnight), with his right side down and feet crossed, he passed away peacefully.
When the officials reported this to the throne, the Emperor’s heart was filled with compassion.
An imperial messenger came to offer condolences, providing exceptionally generous funeral gifts.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Great Realization Chan Master (Dazheng Chanshi).
A mandate was issued for his remains to be returned to Xiangyan Temple in Dangzi, following the principle of returning to one's origins.
He provided the necessary provisions from his own resources for the funeral rites and the final adornments, mourning deeply at the site of the Dharma-assembly.

By imperial decree, he ordered the monk Dajie of Xingtang Temple—who served as the Director of the Palace Attendants—to oversee the arrangements; having long engaged in Buddhist discourse with him, Dajie’s mind was as expansive as one who has cleared away the clouds. Although not a formal disciple, his grief surpassed that of a dharma-heir.
Whenever he presented memorials or petitions, the Emperor granted them all approval.

Among his lay disciples were Sun Zhigu, a Grand Master of the Palace Gate (Kaifu), along with his younger brother Zhao Jin, an Inner Attendant (Neichangshi), and the brothers Jushi Jingchao and others; among his monastic disciples were Zhi Cheng of Qianfu Monastery, Zhide of Guangzhai Monastery, Dao Mi, the Abbot of Xiangyan Monastery, and others—numbering some tens of thousands in total.
I lament the final tally of the stone chambers and grieve for the towering pagoda on the cloud peaks;
the morning bell is struck in vain within the lofty hall, and the evening chants are performed in silence upon the mountain ahead.
"The wise man has passed away; who will now have a model to look up to?
The *śramaṇa* Fēixī, a translator of scriptures, composed a stele inscription to record his virtues.
Biography of Zhìxián of Gānquán Monastery in Tàiyuán, Táng Dynasty. The *śramaṇa* Zhìxián, surnamed Jiāng, was a native of Jiānyáng.

His innate mind was firm and disciplined; even in his youth, he established a standard for himself. Having fulfilled the requirements for renunciation, he soon received the full precepts. Having partaken of the gradual teachings, he guarded his sense faculties, maintained his integrity in cultivating the mind, and never deviated from the monastic rules.

In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era, he attended upon Chan Master Dàoyī at Fójíyán in his native province; he served him without interruption, fetching water and gathering firewood, devoting himself solely to diligent toil.

While traveling, he visited Mount Jinhua and the Red Pine Cave (Chisong Dong), the site where Huang Chuping transformed stones into sheep; there, steep ridges rose in dense clusters, and a spring-fed lake lay about a hundred paces away.
His disposition was eccentric; having settled upon a mountain peak, an old man from the wilds carried fragrant rice and vegetables to provide for him.
Once, during a great drought, Xian struck a stone against the sky and cursed the dragons, saying:
"You are but dragons of karma; you have no power at all."
"Why do you, O Bodhisattva Dragon King, not follow the Buddha’s command to save the common people?
As soon as he finished striking the stone, it rained down in torrents, and the people of Wulu were all filled with joy.

Later, while traveling to Chang’an, eminent officials and men of great virtue petitioned him in succession to serve as the preceptor for the meritorious works of a great monastery; Hui-xian was struck with awe and refused them.

The next day he set out, ascending Mount Wutai, where he eventually stayed at Ganquan Monastery in Taiyuan. Monastics and laypeople who wished to study the principles of Chan meditation arrived there one after another.
He passed away without illness, and was posthumously granted the title of Chan Master Dayuan, thereby commemorating his virtue.
Biography of Weizhong of Huanglong Mountain, Tang Dynasty. Shi Weizhong, surnamed Tong, was a native of Chengdu Prefecture.

In his youth, he served under the Chan Master Daoguanyuan at Mount Daguang; though this divine steed was currently tethered in its stall, were it to lift its hooves, it would leap over a thousand li in an instant.
While traveling to Mount Song, he met Chan Master Shenhui; his doubts were resolved and he fell into profound silence, abiding in the Great Dharma.
Upon surveying the sacred sites, he saw that Huanglong Mountain was lush, verdant, and extraordinary, so he established a thatched hut there.

At the ends of its streams and the depths of its valleys dwell many venomous dragons; when they exhale their breath, a misty haze arises, and those mountain folk who encounter it often fall as if stricken by miasma, for medical practitioners find little efficacy in treating them.

Zhong was initially unaware of this; he dwelt alone in meditative stillness, drinking from mountain streams and eating forest fruits, whereupon the monsters all curled up and withdrew, leaving the mountain folk unharmed.
Someone heard a voice in the air saying:
"That you, Master, dwell here is a great blessing for the people; it has brought us liberation."
Consequently, the local people named this mountain "Subdued Dragon," saying that Zhong had subdued the king of scaly creatures; thus it was so called.
He entered parinirvāṇa in the third year of the Jiànzhōng era, at the age of seventy-eight.
In the ninth month of that year, the stupa was moved.

This concludes the Biography of Xiqian of Mount Shitou on Nanyue during the Tang Dynasty. Biography of Shi Xiqian of Mount Shitou on Nanyue during the Tang Dynasty: Shi Xiqian’s secular surname was Chen; he was a native of Gaoyao in Duanzhou.
When his mother was pregnant with him, she had no desire for meat or blood.
Upon his birth, he was precocious; though still a mere child, he required no nursemaid's care.
After his capping ceremony, he was reliable in his word and honor, never once offending others with his temper or countenance.

The local villages were inhabited by the Qiang and the Dong, whose people feared ghosts and spirits and practiced many superstitious sacrifices. They generally used oxen and wine to pray for blessings from the "sages" they venerated.
Whenever [Huiyuan] moved to a new location, he would go to destroy their shrines and take back the oxen to return them to the owners.
Over several decades, the elders of the district were unable to restrain his conduct.
Hearing that Master Dajian had come from the south, students followed him one after another.
Huian went straight to him; Dajian joyfully took his hand and playfully said to him:
"If you truly become my disciple, you shall surely resemble me.
Xian raised his eyebrows and smiled,
saying, "Yes."
Soon thereafter, his spiritual faculties were suddenly awakened, and he felt as vast and clear as after a fresh clearing of the skies.
From then on, he traveled between Mount Luofu and the Three Gorges.

In the sixteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, he received full ordination at Mount Luofu; that same year, he returned to the mountain, where he dreamed that he was riding a tortoise with Dajian, swimming together in a deep pool.
Upon waking, he performed a divination and said:
"The tortoise is spiritual wisdom; the pond is the ocean of nature.
I and my teacher have long been riding upon spiritual wisdom to roam through the ocean of nature—what need is there for a dream?"
Later, hearing that Master Si of Mount Qingyuan in Luling was the successor to Caoxi, he again adjusted his robes and followed him.
At that time, students flocked to Master Si’s gate like deer.
When Huaijian arrived, he said:
"Though there may be many horns, a single unicorn is sufficient.
At the beginning of the Tianbao era, he first established Nan Temple on Mount Heng.
To the east of the temple was a rock shaped like a platform; he built a hermitage upon it and dwelt there atop the precipitous peak.
The assembly looked up to him and called him Master Shitou.
Initially, there were three Chan masters in Mount Yue—Gu, Zan, and Rang—all of whom were disciples of Caoxi. They said to their followers:
"That Shitou delivers a true lion’s roar; he will surely cause your eyes to become clear and cool."
Consequently, his disciples returned to him with devotion.
When someone asked about liberation, he replied:
"Who is there that can bind you?"
When asked about the Pure Land, he replied,
"Who could defile you?
His responses were all of this nature— concise and swift.
In the second year of the Guangde era, his disciples requested that he descend from the end of the beam.

Since then, those who presided over Daji in Jiangxi and Shitou in Hunan have been as numerous as travelers on a busy road; yet, had they not encountered these two great masters, they would have remained ignorant.

On the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month in the sixth year of the Zhenyuan era, the year of Gengwu, he passed away peacefully at the age of ninety-one, with sixty-three years of monastic seniority (*bhikṣu-vaṣa*).
His disciples Huilang, Zhenlang, Bolì, Daowù, Daoxiàn, and Zhizhōu together erected a stupa for him on the eastern ridge.

Thirty years after the stupa was completed, Liu Ke—the Court Doctor of the National University, who had long understood the profound principles of the Way and deeply admired the ancestral tradition—met with Daoxian and extensively recounted the teachings of his late master.
In the Chángqìng era, Kē (Báo Zǐ) looked back upon the illustrious deeds of his predecessors and erected a stele to record their virtues.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled the Great Master Wújì (Boundless), and his stūpa was named Jiànxiàng (Manifesting the Marks).

Biography of Shénhuì of Jìngzhòng Monastery in Chengdu Prefecture, Tang Dynasty. Shí Shénhuì, whose secular surname was Shí, was originally a man from the Western Regions. His family name was Shí. He was a native of the Western Regions.
His grandfather moved his residence and settled in Qí, so he became a native of Fèngxiáng.
By chance, his innate nature was liberated from constraints and his brilliant wisdom emerged from within; yet, as his great gem remained unpolished, no one at the time recognized his potential.
At the age of thirty, he entered Shu to pay his respects to Master Wuxiang. Possessing keen faculties, he attained sudden enlightenment, achieving a profound resonance with the Mind-Seal.
Master Wuxiang sighed in admiration, saying:
"The Way of my school now rests with you!"
Thereafter, his virtue was fulfilled and his wisdom expanded, and he flourished as a master of the Chan school. Its general outline is as follows:
"Quiescent illumination extinguishes objective realms; through transcendent realization, one is free from discursive thought. The mind itself is the Buddha; one perceives no self-existent body."
"When they are stilled and closed, devoid of manifest form, their substance is like that of earth and wood.

Yet when their wondrous function silently brings salvation—like the movement of clouds and the falling of rain—the simple masses joyfully perceive the transformation; they observe appearances and shift toward goodness, hearing words and reforming their errors."

Upon reaching a state of vast openness, he purified himself of all attachments and fetters, leading those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities to enter the Way according to their respective levels.

On the twelfth day of the eleventh month in the tenth year of the Zhenyuan era, he manifested illness; sitting upright in the full lotus posture, he passed away. He was seventy-five years of age and thirty-six years of *dharma-lakṣa* (monastic seniority).
The śramaṇa Nadi attained the Way of his master and transmitted it to future generations.

On the twenty-second day of the second month in the twelfth year, his disciples—both monastics and laypeople—moved his seat to the northern corner of the monastery. Out of deep longing for their master’s virtue, they wailed and wept so loudly that the mountains and forests were moved to change color.
Initially, when Huì was transmitting the Dharma in the region of Kunwei (Sichuan), monastics seeking Chan from all directions flocked to his monastery.

At that time, Wei Gao, the Prince of Nankang, placed his heart’s deepest trust in Huì; upon the Master's death, he wept with grief and looked back upon him with longing, for he had roughly entered Huì’s gate and attained the essentials of his Chan teachings.
A stele was erected for him; he composed the text himself and also calligraphed it, which brought glory to the Chan school.
Biography of Fazhin of Mount Jing in Hangzhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Fazhin, whose secular surname was Zhu, was a native of Kunshan in Wu Commandery.

His family lineage was refined and elegant; both his grandfather and father were masters of both the profound mysteries of Buddhism and Confucianism, yet they lived with haughty indifference in the forest retreats and did not serve in office.

When Faqin conceived him, his mother, Lady Guan, suddenly dreamed that a lotus flower grew in the courtyard; she then plucked one bud and tied it to her garment. Upon waking, she immediately began to loathe the smell of meat and pungent spices.
By the time he reached the age of ten, while still wearing his hair in braids, he took pleasure in Buddhist devotions.
By nature gentle and refined, with a taste for the noble and sublime, he applied himself diligently to the classics and histories, subsequently gaining admission through the local examination system.
At the age of twenty-eight, he prepared his luggage to travel to the capital; on his way through Dantu, he encountered the Chan Master Sù of Helin.
Recognizing him intuitively through profound discernment, the Master perceived his extraordinary character and said to him:
"Observing that your spiritual treasury is warm and refined, you are almost one who possesses innate knowledge."
"If he can leave the household life, he will surely realize the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.

Having heard this, [Hui]qin awakened to his original mind; he personally shaved the boy's head and said to his disciple Fajian, "This child shall, in days to come, greatly promote my teaching and serve as a teacher to others."

He immediately ascended the altar to receive the precepts, refining his conduct and settling into dhyāna. Having grasped the single word "direct path," he transcended the three trainings of circumstantial practice.
From this point on, he took leave of Huisu to travel south;
Huisu said, "As you follow the current of your journey, stop whenever you encounter the 'Direct Path'."

Later, arriving at Lin’an, he gazed upon the lofty peaks to the northeast, which were part of the Tianmu range. He casually questioned a woodcutter, who told him they were Mount Jinshan; he then planned to hang up his monk’s staff there.
Seeing thatched covers spread over snares and nets, he approached them and sat down calmly. He remained seated with solemn composure.

At that time, the snow and rain had just cleared, and there was no smoke or fire nearby. When the hunters arrived and were about to take his things, they were greatly astonished and marveled at him; they all burned the nets, broke their bows, and ceased their killing.
He descended the mountain to recruit people to build a small chamber for him, inviting him to reside there.
As he lived near the mountains with the sea before him, the local official Wu Zhen donated a private villa to support him.
From that time on, his influence flourished and those who came to study under him became numerous.
In the second month of the third year of the Dali era (the Wushen year), Emperor Daizong Ruizu issued an edict stating:

"I have heard that in the region east of the Yangtze River there is a Chan master who embodies the Way, whose virtuous nature is as pure as ice and frost, and who dwells in the forests and wilds in pure conduct. With a humble mind, I gaze toward him with longing, my thirst for his presence hanging heavy."

Where there is resonance, there is surely penetration; this is a source of great celebration for the nation. We pray that you, O Venerable Monk, will descend far to the Central Kingdom so that we, Your Majesty, may fully turn toward you in devotion.
May you not fail the power of your vows, manifesting forms in response to sentient beings.
I now dispatch the Inner Attendant Huang Feng to proclaim this decree, specifically arriving to issue an imperial summons to welcome you; may you swiftly comply with my wishes.
The spring is warm; I hope the Master is well.
I send this message and shall not write further.
An imperial edict was issued:

"The local province shall provide for his transport; wherever he arrives at a prefecture or county, a pure courtyard must be opened and prepared for his lodging. Officials are not permitted to visit him, lest they exhaust the Master’s mental and physical strength."
"The disciples are not many; let them attend upon him as they please.
When the Emperor saw this, he respectfully inquired about the essentials of the Dharma and provided offerings with great diligence.

Yang Wan, the Minister of Education, was deeply devoted to the pivot of the Way, and his conduct surpassed that of ordinary men. Upon seeing [the Master], he was held in high esteem by all; withdrawing, he sighed and said:
"This is truly a transcendent gentleman beyond the mundane world; it is difficult to find his name!
The Emperor repeatedly bestowed upon him silks and fabrics and presented imperial delicacies, yet he declined and would not accept them all.
He lived simply in plain clothes and on coarse food, requiring his disciples to go on alms rounds for their sustenance, and he used only earthenware vessels for his meals.
Possessing few desires and being content with little, he was beyond compare.
When the Emperor heard of this, his reverence increased further, and he said to Chan Master Zhong of Nanyang:
"Grant him the honorific title of 'Qin Yi'.
By imperial decree, he was bestowed the title Guoyi.
In the fifth year of the Zhenyuan era of Emperor Dezong’s reign, an envoy was dispatched bearing an imperial letter to commend his services, along with generous gifts and rewards.

While [Wang] Qin was in the capital and upon his return to Zhejiang, those who served as his attendants and were eminent worthies who governed prefectures and counties, and who observed the ritual of disciples toward him, included Chancellor Cui Huan, Pei Jin Gong (Du), Di Wushi Qi, Chen Shaoyou, and others.
From the Huai River southward, women who requested the honorific title of "Gigi" were all designated as "Mount Gongde.

In the sixth year, the Prefect Wang Yan requested that she be moved to the Pure Court of Longxing Monastery within the prefectural seat, so as to elegantly avoid the destruction of her mountain retreats by Han Hang.

In the twelfth month of the eighth year, the *renshen* year, he manifested illness; after preaching the Dharma, he passed away. His age was seventy-nine, and his years of ordination (*dharmakṣapa*) were fifty.
Emperor Dezong posthumously conferred upon him the title "Dajue" (Great Enlightenment).
The disciples he taught were Chan Master Chonghui; next, Chan Master Yan of Mount Dalu; Chan Master Wu of Mount Xing in Fanyang, whom he studied under; and finally, Chan Master Guangfu of Qingyang.
At that time, his disciples Shixiang, Changjue, and others performed the funeral rites and erected a stupa containing his entire body at the Jingyuan Monastery of Longxing.
Previously, while Huiqin resided on the mountain, fierce beasts and birds of prey had become tame and familiar with him.
A white rabbit once knelt twice between his staff and sandals.
Furthermore, he once raised a chicken that would not eat living creatures; it followed him like a shadow and never wandered elsewhere.
When he entered Chang’an, his crowing ceased after three days of loud clamor.
Today, his tomb lies upon the summit of the mountain.
His physical appearance was imposing and grand; he stood seven chi tall, and his skeletal structure was extraordinary.
The sculptor’s likeness within the stupa today still appears lifelike as he leans upon his desk.

During the Tianfu renxu year while the Qian family ruled the state of Hangzhou, a rebel named Xu Si incited a riot; soldiers from Xuancheng joined the fray and opened this stupa, believing that treasures were contained within.
They saw two jars joined together, top to bottom; the body was preserved within, its hair grown long enough to cover the face.
The soldiers closed the jars and departed.

Wang Yan, the Regional Inspector (*cishi*), composed a stele to recount his virtues. Cui Yuanhan, Director of the Ministry of Revenue (*bilibu langzhong*); Cui Xuanliang, Regional Inspector of Huzhou; and the late Chancellor Li Jifu, along with Qiu Dan, each erected their own memorial steles.
Biography of Dao-shu of Mount Sanfeng in Shouchun, Tang Dynasty. The monk Dao-shu, surnamed Wen, was a native of Tangzhou.
From his youth, he possessed eloquence and wisdom; he was profound, serene, and open-minded, devoting himself to the study of the scriptures and classics without the slightest slackening.
As a person, he was steadfast and firm enough to manage affairs, and possessed the integrity to rectify the times.
Encountering the monk Dennyu by chance, he vowed to leave the mundane world.

Depressed that his years were approaching forty and that his pursuit of the Dharma had been delayed, he paid homage to Master Hye-mun of Daegwang-yeon on Mount Myeongweon in his own province to receive instruction, and immediately underwent tonsure and ordination.
Having received full ordination two years later, he then observed the direction of the Way, traveling everywhere including Tiantai and Nanyue.
Later, returning to Eastern Luoyang, he encountered the lineage of Master Huixiu; like a lotus in bloom, his understanding became thorough and his mind tranquil.

His secular name was Xuanzong. He was born in the year of the *dingwei* (586) during the reign of Emperor Wen of the Northern Zhou. His father, Ma Shizhen, served as the Governor of Hanzhou. At birth, his mother dreamed that she saw a golden statue enter her mouth; upon waking, she gave birth to him. When he was seven years old, he entered the school of Confucius, where he studied the classics and histories with great diligence. By the age of thirteen, he had mastered the *Lunyu*, *Analects*, and the *Zuo Zhuan*. He was exceptionally intelligent and possessed a profound capacity for understanding. He could recite the *Book of Changes* from memory and was well-versed in the *Book of Documents*, the *Book of Poetry*, and the *Spring and Autumn Annals*. He also excelled in calligraphy and painting. At that time, the Chan Master Huiming resided at Jingshan Temple in Jingzhou. Hearing of Daoyi’s reputation, he summoned him to the temple to serve as an attendant. After three years, Daoyi’s conduct became increasingly refined, and he began to study the Buddhist scriptures. He eventually received full ordination and took up residence at Dongshan Temple in Yuzhang. There, he encountered the Venerable Zhixian, who tested him by asking, "What is the meaning of Bodhidharma coming from the West? Daoyi replied, "The Great Way has no gate. Zhixian said, "If there is no gate, how can one enter? Daoyi replied, "Entering is not difficult; it is only that there is no gate. Zhixian then asked, "How do you enter? Daoyi remained silent. Zhixian remarked, "Your words are indeed eloquent, but you have not yet attained the essence. Daoyi then bowed and withdrew. Later, Daoyi traveled to Mount Lu, where he visited the Venerable Huiming. Huiming asked, "Where have you come from? Daoyi replied, "I have come from the place where there is no coming. Huiming asked, "Where are you going? Daoyi replied, "I am going to the place where there is no going. Huiming asked, "Who is this person who has no coming and no going? Daoyi replied, "It is precisely because there is no person that there is no coming and no going. Huiming said, "Excellent! You have truly seen the Buddha-nature. Subsequently, Daoyi traveled to Jiangxi. While staying at the Longxing Temple in Xinfeng, he encountered the Venerable Huairang. One day, Huairang was tending the fire, and Daoyi asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Huairang struck the hearth with his staff and said, "Do you understand? Daoyi said, "I do not understand. Huairang said, "If you had understood, you would have been a Buddha. Daoyi remained silent. Huairang said, "You have already attained it; why do you seek further? Daoyi bowed and withdrew. In the second year of the Yongchun era of the Tang (683), Daoyi traveled to the capital, Chang’an, where he visited the Venerable Fatai at the Xingfu Temple. Fatai asked, "From where do you come? Daoyi replied, "I come from the place where there is no coming. Fatai asked, "Where are you going? Daoyi replied, "I am going to the place where there is no going. Fatai asked, "Who is this person who has no coming and no going? Daoyi replied, "It is precisely because there is no person that there is no coming and no going. Fatai said, "Excellent! You have truly seen the Buddha-nature. Daoyi then returned to Jiangxi and settled at Kaiyuan Temple in Hongzhou. He lived there for over forty years, teaching and transforming disciples. His followers numbered in the thousands. In the first year of the Tianbao era (742), he passed away at the age of seventy-seven. He was buried at Mount Gonggong in Hongzhou. The Emperor bestowed upon him the posthumous title of "Great Master Dajian" (Great Mirror). Suddenly, heavy rain poured down from the distant sky, and the exhausted stream quickly transformed into a deep ford. This, moreover, clearly illustrates another instance of the spiritual resonance between the One and the myriad things.
To know that truth alone resides in emptiness and that there is no self within existence—to be free from both of these and to provisionally designate "One" as the vehicle—is the teaching.
It shows that those in the cycle of birth and death can become Buddhas, and it clarifies that even demons may appear like sages when distinguishing between the heterodox and the orthodox.
The Great Being manifested his form and did not remain; the Sage turned his back and suddenly withered away.

His disciples Zhizang, Haoying, Chongtai, and others attended to the funeral rites. Emperor Xianzong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Daji (Great Quiescence). Bao Ji, Duke of Danyang, composed an inscription to commemorate his deeds, and Quan Deyu wrote the epitaph for his stupa.
The memorial hall (yingtáng) now exists in Haihun County.
Furthermore, there was the monk Zhizang of Xitang in Qianzhou during the Tang dynasty; his secular surname was Liao, and he was a native of Qianhua.
From birth he possessed extraordinary features, and his kinsmen marveled at his magnificent potential.
At the age of eight, he followed a teacher, and his spiritual aspirations became lofty and far-reaching.

He accompanied Daji in moving to Mount Gonggong; later, he visited Chan Master Guoyi of Mount Jing, with whom he engaged in extensive discussion and debate, causing everyone to change their perception of him.
When the Commander-in-Chief Lu Sīgōng invited Dàjí to reside at his headquarters, Huìzàng returned to the commandery and received the transmission and the *kāṣāya* from Dàjí.
At that time, the Vice Minister Li Gōngjiān, the State Councilor Qí Gōngyìng, and the Palace Attendant Pèi Gōngtōng all inclined their hearts toward and followed his teachings.
He passed away on the eighth day of the fourth month in the ninth year of the Yuanhe era; he was eighty years of age and had fifty-five years of *śrāmaṇera* and *bhikṣu* ordination (*varṣa*).
He was immediately interred in a stupa. Wei Shou, the Grand Master for Remonstrance, subsequently inquired after his preserved teachings and conduct, which were compiled and included in the *Tujing*.
The Prefect Li Bo requested that he be honored with a commemorative plaque; in the first year of the Changqing era, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Dajue.
Biography of Zhiman of the Lingtangquan Hermitage in Xuanzhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Zhiman’s secular surname was Kang, and he was a native of Luoyang.
In his youth, he was entrusted by his family to the śramaṇa Chen Fohui; as his heart’s desire remained unyielding, he subsequently entered the monastic life at Longxing Temple in Yingchuan.
Having heard that the Dharma assembly of Chan Master Shenhui in Luoyang was flourishing and that he had attained the essential point of the mind,
he traveled south to the site of the miraculous hot springs at Mount Huang, where he built a thatched hut and took up residence.
Later, when he gathered *huanglian* (Coptis teeta), the local villagers saw him and were filled with joy.
Man asked, "Where is this place?
The villagers replied:
"Huanglian Mountain belongs to Xuancheng.
We wish for you, Master, to settle there; however, tigers and leopards cause much harm. Faman said:
"Even tigers possess Buddha-nature.
He then burned incense and performed a ritual of exorcism; from that time on, the disturbances subsided, and it was subsequently established as a great Chan monastery.
Later, he passed away at the age of ninety-one.
In the first year of the Yongzhen era, he entered the stupa.
Biography of Guangyao of Baozhen Monastery in Yizhou, Tang China, by Daojian: Guangyao, whose secular surname was Zhou, was a native of Beiping.
Having suffered the bitterness of early loss from childhood, he was utterly unable to bear his grief and vowed to leave the household life.
Abandoning the lecture halls, he entered the monasteries, seeking instruction and benefit from every master he encountered.
Later, having met Master Huihui, he was like golden tweezers removing a cataract, seeing clearly throughout the ten directions.
Subsequently, he went to Mount Meng in Yishui, where he thatched grass to form a hermitage and sat in meditation with serene composure.
The people of Huai and Fei followed this transformation with one accord.

At that time, the District Magistrate of Shen, Zhi Zhong, first established a meditation hall. Subsequently, Wang Liao, the Regional Inspector of Yanzhou and Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, personally requested him to enter the province to propagate his teachings; he then memorialized the throne to grant the institution its official title, "Baozhen."
Students flocked to him from all directions, and many received great benefit.
He entered nirvana in the second year of the Yuanhe era at the age of ninety-two.
Furthermore, there was the monk Shi Daojian of Ci'en Monastery in Xiangzhou during the Tang dynasty; his secular surname was Wang, and he was a native of Danyang.
He first resolved his mind on the path under the Chan patriarch Huizhong at Mount Niutou.
In the first year of the Dali era, he lived in seclusion at Nanquan Mountain in Chizhou.
Later, he traveled to Xianghan and stayed at Cien Temple.

At the beginning of the Yuanhe era, the Chancellor Yan Gong was stationed in Hannan; he held him in profound esteem and inquired after his well-being with great diligence, providing a continuous stream of offerings.
Consequently, he constructed a monastery outside Fenglin Pass and invited him to reside there.
He manifested his parinirvāṇa in the second year [of the Kaihuang era], at the age of seventy-three.
This is the biography of Shi Lingtan of Hualin Monastery in Yangzhou during the Tang Dynasty. Shi Lingtan’s secular surname was Wu; he was a native of Wen-shui in Taiyuan.
He was the nephew’s grandson of Empress Wu Zetian.
His father’s name was Xuan, who served as the Magistrate of Luoyang County.

His mother was Lady Xiahou; when she first became pregnant with Tan, she dreamed that a divine monk bestowed upon her a precious mirror, its interior and exterior both brilliantly clear, and said to her:
"I entrust this to you; protect it well.
When he was born, his parents suffered no distress.
At the mere age of seven, he had mastered all his studies and passed the examination for young scholars.
At thirteen, he entered government service and was soon promoted to Palace Attendant for the Crown Prince.
Thus, he delighted in study without ceasing, and his profound mastery of the scriptures of the Three Teachings continued to increase.

Nevertheless, ever sighing over his dilapidated dwelling, he vowed to enter the Gate of Emptiness; having already prepared the provisions for the Mahāyāna, he was destined to reach the realm of Nirvāṇa.

At that time, Master Shenhui of Heze Temple was flourishing his teachings in the capital of Luoyang, just as the light of Pujici was being eclipsed and the path of Master Xiushan was gradually fading. Tan went there to pay him a visit.
He skillfully employed expedient means to guide him, and upon suddenly perceiving his mind, he silently granted his request and permitted him to serve as an attendant.
His parents were unable to turn his resolve.
Like a bird soaring through the air beyond restraint, [the Master] refined [his understanding] from beginning to end until he was able to shatter all doubts and obstructions.
In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era, he summoned Dàntán and said:
"I have a single phrase that has been transmitted from patriarch to patriarch down to Cáoqī; Cáoqī entrusted it to me. You must receive it with careful attention."
"I shall surely encounter obstacles," he said,
and thus took his leave to travel abroad.
Before long, as expected, an imperial decree was issued to transfer the assembly to Yiyang.
Tàn then proceeded to Fucha Temple in Luzhou to examine the Tripitaka.
Later, hearing that National Teacher Zhōng had been summoned from Nanyang, he went to pay his respects to him in the fifth year of the Dàlì era.
In the eighth year, when he wished to pass through the Pass, Zhong memorialized, saying:
"This man is a fellow disciple of mine; both are disciples of Shenhui.
By imperial decree, he was granted the title "Great Compassionate One" (Dabei) and was presented with an official edict.
While traveling to propagate the teachings at Liangyuan, he was received with offerings by the Chancellor, Lord Tian Shengong.
As he proceeded gradually toward Wiyang and Lihexi, sighing over the decline of the Great Dharma, he suddenly heard a voice from the air saying:
"Open the ground of the mind."
He immediately saw the Bodhisattva appearing like Mañjuśrī, who said, "I shall provide you with a seal of verification.
He ordered him to lift his neck and pressed down upon it with his palm; he then observed four finger-width marks of redness, the impressions of which remained constantly visible.
Furthermore, he stayed on Mount Jinshan in the Yangtze River at Zhizhou; this is the present-day Zexin.
On the northern face of that mountain there was a dragon’s cave, which constantly emitted poisonous gas like clouds; those who approached it frequently fell ill or perished.
As he settled there, the poisonous clouds vanished without a trace.
Later, while he was dwelling in a hermitage on Mount Ding in Jiangyin, he suddenly heard the sound of voices chanting praises.
Looking toward the source, he saw two white tortoises; Tan then received the precepts of taking refuge from them.
He also saw two large white snakes, several zhang in length, likewise receiving the precepts and repenting.

Thus he returned to the forests of Wuxing and established an araṇya there. Three men dressed in purple-gold robes, whose gait was slow and upright, praised the site of the practice hall as being excellent alone; many of the villagers abandoned their nets and traps.

In the fifth year of the Yuanhe era, while Li Gong Xiong was serving as the Chancellor (Xiangguo) governing Guangling, he governed his subordinates with severe laws and was stern and decisive, showing little compassion. Yet, upon first meeting Tan, he treated him with great respect and ceremony, summoning him to reside at Hualin Temple.
Within the temple was the tomb of the Great General Zhang Liao, and many of the monks were frequently bewildered and disturbed by malevolent spirits.
When Dao-tan resided there, he remained solemn and showed no sign of agitation.
Furthermore, many people in Yangzhou suffered from the delusions caused by mountain sprites and forest monsters; Dao-tan warded them all off.
People vied with one another to take refuge in his teachings.

In the tenth year, he suddenly saw two Hu people who claimed to have come from the kingdom of Kucha, saying, "There is no supreme teaching there; we have come from afar to invite the Venerable Master to expound it."
On the thirteenth day of the fifth month in the eleventh year, during a memorial service for Heze, he addressed the assembly:
"I have accepted an invitation to travel afar.
In the seventh month I shall manifest illness, and in the ninth month I shall pass away; this is my advance notice."
On the eighth day of the eighth month of autumn, he indeed passed away in profound stillness.
His stupa was enshrined on the southern ridge of Xunzhai Ward in western Yangzhou; Zheng Jian, the Assistant Administrator of Yue Prefecture, constructed the stupa.
His secular age at death was one hundred and eight, and his monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera-vassa*) was eighty-four.
Tan was the grandson of Caoxi and the son of Heze.
Biography of Shi Daotong of Mount Ziyu in Tangzhou, Tang Dynasty: Shi Daotong’s surname was He, and he was a native of Lujiang.
In his youth, he was grave and reserved, speaking little; whenever he beheld a Buddhist image, he would invariably pay homage, offer praise, and remain in contemplation without ceasing.
Because his father held office in Nanan, Quanzhou, he requested permission to leave home life, shave his head, and don the monastic robes.
Having successfully completed his recitation of the scriptures, he received an imperial decree for ordination during the early years of the Tianbao era.
At that time, Chan Master Daoyi was beginning his propagation in Jianyang; he went to visit him at Foji Rock, where the master was gathering disciples.
One master also followed him like a shadow to Mount Gong in Nankang, Linchuan;
yet he vowed to travel throughout the regions of Wu and Yue, ascending every mountain valley of Tiantai and Mingzhou.
Upon returning his staff to Mount Ledong in Jiangxi, he devoted himself to monastic affairs with a resolute mind, never shrinking from toil and hardship.
In the second year of the Zhenyuan era, he traveled to Mount Nanyue to visit Master Shitou, which was like adding vermilion and indigo dye to a thread already woven into fabric.
In the fourth year, when the Great Master of Chan was about to pass away, he spoke with clarity, saying:
"The jade and stones of this mountain provide moisture and its peaks offer beauty and benefit; they will further your path of practice. When you encounter a suitable place, you may dwell there."
Tong heard these words, yet he remained as if concealing a prophecy and did not investigate them in detail.
That autumn, he traveled with Master Zizai of Mount Funiu through the capitals of Jing and Luo, returning to the west of Tangzhou.
There was a mountain peak with solitary peaks and dense forests, cut off from human habitation on all four sides; it truly possessed a transcendent charm beyond the mundane world.
He then questioned the local people, who told him that this mountain was Mount Ziyu.
Reflecting upon the far-reaching prediction of the Great Sage (Daji), he thought, "It is fitting that I should dwell upon this peak.
He then ascended the craggy heights and saw a square stone upon the mountain ridge; its color was like that of lustrous purple jade.
He sighed and said, "That which is called 'Purple Jade' truly lives up to its name."
"The words of my former master were no empty record.
Hanging up his staff and opening his satchel, disciples gathered like mist to study under him.
At first, he cleared away the weeds to construct a dwelling; subsequently, the Regional Inspector Li Daogu took it upon himself to build a Chan temple for him.
In the eighth year of the Yuanhe era, the disciple Jincang went to pay his respects to Chan Master Baizhang Shanhai;
upon his return, he met Baotong.
Baotong’s expression turned somber as he said, "Now that you have come, this mountain has its master."
Carrying his staff, he went straight away; the monastics and laypeople of Xiangzhou all came out to welcome him.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, he passed away without illness at the age of eighty-three.
One source states that the former Prime Minister Yu Di placed his utmost trust in him, and the Minister Li Ao held him in high esteem.
Biography of Shi Huahui of Changjing Monastery in the Capital of Yong during the Tang Dynasty: Shi Huahui, surnamed Xie, was a native of Quanzhou.
Having planted deep roots in past lives and harboring a far-reaching resolve to transcend the mundane world, he pursued full ordination and thereafter esteemed the life of a wandering monk.
At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era, he paid homage to Chan Master Daji of Hongzhou and suddenly realized the essential point of the mind.
At that time, Liu Ji of Pengcheng was deeply impressed by his virtuous brilliance, and they mutually recommended and validated one another.
Later, he went into seclusion at Mount Qulu; subsequently, he stayed at Lingyan Temple in Qizhou.
He then moved to Baijia Rock, where the springs and rocks were secluded and wondrous.

Distressed by the profusion of questions from his meditation disciples, he went to Mount Tiaoshan in Shangzhong to practice the dharma of Chan; those who sought the Dharma followed in his footsteps, and the people of Puzhen were all transformed by him.

In the third year of the Yuanhe era, Emperor Xianzong issued an imperial decree to have [the image] installed in the Vairocana Hall of Changjing Temple. This was because, during the Dali era, an edict had decreed that all renowned monks and virtuous masters from throughout the empire who were well-versed in the three studies should be gathered there; on the emperor's birthday, many would perform vegetarian feasts and ordain monks at this location.
Since Huī resided in the Upper Hall, he expounded the essentials of Chan meditation for the people; eminent officials and scholars came daily to seek his instruction.
Furthermore, by imperial decree, he was summoned to enter the Lín Dé Palace to receive a vegetarian feast, where he was honored as the presiding elder (*upādhyāya*).
In the winter of the tenth year of the Yuanhe era (the year of Yiwu), he manifested illness; on the eleventh day of the twelfth month, he passed away at the age of sixty-two.
In the second month of the following year, his disciples Zhilang, Zhi Cao, and others enshrined his entire body for burial on the northern plain of Baqiao.

An imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title of Great Master of Propagating the Teaching (Daxuanjiao Chanshi). A stele was erected at the gate of the monastery, with the text composed by Jia Dao, the Director of the Granary in Yueyang, to recount his virtues.

Biography of Vikuang of Xingshan Monastery in Jingzhao, Tang Dynasty. Vikuang, whose secular surname was Zhu, was a native of Xin’an in Quzhou. He was a disciple of Baoxiu. His family name was Zhu, and he hailed from Xin’an in Quzhou.
His grandfather’s name was An and his father’s name was Jiao.
At the age of thirteen, upon seeing those who slaughtered living beings, he was struck with such compassion that he could not bear to eat meat.

He subsequently left the household life to seek the tonsure from the monk Tan, receive the *śīla* (precepts) from the monk Chong, study the *vinaya* under the monk Ru, realize the Mahāyāna teachings through *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, and achieve the Supreme Vehicle under Da Ji Dao Yi.

In the sixth year of the Zhenyuan era, he first began to propagate his teachings in the regions of Min and Yue; within a little over a year, hundreds had turned their hearts toward the Dharma and changed their attire.
In the seventh year, he subdued a fierce tiger at Kuaiji and established the Tengjia Daochang.
In the eighth year, he received the *śaraṇagamana* precepts from the mountain deity at Poyang and established a *pariṇāmanā* ritual site.
In the thirteenth year, he was moved by the appearance of a non-human being at Shaolin Temple.
In the twenty-first year [of the Kaiyuan era], he performed conditioned meritorious deeds at Weiguo Temple.
The following year, he bestowed unconditioned meritorious deeds at Tiangong Temple.
In the fourth year of the Yuanhe era, Emperor Xianzong Zhangwu issued an imperial decree at Anguo Temple.
In the fifth year, he was questioned regarding the Way at Linqide Hall.
In that same year, he restored the Lingquan Pond to its original state for the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra.
On the final day of the second month in the twelfth year, after concluding a grand exposition in the Chuanfa Hall, he suddenly passed away.
He was sixty-three years of age and had spent thirty-nine summer retreats as a monk.
He was buried at Xiyuan in Qianling, and by imperial decree was posthumously titled Chan Master Dache; his stupa was named Yuanhe Zhengzhen.

Initially, Daochuan preached the essential Dharma for thirty years, ordaining nearly hundreds of thousands of monastics and laypeople; as he administered medicine according to their ailments, how could one ever reach the end of his deeds?

When Bai Juyi served as Palace Attendant, he once visited Master Yuanzhao at the Dharma Hall four times; each time he arrived, Yuanzhao posed a question, to which Yuanzhao replied with effortless fluency, leading Bai Juyi to treat him as his teacher.
His disciples numbered nearly one thousand, and those who attained the Dharma were thirty-nine; those who entered the inner chamber and received his final entrustment were named Yichong and Yuanzhao.
During the Tang dynasty, there was the monk Baoxiu of Mount Luofu; his secular surname was Zhou, and he was a native of Zizhou.
He studied under his teacher at Chunde Temple, seeking the profound principles with resolute intent; there, he resolved his lingering doubts under the guidance of Master Ren of Qizhou.
Later, he took up residence in a stone chamber on Mount Luofu, where a patron built a Buddhist monastery for him, which flourished into a great temple.
One day, he told his disciples:
"Circumstances press upon me.
He appeared somber and unhappy, and none of the assembly could fathom the reason.

Emperor Shunzong held the Buddhist tradition in high esteem and was aware of Xiu’s reputation; he issued an imperial decree for him to enter the capital to engage in debate with the Tripitaka Master and respond to inquiries regarding the principles of translation, to which Xiu replied with clarity and fluency like a flowing stream.
He remained residing in the capital for three years, where he passed away at a temple in the metropolis.

This concludes the "Biography of Yize of Fuku Yan on Mount Tiantai during the Tang Dynasty. As for the biography of Śramaṇa Yize of Fuku Yan on Mount Tiantai during the Tang Dynasty: his secular surname was Changsun, and he was a native of Chang’an in Jingzhao.
His grandfather, Ze, was the Sima of Ezhou;
his father, Lishi, lived in seclusion in Jinling.
From a young age, he did not mingle with the secular world, remaining serene all day long without any worldly pursuits.
He first studied cursive script under Zhang Huai-guan, alone mastering the subtle essence of the brush.
He was refinedly devoted to the classics and histories, but took particular delight in Buddhist scriptures, considering them to have captured his own mind.
One morning, he abandoned his family estate and followed Huizhong of Mount Niutou—Huizhong being what is known as the Sixth Patriarch of Niutou.
Originally, Bodhidharma of India arrived with the essential teachings of the Śākya clan; those who transmitted his Way were Huineng of Caoxi and Huiyou of Mount Song.
Those who studied for proficiency were called the School of the Southern Lineage, while those who studied for excellence were called the School of the Northern Lineage.
Furthermore, the Patriarch Xinxing transmitted his Way to Huirong; having received it, Huirong resided at Mount Niutou, where his disciples passed it on.
From this, the Dharma of the mind gave rise to the Oxhead school.

Having transmitted the Way of Zhong, they practiced profound contemplation for a long time and concluded that heaven and earth contain no things, and the self contains no things; yet, although there are no things, it has never been the case that there are no things.
In this way, the sage is like a shadow and the common people are like a dream; who, then, undergoes birth and death?
It is through this that the Perfected Person is able to shine alone and act as the lord of all things—I have understood this.

He then traveled south to Mount Tiantai, reaching the Buddha’s Cave Rock. There he thatched his dwelling with *bìlì* vines and used fallen leaves as a mat, living there like a corpse. He drank from mountain streams and ate the fruits of trees to fill his hunger; tigers and leopards became his guests, and deer and elk his companions, until he sat motionless like a withered tree.
Later, when those who hewed wood saw him, they informed one another in turn.
One who admired his Way said, "The Way has no disciples yet.
They joined together to build a dwelling for him, where they depicted the Buddha and seated the monks, until it flourished as a vihāra.
Therefore, since the Yuanhe era, those who transmitted the Dao have also referred to it as the "Buddha-cave School" (*fokuo xue*); the title "Buddha-cave" originated with Zhe himself.

For forty years he sat in one posture; when high officials or titled nobles arrived bearing letters of inquiry and offerings for his sustenance, he never once returned thanks, nor did he ever rise from his seat to perform a prostration.
At that time, when the year was gengxu, on the thirteenth day of the final month of summer, he summoned his disciples and said,
"You must exert yourselves!
On the night of the fifteenth, he sat down and passed away.
That night, the people at the foot of the mountain heard it as if a mountain were collapsing; when they looked toward it at dawn, they saw colored clouds hovering and settling upon the cliffs.
The elders all wept and said, "The Master has passed away!"
Upon examining him, it was indeed so.
He had been a monk for twenty years and passed away at the age of fifty-eight. He was skilled in composing prose;

beginning with his instruction in the Way at Mount Zhongshan, he compiled the *Preface to the Collected Works of Master Rong* in three fascicles, wrote the *Twenty-four Chapters on the Explanation of Titles* for Baozhi, the *Preface to the Legacy of Master Fu during His Southern Tour*, and also the *Meanings of Non-arising and Other Doctrines*.
All his writings were characterized by their brilliant diction and profound reasoning.
Furthermore, several dozen of his other songs and poems were all circulated throughout the world.
Thus, Zhiyuan resided at the original site of the Buddha Cave Hermitage to the west of the Waterfall Spring, where he constructed a stupa and a niche for enshrining relics.
During the Huichang era, it was demolished according to precedent, and the monastery came under the possession of the Daoist community.

Later, in the year of Yiyou of the Xiantong era (867 CE), the monk Zhengfaguang of Kaiyuan Temple moved the stele to its present location; Han Yi, the Governor of Henan, composed the inscription for the stele.

The Biography of Lingmo of Mount Wuxie in Wuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, Transmitted by [the Compiler]. Lingmo, whose secular surname was Xuan, was a native of Piling. His courtesy name was Zhixian. He was a layman from Piling.

In the year I first attained my degree, I delighted in study and forgot all fatigue; I vowed that by succeeding in the examination through the "shècè" method, I would bring honor to my parents and my hometown.
Later, I encountered the Great Master Mǎ of Yùzhāng, who gathered a great assembly to expound the Dharma.

When the meditation hall was being constructed, Master Ma manifested his countenance to reveal his true form; silently and secretly attuning to the profound mechanism [of the Dharma], he immediately sought ordination, like a ripe boil awaiting incision.
After receiving full ordination, he underwent rigorous training in the gates of practice with unwavering resolve.

In the early years of the Zhenyuan era, he entered Mount Tiantai, where there were twelve hermitages (*aranya*) established by the Sui dynasty’s Zhiyi. Zhiyi had made a prophetic declaration regarding them, saying:
"This place is solemn and sublime; it is not a dwelling for those of inferior capacity. If one can reside here, they will be no different from me."
Moyin resided at the White Sand Meditation Hall for two years.
A fierce tiger came to tame itself before him and gave birth to cubs near the forest, finding its purpose in his presence.

He then stayed at the Eastern Meditation Hall; the location was secluded and sparsely populated, and one night, a mountain deity unleashed a storm of thunder and torrential rain, causing a precipitous cliff to collapse.
At dawn, the great tree collapsed and leaned over, its branches entangling the side of the hut; yet the thatched roof of reeds was not damaged in the slightest.
News of this spread far and wide, and people from all directions came to behold it and marvel.
Later, while traveling to Mount Dongbai, he was suddenly poisoned; yet he sought no medical treatment, instead closing his quarters and sitting in meditative repose.
Before long, the poison was transformed and flowed out as sweat that dripped away, whereupon he returned to his normal state.
During his travels, he arrived at Puyang, where his influence flourished; there, Li Wang, a commander of the Yangling Garrison, invited him to reside at Wuxi.
At the beginning of the Yuanhe era, a severe drought occurred, leaving the farmers in a state of great anxiety.
Silently following the stream, he saw a green snake coiling and twisting; it stared with fixed eyes as if watching a passerby, remaining motionless.
He rebuked it, saying:
"The people's streams have run dry and their crops are dying; why do you not send down rain to save them?"
That night, it indeed rained heavily; the clouds satisfied the entire region, and the people were graced with this bounty.

It so happened that Meng Jian, the Surveillance Commissioner of Pingchang, was on an inspection tour of the abandoned monasteries within the jurisdiction of Zhejiang, where the students had dispersed.
At that time, Li Zhou, the Magistrate of Jiyang, submitted a formal petition recommending Ling Shan for permission to rebuild the monastery.

On the twenty-third day of the third month in the thirteenth year, having bathed and burned incense, he sat upright upon his rope-cot, entrusted his final instructions to the assembly, and suddenly passed away.
He lived to the age of seventy-two and had forty-one years of ordination seniority.

The eminent monk Zhixian was preeminent in his spiritual practice and possessed elegant literary style; he was a preeminent talent of the Jiangzuo region, for whom this *Moxing lu* (Record of Silent Practice) was compiled.
The Biography of Daowu of Tiantai Monastery in Jingzhou during the Tang Dynasty. Chongxin venerated the monk Daowu. His secular surname was Zhang, and he was a native of Dongyang in Wuzhou.
Having received the refined essence of Heaven, he became a Prince of the Dharma; from birth his spirit was brilliant, and as he grew, he was prudent and sincere.

At the age of fourteen—when the golden-winged bird first sprouted its feathers and the qilin was just beginning to grow its horns—he addressed his elders, intending to seek ordination. However, out of a sense of compassionate affection, his request was not granted.
He immediately reduced his regular meals, eating only once a day; although his body and belly became emaciated and famished, he remained increasingly steadfast for many years.
His parents, having no other choice, finally granted him permission.
He then went to Mingzhou to receive the tonsure from a virtuous elder (bhadanta).
At the age of twenty-five, he received full ordination under a virtuous elder at Zhulin Temple in Hangzhou.
With the power of valor and a firm, steadfast mind, he cultivated all pure practices within the gateway of the six perfections.

I have always maintained that those who treat the most critical ailments must rely on the finest medicines, and those who seek to dispel the darkness of ignorance must seek out virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra).
Without relying on a boat or oars, how could one cross over?
He then suddenly snapped his whip and set out for Mount Jing, where he threw himself at the feet of National Teacher Guoyi.
As soon as his prostrations were completed, he secretly received the essentials of the school.
Amidst the flow of words, he recognized the pearl within his own robe.
Body and mind become suddenly clear and expansive, as both the real and the false are cast aside.
All doubts and obstructions are severed; one attains fearlessness and sovereignty, directly perceiving the Buddha-nature, which remains untainted within.
Having served with diligence for five years, Sui also granted his seal of approval, intending that the rain of his Dharma might nourish all the monastic groves.
Wù had accumulated strength while moving toward obscurity, penetrating ever deeper into remote and difficult places; he truly hoped for a single flight that would reach the heavens.

When people came to inquire about him, he would simply remain silent. He did not preach the Dharma extensively. He only taught through his conduct. He passed away at Mount Funiu in the year [year].
