As he grew older, he sat in the full lotus posture even when at rest, which his relatives found extraordinary.
He took leave of those he loved to enter the monastic life at Mount Jing; there, in Xin-ding, he received full ordination.

Subsequently, he traveled to various regions to study under the dharma seat of Chan Master Dao-yi of Nan-kang, where he attained a profound understanding of the true doctrine. His spiritual traces surpassed his contemporaries, his reputation for the Way shone brightly, and his conduct was characterized by ease and grace.
He frequently dwelt in mountain valleys, where practitioners from all quarters gathered at his gate.
During the Yuanhe era, he resided at Mount Xiangshan in Luoyang and formed an inseparable bond with Chan Master Tianran.
Wherever he traveled, he was invariably fond of antiquity, seeking out the remains of former sages to satisfy his desire for elegant sights.
At Longmen Mountain, he discovered the site where the Tripitaka Master of the Later Wei dynasty translated the scriptures;
at Wangwu Mountain, he found the place where Chan Master Chou resolved a tiger fight, and because the mountain’s waters were sweet, he renamed it Ganshui (Sweet Spring) Temple.
At Mount Song, he obtained the "Horse-Track Spring" from Dharma Master Fan;
dwelling there, he was free from attachment. His composition, the "Three Laments," is exquisite both in diction and reasoning, awakening those who are deluded and providing great benefit to the age.

At the beginning of the spurious Qiande era of the Former Shu Wang family, there was a minor military officer named Chen Gong who married the granddaughter of the late Magistrate Zhong Ping. This man had maintained the practice of non-killing for over twenty years; later, while serving in Shu, he was required to slaughter animals for the wedding rites of his son.
At first, Gao was unwilling, but his relatives said,
"If you maintain the precepts yourself, how will you entertain your guests at a formal banquet?
Caught between these conflicting pressures, he eventually prepared many dishes and carvings.
Before ten days had passed, she fell ill with a most extraordinary affliction; her speech became merely delirious, but after three nights, she revived and recounted the events of the underworld.

Initially, she was pursued and captured by messengers in black robes and brought into the City God Temple of Qifeng. There, the temple deity—wearing a high crown and voluminous sleeves—sat facing her, together with a golden-armored warrior.

The messenger led Kōken Shin, and the warriors engaged in a heated exchange, reproaching him for his violation of the precepts; they then wrung their hands in indignation and cursed him, saying, "I am a general of the deities who protect the precepts!"

For twenty years, I have had no leisure for food or sleep on your account; how could I have expected that you would suddenly give rise to a murderous intent and abruptly violate your precepts and restraint?
Although your life has not yet ended, your transgression is already profound, and you must be sent to the Office of the Netherworld to be punished for this deliberate offense.
The City God asked Gao, "What further good deeds have you cultivated to redeem your transgressions?
Gao had frequently recited the *Sūtra on the Upper Birth*, though he had already lost count; at that moment, he was utterly bewildered and could remember nothing. In his state of fear, he said:
"I can recite the *Three Verses on Sorrow* and the *Song of the Monk Ippō*.

He then pressed his palms together toward the deity and recited them with a resonant voice; the deity and the warriors stood listening with ears pricked and fists raised, their countenances gradually brightening.
Upon reaching the final chapter, the deities all shed tears and said to Gao, "Return now to the human realm;
you should diligently cultivate merit.
Before he had finished bowing in farewell, they suddenly rose from their seats and related the matter in full detail.
From this point on, the songs and hymns of "The Three Laments" and "The Single Almsbowl" were transmitted, copied, and recited by all people.

Regarding "The Monk with the Single Almsbowl," its lyrics accord with reason and deeply stir feelings of sorrowful exhortation; however, as its literary style is colloquial, how could it surpass the elegance of "The Three Laments"?
When he sent his disciples south of the Yangtze River to select the most excellent landscapes, he said, "I wish to go there to spend my final years.
Upon arriving at Duchang County in Jiangzhou, he found fine groves and springs and sent word back.
Upon arriving at Ye County, he was detained by both monastics and laypeople.
He proceeded to Kaiyuan Temple in Suizhou, where he manifested his parinirvāṇa at the age of eighty-one; this was the first year of the Changqing era.
The commentary states:

Examining the Vinaya-piṭaka, when one who has left the household life violates a precept, they incur two types of offenses: first, a transgression of the regulations; second, an offense of the path of karma.

Since the Master Gao was a layperson and had never formally received the precepts, he could not have committed a transgression of the regulations. While as a layman he might have incurred an offense of the path of karma, how could he possibly have possessed a deity for protecting the precepts?
Moreover, since the Gao family has maintained the precept against killing, they have naturally been moved by a profound resonance to cultivate the merit of non-action.

Yet, because they "rarely succeed in reaching the end," they have incurred the retribution of the unseen realm; thus, I address the fivefold assembly: you should all stand in awe of and protect the deities who guard the precepts.
Thus it is that in the realm of light there are the laws of precepts, and in the realm of darkness there are ghosts and spirits!
Next is Shi Nan-yin of Yuanhe Shengshou Temple in Chengdu Prefecture, whose secular surname was Zhang.
The nature of clear awakening benefits others without ever being satiated; having attained the profound purport of Caoqi, he found no further need for external verification.
Upon meeting Master Hui of Jingzhong Temple, it was as if brocade from a loom were washed to enhance its brilliance, or as a dragon holding a torch that moves forward to dispel the darkness.

Master Yin traveled from Jiangling to Shu; on the southern bank of the Shu River, he cleared the weeds and thatched a hut. The masses all turned to him with devotion and reverence, and gradually a Buddhist monastery was established—this was at the beginning of the Zhengyuan era.
After Gao Si-kong Chongwen suppressed Liu Pi, he renamed this temple "Yuanhe Shengshou" (Holy Longevity of the Yuanhe Era), though it was originally named Baoying.
When his work of transformation was nearing completion, at the beginning of the Changqing era, he manifested illness and entered parinirvāṇa.
A stūpa was constructed and he was buried within the monastery.

During the Huichang era, the stūpa was destroyed; however, during the Dazhong era, the monastery was rebuilt upon the old foundations of Baoying Temple north of the Yangtze River, and its name was restored as "Shengshou."
Yin’s disciple Yifu succeeded him and restored the practice of Chan.
Regarding the lineage of Wuye of Kaiyuan Temple in Fenzhou during the Tang Dynasty: the monk Wuye, whose secular surname was Du, was a native of Shangluo in Shangzhou.
Her mother, Lady Li, suddenly heard a voice from the air saying,
"May you have a place to dwell?
Shortly thereafter, she became pregnant.
On the evening of his birth, an extraordinary light filled the room.
By the time he reached the age of childhood, he never engaged in play; when walking, his gaze was always straight ahead, and when sitting, he immediately assumed the full lotus posture.

When the merchants and the assembly of monastics saw him, they were all struck with wonder and sighed in admiration, saying, "This is an unsurpassed vessel of the Dharma; let him quickly leave the household life so that he may uphold and flourish the Triple Gem.

At the age of nine, he petitioned his parents for permission to follow Master Zhiben of Kaiyuan Temple in his native commandery. The master then bestowed upon him the *Vajracchedikā*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Vimalakīrti*, *Viśeṣacinti-brahma-paripṛcchā*, and *Avataṃsaka* sūtras; he could read five lines at once, and after a single recitation, he retained them without omission.
At the age of twelve, he was permitted to undergo tonsure.
Whenever he attended lecture sessions, he understood the teachings upon merely hearing them.
If his fellow students had anything they did not comprehend, he would analyze and explain it for them accordingly, such that they all reached the profound mysteries of the Dharma.

Upon reaching the age of twenty, he received full ordination from Master You of Xiangzhou; having practiced and studied the *Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya* (*Sifen lü shu*) during a single summer retreat, he was already able to expound upon it.

He also lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for the assembly of monks; the dharma feast was opened long and wide, without weariness in either winter or summer. It may truly be said that the legacy of Daosheng and Sengzhao has not perished, and that Tanlin and Huiyuan have been revived once more.
Later, hearing that Daji of Hongzhou was the preeminent leader of the Chan school, he went specifically to pay his respects.
Daoye’s body exceeded six feet in height; he stood as immovable as a mountain, gazing with a fixed, steady look, and his voice resonated like a great bell.
Daji saw this at once and, smiling, said,
"In this lofty Buddhist hall, there is no Buddha.
Thereupon, Daoye prostrated himself on his knees and said:
"As for the literature of the Three Vehicles, I have roughly exhausted its essential meanings.
However, I have heard that in the Chan gate, 'the mind itself is Buddha,' yet I truly have not yet understood this. Daji said:
"Nothing other than this very mind that has not yet been understood exists;
there is no separate thing. When it is not understood, that is delusion;
if it is understood, that is awakening."
Delusion is precisely the sentient being; awakening is precisely the Buddha.
The Way does not depart from sentient beings; how could there be a Buddha existing separately!
It is just like a hand forming a fist: the fist is entirely the hand.
Upon hearing these words, Huiye attained sudden enlightenment;
weeping and sobbing with grief, he said to Daji, "I had originally thought that the Buddha-way was long and distant, requiring diligent toil through vast eons before one could finally achieve it."
Only today do I come to know that the true mark of the Dharmakāya is inherently complete; all phenomena arise from the mind and possess nothing but names, having no substantial reality.
Daji said: "So it is, so it is.
The nature of all dharmas is neither arising nor ceasing; all dharmas are fundamentally empty and quiescent from the beginning.
As the Sūtra says:"
"All dharmas, from their very origin, are eternally characterized by quiescence.
It is also said:
"The ultimate abode of emptiness and stillness."
It is further said:
"The emptiness of all phenomena is the seat.
This refers to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, dwelling in this place of non-dwelling.

If one knows in this way, one dwells in the abode of empty stillness and sits upon the seat of the emptiness of dharmas; whether lifting the foot or setting it down, one never departs from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Understanding is attained in an instant, with no further gradual stages—this is what is meant by "ascending the mountain of nirvāṇa without moving one's feet."

Having already received the transmission of the Mind-Seal, he traveled to Caoxi to pay homage at the ancestral stupa; thereafter, he journeyed to Mount Lu, Tiantai, and various other famous mountains, seeking out sacred sites everywhere.

From Luoyang to Yong, he stayed at Ximing Monastery; the assembly of monks all wished to nominate him as a Great Virtuous One (Mahādeśaka) for the two streets, but Fayue remained silent and sighed, saying:
"To draw near to kings and high ministers is not my aspiration!"

Thereupon, he went to Shangdang. The Regional Commander and Minister of State Li Baozhen and Ma Sui had repeatedly achieved military victories; furthermore, they had inspired Wang Wujun to join them in defeating Zhu Tao. Their merits were numerous and their power great. Nevertheless, they delighted in hearing of the virtuous and good, and even if such persons were a thousand *li* away, they would certainly present ceremonial gifts to invite them.
His heavy and profound karmic burden was called "action" (saṃskāra); morning and evening he performed prostrations and circumambulations, and his banners and standards moved back and forth.
He often showed signs of weariness and said to his disciples:
"I originally sought to avoid the clamor of fame and profit in the great capital; now I am again troubled by receiving these lords—is this truly my heart's intent?"
Having finished speaking, he roamed at ease upon Mount Mianshang Baofu.
He then went to Mount Qingliang, where he read the Tripitaka at Jinget Temple; after eight cycles of the heavens had passed, his vow was finally fulfilled.

Again he took up his mendicant’s staff and traveled south, arriving at the West River. Initially, he stayed at the Zhongxiang Buddhist Monastery, where the provincial governor Dong Shuchan invited him to reside at the Kaiyuan Vihara.
Dharma Master Jie said to his disciples, "Since I arrived here, I have no longer had the intention to travel elsewhere; could it be that my karmic conditions lie here?
Thereupon, he struck the bell to summon the assembly, let out a lion’s roar, and rained down the great Dharma rain for nearly twenty years.
The people of Bing and Fen were all converted to his teachings.

In the fourteenth year of Emperor Xuanzong’s reign, having long admired his virtuous reputation, the Emperor issued an edict inviting him to enter the palace; however, he declined on the grounds of illness and did not go.
The following year, another imperial edict was issued, stating that he remained ill as before.

In the year Emperor Muzong ascended the throne, his sacred heart was filled with devotion and he longed to pay his respects; he therefore commanded Lingzhun Gong, the Monastic Registrar of the Two Streets, to travel afar bearing the imperial decree to invite him.
He approached and paid his respects, saying:
"I know that you, Master, have transcended the mundane world and treat worldly affairs as mere chaff.
Since the Dharma has been entrusted to the King, I pray that you will give this mature consideration!"
This reversal of the imperial decree is not like those of ordinary times; we pray that you, Master, will surely comply with the Will of Heaven and must no longer decline on account of illness.
Act according to the circumstances of the moment, so as not to burden future generations.
Kaiye laughed and said,
"What virtue do I, a poor monk, possess to trouble the Holy Sovereign so often?
I shall depart immediately."
"The paths differ.
Thereupon, he shaved his hair and bathed; when midnight arrived, he addressed his disciples, including Huiqin, saying:
"The nature of your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is coeval with the great void; it neither arises nor perishes."
All objective realms are fundamentally empty and quiescent; not a single dharma can be apprehended.
Those who are deluded do not understand this and are thus bewildered by objects; once bewildered by objects, they transmigrate without end.
"You all should know that the nature of the mind exists inherently from the beginning and is not produced through artificial effort; it is like a diamond, indestructible.
All phenomena are like shadows and echoes, having no reality. Therefore, a sutra says:
'Only this one thing is real; the other two are not true.'"
"Constantly realize that all things are empty, so that not a single object remains within the sphere of the mind;
this is the place where all Buddhas apply their minds. You should practice this diligently!
Having finished speaking, he sat cross-legged and suddenly passed into stillness.
Alas! It may be said that he attained mastery over birth and death!
At sixty-two years of secular age and forty-two years of monastic seniority (*saṃgha-rakṣā*), both clergy and laity mourned him as if they had lost their own parents.

They prepared incense, flowers, banners, and streamers, and escorted his entire remains to a *nyāya* (meditation hut) west of the city, where they piled fragrant firewood and performed the cremation (*dhyāpita*).

Then there appeared auspicious clouds from the heavens, their five colors coalescing in the sky; a wondrous fragrance wafted from the west, rich and pervasive, which all the officials and commoners throughout the realm both smelled and beheld.
When the fuel was exhausted and the fire extinguished, he obtained śarīra relics that were as brilliant as pearls and jade.
His disciples included Huìqín, Xíngqín, Qiánzòng, Yìyōu, Yuándù, Héngtài, and others.
Weeping with blood, he collected the remains and enshrouded them in a golden coffin.

He then commissioned a master carver from Ying to carve stone for a stupa, and on the twenty-first day of the twelfth month of the third year of the Changqing era, he interred it within the courtyard of the *lianye* (monastic retreat).
In the year of his passing, the provincial governor Yang Qian obtained a detailed account of his deeds from the Monastic Registrar, Master Zhun, and subsequently composed an inscription for a stele.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled National Teacher Dada, and his stupa was named Chengyuan.
Biography of Ruhuī of Dongsi Temple in Changsha, Tang Dynasty Śramaṇa Ruhuī was a native of Shixing in Shaoyou Prefecture.
In the eighth year of the Dali era, he stayed at the gate of National Teacher No. 1 (Guoyi Chanshi); later, he returned to the Dharma assembly of Daji (Mazu Daoyi).

At that time, Zen practitioners looked up to him with admiration and sought the essential point of the mind with determination; the beds and couches within the Sangha Hall were worn down and broken by their constant use, so it was known as the "Broken-Bed Assembly," which is like saying they were carving into the Buddha’s own bed.
Later, at the request of many, he resided at Dongsi (East Temple) in Changsha.

Since the passing of Daji, his dharma lineage had flourished to such an extent that none could rival it at the time; thus, it can be known for certain from the popular saying that Dongsi was a "cave of Chan."
At that time, the Chancellor Cui Qun admired Hui’s character and came to visit him at his gate; their conversation was clear and resonant, and every word reached the essence of principle.
From then on, they formed a bond as teacher and friend.

Initially, Yuanqun consulted with Huangfu Bo regarding the proposal for Emperor Xianzong’s posthumous honorific title; consequently, he was framed by Bo and sent out as the Inspector of Hunan, where he lived in leisure and turned his heart toward Zhihui.
In the year of Gui-mao during the Changqing era of Emperor Muzong, he passed away at the temple at the age of eighty.
At that time, the well and springs dried up in advance, and an extraordinary fragrance wafted through the air; his stupa was subsequently enshrined south of the city.

Li Ao, the Intendant of the Circuit, demolished all the stupas and pagodas near the city, leaving only the stupa enshrining the remains at the assembly hall, upon which he inscribed with his own brush:
"I have left this stupa alone to distinguish between the worthy and the foolish."
Liu Shenbu Ke composed a stele for him.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Great Master Chuanming, and his stupa was named Yongji.
It is likely for this reason that his residence was also referred to as "Master Jia Shan."
Biography of Tianran of Mount Danxia in Nanyang, Tang Dynasty Shi Tianran was a man of unknown origins.

Having entered the Dharma-gate in his youth, he possessed a straightforward and uncompromising nature. He went to visit Master Shitou, who silently recognized him; intending to summon forth that which is realized within his own essence, the Master bestowed upon him the name "Tianran" (Natural).
He personally attended to the cooking for three years before finally shaving his head and abandoning his lay appearance.
Later, he received the precepts from Master Xi at Yuesi Temple.
He traveled to the assembly of Daji in Jiangxi; when Daji attempted to entice him with words, the Master’s responses were refined and correct.
Da Ji marveled at this as most extraordinary.
He subsequently resided for three years on Mount Tiantai’s Huading Peak and again paid homage to National Master Guoqing.
During the Yuanhe era, he ascended Longmen and Xiangshan, where he formed a bond beyond the mundane world with Chan Master Funiu.
Later, while at Huilin Temple, he encountered a severe cold; he then burned a wooden Buddha statue to ward it off.
Some people ridiculed him, saying:
"You are cremating a relic."
He asked,
"What does a block of wood possess?
Yanran replied:
"If that is so, why do you reproach me?
In the third year of the Yuanhe era, he passed Tianjin Bridge at dawn and lay across it; he encountered the Imperial Resident, Lord Zheng, who came out and scolded him for not leaving.
Thereupon, he slowly looked up and said,
"I am a monk of no affairs.
The Regional Commander was struck by this and presented him with two sets of plain silk robes and provided him with a monthly ration of rice and flour.
The people of Luoyang were moved to faith by the wave of acclaim.
In the spring of the fifteenth year, he remarked, "I long for the forests and streams," and subsequently selected Mount Danxia in Nanyang to construct a hermitage.
In the sixth month of the fourth year of the Changqing era, he told his disciples:
"Prepare my bath; I am about to depart.
He then donned his bamboo hat, took up his staff, and stepped into his sandals; with one foot hanging down, he passed away before it had even touched the ground, at the age of eighty-six.
Liu Ke, an Extraordinary Censor of the Department of Provisions, composed an inscription to commemorate his virtues.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Zhītong, and his stupa was named Miaojue.
Biography of Shi Tàiyù of Mount Fúróng in Chángzhōu, Tang Dynasty: Shi Tàiyù’s secular surname was Fàn; he was a native of Jīnlíng.
When he was only twelve years old, his aspiration was set on leaving the household life; he thus paid homage to Master Zhong of Mount Niutou and served him as his teacher.

Thereupon, with courageous and diligent effort, he sought its profound principles. As a vessel of the Dharma, his external demeanor was radiant, while his spiritual mind was harmoniously integrated within.
Although he clearly understood the One Vehicle, he fully practiced the myriad deeds.
He traveled to An Guo Temple in the capital of Yong to receive full ordination, where he stood out preeminent among the assembly.
Furthermore, his deportment was solemn and dignified, and his wondrous physical marks were extraordinary; he was as unfathomable as the great ocean and as immeasurable as space.

When visiting places of practice to collect the mind and purify one's domain, although one’s wisdom may be capable of penetrating all things without depending on a teacher, the seal of approval and certification must necessarily come from those who have attained awakening first.
He then visited Master Daji of Hongjing, and upon beholding the Master’s countenance, he attained a thorough realization of the Dharmakāya; in an instant, he suddenly perfected the Great Way.
At that time, the Buddha-dharma throughout the world was most flourishing in Hongfu, where holy sages sat shoulder to shoulder and those who had attained the Way were quite numerous.

Yù was a brother to Chan Master Dàchè, Chan Master Dàxuān, and Chan Master Dàzhì; subsequently, they traveled north and south to survey the various regions, never once showing any reluctance, so as to broaden their learning and见闻 (knowledge and views) and leisurely nurture the "sacred embryo" of enlightenment.
In the thirteenth year of the Yuanhe era, he settled at Mount Fuyong in Yixing, Piling; thus he derived his name from that mountain.

With cultivation as the cause and conditions as the catalyst, his responses were spontaneous and unattached; consequently, wherever he dwelt there was transformative influence, and wherever he traveled, people followed him with joy. Monastics and laypeople alike looked up to him, their numbers often reaching ten thousand.
From this time forward, many people in Jiangnan awakened to the principles of Chan.

At that time, Prime Minister Cui Gongqun was dismissed from his post for failing to maintain security and assigned to a provincial office; he subsequently served as Governor of Huazhou and later departed from Sanfeng to govern Xuancheng.
Although the land was near, the man was far away.

Lord Cui took great pleasure in paying his respects and made a sincere request with all his heart. Sengyue, moved by this devotion, manifested himself; taking great compassion as his heart's core, he fulfilled their desires according to conditions and traveled through various regions in accordance with his destiny.
In the first year of the Baoli era, he went to Chandingsi in Wānlíng to propagate the teachings in accordance with the needs of the time.
The following year, he announced his departure to return to Qiyún Mountain.

On the new moon day of the ninth month, his physical form remained unmoving as he manifested his passing at the mountain monastery; he had reached eighty years of age and fifty-eight years of monastic seniority.
On that day, heaven and earth seemed to mourn, plants and trees appeared withered, birds and beasts wailed in grief, and the clouds and springs were choked with silence.
The monastics and the common people were filled with longing and grief.
In the tenth month, his spirit was enshrined in the courtyard of the monastery, which was appropriate for the occasion.
His disciples Zhifu, Qizhen, Qinghua, and others lamented that while their teacher had entered extinction, the students remained behind.

In the second year of the Tàihé era, the Chancellor Wèi Chùhòu, who had long cherished the profound teachings of the Mysterious Way and possessed a sincere and steadfast devotion to the Dharma, submitted a memorial regarding these matters.
Thereupon, the Emperor issued a gracious edict, honoring him with exceptional rites and bestowing upon him a posthumous title and a name for his stupa.
Lu Xing, the Prefect of Yuezhou, composed this record with his brush.

Biography of Tanchang of the West Garden Hermitage on Mount Nanyue, Tang Dynasty. Tanchang, whose secular surname was Lingtuan and whose style name was Cha'an, was a person of unknown origins. He received the secret instructions of Chan from the gate of Daji (Huairang).
Later, he met the Chan Master Shitou Xiqian—this is what is meant by "re-dyed, it becomes crimson.
In the second year of the Zhenyuan era, he withdrew in seclusion at Mount Heng, taking up residence on its highest peak.

In his later years, he suffered from a chronic ailment of the feet and moved down to the Western Garden to build a thatched hut; those who came to seek his instruction became numerous and flourishing.
He passed away among the mountains in the first year of the Taihe era at the age of seventy.

Previously, he had kept a dog that was exceptionally intelligent. Once, while Zang was walking about at night and sat down to rest, the dog took his robe in its mouth and returned to the room; it then lay down and waited guardedly beside the threshold, barking incessantly and repeatedly lunging forward with the intent to bite ferociously.

At dawn the next morning, he went to look and found a great python in the eastern kitchen; its body was several *zhang* in length, coiled around the small shed so that it seemed precariously perched upon it.
It gaped its mouth wide and let out a roar like a wild beast, while its poisonous vapor spread everywhere.
The attendant said, "Zangqi, go back and avoid him.
Zang replied, "If death could be escaped, how could there be any distance?
He comes with poison; I receive it with compassion."
Poison has no inherent nature; it becomes potent when provoked.
If compassion lacks a causal condition, enemies and kin are of one and the same essence.
Without person and without self, the dharma-nature is universally empty.
Having finished speaking, the python lowered its head and moved away slowly, vanishing in an instant.
On another night, there was a band of thieves; his dog likewise seized their hidden garments in its mouth.
The thief said, "Gentlemen, there is something of my heart's desire within this old man’s thatched hut; you may take it as you please, for I shall never feel even the slightest sting of regret.
Touched by these words, the thieves distributed the goods among themselves and descended the mountain.
Furthermore, there was the monk Shi Lingtan of Yongtai Temple in Jingzhou; his surname was Xiao, and he was a native of Lanling.
As for his lineage, after the Later Liang was destroyed by the Northern Zhou, its branches were scattered like stars, and Lingtan’s father became a commoner resident of Changsha.

From his youth, Shengtuan possessed a vow to transcend the mundane; whenever he encountered Zen assemblies, there were few where he did not attend. Dwelling and resting at Weiqing, he lived with ease and self-satisfaction.
In the first year of the Changqing era, he resided at Baijia Rock Temple.
Not long thereafter, he traveled on foot to Jiangling, where the Prefectural Governor Wang Qian invited him to dwell at Yongtai Temple.
On the twenty-third day of the sixth month in the third year of the Taiping Xingguo era, he passed away at his residence temple at the age of seventy-five.
A stupa was erected to his north of the prefecture, which remains there to this day.
Furthermore, there was Shi Cha’an, a native of Danyang.
Previously, he had met Chan Master Su of Heilin, yet among the assembly he remained merely silent and deferential.
In the second year of the Tiānbǎo era, he arrived at a *ārāma* in Fǔzhōu and received the awakening of Great Quiescence (*Dàjì*).
Monastics from the four quarters relied upon him.
Biography of Wúděng of Dàjì Yúan in Èzhōu, Táng: The monk Wúděng was surnamed Lǐ; he was a native of Wèishì in the present-day Tōngjīng.
His aspirations were lofty and his speech was upright and sincere.

In his youth, he accompanied his father while serving as an official in Nan-kang; he frequently visited Buddhist monasteries, and whenever he approached the monks or gazed upon the sacred images, he would forget to return home.
Having become a śramaṇa, he encountered Chan Master Daoyi at Mount Gonggong, where his disciples flocked to him like ants.
While others sought the Dharma among them, he rose preeminent, standing out from the rest.
In the seventh year of the Yuanhe era, he traveled to the region along the Han River.
Later, arriving at Wuchang, he beheld the extraordinary beauty of Mount Huanggu to the west of the commandery and thereupon settled in a thatched hut to practice alms-gathering.
From this point on, those throughout Ba, Shu, Jing, and Xiang who venerated the profound principles of the Way came from afar to visit him.

In the first year of the Daye era, when the Chancellor, Lord Niu Sengrou, was dispatched to govern the Three Rivers, he heard that the fragrance of [Hui]deng’s Way permeated both near and far; he ordered his carriage to visit him in person.
The wind and the tiger require one another; thus, for the sake of the Dharma, he honored the person.
Master Niu, concerned that his fragrant virtue might not be registered in the official records, specifically submitted a memorial to bestow upon him the title "Daji" (Great Quiescence).
People came and went in constant succession, and there was never an empty seat in the hall.
In the tenth month of the fourth year, he manifested his passing at the age of eighty-two.
His disciple Shi Tong enshrined his entire body in a stupa.
The Biography of Mingjue of Qianqing Monastery on Mount Tiangmu during the Tang Dynasty. The monk Mingjue’s secular surname was You; he was a native of Henei.
His ancestor served as an official in Lingnan and later moved his residence there, becoming a native of Jianyang.
Daowu was the son of a Confucian scholar; he possessed refined elegance and a profound inner character, and he was ever eager to inquire and seek knowledge without ever growing weary or indolent.

Having long harbored the nature of the Way, he heard that Chan Master Daoyi was practicing the dharma of meditation at Mount Fotuo; he went there to visit him and subsequently sought refuge under him to receive the tonsure and ordination.
From this point on, he vowed to travel to various regions—Mount Heng, Mount Tiantai, and Mount Siming—to experience the flavor of the Dharma everywhere.
Furthermore, he devoted himself to seeking resolution at Mount Jing for several summers, carrying firewood and developing calluses on his face and hands from manual labor.
Upon descending the mountain, he arrived at Dayun Temple in Hangzhou and confined himself within the gates of the monastery.
He subsequently moved to the summit of Green Mountain by the lakeside, where he built a hermitage and resided.
At that time, Vice Governor Lu of Fanyang, having heard of his reputation, came in person to pay his respects and invited him back to serve as the abbot of Dayun Temple in the provincial seat.
In the fifteenth year of the Yuanhe era, seeking to avoid suspicion and distance himself from clamor, he went into seclusion on Mount Tianmu.
This mountain is exceptionally beautiful, its foundations spanning across four prefectures.
It contains Upper and Lower Dragon Pools, whose depths are unfathomable, and from which strange creatures frequently emerge.
There was a white deer with extraordinary fur and markings, whom the local people called a mountain deity.
Daojue took refuge within this place, and lay devotees built a meditation hall for him.

In the spring of the third year of the Changqing era, reaching as far as the winter solstice and continuing until the second month of the following year, there was a great drought. Wildfires spread and were about to burn down the monastery; the monks were terrified, but Daojue said:
"I have a karmic affinity with this mountain; the fire shall be extinguished quickly.
After a short while, thunder and rain broke out suddenly, and the fire was completely extinguished, causing people near and far to marvel in astonishment.
On the nineteenth day of the seventh month in the fifth year of the Taihe era, he manifested illness and passed away.
This is the biography of Shi Yuanxiu of Qinwang Mountain in Hangzhou, Tang China. Yuanxiu’s surname was Pan, and he was a native of Min in Fuzhou.
He was precocious from birth and became outstanding as he grew up.

Suddenly feeling a desire to transcend the mundane world, he sought out renowned masters; he shaved his hair, changed his attire, and upon reaching the required age, received full ordination at Huishan Temple in Songyang.
Thereafter, his deportment was composed and graceful as he daily renewed his virtue; he investigated the sutras and treatises until, in a short time, he had mastered their essential principles.
Encountering Chan Master Shanhai of Baizhang, whose fundamental teachings harmonized with his own, he finally clarified the essentials of the mind.
Carrying his bowl and shaking his staff, he arrived at Hangzhou.
Seeing the towering majesty of Mount Qinwang and its long pines with dense branches forming a canopy, he took up residence upon the pine-topped peak.
At that time, a magpie was moved to nest again upon a horizontal branch; having forgotten both self and others, the feathered species became tame and familiar.
From then on, it did not descend [to the ground] for nearly forty autumns.
Whenever a new Governor took office, he would go there to pay his respects and gaze upward, and thus the bird was called Chan Master Niaoke (Nest-Bird).

By the beginning of the Yuanhe era, the provincial governor Pei Changdi deeply revered his Way and requested that the hermitage be established three or four times. On various occasions, he preached the Dharma for those who came to seek instruction. Lord Pei then commanded the magistrates of the eight subordinate districts to join forces in constructing a monastery, renaming the site formerly known as "Fai" to "Zhaoxian" (Inviting the Wise) as a residence for him.

On the twenty-second day of the ninth month in the seventh year of the Taihe era, the year of Gui-chou, he sat upright and passed away with a serene countenance. He was ninety-nine years of age and had maintained the monastic precepts for eighty years.

Successive administrations and virtuous governors of Hangzhou have all held him in high esteem; they would halt their carriages beneath the shade of his trees and request discussions on the ultimate mysteries of the profound, unaware that the servants had been changed and the hours had passed.
Now, the stupa stands at the foot of Mount Shizeng, where the monk Weizhen of Nanyue composed its inscription.
Recently, someone attempted to plunder his stupa, encountering many strange and ominous omens; they managed to recover nothing but the inscription.
Biography of Puyan of Nanquan Monastery in Chizhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Puyan’s secular surname was Wang; he was a native of Xinzheng in Zhengzhou.

His lineage succeeded that of Daji of Jiangxi; Master Daji was the successor of Guanyin of Nanyue, and Let was the eldest son of Caoxi—thus he may be considered my great-grandfather, from whom his own grandfather and great-grandfather can be known. Therefore, the Chan of Nanquan has a long and distinguished ancestry.
While she was pregnant, her mother took no pleasure in meat or blood.
In the second year of Zhidu, she knelt before her parents and requested permission to leave the household life; she appeared suddenly free from the burdens and fetters of the world.
He then went to Mount Daowei in Mì County to receive instruction from Chan Master Dàhuì.

He applied himself with rigorous discipline and earnest diligence; his skin became calloused and cracked, yet he did not dare regard his own body as his master, which caused his teacher to marvel at him.

In the twelfth year of the Dali era, at the age of thirty, he went to Gaoseng Heshang Monastery on Mount Song to receive full ordination from Vinaya Master Gaofa; there he studied the ancient regulations of the Xiangbu school and mastered the learning of the *Viniya* chapters and sections.

Later, he frequented lecture halls, ascending to the summit of the *Laṅkāvatāra*, entering the oceanic assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, unlocking the keys to the contemplations of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Śataka-śāstra*, and the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, and grasping the profound mechanisms beyond the commentaries and treatises.
Those who encountered his vanguard found their banners collapsing and their tracks thrown into chaos.

Among the eight hundred or so disciples under the gate of Daji, whenever they attended his lectures and subsequently reflected upon the Master’s teachings, disputes over right and wrong became muddled and confused.
He would sometimes remain silent and speak on his own initiative, causing all the debates to cease, saying:
"It is only when a man does not speak that he speaks.

Thereafter, he concealed his brilliance and hid his luster, appearing as if unable to speak; because people thought he had no doctrine to expound, even when they pressed him on the essential points, he firmly refused to reveal anything.

At that time, there were those who perceived his profound potential; they subtly revealed their own insights and came to realize that he was not one who lacked the ability to preach the Dharma, but that the time had simply not yet arrived.

In the eleventh year of the Zhenyuan era, he hung up his staff at Nanquan Mountain in Chiyang. There, he filled in valleys and cleared timber to construct a Chan monastery, wearing a straw raincoat and hat while tending oxen for fodder, mingling among the cowherd boys.
Clearing mountains for slash-and-burn fields, they cultivate food until it is abundant.
It has been thirty years since my feet have left Nanquan.
Now, a great bell does not sound when struck by a blade of grass; that which causes it to sound must have something upon which to depend.

At the beginning of the Taihe era, the Imperial Messenger Lord Lu Xuan and the former Governor of Chiyang both recognized that he had established his traces beyond the mundane world and served as a "Dharma-eye" for the four quarters; they, together with the Protector General Lord Liu of Pengcheng, went down the mountain to welcome him and paid him homage from the north.
Before a full year had passed, several hundred followers clad in coarse woolen robes were traveling along the roads.
On the twentieth day of the tenth month in the year Jia-yin of the Taihe era, he manifested illness.
On the twenty-third day of the twelfth month, a white rainbow pierced the peak behind the meditation hall. Those who interpreted the omen asked:
"Could this not signify that Nanquan has passed away?"
On that day, a massive rock collapsed on the western peak, its sound heard for several dozen li.
During the day, a tigress with milk in her teats roamed the meditation grove and let out a roar; everyone marveled at this.
On the twenty-fifth day, as the eastern sky grew bright, he addressed his disciples, saying:
"The fading of stars, the lamp, and illusions have long been so; do not say that I come or go."
Having finished speaking, he took his leave. He was eighty-seven years of age and fifty-eight years since his ordination.
Qi Yuan, Wen Chang, and others, numbering nine hundred in all, were dressed in plain robes and black caps, weeping blood at the mountain gate.
Those who went to attend his funeral procession followed one after another along the roads, the sound of their lamentations shaking the cliffs and valleys.
In the year of Yimao, his disciples enshrined his entire remains in a spirit stupa, following his teachings.
Liu Ke, an Extraordinary Censor of the Ministry of Provisions and Compiler of the Imperial Library, admired the former heroism [of his predecessor] and composed this eulogy to commemorate his virtue.
**Biography of Dharma Master Tansheng of Yunyan Temple in Liyang, Tang Dynasty** Dharma Master Tansheng’s secular surname was Wang; he was a native of Jianchang in Zhongling.
Upon his birth, he naturally had a fetal membrane draped over his right shoulder like a black monastic robe.
He subsequently requested ordination at Shimen; once he reached the required age, he received full ordination and went to visit Chan Master Baizhang Shanhai.

For twenty years he served as an attendant, his duties equivalent to those of Ānanda; he received the Dharma through direct hearing, yet his body remained like that of a palace eunuch while his mind dwelt in a state of non-attachment.
Subsequently, having been exhorted by Yaoshan, he attained complete realization without doubt; he labored diligently in training disciples, and many benefited from his teachings.
He manifested his passing on the twenty-seventh day of the tenth month in the third year of the Taihe era (the Jihou year).
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled the Great Master Wuxiang, and his stupa was named Jingsheng.
The commentary states:

Saṃgharakṣita means "womb-cloth" in the language of China. He was born wearing his birth-cloth; it was not made of silk or flesh, but served as a swaddling band in infancy and remained fitting to his body as he grew.
Upon leaving the household life, it became his Dharma robe, and only when he entered parinirvāṇa and was cremated did it finally turn to ashes.

Master Sheng’s possession of a fetal membrane was merely to prevent it from becoming a garment for a deceased infant; this is close to the practice of Śāṇakavāsin and Śāṇakara, and its merit already exceeds half [of what is required].

Why is this so? Master Sheng is separated from the Sage by a vast distance; Huiguo showed the fetal garment to those who possessed the fruits of practice a hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, yet now Sheng attempts to transform the world through the principles of his teaching while clad only in a loincloth—is this not difficult?
Therefore it is said: "The greater part of the task is already accomplished through reflection.
Biography of Master Zhen of Fushou Monastery in Jingzhou, Tang Dynasty Shi Zhen, whose secular surname was Lu, was a native of Jiangling. His family name was Lu. He was a man from Jiangling.

From his youth, he was alert and wise; at the age of seven, he could recite and master the "Ya" (Elegant) section of the *Shijing* (Book of Poetry). He subsequently entered the provincial examination system and passed it three times, yet had not yet donned the official robes.
Engaging in discussions on profound principles with śramaṇas, he then aspired to don the black robes and sought out Dharma Master Bianchu of Fushou Temple to serve as his model and guide.

Later, at Zhaocheng Temple in the capital Luoyang, he lectured on the Dharma on several occasions. Thereupon, he paid homage to the Chan Master of Mount Song, through which his mind was thoroughly clarified and his doubts resolved.

He subsequently traveled to Maoshan in Danyang and eventually hung up his staff at Lengqia Mountain in Suzhou; seekers of the profound mystery from all directions flocked there, crowding shoulder to shoulder and foot to foot.

At that time, Bai Juyi was serving as the governor of this commandery; as he engaged in conversation with him regarding the Way, he unconsciously opened his breast and loosened his girdle, his mind wandering into the realm where no things exist, thereby reaching the threshold of the Sage’s realization.
He then firmly requested to leave Shui Liu Temple, finding no pleasure in remaining there; he took the mountains and rivers as his source of aesthetic delight.
In the third year of the Taihe era, he manifested illness and stated that he had reached the age of ninety.
On the seventeenth day of the fourth month of that year, he was enshrined in the stupa.
Biography of Chongshen of Dongyuan in Zhaozhou during the Tang Dynasty: Shi Chongshen was a native of Linzi in Qingzhou.
In his childhood, he was solitary and unconventional, not conforming to the crowd; he cast off the bonds of his parents and transcended worldly life.
He then entered the Longxing Monastery in his native province to undergo tonsure under a master.

He then went to Mount Song to receive the full precepts at the Lapis Lazuli Altar. His master encouraged him to listen to and study the teachings, yet he only managed to "dip his finger" into the sutras and vinaya.

Hearing that Master Yuan of Chiyang’s spiritual influence was flourishing like a rising tide, Xian held fast to his resolve and fixed his will, drilling into and admiring the teachings until he forgot all fatigue.
Nanquan secretly transmitted [the Dharma] to him; he erased his traces and concealed his presence, remaining serene and at ease.
Later, in Zhaojun, he opened up the world for all things and transformed the deluded, widely propagating the Way of Chan.
Because Wang Shi of Zhenshuai had obstructed the military lines and caused many border regions to be blocked, the imperial court was distressed by this.
Wang Shi’s resistance exceeded all bounds, yet he remained single-mindedly devoted to Shen.
Xian once entrusted a fly-whisk to the Wang family, saying:
"If Wang asks where he obtained this whisk, answer him:
'It is an object that this old monk has used throughout his life without exhausting it.'"
Whatever he proclaimed was transmitted throughout the world, becoming known as the "Virtuous State (Zhaozhou) Dharma Way.
His recorded sayings circulated widely and were held in high esteem by the age.
Biography of Zhizang of Huayan Monastery in Jingzhao, Tang Dynasty: The monk Zhizang, whose secular surname was Huang, was a native of Shanggao in Yuzhang.
His father served as an official in Hongzhou.

Sengzang accompanied his father to Baoguo Temple, where he saw the court chaplain Haoyue lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. He gained a subtle understanding of the sūtra’s meaning and took delight in entering the Buddha-dharma.
At the mere age of thirteen, he severed his bonds of affection and took leave of his parents to study under Master Zong of Kaiyuan Temple.
Later, he cultivated the methods of Chan and realized the essential tenets of the Great Stillness (Daji) tradition.
In the first year of the Jiànzhōng era, he entered Chāng’ān.

Lú Yuànhào, who had long been a devotee of his Way, submitted a memorial recommending him for entry into the palace to provide offerings; by imperial decree, he was ordered to reside at Huáyán Monastery.

In the capital, the study of the profound mysteries flourished most vigorously; those who sought the gates of the scriptural repository were as numerous as the waters of the sea pouring into the valley of Mount Qín.
He passed away at his residence temple in the ninth year of the Tàihé era and was enshrined in a stūpa on the twelfth day of the third month.
The Biography of Yuanzhi of Mount Daowu in Tanzhou during the Tang Dynasty. The monk Yuanzhi’s secular surname was Zhang; he was a native of Haihun in Yuzhang.
From his youth, he sought liberation with resolute intent; he paid homage to Master Niepan and personally attended to his needs by carrying his water jar and sandals.
Upon ascending to the stage of ordination, he vowed to enter the gates of Chan and, meeting Master Yaoshan, was shown the decisive resolution of the mind.
Later, he resided at Daowu Mountain in Changsha, where the assembly gathered around him like bees and ants flocking to a king.
He passed away on the eleventh day of the ninth month in the ninth year of the Taihe era (the year of Yimao), reaching the age of sixty-seven.

Upon cremation, several fragments of bone that did not turn to ash were obtained, as well as a single section of the cranial cap; these were exceptionally unique and translucent, their color like gold and their resonance like bronze.
Thereupon, a stupa was erected on Mount Shishuang, and by imperial decree it was posthumously titled "The Stupa of the Great Master Xiuyi, Precious Appearance.
Those who attained his Way gathered there in great numbers.
When Master Zhi first realized the essential principles of Yaoshan, Master Yan instructed him, saying:

"I have no precious jade or great bow to serve as a vessel for distribution; I now grant you a single pair of ox-hide sandals. Though they are trivial and insignificant, do they not nonetheless manifest my intimate familiarity with you?"
The monk Xuantai of Mount Nanyue composed an inscription and eulogy for him.
Biography of Fachang of Mount Damei in Mingzhou, Tang Dynasty: Shi Fachang’s secular surname was Zheng, and he was a native of Xiangyang.
In his childhood, he followed a teacher at Yùquán Monastery in Jīng.
Regarding all the various scriptures, once he had glanced over them, he could recite them from memory without ever forgetting anything again.
Upon reaching the age of twenty, he received full ordination at Lóngxīng Monastery.

His appearance was dignified and refined, and his character was firm yet quick-witted. Wearing patched robes and carrying a bowl, he devoted himself entirely to the practice of eating only at the hour of the Rabbit (morning).
In the twelfth year of the Zhenyuan era, he traveled from Tiantai to Siming and settled seventy li south of Yuyao in the former hermitage of Mei Zizhen, the Immortal Commandant.

In the past, when Mei Fu first entered the mountains, he saw many dragon caves where divine serpents would frequently exhale breath that formed multi-storied pavilions, while clouds and rain obscured the heavens in darkness.
Beside them was a stone treasury, within which were stored elixirs of immortality and the scriptures of the transcendents.
He was frequently lodging in a room when he dreamed that a divine being spoke to him, saying:
"You are no ordinary man.

Thereupon, they discussed the sacred scriptures found within a stone repository, which contain prophetic records of past and future events; it was said that whoever receives them shall become a lord of the underworld, and otherwise, a tutor to an emperor.
I often said to him:
"Books from the Stone Library are not what I delight in.
In the past, when Sengchou disregarded the scriptures of the immortals, their scrolls vanished of their own accord."
"I take Nirvana as my joy; how could my lifespan stop at merely growing old together with the heavens?
The spirit said, "This place is a sanctuary of the numinous; those of worldly temperament find it difficult to dwell here, for strange portents immediately arise."
Chang said:
"I am merely lodging my traces in the district of Meiwei; I do not intend to occupy it for long.
For this reason, he styled himself Mount Mei.
Consequently, he thatched with reeds and felled timber to construct a sheltered dwelling; after residing there for barely forty years, it was evident that he was truly an extraordinary person.

At the beginning of the Kōei era, when his monastery was completed, disciples gathered from all directions like spokes converging at a hub to seek instruction and resolve their doubts, numbering some six or seven hundred monastics.
In the fourth year, he suddenly manifested illness.

On the nineteenth day of the ninth month, the mountains and forests shook and birds and beasts wailed in sorrow; he took his leave of the assembly and passed away at the age of eighty-eight, with sixty-nine years of ordination seniority.
On the nineteenth day of the tenth month, he was cremated at Nanjian, where his *śarīra* were collected; they were brilliantly multicolored and rolled in circles.
Previously, Changxian had been hiding at Meiling; when a monk seeking a staff encountered him there, he introduced him to Chan Master An of Yanguan.
He said:
"The plum fruits have ripened; you all may go to seek them, for they can fortunately quench your thirst.
Thus did the Jinshi Jiang Ji compose the inscription for the stele.
Biography of Shi Chongyan of Huizhao Monastery in Yangzhou during the Tang Dynasty. Shi Chongyan, surnamed Duan, was a native of Dongping.
He left the household life at the temple of Longxing in his native province under the guidance of Dharma Master Huichao.
Traveling to seek the Way, he met Chan Master Shanji of Songyang, who revealed the Dharma of the mind to him.
Later, he resided at Mount Duliang by the banks of the Huai River; merchants from all directions came there, and travelers from distant lands flocked to him like shadows.
While Prime Minister Li Shen governed Guangling, his character was stern and severe, and he rarely associated with others, showing particular disdain for Buddhist monks.

Whenever they were permitted to meet, [Wang] Shen would invariably launch a barrage of difficult questions; those who failed to provide adequate responses were often rebuked with shouts and sent away.

Shen dispatched his official, Zhang Youcheng, to convey his intention to summon Wang Yan to the prefectural residence. Upon entering, Yan responded with reasoned precision, and their discourse was resonant and profound.
The local gentry were bewildered, unable to fathom his boundaries, yet they placed exceptional faith in him and requested that he reside at Huizhao Temple to guide and transform them.
Like a resonance of kindred spirits, he gathered only a thousand followers.
In the second year of the Kaicheng era, he passed away at Jingyuan Temple at the age of eighty-four.
On the twenty-third day of the tenth month, his remains were interred in a stupa.

Biography of Qi’an of Haichang Monastery in Yanguan County, Hangzhou Prefecture, Tang Dynasty. Shi Qi’an’s secular surname was Li; he was truly a distinguished scion of the imperial lineage of the Tang.
His ancestors were displaced and scattered, so he was born in Haemun-gun; deeply avoiding worldly glory, he kept his clan lineage secret throughout his life.
While he was still in his mother’s womb, she had a dream of the sun as an auspicious omen.
Upon his birth, a divine light shone downward.
When he was several years old, a strange monk came to his door and requested an audience; stroking the child’s head, he said:
“The phoenix’s nest stirs its majestic presence, and the dragon palace conceals its treasure; the continuation of the ultimate enterprise rests with him!”
When he reached the age of childhood, he repeatedly requested to leave the household life, but his parents rebuked and forbade him.
Dao’an said:
“The nourishment provided by official emolument and profit ends with one’s own parents.”
Is not the benefit of karmic retribution in the afterlife far-reaching?
Is not the glory of official rank and emolument limited merely to one's family?
Is not the benefit of salvation and deliverance vast indeed?
His two parents were moved by these words and complied with his request; he subsequently followed Master Yunzong of his native commandery.

Although he was diligent, humble, and silent, blending his light with the dust of the world, he remained as distinct in brilliance as a firefly from the moon, and as different in nature as a cock from a crane.

Upon reaching the age for full ordination, he went to the Vinaya Master Zhìyán of Mount Nanyuè; externally he examined the monastic precepts, while internally he illuminated the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Later, hearing that the Great Master Dájì of Gōnggōng Mountain in Nánkāng was transforming people according to their needs, his compassionate affinity was deeply moved.
Wrapping his feet in cloth and shaking his mendicant’s staff, he arrived there in a single day.
Daji rejoiced at having such a companion and discussed the maintenance of practice with him tirelessly.
When [the companion] passed away, Dao’an exerted all his strength to conduct the funeral rites.

At the end of the Yuanhe era, when An was already over seventy years of age, he traveled to Faluo Temple in Xiaoshan, Yue. Because the ancient structures of the walls and buildings were dilapidated and incomplete, he repaired the ruins and propped up the leaning walls, unable to remain in tranquil meditation.
At that time, there was one named Faxin in Haichang, a preeminent figure among the monastic community, who began to restore a Chan hermitage on a piece of abandoned land bordering the Fangsheng Pond.
Faxin was humble and unassuming, yet he invited Master An to take charge of it; consequently, seekers from all quarters arrived like a swarm of deer.
The flourishing influence of his Way caused all to submit with unanimous admiration.
Dao’an paid no heed to cold or heat, never descending from the hall or its corridors; he cast no sidelong glances and gave no ear to external sounds, remaining thus for many years.

Furthermore, he was of towering and stately stature, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence; the hair between his eyebrows was deep blue and hung down, and his cranial protuberance was perfectly rounded and prominent. To those who gazed upon him, it was as if they were looking up at Mount Song or Mount Hua while bowing toward the vast ocean—none could fathom his height or depth.
On the twenty-second day of the twelfth month of the second year of Huichang (the Renxu year), he sat in serene meditation and suddenly manifested his passing.
Previously, the bamboos and cypresses had all withered, but at this moment, their luster and vitality were even more vibrant.

Thereupon, a clear resonance struck the door and auspicious light filled the chamber; it was like the tinkling of jade rings and pendants, or as if swords and halberds were flashing against one another.
The auspicious manifestations were exceedingly numerous, and their details are recorded separately.

Furthermore, Anxuan knew in advance that Emperor Xuanzong was secretly practicing the monastic life; anticipating his future attendance at a Dharma assembly, he pre-emptively instructed the administrators, saying:
"A person of extraordinary character will arrive here. Prohibit idle chatter and cease all disruptive activities, for I fear they may bring reproach upon the Buddha-Dharma."

The next day, several itinerant monks came to pay their respects; Dao’an silently recognized the Emperor and consequently ordered the *weina* to seat him in a position of high rank, such that his ritual honors were distinguished from those of the others.
Whenever Dao’an engaged in conversation with him, he increasingly recognized his noble bearing and remarked, “I, this poor monk, am falsely surrounded by a vast assembly;
I am troubled that my offerings for the vegetarian feast are insufficient.
I shall request a memorial for the offering from the Head Seat.”

The Emperor composed the draft and provided the wording; when Dao’an read it, he was struck with awe and alarm, realizing that the offerings for the monks had been brought away and that the rewards obtained were so abundant as to be almost beyond ordinary measure.
He then said to the Emperor, "The time has come; do not linger like a snake coiled in the mud.
Having entrusted him with the future affairs of the Buddha-dharma, he departed.

The Emperor was originally the fourth son of Emperor Xianzong and the half-brother of Emperor Muzong. Emperor Wuzong constantly feared and resented him, so he cast him into the palace latrines; however, the eunuch Qiu Gongwu secretly provided rescue and protection, causing him to shave his head and become a monk, after which he was released and escaped.
He traveled throughout the empire, experiencing every kind of hardship and peril.
By circumstance, he was appointed as the Junior Prefect of Jiangling; this was merely because [the Emperor] disliked his presence at court.

Upon the demise of Emperor Wuzong, Yang Gong, the Commander-in-Chief of the Left Shenche Army, exhorted the Prime Ministers and the officials to welcome and install him on the throne. When he heard that An had already passed away, he mourned him for a long time.
An imperial edict posthumously conferred upon the Great Master the title Wukong, and the Emperor composed a poem in his memory.
Later, Lu Jianqiu, a Grandee of the Right, erected a stupa for him.
Biography of Shi Hengzheng of Shengshou Monastery in the Tang Capital: Shi Hengzheng’s surname was Zhou; he was a native of Pingyuan.
Before entering the Dharma, he attended local schools and had no particular fondness for books;
however, whenever he encountered Buddhist scriptures, he would immerse himself in their flavor and never let go of them.
Later, he renounced secular life to follow a teacher, going to Master Shuancheng of Yanhe Temple in his home province to receive instruction in the recitation of the sutras.
Having received full ordination, he sought instruction at Mount Song and Mount Shao; his realization was complete and unobstructed. He withdrew to the Three Peaks, living in carefree independence.
Before long, he entered Taiyi Mountain, where he had only just begun to propagate the teachings when students flocked to him like ants.

During the Taizhong era, Emperor Wenzong was particularly fond of oysters and clams. Officials along the coast had previously been required to present them in succession, which caused great exhaustion for the people.

One day, a platter full of them was served as part of the imperial meal; among them was one that would not open its shell even when pried. The Emperor, observing this anomaly, immediately burned incense and offered a prayer.

Suddenly, he took the form of a Bodhisattva, his Brahma-like features perfectly complete and his countenance lovely to behold; he was then placed within a casket of *suvarṇa-kṣetra* sandalwood, covered with jade-wool and brocade, and bestowed upon Xingshan Temple with instructions that it be treated with due reverence.
The Emperor then issued inquiries to his ministers, asking,
"What auspicious omen is this?
Li Gongdeyu, the Chancellor, submitted in response:
"I am not worthy to know such things; I only know that Your Majesty’s sagely virtue is manifest and responsive.

Regarding the principles of the Buddhas, I have heard that there is a Chan Master named Hengzheng on Mount Zhongnan, who has a profound understanding of the Buddha-dharma and possesses vast learning and a powerful memory."
The Emperor issued an edict for him to enter and inquire; Daosheng replied:
“I, this poor monk, have heard that no phenomenon responds in vain; this is merely to awaken and nourish Your Majesty’s faith.
Thus, as stated in the sūtras, for those who are to be delivered by means of this very body, one manifests this very body to preach the Dharma.”
The Emperor said,
"I have already seen the body of the Bodhisattva, but I have not yet heard him preach the Dharma.
Zheng replied:
“Does Your Majesty regard this as permanent or impermanent?
Is it real?”
"Is this not a matter of faith?
The Emperor replied, "It is a rare and extraordinary matter; I believe it deeply."
The Minister said, “Your Majesty has already heard the Dharma teaching.

The Emperor’s heart was filled with joy, a state he had never before experienced; he issued an edict that every temple throughout the realm must establish an image of Avalokiteśvara to express his gratitude for this extraordinary blessing.
When that Bodhisattva reached the time of the Huichang persecution of Buddhism, he vanished without a trace.

He subsequently remained at the Zhengnei Daochang, where he repeatedly declined offers to enter the mountains; Xuan then resided at Shengshou Temple until Emperor Wuzong ascended the throne, at which point he suddenly entered Zhongnan Mountain.
Someone asked him the reason for this, and he replied, "I am fleeing from my enemies; how could I stop?
Later, he passed away in a mountain hermitage at the age of eighty-seven.
He was cremated, and forty-nine śarīra relics were collected and enshrined in a stūpa on the fourth day of the ninth month of the third year of the Huichang era.
Later, an imperial decree was issued to suppress the Buddhist teachings; his foresight in governance was as if two tally-sticks perfectly matched.
The commentary asks:
"How could a Buddha image possibly emerge from within a clam?
Tōng replied:
"Whenever there is a stimulus, it manifests itself for a brief moment.

Recently, I heard that the territory of the illegitimate Tang dynasty under the Li clan has suffered successive famines; consequently, many *li* and *bang* shellfish have grown in the ponds and lakes, and the common people are vying with one another to harvest and eat them."
That year, seven or eight out of ten people were spared from starvation.
The following year was a year of abundance, yet the people continued to gather them.
Not long after, someone obtained a giant oyster over two chi in length; carrying it home, he split it open and struck it with a hammer, yet it suffered not the slightest damage.

The man recited a mantra and let it drop; immediately, it opened of its own accord and disgorged a Buddha image about a foot in height, complete with all the marks and signs of perfection, and the color of a pearl.
It was thus called "Pearl Buddha."
He offered them to the Li family, who later gave them as gifts to Buddhist monks.

As for those instances where he manifested forms in places beyond the reach of his intention, it was likely because, as described in the sutras, he transformed mountains of flesh and fish and rice to provide sustenance during famines.
"The harvests have been bountiful; why not be fully satisfied? Therefore, he manifests the ground of contentment.
The Biography of Lingyou of Mount Daopei in the Tang Dynasty. Shi Lingyou’s secular surname was Zhao; both his grandfather and father were natives of Changxi County in Fuzhou.

When Sengyou was in his childhood, he was playing in the front courtyard when he looked up and saw auspicious vapors and propitious clouds lingering and swirling in dense masses; it was as if celestial music were being played in clear tones, and a true embodiment of the spirit had descended. Those in the streets and alleys gazed at this intently, yet the elders could not fathom its meaning.
Suddenly, there appeared an old man from Mount Hua, whose appearance resembled that of a person from Kaśmīra;
he said to the family elder, "This multitude of spirits and sages have manifested their distinction.
This child is a true son of the Buddha; he shall surely cause the Buddha-dharma to shine forth once more."
After a long while, he snapped his fingers four times and departed.
Sengyou, wearing his hair in a topknot and dressed in coarse cloth, followed the Vinaya Master Faheng of his home commandery, performing manual labor with twice the diligence of the other workers.
At the age of twenty, he shaved his head, and after three years, he received full ordination.
At that time, the eminent layman Yi-bin of Qiantang taught him the Vinaya precepts.
Upon entering Tiantai, he encountered Hanshanzi on the road, who then said to Huizhou:
"Across a thousand mountains and ten thousand waters, one stops whenever a pond is encountered.
Having obtained a priceless treasure, one provides relief to all children.

As Daoxuan traveled along the way, he contemplated these words and sat in meditation; soon thereafter, he arrived at Guoqing Temple, where he met the extraordinary person Shidi, who expressed his previous intentions, their faith coinciding like the joining of two tally-strips.
He then traveled to Letan to pay his respects to Master Dazhi, through whom he suddenly realized the intent of the Patriarchs.
Toward the end of the Yuanhe era, while wandering at leisure in Changsha, he passed by Mount Daowei and decided to take up residence there.
The mountain was ten *she* distant from the county seat, a place so remote that it was devoid of human habitation and served as a den for wild beasts.
Thus, he lived among monkeys and langurs, subsisting on acorns and chestnuts.
Within ten days, a mountain dweller saw him, and a multitude of believers together constructed a Buddhist temple.

At that time, Li Jingrang, the Regional Commander of Xiangyang, was governing Xiangtan; wishing to participate in this auspicious occasion, he submitted a memorial requesting that the name of the monastery be "Tongqing Temple."
Later, Prime Minister Pei Gong shared a deep spiritual affinity with him.

Because Xu had encountered the purge of the Huichang era, he was further honored and treated with exceptional courtesy by Prime Minister Cui Gong Shenyou. On the ninth day of the first month of the year Dazhong Guiyou, having finished washing and rinsing his mouth, he spread his mat, closed his eyes, and passed away.
He lived to the age of eighty-three and had been a monk for fifty-nine years.
He was reinterred at Zhiziyuan on the right side of the mountain.

Lu Jianqiu, the Commissioner of the Four Garrisons of Beiting, the General of the Xingjun and Jingyuan Prefectures, and Right Attendant-at-Large, composed his stele inscription, while Li Shangyin inscribed its title.
Biography of Xuance of Jiujing Mountain in Huangzhou during the Tang Dynasty. Xuance, whose secular surname was Lu, was a native of Kuaiji.

In his youth, he followed his father on a merchant journey to attend the Guangming Assembly at Mount Tiantai. This assembly was established by the Sui dynasty Chan Master Zhiyi; held annually in the ninth month, it drew together a vast gathering of both monastics and laypeople from distant provinces and local districts.
Having witnessed these extraordinary signs, Ce subsequently left the household life under Master Zhiguang at Chanlin Temple.
While traveling, he met Daji of Jiangxi, whereby his mental obscurations were instantly cleared away.

After traveling extensively to seek instruction from various masters, he beheld the extraordinary beauty of Mount Jiujing at Huangpi and thereupon thatched a hut to dwell. His disciples gathered like cicadas hastening toward the light.
Someone once comforted and urged him, saying:
"Is the Master’s endurance of solitude such as this?"
Cai said, "One who attains the Way forgets the mind; how great is my joy!
In the eighth year of the Dazhong era, he manifested illness and passed away.
A subsequent imperial edict posthumously conferred upon the Great Master the title Yuanji (Perfect Quiescence), and his stupa was named Zhijue (Wisdom Enlightenment).
*Song Gaoseng Zhuan*, Scroll 11;
*Song Gaoseng Zhuan*, Scroll 12.
