Part Five: The Section on the Practice of Meditation, Chapter Three, Part Five. Twenty Biographies of the Main Lineage, with Four Additional Entries. Biography of Huanyong of Mount Daci in Hangzhou during the Tang Dynasty. The Śramaṇa Huanyong, surnamed Lu, was a native of Puzhak in Hedong. His secular surname was Lu. He was a man from Puzhak in Hedong.

Endowed with a spirit uniquely extraordinary and a physical form transcending all peers, his limbs were well-proportioned and his cranial bones were rounded and lofty; his voice resonated like the tolling of a bell, and his complexion was as pure as congealed fat.
His learning spanned all antiquity and his prose was truly abundant.
At the age of twenty-five, he passed the imperial examination and ranked among the first class; yet, this did not satisfy his aspirations, and he resolved to seek further success.
Before long, he encountered the sorrow of his mother’s death and consequently lived in a hut at her grave site.
When his period of mourning ended, he went directly to Tōji Temple in Heian-kyō to become a monk.
Before two years had passed, he had already studied all the various sutras.
The following year, he went to Mount Song to receive the full precepts and practiced the Vinaya-piṭaka.
Having mastered it thoroughly there, he suddenly came to admire the Supreme Vehicle (Mahāyāna) and resolved to go to Baiyang Mountain, where he deeply grasped its profound principles.
Later, he lived in seclusion at Changle Temple on Mount Nanyue, where he thatched a hut upon the mountain ridge.
Cui Gong, the Grand Master for Remonstrance, held his integrity in high esteem and consequently established a separate "Fangzhang" (a small hermitage) for him.
As the sun’s rays fade at the Pool of Yu, a single meal seems to last an entire day.
Yet, lacking water, he had to laboriously seek it from afar with a worn-out pitcher.
Suddenly, in the deep of night, a tiger roared beside his hut; when he went to look at dawn, a spring indeed burst forth from the earth, providing him with sufficient water for his needs.
Later, when he traveled to Hangzhou, there was a mountain to the north of the Zhejiang River called Daci.
Not long after he settled there, donors and believers arrived;
soon it became a great monastery, with monastics from all quarters coming to pay their respects like clouds.
During the reign of Emperor Wuzong, when the Buddhist teachings were suppressed, he wore inner robes and coarse cloth garments; some requested that he reside at the villa of the Dai family.
In the year Renshen of the Dazhong era, Prefect Liu was the first to command his tonsure and ordination, thereby restoring the flourishing of the Chan forest.
On the fifteenth day of the second month in the year of Renwu, he delivered his final instructions; as soon as he finished speaking, he passed away.
Although the weather was becoming increasingly sweltering, his body showed no signs of change, yet the crown of his head remained warm and moist.
In winter, he was interred at the site of the stupa; he had reached the age of eighty-three and held fifty-four years of Dharma seniority (*dharma-varṣa*).
According to some accounts:
at Mount Hu-pao Spring in Chang-le Temple, on the very day Master Zhong passed away, the spring suddenly ran dry.
How extraordinary!
It was merely for the sake of providing sustenance during his lifetime.

In the year of the Dingsyou cycle of the Qianfu era, an imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title of "Great Master," with the honorific name Xingkong (Nature-Emptiness) and the pagoda named Dinghui (Samādhi and Prajñā).
Duan Chengshi, the Prefect of Jinyun, composed a eulogy for him.
Regarding the biography of Shi Huanyu of Shaoshan in Luoyang during the Tang dynasty: Shi Huanyu was a man of unknown origins.
Endowed with a pure and refined physical form, he possessed an inherently humble and modest nature.
Dwelling among his peers, he would seek instruction from those of lower status; his profound and expansive character was such that his intellectual capacity could hardly be gauged.
After receiving full ordination, he studied the sutras and treatises with diligence.

Subsequently, carrying his staff, he traveled south to Liyang, where he met Jia Shan and attained a profound spiritual resonance. Whenever he encountered those seeking instruction who posed questions, he would extend his hand to lead them back, ensuring that not a single opportunity for guidance was lost.
Regarding those whom he did not personally recommend, he encouraged them to study and contemplate the sutras and the Dharma;
this was also in keeping with the legacy of Xiu and Ji. Biography of Shi Rizhao of Mount Heng’s Angtou Peak, Tang Dynasty. Shi Rizhao, surnamed Liu, was a native of Qifu.

His family lineage was noble and prosperous; having received the instruction of his ancestors from childhood, he read widely through the classics and scriptures, and further delved into the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*. His innate wisdom manifested itself, leading him to desire to follow the sons of the Śākya.

He immediately went to Dharma Master Tanguang at Daxingshan Monastery in Chang’an, where he received instruction and took the precepts. He transmitted and studied the sutras and teachings until there was nothing in which he was not proficient.
Subsequently, while traveling to Mount Song, he inquired after the secret instructions for attaining *yuantong* (perfect penetration) and entered with joyful anticipation.
Later, he traveled to Mount Nanyue and ascended Mount Angtou, where its towering peaks rose steeply amidst lush greenery; thereupon, he conceived the resolve to spend the remainder of his life there.

He lived in a hermitage for twenty years until, during the suppression of the Buddhist teachings by Emperor Wuzong of the Huichang era, Daozhao retreated deep into a mountain cave, subsisting on chestnuts and drinking from mountain streams to sustain his breath.
During the Dazhong era, Emperor Xuanzong revived the Buddha-dharma; he led about sixty disciples back to the old foundations of Mount Angtou, where they thatched a shelter and constructed dwellings.
He resided there for another fifteen years, and students gathered like surging waves.
During the Xian-tong era, he passed away at the age of one hundred and eight.
On the third day of the second month in the third year [of the Xian-tong era], he was interred in a stupa, and a stele was erected to commemorate him.
The world says that his Chan practice was "lifting the head to illuminate what is"—is this not so?
This is the biography of Xuanjian of Deshan Monastery in Langzhou, Tang China. Śramaṇa Xuanjian, surnamed Zhou, was a native of Jian-nan.
Born amidst foul odors and pungent scents, yet naturally gifted with intelligence from youth;

having long harbored extraordinary resolve and earnestly vowed to transcend the mundane world—just as a great dragon is not confined by a small courtyard, and a soaring falcon must surely ascend to the high heavens—you have now discarded all finery and shall henceforth join the ranks of the Sangha.

From the moment he received full ordination (*upasampadā*), he thoroughly mastered the Vinaya-piṭaka; its various natures and characteristics were all internalized through his constant study and practice.

Hearing that the Way of Chan was flourishing in the region between the two lakes (the Yangtze and the Huai), he resolved to travel afar as a wandering monk. He visited Master Xin of Longtan, who was the second-generation successor of the patriarch Shitou.
At first, he lived alone in a single room, and Nanquan provided him with service and attendance.
One night, Longtan held up a branch of fire and handed it to Nanquan;
Nanquan took it and walked several paces, saying, "I have long heard that Longtan has arrived; yet neither the dragon nor the pool is to be seen?"
Huishin said, "The Master has come in person.
Thus, his innate capacity and the teaching were in accord; for over thirty years, he attended the Master’s chamber daily.
Later, he settled in Liyang.
Not long after, he encountered Emperor Wuzong’s suppression of the Dharma.
When the Great Zhong era arrived, the Buddhist rites were restored.

At the beginning of the Xiantong era, Xue Yanwang, the Prefect of Wuling, earnestly invited him; he then first took up residence at De Mountain. His Way was so fragrant that monastics from all quarters flocked to him like spokes converging on a hub.
During the fasts and the *laba* festivals, there were always five hundred people in the hall.
As for his instruction, it was as profound as the heavens and deep as the ocean; its limits were difficult to fathom.
When Xuefeng came to visit him, [Zhaozhou] recognized the depth of his realization and affirmed his excellence.
On the third day of the twelfth month in the sixth year of the Xiántóng era, the year of Yǐyǒu (865 CE), he suddenly addressed his disciples, saying:
"To grasp at emptiness and pursue echoes—is this not merely exhausting your spirits?"
"When one awakens from a dream and realizes it was not real, what further matter remains?
Having spoken these words, he sat peacefully and passed away at the age of eighty-four, with sixty-five years of monastic seniority.
He remained seated upright upon his couch for seven days, appearing as if he were still alive.
Among those in the world who speak of the "swift arrow" style of Chan practice, there is the school of Deshan.
Those who currently flourish as the dharma-grandchildren [of this lineage] in Xiang, Deng, and the region east of Han are precisely these people.
Biography of Canghai of Qixin Temple in Mingzhou, Tang Dynasty. The monk Canghai’s secular surname was Zhu; he was a native of Huating in Suzhou.
From the time his mother conceived him until his birth, she constantly smelled a rare fragrance.
When he was a child, he once fell into a well, but a divine being caught and pulled him out.
At the age of seven, he left home to become a monk and paid homage to the Chan Master Daokuang.
Upon reaching the age of twenty, he went to Mount Song to receive full ordination.
His mother wept whenever she thought of him, and as a result, one of her eyes ceased to see; when he returned home to visit her, that very day her sight was restored.

Upon the death of his mother, he grieved so deeply that he emaciated himself; while dwelling in a hut at her grave, there were many auspicious omens. His filial piety was such as this, and by this means he became renowned.
He then traveled abroad to seek the Way, eventually arriving at Mount Wuxie, where he met the Great Master Lingmo.
With a single word of analysis, their essential intent accords; the way of manifestation and concealment is as it is for the sun and moon.
During the Huichang and Dazhong eras, [the Dharma] declined and then flourished once more.
Only Huian dwelt there; [the light] was so brilliant that it could not be dazzled by glare, could not be heated by fire, and could not be moistened by water.
When the Longshou Temple was rebuilt at Luoyang during the Zhou dynasty, an imperial edict granted him ordination and he resided therein.

At that time, the internal scriptures had been burned and destroyed, and the Sanskrit manuscripts reduced to ashes; he personally collected the scattered fragments to form what truly became the Great Canon.
Subsequently, when Master Yang of Nanhai recovered the canon at Gusu, he invited Huian to return to his native forest to establish a vihāra.
In the twelfth year of the Dazhong era, the lay patron Ren Jingqiu of Yinchui donated his residence to establish a monastery and invited Huian to dwell there.
When the rebel Kou Qiufu led two thousand followers and entered with weapons at midday, Huian sat in meditation with eyes closed; his countenance remained unperturbed.
The bandits were all struck with terror and prostrated themselves, apologizing for their transgressions.
Once the raid was quelled, the provincial governor submitted a petition requesting that the temple’s name be changed to Qixin Temple (Temple of Dwelling in the Mind) to commemorate Huian’s virtue.
Whenever there was any movement or pause, practitioners would inevitably assemble, surrounding the hall and crowding the meditation seats, standing shoulder-to-shoulder like gathering clouds.
Huian’s learning and insight gushed forth like a spring, and his guidance and discernment distinguished all paths with clarity.

The multitudes who challenge and dispel doubts, and the scholars who attack the solid and seek out the hidden, all stand up and brush away the bitter mist, sit and melt the hard ice; with a single word that enters the spirit, they forever shatter deep-seated delusions.

On the third day of the eighth month in the autumn of the seventh year of the Xiántóng era, he manifested illness and passed away. He was seventy-seven years of age and fifty-seven years since his ordination (*bhikṣu-vaśa*).
Having prepared perfumed water for the ritual shaving of his hair, he said to his disciples:
"I shall remain for seven more days."
When the appointed time arrived, he passed away.
His disciples, mourning him with deep longing, temporarily interred his remains at Tiántóng Yán.
After three years had passed, one day a wondrous fragrance filled the air, its intense scent pervading both far and near.
The disciples said to one another, "In the past, our Master entrusted us with the instruction: 'Three years hence, you must cremate my body. Now, such a wondrous fragrance as this has arisen.
They then opened the stupa to look at him; he sat there as solemnly as when he was alive.
On the third day of the eighth month of that year, he was cremated according to the rites of the Western Regions, yielding several thousand śarīras of a crimson-green hue.
In the thirteenth year, his disciple Jie Xiu brought these relics and a record of his life’s conduct to the Imperial Palace to request a posthumous title.
By imperial decree, he was praised with a eulogy, his name was changed to Xīnjiàn (Mirror of the Mind), and his stupa was named Shòuxiàng (Sign of Longevity).
While Huàn was at Chángshòu Monastery in Luòxià, he said to the assembly:
"In the past, the monk Táncuì of Mount Tóngtóng in Míngchéng was my previous incarnation; his tomb and stupa still exist there."
The distance between them was vast, and some people harbored doubts; yet when they subsequently verified the facts, everything accorded exactly with his words.
When Ren-sheng was first about to go and welcome Huian, some people raised objections.
He replied:
"At the beginning of the construction of this residence, a strange monk ordered that its gate be made large, saying, 'Twenty years hence, a sage shall dwell herein.'"
By the time Huian arrived, twenty years had indeed passed.
Furthermore, as Huian was about to depart from Gusu, he was detained and surrounded by his disciples;
he then gave them a *zongfu* (palm-leaf whisk) and said, "I am here with you; why do you have doubts?"
When he had entered into seclusion, the assembly finally came to understand the profound meaning of his intent.
Furthermore, he ordered that five hundred mounds be constructed at the northwest corner of the monastery to suppress [the local spirits].
Some said:
"What strength is required to achieve this?
Huian replied, "Not so;
it can be done by building a small mound and planting five cypress trees upon it."
All such subtle words and profound principles are of this nature.
Cui Qi, the Regional Inspector, composed the inscription for the stupa, and Shao Lang, the County Magistrate of Jinhua, inscribed the title.
The Biography of Yixuan of Linji Monastery in Zhending Prefecture, Tang Dynasty. Shi Yixuan, whose secular surname was Xing, was a native of Nanhua County in Caozhou.
He traveled to various regions to study under masters, undaunted by hardships.
Upon meeting Chan Master Yun of Huangbo Mountain, his realization was suddenly and completely perfected, like the simultaneous sound of pecking and calling.
He then returned north to his native land and, in accordance with the request of those from Zhao, resided at Linji south of the city.
He dismissed those who were chanting sutras and treatises, and all gathered in the main hall; he revealed the essential points of the human mind, which was quite similar to the approach of Deshan.
On the tenth day of the fourth month in the seventh year of the Xiantong era, the year of Bingxu, he entered nirvana.
An imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title of Great Master Huizhao, and his stupa was named Chengxu.
His teachings were widely practiced in the world; today, the region of Hengyang is known as the Linji Chan school.

Biography of Congjian of Guang’ai Temple in Luoyang, Tang Dynasty. Shi Congjian, surnamed Zhang, was originally a native of Nanyang. His family moved to Guangling, and he was born in the Huaidian region.
By nature he was unconventional and noble, possessing a dignified and towering presence; among his neighbors, he was held in awe and respect.
Once, meeting a physiognomist, he said:
"Your height is eight chi, and your features are refined and bright; in the future, you will surely be entrusted with a position of honor."
He admonished him, saying:
"If your heart has no desire for office, what place is there for glory and honor?
The physiognomist said:
"The burden entrusted to me is unfathomable.
Having passed his prime years, he suddenly developed deep faith in Buddhist principles; he subsequently abandoned his wife and children to seek ordination as a monk.
Having just ascended the stage of the precepts, he was able to well protect the jewel of his mind; consequently, he awakened to *dhyāna* and suddenly comprehended the profound principles.
Within only several decades, those who shared his affinity came from afar to seek instruction.
He admonished each person with precise instruction to bring them to awakening.
Subsequently, he traveled to Guang’ai Temple in Luoyang, where he hung up his staff to reside.
At that time, Zen practitioners gathered there in great numbers, attending upon him as filial sons serve their parents.
In Luoyang, whenever invitations were issued for the offering of meals, seats were invariably arranged to face those of Venerable Piṇḍola; such was the nature of the reverence he inspired in people.

It happened during the fifth year of the Huichang era that an imperial edict was issued to abolish Buddhist stupas and temples, ordering śramaṇas to return to their native villages, and thus he too was subjected to the general purge.
Wearing a black cap and hempen robes, he lived in seclusion at the hot spring villa of the Huangfu family.

Later, on a ridge where tall trees grew densely together and a massive boulder lay level as a grindstone, he would often enter meditative concentration during the summer months or engage in mending coarse woolen garments.
Suddenly, they encountered collapsing clouds and rushing rain, with thunder and lightning striking the rocks as a fierce wind arrived all at once;
everyone there fled in terror and cowered in fear, yet Jian alone sat cross-legged with joyful composure, as if he had heard nothing at all.
Someone asked him about remonstrance, to which he replied, "I detest being treated like a beast; why must you be so?
At the beginning of the Dazhong era, Emperor Xuan issued an edict to promote the teachings of Śākyamuni, and [the Master] remonstrated that they should return to his former residence in Luoyang.

One day, his son came from Guangling to pay his respects; he happened to encounter Jian at the gate of the monastery. Jian’s appearance was so solemn and majestic that the son could no longer recognize him.
He then asked, "Where does the Venerable Congjian reside?"
"Admonish him and point him toward the southeast; he can be found there.
Once her son had departed, she closed the gates and would not come out; thus was her severing of the web of affection.
In the fifth month of summer in the seventh year of the Xiántóng era, the year of Bǐxū (766 CE), he suddenly went out to visit a donor’s home and took his leave, saying:
“May you cultivate meritorious deeds; I, a poor monk, shall travel afar at the beginning of autumn, and thus I have come to inform you.”

On the first day of the seventh month in autumn, at dawn, he washed his hands, burned incense, and after reciting the name of Maitreya Tathāgata, lay down on his right side. He called his disciple Xuanchang and instructed him, saying:

"A human body is difficult to obtain and easy to lose; it is urgent! Be without attachment to external things, do not undergo the cycle of rebirth, and realize that there is no phenomenon of birth or extinction—everything exists in the present."
"Now that life has its limits, I part from you for a time.
On that day, he passed away without illness; he was over eighty years of age.
Xuanchang and others, following his final instructions, carried his body outside the Jianchun Gate to the Śītavana forest to offer it to the birds and beasts.
On the third day, he went to look again; the flesh and features were as if alive, with no one nearby at all.
He then covered it with cakes and food; after one night, there were traces of foxes and wolves, which had eaten only what was covering it, while the body remained solemnly intact.
Thereupon, it was decided to cremate the body according to foreign rites; the remaining ashes were collected, and a white stupa was erected by the roadside.
People placed even greater faith in it, and the offerings of incense and lamps have never ceased.
Next was Shi Jianzong of Jingshan Monastery in Hangzhou, a native of Changcheng in Huzhou.
His surname was Qian; he was the grandson of Qian Hui, the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites.
When his father, Sheng, fell ill, Zong cut flesh from his own thigh to feed him, falsely claiming it was "the meat of another animal. Before long, the father’s illness subsided;
the fame of Zong’s filial piety spread throughout his village and neighborhood, whereupon he sought permission to leave the household life and become a monk.

At that time, there was at Kaiyuan Temple in the prefecture a high-ranking monk of the Inner Palace, Gao Xian, who held the rank of one of the ten most eminent masters authorized to preside over ordination platforms in the capital. Xian was skilled in cursive and clerical scripts; he had once written before Emperor Yizong’s presence, earning him a reputation for great elegance and prestige, and Zongshi took him as his teacher.
Later, upon leaving the academy, he delved into and mastered the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*, whereupon he constantly lectured and studied them.
Master Xian also instructed him in the methods of calligraphy, and he gradually attained the "feather of the phoenix."
He suddenly went to visit Master Wukong of Yanguan, where he joined the assembly for formal inquiry and attained sudden, thorough penetration of the source of the mind.
He then returned to his native place and exhorted others to cultivate merit.
In the third year of the Xiántóng era (782), the year of Xīnyǐ, he traveled through famous mountains and eventually settled at Jìngshān on the eastern peak of Tiānmù.
Monastics and laypeople turned their hearts toward him, and he extensively propagated the teachings of the Dharma.

Among his outstanding disciples were Cheongdongsan Hyeongi, who was granted purple robes by imperial decree; Baksan Haengjin; and Daesimsan Haengman. All of them propagated the Dharma by establishing their own branches. On the fifth day of the intercalary third month in the seventh year, the Bingxu year, [the Master] manifested his passing.
The stupa was relocated beneath the Great Silence Rock (Dajiyan).

In the fifth year of the Qianhua era of the Liang dynasty, the King of Wuyue, the Senior Uncle (Shangfu) of the Qian clan, submitted a memorial requesting that the Great Master be posthumously conferred the title "Unsurpassed" (Wushang). Thus, he was transmitted within the ancestral gate as the Second Patriarch of Mount Jing.
At that time, Shen Xiu of Wuxing, who styled himself the "Master of White Teeth," composed a eulogy and record in praise of his virtue.
Biography of Liangjia of Dongshan in Hongzhou during the Tang Dynasty: Shi Liangjia’s secular surname was Yu; he was a native of Zhuji in Kuaiji.
In his youth, Shaoru followed a teacher at Wuxi Mountain Temple.
When he reached the age of twenty-one, he went to Mount Song to receive full ordination.
Immediately thereafter, he traveled to various regions and met Chan Master Nanquan, from whom he deeply realized the profound resonance of the ultimate truth.
He continued to build at Yunyan, where doubts and stagnations were suddenly brought to rest.
Toward the end of the Dazhong era, he widely practiced the Dharma at Mount Xinfeng.
Later, he flourished in his teachings at Dongshan in Gaoyang, Yuzhang—present-day Junzhou.

On the first day of the third month of the tenth year of the Xiántóng era (the Jǐchǒu year), Guǎngjià ordered his hair to be shaved and his robes donned; he then had the bell struck and passed away suddenly.
At that time, his disciples wailed in grief, but Guǎngjià suddenly opened his eyes and rose, saying:
"For one who has left the household life, the mind does not rely on external things; this is true cultivation."
"To toil in life and seek rest in death—what sorrow could there be in that?
To be submerged in and lost to worldly emotions—is this not far too coarse and attached?
He then summoned the administrative monk and ordered him to prepare a vegetarian feast.
"Once the fast is concluded, I shall depart!
However, because the assembly’s hearts were filled with longing and devotion, they entreated him to prolong his stay.
When the seventh day arrived and the provisions for the meal were finally prepared, the Master also attended the fast and said to the assembly:
"This fast is called 'ignorance' (mūḍha)," which likely reproaches them for lacking *prajñā*.
When the monks chanted the *svacchanda* (the ritual of expressing one's wishes), he said:
"The Sangha should not be so casual; at the moment of departure, there was such clamor and commotion.
On the eighth day, after completing his ritual bath, he sat upright and passed away. He was sixty-three years of age and forty-two years of *dharma-śrāmaṇera* seniority.
The imperial edict conferred upon the Chan Master the posthumous title Wuben (Awakening to the Source), and his stupa was named Huijue (Wisdom Enlightenment).
The commentary states:
That he remained behind for several days is something that has occurred in antiquity as well.
In recent times, there has been but one person who could come and go as freely as a merchant.
This is the biography of Tang Sūzhōu’s Cángyì. Regarding the monk Cángyì: his secular surname was Chéng, and he was a native of Xì'ān in Qúzhōu.
In his youth, his spirit was bright and expansive, and his physical presence was imposing.

During the Yuanhe era, he informed his parents of his desire to leave the household life; as his resolve could not be turned back, he went directly to Mount Yuelu in Changsha, where he sought out Master Lingzhi to request ordination.
Master Zhi observed that his aspirations were exceptionally strong and extraordinary, and thus he took him under his care and ordained him.
Once he had donned the dharma robes, he subsequently received the full precepts (upasampadā-śīla) from Vinaya Master Zhizong at Kaiyuan Temple in Wuling during the third year of the Changqing era.
Having studied the Vinaya rules and thoroughly mastered the *pien-chu* (the collection of precepts), he said to his fellow practitioners:
"The teachings of the Dharma-gate are vast and extensive, yet there is a general gateway.
Among the most urgent matters of this general gateway, nothing surpasses the relinquishing of the raft."

He then traveled extensively to study under the Chan school and encountered a high-ranking disciple of Master Masu who was residing at Longya Mountain. Recognizing that Daoyi was a vessel of the Dharma, the master told him one day:
"The aggregates and elements are not real; the Buddha's birth is not the self."
"As for the root of your correction, what should it be named?
And from whom did you obtain it?
Xi understood this in a single word; though there are a thousand paths, they all return to the same source.
Longya said, "My Dharma-eye shall no longer be obscured.
Having thus attained his objective, he found great peace and security; he subsequently returned to Mount Ke to avoid the searches and seizures of the Huichang era.

In the sixth year of the Zhizhong era, the regional governor, Duke Cui Shou, held him in high esteem and constructed a separate meditation hall at Longxing Temple in the prefecture to invite him to reside there.
After several years, he traveled north to Jiahe, where lay devotees took refuge in him and requested that he remain at Zhide Monastery.
He then traveled to Gusu, where at that time Lord Cui Jun was serving as the governor of the prefecture. Having long heard of Huixi’s reputation, he invited him to reside at Nanchan Monastery.
In the eighth year of the Xiantong era, Zhou Bao, the Integrity Commissioner of Zhexi, commissioned him to preside over Zhaoyin Monastery.
In the autumn of that year, he returned to Jiahe, where the lay devotee Lü Jing donated a private villa to establish the present-day Yong’an Monastery.
During the Qianfu era, bandits were in turmoil and the monastic community was dispersed.
Xì said, "The bandits will certainly not come this way.
When the appointed time arrived, the raiders traveled by another route; as predicted, no damage was done. His prescience was like this.

On the twelfth day of the tenth month of the fifth year, dark clouds filled the courtyard; as pheasants cried and crows clamored, he passed away while sitting peacefully. His disciples wailed and wept, but he revived. On the morning of the third month of the sixth year, after bidding farewell to the assembly, he finally passed away at the hour of Chen, having reached the age of eighty-two and completed fifty-six years of monastic seniority.
At that time, Danjiao composed a true eulogy (zhenzan) for Xi.
During the Qianning era, the monk Shenzan submitted a formal petition requesting a posthumous title and a name for his stupa.
The renowned scholar Wu Chongyu inscribed the stele.
The Biography of Dà'ān of Yishān Monastery in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty. Śramaṇa Dà'ān, whose secular surname was Chén, was a native of Mínpíng City.
Entering the Way in his youth, he suddenly brushed away all worldly defilements.
In the twelfth year of the Yuanhe era, by imperial decree, the Qianyuan Temple in Pucheng County was established to set up the Tushita Altar, where he first fully perfected the precepts.

At that time, the heavens rained cassia seeds and the earth produced vermilion grass. The Prefect Yuan Xi personally drafted a report on these auspicious omens, which reached the Emperor’s imperial ear. Consequently, the Emperor issued a decree, changing the name of Fengqi Temple to Linggan Tan (The Altar of Spiritual Response).
Dao'an traveled to Hongjing, and while his route led through Shangyuan, he suddenly encountered an old man who said, "If you go to Nanchang, you will certainly achieve something.

Upon there consulting with and studying the Vinaya under masters, he heard two monks discussing the teachings one night; he immediately attained a thorough understanding of the principles of the Three Vehicles and subsequently entrusted what he had mastered to his fellow practitioners.
He went to Linchuan and visited Chan Master Huizang of Shigong Mountain.
Whenever Huizang gave a formal teaching, he would invariably hold a bow and arrow to threaten his students.
Before An had even finished prostrating and rising from his knees, Huizang shouted:
"Watch the arrow!
An replied without wavering, his answer precise and flawless.
Shigong then cast aside his crossbow and said:
"After practicing archery for several years, he finally began to hit the mark at the height of a man.

He traveled freely to Mount Wutai and entered the Dragon Pond to bathe; although he remained submerged for a long time amidst the rippling waves, there was no sign of the strange phenomena of sudden rainstorms or hail, which left the onlookers both amazed and terrified.
Later, he resided at Mount Gui and paid homage to Chan Master Dayuan, further verifying what he had previously heard as the realization of his prior understanding.

At that time, the Imperial Commissioner of Yuzhang, Duke Cui Zhenxiao—who held the rank of Grand Marshal and was the younger uncle of Duke Wei—profoundly resonated with the profound mechanism of the Dharma and the path of peaceful stability; he dispatched an official missive to summon him, whereby the Master’s reputation flourished even more.
In the fourteenth year of the Xiántóng era, an imperial edict was issued bestowing upon him the title of Great Master Yánsì and granting him a set of purple monastic robes.
In the second year of the Zhōnghé era, he manifested illness; while staying in the Dharma Hall, a massive beam suddenly snapped in two.

On the twenty-second day of the tenth month of the third year, the Gui-mao year, he passed away while seated in his quarters at Mount Yi; he was ninety-one years of age and sixty-seven years since his ordination.
A subsequent imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title of Great Master Yuanzhi, with his stupa named "Realization of Truth" (Zhengzhen).
Daoan never spat on the ground nor lived in a heated chamber; he wore clothing according to the season and bathed when it rained.
The disciple Huizhang, who had consulted on the Dharma, entered Guanzhong and extolled the virtues of Foyang Dao’an; thus, he was posthumously honored with a title.
Sima Xiangguo of Boling, admiring the former hero’s achievements, subsequently composed a literary eulogy to celebrate his virtue.
The poet Zhou Pu was deeply devoted to An; he would frequently enter the mountains to pay his respects to him.
Biography of Qingzhu of Mount Shishuang in Changsha, Tang Dynasty. Hongyin Lingda, Shi Qingzhu: His secular surname was Chen, and he was a native of Yusi Township in Xingan County, Luling.
His ancestors and his father had all refrained from serving as officials, devoting themselves instead to pure discourse and a life of leisure.
At the age of thirteen, Zhushì received the precepts from Master Luànshàn as his teacher and shaved his head at the western mountains of Hóngjǐng.
At twenty-three, he went to Mount Song to receive full ordination and subsequently proceeded to Eastern Luo to study the Vinaya.
Having mastered both the prohibitions and permissions, he concluded that these represented the gradualist school; he then returned to Mount Nanyue and entered Mount Daming.
Next, he went to Yunyan, where he met Daowu; when Daowu posed a question and understood his intent, he was then considered a monk of two summer retreats.
Upon reaching Shishuang Mountain, he resolved to spend the remainder of his life there.
Daowu went in person to Shishuang Mountain and served him with diligent devotion; their exchanges and dialogues during these visits are recorded in a separate record.
His appearance was ancient and his spirit authentic, such that no one in the world could recognize him.

At that time, Dongshan had recently passed away; soon, he was surrounded by fellow practitioners from afar who, having entered a deep mountain wilderness devoid of human presence, were sitting in meditation within a thatched hut.
When the crowd went searching for him, someone suddenly saw him and all wailed in lamentation, entreating him together, "Please come out for our sake."
"Where would all these generals go?
From this point on, he was visited morning and evening by wandering students who came to strike him in inquiry; could he not respond with the "unstruck sound"?

Thus, for twenty years, the veteran monks in the hall sat perpetually without lying down, standing firm like weathered stumps; it is for this reason that the world calls them the "Stone Marsh Community of Withered Trees."
That which is called a "grove" (conglin) in the south is a translation of *dhyāna* as a "grove of merit," for among those who purify the four quarters, none surpasses it.

On the day of Jihai in the second month of the fourth year of the Guangqi era (the Wushen year), he manifested illness and passed away at his mountain hermitage at the age of eighty-two, with fifty-nine years of monastic seniority (*bhikṣu-vaṣa*).

Three months later, on the fifteenth day, he was buried approximately two hundred paces from the northwest corner of the monastery; his disciples constructed a stupa for the tomb in the shape of a śikhā (topknot).

On the first day of the fourth month in summer, the monk Chune of Guanghua Temple, out of deep reverence for the deceased’s virtue and fearing that his sublime reputation might fade, commanded Xuantai of Mount Nanyue to compile a record of his words and deeds.
Disciples from all directions followed and propagated his path.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Great Master Puhui, and his stupa was named Faxiang.
Next was Shi Hongqin of Jingshan Monastery in Yuhang; his secular surname was Wu, and he was a native of Wuxing.

At the age of nineteen, he received the tonsure and left the household life at Kaiyuan Temple under the Great Master Wushang, where he applied himself diligently to Buddhist services without ever neglecting his ritual duties.

At twenty-two, he was sent to Huishan Temple on Mount Song to receive the full monastic precepts (*upasampadā*); there, he was made to recite the *Mahābhikṣu-śīla-sūtra*. After seven days of continuous recitation, he began his formal study of the Vinaya.
Subsequently, as he transmitted the scriptures and gave lectures, he considered himself a monk of extraordinary achievement; yet, upon returning to pay homage to his original teacher, he said:
"During the twelve periods of the day, with what do you repay the four debts of gratitude and the three realms of existence?"
Upon hearing this reprimand, Huian was struck with dismay and lost his composure; for three days he forgot to eat.
His original teacher then summoned him and led him by the ear, only then clarifying the fundamental matter.
Thus they traveled back and forth between Yunmen and Yuezhong, and subsequently to Guishan, where they refined one another until both had become master craftsmen.
Shortly thereafter, during the Huichang era, he was dismissed from office according to precedent; while others wept with grief and sighed in lamentation, Yin remained as composed as ever, saying:
"A man of great character encounters such a calamity—is this not simply fate?"
"Why do you act with the sentiments of a child?
At that time, he encountered the lay devotee Luo Yan in Changsha, who invited him to his home to provide offerings.
Daogui Gan kept the precepts of a white-robed bhikṣu without the slightest transgression; for two years, he conducted himself as if he were a guest of the household.
At the beginning of the Dazhong era, when the regulations that had suppressed the Dharma were abolished, he restored the ritual protocols and returned to his hometown at Xifeng Monastery.
In the sixth year of the Xiantong era, he ascended Mount Jing to visit his original teacher.
The following year, the Supreme Master passed away, and the assembly requested that Huian succeed him in the dharma seat.
At first there were only about a hundred monks, but later their number filled a thousand.
At that time, the fourfold assembly lived together in solemnity, free from transgression.
Emperor Xizong bestowed the temple plaque name "Qianfu Zhenguo.
In the third year of the Zhonghe era, he further granted him a purple *kāṣāya*.
In the second year of the Jingfu era, the King of Wuyue, the Senior Uncle Qian, submitted a memorial recommending him for the title of Dharma Master Fajie.
On the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month in the fourth year of the Gwanghwa era, he took leave of the assembly and passed away.
Qi Changshi of Xixi painted his portrait, and King Wusuku composed a eulogy for it. His dharma heirs were Master Ji of Qixian Temple on Mount Lu, Yi-zhi of Linchuan, and Lingda of Gongchenyuan.
He traveled through the two provinces of Zhejiang, where he widely propagated his spiritual transformation; upon his death, he was posthumously titled Master Guiji.
Initially, Yìn possessed prescient insight.
When King Wusuku resided at Mount Shijian and later enlisted for military service, Yìn took his hand upon seeing him, cleared the attendants from his side, and said to him:
"Take good care of yourself.
In the future, when you reach the pinnacle of nobility, you shall become a leader of the Buddha-dharma.

Later, he repeatedly established military merit and served as the Governor of Hangzhou; consequently, he memorialized the throne to bestow the title of Master Yin upon him, bowing and kneeling whenever he saw him, and his offerings were exceptionally generous, far exceeding the ordinary standard.
At the time of his death, while observing the mourning rites, [the disciples] recalled the words he had spoken during his humble years.
Biography of Daoying of Mount Yunju in Hongzhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Daoying, whose secular surname was Wang, was a native of Yutian in Jimen.
From birth he was extraordinary, his spiritual countenance radiant and clear.
While still in his childhood, he drew his vital energy from Mount Kōngtóng.
His innate mind transcended the mundane, vying to depart through the gates of the burning house.
Wiping his eyes in anticipation, he sought out a master and eventually became a disciple under the Hammer-and-Anvil Master.
The master bestowed upon him the scriptural teachings; having mastered them through recitation, he sought further instruction.
At the age of twenty-five, after some years had slipped by, he finally received full ordination at Yanshou Temple in Fanyang.
He was then ordered to practice the śrāvaka vinaya, to which he responded with a sigh:
"Can a great man be constrained by shackles?
Thereupon, he took up his hempen robes and shook his staff and ring, traveling to Mount Cuimei to seek the Way for three years.
While at leisure in his residence, he suddenly beheld two messengers whose headgear and robes were quite extraordinary.
They urged him, saying, "Why do you not go south to visit a spiritual teacher?
Not long after, a monk arrived from Yuzhang, highly extolling the essential teachings of Chan Master Dongshan.
Ying was moved by a divine inspiration and thus devoted himself to its creation.
Thus, he was able to comprehend the teachings transmitted from Dongshan.
Once, he asked:
"I have heard that the Great Master Wenshi is currently serving as king in Japan;
is this a rumor or a fact? He replied:
"If one is contemplating the Master, even the Buddha would not act [as such], let alone a king.
From that time on, Dongshan granted him his seal of approval.
Initially he resided at Sanfeng, and later he took up the position of *tichang* (head lecturer) at Yunju.
During the final years of the Tang dynasty, the Zhong clan held sway over Hongjing and offered him his utmost trust and sincerity.
Each time he was invited to enter the prefecture, they would first purify the Gansidang Hall to receive him with due ritual.
He then submitted a memorial to Emperor Zhaozong, who bestowed upon him a set of purple monastic robes and a formal title; yet he paid no heed to these honors.
Among those he converted, there were over a thousand followers by the time the cold and hot seasons alternated.
Those surrounded by ox-head incense trees are all sandalwood; the golden-winged bird kings soar and wheel about, far surpassing the common quail;
offerings come from the four quarters, and their fame spreads a thousand li like the wind.
For instance, Cheng Rui, the Regional Commander of Jingnan, dispatched messengers to deliver offerings that frequently amounted to tens of thousands.
He manifested signs of illness in the autumn of the first year of Tianfu (the *xin-you* year), and passed away on the third day of the first month of the following year.
The Prince of Nanyang of Yuzhang, surnamed Zhong, provided for his funeral rites.

At that time, various monastics from different schools followed the local customs of their respective regions; wherever the sacred shrine (lingkan) stopped, they would arrange flowered canopies and curtains and prepare offerings of flour-based delicacies, which were called "zhuo-jì" (table-offerings).
Among the grand funeral rites of a lifetime, none surpasses this occasion. How admirable!
Having received the mandate to transcend the world and deliver sentient beings for thirty full years, his enduring benevolence is evident to all.
The Biography of Shi Youyuan of Lianyun Monastery in Jin’yun, Tang Dynasty. Shi Youyuan’s secular surname was Feng; he was a native of Zizhong in Dongchuan.
In my early childhood, I went to Fugan Temple in Chengdu to serve the lay practitioner Dinglan—who was the Master Xuanzong.
I attended him closely as he moved about, spending most of my time within the inner quarters.
Once summoned, the Emperor wrote upon the back of his robe with a brush, saying:
"This youth shares a karmic affinity with me. From this point on, he was known by the title "Summoned-body" (Jōtai).

In the ninth year of the Dazhong era, he encountered Lord Bai Minzhong, who was stationed as governor in the region of Yibu; [Minzhong] opened a *śīla*-platform, and [the Master] thereupon received the full precepts (*śīla*) at Jingzong Temple.
Subsequently, while in the capital, he studied the Sūtras and Vinaya for five years until his ordination anniversary reached five years (*pañca-varṣa*).
Later, he donned coarse cloth garments and carried a brush and ink-slab as he traveled throughout the land.
He visited Xiaoma Shenzhao; indeed, there were no masters of the Chan school in the monastic forests of that time whom he did not pay his respects.
He then resided at Mount Hua in Chuzhou and traveled south to Mount Wuyi, where the Provincial Inspector Li Hui constructed a meditation hall for him.
In the third year of the Qianfu era, he arrived at Daisai Mountain in Longquan, Jin’yun, and established a monastery there.
He petitioned the Ministry of Sacrifices (Cibu) for an official quota, and it was named Long’an.
By imperial decree, seven monks were ordained; he resided there for eighteen years.
Being able to remain while also being able to move on, he eventually retired to Lianyun Yuan.
The Prefect, Lu Yue, out of sincere faith and trust, invited him to the separate courtyard of Kaiyuan Temple in the prefecture, where he provided him with the four requisites for his support.

On the eighth day of the fourth month in the year of Tianyou Dingmao, he manifested illness; on the first day of the sixth month, he passed away at the official residence. He was seventy-three years of age and fifty-two years since his ordination.
In his final testament, he entrusted the Minister of Works, Yang Xi, to oversee the funeral arrangements; the cremation was performed in the southern garden of the monastery.
When the fire was extinguished, several hundred grains of *śarīra* were distributed.
Later, forty-nine grains [of relics] along with a bottle containing his remains were collected and interred within a stone stupa.
In the third year of the Kaiyun era of the Jin dynasty, the year of Yisi (1045 CE), Vinaya Master Wentai composed the inscription for the stupa.

Biography of Yicun of Guangfu Monastery on Xuefeng Peak in Fuzhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Yicun was born in the second year of the Changqing era (the Renyin year) in the Zeng family of Nanan County, Quanzhou.
From his grandfather downward, all had been friends with monks and devoted to the Buddha, being pure, conscientious, and upright.
He was naturally repelled by the smell of pungent meats and blood.

Even while in his mother’s arms, whenever he heard the sound of bells or chimes, or saw the image of a monk, his countenance would invariably change; for this reason, his parents showered him with special affection from the time he was on their knees.
At the age of nine, he requested to leave the household life, but his father was angry and did not grant permission.
At twelve, he accompanied his father to visit Pūtian Yùjiàn Sī Temple, where there was a Vinaya Master named Qìngxuán, whose conduct was lofty and pure.
He immediately prostrated himself before him and said, "This is my teacher.
He then remained there to serve as his attendant.
At seventeen, he shaved his hair and came to visit Master Hengzhao of Mount Fuyong. Seeing him, the Master marveled at his extraordinary character and thus allowed him to remain there.
When Emperor Xuanzong restored the Buddhist faith, [the Master’s] Way remained unstained by worldly affairs (*nie er bu zhi*), yet his person emerged preeminent and distinguished.

He traveled north through Wu, Chu, Liang, Song, Yan, and Qin; having completed his reception of the full precepts at Baocha Temple in Youzhou, he toured famous mountains and visited various Chan masters, moving with sudden vigor and drifting like a cloud or a soaring bird.
When he reached Wuling, he met Deshan for a single moment; having merely said "Take care," he departed.
His several hundred followers were all unable to fathom this.
Deshan said:
"This has no steps; I have attained it.
In the ninth year of the Xiántóng era, he returned to his old mountain at Fúróng.
That same year, Dàshī Yuánzhì also came from Wéishān with his disciples to Yíshān, the place where the Perfected Lord Wáng had ascended to heaven.
Among his disciples, those who had already succeeded to Master [Xuan]’s virtue came in a continuous stream to knock at the gate; yet Xuan refused them for a long time.
Then there was one named Xingshi, who, sharing Xuan’s sentiments, proposed:

"My Way is lofty and majestic; this is a place surrounded by the gates of the Dharma, where one must not act with haste. As for its location, it ought to be like the auspicious site of 'spreading gold' (Jetavana)."

Two hundred li to the west of the Prefecture lies a mountain that encircles and commands four districts; it rises steeply for ten thousand *ren*, its towering peaks supporting the azure sky, while its smaller mounds overlook the surrounding green hills.

Biography of Yuan’an of Suxi in Langzhou during the Tang Dynasty. Yuan’an, whose secular surname was Tan, was a native of Linyou in Fengxiang.

Biography of Wei Jing of Mount Fulong in Mingzhou during the Tang Dynasty The monk Shi Wei Jing was a native of Wumen.

When Jingxù took refuge in this mountain, the Governor Huang Shèng frequently invited him to leave the mountains for the capital, providing him with abundant offerings and support.
Finally, he established a monastery on the northern mountains of Fengchuan and passed away while sitting in meditation after manifesting signs of illness. He was over seventy years of age.
He was interred at the foot of the mountain, where his burial mound and stupa remain to this day.
