Thereupon, incense and flowers were offered for seven days; those from near and far came to gaze upon and pay homage, praising the rarity of the event.

Afterward, the cremation was performed, and from within the flames emerged divine light of five colors. Over a hundred grains of *śarīra* were collected; the fourfold assembly sifted through them according to their inclinations and obtained nearly one thousand grains—smooth and lustrous as jade, brilliant and radiant as pearls. This attests that they were formed by the熏 (*xūn*, perfuming/imprint) of five lifetimes, rather than being accumulated over the course of a single life.
The fourfold assembly, filled with reverent devotion, again welcomed him into the stupa; this was the year Wuwu of Emperor Zhaozong’s reign.
At that time, the Chancellor of Xuyang, Yuan Xiangxian, was governing the capital region.

The disciples Huiai and others, having been nurtured by the Dharma-milk until their final moments, submitted a formal petition requesting the performance of the posthumous title ceremony. In the third year of the Qiandehua era of the Liang dynasty (Guiyou), Emperor Taizu issued an imperial edict renaming him Dingjue, and his stupa was named Linghua.

In the ninth month of the fourth year of the Zhenming era, Hui’ai and others wished to commemorate the Master’s virtue by erecting a stele; the Emperor granted permission, and the inscription was composed by Wang Gongzan, the Governor of Kaifeng.
Biography of Fapu of Mount Huanggang in Qizhou during the Tang Dynasty. Shi Fapu, surnamed Pan, was a native of Lujiang.
His appearance was ancient and his temperament broad; he took up residence at Nanfang, embracing its dilapidated state.

During the Yuanhe era, seeing that the scenery of Mount Huanggang was extraordinary and beautiful—with its peaks jagged and precipitous and its forests dense and lush—he found within it a stone altar, level and rising high.
He then unslung his bag and hung up his staff, taking up residence among the thorny thickets.
After some time, he sought out a spot beneath a tree and constructed a thatched hut, barely large enough to accommodate his body.
Not long after, someone came along a small path; seeing Baopu, they were struck with wonder and asked:
"For what reason have you come here?

He replied, "I was originally walking at the foot of this mountain when I saw purple vapors surging from its summit, swirling in a lovely manner. Thinking that there must be some extraordinary object upon this mountain, I have come."
Having gazed intently at Pǔ, he turned back and departed.
A traveler on the mountain below heard of this and went to seek him out.
Within a few years, the number of disciples studying Chan had suddenly reached over a hundred.
Fubei Queduo said, "I am an old monk living alone; I have nothing to benefit others, and you all lack for nothing.
From this, mountain huts where they lived like stars became numerous.
His disciples, including Guangyan and others, constructed a great monastery where Zen practitioners gathered in great numbers; those who transmitted his Dharma were beyond counting.
One day, he assembled the assembly and said in farewell:
"I am now coming to my end."
"You all must dwell [in this] well and cherish it!
Having spoken, he sat cross-legged on a low stool and passed away.
His body did not decay or disperse; later, it was coated with fragrant clay and painted.
During the Qianfu era, a stele inscription was re-erected, which states:
"Next, Shi Xiujing of Huayan Temple in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang)—it is unknown where he was from—encountered a time when the Chan teachings of Dongshan were flourishing.
Xiujing went there to visit him, resolving his doubts as thunder returns to its original place."
Returning north to Luoyang, he began his public teachings.
On one occasion, while attending an imperial banquet, various eminent officials were all reciting their scriptures, yet only Huijing and his disciples sat in silence.
The Emperor issued an inquiry, saying,
"Why do you not recite the scriptures?
His responses were prompt and eloquent, with every answer perfectly matching the question, which greatly pleased the Emperor's mind.
He subsequently returned to Pingyang, where he manifested his parinirvāṇa.
His śarīra were collected, and stūpas were erected at four locations.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Great Master Baozhi, and his pagoda was named "Non-action" (Wúwéi).
Biography of Zhixian of Mount Xiangyan in Dengzhou during the Liang Dynasty Zhixian of Mount Xiangyan in Dengzhou was a contemporary of the Liang era. He was a native of Qingzhou.
Standing seven chi tall, he was widely learned, possessed a powerful memory, and was endowed with administrative skill and strategic acumen.
His relatives observed his disposition and said to him,
"If you apply yourself diligently to study, you will later become an excellent vessel for assisting the times. Shortly thereafter,
he took leave of his family and left the secular life.

Soon thereafter, his aspiration for the Dharma became firm, and he traveled to the south to attend the grand assembly of Chan Master Dayuan of Mount Wei. Everyone commended Xian as being exceptionally talented and quick-witted.
One day, Mount Wei summoned him for an audience, but Xian was utterly at a loss.
He set aside all regional dialects and essential points at once, saying,
"A painted cake cannot satisfy hunger.
He then went to dwell at the site of National Teacher Zhong of Nanyang.

Once, while clearing away grass and wood and striking against tiles and rubble, he let out a laugh; there was a realization in the darkness that moved him to compose a verse to sing. From this, his teachings flourished.
After his passing, an imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title Master Xideng, and his stupa was named Yanfu.
Next was Shi Datong of Mount Toudi in Tongcheng, Shuzhou; his secular surname was Liu, and he was a native of Huaining in Shuzhou.
From childhood, his character was upright and firm, possessing the mature bearing of an elder.

He went to Luoyang to take refuge with Chan Master Baotang Man and left secular life behind. Initially, he practiced the *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing), and as his practice was nearing completion, he then sought the ocean of nature within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Again, carrying his *khakkhara* staff, he went to pay his respects at the Dharma assembly on Mount Cuīwēi. There, together with Yuántōng of Fóniú, he was inspired to seek further instruction and clarify the intent of the Patriarchs.
From then on, he wandered freely through various lands before returning to his native soil. He retired to Mount Tóuzǐ, where he thatched a hut and settled there to pursue his aspirations.
During the Zhonghe era, the rebel Chao ravaged the capital region, and the empire fell into chaos.
A bandit wielding a blade asked Tong,
"Why are you staying here?"
He responded with the Buddha-dharma.
When the leader heard this, he prostrated himself, stripped off his own garments, and offered them as alms before descending the mountain.

On the sixth day of the fourth month in the year of Jiashu, the fourth year of the Qianhua era of the Liang dynasty, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture at the age of ninety-six and forty-six years of Dharma seniority.
It is said that he resided on this mountain for more than thirty years.

This is the biography of Guangren of Shushan in Fuzhou during the Liang Dynasty. Regarding the biography of Guangren of Shushan in Fuzhou during the Liang Dynasty: Guangren, whose secular surname was Benren and who styled himself Jundun, was a man of unknown origins.
His stature was short and his frame slight; yet from childhood, his spirit and resolve surpassed all things, and his mental acuity seemed almost unlike that of ordinary men.
Early on he joined Dongshan, where he penetrated the profound mysteries, and his eloquence was even greater than that of most people.
Once he asked Master Xiangyan, who replied with a slight air of self-importance:
"I have come here with calluses on my hands and blisters on my feet; have I not been weary?"
He spat on the ground and departed.

Later, while residing at Shushan in Linchuan, he was frequently requested by visiting guests to speak; his eloquence was considerable, and he composed the *Brief Verses on the Four Elements* and the *Treatise on the Elder of the Avataṃsaka*, both of which circulated in the world.
When he finally entered the shrine, a white deer arrived before the altar, knelt down, and then rose; at that time, the assembly took this to be a sign of mourning for him.
Next was Shi Benren of Baishui Monastery in Junzhou, whose origins were unknown.
He attained realization at the Dharma seat of Dongshan.
Renhan rarely spoke of the Way, yet people from all quarters followed him like shadows following forms; even when he tried to turn them away, they would return again.
Thus, yielding to the request of a person from Danyang, he resided there for only a short time.
During the Zhong period of the Tianjian era, he arrived at Baishui Yuan in Ga’ang, Hongjing, where he gathered disciples.
As he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he first visited various locations to bid his final farewells. He then assembled the congregation and burned incense, saying:
“When the incense smoke has completely vanished, that shall be the time of my nirvāṇa.”
Just as he had spoken, he sat upright and passed away.
Next was Shi Judu of Longya Mountain; his surname was Guo, and he was a native of Nancheng in Linchuan.
At nearly fourteen years of age, he was awakened by the world’s impermanence and maintained a state of tranquil detachment.
Baizhang went to Luling Mantian Temple to seek ordination from his kinsman.

After receiving full ordination on Mount Song, he reflected upon the principle of "choosing a tree," and thus joined the Chan assembly at Cuiwei. Having lost his way and not yet returned, he did not know where to turn for guidance.
Hearing that Dongshang’s words were profound and his principles lofty, Daoxun went to visit him in person.
Upon arriving, he first asked:
"What is meant by the 'intent of the Patriarchs'?"
He replied,
"If the waters of the cave should flow upstream, then I shall preach for you.
At these words, [the other] realized the profound and subtle essence.

While living in seclusion among the masses for seven or eight years, he diligently concealed his brilliance; though people did not recognize him at the time, after a long period, his reputation spread.

Prince Ma of Chu, who served as a Military Counselor, had long admired his virtuous fame and treated him with the reverence one shows to an elder brother or a parent within a family of filial piety and fraternal duty.
He was subsequently invited to reside at Miaoji Chan Monastery on Longya Mountain, where a multitude of disciples constantly gathered, numbering nearly a thousand.

Thereupon, he was recommended for official recognition, and by imperial decree was granted a purple *kāṣāya* and the honorary title "Zhèngkōng" (Certified Emptiness), which occurred during the early years of the Zhenming era of the Liang dynasty.
Beneath the provincial governor’s seat, he was renowned as a "Chan Cave"; those who peered into his chamber and mastered his gate followed one after another.
In the eighth month of the third year of Longde, the year of Guiwei, he fell ill and remained bedridden; on the thirteenth day of the ninth month, he entered nirvana.
Master Dun left the world some forty-odd years ago; his life story is detailed in a separate record.
The Biography of Master Shibei of Xuansha Monastery in Fuzhou during the Liang Dynasty: Shi Shibei’s secular surname was Xie, and he was a native of Min.
From his youth, he was clever and resourceful, possessing a fervent passion for fishing; he often took a small boat out upon the Nantai River to amuse himself.
His vessel appeared as empty as space, such that his peers could not fathom him.

One day, he suddenly conceived a desire to transcend the mundane world; casting away his fishing line and abandoning his boat, he ascended Mount Furong to enter the monastic order during the early years of the Xiantong era.
Later, he received full ordination at Kaiyuan Temple in Yuzhang.
Upon returning to his native village, he took the lead in all manual labor for the mountain monastery.

He added hemp to his coarse robes and mended his straw sandals with grass; he reduced his food intake yet remained content, maintaining a constant rhythm in both speech and silence. All people stood in awe of him; his vast and magnanimous character was such that even the clever schemes of Yan and Sang could not fathom it.
My fellow student Beifu was the master Xuefeng Cun; they met twice, and because Cun bestowed much upon him, he was thus titled "Beifu the Dhūta."
One day, he teased him, saying,
"Why does the dhūta not go forth to study under all the masters? Bei replied:
"Dharma did not come to the Eastern Land, and the Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven.
Cunen held him in high esteem and deep regard.
He first cleared the wilderness at Xuefeng, exerting great effort in all his endeavors.
When the Wang family first gained control of the Min region, he was granted purple robes by imperial decree and bestowed with the title of Great Master Zongyi.

On the twenty-seventh day of the eleventh month of the second year of Kaiping, the Wuchen year, he manifested illness and passed away at the age of seventy-four, having been a monk for forty-four years.
King Wáng Zhōngyì of Mínyuè erected this stupa.

He had prepared for thirty years of transforming through teaching, with approximately seven hundred fellow practitioners of Chan; many attained his Dharma, and Guìchén was esteemed as his "divine foot" (chief disciple).
To this day, the mountain monasteries throughout Zhejiang widely propagate this school, and its lineage of dharma heirs has flourished.
Its establishment serves as a gateway through which one penetrates the initial door of the Mahāyāna.
Among the scholars of the region south of the Yangtze River, was there anyone who did not follow him like grass bending before the wind?

The Biography of Cunsou of Mount Qiyuan in Hedong Prefecture, Liang Dynasty. As for the monk Cunsou, it is unknown where he was from. He resided at Mount Qiyuan in Hedong Prefecture during the Liang dynasty. His life story is as follows: [text continues].
His pure character and exemplary conduct were beyond reach even in moments of haste.
Having ceased his search for sutras and treatises, he became preeminent among his peers in courage.
He went to ask Stone Rain (Shishuang) Chan Master about the Vinaya to resolve his prior doubts.
Like an empty boat unmoored, he became like a withered tree among the forest—a source of refuge for all.
Later, upon returning to Pusa, both monastics and laypeople turned their hearts toward him.

At that time, Prince Youqian of Ji was invested as a regional protector; being one who delighted in the extraordinary and sought out the unique, he would treat anyone who spoke of another’s virtue with great courtesy and humble respect.

The King summoned him into the palace to partake in a vegetarian feast; there they discussed the Way and expounded upon the profound mysteries. Unconsciously, the Master moved forward in his seat, and the King’s reverence and admiration increased greatly. Consequently, he was appointed as the Preceptor for the Bodhisattva Precepts, and the King provided him with abundant offerings and support.
He ordained approximately four hundred disciples and over a hundred nuns.
During his lifetime, he rarely spoke; when he did speak, it was invariably for the benefit of others.
People never witnessed expressions of joy or anger on his face; from afar, he appeared like a solitary pine tree towering above the snow.
At the time of his passing, he was ninety-three years of age. He sat in the full lotus posture, and after one month, his beard and hair grew back; he shaved them again and was enshrined in a stupa.
At the pavilion of the stupa, tigers would frequently circle about, leaving many traces of their claws.
An imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title of Great Master Zhenji (Tranquil Quiescence).
Biography of Master Yan of Ruiyan Monastery in Taizhou during the Liang Dynasty: Master Shi Yan, whose secular surname was Xu, was a native of Minyue.
Having early realized the nature of worldly entanglements, he suddenly sought to transcend the mundane; while adhering to monastic discipline, he soon desired to travel abroad.
Upon meeting Chan Master Yantou, he attained realization without doubt.
Initially, Du Mo delighted in silence, appearing as though he were unable to speak.
Later, urged by those who knew him well, he consented to the request to reside at Ruiyan Mountain Monastery in Taizhou.
At that time, Daofu went there to seek instruction; his responses were swift and resonant, leaving Master Daofu in awe.
Later, when the two assemblies lived together, Yan’s majestic virtue was as chilling as severe frost.
He corrected the monks and nuns, allowing no errors or deviations; thus, regarding those who govern and discipline the masses in the region south of the Yangtze, Ruiyan was considered the foremost.
Once there were three monks with Central Asian features, refined and striking; their eyes rolled like flashing lightning as they stood shoulder-to-shoulder, feet together, to pay their respects.
Huian asked them, "From where have you come?"
He replied,
"I have come from India.
[The other asked,] "When did you depart?"
He replied,
"I arrived this very morning. Yan said:
"Are you not weary?
He replied,
"I have forgotten my weariness for the sake of the Dharma."
He then gazed at him intently and saw that his feet did not touch the ground.

Yan invited him into the hall and seated him in the place of honor; however, by the following morning, he had suddenly vanished. It was said that he was one who had attained the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha, yet no one knew his specific rank.
At that time, there were individuals of unpredictable character who entered the Dharma assembly more than once.
When Yan was studying, he was known as "Little Yan" Elder.

Although the Wusu King of the Qian family of the Two Zhe regions summoned him repeatedly, he only consented to attend after much persuasion, yet eventually declined with great reluctance and departed.
The temple storehouse was always full.
Once, a village woman came to pay her respects, and En said to her, "Cease your prostrations and kneeling;
it would be better for you to return home quickly and save the lives of several hundred creatures—this would be of great benefit."
The old woman hurried home, where her daughter-in-law was returning from the fields carrying a bamboo basket of collected snails.
The old woman took them and released them into the water's edge.
Furthermore, several households invited him for a vegetarian feast, and on each occasion, they saw Yan arriving to eat at the same time.

Upon reaching the final cremation, a giant serpent climbed to the treetop and threw itself into the mass of flames; as the firewood was exhausted, the *śarīra* relics scattered and flew about, falling in profusion upon the grasses and trees, driven by the wind.
His divine wonders were exceedingly numerous, as detailed fully in the separate record.
Biography of Shenhui Benji of Caoshan in Fuzhou during the Liang Dynasty: Shi Benji, whose secular surname was Huang, was a native of Putian in Quanzhou.
In that district, during the late Tang dynasty, many scholar-officials and students resided as émigrés; the scholarly tradition flourished so much that it was called the "Little Jixia.

From his youth, Jing was steeped in the customs of Lu and generally possessed a powerful drive for learning. From that time on, his purity and refinement were uniquely concentrated, and his spiritual nature blossomed from within.
At the age of nineteen, his two parents first permitted him to leave the household life.
He entered Mount Lingshi in Fuzhou.
At twenty-five, he received full ordination; in all his conduct and deportment, he was like a veteran bhikṣu.
At the beginning of the Xiantong era, the Chan school flourished; while the influence arose from Dayi, the reputations of such masters as Shitou and Yaoshan had declined.
However, when Dongshan took pity on sentient beings and held Shitou in high esteem, he went back and forth to seek instruction, his studies rivalling those at the banks of the Zhu and Si rivers.
While dwelling in seclusion, he appeared among the assembly like a simpleton, and his speech was as if stammering.
Later, he was invited to reside at Caoshan in Linchuan; those who came to seek instruction filled the hall and crowded the chambers.

His responses were sharp and unceasing, serving specifically as a standard for the monastic community. Thus, he established the Five Ranks (*wù wèi*) to measure the various domains, such that none failed to reach their full potential.

He further annotated the *Verses in Response to Han Shanzi*, which circulated throughout the realm; because his studies for the civil service examinations were excellent, his prose was forceful and elegant, and he was renowned for possessing great literary talent.
Shortly thereafter, he manifested illness and passed away on the mountain at the age of sixty-two, with thirty-seven years of monastic seniority (*bhikṣu-vaṣa*).
His disciples enshrined his remains in a funerary casket, interred them, and erected a stupa.
Later, Xuantai of Nanyue composed an inscription for the stupa, which states:
The Biography of Gui Chen of Lohan Monastery in Zhangzhou during the Later Tang Dynasty. The monk Gui Chen, whose secular surname was Li, was a native of Changshan.
When he was still a young child, he earnestly sought the transcendent way; he observed a single meal of vegetarian fasting and regulated his breath throughout the entire day.
His resolve was singularly firm, and he was held in high esteem by his fellow villagers.
Bound by affection for his two parents, he could not bid them farewell; entangled by the sentiments of his kinsmen, he found it difficult to escape.

Once he had reached the age of majority, he followed in the footsteps of those who left the city walls, seeking a teacher among the ranks of the "Tigers' Companions," and thus served Great Master Wuxiang of Wansui Temple in the local prefecture.

Having first ascended the stage of precepts, you followed the precedent of studying the Vinaya; now that you have finished proclaiming the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* from the high platform for the assembly, one wonders whether your great aspirations will be confined to the Lesser Vehicle.
He then instructed himself, saying:
"To bind oneself with the rules of observance and transgression is not liberation.
To rely on the literal text for understanding—how could that give rise to sagehood?"
Thereupon, he vowed to seek out the Southern School, traveling a journey of ten thousand li.
He first visited Yunju, and later attended the two assemblies of Xuefeng and Xuansha, where he questioned them with diligent devotion.

It was truly because his karmic conditions were destined to continue that he received the essential meaning from Master Zongyi; regarding light and darkness, form and emptiness, he attained a state of vast clarity free from delusion.
He practiced in secret for many years, remaining concealed while dwelling among the masses.

Although the nocturnal radiance may be concealed, the precious vessel remains ultimately distinct; thus, at the earnest request of Wang Gong, the former Governor of Zhangzhou and Duke of Taiyuan, a lotus temple was established on the western stone mountain of Min City to serve as his dwelling.
He remained in residence for twelve years and a half, with two hundred followers coming and going.

Because Baoshan Chén regarded the wondrous Dharma as secret and weighty, he did not lightly reveal it to his disciples; however, whenever there were those earnestly seeking the esoteric teachings, he would occasionally expound them for them.

Later, when Longxi served as a military magistrate in Qinzhou, the Grand Guardian Langya Gong requested that he preach the Dharma for the assembly at Luohan Monastery; though he declined the invitation, he eventually opened the way of skillful means.
Within a few years, those disciples from the north and south who went forth having resolved their doubts were beyond counting.

Among them were the preeminent figures Cao Shan Wenyi of Fuzhou and Dongchan Huiru of Jiangzhou; both transmitted the essential teachings of [Zhao]qin and each became a Dharma-eye for a school. By observing their sons, one could know their fathers.
In the autumn of the third year of the Tiānchéng era (the Wùzǐ year), he returned once more to his former residence in the city of Mǐn and visited all the Buddhist temples in the vicinity.
After a short while, he manifested illness for several days; then, sitting peacefully, he announced the end of his life. He was sixty-two years of age and had forty years of monastic seniority.
In accordance with his final instructions, he was not to follow secular rites regarding coffins or tombs.

Thus, he was cremated on the eastern ridge of the West City Monastery; his relics were collected, and a stupa was erected to the west of the monastery in fulfillment of his testamentary teachings. This took place on the full moon day of the twelfth month in the second year of the Qingtai era.

When Facheng received the Dharma and was entrusted with its secret transmission, he encountered Master Shenyuan of the Wang clan, whom the Wang family held in high esteem. Shenyuan used political matters to intimidate Facheng, ordering him to renounce his succession to Xuefeng; yet Facheng remained firm and unshakable. In the end, he was slandered by Shenyuan and suffered oppression—how lamentable!
The Biography of Huileng of Changqing Monastery in Fuzhou during the Later Tang Dynasty. Shi Huileng was a native of Haiyan in Hangzhou; his secular surname was Sun.
At his birth, he was enveloped in a purple-colored placenta.
During his childhood, he was brilliant and possessed high principles; at Tongxuan Temple in Wuyuan, he received the full precepts.
Having heard that there was the study of Chan in the south, he traveled to the Min Ridge to visit Xuefeng. Through the master’s guidance and instructions, he suddenly realized his original nature.
He then composed a verse, saying:
"In the past, I studied in vain upon the road; today, I see it is ice within fire.
Thus he remained in close reliance [upon his teacher], never descending from the mountain peak for approximately thirty years.
He followed his karmic destiny with profound dedication, maintaining strict discipline and solemnity.
Wang Yanbin, the Prefectural Governor of Quanzhou, summoned Faling to reside at Zhaokong Monastery; the assembly of Chan practitioners flocked to him, fearing only that they might arrive too late.
He resided at Changqing Yuan in the Changle Fu for over twenty years, where his monastic community never fell below fifteen hundred members. His nature was one of stability and compassion;
he was patient and forbearing, and would not recklessly grant permission to anyone.
Being able to apply this principle to other cases by analogy, he was subsequently granted formal certification.

On the seventeenth day of the fifth month of the third year of the Changxing era (the Renchen year), he passed away; he was seventy-nine years of age and had sixty years of monastic seniority (*bhikṣu-vaṣa*).
The Wang family of Min composed a private eulogy for him as "Grand Master," bestowing upon him the title Chaojue (Transcendent Enlightenment).
His interment in a stupa was entirely provided by official funds.
Lin Wensheng, a judicial officer, composed an inscription to commemorate his virtues.
Biography of Daofu of Longce Monastery in Hangzhou during the Later Tang Dynasty. Śramaṇa Daofu’s secular surname was Chen, and he was a native of Yongjia.
In his childhood, his nature was extraordinary; he loathed the smell of blood.
When his relatives forced him to eat dried fish, he feared he would vomit.
He sought ordination at Kaiyuan Temple.

Once he had received full precepts, he traveled through Min and entered Chu, intending to consult virtuous spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) to resolve his doubts regarding the fundamental source of birth and death.
He visited Master Jì of Cáoshān in Línchuān, who subjected him to extensive interrogation, much like Tánxún’s questioning of Sēngchóu.

Ultimately, he resolved his doubts at Xuěfēng; those in Míngzhōng called him "Little Tófú," as there was a man of the same name from Tàiyuán at the time, though this was due to the seniority of his years and ordination.
Upon returning to Zhejiang, he resided at Jianqing Yuan in Yuezhou.

At that time, Pi Guangye—the son of Ri-xiu—was a man of vast and extensive learning; having delved into the mysteries of the Chan gate, he had frequently engaged in profound challenges and debates with him.
Withdrawing, he said to others:
"As for Master Fuyou’s Way, his lofty discourses and grand deliberations have reached a pinnacle that none can surpass.
King Qian of Wusuku, filled with admiration, ordered him to reside at Tianlong Temple and privately conferred upon him the title of Grand Master Shunde.
Next, during the reign of Emperor Wenmù of the Qián dynasty, the Lóngcè Temple was founded, and he was invited to reside there; from this point on, the Chan school flourished in Wúyuè.
He passed away in the eighth month of the *tiānfú* *dīngyǒu* year at the age of seventy.
He was cremated in the valley of Mount Daci; his relics were collected and a stupa was erected before Mount Longmu.
Thus, the monastic leader Hui Zheng composed the inscription for the stupa.
The present Śarīra Hall is presided over by his disciples, where the incense and lamps have been maintained in succession.

Biography of Shi Quanfu of Qinghua Monastery in Kuaiji, Jin Dynasty: Shi Quanfu was a native of Kunshan in Wu Commandery. His lineage was transmitted from Qinghua Monastery in Kuaiji during the Jin Dynasty. His full biography is recorded as follows: Shi Quanfu was a man of Kunshan in Wu Commandery.

In his youth, he accompanied his father on a merchant journey to Yuzhang, where he heard the teachings on meditative stillness (*dhyāna-śamatha*) and consequently conceived a resolve to renounce the world.
He requested permission to leave the household life, which caused his father’s displeasure to manifest in his countenance.
He ceased his anger and repeated his request three times; the father, moved by his sincerity, gave him a brief and general permission.
He then traveled to Jiangxia and sought out the Great Master Qingping, asking:
"What do you seek by coming here?
Hu replied, "I seek the Dharma."
Master Qingping, pitying his youth yet perceiving his great potential, took him in and raised him.
From dawn until dusk, he distinguished himself from the other children.
Upon reaching maturity, the master ordained him by shaving his hair, and he soon received full monastic precepts.
He served his teacher with ever-increasing reverence and examined himself with ever-greater rigor; he questioned the Dharma without weariness and perceived his own nature without narrow-mindedness.
Qingping nodded in approval and granted him permission. One day, he said to others:
"I have heard that in learning there is no constant teacher. I am not a bitter gourd; how could I remain tethered here while neglecting what lies beyond?"
He then took leave of his teacher and traveled to Mount Yang in Yichun, where he paid his respects to Chan Master Yong of the Southern Pagoda.
Through their dialogues and exchanges, he deeply recognized the significance of Mount Yang and suddenly attained a thorough realization of the mind that lies directly beneath.
Yangshan smiled with appreciation and held him in high esteem.
He devoted himself to his teachings with earnest reverence, dwelling in his spirit for many years.
Later, while traveling through Luling, Yangshan was invited by Yang Gongjian, the Magistrate of Anfu County, to reside at the newly established Yingguo Chan Monastery.
Disciples of the Chan school flocked to him until his hall and chambers were filled to capacity.
When Magistrate Yang completed his term of office, the local people built a monastery on Gehu Mountain and invited him to reside there.

The Intendant reported this to the Emperor, who bestowed upon it the name Qinghua Chan Monastery. Zen practitioners flocked there like deer, and those who came to inquire about the Way arrived in such numbers that they seemed to press against the walls; yet none could best me in debate—was this not because I held myself in high regard compared to my predecessors?
A monk from the same village said to Huifu, "How can you abandon your parents' hometown?
You should follow your karmic conditions and conform to the ways of the world; I hope the Master will return!"
He then took his leave of Hege Lake and returned to his native land.
At that time, Qian Shu, the Prince Wenmu of Wuyue, ordered him to ascend the steps and bestowed upon him robes, bedding, an alms bowl, and other utensils, treating him with exceptional honor.
In the year of Dingyou, the military commander of Qiancheng opened up Yunfeng Mountain and established the Qinghua Chan Monastery, summoning him to reside there.

Subsequently, the late Prince Zhongxian of the Qian family dispatched an envoy to bestow upon him a purple *kāṣāya*; he submitted successive memorials declining the gift, yet it was bestowed again, and he declined once more, finally accepting it only as a garment for the inner robe (*nàiyī*).
Fufu replied, "It is not that I do not honor the gift or wish to embellish my refusal; rather, I fear that later generations might imitate me and indulge their desires.
He subsequently declined the bestowed title of Chunei Zenji, firmly refusing it once again.
Because he did not employ sentiment to forget sentiment, his sentiment was true;
because he did not seek the Way by means of the Way, the Way was straightforward.
The halls, pavilions, and chambers of the monastery where he resided were vied for and magnificently constructed by others.
He cast a bell weighing over a thousand jin.
He changed the new plaque to read "Yunfeng Qinghua Chan Monastery," and practitioners from all quarters flocked there like spokes converging at a hub, gazing longingly as if unwilling to leave.
In the seventh month of autumn in the fourth year of Kaie (the Dingwei year), he manifested illness and said to the assembly:
"Birth is the arising of the Dharma; death is the cessation of the Dharma. This arising and cessation are beyond the reach of verbal discourse."
He passed away peacefully; at that time, there was a great rain and a violent wind that shook the forest until the trees were uprooted.
He lived to the age of sixty-six and had been ordained for forty-five years.

He was interred in a northern cove of the mountain; his disciples, including Yingqing and others—some ten people in total—honored their master’s final instructions and did not let his Way fall into decline.
Sengzhu Huizheng composed the inscription for the stupa, which was erected in the second year of the Jianlong era.

Biography of Shanjing of Yong’an Temple in Yongxing, Jin: Shanjing, whose secular surname was Wang, was a native of Jincheng in Chang’an. His religious name was Lingzhao. He was a man of the Jin dynasty.
His father was Lang, the Regional Inspector of Wei Prefecture during the Tang dynasty.
His mother, Lady Li, became pregnant after dreaming that a sacred countenance shone with a brilliant golden luster;
when he was born, he was precocious and outstanding.

He was nearly a master of learning, having extensively mastered a multitude of doctrines; consequently, he served as the scribe for official reports at the Shen-ce Army, where the Commander-in-Chief held him in high esteem.
Suddenly weary of worldly illusions, he secretly traveled to Fengde Monastery on Mount Zhongnan to pay homage to Chan Master Guangdu, at which time he was twenty-seven years old.
Upon shaving his head and receiving full ordination, Tianfu traveled south to Youlepu, where he met Yuan’an, a successor of the Chan lineage, and thereby integrated the essentials of the mind.
Returning north, he converted disciples in his hometown and built a hermitage on Yunjushan in Zhongnan, where monastics and laypeople flocked to him like a marketplace.
He again set out on a journey to Mount Emei to pay homage at the Silver World of Samantabhadra.

Upon returning to Xingyuan, the regional commander, Lord Wang, treated him with great respect and wished to retain him; however, when he later returned to his native village, it was already a scene of desolation like that described in the "Shu Li" ode.
The Retained Prince established the Yong’an Chan Monastery for him to reside in.

In the winter of the Kaiyun Bingwu year, he struck the wooden mallet to assemble the monks and delivered his final instructions. He then returned to the abbot’s quarters, turned toward the east, and passed away in the lotus posture on his right side. His secular age was eighty-nine, and his monastic seniority was sixty years.
The assembly of both monastics and laypeople mourned him as if they had lost a close parent.
On the eighth day of the first month of the following year, he was cremated south of the city, where several thousand *śarīra* relics were obtained.

On the eighth day of the eighth month of the third year of the Qianguo era of the Han dynasty (the *gengxu* year), his stupa was relocated to Yiyang Township in Chang’an; the stone stupa stands loftily there to this day.
Initially, Jing was frequently possessed of prescient insight; he traveled to Bǎodào to avoid the chaos caused by Emperor Zhaozong’s flight from the capital.
Furthermore, throughout his life, whenever he washed himself, śarīras would fall from his body; he collected them all and kept them secret, refusing to allow his disciples to show them to others.
Furthermore, once while he was in meditative stillness, a white crane appeared outside his window and became tame and familiar in the courtyard, as if it intended to listen to the Dharma.
Jing ordered someone to drive it away.
All these extraordinary signs were present yet non-existent.
Guo Gong, the Commander of the Jinchang Military Command, placed his faith in them; he constructed a Chan temple and commissioned it for their residence.
Yu Chongliang, a Hanlin Academician, composed the stupa inscription to recount his virtues.
Next was Shi Lingzhao of Longhua Temple in Hangzhou, who was originally a native of the kingdom of Goryeo.
Having traveled here from afar after translating the scriptures, he studied the ancestral Dharma and entered Min and Yue, where he attained realization at Xuefeng.
With resolute dedication, he attended the master’s side and applied himself to communal affairs with frugality and diligence; thus he was known as Zhaobuna.
A thousand people were awed and submissive to him, yet his speech resembled that of the islanders.
By nature he was solitary and independent, maintaining himself through tranquility and detachment.
Initially he resided at Mount Qiyun, and subsequently lived at Jianqing Monastery in Yuezhou.
Once, when he was summoned for an audience by the Vice Commissioner Pi Guangye, their conversation did not harmonize; consequently, he was dismissed and banished to Longxing.
Later, when the Prefect of Huzhou, Lord Qian, invited him to reside at Baoji Monastery, his disciples gathered there in great numbers.
In the regions of Wu and Kuaiji, monastics who had renounced the three robes and donned the five-fold patched garment were beyond counting.

When Prince Qian, the Loyal Contributor, established Longhua Temple, he invited the sacred relics and ritual implements of the Great Being Liang Fu Xi of Jinhua; these were enshrined in this temple, where a stupa was erected, and he appointed Zhao as its abbot.
He passed away at this temple, and his stupa was enshrined on a peak of Mount Daci.
Biography of Wen Yi of Qingliang Monastery in Jinling during the Zhou Dynasty: Shi Wen Yi’s secular surname was Lu, and he was a native of Yuhang.
At the mere age of seven, he stood out as one transcending the mundane; he shaved his head and donned the dyed robes at Xinding Zhitong Yuan, relying upon the Chan master Quanwei.
In his youth, he received the "Formless Ritual for Simultaneous Ordination" (*xingju wuzuo fa*) at Kaiyuan Temple in Yuezhou.
At that time, he cast off worldly burdens and brushed aside his robes, emerging from the cage to stretch his wings.

It coincided with the period when the master of the Vinaya, Master Xijue, was flourishing his teachings among his disciples at Yuyang Temple on Mount Mao; [Huijiao] thoroughly grasped the essential principles of what is permitted and what is prohibited.
Furthermore, as he frequented circles of literary elegance, Master Jue recognized him as a "Yu" or "Xia" among his disciples.
Thereupon, once the profound mechanism was set in motion, all miscellaneous affairs were cast aside.
Shaking his mendicant’s staff, he traveled south and stayed at the dharma assembly of Chan Master Changqing.
Having resolved his doubts and lingering attachments, he further arranged for companions to travel west out of Huxiang.

On that day, due to heavy rain, they could not proceed; they looked toward Xiyuan for a time to spend two nights there, merely to avoid the danger of rising river floods. Thereupon, he visited Master Xuangfa—who had previously resided at Luohan Monastery in Zhangpu (the people of Min simply called him "Luohan").
Luo Han had long known that Fayi was outstanding among those at Changqing; he resolved to welcome and guide him.

Because Xuefeng’s spiritual lineage was distinct from that of Xuansha, Fayi felt as though a mountain of doubt had suddenly collapsed and the true path had finally been found. With great joy, he hung up his bag and settled there, changing his course and altering his trajectory, remaining firm and unshakable.
Traveling through various regions, he eventually arrived at Linchuan, where the local governor ordered him to reside at Chongshou Monastery.
Monks from all directions seeking his instruction numbered no fewer than a thousand.
Li Shizu, the founding ancestor of the Prince of Jiangnan, recognized his worth and invited him to preside over Ba’en Chan Monastery, bestowing upon him the title Jinghui.
Thereafter, the subtle words were on the verge of being lost, and who could awaken from the great dream?

Having transmitted the Dharma and found his place of return, he likewise manifested extinction like an ordinary person. On the seventeenth day of the seventh month in the autumn of the fifth year of the Xiande era of the Zhou dynasty, the year of Wuma (548), he fell ill; the Sovereign of the State visited him in his quarters to inquire after his illness.

On the fifth day of the intercalary month, he shaved his head and bathed his body, bidding farewell to the assembly. He sat cross-legged until his passing; his countenance remained as if alive. He was seventy-four years of secular age and fifty-five years of monastic seniority.
I posthumously conferred upon him the title Dàfǎyǎn (Great Dharma Eye), and his stupa was named Wúxiàng (Formless).
I ordered the monasteries within the city to provide a full ceremonial procession to escort his remains to Danyang Township in Jiangning County, where a stupa was erected for them.

He increasingly delighted in literary composition, particularly admiring the style of Zhi Dun and Tao Yuanming. He frequently composed verses, hymns, and true eulogies, which he separately compiled and recorded.
His Dharma heirs were Tiantai Deshao, Huiming; Zizhou Zhiyi; Zhongshan Daqin; Runzhou Guangyi; and Jizhou Wensui.
The Later Ruler of Jiangnan composed an inscription to commemorate his virtue; Han Xizai wrote the stupa epitaph, which states:
"Regarding the account of the monk Xingyin of Foshouyan on Mount Lu: Xingyin, whose secular surname and origins are unknown, was a native of Yanmen."

While traveling through the Jianghuai region in search of the Way, he saw a cliff to the north of Mount Lu that appeared from afar like a hanging hand; beneath the hand, the cavern was deep for about thirty or fifty feet.
Consequently, he dwelt alone in secluded meditation within it.
When the Emperor Yuanzong of the spurious Tang dynasty heard of him, he summoned him three times, but he did not rise to accept the call.

Deep into the night in the crag, a strange deer lay down beside Yin’s stone hut, and a bird with a scarlet pouch settled to roost beneath the rock wall; neither creature showed the slightest sign of alarm.
Because he did not ordain disciples, a monk from a neighboring hermitage served him.
One day, falling slightly ill, he said to his attendant:
"Roll up the curtain; I am going."
Just as she was reaching for the hook of the curtain, she stood for three or four steps from her bed and suddenly passed away, at approximately seventy years of age.
Emperor Wonjong ordered an artist to paint her portrait, and after her cremation, her remains were collected; a white pagoda stands on the back of the cliff.
Initially, he transmitted the Chan dharma at Lumen Mountain in Xiangyang.
Subsequently, at the earnest request of Emperor Yuanzong, he opened the hall to proclaim the Way at Qixian Temple; yet before a full month had passed, he secretly returned to a mountain cave.
At first, the cliff resembled five fingers; atop the middle finger grew a single pine tree, which withered away on the day of his death.

Because he possessed learning in the classics and scriptures, whenever he was questioned, he would point out the strengths and weaknesses of former scholars and the correctness or error of their commentaries.
His discourse did not stagnate within any particular regional bias, and his expositions invariably contained elements of spiritual transformation; he was truly a gentleman who had attained the Way.
The concluding verse says:
When ordinary people relinquish their retribution, their corpses are necessarily one and the same.

The Buddha passed away seated in the full-lotus posture on his right side; those who rested their heads upon the ground manifested supernatural powers, while those whose bodies remained upright displayed extraordinary signs.
As for those who intended to transform others through the act of walking, apart from the later assembly of monks, there was also the case of Master Yin.
Next was Shi Daopian of Yongming Temple, Huiri Monastery, in Qiantang. His secular surname was Wu, and he was a native of Pujin.
From birth he was robust and strong, with a dignified and elegant appearance.
When he was established [in his studies], he stood about seven chi tall; there were seven black moles on his chest, like the handle and stars of the Dipper constellation.
He retired to Qiyuan Dàtōng Chan Monastery in Zhōngtiáoshān to pay respects to Chan Master Zhēnjì, who served as his preceptor.
His observance of the precepts was strict and clear; he was reticent in speech but swift in action.
After his teacher passed away, he vowed to enter Mount Wutai in Yanmen, and due to his diligent devotion, he beheld the sacred countenance of Mañjuśrī with his own eyes.
Thereafter, he traveled without a fixed destination through various regions.
Upon arriving in Linchuan, he met Chan Master Yì of Chōngshòu Monastery, where he attained sudden enlightenment and reached a definitive resolution regarding the mind.
Subsequently, he resided at an ancient temple in Qúzhōu, where he perused and studied the Tripitaka.
Once, while sitting in meditation, he beheld the manifestation of Mañjuśrī; unable to contain his emotion, he rose spontaneously to pay homage.
Upon arriving in Hangzhou, he visited the Aśoka Stūpa, where he knelt and placed it upon his head in veneration, his tears falling like rain.
He asked the monk in charge of the stupa,
"If people have not witnessed the śarīra with their own eyes, can it truly be said that they exist?
The monk replied:
"According to the biographical records, it was hidden within the inner corner, appearing from afar like a suspended bell.
While his doubts remained unresolved, he proceeded with arduous devotion, prostrating himself in worship without ceasing for even a moment.
Suddenly, he saw the red-colored śarīra outside the suspended bell, crawling along with a quivering motion.
Secretly, his grief and joy mingled within him.

Furthermore, Dashi Guangwen Hui Zheng, who was exceptionally inclined toward the Dharma, personally served as a donor and invited [the Master] to perform the *Samantabhadra Repentance* for twenty-one days at his mountain retreat. Suddenly, he saw the elephant of Samantabhadra beneath the pavilion at the triple gate of the temple; the elephant’s trunk extended straight out, resting directly upon the place where the repentance was being performed.

The King of Hainan, the Qian family, commanded him to enter the royal palace to receive the Bodhisattva precepts; he then constructed a great monastery named Huiriyongming and invited him to reside there.
He was posthumously titled Chan Master Cihua Dinghui; a separate monthly stipend was granted for his support as a mark of special honor.
On the eighteenth day of the ninth month in the second year of the Jianlong era (the Xinyou year), he manifested illness and passed away.
At the moment he was placed in the coffin, a white light radiated during the day, shimmering and brilliant, which all those present witnessed.
Within the tenth month, his body was cremated at Longjing Mountain; the relics collected were numerous.
There was a butcher who, reflecting upon his own evil karma, approached a pyre with bared chest and made a plea;
in an instant, he obtained seven pearls, which he then brought to the stūpa of the Ikṣvāku clan.
In the year Kaimao (790) of the Kaibao era, Chan Master Shao of Tiantai erected a stone stupa to enshrine his true remains; in the year Guiyou (793), a white light radiated from the top of the stupa.
The Biography of Yuan De of Yuantong Monastery on Mount Lu during the Song Dynasty. The monk Yuan De, whose secular surname was Huang, was a native of Qiantang.

His father, Chao, studied Confucian arts and excelled in painting; he transmitted the Buddhist draft models of Zhou Fang and received the methods of brushwork from Li Zhao, the Grand Master of the Imperial Secretariat in Wuxing.

From his youth, Dezhi harbored the aspiration to leave the household life; as his character was solitary and he found few with whom to harmonize, he subsequently traveled to Tiantai to receive full ordination and studied the methods of Chan meditation under Chan Master Daofu at Tianlong Temple.
He subsequently traveled to Jiangxi to seek the Way, going from Yunju to Mount Lu; his solitary integrity was lofty and austere, and in truth, he appeared to have no desires whatsoever.

When the Prince of the Southern Kingdom, the Li family, summoned him to reside in the inner chapel, he feared that [the Master] was beyond the common crowd, so he constructed a separate Lohan Cloister to house him.
He sought earnestly to enter the mountains and requested to reside at the new monastery on Mount Lu; thereupon, the master arranged the formal ceremonial procession to lead him in.
Having donned his robes and taken up his staff, he entered, whereafter he ascended the seat to respond to the inquiries of the assembly.
Whenever the ruler of that state bestowed gifts upon him, he never sent a memorial or letter to express his gratitude.
There was an elder statesman named Song Qichu, whom he treated with the etiquette due to a teacher.
He passed away in a mountain hermitage during the Kaibao era.
Throughout his life, Huide wore nothing but trousers and socks made of processed leather.
He practiced the dhūta austerities and provided for all his fellow meditators, so that the kitchen was never lacking in provisions.
Some claimed that Huide possessed the arts of alchemy and the transformation of base metals into gold.
The Biography of Shidechao of Mount Tiantai during the Song Dynasty. Shi Dechao’s secular surname was Chen, and he was a native of Jinyun.

Having left home to become a monk in his own prefecture at a young age, he received full ordination and subsequently traveled to visit famous mountains and seek out enlightened teachers (zhishi) during the Tongguang era; those he encountered were beyond counting.

He first resolved his mind under Master Touzi Shan; later, he met Chan Master Fayan of Linchuan, through whom he again clarified the essentials of the mind and subsequently received dharma transmission.
He then entered Mount Tiantai, where he established monasteries and practice halls.
Before long, Daochao greatly promoted the Dharma-way of Xuansha, and those who took refuge in him became numerous.
Once, when the King of the Southern Han, the Qian clan, was governing Danqiu, Daochao possessed foresight and said to him:
"In the future, you shall become a king and you must cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish."

His words were indeed trustworthy; messengers were dispatched to the mountains in great numbers, and later he was bestowed with the title of Great Chan Master (Dà Chánshī). Whenever he spoke, there was nothing that did not accord with the truth.
Qian Renfeng, the military commissioner of Suzhou, fell ill and dispatched a messenger bearing incense to offer prayers for his recovery.
He then inscribed a petition stating:
"The Lord Commissioner shall live to eighty-one."
Ren received it with great joy and said,
"My lifespan shall be eighty-one years.
On the eleventh day of the eighth month of that year, he passed away.
There were many such instances.

Before Shao had finished his term, a rock on Mount Huading collapsed, sending shockwaves for a hundred li; the mountain appeared like a wild fire spreading over a banquet mat, and thus it was fulfilled that Shao’s term would end.
The cremated relics were numerous; a stupa was constructed, and the Imperial Preceptor for Monks (Dusengzheng) Zan Ning was commissioned to compose the inscription for its stele.
He reached the age of eighty-two and had been a monk for sixty-four years, passing away on the twenty-eighth day of the sixth month in the fifth year of the Kaibao era, the Ren-shen year.
His *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) circulated widely.

He produced some one hundred disciples who transmitted the Dharma, and he further established dozens of Zhizhe monasteries. Having accomplished these great works, he remained unassuming as a master; his mind-ground was level and serene.
He was especially proficient in the arts of divination and calculation, prioritizing the benefit of others above all else.
To this day, those in the Jiangzhe region refer to him as the "Great Monk" (Dàhéshàng).
The commentary states:
The Sanskrit term "dhyāna" is translated into Chinese as "contemplative cultivation.
This is because, while engaging with mental objects, one remains without thought; and though practicing throughout the day, there is no practice.
It is also called "right concentration" (*samyaksamādhi*) and "right reception" (*samyaksamāpatti*);
being "right," it is vast, profound, and settled, while "right reception" excludes erroneous conceptualization and increases thorough discernment (*parikalpa*).
Therefore, because *śamatha* is characterized by tranquility and *samādhi* by the contemplation of things as being like an illusion,
whereas *dhyāna* is that which is free from both tranquility and illusion,
it is only then said: "The Bodhisattva does not abide on this shore, nor does he abide on the other shore, yet he delivers sentient beings so that they may ascend to the other shore."
If this is so, since the abodes of the various sages were already like that, how did the sages further deliver sentient beings?
When we examine the Dharma being propagated in the Han court, the name of ultimate realization had not yet become prominent;
when the wind of the teaching spread across Mount Lu, the study of *dhyāna* (meditation) first began to sprout.
Buddhabhadra arrived during the Qin dynasty; Prajñātāra came during the Jin dynasty.

At that time, Master Huiyuan secretly transmitted the methods of seated meditation and profoundly manipulated the profound mysteries. Others gradually became imbued with these practices, following and perpetuating them according to their own inclinations.
Senghui of Wu also manifested signs of a karmic affinity, yet both remained indistinct, leaving much concealed and secreted.
It was not until the Great Being Huiwen that the lineage of Nāgārjuna was first sought out;
and with the Venerable Dhyāna Master Zhiyi, the subtlety of the Three Contemplations was successively transmitted.
Tiantai Zhiyi drew upon these teachings and extended them to guide the Chen and Sui dynasties, titling his work *Zhi Guan* (Cessation and Contemplation).

Subsequently, Bodhidharma from Central India took pity on our masses of sentient beings; he perceived that although the Sanskrit scriptures had been transmitted, people were drowning in mere names and characteristics—mistaking the finger for the moon and clinging to the trap once the fish was caught. They prided themselves on recitation as their spiritual merit, yet failed to believe that they themselves were inherently Buddhas.
Therefore, he proclaimed:
"I point directly at the human mind, see one's nature and become a Buddha; I do not establish written words.
This is to ride upon the *pāramitā* of skillful means, crossing over directly and avoiding immeasurable detours.
Alas! The scriptures contain indirect indications; such indirect indications refer to gradual cultivation.

As for "seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood," it means suddenly awakening to the fact that one's own mind is originally pure, fundamentally free from afflictions, and that the nature of untainted wisdom is inherently complete.
This mind is itself the Buddha; it is completely realized as being without difference.
To practice and realize in this manner is the Chan of the Supreme Vehicle.
Regarding "not establishing words," a sutra says:
"Do not cling to words, nor depart from words. It is not that there are no words;
if one can practice in this way, one does not perceive the characteristics of practice.
Furthermore, the Dharma established by Bodhidharma consists essentially of two kinds: namely, principle (*li*) and practice (*xing*).
Thus, it was direct yet not circuitous, unhurried yet swift; to say that "words and letters were not established" was, in fact, to employ expedient means in accordance with the Way.
At that time, Emperor Wu of Liang did not understand this, nor was it esteemed by the people of Wei; facing the Shaolin wall, he could only commune with Huike through the spirit.
It is also like the song "White Snow," which, though sung, was rarely harmonized with by the children of Ba.
Later, when [the Zhou] were at Qian as herdsmen and stable-keepers, their descendants ultimately raised cries of protest against the powerful Qin;
yet by fleeing the Di tribes from Qi and Bin, Wen and Wu were able to establish their Way of Kingship.
Ke may give birth to Can; Can shall give birth to Xin.
Under Xin there are two branches: first, Ren; second, Rong.
Rong is of the Niutou lineage.
Ninsō gave rise to both Shū and Nō.
Nō transmitted the robe of faith, much like the feudal lords handing down their ancestral vessels to their descendants; thereafter, this school flourished even more extensively.
A hundred chariots provided shade, as the branches of the *nyagrodha* tree spread out and hung down;
a myriad directions were covered by rain, as the *Anavatapta* dragon spread its moisture across the mats.
At that time, responding to his prophetic prediction, it was destined for this man—were not those who later attained the Way indeed beyond counting?
I comment on this, saying:
"As for the nature of dhyāna, how great it is!

All Buddhas attained it to ascend to the levels of Equality and Subtlety; the female dragon attained it to shatter the hindrances and entanglements. Among all gates of rapid progress, none surpasses this."
Thus, in these present degenerate times, strife has arisen once more; the Master’s feet have already been injured, yet the struggle for resources remains unresolved.
Hearing that this mind is the Buddha, they immediately ask: "Why are the thirty-two marks not present?"
If one hears that there is but a single path to nirvana, they may ask, "Where then are the eighty thousand dharma-gates?
They fail to realize that within the sutras, the arousal of the bodhicitta is precisely what constitutes the seeing of the Buddha-nature.
How does one cultivate the bodhisattva practice? This refers to the cultivation of the *pāramitās*.
Because faith is insufficient and one is deluded by ignorance, like a lost child who forgets the way home, by what means can one restore one's original vocation?
If he were presented with a passage from a sutra, he would reply,
"This is a teaching of the Dharma of Nature (Xingzong)";
or someone might say to him:
"Is this not the teaching of Māra? Should it not be burned and destroyed?
Let us set that aside for now and not discuss it further.
Yet, you wish to discard it on one hand and wish to preserve it on the other—is this not delusion?

In the past, the various clans of Khotan regarded the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* as a Brahmanical text, while the Hīnayānists of Oḍḍiyāna slandered the Mahāyāna practitioners as followers of the "Empty-Flower" heretics.
If it is so even in the Western Regions (India), why should this cause surprise?

It is simply because the Patriarchs of the Six Generations, in their timely proclamations, merely sought to dispel the darkness of a hundred years; they did not concern themselves with the ruin of a single room.
Little do they realize that Chan possesses both principle and practice.

If one were to apply oneself with equal urgency to both the precepts and the vehicle, and if the eyes and feet mutually assist one another, then practice will not be neglected while principle becomes ever more clear; the Dharma will remain without partiality, and its efficacy will provide comprehensive benefit.
Only then can one begin to speak with them of dhyāna.

This is because those of the "Dark Learning" (xuanxue) school frequently disparage the exponents of the commentaries, regarding them as people who merely count their treasures while ultimately remaining trapped in rooms of perpetual emptiness.
That sutra is not seen to be the Buddha’s word, yet meditation is the Buddha’s intent; the mind and speech of all Buddhas are certainly not in contradiction.
Expedient devices are established to accommodate various capacities, and their application depends on the specific time and place.
How much more so when considering that the name of the Kingdom of Gao is recorded in the annals of the River Ji;
that the sea is discussed as the great assembly where all tributaries flow toward the source;
and that the single study of the Vinaya serves as the model for a thousand paths.

Having been granted the foundation for the Śākya disciples by constructing their dwellings together with them, and having proclaimed the practice of purity as the vocation of a śramaṇa, how can one who intends to abandon the three matters yet be driven toward the One Vehicle?
Such a person will ultimately suffer the shame of insufficiency; how could they ever reach the stage of the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti)?
The man of comprehensive understanding does not mock; what could a mere child know?

Within the gateway of Buddhist practice, not a single dharma is abandoned. To bark at sounds is to invite reproach; to transfer one's anger and harm others is like breaking a basin while striking a rat, or biting one’s master while struggling over a morsel of food. Both self and other possess [the same nature]; "other" and "self" must be treated equally. When纵横 (zōnghéng) are fully realized, they become the One Qin; when the various temperaments are harmonized, they become a single flavor.
From the Zhenguan era down to the Song dynasty, they have selected the peaks among mountains, causing Mount Sumeru to emerge from the sea;
they have sought the feathers among plumage, releasing the golden-winged bird to soar through the void.
This will cause those who look up to us with reverence to admire this firm and lofty Way.

Among our followers, there is no need for one to usurp the position of another; it is like the arts of civil and military governance belonging to a single person—if one cannot master both, they merely criticize one another.

If you honor and support one another, the Buddha-Dharma will flourish and become more luminous; this will repay the King’s grace in providing for your passage across the sea and answer the Buddha’s instruction that He is your teacher. Be careful!
Be cautious! *Biographies of Eminent Monks Compiled in the Song Dynasty*, Volume Thirteen;
*Biographies of Eminent Monks Compiled in the Song Dynasty*, Volume Fourteen.
