In the twenty-fourth year of the Kaiyuan era, the Emperor personally annotated the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and issued an edict to promulgate it throughout the realm, ordering that it be preached everywhere.

Yuan Yan-chong, the Governor of Henan, personally entreated [the Master] Huiyan to once again illuminate the sacred sun; he subsequently propagated and assisted in this cause, perfectly aligning with the Will of Heaven, so that the blind might see the light of the sun and moon, and the deaf might hear the roar of thunder.
Yan’s extensive exposition was indeed of great benefit.
For those who delight in minor dharmas are deluded by the self and thereby fall ill, while those who seek to penetrate the Great Vehicle are bewildered by the dharma-path of opening up emptiness.
As for those who synthesize the three vehicles into the One and touch upon the principle while merging with its phenomena, even those from Upāli downward may still suffer from various ailments.
Yet [Hui]yan regulated the framework of the Hīnayāna and expounded the Great Dharma; he realized that the Buddha-realm is non-existent and recognized that the realm of Māra is empty.

Therefore, one can cause nirvana and samsara to be as one, and afflictions and bodhi to reach the same goal; by giving rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, one ascends to the stage of Buddhahood—if it is not I, who else could it be?
Those who take refuge in the Triple Gem, whether white-robed or black-robed, should practice benevolence without hesitation.

Formerly, the Dharma Master Senghu resided constantly at Shicheng, where he sat in meditation against a green cliff. Looking up at its central peak, he perceived what appeared to be a Buddha image; he then vowed to construct a ten-fathom statue in order to visualize the Tuṣita Heaven.
Before his noble aspirations could be fulfilled, Master Hu passed away.

Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty issued an imperial decree for Vinaya Master Sengyou to travel by express courier to manage the project; the scale and design were already established, and the master’s creative vision had only just been applied.
Suddenly, the mountain tomb collapsed, and his entire body appeared seated, reaching a height of over one hundred feet.
Although the sounds of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo—the offerings of the Four Heavens—were constantly heard;
even the carvings of the Ten Stages (Daśabhūmi) could not surpass the majesty of his meritorious adornments.

Yan then turned inward to offer his robes and alms bowl, while outwardly he exhorted donors to provide gold for its color and refined silver for its appearance; with copper, tin, lead, and zinc, as well as *jīva-jīva* and *maṇi* gems, the seven treasures were thus fully integrated and the eight precious substances were thereby made complete.
Although Ratnākara offered his parasol, its boundaries manifested throughout the three thousandfold world system;
and although Kāśyapa presented his robes, their golden hue surpassed a hundred thousand [in brilliance].
Like Mount Sumeru appearing within the great ocean, or like the bright sun rising from a high mountain—this, moreover, is the inconceivable merit of Huìyán.
Thus, Xu Jiao, the Prefect of Luozhou, and Xu Anzhen, the Minister of Works, both being members of the imperial clan, established the etiquette of dharma-friends with him;

while Kang Xixian, Director of Studies at the National University, He Zhizhang, the Palace Attendant, and Zhu Yuanshen, the Grand Master for Splendid Happiness and Magistrate of Lin’an County in Hangzhou, likewise formed bonds of dharma-comrades based on their shared local origins.

In the twenty-sixth year of the Kaiyuan era, by imperial decree, people were sent to receive instruction; the Circuit Intendants Qi Han, Prefect of Runzhou, and Jing Cheng, Governor-General of Yuezhou, along with Lu Jianyi and Wang Bi, Prefect of Sizhou, all halted their carriages at this pure realm to receive the teachings of the Dharma.

The Duke of Qi then prepared a fleet of linked boats and traveled to the prefectures of Danyang, Yuhang, and Wuxing to welcome Huiyan, commanding that newly ordained monks personally receive the full precepts from him.
From Guangling to Xinan, over an area of a thousand *li*, those among both the clergy and the laity who received the Dharma numbered nearly ten thousand.

He recited the *Buddhanāmasūtra* one hundred times and established ten banquets for the *Unrestricted Great Assembly*; in his conduct upon entering regions and presiding over monasteries, there was none who could equal him.

As for those who upheld the Dharma and transmitted its teachings, they were born from the very mouth of the Buddha. Among his disciples were Fahua, Tanjun, Chongmo, Longxing Chongyi, Kaiyuan Zhifu, Chengxin Chongyi, Xiangyan Huaijie, Baolin Hongpai, Jueyin, and Guanding; all of them did not spill a single drop from the oil bowl and remained without leakage in their life-preserving bags.
Does not the Sūtra say:
"Like a sandalwood forest surrounded by sandalwood trees;
like a lion king surrounded by lions"?
I believe that Xian’s majestic spiritual power truly exists, and that the meritorious virtues of the Master of the Dharma are indelible.

One should know that there is no peace within the three realms and that all spirits eventually perish; this present life has already transitioned toward the next breath, and in another world, one shall surely encounter the mind from before.
In the first year of the Tianbao era, the cyclical year being Renwu, his work of transformation was completed.

On the third day of the eleventh month, he manifested illness upon his corded bed; on the seventh day at noon, he passed away while seated in the Jitan (Precept Platform) Hall at the age of sixty-eight.
On the twenty-fifth day of that month, he was interred beneath Qin Mountain to the south of the monastery.
Twin pagodas were erected on high, their radiance surpassing white clouds;
a thousand pines were planted in rows, their elegant beauty arrayed before the bright moon.

At the commencement of the project, Shen Yong and Chong Xiao served as abbots; subsequently, Wei Zan and Daozhao held the office, both personally protecting the sacred precincts and directly transmitting the seal of wisdom (*jñāna-mudrā*).

As for the remaining three thousand gate-disciples and five hundred followers, they inherited the profound Dharma of Prajñā and received the secret practices of Vinaya; all were renowned as masters who had reached the pinnacle of their respective schools, requiring no further instruction from Maitreya.
In the fifteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era, the cyclical year being Jǐngshēn, Wàn Qíróng composed the "Stele Praising Virtue.
Biography of Shì Dèxiù of Língzhì Monastery in Hángzhōu, Táng: Shì Dèxiù’s secular surname was Sūn, and he was a native of Fùyáng.
Having emerged from the mundane world at an early age, he took refuge in the Buddhist monastery in his youth.
When he was about to receive full ordination, he correctly protected his "raft" of precepts; though he did not have a fixed teacher, he focused his mind on the treasury of the Vinaya.
Aside from his lectures, he often lamented that ghosts and spirits lacked food, and he habitually offered them meals during the deep hours of the night.
The people along the banks of the Zhe River were moved by his sincerity and submitted themselves to him with awe.
His life concluded at Mount Ding, where many miraculous occurrences took place during the early years of the Tianbao era.
When his remains were moved into the stupa, seven śarīra relics descended from heaven; the disciples collected them in a flask and sealed them within the stupa.
When it was excavated, one saw exquisite teeth from which śarīras were produced, falling down in profusion.
Later, people piled bricks to construct a stūpa there.
The local people say:
"A white snake was constantly coiled there, guarding the stupa; none of the children who tended to wood or herded cattle dared to approach.

This is the biography of Aitong of Kaiye Monastery during the Tang dynasty. Regarding Aitong of Kaiye Monastery: his religious name was Aitong, and he was surnamed Zhao by birth; he was originally a native of Tianshui.
Inheriting the crown and ceremonial cap from his predecessors, he was already upright and distinguished in his youth; he came forth with gracious ease to become a son of the Buddha.
After receiving full ordination, he lectured on the Mahīśāsaka-vinaya, becoming a teacher to those near and far, who followed him as scales and feathers flock to the Kunlun and the phoenix.

In the past, during the Southern Song dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Jueśou of Kaśmīra translated this Vinaya and produced one fascicle of the *Karmavācanā*. As time passed, the original manuscript fell into disrepair and was lost; unable to find it, students have been left without a reliable source.

Consequently, Tong also extracted one fascicle of the *Karmavācanā* from within the Great Vinaya; this was widely propagated and transmitted by scholars of that school, until the ritual procedures were finally made complete.

During the reign of Emperor Xiaohé (r. 710–712), in the Shénlóng era, he was highly esteemed and active in the propagation of the teachings; together with Wénɡāng and others, he participated in the translation bureau and was appointed as the *zhèngyì* (certifier of meaning).
He played a significant role in the scriptures produced by Yìjìng.
He composed the *Wufen lü shu* (Commentary on the Five-Part Vinaya) in ten fascicles and further bequeathed his instructions to the Vinaya Master Xuántōng of Xīmíng Monastery to revise and polish it.
Later, during the disturbances caused by the An Lushan and Shi Siming rebellions, the monastery was burned to the ground and lost; today, not a trace remains.
Biography of Dharma Master Shuan of Mount Wutai during the Tang Dynasty Dharma Master Shuan was a native of Wutai County.

He entered the monastic order while still wearing his ceremonial robes and received full ordination upon reaching the age of twenty. His deportment was refined and elegant, and the assembly looked to him for guidance in observing the monastic precepts.
He studied the principles of the Vinaya while keeping the practices of a Bodhisattva secret.

Aside from providing exegesis and training his disciples, he maintained silence without wavering. Whether matters arose near or far, there was nothing he did not know in advance; people said that he had attained the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others.
He ate but one meal throughout the day and wore tattered clothes to cover his body; he did not store a single grain, nor was there a thread of silk in his room.
His strength of fundamental principles and austerity in expenditure were such that even those in moments of haste could not equal them.
On the day he entered parinirvāṇa, auspicious clouds gathered densely and celestial music resounded. All the monks of the monastery perceived a wondrous fragrance wafting through the air.
He then summoned the assembly of the temple, took their hands in farewell, and entrusted his disciples with final instructions; finally, sitting cross-legged, he passed away.
Biography of Fashen of Longxing Monastery in Yangzhou during the Tang Dynasty. Shi Fashen, surnamed Guo, was a native of Jiangdu.
From the age when I was held in my arms, I vowed to enter the Gate of Emptiness; though my affection was deeply concentrated upon worldly ties, my resolve could not be diverted.
I subsequently received the full precepts from Vinaya Master Cheng of Yaotai.
Relying on the Eastern Pagoda of Taiyuan Temple, he mastered and interpreted the Vinaya texts, resolving all points of doubt; thus, his contemporaries esteemed and submitted to him.

Sometimes a single word would provide a subtle analysis beyond the manifest form, while the essential principle was spontaneously realized within the center of the cycle; his reputation resounded through the capital like the morning sun dawning upon the dew.
When the monastic communities of various temples requested him to serve as their leader, he returned eastward in silence.
Upon his arrival back in the capital of Yangdu, he humbly granted their request; he constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Sūryavairocana-cakra-mantra*.
Prajñā is the Buddha-mind; I have attained this mind, and sentient beings shall also attain it.
My supreme vows are as follows: as I am, so shall sentient beings be.
It is said: "The Tiantai *zhiguan* encompasses the meaning of all sutras;
the Dharma-gate of Dongshan is the vehicle of all Buddhas.
Where both form and emptiness have perished and both concentration and wisdom shine forth together, it is beyond description."
In careful observance of the heat, he did not adjust his lower garment; in eating, he did not seek satiety; and in his dwelling, he did not change his seated posture.

Whatever he bestowed as alms in the four directions was dedicated to the great assembly; whether his own person possessed anything or not, he maintained an equanimity toward those at the lowest level.
Scholars of the court who carry out and return from imperial missions pass through Weiyang by the hundreds each year; yet, if they do not cross your threshold, they consider it a great disgrace.
To receive even a single glance from you would be like washing away their hunger and thirst.

Be cautious when speaking with the sons of others, relying on filial piety; when speaking with ministers, rely on loyalty; when speaking with superiors, rely on benevolence; and when speaking with subordinates, rely on ritual propriety.
The Buddhist teachings and Confucian conduct were unified as one.
Because scholars had fallen into error, he personally collated the sutras and treatises;
because he invited those who came to listen and receive instruction, he extensively constructed monasteries.
To warn the multitude against delusion, he extensively illustrated the stages of a bodhisattva’s causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*).
To well protect all lives, he skillfully extended the life-span of sentient beings.
To deliver people through written characters, he excelled in calligraphy and brushwork.
Since all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma, he concurrently adopted the traditions of Confucianism.
Because he took the pride of self (māna) as his defense, he personally carried his own robes and bowl.
Because he made meticulous attention his responsibility, he rectified the framework of the monastic community.
In order to propagate the fundamental tenets of the Way, he respectfully observed the rites of the highest conduct.
Out of deep veneration for the traces of the past, he did not travel far to other lands.
Because of the deliberations with the "dragons and elephants" (eminent monks), he returned once more to the capital.
Because his conduct was so upright and lucid, he indeed devoted himself to the meticulous study of the Vinaya-piṭaka!

Lu Zangyong, the Gentleman Attendant for the Yellow Gate, possessed great talent and a high reputation; he rarely showed deference to others, yet upon meeting Yu Shen once, he admired him so deeply that he could not leave his seat.
Withdrawing, he sighed and said:
"Within this universe, there truly are men of lofty character!
The eunuch established a scripture repository within the courtyard and adorned it with incense and lamps; as the heavens and earth are boundless, so too shall the Semblance Dharma endure forever.

Prince of the Household Lu Xiangxian, Minister of War Bi Gou, Director of the Imperial Treasury Lu Yucheng, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel Yan Tingzhi, Governor of Henan Cui Xiyi, Grand Marshal Fang Guan, Chief Secretary and Chancellor Cui Huan, Minister of Rites Li Cheng, poet Wang Changling, and Court Historian Qimuzhan—all these men look up to and revere [the Master], and they wish to join in sweeping and cleaning [his dwelling].
He moved the ministers and officials of the court in this way.

On the morning of the fourteenth day of the tenth month in the seventh year of the Tiānbǎo era, he rose at dawn, rinsed his mouth and washed his face, and sat cross-legged upon a folding chair with his mind directed toward the Western Quarter. At sunset, he passed away in the detached quarters of Longxìng Monastery; he was eighty-three years of age, having completed sixty-two summers.

His disciples, both ordained and lay, extended from the Si and Yi Rivers in the north to beyond the Ling and Jiao ranges in the south. Those who came to wail at his sight numbered in the thousands, and those who assembled for his funeral reached ten thousand.

Among his foremost followers were Tan-yi of Kuaiji; the monk Huai-yi of Min; Chong-rui of Nan-kang; Yi-xuan of Jin-ling; Hui-luan of Shan Mountain Temple in Qiantang; Fa-yu of Luojing; Chong-yuan; Fa-li of He-lin Temple; Fa-hai; Hui-ning of Wei-yang; Ming-you, Ling-yu, and Ling-i. All of them had attained the eloquence of *anupapatti-pratibhāna* (unimpeded analytical exposition) and entered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
Known and revered by all, he is the refuge of all beings.
Like the nectar of immortality in the heavens, his true flavor is harmonious and gentle;
like the elephant king among men, his faculties are sharp and fully matured.
Beneath the tree of music, the spring of merit and wisdom flows forever;
atop the peaks of the Snowy Mountains, one gazes upon the moon of cool clarity.
With adamantine certainty, afflictions are exhausted without remainder.
The udumbara flower has blossomed, its fragrance pure and its scent filling all.

Moved by the grace of the Dharma-gift and the profound sentiment of his local residence, he mournfully attended to the physical remains and commenced the construction of a spirit-stupa on the plains of Shugang to the west of Wucheng, thereby manifesting the teachings of the Image-Religion.

From his youth until his decline, [Yonggong] was constantly attended by [the subject]. Later, he requested Li Hua of Zhaojun, an Extraordinary Councillor of the Ministry of Personnel, to compose an inscription to commemorate him; this was done in the twelfth month of the eighth year of Dali (the Gui-chou year).
The calligraphy was by Zhang Congshen, Rectifier of the Court of Judicial Review, and the inscription for the title plaque was by Li Yangbing of Zhaojun.
The stupa itself was planned and constructed by Master You;
the site where the stupa stands is as level as a plain, with its height and proportions perfectly balanced.
Surrounded by four avenues, it commands a panoramic view of a thousand *li*.
Disciples have planted cypress trees in rows around the gate and offered famous incense.
During the Huichang era, this pagoda was destroyed according to the general proscription.
The Biography of Dao Guang of Huayan Monastery in Hangzhou during the Tang Dynasty. Shi Dao Guang, surnamed Wang, entered the monastic life after his teeth had fallen out.
Upon receiving the full precepts while still wearing the square cap, he went to the Upādhyāya at Guangzhou, where he mastered the Vinaya.

At that time, though his years were few, his virtue was already eminent; the monastic assembly looked up to him with high expectation. Truly, Heaven had bestowed a true sage upon the world, serving as a "Tiger of Meaning" for the Southeast. Like clouds and rain, he showered the flavor of compassion; like the music of the *sheng* and *yong*, he resonated the sound of the Way.
Guangchi upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and first established stūpas and temples; until his death, he never grew weary of these efforts.

In the second month of autumn in the year of Gengzi, the first year of the Shangyuan era, he manifested illness and passed away at this very temple at the age of seventy-nine and with fifty-eight years of Dharma seniority.

On this day, the sun’s brilliance faded as it hurried its course; torrential rains poured down incessantly, and a fierce wind blew for a full morning, breaking the noble trees—this was a portent that the blessings of the eastern lands had reached their end.

Suddenly, an auspicious radiance of five colors appeared, standing tall like a canopy; it did not disperse for the duration of a watch, casting its light specifically upon the hermitage, which was a manifestation of the intent for rebirth in the Western Paradise.

Before the initial light had faded, at dawn on the third day of that month, Zhi concentrated his spirit and practiced the contemplation of the physical body; Amitābha Buddha, complete with all his marks, appeared before him.
The courtyard was filled with verdant flowers, the likes of which had never been seen before.
At dawn on the fourth day, a strange man requested that Guang become his preceptor; he then opened his eyes, snapped his fingers, and said:
"Simply give rise to the bodhicitta."
On the fifth day, *mandārava* flowers rained down from the heavens.

His disciples Shenlie and Yijin, unable to bear their longing for him, each partook of the flavor of the Dharma and spread his teachings through their own transformative work; thus, the lineage of his offerings has continued without end.
The Biography of Jñānagupta (Jianzhen) of Dayun Monastery in Yangzhou during the Tang Dynasty. The monk Jñānagupta, surnamed Chunyu, was a native of Jiangyang County in Guangling.
From his youth, he was exceptionally brilliant and possessed a broad and magnanimous character; he was capable of managing formal audiences.
Accompanying his father to Dayun Temple, he beheld a Buddhist statue and was moved in his heart from early on, whereupon he informed his father of his desire to leave the household life.
His father marveled at his resolve and granted him permission.
Deng then went to Master Zhiman to follow his guidance and instruction.
It happened that in the first year of the Chang’an era of Empress Wu’s reign, an imperial edict was issued to ordain monks throughout the empire.
He was then appointed as the *śikṣamāṇā* (xi-cí) to reside at his home temple, which was later renamed Longxing.
It was likely during the first year of the Shénlóng era of Emperor Zhōngzōng Xiàohé that he received the Bodhisattva precepts from Vinaya Master Dà'àn.
In the first year of the Jinglong era, he traveled to Chang’an.
On the twenty-eighth day of the third month of the second year, he received the precepts from Vinaya Master Hengjing of Jingzhou at Jishi Temple.

Although he had only recently resolved his mind [to seek enlightenment], he possessed the air of one long experienced; having traveled to observe the two capitals, he was molded and guided by renowned masters.
Having mastered the teachings of the Tripitaka over several years, he always investigated the subtle nuances of every action and never indulged in self-aggrandizement.
Upon returning to the Huai and Hai regions, he transformed and guided others through the Vinaya, becoming a preeminent leader of the school in that quarter.
Like a moon reflected in a pool of ice, his presence brought clarity and purity;
like a lion’s roar from its throne, his teaching elicited many resonant responses.
At that time, there were śramaṇas from the kingdom of Japan, including Eiei and Fushō, who came from the east to seek the Dharma in order to remedy its deficiencies.
During the Kaiyuan era, they arrived in Yangzhou and came to inquire about the teachings, prostrating at the feet of the Venerable [Daoxuan] and saying:
"Our country lies within the midst of the ocean; we do not know how many tens of millions of li it is distant from Qizhou."
"Though the Dharma exists, there is no one to transmit it; this is like seeking something throughout the entire night in a dark chamber—without a lamp, how can anything be seen?
We pray that you, Master, might cease these benefits and joys for this region and become a guide for the lands beyond the sea!"
Zhen carefully observed his demeanor and scrutinized his diligent efforts, then asked him:
"I have heard that in the past the Chan Master Sengsi of Mount Nanyue was reborn there as a king to cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish; is this true?"

Furthermore, I have heard that the ruler of that country, Changwu, once commissioned a thousand *kāṣāya* robes to bestow upon the renowned and virtuous masters of China; moreover, he embroidered a verse upon the borders of the garments, saying:
"Though mountains and rivers separate our lands, the wind and moon share the same sky; I entrust these to the sons of the Buddha, that we may together forge a karmic bond for the future."
Reflecting on this, it is truly a land with which the Buddha-dharma has a karmic affinity.
He silently consented and acted accordingly.
As for the one called Changwu (Jōgaku), he was the Chancellor (Sang-kuo).

Zhen then recruited fourteen bhikṣus, including Situo and others, and purchased a boat at Guangling; they carried the Sūtras and Vinaya texts with them as they departed from the shore, which was in the sixth month of the second year of the Tiānbǎo era.
Upon reaching the harbor of Yuezhou, he stayed at Fengshan.
That very night, he had a most miraculous dream.
Just as he was setting out across the ocean, he encountered a violent storm; seeing the ship on the verge of sinking, some of the sailors cast away aloeswood.
A voice was heard from the air saying, "Do not cast it away.
At that moment, they saw divine generals clad in armor and wielding weapons at each of the ships' sterns and prows; immediately, the wind subsided.
Suddenly, he was drifted into the Sea of Snakes; the snakes there were over thirty feet long, their colors like brocade patterns.
Later, he entered the Sea of Fish; the fish were over a foot long and filled the air as they flew.
Next was one ocean where they saw only birds flocking onto the back of the ship, nearly overwhelming it with their weight.
Upon emerging from the Sea of Birds, they were short of water.
Suddenly, they anchored at an island; there was a deep, clear pool, and the water was sweet and delicious for the people to drink.
In succession, they arrived in Japan; the King welcomed them with joy and led them into the city, where they were settled in a great temple.
Initially, an altar was established before the Vairocana Hall, and the Bodhisattva precepts were conferred upon the King.

Next, after the queen, the princes, and others had been instructed, he then taught ten virtuous śramaṇas from his native land to fulfill the required quorum; they then conferred the *śrāmaṇera* ordination upon four hundred people, including Cheng and Xiu, by means of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations).
Furthermore, there was a prince of the first rank who donated his ancestral fields and residence to build a temple named Zhaoti, granting one hundred *qǐng* of irrigated land.

From that time forward, the Vinaya-piṭaka was extensively propagated; those who received its teachings were numerous, and he was titled "Great Master" (*Dàhéshàng*) by that country, being the progenitor of the transmission of the precepts and the Vinaya.

On the fifth day of the fifth month in the seventh year of the Tenpyō Hōshi era, the year of Gui-mao (763 CE), he bid farewell to the assembly without illness and passed away while seated; his body did not collapse or decay. This was the first year of the Guangde era of Emperor Daizong of the Tang dynasty.
He was seventy-seven years old.
To this day, his body has not been treated with hemp cloth or lacquer; instead, kings, nobles, and faithful lay practitioners occasionally apply precious incense to it.
The monk Si entrusted the details to the *Dongzheng zhuan* (Account of the Eastern Expedition).

Biography of Shi Shouzhi of Lingyin Monastery on Mount Tianzhu in Hangzhou during the Tang Dynasty: Shi Shouzhi, whose courtesy name was Jiandao, was a native of Qiantang. His surname was Fan, and he was the eighth-generation descendant of Fan Huang, the Governor of Xian’an during the Qi dynasty.
Having already been honored as a leader among those who have undergone the capping ceremony, the gentleman was esteemed for his talents.
Having long harbored the aspiration for the life of a recluse in the hills and gardens, he disregarded the imperial bestowal of the black and vermilion robes.
He subsequently proceeded to Zhiying Temple in Suzhou to receive the full precepts from Master Yuan.
That night, a light appeared from his eyes, more than a zhang in length, which only faded after remaining for a long time; this was a sign of his attainment of the precepts.
Later, he arrived at Jiangling and relied upon Master Zhen.
After three years of ascetic training,
he traveled throughout more than two hundred commanderies across the empire, visiting every site where sacred traces were found.
There he met the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi and received the Bodhisattva precepts from him.
He heard the Great Master Pujì transmit the mind-seal of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
He lectured on the *Awakening of Faith in Mahāyāna* more than twenty times and the *Nanshan Vinaya Commentary* forty times;
like a single rain falling equally upon all, his perfect voice simultaneously addressed both the Great and Small Vehicles without ever showing the slightest variation.
He then made a vow to recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and during the middle of the night, he dreamed that a divine being bestowed upon him a single pearl.
Upon waking, he felt a sense of wonder as if the pearl were still held in his hand.
In this year, he entered Mount Wutai and recited the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* two hundred times to fulfill his long-held aspiration.
He perused the Tripitaka three times through to gain a broad and correct understanding of the teachings.

In the twenty-sixth year of the Kaiyuan era, by imperial decree, he was summoned for his eminent conduct; at the request of the secular clergy and monastics, he was formally registered under Dailinsi. Later, he transferred his records to Tianzhu and resided on Lingyin Peak; this was in the second year of the Dali era.
In the third month of the fifth year, he stayed at the Jingtu Monastery in Longxing and said to those around him:
"The Perfected One comes riding upon the Suchness (tathatā) and departs riding upon the Suchness; this demonstrates the nature of his mind."
Yet how could a fool hope to bind that bright sun with a long rope—how could it ever be possible?
My shadow has already fallen upon the mulberry and elm trees; how could I remain for long?
On the twenty-ninth day of this month in this year, he passed away at the age of seventy-one, having been a monk for forty-five years.

During that time, he presided over ordination platforms for many people; those whose names were prominent included Bianxiu of Dongting, Jiaoran of Huzhou, Huipin, Daozhuang, Qingjiang and Qingyuan of Kuaiji, Zeli of Hangzhou, Shenyen, and Daojin of Changzhou.
The epitaph for Master Zhù by Zhìrì states:
"The Biography of Yánjùn of Dàmíng Monastery in Hóngzhōu during the Táng Dynasty. Śramaṇa Yánjùn, surnamed Fán, was a native of Wéizhōu."
His father served as the Prefectural Administrator of Xiaozhou and the Vice Director of the Prince Zhao’s Household.
Li Jun possessed a naturally serene disposition and was sharp and discerning in his studies.
Upon reaching the age of nineteen, he sat for the jinshi examination.
Suddenly struck by bitter grief for his parents, he sought to repay their labors and entered a Buddhist temple in Nanyang.
Later, he arrived at a hermitage on Mount Yuquan in Jingzhou, where he met Master Zhen, who instructed him in Chan meditation; subsequently, he entered the city and stayed at Dayun Temple.
Jùn upheld the seal of the precepts, employing them without ever letting them wear thin;
relying upon the life-preserving float, he crossed over wherever he went.
When the assembly requested him to preside over the ordination platform, they further proposed him as the master of the Vinaya; he acquiesced and accepted the command.
He suddenly encountered Chan Master Guanjing, through whom he attained immediate enlightenment regarding the Dharma of the mind.

In the first year of the Dali era (766 CE), he set out for Mount Qingliang; before reaching Luling, he met Yan Zhenqing (Lord Yu). Their words accorded with one another in a single instant, and they became as inseparable as glue and lacquer.
In the spring of the second year, the Governor of Yichun dispatched a monk-official to send a memorial requesting his summons.
In the spring of the fourth year, Li Hua, the Vice Minister and Prefectural Governor of Hongzhou, invited him to reside at Daming Monastery.
In the third month, he suddenly ordered himself to bathe and change his robes; looking up toward the empty sky, he joined his palms and passed away at the age of fifty-nine.
When his stupa was moved, his disciples Yuan Yue and others erected a stele by the great spring pond in front of the temple, which remains there to this day.
Biography of Tanyi of Kaiyuan Monastery in Kuaiji, Tang Dynasty. Śramaṇa Tanyi’s secular surname was Zhang, and he was likely a native of Han.
His lineage originally received its surname from Xuanyuan; reaching the time of Xiao Liang, he served as a minister to the Han dynasty and was enfeoffed at Liu.
From the Wei and Jin dynasties onward, his family continued to produce generations of scholar-officials.
His great-grandfather, Heng, served as the Grand Master of Ceremonies under the Sui dynasty; while attending the imperial entourage at Yangdu, he settled in Yue.
Hengsheng gave birth to Xiaolian Yi; Yi gave birth to the retired scholar Chu; Chu gave birth to Yi, whose reputation spread throughout Jiangnan; this is now the fourth generation.
Yi cultivated the seeds of pure causes in his former lives, possessing innate wisdom from birth; he was quick-witted in his youth and became exceptionally intelligent as he grew up.
At the age of fifteen, he followed Master Li Tao to study the *Shijing* and the *Liji*, never departing from them all day long.
At sixteen, he listened to Dharma Master Moliang of Yunmen Temple lecture on the sutras and treatises; upon hearing them once, he attained profound understanding.
The Dharma Master marveled at this and said to his mother, Lady Meng:
"This is a son of the Buddha!
You should have him shave his head; I shall bestow upon him a prediction of enlightenment."
Faliang was the Bodhisattva Precept Master to Emperor Xiaohé.
Upon hearing [the Dharma] once, he rejoiced and conceived the aspiration for transcendence.
During the Jinglong era, he received imperial favor to enter the monastic order and was enrolled in the Registry of Monks (Senglù).
Upon reaching adulthood, he received full ordination from Vinaya Master Xuanchang of Danyang and mastered the *Shisao* (Commentary on the Essentials) under Vinaya Master Tansheng of Dangyang.
Subsequently, like drilling wood until smoke appears, he penetrated the texts; like peering through a wall, he beheld their profound mysteries.

In the fifth year of the Kaiyuan era, he traveled west to Chang’an, where he relied upon Master Daliang of Guanyin Temple to transmit the Vinaya-piṭaka; he studied treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Abhidharmakośa* under Master Tanzi of Chongsheng Temple, and received the Bodhisattva precepts from an Indian śramaṇa at Anguo Temple.
Thereupon, regarding the meaning of the lotus being unstained and the profound purport of the ambrosia, he alone transmitted the torch of wisdom and fully realized the state of a Brahma-hero.
Those from far and near gazed upon him with reverence, as if toward a patriarchal master.

However, as his scholarly pursuits had not yet reached their full potential, he simultaneously studied external disciplines; he frequently consulted Zuo Wuliang, the Attendant-in-Ordinary, on the *Book of Changes*, and discussed the *Records of the Grand Historian* with Ma Zhen, the Director of Studies at the National University.
He then fished and hunted through the works of a hundred schools and encompassed the Six Classics, thereby broadening his knowledge and vision.
From this point on, Confucianism, the teachings of the Tamer (Śāstṛ), and the Way of Humans and Devas all derived from Buddhist matters.
The high officials looked up to him with admiration, and his fame was widespread throughout the capital.

At that time, Chancellor Zhang Yue of Yan State, Song Jing of Guangping, Minister Su Gui, Lu Xiangxian of Yanzhou, Secretary-General He Zhizhang, and Wan Qirong, Magistrate of Jing County in Xuanzhou, all shared a common voice and served as his teachers and friends; even the assemblies of Zhi Dun and Xu Xun at Lingjiashan, or the gatherings of Huiyuan, Huiguo, and Lei Ci at Mount Lu, would not be considered numerous by comparison.

As for the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas, a monk from India, transmitted it to China during the Later Qin dynasty; together with the Dharma Master Kumārajīva, they translated it. The current tradition of its exposition and instruction has descended from this lineage.
The Vinaya Master Fǎcóng of the Wèi dynasty was the first to expound [this text]; Fǎcóng transmitted it to Dào Fù, and Fù transmitted it to Guāng.

Reaching the Sui dynasty, Vinaya Master Lì of Xiāngbù composed a commentary in ten fascicles. Vinaya Master Mǎnyì of Chóngfú Monastery in the Western Capital widely propagated this commentary and transmitted it to Vinaya Master Liàng.

That which has been transmitted is based entirely upon the sub-commentary of Vinaya Master Yili and the three-fascicle *Sifenlü chao* by Vinaya Master Xuan of Zhongnan during the early Tang dynasty; their details and omissions, as well as their similarities and differences, are consistent.
He himself composed the *Fajingji* (Record of Clarifying the Righteous Meaning) in ten fascicles.
It elucidates the discrepancies between the two schools and unlocks the keys to the five sections [of the Vinaya].

For later students, it provides enlightenment—like obtaining a torch for walking in the night—and dissolves prior doubts—like ice melting under the spring sun. Thus, the Buddha-sun shines brightly once more, and the pillars of the Dharma stand loftily and majestically.
This can be seen in the "Refutation of the Nanshan School’s Observance and Transgression" section of the *Fazheng ji*.
In the twenty-fifth year [of the Kaiyuan era], he took up his staff and returned east.
The following year, an imperial decree established Kaiyuan Temple; Zhang Chujü, the Regional Inspector, appointed him as the temple head, and he resided there accordingly.

A single voice resounded throughout the capital, his Way exalted across the regions of Wu and Kuaiji. He gathered the multitude through the exercise of great compassion and manifested his dignity by cultivating the myriad practices.

Those who came to inquire about the Way followed like a crush of wheels or a shoulder-to-shoulder throng; those who sought instruction within the space of a fathom arrived in waves and gathered like clouds.

According to the capacity of those who received [the teachings] in vain, he expounded them accordingly; thus, he lectured on the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya) thirty-five times and on the *Shanbu chao* (Annotated Commentary on the Revised Vinaya) more than twenty times.

Among the Buddhist monks of Jianghuai who received the Prātimokṣa, there were not just one or two who ascended the altar; yet they did not consider themselves to have attained the Dharma, instead adhering strictly to the monastic discipline.
In total, they ordained approximately one hundred thousand people.
During the era of Zhide, the state faced many hardships; the monastic community was negligent toward the Dharma, and few adhered to the scriptural teachings.
The Chancellor, a Prince who had been stationed in Yue, possessed a singular virtue and a long-standing reputation for high character, so he requested that [the Master] serve as the Sanghasthavira.
In one transformation he attained purity and extensively propagated his cultivation; within ten days, those who had followed deviant paths turned toward the correct path.
Such instances of skillful guidance and subtle transformation were all of this nature.
At first, when he entered the pass and paid his respects to Master Mingda, the master looked at him and said:
"You are a lion among men.
Later, he encountered the nun Cihua of Zunsian Temple, who sang:
"Master Tan is a master of the Vinaya, possessed of great intelligence and free from any doubt.
This was a saying frequently uttered by men of discernment.

In the fourteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era, the tide of the Zhè River surged southward toward Qiántáng; the Dàyún Monastery stood right at this turbulent rapids. Consequently, [the Master] was invited to lecture on the Vinaya, and his thousand disciples all made great vows.
Each time he ascended [the mountain], he would recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* until the surging waves subsided, thereby bestowing merit upon the Dragon King of Wu-xu.
Through this adornment, he prayed for protection.
On the night of the last day of the fifth month, while in a state of dazed reverie, he beheld a divine being whose robes and cap were most magnificent. The being bowed his head in thanks and said:
"Having received the gift of the Dharma you bestowed, I have immediately altered my course from the flow of the waves."
Before ninety days had passed, the shifting sands had advanced fifty li; both monastics and laypeople were struck with wonder and sighed in amazement at such an unprecedented occurrence.

He alone became a sovereign of the Dharma, greatly propagating the traces of the teachings, elucidating the entrustment of the former Buddhas, and guaranteeing the protective mindfulness of the future Buddhas.
Through the four-line verses of the gāthās, those who uphold them understand what was previously unclear;
through the Dharma preached in a single sound, those who listen attentively hear what they had not heard before.

Were it not for one whose essence is the pure quintessence of heaven and earth and the refined spirit of the rivers and mountains, who takes the Dharma as his standard and appears in this world at an interval between eras, [such a thing would not be possible].
Who could have achieved such profound penetration and secret realization on a scale so vast?
The great bell within the monastery was crafted by one man; it summoned the excellence of Fu Xi from afar and emulated the splendor of the Leimen Gate nearby.

Having lived for many years, he perfected its design; three days after his passing, it was completed through casting. Its resonance reaches a hundred *li*, and it can support ten thousand *qun*. When the Pu-lao bell calls, the earth trembles; when the lion roars, the mountains shudder. To awaken the deafening masses and guide those lost in their direction—how can this be described in words!

When the Dharma departed and the physical form was left behind, and the fuel was exhausted so that the fire was extinguished, he passed away at the Vinaya Hall of the monastery on the seventeenth day of the eleventh month in the sixth year of the Dali era. His age at death was eighty, and his years of monastic seniority were sixty-one.
On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month of the following year, he was moved to his seat at Qinwang Mountain, to the burial grounds of his late preceptor.
Although his years were already advanced, his spirit remained exceptionally vigorous; neither physically exhausted nor suffering from illness, he showed no signs of decline.
Suddenly, he said to his attendant,
"I shall go to sweep and pay respects at the stupas and pagodas,
and then return my remains here. A few days later, he passed away peacefully.

To the south of the Jianghuai region and beyond the Yellow and Luo rivers, those wearing mourning garments and observing the prescribed rites escort the funeral processions, their wailing filling the mountains and their banners and flowers covering the wilds; how can this be compared to Ju Meng’s mother sending out a thousand chariots, or the ten thousand trees planted at the tomb of Kong Qiu? They may well be considered of a kind!

His disciples—Changzhao of Miaoxi Temple in Yuezhou, Qingyuan of Jianfa Temple, Shenwan of Longxing Temple in Huzhou, Da’ang of Yinjing Temple in Xuanzhou, Yibin of Longxing Temple in Hangzhou, Zhanran of Guoqing Temple in Taizhou, Bianxiu of Kaiyuan Temple in Suzhou, Zhaoliang of Qixia Temple in Runzhou, and Fajun of Longxing Temple in Changzhou—had all been enlightened from their youth and had received his instruction and guidance. Now, these three thousand disciples look up at the great timber of the hall with deepening sorrow, and these eighty thousand followers gaze toward the sandalwood tree, unable to reach it.

His spirit was clear and his qi harmonious; his inner mind was vacant and still, merging with the pure essence of the Great Harmony.
When he reached the age of nine, he shunned his humble dwelling and resolved to enter the Garden of Dharma. He joined the ranks of the *śrāmaṇera* and received the precepts for renunciation.
Upon reaching the age for the initial capping ceremony, he received the full precepts; he studied without weariness and cultivated the rules of discipline (*vinaya*).
In his speech and laughter, he manifested the intent to clarify liberation.
He displayed literature and the arts to entice those of worldly wisdom.
From the beginning, he did not reckon that there was a self within the body, nor a body within the self.

When his virtue was perfected and the Way accomplished, his karmic conditions were severed and his physical form passed away. On the sixteenth day of the tenth month of winter in the first year of the Baoying era, he entered nirvana at Longxing Temple in Hangzhou at the age of thirty-five, having completed fifteen full periods of the *an-gu* (rainy-season retreat).
At the time of his death, he looked toward his disciples and instructed them to perform the *chāyī* (cremation) rites and erect a small *stūpa*.

At that time, Li Shu, General of the Staff of the Left Guard; Li Tang, Magistrate of Jiaxing County; and Du Guji, Assistant Director of the Military Office of the Left Golden Wolf Guard, together lamented that the "main beam" had already collapsed. His family was wealthy and had accumulated vast riches; however, he subsequently shaved his hair and, relinquishing his fortune of a thousand pieces of gold, bestowed it all upon his orphaned brothers and sisters, taking for himself nothing but the saffron robes and the mendicant’s staff.
From that time on, he visited Master Fashen of Yangzhou to study the Vinaya of the Dharmaguptaka school; he penetrated its subtleties and reached its ultimate depths.

His virtuous friends were Huining, Mingyou, Lingyou, Tan’i of Kuaiji, and Yixuan of Jinling—these three being his "beneficial friends" (sanyì) from the same school, bringing the total number of his associates to seven.

At the slightest sound of coughing or spitting from the surrounding world, he would continue his walking meditation throughout the day; for seated meditation, he invariably chose mountain peaks or beneath trees.

Initially, he stayed at Xuānlíu Temple on the southern side of Mount Kuéijī, where he engaged in discussions on the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*) with the practitioners of Chan, Yìnkōng, Qián, and Jìng.

Whenever there was an interval between meditation and recitation, he would invariably compose poems and songs; his thoughts entered into the profound and uninterrupted, and his inspiration embraced the soaring and the moving.
He would surely be able to continue the lingering melodies of Pan Yue and Ruan Ji, and fill in the missing texts of Jiang Yan and Xie Lingyun, thereby standing without shame beside the ancients.
He was patient and skillful in his guidance; his disciples received his teachings as a fertile field receives a drenching rain of dew.

He never once entered the gates of the laity, yet he formed friendships beyond the mundane world with the Tiantai Daoist Pan Zhiqing, Zhu Fang of Xiangyang, Zhang Ji of Nanyang, Huangfu Ceng of Anding, Zhang Nanshi of Fanyang, Lu Xun of Wu Commandery, Xu Yi of Donghai, and Lu Hongjian of Jingling. Biography of Shi Qihan of Donghuqiu Monastery in Wu Commandery, Tang Dynasty. The monk Shi Qihan, whose courtesy name was Dengzhi, was the son of Shen [surname] of Wuxing. He was a native of Wu Commandery. His father, Shen Xuan, served as the Magistrate of Changzhou during the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty. Qihan entered the monastic order at the age of twelve. He was diligent in his studies and possessed a sharp intellect;

he was well-versed in both Buddhist and secular classics. He composed poetry with great skill, and his style was refined and elegant. During the Tianbao era, he resided at Donghuqiu Monastery in Wu Commandery, where he became renowned for his literary talent. His works were highly esteemed by his contemporaries. He passed away in the second year of the Zhenyuan era at the age of sixty-three. He was buried at the monastery grounds, and a stele was erected to commemorate him. His disciples compiled his writings into one volume. His collected works were widely circulated throughout the realm. His fellow monks, including Zhixian and others, lamented his passing and composed verses in his memory. His legacy remains celebrated among the literati of the time.

His great-grandfather served as the Director of the Imperial Academy in the Chen dynasty; his great-great-grandfather was the Governor of Weizhou in the Sui dynasty; and his grandfather and father, for three generations, did not hold office.

Biography of Shi Langran of Zhaoyin Monastery in Runzhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Langran’s secular surname was Wei; his family had held high office for generations. His ancestors followed the Eastern Jin dynasty during its southward migration, and thus he was a native of Nanxu.
He entered the monastic order during the Kaiyuan era and received his training under Master Qi of Kaiyuan Temple in Danyang.
At the beginning of the Tianbao era, he received full ordination from Vinaya Master Guang of Huayan Temple in Hangzhou.

Later, he moved to Lingyin Temple and relied upon Master Yuan as his preceptor. He mastered the *Sifenlü chao* (Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya) and further received instruction from Master Tanyi of Yuezhou. He specialized in the study of the Vinaya-piṭaka, lecturing and instructing his disciples, drawing enthusiastic responses from all directions.
In the second year of Emperor Suzong’s Zhide era, by imperial decree, he was transferred and his name was registered at Cihesi.
During the Shangyuan era, the Prefectural Governor Wei Xuan further requested that he serve as the Great Virtuous Head of the Zhaoyin Monastery.

In the same year, during his leisure time from lecturing and teaching, he composed the *Jin-gu-jue* (Decisions on the Ancient and Modern) in ten fascicles. He provided explanations for the *Sifenlü chao* (Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya) totaling several hundred thousand words; its complex rules and categories were rendered with great clarity, and it circulated widely throughout the world.
Observing that there were points of unease regarding the principles of the ancients set forth previously, he resolved them; thus it is titled "Decisions" (*Jue*).
In the preface to the *Jue*, he states:
"At first I relied on Master Wei of India for my studies, and subsequently followed Masters Huiyuan and Huichi."
In total, there were twenty-six ascents to the ordination platform (jie-tan),

According to the *Lüchāo*, he lectured on it twenty-eight times in all.
When receiving gifts, whether they were abundant or meager, he accepted them and redistributed them to the two fields of compassion and faith.
Regarding all matters of doctrine and principle, his ability to examine the texts and investigate their meanings was entirely attributed to the power of his past cultivation.
He maintained his observance of the precepts and restraints without deviation for even a moment.

In the winter of the twelfth year of the Dali era, on the day of Gui-mao, he sat cross-legged as usual and passed away in serene tranquility. He was fifty-four years old at the time of his death, having been a monk for thirty-five years since his ordination.
