thus, the Prefectural Governor Wei Shu accorded him exceptional honor and respect.

His body was not clothed in silk or cotton, and his dwelling was merely covered by *bìluó* vines; the fourfold assembly knew where to turn for refuge, and those from all quarters admired his transformative influence—his purity was like that of white cranes and egrets.
In the twelfth year of the Xiántóng era, the monastics and laypeople of the surrounding district requested that he provide instruction to the fourfold assembly.

At times he would roam through the remote pastures, and at others he would stroll leisurely along the coastal shores; never venturing beyond the forested foothills, he remained there for several years at a time.
Although he was a nobleman, when scholars arrived at his gate on single carriages, none were permitted an audience.

Regarding his seven-character and five-character regulated verse, he followed the style of the Yuanhe period to compose the "Song of Green Mountains and Following the Way," which spread through the lips of the people.

Suddenly, on the morning following the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, he gathered the assembly in the long corridor and, with palms joined, bid them a final farewell; his parting words were exceedingly firm and upright.

Consequently, he remained bedridden without rising, fasting for seven days before passing away on the sixteenth day of the ninth month in the fifteenth year of the Xiántóng era. He was seventy-four years of age and fifty-one years since his ordination.
The disciples Huiqing and Chuanlang escorted the spirit coffin and enshrined it three hundred paces southeast of the temple.

In the following year, they raised a mound and erected a stupa; Chen Yan of Yingchuan composed the stupa inscription, and Zhou Siyi, the district magistrate of Runan, served as the patron for the faithful, with the stele being established in the fourth year of the Qianfu era.
Biography of Danfu of Kaiyuan Temple in Yuezhou during the Tang Dynasty. As for the monk Danfu, it is unknown where he was from.
By nature he was highly alert and perceptive; his speech was invariably firm and upright. He was solely diligent in lecturing and instruction, maintaining a refined and correct demeanor.
The local customs of Kuaiji were a profound repository of monastic discipline and models of conduct.
When Fǔ began his exhortations, those who followed him were like black iron drawn to a magnet.
He originally studied under the Dharma-assembly of Vinaya Master Guǎnwén; Guǎnwén was the "Yóu" or "Xià" to Master Shěnggōng, and Fǔ was the direct descendant of Gōng.
The Chapter on Right Livelihood penetrates the profound mysteries of the secret teachings.
Since the time of Tanyi and Xuanyan, few have been able to follow in their footsteps; Fayu’s reputation now surpasses that of his predecessors.

However, at that time, the masterful hand of Master Yunwen prevailed throughout the regions of the Vinaya; as he was just beginning to mediate within the Great Vinaya, when it came to the performance of rituals, all followed his lead like grass bowing before the wind.
At the end of the Xiántóng era, Dàchūn produced disciples such as Zhìzhāng, who transmitted and lectured on his teachings; even now, his dharma heirs still exist.
It is said that he authored a *Shǒujì* (Handwritten Record), which has yet to be obtained. Alas!
How lamentable!
This is the biography of Dharmakṣema of Lingguang Monastery in Jiahe, Wu Commandery, during the Tang Dynasty. Śramaṇa Dharmakṣema’s secular surname was Yu, and he was a native of Changshui in Wu.

He was born during the Tiānbǎo era; as an infant, he was exceptionally gifted. At the age of seven, he entered the service of a teacher, and within three weeks of receiving the scriptures and Dharma, he had mastered the entire *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* through recitation.
In his early twenties, he went to Chang’an and received full ordination at An-guo Temple during the Dali era.
Thereupon, he studied the Vinaya path in the capital; he mastered all the various schools and their differences, and after eleven years, he had flourished in his mastery of the discipline.
When he returned to the East after transmitting the Dharma, seekers gathered around him like a forest.
The Governor of Wu Commandery memorialized the throne to establish a *śīla*-platform at Kaiyuan Temple, and [the Master] was selected to preside over the ordination ceremony.

Xunqiong served as his attendant and was simultaneously appointed by the assembly to oversee the affairs of the monastery; he constantly bestowed the precepts upon the two assemblies of monks and nuns.
He wore a water-strainer at his waist and did not keep any utensils beyond those required for immediate use.
Every time a bird perched beside his seat, he would drive it away so that it would not remain.
On the third watch of the hour of the horse (noon) on the tenth day of the second month in the first year of the Huichang era, he informed his disciples Qingjun and Qinggao:
"I am about to pass away."
He remained solemnly with his feet stacked one upon the other and passed away while lying on his right side.
At that time, the assembly heard the clear and resonant sounds of pipes and strings during the day, which were celestial music;
at night, they beheld extraordinary light.
He was eighty-nine years of age and had been a monk for sixty-nine years.
In the fourth month, his stupa was moved to the grounds of Laisu Township; this is the white stupa that stands there.

Later, his disciples, together with Cao Xin, the Regional Inspector of Yizhou, and Wu Fang, the Rectifier of the Court of Judicial Review, renovated the stupa. Upon opening it, they found the remains of the Master’s physical features appearing like copper-colored metal; his tongue remained intact like a lotus flower, and all forty-two of his teeth were complete.
He was bathed with fragrant water and reinterred on the twenty-second day of the fifth month in the second year of the Jingfu era, the *guichou* year.

His senior disciple was Gongjing; Jing’s disciple was Xingyun; Yun’s disciple was Renbiao; and Biao’s disciple was Xuangao. Xuangao was originally a monk of pure character who, together with Hongqi, reconstructed Lingguang Monastery following its destruction during the chaos of war.

Master Gao and Master Qi subsequently retired together to Mount Tiantai to practice *dhyāna* and contemplation; they both passed away on the mountain in succession, and upon their cremation, śarīras were obtained from both.
Biography of Shi Wenju of Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai during the Tang Dynasty. Shi Wenju’s secular surname was Zhang, and he was a native of Dongyang in Wuzhou.
When he had just reached the age of fifteen, he went to a master to request the Dharma.
At nineteen, he shaved his head and first entered the order as a novice.
In the third year of the Zhenyuan era, by imperial decree, he was ordained and received the full precepts.

During the subsequent fifteen years, he studied the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, mastering its methods and practicing with such diligence day and night that he eventually ascended to the platform of lecturing and instruction.
Subsequently, he thoroughly mastered the commentaries and meanings of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, attaining the very essence of Zhiyi’s teachings.
His stature was over six chi tall; his form was like a mountain and his countenance like jade. He was as still as a placid pool and as mobile as drifting clouds.
His eyes never glanced about, and his mouth uttered no frivolous words; within the four modes of deportment, there was nothing that did not conform to the monastic discipline.
The two assemblies of Dancheng look up to him as their standard and model.
Those who travel to other regions to receive his teachings vie with Master Zekong of Foku to excel one another in the path of Chan.
Soon after, he was appointed by imperial decree as the Great Virtuous One (Dade) of Guoqing Temple.

Previously, when the Great Master Zhiyi had answered the inquiries of Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty, he established the "Seven-Day *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Ritual Site" (*jinguangming daochang*). Every year in the ninth month, officials from distant and nearby prefectures, governors, and regional lords would dispatch people to deliver offerings. Since these matters were carried out without hindrance, both the monastic and lay communities arrived from far and wide; however, as the crowds gathered in such great numbers, food and drink became scarce.
The *dianzuo* (head cook) monk was troubled by this.
During the Dazhong era, the administrative monk Qingyun consulted with Huiming about establishing monastic estates and fields totaling twelve *qing*.
From then on, the *Guangming* assembly was never heard to lack for provisions; was this not the achievement of Huiming?
He passed away in the fifth month of the second year of the Huichang era. His disciple Youqing erected a stupa on the western peak of the temple.
He was eighty-three years of age and had fifty-five years of summer retreats as a monk.
Han Yi composed an inscription to eulogize his virtue.
Biography of Shi Yunwen of Kaiyuan Monastery in Kuaiji, Tang Dynasty: Shi Yunwen, whose courtesy name was Zhijing and whose family name was Zhu, was a native of Jiahe in the present-day Xiuzhou.
At the age of nine, Quan Yu lost his father; however, he accepted his destiny and set aside secular learning to devote himself to Buddhism.

His teacher instructed him in the two sutras, the *Vimalakīrti* and the *Lotus Sūtra*; due to his quick-witted nature, he mastered both within two years. Men of great erudition remarked that he was one who "repeatedly grasped the underlying principles."
Someone asked Wen in jest,
"After you have left the household life, what kind of occupation do you intend to pursue?
He replied spontaneously:
"When you ascend the lotus pedestal, you shall let out a lion’s roar.
Or some would mock him, saying:
"How dare you act thus before the elders?"
Some said, "His aspirations are great; this youth's future is not easily fathomed.
When he reached the age of sixteen, he shaved his crown hair and donned the *antarvāsaka*.

Subsequently, he bound his feet and traveled westward to seek out the Great Virtue Master Yuan, who presided over the ordination platform at Mount Song; there he attained the Dharma of Non-action, at which time he was twenty-three years of age.

That summer, he proceeded to the Central Capital to study the Vinaya school of the Xiangbu lineage and the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*. Wearing patched robes and subsisting on alms, he spent four seasons amidst both cold and heat.

Having knocked at the gate of doctrinal inquiry, he invariably entered the master’s chamber; thus, regarding the profound pivot of the Vinaya rules, he attained an especially refined and subtle understanding.
In the fifth year of the Taika era, while on a visit to his parents for filial reflection, he suddenly sighed, "I shall return.
Having returned to his native village, he remained there for some time before falling ill; thus, he had no leisure to engage in lecturing or chanting.
Later, hearing that the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* was being lectured at Tianzhu Monastery in Qiantang—a gathering renowned for its excellence—Wen went there to study.
Before even a full year had passed, his brilliance had already begun to manifest.

In the first year of the Kaicheng era, while traveling to Mount Taiqiao, he stayed at Jiaxiang Temple in Yue; the assembly, inspired by his pure fragrance, requested that he expound upon the sutras and vinaya.
Wen Ziyue was a student of considerable rigor and gravity; he would often instruct them, saying:

"The conduct of a bhikṣu is not that of a householder. To be fully endowed with the prātimokṣa and the communal discipline (saṃvara) is its essential nature. This is because of one's diligence regarding form and color, because of fear [of transgression], and because of guarding [the senses]."
"In this way, one will swiftly attain the fruits of the Path!
Otherwise, the disciple would fall and the Master’s Way would be bestowed in vain.
Upon hearing these admonitions, his tears flowed profusely; he reformed his heart and changed his conduct, realizing that more than half of his faults had been exposed.
In the third year of the Huichang era, he moved to Jinglin Temple, where he devoted himself exclusively to preaching the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
It was during the reign of Emperor Wuzong that the purge of Buddhism occurred, and he was consequently subjected to a search and seizure of his belongings.

By day he wore the wide-sleeved robes of a scholar, and by night he donned the simple hempen garments of a monk; thus he did not fail in his monastic conduct, while merely avoiding the censure of the laity.

At the beginning of the Dazhong era, he once again revitalized the Buddhist gate, reestablishing the ritual protocols of the Dharma, and was subsequently enrolled among the thirty monks of Kaiyuan Temple.
Seven years later, the senior monks of the monastery commissioned him to lecture on the Vinaya and the Mahāyāna sūtras.
In the autumn of the third year of the Qiánfú era (the Bingshén year), he concluded his lectures and began perusing the Tripiṭaka.

On the twenty-ninth day of the sixth month of the second year of the Zhōnghé era (the Rennyín year), he passed away after a slight illness at the age of seventy-eight, with fifty-five years of ordination seniority.
On the twelfth day of the seventh month of that year, he was buried on the southern slope of Shiqi Mountain;
by his final testament, he had forbidden the planting of trees or the raising of a mound over the grave.

When he first ascended the seat to lecture on the scriptures, his disciples were struck with awe and trepidation; yet, during the moments when he uttered a single groan, everyone would fall into prostration. Such was the power of his disciplined majesty.
At Jiaxiang, Jinglin, and the present Dashi'an Monasteries, he lectured on twenty-seven commentaries on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and twenty-five lectures on the *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra*.
As for his personal character:

his appearance was ancient and tall, with a sharp-featured head and a dark complexion; he was meticulous in his conduct, such that even "cranes in the courtyard" would fall short of matching his purity.

Nevertheless, he also forayed into the teachings of Confucius and Mozi, and admiring the example of Bai Juyi (Bait Fu), who composed his own epitaph and pre-wrote an inscription for his square grave (*fangfen*), he placed it within his chest.
His disciple Huaiyi, while searching through the master’s literary collection, saw this and was moved to tears; he thus fulfilled his late teacher’s intention by erecting a small stupa.
Later, his disciples Huaisu and Sijie named the work *Mingde xushou* (The Postscript on the Virtuous Name) and added this postscript.

When Zanning traveled to Kuaiji, he once paid homage to the true image of Wenxian and met his dharma-grandson Kexiang, who was practicing with rigorous discipline and diligent cultivation, embodying the conduct of a Dhūta.
Therefore, his life and deeds have been fully recorded.

**Biography of Huize of Ximing Monastery in Jingzhao during the Liang Dynasty** The monk Huize, whose secular surname was Mi, was a native of Kunshan in Wu Commandery. His original name was Yuanbiao. He was a disciple of [the master] Shi Huize. His family name was Mi, and he was a man from Kunshan in Wu Commandery.
At the age of nine, he traveled extensively to study talent and righteousness, thoroughly immersing himself in the Confucian classics.
As his virtuous seeds began to sprout, he became resolutely weary of worldly customs; in the seventh year of the Dazhong era, he entered the monastic order at Ximing Monastery in the capital.
He was diligent in his knowledge of recitation and chanting, mastering them all as if he had practiced them for years.
In the ninth year, while at his home temple, he received imperial favor and attained ordination.

In the fourteenth year, he resided at the Dharma seat of Master Fabao and lectured on the scriptures; that same year, by imperial decree, he was appointed to serve as a member of the assembly of Great Virtues (Dade).
In the third year of the Xiantong era, he lectured on the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* and the *Sangfu yi* at Chongsheng Temple, and produced one scroll of the *Sanjie tu*.
In the seventh year [of the Dali era], he took the place of Master Chang to lecture at the ancestral monastery.
In the fifteenth year, by imperial decree, he was appointed as a regular member of the ordination platform.
In the first year of the Guangming era, when the Nestle rebels (Chao Kou) violated the capital and Guanzhong was in turmoil, he departed for Xiagui in Huazhou to seek refuge from the chaos.
In the second year of the Zhonghe era, he arrived in Huainan, where Lord Gao Bian summoned him to Fayun Temple.

Upon concluding his lectures, he returned to Wu, but was earnestly detained by the Regional Inspector, Lord Yang; consequently, he traveled to Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai to take up residence there.

In the first year of the Qianning era, he went to Yuyang Monastery in Mingzhou, where he composed one scroll of the *Taji* (Record of the Stupa) and produced twelve scrolls of the *Jiyaoji* (Record of Collected Essentials).
King Qian of Wusu commissioned him to preside over ordination platforms in Yuezhou.
On the eighth day of the eighth month in the second year of the Kaiping era, he manifested illness and passed away while seated.
He had lived seventy-four years and held fifty-four years of Dharma seniority.
He was interred on a ridge of Mount Mao.
The lay disciple of the Eight Precepts, Regional Inspector Huang Sheng, established a stupa for him.
Zisheng was by nature not fond of being blunt or outspoken; he held the practice of modesty and deferring to others as paramount.
Aside from his formal lectures, he devoted himself to the oral recitation of sutras and mantras—some thirty or forty texts in total, beginning with the *Lotus Sūtra*—to cultivate his verbal karma.
He perused the entire Tripitaka twice, lectured on the commentaries seventy times, and read the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Sangyi*, and the *Analects* several times each.
His austere and steadfast adherence to discipline was rarely seen since ancient times.
Among his入室 (入室) disciples, Xi Jue was the most prominent in displaying his sharp intellectual acumen.

Furthermore, there was Yuan Biao, a man of integrity and sincerity whose speech was often incisive and direct. He delighted in evaluating human affairs and possessed lofty insight; he followed the study of the Vinaya while also diligently pursuing secular learning, such that there were no works of history, literature, or technical arts that he did not master.

Early on, he attended the lecture hall of Master Fabao at Ximing Monastery in the capital. By the Guangming era, the Divine Capital had fallen into chaos; he subsequently departed for the region south of the Yangtze River and resided at Dashi Monastery in Yuezhou, where he lectured on the *Nanshan Lüchao*.
Scholars from all the commanderies flocked to him without exception.

His exposition of principles was comprehensive and profound, and he excelled in his eloquence; whenever he brandished his fly-whisk, the listeners forgot their fatigue, and he was thus titled the "Kamalaśīla (Mie-shui) Ācārya."
He composed the *Yiji* (Record of Meaning) in five fascicles, also titled *Jianshui* (Mirror of the Waters).
His disciple Qingfu served as its editor-in-chief.
Biography of Shao Shami Shi Yancheng of Poshan Xingfu Temple in Suzhou during the Liang Dynasty. Shao Shami Shi Yancheng, surnamed Gong, was a native of Changshu in Wu Commandery.
He upheld the precepts with rigorous intensity, regarding even the slightest worldly affairs as trivial. Diligently seeking a master for his model, he followed only that which was virtuous.

Eventually, he sought out the author of the *Jizong ji* (Record of the Succession of the Lineage) and gained entry through its gateway; thereupon, he began teaching and guiding in his native land. Those of like mind gathered around him, and the influence of the Vinaya spread widely, such that the place became known as the "Abode of the Vinaya."

Previously, this corner of the sea was the ancestral domain of the sorcerer Wuchan and the ancient ruins of Zhaozhentzhi; the surrounding walls of the old temple were incomplete, reduced to nothing more than crumbling enclosures.
Once, one night, a tiger struck by a hunter’s arrow lay crouched on the temple gallery, its roars and growls never ceasing.
Fenyang Chenming took pity on it; he hurriedly fastened his sandals, took up a torch, and descended from the gallery, saying he intended to extract the arrow.
His disciples supported him and tried to stop him three or four times, but he waited until the night was deep and everyone was asleep; he then took a torch himself and went to extract the arrow.
The tiger licked the blood from the tip of the shaft with its tongue and ears drooping, and having looked at him, it closed its eyes.
At dawn, the hunter Zhu De went to the temple to search for the tiger; Xingcheng showed him the arrow, whereupon Zhu De repented his heart and ceased hunting.
King Qian of Wusuku, recognizing and honoring his worth, would summon him whenever he established memorial vegetarian feasts to perform the rites of the *vidyā-dhara* (Holding the Bright Dharma).
At that time, his shoulder-covering robe fell from his arm, yet it returned and draped itself back over him; at times, he even saw ghostly beings attending upon him.
This is what is meant by the saying: "When one's virtue and moral cultivation flourish, ghosts and spirits provide assistance."
In the sixth month of the sixth year of the Zhengming era, he passed away in his mountain retreat at the age of ninety-nine.
As for the Venerable Shou who followed him, throughout the regions of the Huai River, his integrity was peerless; in guarding right mindfulness, few of his time could equal him.
His commentary on the *Nanshan Lüchao* was so thoroughly perfected that he never looked to others for guidance.
During the late Tang dynasty, when the Yang family seized control of Guangling, they repeatedly summoned him to receive offerings.
He was revered from all quarters, yet his sustenance consisted solely of what was obtained through right livelihood.
He did not keep surplus goods in storage, nor did he install bolts on his doors.

When he was presiding over the ordination platform to confer the precepts upon disciples and was correctly performing the *karmavācanā*, before the three proclamations were completed, he suddenly passed away while seated beside a covered cauldron; those who heard of it or witnessed it were filled with wonder and admiration!
Biography of Congli of Futian Monastery on Mount Tiantai during the Later Tang Dynasty. Shi Congli was a native of Xiangyang.
He served his parents with filial piety and was widely praised for his reputation within the local community.
Upon the death of one parent, he resolutely renounced the household; at that time, he was already in the prime of his life.
Upon reaching the stage of full ordination (*upasampadā*), he requested his preceptor to transmit the ritual text for the precepts.
However, his mental nature was fundamentally discordant; he found it extremely difficult to abandon his former habits, and he was frequently disturbed by the demon of sleep.

Outraged by his own turbidity and delusion, he struck his forehead and palms with an iron awl until blood flowed. It was only after more than half a year that he finally succeeded in memorizing and reciting the text.
From that time forth, he maintained the disciplinary rules with meticulous care, adhering strictly to them even in moments of haste or distress.
During the Qiandehua era of the Liang dynasty, he traveled to Mount Tiantai and took up residence at the Pingtian Monastery.
Later, he was promoted to the position of *upādhyāya* (abbot) of the monastery.
He was grave and composed, never showing joy or anger on his face, practicing only compassion and patience.
He constantly instructed the assembly, saying:
"The Prātimokṣa is my great teacher; you must know that for one who has left the household life, the absence of the precepts is like a monkey escaping from its shackles.
In every practice he undertook, he was most diligent in the Poṣadha ceremony, admonishing the assembly to cherish and protect their "life-preserving bag" (the precepts).

At that time, the summer was marked by extreme drought, and the presiding monk came to inform him, saying, "We are about to prepare a vegetarian feast for the Arhats, but alas, the garden vegetables have withered!
We pray that you, O Kalyāṇamitra, will offer prayers on our behalf."
The ritual manual states:
"Simply burn incense in the Hall of the True Lord.

As for this True Lord, he was the crown prince of King Ling of the Zhou dynasty. It has long been heard that he ascended as an immortal; having received an appointment as an immortal official, he became the True Man of Tongbai, the Right Assistant (Youbi Wang), who presides over the Five Peaks and serves the Celestial Dawn. Prince Zhaoqiao came to govern this mountain, and for this reason, in the monasteries and Daoist observatories of Mount Tiantai, the image of the Right Assistant is enshrined, where one merely offers incense and fruit.
From then on, people in the secular world called it the "Local Deity of Mount Wang," but this was not so.
At that time, the presiding official faced the shrine of the immortal and incanted:
"The Elder desires rain to nourish what is withered and parched."
When night fell, clouds rose and rain poured down, ceasing after three days.
Furthermore, the monastery kitchen was lacking a wooden trough for water, and there was a red tree on the mountain whose wood would serve as the necessary material; [the monks] came to inform Huili.
Li said, "I have informed the True Lord that I am going; you need only prepare your followers and equipment to await him.
Before long, a great wind suddenly arose, uprooting and felling trees, which provided sufficient materials for his use.
His ability to move ghosts and spirits was mostly of this kind.

When the Wudukuang of the Two Zhe regions, the Qian family, heard of him, they summoned him into their provincial administration and established a *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* ritual site (*jinguangming daochang*), providing him with abundant offerings and alms.
He dedicated his possessions to the community of monks, possessing only a single cloth for his body.
He remained awake throughout the night, ate but one meal daily, and sat constantly without ever lying down; moreover, he had no surplus or excess.
In the eleventh month of winter in the third year of Tongguang, the year of Yiyou (865 CE), he entered parinirvāṇa at the age of seventy-nine and with fifty-two years of monastic seniority.
He was cremated; his *śarīra* relics were collected, and a stūpa was erected where they remain to this day.
Regarding the biography of Jingxiao of Zhenshen Baota Temple in Hangzhou during the Later Tang: Jingxiao, whose secular surname was Xu, was a native of Danqiu.
Initially, his studies were centered on the public gates of the imperial court; later, he came to admire the commentaries and collections of the Dharma Master Shouyan, which were expounded in Danqiu.
He was stern and resolute by nature, and seldom associated with others.
He was irascible and self-reliant, often treating others with contempt, and his physical constitution was frail.
Later, at the request of others, he went to Dongbai Mountain in Jinhua to instruct beginners.

At that time, there was a Vinaya master from Huiyou in Jiangxi who produced a commentary on the *Śīlaparivarta* titled the *Guijian Lu*. His scholarship was extensive and his exposition grand; he arrived at Xiaoseng Temple with his disciples just as the lecture was reaching the section on "Observance and Transgression" (*chifan pian*), whereupon he repeatedly expressed his admiration and praise.
From this point on, his reputation spread and his works became highly valued.
Every morning when he brewed tea, it would suddenly transform into milk.

He composed twenty fascicles of writings titled *Jianzheng* (Simplified Rectification), which stated that by means of the power of discernment (*cintā*), he had eliminated erroneous doctrines and selected the correct principles.
King Wusuku of the Qian clan summoned him to his native hometown of Lin’an to serve as the abbot of Zhulin Temple.
Not long after, he was ordered to attend the ritual platform at Beitasi; this was in the second year of the Tiānchéng era.
Next, he was appointed to reside at the True Body Jewel Pagoda Temple in the south, where he spent the remainder of his life.

He was subsequently buried in a valley of Daesimsan Mountain; the pagoda there was named "Choryang" (Pure Coolness), which corresponds to the title bestowed upon him by his original preceptor. This is likely the case.
Biography of Shi Zhenjun of Xiangguo Monastery in Dongjing during the Later Tang Dynasty. Shi Zhenjun’s secular surname was Zhang; he was a native of Xinzheng in Zhengzhou.
He was a descendant of Mr. Zhang Guo of the Tang dynasty.
Today, there is a village called Zhangguoli in Yingyang, where his tomb and its surrounding catalpa and camphor trees still remain.
His character was lofty and his demeanor broad and generous; even in his childhood, he did not engage in frivolous play.
At the age of fourteen, he suddenly and transcendentally departed from secular life, such that no one knew his intent.

Although his parents bared their legs to block his path and his brothers cut across the road to stop him, they were ultimately unable to dissuade him; he thus went to Xiangguo Temple to take refuge under the Vinaya Master Guizheng and enter the monastic order.
His divine faculties sprang forth with remarkable brilliance, such that he was startling at first sight.
Although his feats of reading inscriptions on stone monuments from behind and reciting chessboard patterns were extraordinary, they were not as much to marvel at as this.
Before long, he had mastered the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the *Benevolent Kings* sutras and other scriptures, totaling tens of thousands of words.
At that time, his peers teased him, saying,
"You are a portable scripture chest with legs.
Xu Jun declined this title with firm humility, remaining only respectful and modest.
Having shaved his head and donned the robes of a monk, he immediately began studying the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. He followed the lectures and recited eight chapters, totaling six hundred stanzas.
By the time he reached the eighteenth chapter, he ascended the lecture seat to debate.

Upon reaching adulthood, he received the full precepts at the Precept Platform Hall of Huishan Temple on Mount Song; subsequently, he resided at Fengshan Temple—which is now known as Kaibao Lüyuan—where he studied the commentaries on the *Vinaya* and its new recensions.
At twenty-three, he registered his name for official service and engaged in lecturing and instruction, earning praise as a prodigy from his seniors.

In the second year of the Dàshùn era, the Guóshì Temple was ravaged by fire; its multi-storied towers, three gates, the Seven-Jeweled Buddha Hall, the Cloud-Arrayed Treasure Pavilion, and the corridors within the Mañjuśrī Hall—totaling over four hundred rooms—were all reduced to ashes.
At that time, the community of the monastery was filled with anxiety, not knowing where to turn for refuge.
Someone said, "If we can request Daoyun to return to the temple, the monastery will be restored.
Thereupon, they went together to Kai Bao Temple and earnestly requested Daoyun to return and serve as the *upādhyāya* (abbot) of their own temple.
Over the course of several years, he renovated the corridors and eaves, and the temple halls were further embellished with splendor.

He was also invited to serve as the presiding master of the new chapter, where he once again opened lectures on the Vinaya; more than fifty monastics and nuns attended daily, holding the commentaries to listen and absorb his teachings.
