When Master Zongmi of Caotang selected and refined [the teachings] to their ultimate point, only Qingliang Chengguan grasped their essential meaning, like a grain of rice held by a young official;
others did not yet embody the vision of Master Li.
Therefore, in the translation activities of the Tang dynasty, Yi served as the preeminent master; thus, Huili referred to him as the "Chief Translator" (yìzhǔ).
The title "Chief Translator" originated with Yi.
He was profoundly versed in the five regions of India and thoroughly integrated the teachings of the Three Vehicles; he was esteemed by both past and present, and few in the world could equal him.
His two-fascicle treatise has been included in the Tripiṭaka; as for repelling the attacks of external critics, this alone serves as his spear and shield.

Biography of Huili of Wei Guo Monastery in Jingzhao, Tang Dynasty. Shi Huili, whose original name was Zili, had his name changed to Huili by the Emperor. His secular surname was Zhao, and he was a native of Tianshui.
His distant ancestor moved his residence to Xinping due to official duties, and thus became a native of Bing.
Both his grandfather and father enjoyed high reputations.
Li Ji was the third son of Li Yi, who served as a起居舍人 (Attendant-in-Ordinary) and 司隶从事 (Official of the Office of the Imperial Secretariat) during the Sui dynasty.
From birth he was precocious and possessed the aspiration to renounce worldly life.

At the age of fifteen, in the third year of the Zhenguan era, he entered the monastic order and resided at Zhaoren Temple in Bingzhou; this temple was the very battlefield where Xue Ju had been defeated.

Li Shi was a man of keen talent and brilliance; his spirit was pure and his realization of the Way surpassed others. He emulated the lofty character of Lin Yuan and possessed the discernment and magnanimity of Zhaorong.

His reputation spread far and wide, leading to an imperial decree summoning him to serve as a Great Virtuous Master for the translation of scriptures at Da Cien Monastery. Subsequently, he was appointed as the Chief Steward (Du Weina) of Ximing Monastery, and later granted the position of Abbot of Taiyuan Monastery; in each case, imperial edicts were issued to appoint him to these monastic offices.

During the reign of the Emperor, he extensively examined both Confucianism and Buddhism, composing elegant writings with such marvelous eloquence that his arguments soared like clouds and his insights gushed forth like a spring. Furthermore, he maintained upright speech and a dignified countenance, never shrinking from imperial severity; even when faced with fire or boiling water, he never yielded or flinched.
He was frequently summoned to the inner palace to engage in debate with the Daoist priest Huangguan;
his arguments always accorded with the Emperor’s wishes, as recorded in a separate biography.

[The Emperor] established that because the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang had sought scriptures in India, if there were no records of his journey, future generations would rarely hear of it; he therefore composed the *Biography of the Tripitaka Master of Cien*, but passed away before its completion.
Later, the śramaṇa Yancong of Guangfu Monastery continued and completed it, comprising ten volumes in total.
Thus, the original title reads: "Originally compiled by the śramaṇa Huili; annotated by Shi Yancong. This refers to that very work.
Having finished carving the inscription, he feared that its many beauties might be lost; he therefore buried it in the earth, so that no one in the world could hear of it.
Later, as he was nearing death, he ordered his attendants to dig it up and reveal it. Just as they were about to bring it out, he passed away.

Initially, when Lü Cai, a Court Physician of the Imperial Medical Bureau, established his views, he falsely composed the three-fascicle *Commentary on the Diagrams for Explaining Hetuvidyā*, in which he slandered and rejected the correct principles of various masters.
Kuiji sent him a letter of reprimand, containing these pointed remarks:

"The Court Physician has little experience with worldly affairs, yet he claims that the True Doctrine can be mastered; how is this different from a field mouse seeing a cauldron or stove and deeming them climbable, then asserting that Mount Kunlun is not difficult to scale?"
"The wolf spider beholds the thorny forest as easy to ensnare, and likewise deems the *fusang* tree capable of being caught in its web.
To fail to measure one's own limits—how is this any different?
Because of these words, Cai ceased his efforts.

Upon hearing of these matters, Liu Xuan, a Doctor of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, returned to his faith and wrote a letter titled "Proclamation to the Monks Translating the Scriptures," stating: "In resisting external insults, he is the Ji-lu of the Buddhist community."
Biography of Shi Xuanyi of Foshouji Monastery in the Tang Capital Luoyang: Shi Xuanyi’s secular surname was Du.

Having entered the Mysterious Gate (Daoism) in his youth, he mastered the scriptures and teachings as soon as they were introduced to him; his peers in yellow caps recognized his brilliance and wisdom, and as he transcended his contemporaries and excelled beyond his peers, he was titled the Master of Refinement, Du Yi.
Having ascended to the highest registers of the Daoist canon, he served as the master of Dahan Guan in the capital of Luoyang.

He immersed his mind in the *Qilüe* (Seven Categories) and attained mastery of the principles of the Three Mysteries; among those in the tradition of Daoist arts and techniques, he was esteemed as their guiding authority.

The Empress Dowager’s heart revered the Great Dharma and she propagated the teachings of the Śākya lineage; moreover, realizing that eating the dock plant was not sweet, she departed for a distant residence, vowing to return to her original attire and turn toward the Buddha for refuge.
He then earnestly requested ordination, and an imperial edict granted him permission to enter the monastic order. He resided at Foshouji Monastery and soon thereafter became its abbot.
Thus we know that it is truly said: "In the grass there are heroes; among birds there are champions."
Continuing his studies and translations, he thoroughly understood the errors of those [non-Buddhist] schools and realized that the True Teaching could be relied upon.
Someone asked him,
"Why do you believe in the Buddha?"
Yi said: "Life and death pass as swiftly as a gale;
one ought to plan for them early, lest one find oneself bracing the reins at a crossroads or pausing with the oar in midstream!
To act like those who circle their chariots while gazing at the Dipper Star, or who exorcise ghosts while seeking immortality—to apply the mind in such a manner is not to reach the ultimate."

He then composed the *Zhengzhilun* (Treatise on Discerning the Correct) in one fascicle, pointing out and refuting their errors to lead them back to the true and correct. He established a format of host and guest in dialogue, making it extremely concise and essential.
Yi did not know its end.
The genealogy says:
To know the enemy's disposition depends upon local guides;
Alternatively, entering a realm where conflict is inevitable avoids the reproach of "not treading upon the ground";
furthermore, it is like holding a torch while marching through the night, which is not at all like a person entering the darkness.
I have long heard that Xuanyi once donned the yellow cap of a Daoist and was well-versed in its fundamental teachings;
yet upon returning to the Buddhist fold, he rejected those false origins.
Without requiring four months to test him, he had already won the submission of an entire city.
Viewed from this perspective, if there were those who opposed him, he would say, "I shall speak the truth to you"—is this not precisely what is meant by that?
The Biography of Dharma Ming of Jiangling Prefecture, Tang Dynasty. Śramaṇa Dharma Ming was originally a native of Jingchu.
He was extensively versed in the sutras and śāstras and proficient in secular literature; his eloquence flowed like a stream, and his observance of the precepts was firm and upright.

During the reign of Emperor Zhongzong, he entered Chang’an to visit and seek out various eminent masters. It happened that an imperial decree had been issued for the monks and Daoists to deliberate upon the authenticity of the *Huahu chengfo jing* (The Scripture on the Conversion of the Barbarians and Attainment of Buddhahood).
At that time, the inner palace was filled with a grand assembly, and the hundred officials waited in attendance.

The eminent figures of high rank, like great elephants, were contending against those in yellow caps; their positions were unstable and overturned, and they were difficult to settle, being as restless as snorting horses.
At the beginning of the Ming dynasty, he was not included in the selection for the imperial examination; yet when he entered the arena, his performance was preeminent.
He asked a follower of the Way, "When Laozi transformed the Hu people into Buddhists, did Laozi employ the Han language to convert them?"
Was it transformed by means of the Hu language?
If it were transformed by means of the Han language, the Hu people would not understand it.
If it were transformed by means of the Hu language, then once this sutra arrived in this land, it would necessarily have been translated.
I do not yet know: in what year and month was this sutra [translated]?
In which dynasty did it occur?
And who recited the foreign (Hū) language?
"Who took down the dictation?
At that time, Daoliu was unable to offer a defense or a reply.
Because of this, the high officials praised him, and it was the first year of the Shenlong era.
On the fourteenth day of the ninth month of that year, an imperial edict was issued, stating:

"I command all officials in their respective jurisdictions to abolish this spurious scripture. A stone inscription shall be carved at the Baima Monastery in the capital of Luoyang to be shown to future generations."
The Imperial Edict stated:

"I, the Emperor, have humbly occupied the precious throne and am renewing and expounding the administration. Having once again brought peace to the ancestral altars, I have performed the great rites of solemn sacrifice and bestowed the vast grace of thunder and rain. These benefits now extend even to those in monastic robes, as I simultaneously issue both warnings and encouragement."

I have heard that in all the Daoist observatories throughout the world, paintings of "The Transformation of Huahu into a Buddha" are displayed, and in Buddhist monasteries as well, images of Xuan Yuan are depicted; the sacred countenances of these two teachings are both improper to display together.
These must all be destroyed within ten days of the date of this decree.
Should they be intentionally retained, the local officials shall be charged with the "crime of violating an imperial edict.

Regarding the *Huahu jing*, successive dynasties have issued clear edicts prohibiting it; yet recently we have learned that it still circulates extensively outside the capital. From this day forward, all versions of the *Huahu jing* and all related records [are hereby forbidden].
"The accounts concerning the 'Conversion of the Barbarians' (Huahu) should all be expunged.
Should anyone retain them, they shall be punished according to the imperial decree.
In that same month, Huan Daoyan, the head of the Dahrng Daoist Abbey in Luojing, and others submitted a memorial persistently defending [the texts]. The Emperor’s response was inscribed as follows:

"I, with my unworthy person, have humbly inherited the great enterprise; though I have failed in many respects in pacifying and stabilizing the realm, I have indeed been devoted to impartiality and leniency.

Moreover, as the three sages have shed their brilliant light and the Mysterious Origin has presided over the order of succession, how could I forget the teachings of Laozi while showing partiality toward the school of Śākyamuni?"
My resolve is sincere in returning to simplicity, and my heart is intent on removing artifice.
If principles are violated and affairs are discordant, even those close to me shall be eliminated;
if righteousness accords and names are appropriate, even those with whom I have grievances must be recorded.
Recently, during the leisure moments between the myriad affairs of state, I have briefly examined the texts of the Three Teachings.
As for the two chapters of the *Daode jing*, they are exquisitely sublime, reaching the realm of the ineffable and the unmanifest.
In India, there exist the two truths of emptiness, wherein the principle of the profound discourse on *tathatā* (suchness) is kept secret.

There is nothing that does not extensively expound the gate of the mysterious and elucidate the most recondite mysteries; why, then, rely upon the falsehood of the "Converting the Barbarians" (*Huahu*) to further propagate the school of the Old Lord?

The meaning contains contradictions, and the text lacks canonical authority; regarding the attainment of Buddhahood, the four individuals differ, and concerning their disciples, the accounts of their learning are inconsistent.
Since Yin Xi is already said to have attained Buddhahood, this is already highly fanciful.
Furthermore, to claim that Ānanda was manifested through transformation is merely to create a "crowd gathered by chance.
Figures such as Guiguzi and Beiguozi had not yet set foot in the Central Kingdom;
those like Śāriputra and Mañjuśrī falsely claimed to have appeared in this eastern land.
The Hu and Han peoples were intermingled, and the eras were also discordant.
To preach *nirvāṇa* while treading upon water lacked any scriptural authority;
to discourse on the *saddharma* while walking through fire was akin to the antics of a court jester.
Deceit and falsehood are self-evident; what need is there for further elaboration?
The scripture was not composed by the Lord Lao; to destroy it does not constitute a deficiency in filial piety.
These texts were merely spoken by a vulgar man; to eliminate them only serves to further manifest the virtue of one's ancestors.
"Although your words are earnest, the reasoning is in fact not yet settled.
You should fully comprehend My intention and immediately cease sending further memorials.
Mingzhi was eloquent and quick-witted, without peer in his generation.
This Dharma-gate provides support, by which one may ward off insults; that evil words do not enter the ears—is this not what is meant?
The colophon says:
Regarding the *Huahu jing*, the two teachings were not equal, and their disputes were many!
There is no dharma that can clarify this; a single word suffices to encompass it all.

Even if one were to concentrate the spirit and exert the mind, it could not be answered after a long time—how much less so before the presence of the Ten-Thousand-Wagon Sovereign? Who could possibly respond instantly?
Formerly, when Yang Su saw the painting of "Converting the Barbarians" at Songyang Monastery, he remarked,
"Why did he not convert the barbarians to the Way, but instead cause them to become Buddhas?
The Daoist practitioners remained speechless.

Observing Master Ming’s inquiry, its meaning contains two points: first, it concerns the transformation of the barbarians into Buddhahood; second, it addresses the fact that the speech of the various celestial immortals differs from that of humans—when the celestial words were transmitted to produce the various scriptures, who was it that translated them?
Is this not like shooting two wild ducks with a single arrow, or like striking two young boars with one shot?
The Biography of Shenwu of Mount Shibi in Runzhou, Tang Dynasty. Shenwu, whose courtesy name was Tongxing, was the son of the Li family of Longxi.
His ancestors had originally belonged to the Western Jin dynasty during its period of upheaval and subsequently migrated to Changshui in Wu.
For generations they had maintained a life of Confucian simplicity; from childhood, he served as a student.
Upon reaching the age of twenty, he was suddenly stricken by a malignant disease that appeared incurable.
With a guilty heart seeking to amend his conduct, what power could he possibly exert?
During the Kaiyuan era, he visited Vinaya Master Xiguang to request the medical prescriptions of Jīvaka and to observe the etiquette due to a disciple.
The Master showed him the teachings for the elimination of karma, which are twofold: first, repentance through principle (li-chan);
second, repentance through ritual action (shi-chan). These two were bestowed by the Sages; their practice will inevitably bear fruit.
Thereupon, before the image of Bodhi, he maintained an unbending resolve and offered his finger—a limb difficult to sacrifice.
At that moment, a wondrous light like the moon shone radiantly within the azure palace; such extreme suffering can move the divine spirits, and such ultimate refinement can shake heaven and earth.
Ah, how difficult it is for a person to achieve such a task!
In the fourth year of the Tiānbǎo era, he received full ordination and first donned the black robes.
In the eighth year, his extraordinary conduct was recognized, and his name was registered at the monastery.
In his later years, his diligent devotion became even more evident.

He frequently established a *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* ritual site for a period of ninety days, entering into the contemplative samādhi of the Buddha through the recitation of the prose sections; thus, he brought about the causes for the Buddha’s manifestation before him.
He said to his disciples:
"Now, how can the clouds obscure the sun? How can the wind move through space without moving it? If one truly understands that all is illusory, who is not of the nature [of reality]?"
He then constructed a dwelling on the east of Laolao Mountain, occupying a stone ruin at its center, where he reached a path frequented by immortals.
Fierce beasts became tame beside his meditation couch, and auspicious clouds lowered themselves over his Dharma hall.
In the middle of the night, a mountain deity manifested its form and said to Wù:
"I am Cao Shì'ān, the former Marquis of Xīnchéng during the Sui dynasty. In life I was a ranked noble; in death, I preside over the Southern Ridge."
"Now that you, Master, have arrived, I wish to offer this place forever for your walking meditation.
Having spoken, he vanished and was no longer seen.

Thus, Li Hua, Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel, and Cui Yi, Palace Attendant Censor, together visited Huizhu to inquire about the relative merits of the holy teachings of Confucius and Laozi, requesting him to provide a critical appraisal.
He replied:

"The scriptures of the Lokāyata are all phenomena external to the mind; those who savor them labor in vain without attaining realization, much like one who seeks flowers from withered marshes or reflects the moon in a dried-up pond. Compared to the teachings of Śākya, how could they be far removed?"
As they exchanged such words back and forth, [Hui]hua and [Dao]yi responded like a flowing stream.
With their hands folded in submission, they had no means to resist.
Who would dare to encroach upon the borders of the Śākya gate that he thus defended?
Hua was a preeminent literary figure of his generation, whose fame rivaled that of Xiao Yingshi; yet his prose and rhetoric surpassed his.
As for a scholar such as this, who could possibly challenge him?

Whenever there were unruly elements who doubted the scriptures or challenged the Dharma, they would inevitably realize that one must draw analogies from what is near, such as one's own body, and from external objects; when answered according to the principle, there was not one who did not hang their head and droop their wings in defeat.
In the spring of the tenth year, the Xinmao year, he fell ill while in bed; sitting in the full lotus posture, he passed away.
He reached the age of sixty-three and had twenty-six years of Dharma seniority (*dharmavarṣa*).
On the day of his cremation, more than five hundred *śarīra* relics were obtained; like clusters of pearls, they were brilliant and clearly visible to the eye.
His disciples, including Zhan-yi and Yuan-yi, presided over the construction and enshrined his remains in a stupa.
Biography of Chan Master Shi Yuanchong of Mount Zhongshan in Jinling, Tang Dynasty. Chan Master Shi Yuanchong’s secular surname was Wang; he was a native of Linyi in Langya.
He was a descendant of Wang Zhihui, the Prince of Shixing and Minister of State under the Jin dynasty; since the fall of the Southern Dynasties, his lineage had lived in Ju’ong.
From his ancestors back, they had been either sages or wise men.
From childhood, Chong was orphaned yet possessed a rare brilliance, as prominent and imposing as a mountain peak rising from the earth.
His mind was like a lotus flower, and his form was as pure as jade; untainted by the dust and winds of the world, he established his resolve in a state of tranquility and simplicity.

At the age of fifteen, he honored the Way and left his home; carrying his book-case, he entered a celestial cavern, where he feasted on the mists and lay among the clouds. Taking Tao Hongjing and Xu Xun as his models, he refined his study of wondrous verses, attaining solitary realization of their subtle and hidden meanings.

Fearing that the ultimate truth had not yet been fully integrated and that liberation was still obstructed, he turned his heart toward the Buddhist scriptures and extensively expounded the Buddha-vehicle; thus, while the three teachings proceeded side by side, his mind reached beyond the mundane world.
Consequently, his reputation resounded throughout Wu and Yue, and both the monastic and lay communities marveled at him.

When Qi Pingyang Gong, the Imperial Commissioner and Governor of Runzhou, heard of his virtuous conduct, he waited for him with great anticipation for a long time; it so happened that an imperial decree was issued to recruit practitioners of the Way, and [the Master] was selected as the foremost candidate.

At the end of the Kaiyuan era, he followed Master Huai’an of Waguan Temple to inquire about and receive the essentials of the mind. Day and night he was untiring, never forgetting to request further instruction.
Master Huai’an then discerned his spiritual potential, recognizing that he was like a swift horse from a thousand *li* away, and consequently transmitted the profound Dharma to him.
The Lingtai Hall was lofty and transparent, capable of housing the hundred deities; his mind was like a mirror suspended on high, where no worldly dust remained hidden.
Subsequently, as his reputation spread far and wide and he became known for the esteem of all, the virtuous monks of Jinling requested that he transfer his residence to Qixia Temple.

As more than a decade passed, he devoted himself diligently to the affairs of the Way; the constant principles of human relations were well-ordered, and the assembly of his time looked up to him with admiration.

At the beginning of the Zhide era, he withdrew from all worldly affairs and, staff in hand, departed from the commandery. He traveled to the capital, where he attended upon various eminent teachers, settled his mind in secluded environments, and rarely associated with the common world.

He then entered Zhongnan Mountain, passed through Uḍḍiyāna (Weizang), reached Bailu, and ascended to Lan-tian; there, at Wangchuan, he obtained the private estate of the Right Vice-Minister, Lord Wang Wei.
Pines grow upon the rocks, and water flows beneath the pines; the Prince burns incense in his quiet chamber and meets with Chong, their spiritual communion severed by circumstance.
At that time, heaven and earth were not yet at peace, and jackals and wolves wrought havoc; the worthies of the court and the treasures of the state were either in exile or wandering in distress.

The Attendant-in-Ordinary Xiao Xin and the Right Vice-Directors and other gentlemen are all men of profound learning and eminent talent who revere Confucianism and honor the Way. Having happened upon this single gathering, they engaged in debate for many days, probing the profound and seeking out the hidden, while their aspirations and mutual esteem were fully shared.
The King sighed with admiration, saying:
"The Buddha-Dharma possesses true people; it is not fitting to disparage it lightly!

When [Hui]yan returned to the region of the Yellow and Luo Rivers, he ascended Mount Song and Mount Shao, cherishing the essential tenets of Bodhidharma and attaining the ultimate convergence of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. His reputation gradually grew high, and the gentry looked up to him with envy and reverence.
The renowned and virtuous masters of the capital all invited him to serve as abbot, but his will was set upon non-action; he remained aloof and indifferent to their offers.

Thereupon, he wandered through the world, following the traces of the Way, and after investigating sacred sites, he traveled east to Wu, Yue, Tiantai, and Siming, where he purified his mind and cultivated his fundamental nature.

Several years later, he looked back longingly toward Mount Zhong and his former dwelling where he had once flown with his monk’s staff; as he examined his cloud-like chambers, both monastics and laypeople rejoiced, and the mountain shone with renewed splendor.

In the fifth year of the Dali era, the Prefectural Governor, Lord Fan of Nanyang, who was deeply devoted to meditative stillness, went on an inspection tour of his subordinate counties. Encountering the Master, he bowed his head in accordance with the prevailing wind and inquired about the essentials of the Way, thereafter treating him with even greater reverence as a teacher.

At that time, both the clergy and the laity considered this monastery particularly sacred and eminent, attracting many visitors who came to stroll and rest; thus, they felt it was necessary to select a person of renowned virtue to serve as its supervisor and guardian.
After collective deliberation, they concluded that no one could surpass the Dhyāna Master.

Chong repeatedly took his leave with earnest and sincere entreaties, and the assembly likewise did so three times over. Having no choice in the matter, he complied and mediated between them for a total of twenty years.

Relying on wealth from the four quarters and through the power of spiritual transformation, the rafters and beams rose like clouds and the vermilion and lacquer were renewed daily; thus it was that while abiding in non-action, there was nothing he did not accomplish.
Having accomplished his work, he withdrew from the world to dwell in meditative seclusion atop a high peak; the disciples who followed him before and after were beyond counting.
In the twelfth year of the Dali era, he manifested illness and announced his return to the ultimate, refusing further medical treatment.
On the second day of the eighth month, he passed away at his mountain hermitage at the age of sixty-five.

At the time of his death, he instructed his disciples not to erect a tomb or plant trees over him. His disciples, including Ruiquan and Chengtian, followed the Master’s final teaching and interred him on the eighth day of that same month on the southern slope of Mount She. They constructed a cave dwelling against the rock face, piling unpolished and unshaped stones; thus they honored his last testament.
Chongsheng stood six chi tall; his appearance was dignified and solemn, inspiring awe upon being beheld and reverence upon being approached.

His intentions were profound and his temperament forgiving; his mind was harmonious and his conduct noble. Possessing the natural majesty of a dragon or elephant, he was born with such exceptional brilliance.
His lifespan was not long; how lamentable!
His disciples jointly erected a magnificent monument to record his transformative deeds, planting it at the entrance of the temple.
Biography of Shi Lishè of Dà'ān Guó Temple in Jīngzhào, Táng Dynasty. Shi Lishè was originally a man from the Western Regions, belonging to the lineage of the Great Brahmā Brahmins.
From his youth, he was strong-willed and possessed an intelligence that surpassed his peers; among his kinsmen, he was esteemed for his profound understanding of the Dharma.

Desiring to travel to Jambudvīpa, he formed a party to journey eastward. Upon reaching Jinsuo Ridge, he encountered the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang; meeting him by chance as the Master was traveling along, he paid his respects and requested ordination from Xuanzang.

Subsequently, the various scriptures and treatises have been used to pierce through the superficial to penetrate the profound; they stand apart from worldly dust and return to the True Path—it is not difficult for Xuanzang to shift and transform them!
The worthy and sages of Xuanzang’s school flocked together like spokes converging at the hub, ranking as juniors to the likes of Daoguang and Huibao.
As for their character, they were as free and expansive as those who sit upon high silk seats.
The Emperor Zhongzong held him in the highest esteem, and the ministers and officials of the court associated with him out of a sense of shared righteousness.

During the Kaiyuan era, he lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at An Guo Temple; the fourfold assembly flocked to the hall, and by the time they arrived late, there was not even enough space for one to sit cross-legged.
Almsgiving was flourishing and widespread, moving people's hearts with its benefits.

There was a man from Yingyang named Wei Ding, who passed the imperial examinations during the Chuigong era; he was appointed as a School Instructor for the Hedong Prefecture, and subsequently promoted to Court Appraiser of the Ministry of Justice and School Curator of the Imperial Library.
Seeing that the lecture halls were overflowing with piles of silk and cloth, he requested to be granted grain from these stores, yet remained unsatisfied with what he obtained.

He submitted a memorial requesting that the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism be pitted against one another to determine their relative merits, asserting that Buddhism and Daoism were parasites on the administration and should be eliminated.

The Emperor Xuanzong issued an edict that each of the Three Teachings should select one hundred followers, who were all assembled in the inner palace. Wei Jing first ascended the high seat and defeated Ye Jingneng and the Buddhist monk Siming; in every case, they were rendered speechless.

Sheshen ascended the seat in succession, resolving doubts and unraveling entanglements; he was more than a match for his opponent, exchanging hundreds and thousands of words with Wei. As their arguments became as tangled as interlacing threads, Sheshen countered them one after another, disentangling the matted skeins until they returned to a state of clarity and rectitude.
Sheshong asked Wei, saying, "You have already taken your seat; can you not be considered the host?
I do not know what the host's surname is."
Ding replied,
"My surname is Wei.
Zhao She took the character "Wei" as his rhyme and began to chant in a long, drawn-out melody.
The verse says:
"My Buddha-dharma is unconditioned; why does it now become conditioned this morning?
It has been but three years since the beginning of the era; I do not know what era this could possibly be."
As Shezhi chanted these verses, the officials were struck with awe.
The Emperor, indeed recalling the matter of He Wei, turned pale with a stern expression and said:
"Ding is but a member of the commoner class, yet he dares to treat with such contempt my teachings of the Mysterious Origin (Xuan Yuan) and to insult the Buddhist clergy."
Ding descended from the hall, prostrated himself to await punishment, and knelt, saying:
"I am not among the ranks of commoners.
Shi Zhe valued his sharp tongue for its ability to resolve matters of negligence and madness, and thus memorialized the Emperor:
"Jing is a person from beyond the passes; he is not of the same lineage as Xuanzhen.
By imperial decree, he was demoted to the rank of commoner in Xiangzhou.
He was granted money and silk to assist in the construction of Mingjiao Monastery, and the title "Mingjiao" was added to his name.
The second reign was doubly prosperous, and this was due to the efforts of Shiye.
Consequently, he composed the *Lifachang lun* (Treatise on Establishing the Dharma Banner) in one fascicle.
Among the high officials, some remarked:
"Shen Gong is the fatal ailment of Attendant Wei.
Shen said, "As for this undertaking, the arrow is already upon the bowstring; it cannot but be released."
From this time on, there was no one in the capital who did not change their perspective; among those who engaged in discourse and lecturing, Heshang Baosheng was considered the foremost.
In his later years, he suffered demotion and exile to Handong, but soon thereafter he was granted amnesty and relocated to Longxing Temple in Nanyang.
At that time, National Teacher Huizhong recognized that Chongshè was renowned for his virtue;

he casually opened the gate to receive him and said, "I am but a humble monk in patched robes who has been brought here by my disciples through their morning duties. Just now, observing you, Master, I see that you possess an air of nobility; you are fit to be one of high attainment and a national virtue, and should not be treated like me."
He then opened the chest and brought forth the garments and belongings, ordering Master Zhong to drag them out.

Because of this, the people of Xiang and Deng were all astonished by such a prescient prediction; furthermore, Master Zhong’s reputation for the Way flourished, largely due to the high standing of Master She.
In the second year of the Shangyuan era, an imperial edict summoned Master Zhong to enter the palace for offerings.
During the reign of Emperor Suzong, he entered the palace to attend upon the Retired Emperor (Taishanghuang); the Emperor then introduced Zhong to the Retired Emperor, saying:
"How does this man compare to Lishi?"
Thus we know that Zhe was a man of superior talent and extensive accomplishments, held in high esteem by the Emperor, and was prolific in his writings.
During the Dali era, the śramaṇa Yuanzhao of Ximing Monastery compiled the *Biography of Zhe* in ten fascicles, which sufficiently attests to the abundance of his words and deeds.

Biography of Shen’ung of Dali Temple on Mount Jiao in Yuezhou during the Tang Dynasty Shen’ung, whose courtesy name was Daogong and whose secular surname was Cai, was a fifteenth-generation descendant of Cai Mo, the Grand Marshal of the Eastern Jin dynasty and the patriarch who first crossed the Yangtze River.
Because his official residence was in Jiyang, Daoyong was born in that district.
When his mother, Lady Xuan, first became pregnant, she frequently experienced extraordinary portents.
Even while in her swaddling clothes, whenever she heard the sound of chanting scriptures, she would invariably display an expression of rapt concentration and attentive listening.
In his childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent and perceptive.
At the age of twelve, he took leave of his parents to study the Way, seeking instruction from Master Jun of Fahua Temple.
Whenever he read the two canons of Confucius and Śākyamuni, he could recite them after a single reading.
Among his peers, there were few who did not admire him with longing.
In the twenty-sixth year of the Kaiyuan era, by imperial decree, he was ordained and registered at Xiangyan Temple in Zhuji.
He followed Master Xuanyan of Fayhua Temple as his teacher and attained mastery of the *Sifenlü chao* (Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya).
Yan recognized his ambition and spirit, and said to others:
"In a few years, this youth will surely become a compass for scholars.
You must all exert yourselves!"

Yan had recently produced his *Fupian lüji* (Record of the Auxiliary Chapters on the Vinaya); Yong extracted its essence and mastered its various methods, such that among the scholars of this school, few were able to keep pace with him or follow in his tracks.

His nature was not narrow or confined; furthermore, he studied the Tiantai *Zhi guan* (Stilling and Contemplation), the Chan gate, the *Fahua xuanshu* (Mysterious Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), the *Fanwang jing* (Brahmajāla Sūtra), and other works under Master Xuanglang of Zuoxi. He thoroughly unlocked the secret keys regarding the meanings of the four teachings and three contemplations. Through contemplating his own nature, he realized emptiness. By the time he had completed five summer retreats, he had indeed mastered the detailed exposition [of these doctrines], and scholars from the regions of Wu and Kuaiji followed him.

During the Tiānbǎo era, Gùomìzhī of his native district requested that he reside in the western ward of Fǎlè Monastery; there, he expanded the Buddhist quarters so that its multi-storied pavilions brushed the clouds and reflected half the image of the clear river, with its corridors and halls fully completed.

Later, he traveled to Chang’an to seek instruction and resided at An-guo Temple. High officials, drawn by his dignified bearing, came to him in such numbers that their carriages formed a continuous stream.

Just as he was about to extensively propagate the teachings of Chan and the Vinaya, he was suddenly confronted by the military chaos of An Lushan. He returned east to the Jianghu region, passing through Xiangyang, where Yu Guangxian, the Imperial Censor-in-Chief stationed there to govern Jingnan, invited him to stay for several months.
At that time, Du Shao, the Palace Attendant, and Yuan Xian, the Secretariat Drafter, revered him all the more for his loftiness and both received the essentials of his mind.
Wei Zichun, the Court Historian—a subject of the Tang dynasty who was both resolute in spirit and extensive in learning—engaged in debate with him.
When Zichun’s horn was broken, the entire assembly was struck with awe and admiration.
Secretary Yuan sighed and said,
"The Acharya may truly be called a mani-jewel beyond the mundane world, a lion among debaters!"
At that time, people considered him a man of eloquent speech.

He soon returned to his hometown at Fahua Temple, where he engaged in a poetic exchange with Dianzhong Shiyushi Huangfu Zeng, Dalilingshi Zhang He, Jinwuwai Changshi Yan Wei, Bingcao Lü Wei, Zhujichang Qiu Dan, and Xiaoshu Chen Yunchu. Lu Shishi composed a preface for these works, so that their friendship might continue the tradition of Zhi Dun and Xu Xun, becoming a celebrated local legend.
In addition to his cultivation of mindfulness, Yong occasionally composed literary verses; these comprise a ten-volume collection for which Huangfu Zeng wrote a preface.

From the Zhide era through the middle of the Dali era, he was repeatedly invited to ascend the ordination platform to confer the precepts. From Danyang to Jinhua, all the śrāmaṇeras during that interval appointed him as their upādhyāya (preceptor).
Furthermore, the southern road of Xian County leads to Wuzhou, yet for over a hundred li along the way there were no monasteries (gā-lan), leaving traveling monks with no place to rest.
Yong wished to spread the bridge of the Dharma to provide lodging for travelers, and thus [determined] that Jiaoshan would be suitable as a Buddhist sanctuary (fan-chang).

Chen Shaolin and others from the local district, who held the rank of *qíduowèi*, led a group of faithful believers to establish a pure monastery (*jìngchà*); it was only after twelve years that the construction was completed.

When Xu Hao, the former Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel, was sent to assist in the administration of Mingzhou, he noted that the site was a significant settlement for the state and requested that the Intendant Huángfù Wēn petition the throne to grant it an official name, which was subsequently bestowed as "Dàlì" (Great Calendar).

Previously, the Daoist Wu Yun of the Central Peak had composed several treatises of heterodox argumentation to denigrate and destroy the Buddhist teachings, thereby deluding those who were ignorant and muddled.

Chen Shaoyou, the Regional Inspector of this province, requested that Huaiyong resolve the question of which of the two teachings—Buddhism or Daoism—is the ultimate Way. Thereupon, [Huaiyong] followed the World-Honored One’s subduing of heterodox views and revived the "Essay on Destroying Mara" by Bao Lin; thus, he took up the defensive position of the citadel to use orthodoxy to restrain the mad.
As soon as the banners and drums arrived, Wu Yun’s failure was overturned.

He subsequently composed the three-fascicle *Treatise on Destroying Perversity and Overturning Delusion*; that the Buddha-dharma flourished once more in the East was indeed due to the power of Huiyong.
Later, he traveled to Mount Tiantai and compiled two volumes of a geographical gazetteer, both of which are appended to his *Xinlun* (New Treatise).

His appearance was majestic and dignified, and his character was brilliant and eminent; successive provincial inspectors all invited him to a private seat and requested that he serve as the Head of the Monastic Community (*Sengtong*), treating him with the most respectful salutations due to a high-ranking official.

On the fourteenth day of the eleventh month in the fourth year of the Zhenyuan era, the year of Wuchen (788 CE), he fell ill; having delivered his final instructions to his disciples, he sat upright in the lotus posture and passed away in the Dali Dharma Hall.
On the fourteenth day of the twelfth month, his sacred remains were enshrined on the northern plain of the monastery, in accordance with monastic regulations.
His secular age was seventy-nine, and his years of ordination were fifty.
In the eleventh month of the winter of the following year, the pagoda was finally constructed.

Lu Huai, a Proofreader at the Secretariat, composed its inscription. His foremost disciples—Zhi’ang, Lingche, Jinming, Huizhao, and others—all displayed their keen talents, transmitting both Chan and Vinaya teachings in tandem.
In the eleventh year [of the Kaiyuan era], Qiu Shangqing, an Assistant Director of the Ministry of Revenue, erected a stele to record his virtues.
Biography of Weiyen of Yaoshan in Langzhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Weiyen’s secular surname was Han; he was a native of Jiang County.
From childhood, he was spirited and joyous, possessing a quick intelligence that surpassed his peers.
At the age of seventeen, he moved to Nankang to serve under Chan Master Huizhao of West Mountain in Chaoyang.
In the eighth year of the Dali era, he received full ordination at Hengye Monastery from Vinaya Master Xicao, who then said to him:
"A great man should transcend all dharmas to achieve self-purification; how could he deign to concern himself with such trivial matters as the ritual of cleansing with a cloth?
He then went to visit Master Shitou, where he secretly realized the mind-dharma and resided at Yaoshan.
One night, under the bright moon, he ascended that steep and lofty peak and let out a great laugh; the sound echoed for about ninety li to the east of Liyang.

That night, everyone in Liyang heard the sound and all said it came from their neighbor to the east. The following morning, they went from house to house inquiring and passed the word along until they reached Yaoshan.
His disciples said, "Was it the Master laughing loudly on the mountain top last night?"
From that time on, his reputation spread, and he was celebrated far and wide.
During the Yuanhe era, Li Ao served as the Vice Director of the Examination Board (Kao-gong Yuan-wai-lang) and was on very good terms with Li Jingjian.

When Li Jin removed him from his post as Counselor for Remonstrance, he recommended Xie Ao to replace him; when Jin incurred reprimand, Ao was consequently implicated and sent out as the Prefect of Langzhou.
While there, Ao visited Huian in his leisure time and subsequently attained awakening.
Furthermore, when Yan first saw Ao, he held his scripture volume and did not look back.
The attendant said, "The Governor is here.
Ao, being of a narrow and impetuous temperament, then spoke out, saying:
"Meeting you in person does not match what I have heard of your reputation.
Yan then called out, and Ao responded with a single "Yes," saying,
"Why does the Governor value my ears while disparaging my eyes?"
Hao folded his hands in gratitude and asked,
"What is called the Way?
Yanyue pointed to the sky and then to the water pitcher, saying:
"Clouds are in the blue sky; water is in the pitcher.
At that moment, Yang Ao’s dark room was suddenly illuminated and the ice of his doubts instantly melted. He then composed a verse: "My body has been refined until it resembles the form of a crane;
Beneath a thousand pine trees lie two cases of scripture. I have long since abandoned the world and its concerns; In this life, I shall surely attain the Way."
"I have come to question you; there is nothing more to say: the clouds are in the blue sky, and the water is in the jar.
Furthermore, he spoke in verse: "I have chosen a secluded dwelling that accords with my rustic sentiments; throughout the year, there is neither seeing off nor welcoming."
"Sometimes he ascends directly to the peak of a solitary crag, / Unveiling the clouds beneath the moon and letting out a laugh.

Initially, Bai Ao was a literary associate of Han Yu, Liu Zongyuan, and Liu Yuxi; together they recounted ancient sayings and modeled themselves after the *Six Classics*, composing prose that rejected the frivolous and ornate in favor of logical coherence. When speaking of those who composed such prose, people referred to Han, Liu, and Liu.
The Director of the Ministry of Personnel once remarked:

"Since the passing of Confucius, the various masters have promoted divergent doctrines; thus, Xunzi and Mencius restored the true path, causing the followers of Yang Zhu and Mo Di to be completely washed away and cast aside."
It was likely during the eras of the Zhou and Sui dynasties that the Way of the King did not flourish; thus, the composition of Wen Zhongzi must have occurred amidst the various schools of thought.

With the rise of the Tang, once Fang Xuanling and Wei Zheng had passed away, the people lost their way and became preoccupied with superficial elegance, eventually leading to the calamities of Empress Wu and the ravages of An Lushan.

I have pledged with you, my fellow students, to together restore the Way of Yao and Shun; we must not abandon pure discourse to neglect Confucianism, nor indulge in Buddhist scriptures to bring disorder to the Middle Kingdom.

Should anyone harbor heterodox thoughts and turn toward the followers of Śākyamuni, or should they violate this oath, may they not enjoy human rank nor live out their natural span of years under Heaven.
May the enlightened spirits of the former sages bind them in judgment and strike them down!
Before long, Lü Ao encountered Zhixian by chance and suddenly attained a thorough understanding of his original mind.
He subsequently served as the Minister of the Ministry of Revenue, the Regional Inspector of Xiangzhou, and was appointed as the Commander-in-Chief of the Shan-nan East Circuit.

He further encountered the Chan elder Ziyu, who further clarified his understanding of the Way’s essence; he then composed the *Fu xing shu* (Treatise on the Restoration of Nature) in two parts, upper and lower.

In general, it states that one's original nature is inherently luminous, yet it is defiled by the six passions; having become lost and failing to return, one must now restore it, which is like the hexagram Fu (Return), where the thunder emerges from beneath the earth, revealing the heart of Heaven and Earth!
This is precisely the inner teaching’s return to the origin and restoration of the source.

Its texts are manifest yet hidden, concealed yet revealed; its writings—such as the *Xiang*, *Xi*, and *Zhongyong*—remain hidden without invoking Buddhist doctrine, yet their principles follow truth and abandon delusion, being clearly revealed as the manifestation of one’s own mind.
I did not set forth my views in words, but merely harbored the intention to grant them.
When Han Yu and Liu Zongyan read this, they sighed and said:
"Our Way has withered and declined; we shall flee!"

Huyan Yan refined those who were difficult to transform through his rigorous training; his merit in protecting the Dharma was great. To turn the minds of such disciples was as easy as moving mountains or lifting a cauldron.
Furthermore, when the Minister of State Cui Qun and the Palace Attendant Wen Zao successively sought instruction from him, Yan was able to awaken them to the intent of the Way.
In the second year of the Taika era, as he was about to pass away, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"The Dharma Hall is about to collapse.
No one understood his meaning, so they took long timbers and propped it up with beams. He solemnly clapped his hands and laughed loudly, saying: [...the rest of the passage continues...]
"You have not yet understood my meaning.
With palms joined, he passed into stillness; it is said that his age was seventy.
The commentary states:

I have once perused the two chapters of Li Wen-gong’s *Restoration of the Nature*, which clarify Buddhist principles without citing Buddhist scriptures; rather, they provide corroboration and evidence by drawing solely from the *Book of Changes* and the *Book of Rites*.
One may say that he was outwardly compliant while inwardly firm and contrary; thus it is said, "Having grasped the image, one forgets the words.
That which the Sūtra describes as "the speech of governing the world all becoming the True Dharma" is exemplified in Master Li.
Master Yan let out a single laugh, the sound of which reached distant lands; though he did not trouble Maudgalyāyana to seek him out from afar, the *Yili* (Examples of the Changes) has it:
"A long sigh on the high steps will surely fill the distant ravines. The resonance of the Way is thus, yet one does not know how it comes to be so!
Biography of Chonghui of Changxin Temple in the Capital of the Tang Dynasty. Shramana Chonghui, surnamed Zhang, was a native of Hangzhou.
In his youth, his capacity and disposition were already evident; like a bird of prey that cannot be caged, his resolve to transcend the mundane world was intense.

He went to pay homage to National Teacher Guoyi of Mount Jing as his disciple; although he applied himself diligently to Chan meditation, he mostly took the teachings of the Three Mysteries as his constant practice.
Initially, he built a thatched hut at the summit of Qianqing Peak in Changhua, where he devoted himself to reciting the *Buddhōṣṇīṣa Dhāraṇī* for several years.
He later went to Dongshan on Yaoguan Xiaoshi, where he erected a small, pointed-roofed grass hut and remained there for many years.
He further vowed to seclude himself at Yunsi Temple in Qianluo; shortly thereafter, a deity appeared to Huì and said:
"The Master’s recitation of the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-śikhara-sūtra* lacks the *svāhā* at its conclusion, causing the secret mantra to be incomplete."
" Svāhā" means "accomplishment.
Now, in this capital, the Buddha-dharma is being trampled upon by non-Buddhist teachings; its peril is like that of hanging tassels, awaiting only your masterful salvation!
Hui hurried his journey westward, and his heart grew weary; for the sake of choosing a tree to rest upon, he hung up his staff at Changxin Temple, which was at the beginning of the Dali era.

On the twenty-third day of the ninth month of the third year, the year Wushen (708 CE), the Daoist priest Shi Hua of the Taicing Palace submitted a memorial, requesting that he engage with the eminent masters of the Buddhist school of the present age in a contest of the relative merits of the Buddha’s Way and the Daoist Law.
During the reign of Emperor Daizong, the imperial court held the Buddhist school in high esteem; heterodox practitioners were indignant at this partiality and thus made this request.
Consequently, they erected a ladder of blades before the altar of Dongming Guan, yet Shi Hua climbed upon it as if it were an ordinary flight of stairs.
At that time, the monastic community looked at one another and pushed back, with none daring to step forward.

When Huì heard of this, he sought an audience with the Commander-in-Chief Yu Chaoen. Yu submitted a petition requesting that a ladder be erected against the courtyard trees of Zhangxin Temple, upon which sharp blades were laid out horizontally like frost and snow, reaching a height of one hundred feet.
The stairs at Dongming were extremely steep.
At that time, high officials of the court and residents of the marketplace crowded together, jostling shoulder to shoulder and foot to foot, to witness this feat.
Then, Hui climbed the lower steps barefoot; it was as if he were walking upon level ground, showing no sign of difficulty whatsoever.

Furthermore, they tread upon blazing fires and reach into boiling oil with their hands; they still eat iron leaves, which are called *biāndòu*, or chew iron nails and wire, making sounds like those of brittle taffy.
Shi Hua was struck with fear and shame; he covered his face with his sleeves and withdrew.
At that moment, the assembly snapped their fingers in admiration, the sound like the roar of thunder.
The Emperor dispatched the eunuch Gong Tingyu to offer repeated words of consolation and bestowed upon him a set of purple square-cut robes.
By imperial decree, he was appointed as Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial and titled the "State-Protecting Tripitaka Master"; an edict was issued to move him to reside at An Guo Temple.
From that time forth, his reputation spread far and wide, and his moral prestige stood loftily high.
When Emperor Daizong heard that this was a direct disciple of National Teacher Guoyi, he treated him with even greater reverence.
He is the one known in the world as Chan Master Jiangmo of Jingshan.
The commentary says:
Some may ask, "Was Master Hui a phantom monk?
Tong replied:

"Generally, the manifestation of the five sensory objects is called 'supernatural power' (abhijñā). However, if one with a defiled mind transforms the phenomena of the five sensory objects, it is an illusion (māyā).

Since the Venerable Master maintains the three mysteries, yoga, and the dhāraṇīs for protecting the Dharma, he employs them to assist his right concentration; thus, when he treads upon blades and walks through flames, what cause for alarm is there?"
"What illusion could there possibly be?
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* contains various accounts of the three types of supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).

The Biography of the Monk Wuming of Tongde Temple in Luoyang, Tang Dynasty. The monk Wuming, whose secular surname was Gao, was a native of Bohai. He resided at Tongde Temple in Luoyang during the Tang Dynasty. His biography is as follows: [text continues]
The Master’s official career has now brought him to the Western Capital, where he is thus a man of Luoyang.

Even at such a tender age, his conduct is extraordinary; his mouth never tastes pungent flavors or blood, and by nature he does not associate with clamor and bustle. He stands far removed from the mundane world, and thus it is difficult to detain him.
At the age of twenty-eight, like a lean wild goose emerging from its cage, he went to a teacher to study, following him at Le-tong Temple.
Once he had mastered the Vinaya-piṭaka, he understood even a single character without doubt;
yet, hearing of the existence of the Chan school, he traveled a thousand li to seek a definitive resolution.
Adjusting his collar and straightening his robe, he opened the lock and found the path; his prose was as vigorous as soaring flight, and his thoughts flowed like a gushing spring.
Consequently, he followed his master on a journey to visit the sites associated with the patriarchs, where he attained the transmission of the mind-seal from the Master.
Before his passing, he addressed his disciples, saying:
"In the transmission of my Dharma, there is no name.
Consequently, he was styled Wuming (The Nameless).

From this point on, he set his mind upon traveling the four quarters and journeyed throughout the Five Sacred Peaks. At Luofu, Mount Lu, Shuangfeng, Wangong, Luzhiling, Niutou, Shanxi, Ruoye, Tiantai, and Siming, there was nowhere he did not inquire about. His character was lofty and far-reaching, and his spiritual resolve was bright and transparent; those of broad learning would submit at the mere sight of him, while those with narrow views were inevitably refuted whenever they spoke.

At that time, Emperor Dezong was just beginning to have Xianyu Shuming and Linghu Hu examine and purge the ranks of monks and nuns; the famous figures named Youbiao and Zhijian were both suspended from their duties.
Shortly thereafter, Xianyu Shuming, Linghu Hu, and others were exiled to Nanhai as commoners.
In the sixth year of the Zhenyuan era, he traveled to Mount Wutai, where he dwelt without a fixed abode.

On the twelfth day of the twelfth month in the ninth year, at Foguang Temple, after having finished his meal, he sat upright and passed away. He was seventy-two years of age and forty-three years since his ordination.
In the eleventh year, his body was cremated, and one *sheng* of *śarīra* relics were obtained.
Li Baozhen, the Regional Inspector of Zhe and Lu, erected a stupa at Foguang Temple; this was the gengwu year, the sixth year of the Zhenguan era.
Some say: "He is known for having authored a commentary on the *Amitābha Sūtra*.

This is the biography of Shi Zhichang of Gui宗 Temple on Mount Lu during the Tang Dynasty. Shi Zhichang was a man of exceptional character who rose above his peers; his conduct was pure and frugal. Having traveled extensively to consult various masters, he followed Nanquan as a disciple and joined him at the gate of Dayi (Mazu), thereby coming to realize the Way of Jiangxi.
During the Yuanhe era, he took up residence at the Jinguan Cloister of Mount Lu.
His disciples responded like echoes, and his Dharma spread like the wind.
Before long, Bai Juyi was demoted to the post of Sima in Jiangzhou and held him in the highest esteem.
Subsequently, the Vice Minister Li Bo went into seclusion at Mount Song and Mount Shao in the sixth year of the Yuanhe era; he was summoned to office as a Court Historian.
However, Du Yuanying opposed him, and he was subsequently dispatched as the Regional Inspector of Qianzhou.
Before a full year had passed since his appointment to Nankang, he was transferred to the post of Regional Inspector of Jiangzhou.
Bo was widely learned and possessed extensive knowledge; there were no books among the hundred schools of thought that he did not master, earning him the nickname "Li the Ten-Thousand-Scrolls."

Upon arriving at the commandery, he was delighted to meet Bai Juyi. They spoke of the preeminence of the mountains and waters of Xunyang and Mount Lu, as well as the virtuous and sagely recluses found there.
While discussing the remains of Huiyuan, they went on to describe how Master Guizong was skilled in expounding the essentials of Chan.
Li remarked, "Before long, the golden tablets of the imperial court will surely include the name of that 'vegetarian monk.'"
He replied, "If that is so,
then I do not yet know if you are a master who eats only vegetables!
Bai strongly urged him to visit the two groves, his intention being simply to see Chang.
Upon arriving at Guizong, Li asked, "In the teachings it is said that 'Mount Sumeru contains a mustard seed, and a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru. How can a mustard seed contain Mount Sumeru?"
Chang asked, "People say that you, Doctor, have read ten thousand scrolls of books;
is this indeed true? Li replied:
"I am unworthy of this empty reputation," he often said.
"From the soles of my feet to the crown of my head, there is only a body of a few feet; where, then, shall ten thousand scrolls of books be placed?"
Li bowed his head and remained silent, reflecting further on the words of praise.
Subsequently, there was the monk Shenjian of Donglin Monastery, who lectured on various sutras and treatises; when asked about "Bodhi before one's eyes," Chang would briefly bring it up.
The divine manifestation lacked a physical form, appearing instead as a state of contention that constantly displayed an evil realm.
At that time, Li Fanqun was widely renowned for his legal acumen.

He possessed extraordinary features, including eyes with double pupils (*chóngtóng*). Consequently, he would apply medicinal incense to his hands and constantly rub them; before long, the corners of both eyes turned red, and he became known as "Red-Eyed Guizong."
The commentary states:
The principles of the Buddha are profound and subtle; that which summarizes them in a single word is the discourse of mystical understanding.
That it accords with those of sharp faculties is proof of the efficacy of a marvelous medicine that swiftly alleviates illness.
Biography of Shi Chunan of Mount Qianqing in Hangzhou, Tang Dynasty, Transmitted by Chunan of Mount Qianqing in Hangzhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Chunan was a native of Min; his secular surname was Zhang.
Already at the age of childhood, he knelt in solemn silence before his parents and declared his resolve to leave the household life.
He then sought out Master Tandai of Kaiyuan Temple to receive instruction.
When he was taught the scriptures and the Dharma, whatever his eyes beheld, he would immediately recite it from memory.
In attending to him with handkerchiefs and water for washing, and in sweeping and responding to instructions, he was quite capable of being diligent and respectful.
Upon reaching the age of twenty, he shaved his hair.
He traveled to Mount Wutai to receive full ordination, studied the Vinaya of the Xiangbu school at Zhaojun,
and went to the Capital to study the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*.
Having briefly mastered the essential tenets of one sutra after another, he realized that those of sudden capacity would not willingly be bound by the gradual teachings.
He subsequently went to Mount Furong, yet his fundamental spiritual nature had not yet been awakened.
He visited Master Huangbo of Mount Huangbo; although their dialogues were numerous, he suddenly attained complete realization of the master’s pedagogical intent.
Shortly thereafter, encountering Emperor Wuzong’s suppression of the Buddhist teachings, Nan went into deep hiding within the mountain forests and valleys.

During the Dazhong era, when the teachings were being revived and he encountered the peaceful reign of Prime Minister Pei Xu, who was governing Wanling, he invited Huangbo to leave the mountains and follow him south as an attendant.
From there, they proceeded to Ba’en Temple in Gusu, where he devoted himself exclusively to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), never crossing the threshold of his quarters for nearly twenty years.
In the fourth year of the Qiánfú era, Zhōu Shènsì, the Governor of Sūzhōu, was drawn by his reputation and invited him to reside at Bǎolín Monastery.
He further requested that he dwell on Zhīxíng Mountain.
In the fifth year, Xú Zhèngyuán, the Magistrate of Chānghuà County, together with Ráo Jīng, the Garrison Commander of Zǐxī, jointly summoned him to reside at Qiānqǐng Cíyún Monastery.
Aside from instructing his Zen disciples, he remained solemnly in meditative absorption for over a month or ten days at a time.
In the third year of the Guangqi era, the former King of Two Zhe, the Qian clan (Wu Su Wang), requested that he descend from the mountain to receive offerings.
When Emperor Zhaozong heard of his spiritual transformation, he bestowed upon him five sets of deerskin robes and specially provided him with purple vestments.
In the second month of the first year of the Wende era, two rainbows suddenly pierced through his hall and chamber; two deer leaped into the temple, and the beam of the Dharma Hall broke.
In the fifth month, he took leave of the assembly; subsequently, while seated upon his meditation platform, he let his two feet hang down and extended both arms over his knees, passing away suddenly.
He was seventy years of age and had fifty-six years of seniority as a monk.
The stupa was moved to the western corner of the monastery.
In the second month of the year Renzi (892), the second year of the Dàshùn era, Sūn Rú of Xuānzhōu invaded the borders of Qiántáng.
His soldiers opened the stupa and saw the body of the Southern Master, intact and undecomposed, with his nails and hair grown long; they repented their transgressions and departed.

In his lifetime, Nanping authored one fascicle of the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra-śloka-gāthā* and one fascicle of the *Poxie lun*, which he used to counter the heterodox schools and external adversaries; these works were highly esteemed by his contemporaries.
Biography of Xuantai of Qibao Terrace Monastery on Mount Heng in the Tang Dynasty. Regarding the monk Xuantai: it is unknown where he was from.
By nature he was upright and square; his words were never uttered frivolously. With a mind of profound stillness, he acted only after deliberating on what was right.
The *āraṇya* where he resided was located to the east of Mount Heng and was known as the Seven Treasures Terrace (*Saptaratnasthūpa*).
He did not wear silk garments, which at the time was considered a coarse cloth robe.

After meeting Chan Master Deshan, his mind became expansive and he felt at ease; he vowed never to establish disciples, instead wandering freely to pursue his aspirations. Regarding his literary style, his brushwork seemed as if possessed by a divine spirit.
When those from the four quarters who were junior to him came on pilgrimage to meet him, they all observed the etiquette of equal-mindedness.

When Emperor Shenwu of the Qi dynasty gave birth to his second son, Yang—the future Emperor Wenxuan—Empress Dowager Wuming saw that their family was in extreme poverty; she spoke with her relatives regarding the household finances, expressing her deep concern that they would surely die of hunger and cold.
When the boy from the Western Regions was only a few months old and had not yet been able to speak, he suddenly said:
"I have lived!
The two characters were distinct and clear.
The Empress Dowager’s attendants were greatly alarmed, yet they did not dare speak, believing him to be a supernatural monster.
At that time, it was rumored that Master Tulu possessed divine powers and was frequently successful in archery; thus, he was skillfully enticed to come.

The Empress Dowager’s mind was preoccupied with her sons; she had previously remarked that they were strange, and so she went to see all her sons—including Wenxiang and the Empress Dowager of the Wei Yongxi era—questioning them one by one regarding their official ranks and positions.
Upon reaching the shore, he raised his hand two or three times, pointing only toward the sky, yet said nothing with his mouth.
As for his disciples, none of them made any further movement or gesture.
His final end was thereafter unknown.
Biography of Xuan Guang of the Silla Kingdom during the Chen Dynasty The monk Xuan Guang was a native of Xiongzhou in Haidong (Korea). From his youth, he possessed keen intelligence and insight;
he grew suddenly weary of the mundane dust of the world and resolutely sought out a renowned master to devote himself exclusively to the cultivation of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
Upon reaching adulthood, he wished to cross the vast ocean to seek the Chan dharma of the Central Kingdom.

Thereupon, he traveled through the state of Chen and proceeded to Mount Heng, where he met the Great Master Si. There, he opened the way for all things and brought about transformation, his spiritual understanding merging with that of the Master.
The Master contemplated him and examined his origins, then secretly bestowed upon him the *Anrakugyōmon* (The Gate of Peaceful Conduct) from the *Lotus Sūtra*.
His brilliance and benefit were like a divine awl, penetrating all things without exception;
he was as fresh as new cotton cloth, with whatever it was dyed becoming bright and pure.
Having received [the teachings], he practiced them with diligence and without error; soon thereafter, he realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* and requested certification of his realization.
Śākyamuni Buddha, desiring to certify him, said:
"That which you have realized is true and not false; guard and cherish it well, and cause the Dharma to increase."
"Return to your native land and employ skillful means (*upāya*); take well under your care those like *mínglíng* (cicada larvae), and they shall all become *guǒluó* (wasp-like beings).
Guāng prostrated himself and wept, whereupon he returned to the south of the Yangtze River with his monk's staff.

When the vessel belonging to his own country arrived to transport him and departed from the shore, colorful clouds dazzled the eyes, elegant music resounded through the air, and crimson staffs and rainbow-colored banners arrived with the sound of heralds' calls.
A voice from the air proclaimed:
"The Celestial Emperor summons the Chan Master Xuanguang of海东 (Haidong).

Xuanguang folded his hands in deference and declined, yet he saw only a servant in green robes leading the way. After a short while, they entered the palace city, which was clearly not a human government office.
In the establishment of the ceremonial guards, there were none who were not scaled or shelled creatures, interspersed with spirits and deities.
Someone said:

"Today the Heavenly Emperor has descended to the Dragon King’s palace; we request that the Master preach the Dharma-gate of Direct Realization. We of the Water Treasury shall receive the Master's benefit."
Having ascended the precious hall, he next climbed the high terrace; they conversed as if in private for approximately seven days.
Thereafter, when the King personally escorted him to his departure, the ship drifted upon the ocean and would not advance.
Faguang boarded the ship again; the crew said it had been only half a day.
Faguang returned to Mount Weng in Xiongzhou, where he planted his staff and tied up a thatched hut, which eventually became a Buddhist monastery.
Like voices responding to one another, those who have attained the Dharma find the door of their hibernation opening;
those who delight in the small and turn their hearts toward it, like ants drawn by the scent of food, arrive in rapid succession.

Yet, as for those who ascend to the hall and receive their prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), there is one person; those who enter the Fire-Light Samādhi, one person; and those who enter the Water-Light Samādhi, two persons—thus each attaining two kinds of Dharma gates.
The designation "Samādhi" is merely manifested from its initial arising.
As for those born through its various gates, they are like the myriad birds perched upon Mount Sumeru, all of which become one color.
When the radiance fades and ceases, there is no knowing where it has gone.
When the Patriarch [Hui]gong constructed the Hall of Shadows at Mount Nanyue, he depicted twenty-eight individuals within it, and I (Guang) was among them.
The same was true for the Patriarchs’ Hall at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai.
The verse states:
Now, if we examine those who have entered the Way after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa by means of the four dharmas—teaching, principle, practice, and fruit—then none can remain hidden or concealed!
Those who are closest to the Sage achieve success in their practice and realize the stage of fruition;
those who are somewhat further from the Sage find it easy to study the teachings and perceive the principles with intimacy;
while those who are even more remote do not refine their study of the teachings and their perception of the principles is not accurate.
When not a single thought arises, the boundaries of past and future are severed; this is the sudden realization of Buddhahood through the mind.
While the Buddha of Principle is fully endowed with sequential cultivation, he never once spoke of the Buddha of Practice.
"Specific yet minute":
Since the Sixth Patriarch, those in the Eastern Continent (China) have mostly discussed the principles of Chan while rarely discussing the practice of Chan.
This is not because the Southern School does not speak of practice; rather, it is so that they may cause one to see the Way with the urgency of one whose hair is on fire.

Master Huisi of Mount Nanyue was earnestly committed to the concurrent cultivation of both the precepts and meditation; he held both equally urgent. Therefore, students may verify this through the fruits of their practice.

For instance, regarding those who enter the Fire-Light Samādhi (*tejovatī-samādhi*), the *Womb Sūtra* (*Garbhavakrānti-sūtra*) states that by using meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) to gather the mind, one enters the Fire-Element Samādhi, whereby the buddha-field becomes brilliantly illuminated.
Fools say that it has been consumed by fire.
If one enters the samādhi of the water-element, fools see it as water and cast objects into it.
That the Bodhisattva’s mind is like space and does not perceive any contact or affliction is something that cannot be fully fathomed by those of the Two Vehicles.
This is precisely why one must be urgent in practicing for the fruit [of enlightenment].
Do not let it be that you merely speak with your mouth while your body and mind do not cultivate [the path]; how then could this assist the Way?

The Biography of Dharma-xi of the Jiangdu Palace during the Sui Dynasty. Shi Faxi was a native of Nanhai. His physical appearance was unattractive; he was short, frail, and simple-minded, appearing to be about forty years of age.
The elders of the region beyond the ridges all say:
"I recognized him when I was a child; his countenance is no different than it is now.
Among the Mian and Yan tribes, the tradition has been passed down that he is already three hundred years old.

He also claimed to have been an old acquaintance of the Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu, recounting events from the Jin and Song dynasties with such vivid detail that they seemed as if they had occurred only days before.

While he remained silent in ordinary circumstances, whenever he encountered someone he would speak, his words invariably containing profound meaning; his prognostications regarding auspicious and inauspicious signs were as certain as echoes following sounds or shadows following forms.
Ordinary people also do not wish to encounter Xi, fearing that his straightforward words regarding calamities and evils would offend their wills.

When Ma Jing of the Chen dynasty was appointed as the Governor of Guangzhou, just as he was about to take office, Xi entered the governor’s hall directly and drew the shape of a horse's head on the ground to show it to Ma’s son before departing.
Jingben was of a distinguished clan from Fufeng; he was bold and courageous and possessed great military strategy, yet he lacked experience in administrative affairs.

Upon arriving at the commandery, whenever he went on an excursion, he led a retinue of tens of thousands of armored soldiers, with banners, standards, swords, and halberds appearing like rainbows reflected against frost and snow, claiming that this could be used to intimidate the frontier regions.
His extravagance and presumption exceeded all bounds, surpassing even those of a king; consequently, he was falsely accused of plotting rebellion.
Filled with apprehension, he immediately dispatched more than a hundred members of his family to the court to demonstrate that he harbored no intention of revolt.
The Chen ruler remained confused and dispatched the Marquis of Linru to observe the situation, saying:
"If there are signs of rebellion, you may execute him immediately;
if there is truly no plot for treason, simply go and replace him."
When he arrived in Linru, he seized the man's property; upon reaching the province, he failed to verify whether the matter was right or wrong.
Jing relied solely on his own mind and felt no doubt, so he went with folded hands to Linru, whereupon [the governor] shouted to his attendants to seize and behead him.
This was a clear manifestation of his power over the earth.
His precognitive insights were all of this same nature.
When Emperor Yang heard of this, he summoned him to Yangzhou.
Not long after, a new hall was completed within the palace.
Overjoyed, he hurriedly ascended the hall to view it, but suddenly, in alarm, he rushed down the steps, crying out, "I nearly crushed to death!"
As night fell, a great rain caused the hall to collapse, killing several people. Subsequently, he again ran about within the palace, crying out that he was searching for a sheep's head.
The Emperor, hearing this, loathed it and rebuked him for his delirious talk, ordering him to be locked in a single room.
After several days, the three guards saw Xitan wandering freely in the marketplace.
Upon their return, they reported this to the Emperor, who ordered the relevant authorities to investigate the place of confinement; the door locks were found to be as they had been before.
The keeper said, "Xijian is inside the room.
Thereupon, the door was opened, and he saw a *kāṣāya* robe covering a heap of bleached bones; the chain passed through his cervical vertebrae and had not been removed.

The Emperor was greatly astonished and strange at this, and issued an edict dispatching his Chief Secretary, Wang Heng, to go quickly and verify it. He found that a *kāṣāya* robe covered the white bones; the bones were all linked together like a chain, and an iron chain bound his neck bone.
Upon hearing this, the Emperor was struck with amazement and offered words of praise; his faith and reverence increased all the more.
He issued an edict that [the monk] not be disturbed or moved, saying:
"The Sage’s spiritual transformations are boundless."
By evening, Xi returned to his room, speaking and laughing as before; the gatekeeper reported this once more.
The Emperor ordered the shackles to be removed, allowing him to go wherever he pleased.
On one occasion, he attended vegetarian feasts at several households; at other times, he drank wine and ate meat, observing no prohibitions whatsoever.
Shortly thereafter, he fell ill; he himself removed the mats from his usual bed, laid out a coffin plank, and lay down upon it.
He ordered people to spread burning charcoal beneath him until it was intensely hot, and after several days, he passed away with half his body charred and mangled.
He was buried beside Xiangshan Temple.
Four years later, the Governor of Nanhai Prefecture reported that Xijian had returned to the prefecture.
By imperial decree, the coffin was opened, but it was empty and contained nothing at all.

The Biography of Master Qin of Mízhōu during the Sui Dynasty. Regarding the monk Master Qin of Mízhōu during the Sui Dynasty: it is unknown where he was from. During the Dàyè era, he arrived at Guǎngpíng;
his physical appearance and spiritual demeanor were eccentric and incongruous, difficult to fathom even in casual moments. His speech was inconsistent, often shifting mid-sentence.
Seeing the five-storied brick pagoda at Lingtong Temple, which was intended to be lofty and spacious but whose construction was disordered and messy,
he looked up at it with a smile and said to the assembly of monks,
"Why have you built this?"
The assembly said, "For a meritorious Buddhist rite, one must employ grand and magnificent displays; why does the Dharma Master ask such a strange question?
