He laughed and said:
"He is building a beacon tower!
At that time, the monastic community criticized one another, saying,
"The words of this madman— how could they be taken seriously!"

By the ninth year, the stupa was still not finished when bandits rose up on all sides and the local officials tightened their defenses. Watchtowers with beacon fires were established atop the pagoda, proving that Faxian’s words had not been in vain.
The elders of the locality did not know where he came from or why they should revere him;
nor was there any trace of his place of lodging.
Nevertheless, from time to time he would transform his body and enter a pigsty, immediately joining the herd of swine.
When the youths Ma Shida and several others witnessed the moment Qin began his transformation, they halted to observe him, intending to see if he would return to human form.
Suddenly, the later manifestation of the fruit reappeared; from behind the onlookers, it cried out loudly, "What do you all wish to behold?
The crowd was struck with awe and alarm, and they joined their palms in prostration before it.
Their transformations are impermanent; all are like this.
When the world fell into chaos and disorder, even the reverent traces of their sounds and footprints were lost.
The verse says:
"Why is it that there were so many manifested monks during the Wei and Sui dynasties?
Tong replied, "The activities of Bodhisattvas involve manifesting transformation bodies according to the species they encounter; they employ supernatural powers as their play."
"While sporting about, he benefited the Lord of the World.
Someone asked:
"The Wei, Qi, Chen, and Sui dynasties were within the range of Master Xuan’s hearing and sight; why were they not included in the *Xu Zhuan* (Continued Biographies)?"
Tong replied, "There are things I do not know; my knowledge is simply incomplete.

It is much like the Great Song, where the civilizing influence of its culture has already unified all lands and its territory is so vast that the wonders occurring daily are truly difficult to know in their entirety."

Even if there were certain monks [among them], since they have not yet been included in the records of the Shi family and there is no basis for their biographies within their own lineage, they likewise remain absent and have not been recorded; this is left for future worthies to address.

Biography of Saṃgha of Puguangwang Monastery in Sizhou, Tang Dynasty; Biography of Saṃgha of Puguangwang Monastery in Sizhou, Tang Dynasty. By Muxia, Huiyan, and Huian. As for the monk Saṃgha, he was a native of the country of He, north of the Pamir Mountains.
He himself stated that his secular surname was He; since Senghui was originally a man from the country of Kangju, he was accordingly named Kang Senghui.
However, he should have possessed both a Hu and a Fan name; while his given name followed the Fan pronunciation, his surname followed Chinese linguistic conventions.
Upon detailed inquiry, it was found that his native country lay to the northeast of the kingdom of Shule; it was merely a dependency of Shule.
Jiā left his homeland at a young age to enter the monastic order.
After becoming a monk, he vowed to travel abroad.
Upon first arriving at Xiliangfu, he subsequently traveled through Jianghuai during the early years of the Longshuo era.
He immediately registered his name at Longxing Temple in Shanyang, whereupon his divine wonders began to manifest.

At first, he took his disciple Huinan with him to Linhuai, where they requested land from a resident in Xinyi Ward; having set boundary markers there, he declared that a monastery would certainly be established at this very spot.
He then dug into the earth and recovered an ancient stele, which belonged to Xiangji Temple of the Qi Dynasty.
He found the robe fragments of a golden image inscribed with the characters "Buddha Universal Radiance King" (Puzhao Wang Fo).
The local residents sighed in wonder, saying, "The celestial eye foresaw this; how could we not have abandoned it?"
The statue on that stele had twice been destroyed by fire during the Zhenyuan and Changqing reigns, and consequently its traces were lost.
Once, while lying in the home of the Heba clan, her body suddenly grew three feet longer than her bed and mat; everyone was filled with wonder and astonishment.

Next, he manifested in the form of Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara; the entire family of his household rejoiced and celebrated, their faith and reverence redoubled, and they subsequently donated their residence.
The site of that Xiangji Temple is the very temple that stands today.
Due to these extraordinary traces, his reputation spread rapidly and could not be contained.

In the second year of the Jinglong era of Emperor Xiaohedao of the Zhongzong reign, an envoy was dispatched with an imperial decree for him to attend the Inner Daochang. The Emperor presided over the Dharma assembly, conversing with him intimately; their discussions on auspicious and inauspicious omens were as harmonious as two halves of a tally fitting together.
He further bestowed upon the temple the name Puguangwang (Universal Radiance King).
In the fourth year, the gengxu year, he manifested illness; by imperial decree, he was moved from the inner palace to be settled at Jianfu Temple.
On the second day of the third month, he passed away while sitting upright and composed; his divine countenance remained as if alive, with only his eyes closed.
He was eighty-three years of age by secular reckoning, while his years of ordination were unknown.
He had spent thirty years in his own country and fifty-three years transforming the land of Tang.
The Emperor was deeply grieved and filled with sorrow.
At that time, although the air was filled with a foul odor, her physical form remained as it had been, and many miraculous traces were manifested.

An imperial edict ordered the relevant authorities to provide three hundred rolls of silk for her return funeral at the banks of the Huai River, and commanded the various officials to escort her; scholars and commoners gathered in great numbers to see her off.
On the fifth day of the fifth month, he arrived at his current location.
The Emperor, never ceasing to look up to him with admiration, asked Master Wanhui:
"Who was that monk Saṃgha?"
He replied:
"This is an emanation of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Does the sutra not say so?"
"Because those who were to be saved by the body of a bhikṣu, he manifested the appearance of a śramaṇa.
Initially, Kāśyapa traveled through the regions south of the Yangtze River and resided at Lingguang Temple in Jiahe.
That land is a marshy realm where the people’s houses have fishing weirs, and nets and arrows crisscross like a grid.
Ga Ku Dun said by way of illustration:
"As for the various karmic acts of killing that cause people to fall into ruin, one should swiftly devise other means of livelihood."
At that time, there were many who had torn their nets and broken their poles.
Ga Xian was resting in leisure when he saw a deity who addressed him, saying:
"Heaven is currently suffering from a severe drought; the crops of the common people are withering to death. Why do you hide yourself away?"
"Is it because he is a lazy dragon? Jia asked,
"What can be done about this?"
The deity said, "If tonight you simply extend your little finger outside through a crack in the window, what can anyone do to you?
Jia followed this advice. That night, there was an extraordinary crash of thunder. At dawn, when he examined his finger, there was a faint red line upon the vessel.
Huijia said, "I have no affinity with this land.
He then traveled to Jinling, where he saw that Guoxiang Temple was in ruins; he left his robe upon the beams of the main hall and departed, after which later generations smelled a wondrous fragrance.
Gaya once recorded this, saying:
"This temple shall be restored by a 'King of Men'.
Thirty years later, there was indeed a layperson and a monk surnamed Chon who acted as its patrons.
Tongtian Wansui, who was among the crowd at Shanyang and had already anticipated their disdain for Ga, spoke out boldly, saying:
"I have five hundred thousand coins to offer as support for this meritorious deed; do not harbor groundless objections."
Jia called out to a boat on the banks of the Huai River, saying:
"If you provide me with a gift of wealth, I shall grant you leniency regarding your legal punishment.
Those goods you are carrying were obtained through plunder."
The thief surrendered everything exactly as he had been told, and thus the Buddha hall was completed.
Not long after, the thief was caught and imprisoned in the jail of Yangzi County.
Guṇabhadra descended from the clouds and comforted him, saying:
There was no suffering.
Before many days had passed, the imperial pardon arrived and he was spared from death.

Previously, while in Chang’an, when the Prince Consort (Fuma Duye) Wu Youji fell ill, Tanqian cured him by sprinkling him with water from his ritual pitcher; his fame thus resounded throughout the capital.

Later, when someone fell ill, he would inform them; some were cured by having willow branches brushed over them, some by being told to wash a stone lion, some by the throwing of a water pitcher, and others by being made to confess their transgressions.
The efficacy is not a hollow fabrication, and the merit is not in vain.
To avert bodily calamities, one seeks horses;
to warn against the perils of wind, one seeks fans.

Some recognized the thief’s money; some bit the neck of one bound by the Black Rope Hell; some sought the well of an Arhat; some realized the drowning of the Pei family; some foreknew the great snowfall; and some brought rain to save from drought.
His spiritual transformations were boundless and unfathomable, exceeding all ordinary measures.

By imperial decree, Emperor Zhongzong bestowed grace upon three disciples—Huian, Huyan, and Mokṣa—granting each a robe and an alms bowl, and ordering them to succeed him in maintaining the incense and lamps.
Many years after his passing, he once manifested his form to go to the southern market of Han to purchase lacquered vessels.
When the merchant Li Shanxin’s ship arrived at the temple, he sought to buy monastic alms bowls.
Suddenly, he saw the image within the stupa and, with a solemn expression, pointed and said,
"It is precisely this monk who has come seeking to purchase me!
Those far and near sighed in admiration.
Furthermore, he once transformed timber at Hongjing by means of supernatural power and arrived there by raft.
During the Dali era, the provincial governor mandated that the temple oversee ten postal stations, requiring it to provide funds for the transport of official envoys.
On the night of the Jia-day in the seventh month of the fifteenth year, he manifested his form in the inner palace and requested exemption from the labor service at the postal stations.

Emperor Daizong issued an imperial edict through the eunuch Ma Fengcheng to grant him release, and further presented him with three hundred rolls of silk, one thousand pieces of miscellaneous colored fabrics, a golden ritual pitcher, and a set of robes for the Crown Prince, ordering that his likeness be painted for worship within the palace.
Furthermore, during the Qianduan era, there was a provincial governor named Li Wuming.
An astrologer calculated that because the Earth Lodging (Tu-xu) was presiding over his position, he would suffer from misfortune and weakness.
Suddenly, [the Bodhisattva] manifested his form and patted Li on the back, saying:
"I have come; blessings have arrived. My sweat has been shed and my calamities have been extinguished.
Thereafter, no further misfortunes befell him.
He once sought felt and woolen cloth from the state of Yan, identifying himself as a monk from a monastery in Sizhou.
The envoy from Yan arrived bearing the requested items; upon comparing them with the image within the stupa, they were found to be authentic.
He then made a copy of its likeness and returned home.
From Yan and Ji, it was circulated and transcribed repeatedly until there was no place where it did not reach.
On the night of the first day of the New Year in the first year of the Changqing era, he sang before the chamber of Su Gong, the Prefect of the province:
“South of the Huai and north of the Huai, from this point on there shall be blessings.”
"From the east to the west, there is nowhere that does not ripen.
That year, it was only within the borders of Linhuai that there was a bountiful harvest.
In the second year, the temples and stupas were all consumed by fire; only the physical form of the stupa remained solemnly intact, as if undamaged.

During the Xiantong era, one Pang Xun—originally a soldier of the Xuzhou garrison—deserted his post in the Gui Circuit and proceeded along the way plundering, eventually attacking Sizhou and besieging its city.
Guṇabhadra manifested his form atop the stupa; while the foreign invaders were all asleep, he emerged from the city by chance to strike them, causing them to flee in terror and fall into Suzhou.
Upon reporting these events to the throne, he was further bestowed the title of Great Master Zhèngshèng (Certified Sage).
In the first year of the Wende era, external invaders launched a raid, and the provincial governor fortified the city walls to resist them.
Guṇabhadra manifested his form at the northwest corner of the city.
Upon seeing him, the invaders realized their strong fortifications were difficult to capture; struck with terror, they fled under the cover of night.

During the Dashun era, Zhang Jian, acting on the orders of Pengmen Commander Shi Pu, launched an attack on the northern city wall. Aside from those who were executed, more than five hundred people were detained within the training grounds. While leaning over his desk, Jian suddenly saw in a state of mental confusion a monk dressed in purple robes instructing him, saying:
"These are but commoners; how can they be put to death?"
"It would be better to let him go.
Having finished speaking, he vanished from sight.
The counselor then released him, and he fled.
In the first year of the Qianning era, the Prefect Tai Meng dreamed of Moga, who said:
"The cold is severe in the southeast; you have made few preparations.
Meng did not understand the meaning of these words, so he offered him cotton quilts and Dharma robes.
On the night of the last day of the twelfth month at midnight, a soldier leaped over the ramparts and entered; Meng did not know it at first.
He then dreamed of a monk placing a *khakkhara* (monk’s staff) upon his chest; its coldness pierced to his very marrow, and he started awake in alarm.
Upon receiving orders to beat the drums and sound the horns, the rebels were startled and fled; a leader surnamed Han was captured, and it was only then that they understood the situation.
From this time on, small monks frequently appeared atop the pagoda, drawing the gaze of the entire province.
Nevertheless, there are omens of good and ill fortune; at such times, those who pray for wind receive wind, and those who seek children obtain children.
Now I have heard that among those who personally pay their respects, there are many who do not see the physical form of the deity at all.
If one sees a smiling face, it is auspicious; otherwise, it is ominous. Such are the matters that cannot be easily fathomed.

When Emperor Shizong of the Zhou dynasty turned his attention to the south of the Yangtze, first attacking and capturing Sishang, Xie Ga appeared in a dream to the local people, saying that they should not underestimate the enemy.
When this was reported to the provincial governor, he did not believe it at first.

However, from then on, every household had the same dream; when they informed him, he finally granted the request, thereby sparing all the people of the commandery and relying upon the protection of the Kāśyapa.
Throughout the world, wherever a refined hermitage was constructed, an image of the Venerable Śākyamuni was invariably established and inscribed with the title "The Great Sage Monk Śāṅgha.
Those who offered prayers there mostly had their wishes fulfilled according to their hearts' desires.
Li Bei-hai Yong and Hu Zhu-zuo Hao each composed stele inscriptions to extol his virtues.

During the reign of the present sovereign, who has set his mind upon this matter, in the third month of that year, a nun returning from Mount Wutai beheld the image of a child atop the stupa; she then ascended the spire and offered her body as an act of devotion.

In the seventh year of the Taiping Xingguo era, an imperial edict was issued for the high-ranking official Bai Chengrui to rebuild the stupa, endeavoring to make it taller and more spacious by adding additional tiers.
In the eighth year, an envoy was dispatched to deliver additional śarīra relics and precious goods, which were interred together at the lower foundation.
On that day, the monk Huaidé had prepared a wooden structure for self-immolation in advance; holding a wax-tapered torch himself, he burned his body as an offering.
Amidst the spreading flames, the sound of the sutras did not cease.

Furthermore, as he was about to construct a stupa, three massive timbers were floating down the Huai River; they came to a halt near the floating bridge and were taken to serve as the central pillars for the tower.
Subsequently, an imperial edict appointed the Palace Attendant Li Tingxun to preside over it.
Previously, because a golden image had been discovered within the burial mound and its inscription read "King Universal Radiance" (Puzhao Wang), that title was adopted as the name of the temple.
Later, to avoid the imperial name of Empress Wu, the character "Guang" (Light) was used as a substitute.

Recently, when the *Sengqie Shilu* (Biography of Saṃgha) was requested for imperial inspection, after the Emperor had perused it, he issued an edict restoring its title plaque to that of Puzhao Wangsi (Puzhao King Temple).
The disciple Mokṣa was named after a term from the Western Regions; in the language of China, it means "liberation.
From his youth, he followed the Venerable Kāśyapa as a tonsured disciple, and thus manifested many miraculous and extraordinary signs.
In the fourth year of the Zhonghe era, the Prefect Liu Rang’s father, the Palace Attendant Zhuhue, suddenly dreamed one night of a monk in purple robes who said:
"I have a disciple, Mokṣaka, who was buried to the west of this temple long ago."
"Could you exhumate it?
He then showed him the location of the burial.

At first, he did not pay any heed to the dream; yet when the dream occurred a second time, just as before, the Vice Minister (Zhongcheng) went to the place indicated in the dream with the intent to have it excavated. There he saw a man surnamed Zhan who resided there, so he paid a large sum of money to purchase the site from him.
They excavated a pit approximately three feet deep and discovered a seated reliquary box; upon opening it, they found that śarīra were emitting light from atop the bones.

They ordered the remains to be cremated and collected over eight hundred śarīra, which they presented to Emperor Xizong. By imperial decree, an image was fashioned from the ashes of the cremation, and he was posthumously granted the title "Great Master True Appearance" (Zhenxiang Dashi).
Now he stands in attendance to the left, as if participating in the sacrificial feast.

His disciple Huinan, whose family name and place of birth are unknown, has constantly followed Master Saṃgha, attending to his water flask and staff. From Chuzhou they traveled to Huaiyin, where together they exhorted the Sima Governor of Donghai; his wife was stingy with her white sandalwood casket, which subsequently fell into the water.
Upon arriving at Xuyi, he opened the Luohan Well and stayed at the home of Heba Xuanji, where Yan attended him by the side of the Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Thereafter, an imperial edict summoned Saṃghavarman to the capital.
Emperor Zhongzong issued a special edict to ordain three individuals—Huyan, Hui’an, and Mucuo—and bestowed upon each of them a separate set of robes and alms bowl.
Biography of Huian of Shaolin Monastery on Mount Song, Tang Dynasty. Shi Huian, surnamed Wei, was a native of Zhijiang in Jingzhou.
His appearance was dignified and elegant, with deep blue-black hair and azure eyes; he descended to earth during the early years of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
By nature, he was calm and broad-minded, remaining untainted by worldly dust; he cultivated and studied the Dharma gates, mastering them all without exception.

In the seventeenth year of Emperor Wen’s reign, an imperial edict was issued to comprehensively register all privately ordained monks and nuns throughout the empire. Upon investigation, it was found that they had no recorded names or surnames and had fled into mountain valleys.
During the Daye era, when the Jiqu Canal was being opened and constructed, laborers were conscripted in great numbers, and those who died of hunger were seen everywhere.
Dao’an traveled about begging for many bowls of food to relieve their illness and exhaustion; those whom he saved and sustained were numerous.
Upon hearing of this, Emperor Yang issued an edict for his arrest; Dao'an thereupon entered Mount Taihe in secret.
When the Emperor traveled to Jiangdu and the realm fell into turmoil, Dao'an took up his staff and ascended Mount Heng to enter a monastery, where he practiced the dhūta austerities.
During the Zhenguan era, he traveled to Qizhou to pay his respects to Master Ren.
In the first year of the Linde era, he journeyed to the Stone Wall of Mount Zhongnan and settled there.
At that time, amidst the plains and valleys where he resided, early frosts damaged the crops; yet at his dwelling alone, there was none.
For forty *li* around, all were suffering from the calamities brought by Qingnü.
When the Great Emperor, the Son of Heaven, heard of this, he summoned her; however, An did not comply with the imperial decree.
In the second year of the Yongchun era, she arrived at Huatai, where she took up residence in a thatched pavilion. She sat upon a rope bed in the center, with the four directions entirely exposed.
An imperial edict was issued to construct a temple for him to reside in, which was named Chaoti;
thus he returned to his hometown at Yuquan Temple. At that time, Zen Master Shenxiu had recently passed away, and everyone requested him to take up the position of abbot.
An did not obey his command.
In the fourth month of the second year of the Shengli era of Empress Wu, he addressed his disciples and students, saying:
"Each of you return to your quarters and close your doors."
At the third watch, a divine being arrived, accompanied by a dense array of guards and the tinkling sound of bells on their carriages. Wind and rain arrived together.
The deity circled the courtyard several times; Dao’an conversed with him, who offered earnest instructions and admonitions before departing after Dao’an had prostrated twice.
Someone asked him the reason for this, and he replied,
"I have received the Bodhisattva precepts from the deity of Mount Song.
Empress Wu once asked him about his age, and he answered:
“I have not recorded it.
[The other] asked:
“Why did you not record it?”
He then said:
"Is the body of birth and death like a revolving wheel?
Since a wheel has neither beginning nor end, what is the use of recording it?"
Furthermore, this flow of the mind is uninterrupted in its midst; even the perception of bubbles arising and ceasing is but a deluded thought.
From the initial consciousness until the point when the signs of movement cease, it is exactly like this—how could one record it by years or months?
The Empress Dowager prostrated herself with her forehead touching the ground.
Having heard that Dao’an’s well was missing, she issued an imperial decree to have one excavated for him.
Dao’an said:
"Below here is a red omen; be careful not to harm living things.
When they reached the spring, they saw a golden toad emerging dully from the marshy ground, which accorded perfectly with his prophetic record.
The Emperor redoubled his respect and esteem for him.

In the ninth month of the second year of the Shenglong era of Zhongzong, he issued an imperial edict ordering an inner court official to bestow upon him a purple *kāṣāya* and silk, and to ordain fourteen disciples.
The Emperor further issued an edict for the Masters Dao’an, Jing, and Chan to enter the inner palace to receive offerings.
In the third year, he was granted a set of monastic robes and then took his leave to return to Shaolin Monastery.
On the third day of the third month in the third year of the Jinglong era, he addressed his disciples, saying:
"After my death, place my corpse in the woods and wait for a wild fire to consume it naturally."
"Do not go against my wish!

Suddenly, Master Wanhui arrived; Huisi greeted him with wild enthusiasm and grasped his hand, and they conversed for some time while those attending by their side strained their ears but understood nothing at all.
On the eighth day, he closed his door and passed away while reclining.
He was approximately one hundred and thirty years of age, from the second year of the Kaihuang era until the third year of the Jinglong era.

After the cremation was completed, eighty *śarīra* relics were collected; five of these, which were reddish-purple in color, were presented to the Emperor, while the remainder were distributed as alms, with stupas being constructed according to the means available.
In the second year of the Xiāntián era, his disciples erected a pagoda there.
The Biography of Wanhui of Wenxiang County, Guozhou, Tang Dynasty. The monk Wanhui, whose secular surname was Zhang, was a native of Wenxiang County in Guozhou.
Still at a tender age, he was white-haired and mentally dull, remaining mute; his parents grieved over his impure spirit.
He was mocked by the children of the neighborhood, yet he never displayed any attitude of contention toward them.
However, he himself would call out "Wanhui" (Ten Thousand Returns), and thus this became his name.

Furthermore, he spoke nothing of cold or heat; he did not show increased disdain toward the poor and lowly, nor did he offer excessive deference to the wealthy and noble. He ran wildly back and forth, never ceasing all day long.
Sometimes laughing and sometimes weeping, his facial expressions were entirely without constancy; saliva and froth constantly dripped from the corners of his mouth, which everyone found strange.
He did not favor luxury or ostentation and spoke very little; whenever he did speak, it was invariably in the form of prophecies, the truth of which was only understood after the events had passed.

When he was ten years old, his elder brother went to garrison Liao Yang—some say Anxi—and for a long time there had been no news of him. His mother was deeply distressed by this and consequently established a vegetarian feast to pray for blessings.
Huishu said to his mother, "It is very easy to know whether my elder brother is well; why should you worry?
He then wrapped up the remains of the meal and went out directly. Returning at evening, he held his brother's letter and said:
"Peace and well-being," [he said].
When asked about his journey, he remained silent and offered no reply, having traveled ten thousand *li* to and fro.
Later, when his elder brother returned, he said:
"On this day, I spoke with Huí, who had just returned from his home; we shared some cakes and snacks together before he departed.
Upon hearing this, the entire family was filled with wonder and joy.

From then on, everyone’s perception of him changed, and his reputation reached the imperial court. Emperor Zhōngzōng Xiàohé issued an edict to summon him for an audience, treating him with great honor and respect.
In the second year of the Shenlong era, an imperial edict was issued granting him a single ordination certificate.
From the end of Gaozong’s reign through the time of Empress Wu, he was frequently summoned to the inner palace chapel, where he was granted garments of brocade and silk and attended by palace women.
Formerly, when he was a child, he built a Buddhist stupa out of stacked bricks and stones at Xingguo Temple in Weixiang.
After he entered the inner palace, that stupa suddenly emitted a brilliant light; consequently, a great pavilion was constructed to cover it.
However, his deeds and actions were all beyond casual measurement; whenever he spoke, there was invariably a profound reason behind it.
By imperial decree, he was granted the title "Master Fayun" (Dharma-Cloud), and no outsiders were permitted to see him.

Previously, during the reign of Empress Wu, when cruel officials were engaged in the practice of "fabricated charges," those whose official rank was even slightly elevated were separated from their wives and children on a daily basis.
Cui Xuanwei of Boling held both the highest position and the greatest prestige; his mother, Lady Li, being a woman of great virtue, grew anxious and said to him:
"You may go one day to welcome Wanhui. This monk is of the same caliber as Baozhi; you can observe his demeanor to discern whether your fortune or misfortune lies ahead."
He then summoned him to his home; his mother wept as she paid her respects and offered him a pair of gold spoons and chopsticks.
Suddenly, he descended the steps, flung the spoons and chopsticks toward the upper hall, and walked away with a甩 (shuǎi—swinging) of his arm.
The family considered this an ill omen.

After several days had passed, they ordered [the child] to ascend the roof to retrieve it; when the spoon and chopsticks were lowered, a scroll of writing was found. Upon examining it, they discovered it was a book of prophetic portents (*chanwei*), and they immediately ordered it to be burned.
After several days, officials suddenly came to his home and searched extensively for prophetic charts and secret texts (*tushen*); failing to find them, he was acquitted.

At that time, many cruel magistrates ordered thieves to cast *gudu* (poisonous charms) or to forge false secret prophecies to frame people; once the accusations were proven true, they would execute the victims and confiscate their families' property. This occurred frequently.
How could Cui Shi, who was not a sage, have known of the forged prophecies when she cast aside her chopsticks and spoons?
Toward the end of Zhongzong’s reign, she once cursed Empress Wei, saying: "You rebel and traitor! I will hack off your head!"
He was subsequently executed.
Princess Taiping had a residence built for him in Huaiyuan Ward, situated directly behind the princess’s own palace.
Furthermore, when Emperor Xiaohé personally escorted Princess Jincheng to her marriage with the Tufan, he visited Shiping; as he was returning, [the monk] went out to welcome the imperial carriage.
At that time, Cui Riyong, Wu Pingyi, Song Zhiwen, Shen Quanqi, Cen Xi, and Xue Ji all bowed respectfully and inquired after his well-being with great solemnity.
The gentlemen said,
"Each of us wishes to seek a single word from the Sage to determine our fortune or misfortune.
They then patted Shen’s back and said:
"You are truly a man of talent," Shen said, overcome with joy,
"The Sage has granted me a prediction of enlightenment; my sons must no longer contend for it."
He also said to Wu, "I shall give you the name Fudong; you shall have no cause for sorrow.
However, Mu Xi and Ji displayed expressions of disapproval.
Cen avoided him on horseback and said to Ji, "These are likely wild foxes; what is there to fear in their words?
He then looked back and said:
"You, too, shall not escape.
When Xie and Ji were executed, people came to value them all the more.
At that same time, there was a monk named Saṃgha, whose traces of transformation were not constant.
The Emperor Zhongzong asked Hui:
"Who is this man? Hui replied.
"He is an emanation of Avalokiteśvara.
During the Zhenguan era, when the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang returned from the West, he stated that there was a Śailaguhya Monastery in India.
When Xuanzang entered it, he saw only an empty room containing nothing but a low wooden stool and a monk’s staff.
He then inquired of the virtuous monks in this room, all of whom said:

"This monk’s karmic conditions were deficient regarding religious affairs, and he was punished by being sent to the East. The country is named Zhendan, and his location is known as Wenhxiang; it has been ten thousand times since he returned here."
When Xuanzang returned and sought an audience with Huiri, he immediately paid his respects.
When asked about the Western Regions, Huiri described them as if he had seen them with his own eyes.
As Xuanzang was about to visit her home, Huiri said to her mother:
"A guest has arrived; please prepare a vegetarian meal.
Shortly thereafter, Xuanzang arrived.
Miraculous occurrences such as these were numerous.
Ming Chongyan, a Grand Master of Rectification and Counselor, was a man of spiritual arts who said of others, "Wanhui is a divine monk.
When the Emperor Xuanzong was still a hidden dragon [a prince],
Ming Chongyan went with his disciple Zhang Wei and others to pay him a visit.

Turning his gaze back toward the Emperor, he saw that the Emperor had become even more insolent and disrespectful; he took up his lacquered staff, called out to him, and drove him away, while all those who accompanied him were likewise expelled.
He dragged the Emperor inside and bolted the door from within. Acting entirely like an ordinary man, he did nothing else, but patted the Emperor’s back repeatedly and said:
"May you, the Son of Heaven, take care of yourself for fifty years; beyond that, I know not."
Zhang Gong and the others heard these words clearly outside the gate; therefore, they devoted their hearts to supporting him.
His statement that "fifty years hence" refers, in fact, to the calamity of An Lushan.
When Emperor睿宗 was still residing at his princely residence, he would sometimes travel among the people.
Upon returning from a journey through the streets and alleys of a village, he called out in a loud voice:
"The Son of Heaven is coming!"
Someone said,
"A sage has arrived.
While he stayed there for two nights, the Emperor was certain to pass by and linger about.
Prince Huizhuang was the second son of Emperor Ruizong. Empress Wu once held him up to show him to [Empress] Wei, saying:
"This child is the spirit of a great tree from the Western Regions; you should raise him as your brother."
Princess Anle—the younger sister of Emperor Xuanzong—had formed an intimate alliance with Empress Wei that was so intense it could have warmed one’s hands; those on the road feared her.
Turning back to look at the imperial carriage, she spat repeatedly, saying, “Foul!
Foul! One must not draw near!”
Before he had even turned his heel, disaster befell him.

The Emperor realized further that Hui was no ordinary man; he sent out two palace women to attend upon him day and night, and issued a special decree to have his portrait painted in the Jixian Academy.
When Hui was nearing his end, he suddenly called out, asking for river water from his native region; his disciples and companions searched everywhere but found none.
Hui said, "The river water is right here in front of the hall; why do you not take it?"
The multitude dug a well at the foot of the stairs, and river water gushed forth; they drank it and passed away.
The wells throughout the surrounding quarters of the residence all became salty and bitter, yet this well alone remained sweet and delicious.
Later, there were those who falsely assumed his identity, some calling themselves "Little Wan-hui," to delude the marketplace; many of them were executed.
After his death, Xu Yanbo, a Right Attendant-in-Ordinary, composed a stele inscription for him, which was erected on the west road at Yujian in Weixiang.
The commentary states:
That the sun travels ten thousand li in a day must certainly not be a human being.
Is it perhaps a ghost or spirit?
"Is it due to some immortal art?
Tong replied, "One observes conduct to know a person; he turns away from all deviant actions and is not a ghost or spirit."
This is not a result of intentional effort or spiritual arts;
it is merely the attainment of "supernormal power" (abhijñā).
Therefore, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, this power is said to be of four kinds:
First, one's single body can fly through the air without obstruction, like a bird;
second, one can cause the distant to become near, arriving there without having traveled;
third, one can vanish from that place and appear here.
"Of the four, which one can reach [the goal] in a single thought-moment? Another asked:
"Among the four, what does 'reversal' (āvartana) entail?"
The Master replied,
"They all exist! Therefore,
it is called the 'Abhijñā of Sovereign Will'."

This is the same as the "Supernormal Powers" (*ṛddhi*) section of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which states that some Arhats possess great capability and can manifest the three types of miraculous transformations (*prātihārya*).
Biography of Daojian of Lingyan Temple in Qizhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Daojian, surnamed Feng, was a native of Wu Commandery.
His origins were unknown, and he resided at Lingyan Mountain Temple in Lixia; his traces were divine and marvelous, and he was a monk whose character could not be fathomed.

During the Yuanhe era, there was a man named Feng, also a native of Wu Commandery, who had failed in his official selection despite his mastery of the classics and thus lived as a sojourner in Chang’an.
One day, he saw an old monk coming to visit Feng’s residence and said to him,
"You bear my surname. Thereupon,
they began to associate with one another.
In little more than a year, he was subsequently appointed as a district magistrate in Dongyue.
Just as he was preparing his travel gear, Sengjian arrived carrying his alms-bowl to announce his departure.
Feng asked:
"The Master is leaving; where will you go?
Jian replied, "My hermitage is beneath the western corridor of Lingyan Mountain in Qizhou."
I have been traveling briefly in the capital for exactly ten years now.
Fortunate as it was to have traveled with you, I am now returning to my former place; thus, I have come to bid you farewell.
However, when you serve as a magistrate in the region of Yue and your path passes beneath Lingyan Temple, you ought to visit me there.
Feng Nuo replied, "I respectfully accept your instruction.
A few days later, Feng departed from the pass while Dong went to his official post. Upon reaching the gate of Lingyan Temple, he halted his horse and gazed toward it, saying:
"Could this not be the temple where the Master Jianshi resides?
He entered immediately to visit him.
At that time, a monk was in the courtyard, and Feng asked:
"Where is the dwelling of Master Daojian?
The monk replied,
"This temple has no Daojian."
Feng, suspecting something strange, pondered silently to himself:
"Master Jian is pure and upright; could he possibly deceive me?

Thereupon, he wandered alone through the temple until he reached the base of the western corridor, where he suddenly saw a monk depicted in a mural whose features were identical to those of Master Jian.
Feng was greatly astonished and sighed, saying:
"Master Jian is truly an extraordinary man!
He is even able to descend his spirit to commune with me."
After a long time, he looked at the true image, beside which was inscribed:
"The son of the Feng family, a native of Wu Commandery.
He studied the Dharma of the Buddha at the age of ten and became renowned for his practice of the Way; he died at the age of seventy-eight."
When Feng read the inscription, he finally realized that the statement "You (Ruo) is my surname" was indeed not erroneous.

According to one account, some twenty li west of the city of Suzhou lies Lingyan Mountain Temple. Beneath the northwest corridor there, a portrait of a śramaṇa was painted, said to have been made in the fifteenth year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, depicting a wandering lay practitioner (*yóufāng jūshì*). Having passed by the mountain temple, [the Master] stayed overnight; he borrowed a brush and inkstone from the monks' kitchen, yet the monastic community paid him no heed.

At dawn, the monks searched everywhere but found no guest. Seeing a painted image of a Brahman monk in a corner of the hall, they observed that his facial features were extraordinary: his skin was weathered and black, his eyebrows were long and drooping, and his eyes rolled like lightning with a bluish-white hue at the corners. He had a prominent nose and a square mouth; his lips were parted to reveal his teeth. With fists clenched, he leaned them upon his right shoulder; his body was bent, appearing about one and a half zhang tall. He wore coarse, patched *kāṣāya* robes, large beads encircled his arms, and he stood barefoot.
The multitude beheld him with awe and trepidation, unable to fathom his origin.
People from far and near all came to him; some burned incense and paid homage with sighs of wonder, while others sought blessings and warded off calamities.
On clear nights, a sound of chanting was heard emanating from within the hall, whereupon birds and sparrows dared not defile the area between the eaves and pillars.
Thus, the people of the district called him Master Lingyan, or sometimes the Holy Monk of Lingyan. Once,
he appeared in person and said to an old woman,
"I, this poor monk, am fond of eating *jiāozòng* (lotus-root dumplings)."

Suspecting him to be a sage, the next day he brought a basket of offerings into the palace to present to him. To this day, on the third day of the third month, the people vie with one another to send these offerings, wrapping glutinous rice and *jiao* leaves in bamboo leaves; the people of Wu call them *jiaozhong*.
In the second year of the Xiān-ān era of the Táng dynasty, the son of Lù Lǔgōng fell ill. As the medical practitioners had not yet achieved results, the official’s anxiety grew increasingly severe.

He encountered a monk on alms-round at his gate and invited him inside; the monk then took a vessel of water, held it in his mouth, and sprayed it upon him, whereupon the illness was immediately relieved.
Lord Lu was delighted and presented him with a generous array of gifts, yet he did not look back at them at all.
He then asked,
"In which monastery does the Master reside?"
He replied,
"I reside at Xilingyan Temple in Wu County, Suzhou. Since you,
young master, serve as an official in Jiangbiao, I hope you will visit the temple to seek me out."
A short while later he departed.
Not long after, he was appointed as a Ministerial Official (Lang) of the Ministry of Justice (Xingbu), and subsequently promoted to the Intendant of Guizhou.
He constantly remembered the monk who had saved his life many years prior; thus, he took a detour through Suzhou and entered Lingyan Temple to seek him out.
He then described the physical appearance [of the deity], to which the monks of the entire monastery replied,
"This is not among those we possess.
Lu lingered about the temple all day, unable to bear leaving, when he suddenly beheld the form of the Sage within the hall, who said:
"The monk who treated me years ago was this very same one," the temple monk said, recounting the circumstances; such a profound resonance is difficult to fathom.
Lu donated tens of thousands of coins to provide for the incense and lamps, and remained for ten days to offer sustenance before finally departing.

Furthermore, among the temple attendants (*śrāmaṇera*), there was one who would regularly inspect the candles and lamps before the images, adding oil and mending the wicks with the intent of stealing the oil to anoint his hair.

Before long, his hair became scorched, curled, and fell out. A bystander advised him to perform repentance rituals and purchase sesame oil to replenish the wicks; consequently, his hair returned to its former state.
Furthermore, when Emperor Wuzong was about to abolish Buddhism, there was a man named Lu Xuan who lived near a temple. He dreamed of a holy being who said to him:
"I have received the offerings and alms of my disciples for many years; now I come to bid you farewell and shall return to the Western Heaven."
He issued an urgent command for an artist to paint his true likeness.
It was only when the monasteries were demolished in the fifth year of the Huichang era that the meaning behind this act of taking leave was finally understood.

Seven years after the Xian Tong era, a locust plague occurred; at that time, they filled the skies and stretched across the fields, devouring people's crops until they even entered people's homes to eat silks and fabrics.
The common people were bewildered and knew not what course to take.

At that time, the citizens Wu Yanrang and others led several hundred elders to the front of the image, where they burned incense and wept as they made their plea; on that very day, the insects flew across the border.

In the fifth year of the Qiánfú era, the monastic community of the temple was due to travel to the imperial court to petition for a bell to be returned to the monastery; they selected a monk and set a date for the journey.
The Sage first entered the headquarters of the Right Shen-ce Army and presented his entrustment in advance.
When the monks arrived for the formal invitation bell, they encountered the administrative official, who asked in surprise:
"A few days ago, there was a monk who came and said he belonged to Lingyan Mountain Temple in Suzhou."
The monk said,
"I travel without companions.
Later, Xu of the Right Army (Wang Xizhi) was traveling in Wu on business and saw a mural painted on a wall that said:
"This was a monk who had previously come to the office during the seventh month to calculate the bells.
Yet, such manifestations of spiritual efficacy were most prominent in the region of Wu, and their underlying causes remained unfathomable.
Once, a monk from India came and prostrated before the painted image, asking,
"By what karmic affinity has the Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa come to be here?
He sighed and marveled for a very long time, and from that point on, the image was titled the "Manifestation Body of Jñānakūṭa."
The commentary states:

Regarding the accounts of identity and difference, historians have often provided many such details. Now, to examine them in detail: that the temple is called Lingyan and the monk’s portrait is there—this constitutes their identity.
That the prefectures are called Lixia and Gusu, and that those encountered were named Lu and Feng—this constitutes their difference.
This is because what was seen and heard was not uniform, and thus the records differ.

To examine the nature of the Sage’s responsive manifestations: they appear sometimes in the south and sometimes in the north, sometimes among the Han and sometimes among the Hu; they may take ordinary forms or extraordinary appearances. Consequently, what is heard and seen must necessarily vary, and as these accounts are transmitted and propagated, it is natural that many different versions arise.
It is like looking at the sun and moon from a thousand li away; they appear identical from that distance, yet their surrounding clouds and atmospheric forms differ.
Since these are inconceivable manifestations, they respond to conditions and accord with stimuli, such that it is difficult for them to be the same.
One may cite an example, saying:
"What has been transmitted differs in its wording.
This is the *Biography of Shi Huizhao of Kaiyuan Temple in Wuling, Tang*. Regarding Shi Huizhao of Kaiyuan Temple in Wuling, Tang: it is not known where he was from.

As a monk, his character was eccentric and lofty; he constantly practiced meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), and his appearance was somewhat emaciated and frail. He delighted in speaking of people's joys and sorrows, and his predictions invariably proved accurate.
When conversing with others, he was neither familiar nor intimate.
He lived in seclusion behind closed doors, with no attendants at his side.
Each day he went out to beg for food; a villager over eighty years old remarked:
"Zhao has resided here for over sixty years, yet his appearance remains no different from that of his youth.
However, his age in sexagenary cycles was unknown.
During the Yuanhe era, there was a man named Chen Guang who, having been appointed as an official in Wuling through the status of a Xiaolian, was a fervent admirer of the Buddha.
One day, while visiting a temple and seeking out various monks, Daozhao saw Daoguang;
moved by both grief and joy, he said, "Master Chen, why have you come so late?"
Guang was startled and reflected that he had never known this monk in his life; how could the monk say he had come late?
He then said, "I have never traveled with you, Master; why do you reproach me for being late?"
Zhaor said, "This is not something that can be discussed in haste; I shall speak with you at leisure for one night, and only then will I fully express this meaning.
Guang was greatly astonished and, at a later time, went to stay overnight with Zhaor to request the details of the matter.
Zhao said, "I am a scion of the Liu clan, the great-grandson of Emperor Xiaowen of the Song dynasty.
My great-great-grandfather, Prince of Poyang Ye Xie, and my grandfather, Shi Hong, are both recorded in detail by the historians."
My late father was proud of his literary talent and was well known to Prince Ziliang of Qi.
When Prince Ziliang gathered together men of exceptional ability and literary refinement, my father was among those invited.
Later, he served during the Qi and Liang dynasties as the Magistrate of Kuaiji.

I was born in the fifth month of the summer in the seventh year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty; it was only at the age of thirty that I entered government service under the Chen dynasty. During the reign of Emperor Xuan, I held a low-ranking post and remained unknown to others, befriending only Shen Yanwen through poetry and wine.

Later, Prince Shujian of Changsha and Prince Shuling of Shixing both gathered many guests and cultivated a great reputation; each relied on their own power and favor, harboring a sense of resentment toward one another.
Wu and Yanwen were both disciples under Changsha. When Shu Ling was executed, I feared I could not escape the same fate;

consequently, we both silenced ourselves and hid our traces within the forested valleys. We gathered acorns and chestnuts for food and cupped water from mountain streams for drink, wearing a single short tunic that we did not change regardless of cold or heat, while awaiting the resolution of our anxieties.
Before long, an elderly śramaṇa came to my dwelling and said, "The constitution of your bones is most extraordinary; you shall surely be free from illness.
Yanwen bowed twice and requested his medicine, saying:
"If you do not possess the longevity of Lord Liu, what can be done?
Even though you take my medicine, it will be of no benefit.
Having said this, he took his leave and was about to depart when he spoke to me again:
"The secular world competes for fame and profit; in the end, what substance is there?
Only the teachings of Śākyamuni can allow one to renounce these things.
He respectfully accepted these words and, from that time on, he withdrew from worldly affairs for fifteen years.
He then went with Yanwen to Jianye; at that time, the Chen dynasty had already fallen, and the palaces were completely destroyed.

The Tai City was desolate, with thorny brambles blocking the roads; the Jingshang Terrace was overgrown and the foundations of the Jieqi Pavilion had collapsed. All cultural artifacts, robes, and caps had been swept away in total ruin.
Thus, when the elders met, they took one another’s hands and wept, saying:
"If the misconduct of a single individual has led to this state of affairs, how truly lamentable it is that the Sui dynasty has been destroyed!"
I further heard that the Later Lord and various other kings had all entered Chang’an; thereupon, I took a single bag and begged for food along the road until I reached Guāngzhōng.
I was formerly a guest of Prince Chángshā, who treated me with great kindness and favor. Hearing that he had been transferred to Guāzhou, I went directly there to pay my respects.
The Prince of Changsha grew up in fine silks and satins and attained high status and prosperity early in life; even during his period of exile, he did not attend to his livelihood.
At that time, he was in the midst of drinking heavily with Consort Shen.
I and Shen bowed twice before him; Changsha was overcome with grief and, after a long time, rose while shedding tears. He then said to me:
"In a single day, our family and state have perished and our kin have been scattered; is this not the work of Heaven?"
"From that time on, I remained at the frontier of the Jin-chang Di and Qiang tribes.

After several years, Changsha passed away; another few years later, Yanwen died. Thereupon, I shaved my head to become a monk and took refuge in a Buddhist temple on Mount Kuaiji for twenty years, by which time I was already one hundred years old."
Although his physical frame was emaciated, his strength did not decline;
he could still travel a hundred li a day.
Consequently, he traveled to Chang’an with a certain monk at a time when Emperor Gaozu of the Tang already possessed the empire and had established the reign title Wǔdé.

In the sixth year, I departed from here, sometimes residing in the capitals of Jing and Luo, and sometimes traveling through the region east of the Yangtze; from the Three Shu to the Five Ling, there was no place where I did not dwell. It has now been nearly two hundred and ninety years.
Despite the intense cold and scorching heat, he never suffered even the slightest ailment.
Toward the end of the Zhenyuan era, while at this temple, he dreamed of a man whose robes and cap were most magnificent; upon looking closely, it was Changsha.
I welcomed him and invited him to sit; we conversed about our past with such poignant emotion as if it were only yesterday.
He then said to me:
"Ten years hence, my sixth-generation descendant Guang shall hold office in this commandery; may you, Master, keep him in your thoughts."
He then asked him, saying:
"What is the King doing now?
He replied:
"The Lord of the Netherworld is most venerable.
Having said this, he wept again, saying:
"That my Master was alive during my sixth generation—how tragic!"

Since I awoke from that dream, I have recorded your name within my collection of scriptures; ten years have passed until last year, yet when I inquired among the people of the commandery regarding your name and lineage, I still marveled at your failure to arrive.
Yesterday, while begging for alms in the village, I encountered a local official who was searching for you, and indeed found you there.
When you arrived today, you still bore that same appearance from Changsha.
"Yet from that dream until now, eleven years have passed!
Therefore, I was surprised by your belated arrival.
Having said this, he was overcome with grief and sorrow, shedding several rows of tears, and then brought out his scripture chest to show it to him.
Guang bowed twice and requested, "I wish to hold your shoes and receive the staff as your disciple.
Zhao said, "You may depart for now; you should return on the following day."
Having received these extensive instructions, he returned; the next day he went to his residence, but [the Master] had already vanished, with no one knowing where he had gone.
This was in the eleventh year of the Yuanhe era.
At the beginning of the Dahe era, Guang served as an official scribe in Bazhou. While traveling on the roads of Shan-nan, he encountered Zhao;
filled with joy and surprise, he prostrated himself twice and said, "I wish to resign my office and request to follow you, Master, for travels beyond the mundane world."
Zhao also consented, and that evening they stayed together in an inn.
When dawn was approaching, Guang rose early to find that Zhao had already departed.
Guang felt as if he had lost something of great importance; his spirit was despondent and defeated, and from then on, he had no idea where Zhao had gone.

Thus, Zhaolai was born in the seventh year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, when the year was Bingwu; from then until the tenth year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, which was Yiwei, a total of two hundred and ninety years had passed, at which point his words accorded with [the historical record] as perfectly as two halves of a tally.
The commentary states:

Since Huizhao has already remained in this world for three hundred years, his past is unfathomable and his future is boundless; he is of one essence with the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja. Why, then, not consider him a descendant of the lineage of the Land of Gratitude?
Tong said:
"Immortals are separated from us by a single speck of dust, yet one cannot yet roam with them.

Furthermore, Guang is a commoner bound by all fetters, while Zhao is a superior man who has transcended the world; a soaring kite and a fish in the deep are worlds apart in their tracks—what is there to wonder at?"
Biography of Chan Master Tang’an: Chan Master Shi’an was a native of Bingzhou. He took the Pure Land as his true place of refuge.
He practiced the Vaipulya repentance rites with diligent devotion and without fail.

Even when slightly ill, he did not neglect his meditative contemplations; he beheld the two Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta appearing in the sky, remaining there for a long time without fading away.

The Prefect summoned painters from within his jurisdiction, but none were capable of painting it. Suddenly, two men appeared, saying they had come from the Western Capital and intended to go to Mount Wutai; they offered their services willingly to provide their labor.
Having completed the painting of the Bodhisattva’s form and features, he presented him with two pairs of shoes, which suddenly vanished without a trace.
Knowing that his karmic conditions for rebirth in the West were ripe, Huian told his disciples:
"I am now to be reborn there; who among you would like to go along?"
A young boy prostrated himself with his forehead to the ground and said, "I wish to follow my teacher.

He was then sent to take leave of his parents; they took it as idle talk, yet they had him bathe, dress in clean robes, enter the dharma hall to recite the Buddha's name, and he passed away shortly thereafter.
Daoshan rebuked him, saying,
"How can you go on ahead?
At that time, Daoshan took up his brush and composed a hymn in praise of the two Bodhisattvas:

"Avalokiteśvara assists from afar to receive them; Mahāsthāmaprāpta aids from the distance to welcome them. The precious vase is manifest upon the crown; the transformation Buddhas are clear before the usnīṣa.
Together they travel through the lands of the ten directions, holding flowers and awaiting the nine births."
"I pray that with your hands of compassion, you will lift me up and travel together toward the West.

Having offered this praise, he took leave of his disciples and entered the meditation hall. He commanded his followers to assist him in reciting the Buddha's name, and sitting upright, he passed away at the age of eighty.
This was the seventh day of the first month in the first year of the Chuigong era.

Regarding the *Biography of the Later Monk Hui* from Yongxin Temple in Kuaiji, Tang: The monk known as the Later Monk Hui was originally a native of the kingdom of Kangju. During the Zhishu era of the Wu dynasty, he presented himself before the Great Emperor (Sun Quan).
Initially, the people of Wu did not recognize the form of a monk, regarding him merely as a "Hu" person entering their borders.
Only after he prayed for śarīra did he cause the Emperor to attain awakening.
In the fourth year of the Tianji era of the last ruler, he attained the "corpse-liberation" (śi-jie), and his true body vanished.

During the Yonghui era of Emperor Gaozong of the Tang dynasty, he appeared in person in Yue, claiming to be a wandering monk (*yóufāng-sēng*). His spirit and appearance were extraordinary: his eyebrows were high, his nose prominent, his chin sharp, and his eyes azure; he was emaciated yet revealed marvelous skeletal structure—truly the countenance of a *brahman*.
Those who saw him were struck with awe, for they knew nothing of his rank or station.
At that time, the monastery officials investigated the matter and, having rebuked him, drove him away.
When Huixing reached the gate, they spoke to him, saying:
"I am Kang Senghui; if you can preserve my true remains, it will bring blessing to your monastery.
Within the space of a few steps, he stood and his breath ceased.
Shortly thereafter, his blue eyes were slightly closed, yet his spirit remained undiminished; he raised his hands as if to receive a greeting and shifted his feet as if about to walk.
The assembly discussed laying his sacred body down and interring it in the tomb, but though human effort was exhausted, the image did not budge in the slightest.
Although his physical body was robust, it was nonetheless treated with great care, being moved to a superior location where a magnificent hall was specially erected for him.

At that time, the people of Yue vied with one another to offer incense, flowers, lamps, silk fabrics, banners, canopies, fruits, and vessels, seeking the fulfillment of their heart's desires; most of these prayers were granted according to their wishes.

Initially, Yue’s military forces were mostly stationed at Yongxin Temple; the births of their womenfolk and the presence of the soldiers' meat and blood defiled the monastic precincts, making it unbearable for people to endure such filth.
Hui then transformed his form and went to visit Li Ruochu, the Intendant of Min, saying:
"Your Excellency will soon take charge of the administration of Yue, while I shall entrust myself to the military affairs of Qian."
Having finished speaking, he brushed off his robes and departed, soon losing his trace.
Master Li was both delighted and startled; he recorded those words, and later, as it turned out, [the monk] indeed went to that commandery.
When the aforementioned matters were concluded, he visited the sacred site; the one who had spoken those words at that time was none other than this monk.
[The Emperor] ordered the military camp to be dismantled and commanded him to proceed to the tented quarters.
Furthermore, there was once a common woman who, while approaching her time of labor at night, had neither oil nor a lamp, and not even a sliver of light from a neighbor’s house reached her.
Suddenly, a monk entered through the window holding a lamp.

When her husband went to the Yongxin Monastery the following morning, he recognized the monk’s appearance; it was the very same monk who had provided the fire to save her from the perils of childbirth.
From that time on, many people in the secular world sought her for the sake of obtaining sons and daughters.
During the Huichang persecution when Yongxin was destroyed, only the present Dashi remained, being renamed Kaiyuan; she subsequently moved her body into this temple.
After Dazhong, the Vinaya Master Tanxiu established a separate hall for the assembly and expanded its ritual implements.

He once went among the common households to beg for straw sandals; to this day, many people in Yue offer them along with oil-fans as offerings. His spiritual responses have been so manifest that they reach every household, beyond what can be fully described.
He is now titled the Great Master Chao-hua.
From the Yonghui era until the present, offerings and alms have never been lacking for him.
The śramaṇa Xushou has composed this stele inscription to record his life.
The commentary states:
Cai Yong was the reincarnation of Zhang Heng, and Zhiwei was originally the former life of Xu Ling; these verifications are all clear and manifest, and their principles are not empty.
As for the sovereign functioning of the Sage, he perishes here and appears there, his manifestation of benefit being without fixed direction.
Since Senghui passed away long ago, his transformation has spread throughout the Tang and Yue regions; he stands firm even in death, a marvel among marvels.
Were it not for one who manifests form in response to beings like the moon in water, who could have anticipated this?
Biography of Daoying of Fahai Temple in Jingzhao, Tang Dynasty Shi Daoying was a man of unknown origins.
His observance of the precepts and his virtuous character were perfectly complete, and his fame resounded throughout the capital. He resided at Fahai Temple in Buzheng Ward.
During the Xianheng era, he saw a ghostly apparition. The temple master Huijian once said:
"At dawn, I saw two people walking without their feet touching the ground as they entered Ying’s quarters.
Huijian questioned them in wonder, and Ying replied:

"Previously, King Zhuangxiang of Qin sent an envoy with a message: 'We have been suffering from hunger for a very long time. Because you possess great compassion, we hope you will grant us food for ourselves and three hundred followers; do not decline this labor.'"
I replied to him, "Tomorrow morning I shall prepare a meal; you may come specifically to wait for me.
When Jian heard this, he said that wine would assist in the matter.
When the appointed time arrived, the fruit came; his attendants were very numerous and the seating was grand, yet he ate in haste and said to Huìyīng, "I have not eaten for eighty years.
When Huìyīng asked the reason for this, he replied:
"Since my birth, I have never committed an offense without cause; yet, I have brought about the destruction of Eastern Zhou and the extinction of the Ji lineage.

Some may hold me accountable for this based on my merit, but in my daily life I have possessed no Buddhist teachings with which to repent and save others. I have sought to compensate for this only through pardons, clemency, and compassion for the orphaned and solitary, but in the end, these have remained insufficient."
"Because your merit is slight while your transgressions are many, the retribution for them is not yet exhausted.
For this single meal now, you shall have to wait another forty years before you can eat again.
Thereupon, he pointed successively at those seated upon the mats, saying:
"This is Bai Qi and Wang Jian; because they committed so many killings, the retribution for their sins has not yet ended.
It further states:
"This is Chen Zhen, on account of his deceit and falsehood."
Ying said, "Why does Your Majesty not seek food from others instead of contenting yourself with an empty stomach? How can this be endured?
The King replied:
"Those with a compassionate heart are few, and others do not see one another.
Because I am associated with a person of noble status, I cannot recklessly inflict calamities; this is why it is so.
Ying pointed to the wine and said:
"The Abbot Jian Gong was about to present [the offering]," [Seng]shen said with deep remorse.
As he was about to leave, he said to Sengying:
"I am deeply grateful for this visit, though it has caused me great expense and fatigue; you may know that I have a small item which I shall send to repay you.
Outside Tonghwam Gate to the east of the city, there is a pointed tomb—so called because its summit is sharp and high—which is the place where my spirit resides."
The people of the world do not know this, and falsely claim it is the tomb of Lü Buwei.
Ying said, “In the past,
when it was excavated by the Red Eyebrows, what objects were found?”
He replied,
"The thief could not take it.
Ying said:
"I am no Lord Qiu who excavates burial mounds; I am a renunciant. I have no use for such things, so do not bring them here by any means.
Having said this, he gave a long bow and departed.
Moved by such profound inspiration, he followed this path until his end, remaining unaware of its ultimate conclusion.
**Biography of Fa-xiu of Jingzhao during the Tang Dynasty** As for the monk Fa-xiu of Jingzhao: it is not clearly known where he was from.

Residing at the capital temple, he traveled between the regions of Xian and Hao, encouraging and leading various devotees to accomplish many virtuous deeds, never ceasing or becoming lax until his old age.
At the end of the Kaiyuan era, he dreamed that someone said to him:
"Take five hundred handkerchiefs and five hundred monastic robes and offer them as alms at Huixiang Temple.
Upon waking, he asked those around him, but they all replied that there was no such place as Huixiang Temple.
He then recruited people to manufacture towels and robes, and further inquired everywhere among the elderly monastics and laypeople as to whether there was such a monastery [as that].
At that time, there was a monk of imposing stature whom no one recognized;
he replied, "I know the location of the Huixiang Monastery."
When asked what was required, including companions and other necessities, he replied:
"It will suffice simply to bring the items to be offered and one *jin* of famous incense."
He then followed these instructions and handed over the items, traveling together with Xiu.
The monk went straight into Zhongnan Mountain; after traveling for two days, they reached a place of extreme depth and steepness where nothing could initially be seen.
Proceeding further, he saw a set of millstones and exclaimed in surprise, "This place is inaccessible to human footsteps; how can such things be here?
He then burned the incense he had brought upon them, offering repeated prostrations and lamentations from noon until evening.

The valley was shrouded in mist that submerged everything, such that one could not distinguish objects even a few feet away; after a brief hesitation, the sky cleared, revealing between the cliffs a vermilion gate with plastered walls, green windows with carved titles, fluttering banners on the stupa, and the straight shadows of the eaves and ridges of the pavilions.
After a short while, he saw a temple clearly appearing on the edge of the clouds; it had three gates, and a large plaque hung above them inscribed with the words "Huixiang Temple.
Xiu and the monk were overjoyed and climbed up until they reached it. It was already dusk, yet they heard the sounds of bells, chimes, and the chanting of *sādhana* mantras.

The gatekeeper questioned him regarding his origins; after he hesitated for a moment, he was led inside to see an elderly monk. After the monk had comforted him with repeated inquiries, he spoke out, saying:
"Is the Emperor of Tang in good health?"
He gave orders that they be accompanied by other monks to inspect the rooms, distributing hand towels and *kāṣāya* robes until only one portion remained.
He pointed to an empty bed in a room where no one was present, yet clothes and mats were there, suggesting someone had recently departed.
Shortly thereafter, they saw an old monk— who appeared to be a leader among them— say,
"The one who went out must have already returned.
That monk and Xiu then wished to go back there to hand over the towels and other items.
"In one room there is only an empty bed; there is no one there either.
When he spoke thus in detail, the old monk smiled and motioned him to sit. Looking into that room, the monk took a *shichibashiku* (bamboo flute) and brought it out; it was a jade *shichibashiku*.
The old monk said,
"Do you see that foreign monk?
He replied:
Having seen him, he said,
"This is one who will come to temporarily replace your master."
"The capital shall fall into chaos, and countless people will die.
This barbarian is named King Annihilation (Mowmie Wang).
That one room is the chamber of your lord."
"Your master was in the temple; because he played the *shichiku* flute out of attachment, he has been punished by being sent into the human world. This is the very instrument he constantly plays.
Now his term of punishment is nearly over, and he will soon return."
The next day, he sent him to attend the vegetarian feast. When the feast was concluded, he said:
"You should return; you may take this rāvaṇahasta flute, along with the kashaya robe and hand towel, and give them to your master to keep himself."
Xiu prostrated himself and returned; the youth escorted him out for only a few dozen paces before clouds and mist closed in from all sides, and the temple could no longer be seen.
Xiu then presented the handkerchief, the *kāṣāya*, and the jade flute to the Emperor. The Emperor summoned him for an audience, and Xiu recounted the entire sequence of events in detail.
The Emperor was deeply moved and delighted; he concentrated his spirit for a long time and took up the flute to play it, finding it to be exactly the one he had previously used.
A few years later, the calamity of Lu Shan indeed occurred; the barbarian monk whom Xiu had seen was none other than Lu Shan himself.
Xiu was moved by what he encountered; his diligence became redoubled and more earnest, such that no one knew his ultimate end.
According to tradition, there was also a dedication [of merit] at the Sacred Temple on Mount Zhongnan.
The colophon says:

In the past, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty sent a *kāṣāya* robe to a mountain by the sea; Fashou visited Huixiang Temple; and the Yan dynasty commissioned an envoy to seek out Zhulin Shengsi. These three instances differ in name but are one in substance. Could it be that they were merely modified versions of one another, like cutting off the neck of a crane to lengthen the legs of a duck?
Tong said:
"The creations of the sages are like building a carriage inside a gate and joining its tracks outside; even across thousands of miles, the principles accord because there is no divergent path."
Thus, it is like the woodcutter who watched the immortals play chess; that the axe handle rotted away was not limited to Wang Qi alone.
There have been many others who encountered the game, for their names differ, and those whose axe handles rotted were not just one.
"Now, the many robes sent to the Shengsi Temple are also like this.
Biography of Shi Puming of Longxing Temple in Huazhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Puming was a person of unknown origin; some say he was a monk from the Western Regions.
Whenever he discussed the methods of Chan, he would expound upon the profound and subtle mysteries; who could fathom the depth and loftiness of his silent transcendence!
At the beginning of the Dali era, at the request of people from Zu County, he resided in an araṇya (hermitage), where students gathered like ants.
As he traveled among the common people, laypeople would pay him homage and offer alms, numbering in the thousands each day.

Sometimes, merely upon seeing his appearance, people would naturally restrain their anger and suppress their desires; like those who eat the *zhèn* fruit while remembering its sound, they followed what was good and reformed their evils. By the year’s end, such instances were beyond counting.

Jia Dan, the Right Vice President of the Secretariat and Military Governor of Yicheng Command—originally a reprobate immortal—was at ease in the study of the Way and followed the broad principles of the Empty Gate (Buddhism).
The moment he beheld him, it was as if Yang Hu had recognized his old ring, or Cai Shun had seen his compassionate mother.
He humbled himself to invite him to reside at the state temple; the entire city turned out to welcome him, leaving not a single person remaining in the streets.
Because of this, he preached the Dharma for others, never weary even in old age.
His gait was as swift as the wind, and his physical appearance remained light and vigorous.

On the tenth day of the intercalary twelfth month in the eighth year of the Zhenyuan era (the Ren-shen year), he entrusted his disciples with final instructions and suddenly passed away while sitting in meditation.
It is said that he was either three hundred years old at birth, as those who were a hundred years old had seen him and his countenance remained unchanged.
According to the Indian custom of cremation, twenty-eight *śarīra* relics were collected.
Jiangu Yuanming. Qunxin established a stupa in the meditation courtyard where Ming resided, and later Ming moved his seat beneath that stupa.

Ten years after Ming’s passing, the royal army launched a western campaign to pacify the frontier; there was a man from Huai named Chai Qing, who was both talented and brave, and he went on reconnaissance against the Xiongnu, penetrating deep into their encampment.
As the patrols were numerous, they lay hidden by day and moved at night; they lost their sense of direction and became disoriented, unable to distinguish between the circuitous and the direct paths.
Qingjian saw clearly and led the way with clarity, acting like an old horse leading the way.
Upon arriving in the capital of Hanseong (Hansung), he suddenly vanished.
He returned to the state and paid homage at the stupa; this was reported far and wide.
*Song Gaoseng Zhuan*, Volume 18.
Biographies of Eminent Monks Compiled in the Song Dynasty, Volume Nineteen.

Part Two of the "Chapter on Responsive Communion," Section Six, Part Two: Twenty-one Main Biographies with Eight Supplementary Accounts. The Biography of Pòzào Duò of Mount Song in the Tang Dynasty. Regarding the monk Pòzào Duò, it is unknown where he was from.

During the reign of Empress Wu, he attended upon Master An of Mount Song—known as Lao’an—and attained profound mastery of the Chan teachings. He wandered freely without constraint; though one constantly sought him, his presence could not be found, and though one pursued him along divergent paths, no one could catch up to him from behind.

I once encountered a woman of the Wu clan who was able to perform rites for the hearth and offer exorcisms for others, much like Li Shaojun during the era of Emperor Wu of Han, who claimed that by worshipping the hearth one could summon material objects; the two cases were identical in this regard.

Whenever he performed his musical compositions, the forms and omens of ghosts and spirits were frequently seen; the people of the neighborhood became terrified one after another, and as the story spread among the masses, those who slaughtered young oxen and sheep to offer sacrifices to him did so in great numbers.

They revere the Lord of the Hearth, surrounding him with banners and canopies; he is kept secret and rarely seen—is this not what Yangzi meant when he said, "The majesty of a sacred site should be experienced at night"?
At that time, Shi Du went to visit him; having first exhorted the shaman and finally preached the Dharma to the spirit, he told him:
"Having heard the Master's teaching, I am certain to be reborn in heaven."
Thereupon, he manifested his form, paid obeisance, and said by way of farewell:
"Having been guided by my teacher’s instructions, I have gained profound benefit and shall be reborn in a most excellent heaven.
Having spoken, he vanished; the hearth was actually a shrine to a deity, which immediately crumbled into ruins of its own accord, not through human effort.

People near and far were struck with amazement; as this master had never previously been known by name, he consequently adopted another’s name entirely and was called "Puo-zao-duo" (The One Who Broke the Oven and Fell).
Biography of Yuan Gui of Xianju Monastery on Mount Song, Tang Dynasty. Shi Yuan Gui, surnamed Li, was a native of Yique.

Endowed with an extraordinary spirit and a disposition that was broad-minded, leisurely, and refined, he resolved to leave the household life due to his past karmic predispositions.
