In the second year of the Yongchun era, he attained full ordination and was subsequently enrolled at Xianju Monastery.
Having practiced the Vinaya, he was diligent and tireless, upholding the discipline with unwavering firmness.

Later, he realized the Chan school of Shaolin Temple, thoroughly penetrating its essential principles and delving deeply into its profound mysteries; he subsequently chose to build a hermitage at Pangwu within the mountain range.
He said to his disciple Rensu:
"When I first lived, I resided on the eastern ridge of this temple.
After my passing, you must enshrine my remains here in a stupa."
Senggui settled in seclusion among the crags and ravines.

At that time, there appeared a man wearing a high cap and trousers with pleated skirts, accompanied by a large retinue of attendants; he moved with light steps and composed grace, announcing his arrival to pay his respects to the Great Master.
Observing that the man’s appearance was imposing and his spirit exceptionally refined, Senggui said to him:
"Welcome, O worthy one! Why have you come?
He replied, "Do you not recognize me, Master?"
Guī said, "I regard the Buddha and sentient beings as equal; I view them all with a single eye—how could I discriminate or recognize them individually?
He replied:
"I am a mountain deity of this peak.
I can bring benefit or harm regarding the life and death of men; how could you, Master, presume to look upon me?
Guī replied:
"You can cause others to be born and die, but I am fundamentally unborn; how then could you cause me to die?
I regard my body as equal to space, and I regard myself as equal to you; can you destroy space or yourself?"
If you can destroy emptiness and destroy yourself, then I shall neither arise nor cease.
Since you cannot even do this much, how could you possibly bring me to birth or death?
The mountain deity bowed his head and prostrated twice, saying:
"I am also intelligent and upright compared to other deities; how could I have known that you, Master, possess such vast wisdom and eloquence?"
"I pray that you bestow upon him the true precepts so that he may transcend the world and assist in his majesty and blessings.
Guī replied,
"Since the deity has already requested the precepts, he is already ordained."
"Why is this? Outside of precepts there are no precepts; what, then, are precepts?
The spirit said:
"I have heard of this principle with a sense of vast obscurity; I merely seek a teacher to instruct my person as a gate-disciple.
Unable to decline, Huigu set out a seat, burned incense, held the censer, and straightened the desk, saying:
"I confer upon you the five precepts. If you can uphold them, then answer 'Yes' to what was said before."
"If you cannot, then say 'no.
The Spirit said,
"Wash your ears to listen attentively, and empty your mind to receive the teaching."
Gui said, "Are you able to refrain from sexual misconduct?
The spirit replied:
"He has also taken a wife.
[The Master] said:
"I do not mean this; I mean that he is free from lustful desires."
The deity said, "I can. He asked:
"Are you able to refrain from stealing?
The spirit replied, "How could I be in want? Why would I take anything by theft?"
He replied, "I do not mean this;
I mean that [the gods] bestow blessings upon the licentious when they are feasted, and bring calamity upon the virtuous when they are not provided for.
The spirit said:
"I can," [he] said. [The Master] asked,
"Can you refrain from killing?"
The spirit said,
"When the reins of government rest upon one's person, how can one say 'I do not kill'?
He replied:
"It is not that I mean this; I mean that there is confusion, error, and doubt. Shen said, "I can."
He asked,
"Can you refrain from falsehood?
The spirit replied:
"I have always been upright; how could I possibly harbor falsehood?
[The Master] said, "I do not mean this. I mean that your actions before and after were inconsistent with the Will of Heaven."
The spirit said, “I can. He asked:
"Can you withstand the ruinous effects of wine?
The spirit replied,
"I am capable."
Guī said: "The above constitutes the Buddha's precepts.
He further stated:
"To maintain with a mind yet to be without the mind's clinging;
to act for the sake of others with a mind yet to have thoughts of self.

One who can do thus is born before heaven and earth without being called 'essence,' dies after heaven and earth without being called 'old age,' undergoes transformation all day long without being called 'movement,' and reaches ultimate stillness without being called 'rest.'"

Upon awakening to this, though one marries, it is not as taking a wife; though one feasts, it is not as receiving offerings; though one holds office, it is not as wielding power; though one acts, it is not as following old habits; though one is intoxicated, it is not as being in a stupor.

If one can be without mind regarding the myriad things, then indulging in desires will not constitute lust; that fortune favors the lewd and calamity strikes the virtuous will not constitute theft; that errors, confusions, and doubts prevail will not constitute killing; that preceding and succeeding actions violate Heaven will not constitute falsehood; and that being muddled, desolate, and inverted will not constitute intoxication. This is called being without mind. Where there is no mind, there are no precepts; where there are no precepts, there is no mind. There is no Buddha and no sentient beings; there is neither you nor me. When there is neither me nor you, who is there to observe the precepts?
The deity said,
"My spiritual powers are second only to the Buddha's.
Guī replied:
“You possess ten phrases regarding supernatural powers: five capacities and five incapacities.
The Buddha, however, possesses ten phrases: seven capacities and three incapacities.
Shen was struck with awe and withdrew from his seat; kneeling with great reverence, he said:
"May I hear it? [The Master] said:
"Can you cause the Supreme Lord to turn back, so that the heavens move eastward while the seven luminaries move westward?"
He replied, "I cannot.
Again he asked:
"Are you able to seize the Earth Goddess, melt the Five Sacred Peaks, and bind the Four Seas?
He replied, "I cannot."
Shui Gui said,
"This constitutes the fifth inability.
He spoke again:
“The Buddha can empty all marks and achieve the wisdom of all phenomena, yet he cannot immediately extinguish fixed karma.
The Buddha can know the nature of all beings and exhaustively comprehend events across billions of kalpas, yet he cannot transform or guide those who lack the karmic affinity.”
The Buddha can deliver immeasurable sentient beings, yet he cannot exhaust the realm of sentient beings.
This is the third "inability. Even fixed karma is not eternal;
even in the absence of conditions, it is said to last for one lifetime. The realm of sentient beings is fundamentally without increase or decrease.
Throughout all time, there has never been a single person who can take charge of existing phenomena.
When existing phenomena have no one to preside over them, this is called the non-existence of phenomena.
When there are no phenomena and no presiding subject, this is called the absence of mind.

As I understand the Buddha, he likewise possesses no supernatural powers (*abhijñā*); rather, it is simply through the penetration of all phenomena with a mind of non-activity that his manifestations appear mysteriously before sentient beings.
"If there is mind and there is action, the operation of that action will necessarily not be all-pervasive.

The mountain deity said, "I am truly shallow and ignorant, having not yet heard the meaning of emptiness. I pray that you, Master, will bestow the precepts upon me; I shall faithfully practice them. Furthermore, what karmic cause could then bind me to this dusty world?"
"I wish to repay your compassionate virtue by doing what I am capable of!
Kui said, "I contemplate the body as being without substance and observe impermanence; the Dharma-cave is utterly empty—what further desire could there be?"

The spirit said, "Master must surely command me to perform a worldly feat to display my minor divine powers, so that five types of people—those who have already resolved their minds, those newly resolved, those not yet resolved, those without faith, and those with certain faith—may behold my spiritual traces and know that there are Buddhas and spirits; that there is capability and incapability; and that there is the spontaneous and the non-spontaneous."
Gui said: "Non-action is this; non-action is this. Shen said:
"The Buddha also commanded divine beings to protect the Dharma; how could you, Master, possibly rebel against the Buddha?
Please grant me your instruction as you see fit.
Guī, having no other choice, spoke:
“The eastern cliff is the screen for the temple—it is vast and treeless.
While there are trees on the northern peak, its back is not shielded or enclosed.
Can you move the trees from the north to the eastern ridge?”
The spirit said,
"I have received your command.
Chen spoke again:
"I shall certainly appear amidst the wind and thunder of a dark night, tossing and shaking with a great resonance; I pray that you, Master, will not be startled.
Having spoken thus, he performed his prostrations with great solemnity and took his leave.
As Guī saw him off at the gate, he watched him depart and beheld his ceremonial retinue winding along like the procession of a sovereign.

Furthermore, emerald mists and crimson clouds, purple vapors and white breaths, intermingled and dispersed in all directions; banners, canopies, and jeweled girdles, along with ranks of spears and halberds, soared high into the void, vanishing into the profound distance.

That evening, as expected, there arose a violent wind with thundering peals, rushing clouds, and crashing lightning. The lofty ridgepoles and stately halls shook violently, on the verge of collapse. The settled monks looked on in alarm; the nesting birds cried out wildly, clashing against one another, as all things found no place of rest.
He then said to the assembly of monks, "Do not fear, do not fear; the deity has entered into a covenant with me.
At dawn the next day, when the sky was clear and bright, all the pines and cypresses from the northern cliff had been moved to the eastern ridge, standing there in dense, orderly rows.
Guī said to his disciples, "After my death, do not let outsiders know;
if they have something to talk about, people will treat me as a supernatural being.
On the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era, the year of Bingchen, he entrusted his affairs to his disciples and passed away like a sloughed-off shell.
At seventy-three years of age,
he subsequently constructed a stupa on the eastern ridge of the mountain, while his portrait hall remains within this very monastery.
Twelve years later, Xu Chou, the County尉 (Commandant), commemorated Guī’s virtue by composing a memorial inscription.
Biography of Shi Huifu of Tianzhu Monastery on Mount Qian in Lujiang, Tang Dynasty. Shi Huifu, surnamed Qi, was a native of Zhuji in Yuezhou.
Upon reaching the age of twenty, his courage surpassed that of others; in wrestling and racing, none could equal him.

However, he was a man of chivalrous spirit who grew weary of domestic life; suddenly, he entered Xiangyan Temple, where he rectified his conduct and softened his heart, undergoing a complete transformation into one of pure and virtuous character.
After receiving the Dharma, he refined his practice with solitary distinction.
Every night he would go along the mountain and sit upon a grass mat, remaining unmoving in dhyāna.

He further studied the sūtras and śāstras, and saw Mount Huo in Qian County—a place where Emperor Wu of Han once relocated the sacrificial rites of the Southern Peak—which was an exceptionally sublime site.
Among them, Tianzhu Temple was suitable for dwelling in spiritual seclusion, so he constructed a hermitage there to reside.
Not long after, a giant serpent appeared with its mouth agape, emitting blazing, poisonous flames.
Fu spoke to Xu in a low voice, saying:
"If you seek to repay your past debts, I may devour you.
Otherwise, cleanse your body and steady your mind; if your karmic destiny is favorable, come to receive the precepts."
After a short while, Mi’an departed in a winding gait; he indeed transformed into human form and came to seek ordination.
Fu shaved his head for him and bestowed the robes upon him; having completed the reception of the precepts, he paid his respects, took his leave, and withdrew.
Later, when Fu was accused of having crossed the border privately, he presented the facts in his defense. Fu said,
"If I am guilty of crossing privately, I am willing to accept the punishment."
The officials, knowing that this was extraordinary, allowed him to leave.
Whenever Fu saw sores or abscesses with pus flowing from them, he would recite incantations over them, and they would all heal.
In the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, he passed away without illness.
He was subsequently cremated, and the appearance of his bone joints remaining interconnected was observed.
This is the biography of Shi Hui’an of Ximing Monastery in Chang’an during the Tang Dynasty. As for Shi Hui’an, it is not known where he was from.
During the Shenlong era, An Shenlong traveled to the capital of Jingzhao, where he frequently displayed prescient insight.
At that time, Tang Xiujing had achieved great military success on the frontier and possessed incomparable wealth and status.
An went to visit him and said:
"Lord, where there is extreme beauty, there must be extreme evil.
A great calamity is imminent, yet it will not be more than a few months away; however, it can be warded off.
Xiu-jing, who had long known that An was capable of performing rites for suppression and victory, gave his assent and bowed to him.
An said, "There is no other method;
I have merely one plan. Is it not the case that the appointment of official ranks arises from the process of molding and refining?
I request that you select a person of talent and capability to serve as the Governor of Caozhou."

Consequently, he obtained Mr. Zhang, who was originally an official of the capital; that very day, Zhang was promoted to the position of Palace Attendant. Shortly thereafter, [the Master] was appointed as the Magistrate of Dingtao and entrusted him with the task of seeking two dogs, more than several feet tall and possessing divine elegance.
When Lord Zhang arrived at his post, he sought with keen determination and found two dogs exactly as requested to present to him.
Xiu-jing was greatly pleased; he summoned An to look at them and said, "Excellent indeed."
After more than ten days had passed, Dao’an returned and said, “The matter will take place this very evening;
I hope you, Excellency, will prepare your defenses strictly.
He then remained there to stay the night with Dao’an.
That night, Xiu Jing sat in the front pavilion of the hall and ordered ten or so attendants to take up bows and arrows and stand at the corners of the couch.
Xiu Jing shared a single couch with An; when the night was deep, An laughed and said, "The disaster that would have befallen you, Minister, has been averted!"
"You may go to bed.
Xiu-jing thanked him with joy, and they subsequently removed their attendants and slept together.
At dawn, An called out, "Xiu-jing, you may rise."
He asked after his health, saying,
"What use have you for two dogs?
He then followed their tracks into the garden, where he saw a man lying prostrate on the ground, deceased.
He observed that there was blood upon its neck, indicating it had been bitten by something.
He further saw two dogs beneath a large tree; looking up, he beheld a man who had bared his chest and concealed himself.
Xu Jing was startled and interrogated him; the man wept and pointed to the dead body, saying, "I and he were both rebels.
Last night we came together intending to harm the Chancellor, but we encountered these two dogs who surrounded us and barked."
"He was bitten by it and has already perished.
I have no place to hide; ensnared by the net of Heaven and watched over by dogs, I now willingly face ten thousand deaths.
He then ordered him to be bound, saying:
"This crime certainly deserves death, yet it was not my own intention; I was merely constrained by another.
He then released him, and the thief bowed in tears and departed.
Xiu Jing bowed in thanks and said to An,
"Had it not been for my teacher, I would have perished at the hands of those two men. An replied:
"This is the fortune of the State Chancellor; how could it be something we are capable of causing?
Furthermore, Lu Zhen, a cousin of Xiu Jing, was at Jingmen when a practitioner of the arts told him:
"You are about to encounter misfortune; you should seek out those skilled in rituals for averting calamity, and perhaps you may escape it."
Zhen knew that An’s extraordinary skills and pure conduct were highly esteemed by his contemporaries, so he wrote a letter to Xiu Jing.
An immediately sent a reply, saying:
"The matter lies within [this very response]!"
When the letter was delivered to Jiangling, Li Zhen had already passed away.
His family opened the letter and found it to be nothing but a single sheet of blank paper, entirely devoid of a single character; Xiu-jing therefore held him in even greater esteem.
Several years later, he departed and was never heard of again.
The Biography of Shi Anjing of the Western Regions during the Tang Dynasty. Master Xuguo, Shi Anjing, was originally a man from the Western Regions.
In the fifteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, he struck his mendicant’s staff and traveled eastward.
Upon reaching Dingtao, he asked directly, “Where is Layman Ding?
A local resident replied to him:
"After three years had passed, he was buried in the suburbs.
Furthermore, it said:

"This man was a lay bodhisattva who devoted himself exclusively to the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). He once paid homage to and served Chan Master Pujì of Mount Song, from whom he claimed to have attained the most profound Dharma."
As he was about to pass away, he sat with his palms joined in the full lotus posture and died in solemn stillness.
The bells and chimes of all the monasteries in Cao City rang out spontaneously without being struck.
Jing went to the burial site and personally opened the tomb.

At that time, five-colored clouds and vapors surged upward; he then took his bones—which were all golden, linked together like chains, approximately five zhang in length—and as they rang out with a clear resonance, he walked along carrying them upon the tip of his staff.
They erected a separate stupa and reinterred [the remains], whereupon the assembly all marveled and sighed in admiration.
After a short while, Jing suddenly vanished from sight.
The commentary states:
The skeletal remains of sentient beings are the residual fruits drawn from prior causes.

In the bodies of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), the joints do not connect; in the bones and joints of a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), they are interlocked in the form of coiling dragons; as for a Buddha, there are the *śarīra* relics of the entire body.

Now, since the bones of the householder Ding possess the form of interlocking hooks and chains, he has transcended the stage of ordinary beings but has not yet attained the Ten Abodes; could this be the characteristic of the joints and bone-ends of the eight-armed Nārāyaṇa being hooked together?
The realization of the layman’s power reaches this point.
It is like gold ore, which is called "dross" (hun); yet it cannot be called mere dross.
It is like a jade-bearing stone, which is called "unworked jade" (pu); yet it cannot be called mere stone.
Furthermore, there was a master named Xu Guo at Dayun Temple in Chengdu Prefecture; he blended with the common world and concealed his brilliance, such that few people could fathom him.
At times he would enter samādhi, yet he never failed to maintain the monastic discipline.
At times he appeared mad or deluded, yet his words were often accurate.
Previously, for the sake of Wei Yuansong, he was an unfathomable man whom people throughout the region of Kunwei often called Master Xu Guo.
Xu is the surname;
Guo is the given name;
Shi is a general title.
This Qianglian was of the same class as Zhigong; his end is unknown.
The Biography of Shi Ruyi of Mount Zhongshan in Fuzhou, Fujian, during the Tang Dynasty. Shi Ruyi was a man of unknown origins.
At the end of the Kaiyuan era, he became a monk and was in charge of the temple seating.
Suddenly, there was a monk whose entire body was covered in sores and scabs, his robes tattered and frayed, as he wandered through the monastery.
When the assembly of monks saw him, there was none who did not feel revulsion.
Seeing him alone, he took pity on him, invited him into the permanent residence’s separate hall, and settled him there for the summer retreat.
At the end of the summer, as the monk was about to depart, he asked:
"Where are you going?"
He replied,
“I have returned to my hut.
He asked again:
"Where is the hermitage?
"It is right to the east of Dàchéng Monastery.
One day he said:
He said, "I arrived from that place only a few days ago; do not look for my hermitage.
[The other] replied, "I do not believe you; come and visit me anyway."
"I shall come specifically two days from now," he said.

The other monk then departed, and indeed saw the former monk waiting for him at the mouth of the cliff. They took each other's hands and entered a vihāra, where multi-storied pavilions rose majestically and halls were interspersed; it was clearly no ordinary human landscape.
On the third day, he sent a monk down the mountain; when the monk looked back, he saw that everything was nothing but rocky cliffs, and only then did he realize it was a sacred temple.
Thereupon, the monk redoubled his efforts in cultivation, vowing to join the ranks of the sages.

The Anonymous Account of a Monk from the Western Regions of the Tang Dynasty. The monk from the Western Regions of the Tang Dynasty was an anonymous person from India, though it is not precisely known which part of India he hailed from.

His appearance was coarse and unattractive; he wore a saffron-colored robe made of strips of cloth, sandals of leather, and trailed an iron staff as he traveled to convert others in the imperial capital.

When Wei Nan-kang Gao was born, being only three days old, his family invited monks for a vegetarian feast. This monk did not come when summoned, yet arrived of his own accord—on such occasions, monks must invariably visit every temple in succession to be formally invited. A servant of the Wei family, resentful that this man was one person too many, grew extremely angry and seated him upon a worn-out mat in the courtyard.
When the vegetarian feast was concluded, Lady Wei had her wet nurse carry the infant out, intending to request that the assembly of monks offer prayers for his well-being.
A foreign monk was the first to rise from his seat; adjusting his robes, he ascended the steps and, looking at him, said:
"It has been a long time since we last met; are you free from ailment?"
The infant, showing a joyful expression, recognized him with an air of familiarity.
The assembly was all amazed by this.
Master Wei said:
"This child has been born for only three days; why does my teacher say we have been parted for a long time?
The Indian monk replied, "This is not something you, a lay devotee, can know."
Wei Jungu questioned him further, and the Indian monk replied,
"This child is the reincarnation of Zhuge Liang.
You are well aware that during the time of the Three Kingdoms, he served as the Prime Minister of Shu."
"Since the people of Shu have long received his bounty, and he has now descended into this world to serve as the commander of Shu, he will surely bring prosperity to those of the Kunwei region.
In the past, when I was at Jianmen, I formed a virtuous friendship with this son."
Since I already knew he was born at the imperial court, I have come from afar.
This son served as the Military Governor of Jiannan for twenty years, reaching the highest ranks of officialdom as Grand Secretary and Grand Marshal.
"Furthermore, this is not something I know.
His father agreed with this, and consequently named him "Wu" as his courtesy name; he was also simply known by the single character "Wu.
When Zhang Yi was appointed as the Regional Inspector (Jiedushi) of Fengxiang and Longzhou, he petitioned for Gao to serve as the Acting Governor of Longzhou.
When Li Yi was killed by Li Chulin, Niu Yun-guang requested that Gao serve as commander.
Having no other choice, Zhu Ci appointed Gao as the Commander of Fengxiang.
Emperor Dezong established the rank of Fengyi Military Governor to honor him, subsequently promoting him to Minister of the Ministry of Rites.
During the Xingyuan era, when the imperial carriage returned to the capital, he was summoned to serve as General of the Left Jinwu Guard.
In the first year of the Zhenyuan era, he became the Governor of Chengdu, succeeding Zhang Yanshak.
Upon taking office, he subdued the Hu and Man tribes and achieved military merit, whereupon he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Nankang.
When Shunzong ascended the throne, he was promoted to Grand Marshal.
He served in Nankang for twenty-one years; in his later years, he held the Dharma in high esteem, constantly holding a rosary and reciting the names of the Buddhas.
The parrot he had raised was taught to recite the sutras;
when it died, it was cremated, and śarīra relics were found among the ashes.
Gao further turned his heart toward the Chan path of the Southern School, studying the Dharma of the mind under Chan Master Shenhui of Jingzhong Temple.

While in Shu, [the ruler] was wealthy and noble yet acted with transgressive arrogance, imposing heavy taxes; contemporary opinion condemned this, yet it coincided with the prophetic prediction of a foreign monk.
The Biography of Bao Yu of Jingzhao, Tang China. Regarding the monk Bao Yu: his religious practice was lofty and extraordinary, and he rarely engaged in worldly affairs.
Whenever he spoke of future events, it was as if he were witnessing them with his own eyes.
Seeing the monk Daguang, he instructed him, saying:
"When you recite the sutras, you should raise your voice so that the sound of the Dharma reaches the heavens and all listen; you will surely receive the assistance and protection of divine beings."
"Later, all events accorded with his prophecies.
Thousands in the capital city took refuge in him in faith.
Every evening he would dwell alone in a single room, closing the door and extinguishing the candles."
Once, a monk peered through a crack in the door to observe what was happening; he saw auspicious clouds emerging from Yu’s mouth, their brilliant colors most lovely to behold.
Later, at approximately ninety years of age, she passed away.
At the time of his death, it was the height of the summer heat, yet the corpse showed no signs of decay.
The minister of state, Di Wuji, was on intimate terms with Yu; upon his death, Di attended the funeral and displayed considerable grief.
Qiji poured fragrant milk into his mouth, whereupon auspicious light issued from his mouth, shining brilliantly in all four directions.
Qiji marveled at this even more.
In the tenth month of the second year of the Qiannuan era, Qiji was demoted to serve as the Prefect of Zhongzhou.

At the beginning of the Baoying era, he entered service as a Guest Attendant to the Crown Prince and subsequently served as the Capital Prefect; throughout these positions, Yu always predicted that his fortunes would alternate between honor and misfortune, and everything occurred exactly as he had said, leading [the Emperor] to apply himself with focused intent to his faith.
The Biography of Master Azu of Mianxiang, Guozhou, Tang Dynasty. Regarding the monk Śramaṇa Azu of Mianxiang, Guozhou, during the Tang Dynasty, his origins and background are not well known.
His physical appearance was dull and coarse, and his spirit seemed dim; yet whenever he spoke, there was nothing that did not manifest as prior awakening.
Although he had no fixed residence and mostly stayed in Weixiang, he followed in the footsteps of Master Fayun;
as people came and went in great numbers vying for the path to pay their respects, offerings accumulated like mountains, yet he never once looked back upon them.
When people harbor hidden sorrows or are afflicted by physical suffering, those who obtain his guidance find its efficacy to be remarkably swift.
At that time, there was a wealthy elder named Zhang Zhen in Shan Prefecture; his estates were numerous and his wealth and goods overflowed.
Having few children, she was constantly fearful that her wealth and silks would have no heir after her death.

Later, she gave birth to a son who was both foolish and dull-witted; his hands and feet were contracted and clenched, and his speech was stammering and indistinct. He took pleasure only in food and drink, being almost different from ordinary people—his mouth was like a gullet, never satiated all day long.
At the age of seventeen, he was doted upon by his parents, who indulged all his desires; they sought out physicians and medicines, traveling no less than a thousand li.
After several decades, the family fortune had been completely exhausted. Someone said to Zhen:
"Master Zu is truly of the same caliber as Baozhi; why do you not reveal your innermost thoughts and seek his help for this illness?"
Thereupon, the husband and wife arrived at Mianxiang, where they prostrated themselves with tears on their faces, entreating him for deliverance.
Azu kept his eyes closed for a long time, then said to Zhen, "Your karmic grievances have not yet been dispersed;
you must still endure several more years. Out of pity for your earnest devotion, I shall eliminate them for you."
He immediately ordered that an auspicious day be selected to perform purification rites by the river;
he summoned a vast multitude to witness his deliverance, and led his son to the site of practice.
At that time, the assembly recognized Ājñāta-kaundinya’s extraordinary nature, and the spectators stood as thick as a wall.
After a short while, he summoned several groups of strong men and, with shouts, had them drag his son and throw him into the river, where he was carried away by the swift current.
Zhen was both sorrowful and alarmed, unable to fathom the reason for this.
Azu said to Zhen,
"I have finished removing the calamity for you."
After a long while, the son suddenly rose to the surface of the water some dozens of paces away, brandishing his hand like a spear and reviling his parents, saying:
"The enmity between us is the result of karmic conditions from past lives; it is only by meeting a holy being that this conflict has been so abruptly resolved."
"If it were otherwise, I would not expect to see the end of this day.
He stood up straight and called out loudly, his words and reasoning clear and distinct, without any appearance of delusion or confusion.
In an instant, he sank into the water, and nothing more was known of him.
From this point on, the teachings spread widely, and those who took refuge in the faith flocked to him like people to a marketplace.
All his activities of conversion and guidance were of this nature; this was roughly during the Dali and Jianzhong eras.
It was likely in the twelfth year of the Zhenyuan era of Emperor Dezong, the Bingzi year, that he was posthumously granted the title of Chan Master Dayuan by imperial decree.
To this day, he is still held in high esteem between the regions of Shan and Guo.

The Biography of Master Feng Gan of Mount Tiantai in the Tang Dynasty. The biography of Master Feng Gan of Mount Tiantai in the Tang Dynasty: Master Muqin, Hanshanzi, Shide, and the Monk Feng Gan originally resided at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai.
With his hair cut even with his eyebrows and clad in coarse cloth robes, his stature was about seven chi or more.
Whenever someone questioned him, he would respond only with the two characters "Acting according to the occasion" (*suíshí*), and utter no other words.
He delighted in husking grain alone and served as a laborer at the city gates during the dawn, assisting with the cooking for vegetarian meals.
He once rode a tiger directly through the pine gate—terrifying all the monks—as he sang the *Changdao Ge* (Song of Chanting the Way); at that time, the assembly came to revere him even more.

After his passing, during the Xuantian era, he traveled to propagate the teachings in Jingzhao; his conduct was not that of ordinary men, and among the officials and commoners who saw him, there were none who did not pay him respectful homage.
Because he followed in the footsteps of Master Wanhui, his character was somewhat similar; his eccentricity surpassed that of the madman, and his words were often prophetic.

Prior to this, there were two practitioners in the kitchen of Guoqing Monastery known as Hanshanzi and Shide; they frequently attended to the cooking in the monks' kitchen, and once the cooking was finished, the two would converse together, though those who listened in secret could not understand their meaning.
They were also extremely deranged, gathering together and associating with one another, as is the way of kindred spirits seeking each other out.

At that time, Lü Qiuyin was departing to serve as the Governor of Danqiu and was about to prepare his carriage; however, he suffered from a severe headache, and the physicians’ efforts proved largely ineffective.
He encountered Gan Zao, who said,
"I have come from Tiantai to pay my respects to you, Excellency.
He then informed him of his ailment, to which Gan replied:
"What are you worrying about?
he asked. He then took a clean vessel, sucked up some water, and sprayed it [upon him]. In a short while, [the man] felt that his body was somewhat better.
Lüqiū was amazed by this and requested a word from him to determine whether the outcome of this journey would be auspicious or ominous.
He replied,
"Upon arriving at my post,
I shall call upon Mañjuśrī. Lüqiu said:
"Where is this bodhisattva? He replied,
"He is the one who tends the hearth and washes the utensils in the kitchen of Guoqing Temple."
Upon entering the mountain temple, he asked,
"Has there ever been a Chan Master Fenggan in this monastery?
They replied:
“There is. “Where is the monastery located?
And who are Hanshan and Shide?”
At that time, Sengdaoqiao replied:
"The old residence of Fenggan is behind the scripture repository; it is currently deserted and uninhabited, with only tigers and leopards occasionally coming here to roar."
"Han and Shi are currently serving as laborers in the monastery kitchen.
When Liu Qiu entered the quarters, he saw only tiger tracks crisscrossing the floor.
He asked again, "What kind of spiritual practice have you been engaged in while here?"
He replied, "I do nothing but husk grain to provide porridge for the Sangha; at night, I sing and recite without ceasing.
Thus he sighed and marveled at this repeatedly.
He then entered the kitchen, where he saw two men burning firewood, appearing as if they were gathered around a hearth.

Lüqiu bowed to them, but the two men repeatedly shouted "Du-ta! at him; subsequently, they took Lüqiu by the hand and treated him with such familiarity as if he were an infant, laughing "He-he" incessantly.
Xing said,
"Feng Gan is too talkative. From then on,
the two walked hand in hand out through the pine gate and never entered the temple again.
Gan once entered Mount Wutai on pilgrimage and encountered an old man, whom he asked,
"Are you not Mañjuśrī?
The old man replied:
"How could there be two Mañjuśrīs?
Before Gan had finished his prostrations and risen, he suddenly lost sight of him.
Next was the master Mudeng, who frequently wandered through the markets and streets of the capital; he was similar to Fenggan, and no one could easily fathom him.

The two characters "fēng" (seal/boundary) and "fēng" (abundant/harvest) appear and disappear differently—Wei Shu, the court historian, uses "fēng" as in "fēngjiāng" (frontier), while Lüqiu Xu, in his *Sanxián zhuan* (Biographies of Three Worthies), uses "fēng" as in "fēngrěn" (bountiful harvest); it is unknown which is correct.
As for Hanshanzi, the world regards him as a destitute man or a madman, and one cannot fathom his nature through ordinary measures.
He lived in seclusion on Mount Tiantai, seventy li west of Shifeng County, in what were known as the two cliffs of Han and An; he made his permanent residence within the deep caves of Han Cliff.
At that time, he came to Guoqing Temple.

There was a man named Shidi, whom the temple monks had appointed to oversee the refectory; he would constantly collect the leftover food and vegetable scraps of the assembly of monks, cutting large bamboo into tubes to deposit them inside.
If Hanshanzi came, he would immediately carry him off on his back.
At times he would stroll slowly along the corridors; at other times he would shout and clamor, intimidating others, or hurl insults into the air.
The temple monks, unable to endure him, pursued him with staffs; he turned around, clapped his hands, and withdrew slowly with "ha-ha" laughter.
Yet his coarse cloth tunic was tattered, his face was withered and emaciated, he wore a crown made of birch bark, and trailed large wooden clogs.
Whenever he uttered words or breathed forth his spirit, they invariably pointed toward a specific destination: the principles of the Buddha.
When Lüqiū first entered the monastery to inquire about Hanshan, the śramaṇa Dàoqiáo replied:

"This man suffers from madness; he originally lived among the cold crags. He delights in composing verses and gāthās, and his speech is erratic—sometimes right and sometimes wrong, ultimately impossible to fathom."
He gathered the temple attendants to serve as his companions; they met together and conversed, though the details cannot be fully related.
When the temple monks saw the Governor bowing before him, they were startled and said, "Why does a high official pay such homage to a madman?"
The two men went out of the temple arm-in-arm, laughing and joking.
Lüqiu went again to Han Yan to pay his respects and inquire after him, bringing clothes and medicinal herbs; however, [Huiyuan] raised his voice and cried out, "Thieves! Thieves!"
He withdrew and his body shrank into a crevice within a rocky cavern.
He spoke again, saying, "Inform all of you: each of you must exert yourselves.
Then the crevice of the rocky cavern closed with a seamless sound, leaving no trace behind.

He then ordered the monk Daoqiao to search for his遗物 (remains/possessions), finding only over two hundred poems—some written by piecing together leaves in the forest and others transcribed on the walls of village houses—which he has now compiled into a single collection that many people recite.
Later, Chan Master Caoshan Ji annotated it, calling it the *Verses in Response to Han Shanzi*—because he had no clan or surname, the people of Yue called him simply Han Shanzi.
There is the line, "What lies within the courtyard? White clouds embrace the secluded rock," which clearly exemplifies an elegant style.
Today, beneath the cliff there is a stone standing tall and upright, known as the "Secluded Rock."

As for Shide: Master Fenggan was once walking along the path to Mount Ou when he heard the sound of a child crying. He went to investigate and saw a boy about five years old; at first, he thought it was a cowherd lad.
Upon inquiring into the details of the matter, he was told:
"There is no one to shelter me; I have been abandoned here alone.
Feng Gan then took him to Guoqing Temple and entrusted him to the head cook (diànzuò).
If someone should come to claim it, it must certainly be returned to them.
Later, the śramaṇa Lingyi took him under his care and had him manage the incense and lamps in the dining hall.
One day, he suddenly saw [the boy] ascend the seat and eat from a dish facing the statue.
He again called out to Kauṇḍinya, addressing him as a "lesser-fruit śrāvaka," and laughed loudly while holding his chopsticks as if no one else were present; the monks then drove him away.

Lingyi consulted with the senior elders and had him removed from his duties in the hall, ordering him instead to wash the utensils in the kitchen. As soon as he finished scrubbing them, he filtered the food scraps and placed them in a tube.
Whenever Hanshan arrived, he would inevitably carry things away on his back.
Furthermore, at the temple of the Guardian Deity of the Monastery, the food daily brought down from the monks' kitchen was scattered in disarray as it was snatched up by crows and birds.
He picked up a staff and struck the earthen figurines two or three times, scolding them, saying:
"If you cannot even protect your own food, how can you protect the monastery?
That evening, a deity entered a dream and said to the monks of the entire temple:
“Shide has beaten me.
The next day, when the monks recounted their dreams, they all matched; the entire monastery was in an uproar, and it was only then realized that he was no ordinary man.
At that time, a report was submitted to the prefecture and county, and the official decree issued from the commandery stated:
"A worthy man has gone into seclusion; as an emanation body of a Bodhisattva, he should be honored.
Thus, Shide was titled "Worthy Man" (Xianshi).
Furthermore, while herding oxen at the temple estate, he would sing and call out to Heaven.
Once, while the monks of that monastery were performing the *poṣadha* ceremony, he picked up a cow and drove it to the front of the assembly hall;
leaning against the door and clapping his hands, he laughed loudly, saying, "A gathering of idle heads!"
At that time, the head monk who maintained the Vinaya rebuked him, saying,
"Wind-man, why do you create such a clamor and disturbance during the recitation of the precepts? Shide replied:
"I am not herding cattle," he said, "but these herds are mostly those who were in charge of monastic affairs at this temple.

Shide called out the posthumous names of each deceased monk one by one; the cattle passed by, each responding to his voice. The entire assembly was struck with amazement, and all resolved to reform their past ways and cultivate themselves for the future, moved by the Bodhisattva’s manifestation in this form to deliver them.
At that time, Daoqiao compiled the words and phrases of Hanshan on the walls of the temple’s local deity shrine; there he saw the verses of Shide and appended them to the *Hanshan ji*.
The commentary states:

According to Feng Gan’s *Xian tian zhuan*, Lü Qiu, Han Shan, and Shi De were all contemporaries from the reign of Emperor Ruizong. How is it, then, that in Master Xuanshi’s *Biographies of Eminent Monks*... Lü Qiu was a military official and lived during the early Tang dynasty?
Liu Qiu’s preface records three individuals without mentioning their dates, which leaves readers in perplexity.
Furthermore, the bestowal of the crimson robe is a civil rank.
Such being the case, there were actually two individuals with the same name, Liu Qiu.

Furthermore, during the reign of Emperor Xianzong, Master Daomiao of Mt. Miao encountered Hanshanzi, who pointed out Leshan Tan; subsequently, he met Shide at Guoqing Temple. From this, it is known that these three individuals still existed during the final period of the Tang dynasty.
As for Fēnggān, he emerged from Jīngzhào after Tiāntái had passed away;
as for Hán and Shí, they were encountered during the Yuánhé era while Xuāntiān was still present.
Is this because their lifespans were longer?
Is this because his appearances and disappearances were not constant?
This is surely what is meant by the *Yijing* hexagram: "The young fox nearly succeeds in crossing [the stream].

The biography of Chan Master Wuxiang of Jingzhong Monastery in Chengdu, Tang China, states: Master Wuxiang was originally a native of Silla. He was the third son of the king of that land. He was born according to the lunar calendar and dates of his own country, received the tonsure and the precepts at Qunnam Monastery.
In the sixteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, he sailed across the Eastern Ocean and arrived in China, reaching the capital.
Emperor Xuanzong summoned him for an audience and assigned him to Chanding Temple.
Later, he entered Shu and went to Zizhong to pay his respects to Chan Master Zhishi.

There was a man of solitary attainment—a man of exceptional character—who had once been summoned by the Emperor into the palace and granted a nine-panel *māṇava* robe; he possessed foreknowledge of all matters and was never mistaken.
Before Xiang had arrived, Ji said,
"A guest from abroad shall be seen tomorrow.
You all should sprinkle water and sweep to await him."
One day later, the appointed time arrived, and Master Ji was given the name Wuxiang (Formless).

In the middle of the night, he was presented with the robes of a *maṇava*. Thus, he entered a deep mountain valley and sat in meditation beneath a cliff. There were two black calves whose horns were entangled; they coiled and sprawled beneath his seat, pressing very close to his body. Their hooves even entered his sleeves, their coldness like ice. He stroked them down to his belly, yet he remained utterly unmoved.
Whenever he entered meditative absorption, it was usually for a period of five days.
Once, when the snow had become deep, two fierce beasts came; he washed himself, lay down naked before them, and vowed to offer his body as food for them.
The two beasts sniffed him from head to foot and then departed.
From time to time at night, he would sit beneath his bed and grasp the tiger’s whiskers.
As he lived in the mountains for some time, his clothes became tattered and his hair grew long; hunters, suspecting him to be a strange beast, intended to shoot him, but then desisted once more.
Later, he entered the city, dwelling among tombs by day and sitting beneath trees at night.
He truly practiced the dhūta austerities.
As people gradually came to hold him in high esteem, they constructed a vihāra before a cemetery of neglected graves.
The Regional Secretary Zhang Qiu Jianqiong came to pay his respects to him.
At that time, as Emperor Ming had fled the capital for Sichuan, he invited the Master into the inner palace.

While they were performing the rites of offering, the Magistrate of Chengdu County, Yang Yi, suspected him of being a sorcerer and a deceiver; he therefore issued a warrant for his arrest and ordered more than twenty guards to drag him away.
As they merely drew near his body, everyone was struck with trembling, their spirits and minds utterly lost.
Shortly thereafter, a great wind suddenly arose; sand and stones flew upward, blowing directly into the hall and tossing aside the curtains and screens.
Yang Yi prostrated himself, bowing his head to the ground, gasping for breath and not daring to speak.
When the repentance ritual concluded, the wind ceased, and he escorted [the image] back to its former location.
Thereupon, he exhorted the donors to establish Jingzhong, Daci, Puti, Ningguo, and other monasteries.
The bell-towers and stūpas in the surrounding villages and hermitages were too numerous to count.
He first resided at Jingzhong Benyuan Monastery; it was likely this that was later called Songxi.
When he arrived in Chengdu, a certain strongman suddenly appeared, claiming to offer his labor to gather firewood for the monks' kitchen.

The younger brother of the Prime Minister has recently ascended the throne in his own country; fearing that [the King] might return, he stands in peril of losing his position. He has dispatched an assassin to kill him, of which the Prime Minister was already privy to through his spiritual insight.
One day, while he was bringing firewood, the wise man came briefly and said to him,
"Tonight there will be a guest.
He replied:
"Truly so," he said. He added,
"Do not harm the sons of the Buddha."

When night fell, the woodcutter took up his knife and sat cross-legged beside the meditation seat. After hesitating for a moment, he perceived what seemed to be something descending from the wall; he sprang up immediately and struck once with his knife, severing the giant Hu’s head and body upon the ground.
There was a large pit behind the gate; he then dragged [the body] there to bury it, covering the traces with soil until they were extinguished before departing.
At dawn, the Magistrate summoned those who had been clearing the brushwood to thank them, but [the monk] was already nowhere to be seen.
Once, pointing to the cypress tree in front of the stupa, he said:
"When this tree is as tall as the pagoda, the temple shall be destroyed.
By the time it was abolished during the Huichang era, the tree was indeed equal in height to the pagoda.

It is further said that before the temple there were two small ponds; when the offerings for the midday meal were few, he would have them dredged and deepened, and indeed, provisions would arrive for the service.
His divine wonders were mostly of this kind.
On the nineteenth day of the fifth month in the first year of the Yizhide era, he passed away without illness at the age of seventy-seven.
As he was nearing death, someone asked him,
"Who should succeed you as the abbot?"
He then requested a brush and wrote over a hundred characters, all of which were obscured and unintelligible, yet they were harmonious and rhymed.
He recorded events from eighty or ninety years prior, and when they were verified, there was not the slightest discrepancy.
Previously, when Emperor Wuzong suppressed the Buddhist teachings, only Daci Monastery remained in Chengdu; Jingzhong Monastery was accordingly demolished along with the others.
The great bell of that monastery was then moved into Daci.
By the time Emperor Xuanzong restored the Buddhist faith, the bell was returned to Jingzhong Temple; because the bell was large and had to be transported across the river, it took two days to arrive.

The next day, he was about to perform a ritual fast; he went to fetch [the image] at the *chen* hour, and by the *si* hour it had already arrived, its momentum as it was pushed and pulled being as swift as if it were flying.
Everyone marveled at its supernatural speed, realizing it could not have been achieved by human effort alone.

When they examined the relics of the image—the fragments of clay and the true form—the faces of those present all broke into sweat. His senior disciple, Li Seng, used a cloth to wipe them repeatedly; where the cloth touched his fingers, the sweat was quite salty. Thus it was known that the spiritual power of the image had caused him to pull the bell himself.
How magnificent is such a transformation!
Later, he was titled the Great Master of the Eastern Sea, and a stupa was erected for him.

In the third year of the Qianduan era, Han Rou, the Regional Inspector of Zizhou, composed a stele inscription. During the Kaicheng era, Li Shangyin wrote the "Stele of the Hall of Four Witnesses" in Zizhou, citing Xiang as one of these four witnesses.

Biography of Huixin of Xiling Stupa Monastery in Yangzhou during the Tang Dynasty. Regarding the monk Huixin of Xiling Stupa Monastery in Yangzhou during the Tang Dynasty: he resided in Guangling and was otherwise without any miraculous deeds.

In the third year of the Huichang era, the Guihai year (843 CE), Emperor Wuzong, under the influence of Zhao Guizhen, persecuted and disparaged the Buddhist community, intending to extinguish the teachings.
At that time, Liu Yinzhi, a literary man from Huainan, was traveling briefly through Siming; one night while lodging there, he dreamed as if he were sailing upon the sea.
Looking back, he saw a stupa to the east; crossing over, he saw it was the stupa of Xiling Temple in Huainan.
That stupa rose loftily, its construction being only slightly inferior to that of Empress Dowager Hu’s Yongning Stupa.
On the third tier of that stupa, Xin saw Yin leaning against the railing and conversing with him, saying:
"I shall temporarily take the stupa across the Eastern Sea and return within ten days."
After several days, Fayin returned to Yangzhou and went at once to visit Huijin.
Huijin asked,
"Do you remember when we met by the sea?"
Huiyin understood this clearly and attained sudden enlightenment.
Several days later, a fire from the heavens broke out and consumed the stupa entirely; however, as torrential white rain poured down, a nearby thatched hall remained completely undamaged.
Viewed from this perspective, those who say that people of the Eastern Sea saw the Yongning Pagoda were not mistaken.
The commentary states:
When the pagoda was burned, everyone claimed it had gone to the Eastern Sea; but would the sea truly accept its ashes and embers?
Tong said:
"The five elements constitute material things, and the seven great natures likewise; how could they not pervade the entire Dharma-realm?
When followed in their natural order, they give rise to one another; when reversed, they harm one another."
Although the conditions of adversity and favor occur at different times, they share the same boundaries as the *dharmadhātu*; one realizes that there is only "consciousness" (*vijñapti*).
Furthermore, celestial beings, immortals, spirits, and ghosts differ from humans:

the superior devas reside in palaces produced by the fruits of meditative concentration; immortals manifest transformations by attaching themselves to material objects; and ghosts and spirits consume the essence of their food—these are all forms subject to physical obstruction, which can be utilized through cremation.
Whenever the spires of pagodas are magnificent and beautiful, they are often taken by ghosts and spirits.

Even the Lords of the Seas and Rivers are not human; for instance, when Chen Chong’s Hall of Clouds was consumed by fire from heaven, people of the Eastern Sea occasionally saw the shadow of the hall there.

Furthermore, when the Ma family was dominating south of the Lake in their later years, the Tiace Pavilion was consumed by a celestial fire. That night, the governor of Langzhou heard voices shouting from the air, "Clear the way! The Tiace Pavilion is coming!"
The clouds billowed and surged as if thousands of people were carrying a heavy load; only after several days did the fire reach Tanzhou.
As for Huaixin’s vision of Liu Yin’s dream, Huaixin was likewise an unfathomable monk.

The Biography of Master Xin Qishi of Shanfu during the Tang Dynasty. Regarding the monk Master Xin Qishi: his monastic name was not revealed; at that time, people called him by his surname and his ordinal number in the lineage. As this had become familiar to the ears of the public, no other appellation was used for him. He was indeed a native of Shanfu.
When he was first a child, he was known for being extremely respectful and solemn; he never engaged in frivolous play and displayed maturity at a young age.
His father, serving as the Governor of Shan Commandery, observed the Master’s conduct and said to his wife, "This son is no ordinary child; you must carefully nurture him."

At the mere age of ten, he clearly understood that the Buddha-dharma was worthy of veneration; regarding any scripture, he could instinctively distinguish between the Chinese and the Sanskrit versions without relying on any teacher’s instruction.
Furthermore, as his grief for Zhong Da-liao and the pain of ascending the hill to mourn his mother grew ever deeper, despite the exhortations of his relatives, he became increasingly emaciated.
Previously, there were seven tile kilns south of the commandery city; one day, amidst his wailing, he went mad and fled, and his household servants followed his tracks to search for him.
Seeing him enter the kiln and sit upright within it, his body radiated a wondrous light, brilliant as gold.
His household servant was startled and went to question him, but he remained silent; the servant, filled with fear, fled on foot.
Next, he peered into one kiln and again saw seven masters, their appearance identical to those before.
Thus he went through all seven kilns, seeing each of them sitting upright and emitting light.
For this reason, the people of the Shan region revered him as if he were a deity, prostrating themselves in rows whenever they encountered him.
The Biography of Huihe of Dajian Guosi Temple in the Tang Capital. Regarding the monk Huihe, his clan, lineage, and origins are not clearly known.
As a monk, he appeared eccentric yet was not disordered; he seemed simple-minded yet possessed true insight, such that his origins could not be fathomed.
His speech often hit the mark, and he was popularly known as a "sage.
He resided at Anguo Temple, where he moved about without any restraints.

He saw that the construction of the halls and pavilions at his home temple was not yet complete. At that time, the Princess of Yue had married Zheng Wanjun of Yingyang; although they were in harmony like the lute and the zither, she had borne no children for several years. When Huo arrived at the princess’s residence, Wanjun burned incense and swept the floor to await him.
The Master prostrated himself and knelt in devotion, making this earnest plea:
"Since I was selected as a consort, I have wished for a son to be my heir; can you, O Master, bring this about?"
The monk replied, "It is easy!
Simply provide me with three thousand bolts of silk, and the mistress shall give birth to two sons."
Jūnqín received it with great reverence as if listening to the Buddha’s own words;
he took out silk as requested and gave it to the patron who was overseeing the merit of repairing the temple halls and pavilions.
He then said:
"The Queen is pregnant; I shall command two devas to descend and become sons for the Princess.
My only concern is whether the Princess will be able to carry two children at once."
"It is merely because they were born while still nursing and are thus ashamed;
I shall cause them to be of the same age, though born at different times.
Indeed, as he had said, one was born at the beginning of the year and the other at the end of the year.
The elder was named Qianyao and the younger Huiming; both were handsome men who later became accomplished through extensive learning.
Their fame spread throughout the capital like surging waves, and considering their status and station, they were truly not to be lightly judged.

The Biography of the Great Master Guangling of Xiaogao Temple in Yangzhou during the Tang Dynasty. The Venerable Master Guangling was a native of Weiyang. He did not disclose his Dharma name; throughout the regions of Huaihai, people vied with one another to call him the "Great Master Guangling."

His physical appearance was coarse and unrefined, and his character was generally shrewd and cunning; his straightforward demeanor resembled that of a butcher or a common tavern-keeper, differing from them only in his monastic garb.

He was fond of wine and meat, and he constantly wore a heavy woolen robe—its thickness was evident—even during the height of summer he would not remove it for a moment, so that fleas and lice swarmed upon it.
He resided as a guest at Xiaogan Temple, occupying a single room alone. Every evening he would close his door and sleep, which he took as his regular practice.

However, when his wild and perverse nature flared up, he would slaughter dogs and pigs, daily gathering rowdy youths to fight and beat others, or he would fall asleep drunk by the roadside; thus, the common people came to detest him.

During the Zhenyuan era, there was a young man renowned for his physical strength. Once, while this youth was gambling with others, the Master became greatly incensed and smashed the gaming table with his hand.
The young man laughed and said, "How dare you, you fool, oppose a great warrior?
The Master then scolded him and spat in his face; thereupon he challenged the youth to a fight, while thousands of onlookers gathered in a circle around them.
In his youth, he was once cornered by a great master and fled from the path;
it was only then that people first realized he possessed supernatural strength.

Furthermore, amidst vast crowds, he boasted of his own prowess, frequently entering the marketplaces to plunder money and silks from others. The townspeople all feared his valor and none dared to resist him.
Later, an elderly monk summoned the Master and admonished him, saying:

"Why do you not carefully observe the precepts? How can you consume wine and meat, slaughter dogs and pigs, forcibly seize money and goods from market-goers, and engage in brawls with rowdy youths? Your conduct is most undisciplined; how could this be the fundamental practice of a monk?"
"Once you are no longer tolerated by the public, the officials who apprehend you will arrest and punish you according to the law; where could you flee or hide?
Furthermore, this would deeply bring discredit upon the Buddha-dharma.
The Great Master, with a look of indignation, replied to him:
"Flies and gnats merely scavenge for carrion; how could you know the aspirations of the great swan?
Thus, my Way is not something you can understand.
Furthermore, as for my integrating the pure within with the turbid without, how could it be the same as your petty, narrow-mindedness?"
The elder was unable to humble him.

One day later, he returned from outside, entered his room, and closed the door. Someone peered through a crack in the door and saw the Great Master sitting upon his mat, emitting a divine light that shone radiantly from between his eyebrows, illuminating all things with penetrating clarity.

Onlookers were startled and reported it; shortly thereafter, the monks of the temple rushed there, prostrating in worship and uttering words of praise. Some repented for their past slanders, while others snapped their fingers in admiration and sang hymns of praise.
The next day, the assembly of monks waited for the Great Master to emerge, burning incense and paying their respects.
When they opened the door, he was found with his eyes closed as if entering meditative absorption; he had already passed away.
From then on, the people of Guangling copied his likeness for veneration and called him "The Great Master.
Biography of Mingzan of Mount Nanyue during the Tang Dynasty As for the monk Mingzan, his clan and origins are unknown.
When he first traveled abroad to Mount Song, Huiji was widely propagating the methods of Chan; Fayuan went there to follow him.
Thus, although they silently realized and attained a heart-to-heart accord, few people recognized or esteemed it.

He subsequently dwelt in seclusion among the crags of Mount Heng; while the assembly of monks were engaged in construction work, he remained at ease. Even when subjected to insults and rebukes, he felt no shame whatsoever, and was thus contemporaneously nicknamed "Lan Zan" (the Lazy One).

There is one who claims that Isengchaiyue and others—whether they partake in communal meals or cook earth in earthenware cauldrons to eat—are the response-bodies (nirmāṇakāya) of Amitābha Buddha; yet it is unknown by what means this is verified.
One account says that he ate the leftover food of the monks; thus he was called "Can" (pronounced with a rising tone).
Alternatively, it is said that whenever he followed after them, he would occasionally utter words that were all in accord with Buddhist principles, though his deeds are difficult to know.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era, he went to serve at Nányuè Monastery; he took charge of all the affairs of the monastery and slept beneath the herd of cattle at night, never once growing weary.
Thus twenty years passed.
Li Mi, the Duke of Ye and Chancellor of the State, fearing harm from the Cui and Li clans, went into seclusion on Mount Nanyue while secretly observing what Wang Zan was doing.
He remarked, "This is no ordinary man."
They listened to the Buddhist chants at midnight, the resonance of which pierced through the mountains and valleys.

Lord Li, who was deeply attuned to the nuances of sound and capable of discerning joy and sorrow, said to Tanzan, "The tone of the sutras is first mournful and then joyful; this must mean that those condemned to exile will soon depart."
Waiting until midnight, Master Li went secretly to visit him; looking toward the door of the matting, he introduced himself and prostrated.
Sengzàn rebuked him vehemently and spat into the air, saying, "This man intends to rob me!"
Li Jia became even more reverent, bowing only.
Zàn was just then stirring up a fire of cow dung and taking out some taro to eat; after a long while, he said, "We can sit on the ground."
He took half of the yam he was eating and gave it to him.
Li knelt, received it with both hands, ate it all, and expressed his gratitude.
He then said to Master Li:
"Be careful not to speak too much; you shall receive the appointment of Chancellor for ten years.
Li bowed and withdrew.
A month later, when the Prefect was performing sacrifices at the mountain, he oversaw the repair of the roads with great solemnity.

Suddenly, in the middle of the night, there was a wind and thunder, and a peak collapsed. The mountain path leading up the slope was blocked by a massive rock; they tethered several oxen to pull it away and several hundred men raised a clamor to push it aside, yet their strength was exhausted while the rock became even more firmly fixed, leaving no other means.
Zan said,
"Why employ such elaborate complexity?
I shall discard it from the outset."
The assembly all laughed loudly; Zàn then stepped upon the stone and it moved, suddenly turning like a wheel and descending with a sound like a peal of thunder.
Once the mountain path was cleared, the monks prostrated themselves and leaped for joy; the entire commandery hailed him as a supreme sage, and the Governor served him as if he were a divine spirit.
Zan became silent and conceived the intention to depart.
Suddenly, tigers and leopards gathered in herds outside the monastery, killing and injuring people every day, and there was no way to stop them.
Zan said:
"Give me a small whip, and I shall drive them away for you.
The crowd said, "A great boulder may still be pushed; tigers and leopards should be easily subdued."
He then gave him a thorn-stick, and they all followed behind to watch him.
Once they had gone out the gate, they saw a tiger seize him in its jaws and carry him away.
After Zàn had departed, the tiger’s tracks also vanished.
At the end of the Tianbao era, when Emperor Suzong traveled north and ascended the throne at Lingwu, he dispatched an envoy to seek out and summon Li Yuegong.
It happened that Li Bi was traveling from Mount Song and Mount Ying to the imperial encampment.

The Emperor was pleased with his service and appointed him to oversee the affairs of the Chancellery; his authority surpassed that of the Chancellor as he presided over the duties of the Vice-Master of the Guangping Prince’s Household.
Suzong said, "You are my teacher and friend."
"Now, father and two sons rely upon you for guidance in the Way and righteousness.
Soon thereafter, however, his abilities were suppressed by Cui Yuan and Li Fuguo; fearing for his safety, Li Bi requested permission to travel to Mount Heng, and the Emperor granted him leave.
Having abstained from grain for several years, he finally beheld Zan.
Later, he ultimately held the position of Chancellor, exactly as Zan had predicted.
He was posthumously granted the imperial title of Grand Master of Great Illumination (Daming Chanshi), and his stupa remains within the mountain range. Thus it is said.

Biography of Daji of Ciyun Monastery in Jianzhou, Tang Dynasty. Daji of Ciyun Monastery in Jianzhou, Tang Dynasty, whose secular surname was Wang, was a native of Jinshui County. His religious name was Huaiyi. He was known as Daji. His secular surname was Wang, and he was a man of Jinshui County.
Chong Ru left the household life as an unusual occurrence; his father bestowed upon him the name Dajia during the final years of the Tianbao era.
He practiced ascetic discipline with such vigor that he was known at the time as a "dhūta."
When Emperor Xuanzong went on a tour of inspection, [the Master] indeed went to the prefectural seat himself to shave his head and become a monk.
At this time, his words that he would "await the imperial carriage to receive ordination" proved true.
When the imperial carriage was twenty *li* from the county seat, he cleared a path and cut away the brambles to dwell alone atop a mountain; later, it became a temple.

This mountain abounds in sacred traces; it was originally named Shicheng (Stone City). When Emperor Ming arrived at Jianmen Pass, the mountain deity manifested his form to welcome the imperial carriage and declared himself to be of the Li clan, whereupon he was granted by imperial decree the title of "Grandson of the Mysterious" (Xuansun).
Later, he ascended the eastern terrace of Wudan and gazed afar at auspicious clouds and purple qi swirling and binding within the void.
He asked those around him, "What place is this? They replied:
"Shichijōzan. Thereupon, he realized the mountain deity's intention to serve as his guardian, and thus renamed Unjō to Jion-ji Temple.
The Emperor passed away at this temple following his departure.

Furthermore, Shi Huaiyi of Lengqia Monastery in Fuzhou, during the Jinglong era, resolved to build a vihāra to the east of Aitong Monastery. Having surveyed the terrain, he found it lacked water for practical use, whereupon he folded his hands and departed.
Suddenly, a mountain bird fought on the ground; finding this strange, he ordered a craftsman to dig a hole over a foot deep, whereupon sweet spring water gushed forth.
From then on, even during the fasts of the伏 (fú) and 臘 (là) periods, there was no increase or decrease in its supply.

Whenever there were auspicious or ominous signs within the temple, the water would invariably diminish for a time; by observing this, one could know [the coming events], and thus local custom referred to it as "Numinous Spring" (Língquán).
He entered nirvana in the second year of the Yongtai era. His disciple Chāowù petitioned Emperor Dàizōng on his behalf to grant a plaque for the temple's name.
The chief disciple was named Zhīhéng, followed by Xíngbì.
Huángfù Zhèng, the Regional Inspector of Yuèzhōu, composed a stele to record his virtues, and Yú Dí, the Military Governor of Xiāngzhōu, inscribed it.

Biography of Shi Huaidao of Aitong Temple in Fuzhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Huaidao was a man of transcendent virtue and lofty character. Compassionate and patient, he sought to save all beings; reflecting upon the realization of the Dharma, he constantly traveled abroad to seek it.
Whenever he encountered a person of great learning, he would humble himself in his conduct to seek their instruction.

On the day he returned to his hometown, he venerated the Buddha with diligent devotion; while folding away his sitting mat (niṣīdana), he obtained a pearl, which he subsequently placed within the forehead of a clay statue of Mañjuśrī to keep it there.
The pearl was perfectly round and lustrous, unlike those born from oyster shells.
Furthermore, śarīra relics descended mysteriously and were subsequently enshrined within the Nanjian Stūpa.
Reaching the second year of the Zhide era, he commanded his disciple, the monk Changchi, to recite the Lotus Sūtra without ceasing day or night.
Suddenly, a set of white cotton *kāṣāya* robes descended into the stupa, though its arrival remained unknown.
This was surely because the mind of Daoxiu’s cultivation had moved the profound principle of the unseen world.
Later, Li Yong, the Governor of Huatai, composed the inscription for the stele and also calligraphed it.
Subsequently, Zhiheng succeeded him in residing at Fahua Monastery—he was a disciple of Huaiyi—and his spiritual practice was equal to that of his master.
After his death, Liu Taizhen, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, composed an inscription for his stele, which was calligraphed by Chu Changwen.
He was followed by Chao Wu and Xing Bi, both of whom were equal in reputation; they transformed the customs of Min, and there was no one who did not hold them in high esteem.

Biography of Huizhong of Zangyan Monastery in Shengzhou during the Tang Dynasty. Huizhong, whose secular surname was Wang, was a native of Shangyuan in Runzhou. He attained parinirvāṇa as a śramaṇa. His family name was Wang, and he was a person from Shangyuan in Runzhou.
While still in his mother’s womb, he suddenly encountered an extraordinary monk who said to him,
"The noble son you shall bear will surely become a celestial being.
Since his birth, he has not eaten meat or pungent foods, distinguishing him from ordinary children.
By nature he was sincere and generous.
At the age of twenty-three, in the first year of the Shénlóng era (705 CE), he underwent ordination based on his mastery of the scriptures.
He was subsequently assigned to Zàngyán Monastery; his resolve and character were lofty and simple, earning him the esteem of his contemporaries.
Having heard that Chan Master Wei of Mount Niutou had followed in the footsteps of Bodhidharma and attained the seal of the Buddha-dharma, Zhong went to the mountain to pay his respects.
Upon seeing Zhong, Wei said,
"The master of the mountain has arrived."
Because he preached the Dharma, [the recipient] attained sudden enlightenment in the Supreme Vehicle.

Having found his destined successor, it was like Laozi meeting Yin Xi; he then commanded him to enter the inner chamber to receive the transmission of the Dharma and the lamp, entrusted him with the affairs of the mountain gate, and subsequently departed from the marketplace.
Huizhong immediately followed in his footsteps at this peak, exerting himself with diligence day and night.
He frequently practiced the dhūta austerities in mountains and marshes, drinking from springs and sitting on mats of grass, subsisting on a single meal that lasted him through the day.
He always used a single cauldron to boil all ingredients together; once finished, he would hang it from the tip of a tree before returning to sit in meditative composure upon his rope bed.

Throughout his entire life, he remained as motionless as a tree stump; his robes did not change with the seasons, and he wore the same garment through both cold and heat for forty years, whereby he manifested manifold spiritual responses.
The wise and virtuous Prefect of the commandery frequently visited the mountain to pay his respects and twice invited him to the prefectural seat to transform and guide both the clergy and the laity.
At the beginning of the Tianbao era, [the Master] first arrived and stayed at Zhuangyan Monastery.

Zhong considered that although Zhuangyan was the most flourishing among the old temples of the Liang dynasty, it had now fallen into ruin due to its great age; moved by a desire for restoration, he subsequently planned to construct a Dharma Hall to the east of the main hall.
Previously there was an ancient tree with a magpie’s nest at its summit. A craftsman intended to fell it.
Zhong said, "Stop for now;
wait until the magpies have moved away before you cut it down."
Thereupon, he went to the tree and made this incantation:
"Since a hall is to be built upon this spot, you must depart quickly.
As soon as he finished speaking, the magpies vied with one another to carry away twigs and moved their nests to other trees.
The lay and monastic residents of the surrounding walls gathered to watch like a wall of people; there was none who did not marvel and express their admiration.
Furthermore, before the foundation had even been settled, two divine beings suddenly appeared and pointed out the location for it, whereupon the site was finally determined.
Although he drew others forth without ceasing and his spirit remained vast and undisturbed, companions from the four quarters came to rely upon him daily.
In the third year of the Dali era—before the stone chamber at the mountain gate grew a "clothing-hanging" vine planted by Zhong—in the height of summer that year, it suddenly withered away.
The divine mushrooms and immortal fungi no longer grew.
In the ninth month, as Zhongyan ascended the high seat to preach the Dharma, water unexpectedly gushed forth and circled around the seat.

On the fifteenth day of the sixth month of the fourth year, he assembled the congregation for the *poṣadha* ceremony; at evening, he then instructed his attendants to shave his hair and bathe his body.
That night, auspicious clouds covered the monastery and celestial music was heard in the sky; on the sixteenth day, he sat peacefully and passed away.

At that time, wind and rain shook the earth and trees were broken and snapped. That evening, the monks of Yanzuo Temple in Hezhou all saw a white rainbow stretching straight from east to west, piercing through the mountains; birds and beasts wailed, and the sound of weeping echoed through the forests, valleys, and crags for several days before finally ceasing.

When Wei Gong Sun, the Duke and Governor, heard of this, he was filled with sorrow and dispatched an envoy with funeral gifts; he further ordered Liu Jun, the Magistrate of Shangyuan, to provide the full ceremonial regalia for the return to the mountains.
At that time, the air was sweltering, but on the seventh day of the seventh month, the heavens sent down rain, bringing profound coolness.
On the eighth day, when the divine coffin was brought forth, not even a speck of dust stirred.
Furthermore, a flock of cranes circled above the hearse, escorting it as far as the mountain gate.
Several days after the interment, light emanated from within the tomb, illuminating the mountains and forests.

In the spring of the fifth year, he was cremated according to foreign rites. An incalculable number of śarīras were obtained; they were round and fine like pearls, with a lustrous and translucent brilliance.

Monastics and laypeople from near and far who had lamented their failure to obtain any relics all sought them within the ashes at the site of the cremation; some ten thousand people in total each received a śarīra.
Thus we know that the Dharmakāya’s perfect response is inexhaustible in its resonance with all things; the Sage’s power penetrates secretly, its radiance soaring through the ages.
His disciples erected a wooden pagoda for him when he was eighty-seven years old.

His stature exceeded seven chi, and his frost-white eyebrows spanned one cun; his appearance was exceptionally magnificent, with a swallow’s jaw and a dragon’s cheekbones. His spirit was solitary and towering, his complexion like a mass of gold, radiant and jade-like in its luster, resembling a monk from India.
He did not spread curtains or canopies where he dwelt, yet mosquitoes and gadflies did not trouble him.

He once resided in a secluded hermitage deep among pines and bamboo; there, tigers and deer would often give birth side by side, wandering about and entering his room with such familiarity that he never showed the slightest sign of fear.
In the twenty-seventh year of the Kaiyuan era, Changsun Suichu, the Magistrate of Shangyuan, being intrigued by extraordinary accounts, went in person to the mountain to investigate.
Upon reaching the midpoint of the slope, a fierce tiger blocked his path and roared; Suichu was struck with terror and did not know what to do.
Hearing this, Zhong went out into the forest to explain the situation to the tiger; the tiger consequently ceased its roar and lay down within the woods.
Terrified and cowed, it pressed its palms together in salutation and gratitude before departing.
