Zhong then proceeded toward Wujun; in the Precepts Hall there was a *lingxiao* vine that had withered during the height of summer, and people were about to cut it down.
National Teacher Wei said,
"Do not cut it!
When Huizhong returns, the vine will grow back."
People did not believe him. When Zhong returned in the autumn, his gourd vines had grown back luxuriantly.
Furthermore, there was once a granary for monks' provisions on the estate; one night, when bandits came to steal from it, a tiger roared and chased them away.
The thieves abandoned their loads and fled.
Their kind were so numerous that it is difficult to describe them all at once.

Zhong composed the "Preface to Seeing One's Nature" and the "Lament on the Difficulties of Traveling," whose essential meanings are subtle and profound, and which have circulated widely throughout the world.
Furthermore, as for Shi Yuanji of Ye, both his clan and birthplace cannot be traced.
Initially, he met the Chan Master Seng'an at Mount Song; their spiritual paths were in perfect accord, and one could not fathom their ultimate limits.
He was born in the second year of the Xianheng era of Emperor Gaozong; calculating from then until his passing, he had already lived for over one hundred years.
Yan Shou, the Regional Commander of Xiangzhou, devoted himself to making offerings to him and also styled him "Master Wusheng" (The Birthless One).
Biography of Shi Huixiu of Tiangong Monastery in Luoyang during the Tang Dynasty. Shi Huixiu’s secular surname was Li; he was a native of Chenliu in the present-day Eastern Capital (Luoyang).
Having emerged from the defilements of the mundane world, he aspired to the state of carefree liberation.
Initially, he adorned himself with the precepts; subsequently, he made meditative concentration his primary pursuit.
Having completed his inquiries with the Patriarchs in the regions of Jing and Ying, he returned peacefully to Tiangong Monastery in Luoyang.

During the reign of Empress Wu, she frequently visited the Divine Capital (Luoyang), and Daoxiu’s reputation for the Way reached the Empress’s ears; she repeatedly issued edicts summoning him to court to honor him with great ceremony. Regarding his prophecies of future events, they accorded perfectly with reality like a matching seal.
While in Chang’an, he went to Zisheng Temple to propagate the Way and transform people; they turned toward him in great numbers.
Suddenly, he instructed the disciples of the Chan hall to extinguish the lamps and candles.
Bai Xiu said,
"May the perpetual lamp be left burning?
He also ordered it to be extinguished.

He spoke because the calamity of fire is difficult to predict and must not be left unprepared. He said that there was once a monastery where, due to a lack of fire-prevention measures, the Buddha hall was consumed by flames; furthermore, another temple’s bell tower was scorched, and yet another temple’s scripture repository was reduced to ashes—truly a matter for profound regret.
At that time, the assembly did not understand his meaning.
When night fell, a fire broke out, and the Buddha Hall, the bell tower, and the scripture repository—all three locations—were completely reduced to ashes and charcoal.
Only then did they realize that Xiu had foreseen this and issued a warning.

Furthermore, when Emperor Xuanzong was still the Prince of Lu, he once visited with several other princes to inquire about the Dharma. During their leisurely conversation, [Dao]xiu presented him with a flute.
After the Emperor had departed, Xiuzhao summoned his disciples and said, "Guard this flute carefully;
when the time comes for it to be needed, you must present it to His Majesty."
When he received the abdication from Emperor Ruizong, his disciples Dharma and others finally realized the meaning of his words and brought him a flute to present.
The Emperor, pleased that he had foreseen this, bestowed upon him generous rewards.
Xiu suddenly manifested a slight illness and instructed his disciples; he then passed away peacefully.
He was one hundred years of age.
Zhang Yue, the Duke of Yan, who had long placed his heart in refuge with him, escorted his remains to be interred at Longmen Mountain.
Several thousand monastics and laypeople rushed to the assembly, mourning him with deep sorrow.

Biography of Shi Weizhong of Fajing Monastery in Pei County, Chengdu, Tang Dynasty. Shi Weizhong became a monk while still a youth. He was diligent in his personal cultivation, and among his peers, there were none who did not revere him as their master.

The Chujiafeng Monastery—originally established during the Yongping era of the Later Han dynasty when the Buddha-dharma first began to spread to China—was founded as the Dejing Vihāra, where divine radiance frequently appeared.
During the Song dynasty, Shi Huichi took his leave of his Dharma-elder, Master Huiyuan, at Mount Lu, vowing to convert the regions of Min and Shu.
It happened that Qiao Zong, being unrighteous, ordered several men to take up blades with the intent to slaughter Huichi.
As soon as Daochi snapped his fingers, the assembly fled in terror, falling prostrate.
In the fourth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, he was renamed Fajing.
The temple houses a sacred image of Maitreya.
During the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, a withered log suddenly drifted down the river; it emitted a brilliant light at night, so it was carved into the head of a Buddha image.
During the Zhenguan era, when Dou Gui served as the local magistrate at Jianmen, the light from the Buddha’s head appeared again and led him to the prefectural seat.
Duke Dou sent men to fetch him, yet even several hundred people could not lift him.
He then ordered a ritual prayer for him, saying, "Go wherever you wish. Thereupon [the spirit] spoke:
"May I be established according to the Dharma?"
Thereupon, a single person was able to lift it.
Dou then constructed a Buddha image, and the Provincial Governor Gao Shilian built a hall to enshrine it.
Later, a monk who was fond of planting trees erected a stupa there and obtained a giant crab, its body and legs measuring over two chi in length.
This stupa possesses many miraculous manifestations; if anyone approaches the presence of the Holy Buddha while intoxicated with wine or meat, they will immediately encounter calamity.
During the Tianbao era, Zhong redoubled his ascetic practices at the temple.

Before long, the stupa was struck by a thunderclap, which uprooted its central pillar and cast it outside; suddenly, a small piece of wood appeared as if to take its place. The assembly all marveled at this, unable to fathom its cause.

Zhong then prostrated himself before the sacred image of Maitreya and addressed the devas and nāgas: "Why have you suddenly caused such a violent tremor, seizing the central pillar of the stūpa? You must all increase your awe and reverence."
Thus we know that when the lowly woman cried out, the thunder struck Lord Jing’s terrace; there was indeed something that moved it.
One day, amidst sudden thunder and fierce winds, there was another shock identical to the previous one.
Upon examining it again, it was found that the dragon-spirits had delivered the old pillar and reinstalled it as before.
When the pillars were being replaced, dark clouds gathered from all sides, and four divine beings appeared, supporting him with their bodies until they stood as tall as the stupa itself.
Such was the power of Zhong’s resonance with the spiritual realm.

Prior to the destruction of the temple during the Huichang era, seven śarīra relics emerged from atop the *cakra* (the pinnacle of the stupa), a white light filling the sky as they flew westward; this was witnessed by all throughout Shu.
When it was about to collapse, a crimson light appeared in the midst of the sky.
Furthermore, there was a large jujube tree in this monastery; in the year before the temple was destroyed, the tree withered away.
When the Dazhong era re-established [the monastery], its jujube trees flourished once more.
Zhong later passed away at the temple.
The colophon says:
Is the rise and fall of the Dharma not determined by destiny?
Once destiny is fixed, not even a moment can be shifted.

Thus, as before the Huichang era, the śarīra pre-emptively flew away and the jujube tree withered first; this shows that when the force of the destiny for decline is strong, the destiny for prosperity must be weak, and prosperity cannot overcome decline.
The rise of the Great [Dharma] is such that its decline cannot surpass its flourishing.
If one does not undergo the transitions of the four marks, it is not because one is exempt from the numerical laws of rise and fall.
The teachings of the Dharma are conditioned phenomena; how could they escape the flow of change? Alas!
Biographies of Eminent Monks Compiled in the Song Dynasty, Volume Nineteen;
Biographies of Eminent Monks Compiled in the Song Dynasty, Volume Twenty.
Great Master Tonghui of Tianshou Temple in the Left Street, under the Song Dynasty.
Compiled by Imperial Decree by the Purple-Garbed Śramaṇa Zanning and Others.

Section Six: Three Accounts of Spiritual Resonance (Sangtong), Part Three. Twenty-two Main Biographies with Four Supplementary Entries. Biography of Chuji of the Northern Mountain Hermitage in Zizhou, Tang Dynasty. Biography of the Śramaṇa Chuji: His secular surname was Zhou, and he was a native of Shu.
He served as a disciple under Master Baoshou, serving him with diligence and maintaining few desires, never contending with others.
He was profoundly versed in the profound mysteries and dwelt in the northern mountains, practicing the dhūta austerities.
When the Empress Dowager heard of this, she issued an imperial decree for him to enter the palace and bestowed upon him a *maṇava-saṃghāṭī* robe; he declined and requested to return to the mountains.
For forty years, his feet never stepped into a village.
Sitting upon a single *huchuang* (a small stool), he remained in serene silence without sleeping.
A tiger was constantly crouching beneath his seat like a domestic animal.
He was highly esteemed by the local people, and those who studied his Way flocked to him from all directions.
For this reason, he appeared remarkably extraordinary,
as in the following instance: when the Great Master Wuxiang arrived from Silla to visit Master Xuanzhen, Huiri gave a prior warning to the assembly, saying,
"A guest from abroad shall come to see us tomorrow."
"You should sweep and clean the grounds to await him.
The next day, as expected, a guest from the East Sea arrived.

At the beginning of the Kaiyuan era, Wang Ye—who had originally been a Daoist priest and had once performed minor meritorious deeds during the Jingyun era—was newly appointed as the Prefectural Governor and dispatched to this commandery; ultimately, however, he harbored malevolent intentions within the guise of a Buddhist monk.
Upon taking office, he issued an edict ordering all those within the borders who were śramaṇas to assemble.
Only Jingji remained without descending from the mountain; someone advised him to go and pay his respects, lest he become a source of calamity.
Ji said to his disciple, "Though you have left the household life, you still do not understand karma. While I am not yet dead, what can Wang Ye do to me?
When the three days of the official’s mourning period arrived, the monastics had all assembled.
Someone said, "Only Sengji treats the regional lords with such contempt that they do not come to offer their congratulations. Fayue was slightly provoked;

he compelled the monks to ascend the hall and take their seats. Just as he was about to voice his indignation and inquire into the reasons for Sengji’s refusal, a look of wrathful fury arose, and the monks all trembled with fear.

Yue suddenly collapsed to the ground; his attendants supported him back to his residence, and when they reached a screen tree behind the hall, there was a sound like someone slapping a cheek, and by the hour of Youzhong, he had passed away.
From this time on, people said that false desires were being imposed upon practitioners of the Way to such an extent.
Jì passed away in the first month of the twenty-second year of the Kaiyuan era, having reached the age of eighty-seven.
Zizhong has revered him to this day.

Regarding the Biography of Wuzhuo of Huayan Monastery on Mount Wutai in Dazhou during the Tang Dynasty: Śramaṇa Wuzhuo was a native of Yongjia. His intellectual capacity was broad and clear, and he maintained a firm and resolute character.

He applied his mind to the Great Way and restrained his aspirations to travel afar; arriving at Yunhua Temple in the capital, he studied the teachings of the Avataṃsaka-sūtra under the Dharma Master Chengguan.
In all the sutras and treatises he had studied, his aspirations reached far and wide; yet, he vowed at last to roam the ocean of the Flower Treasury (Avataṃsaka).
In the second year of the Dali era, he entered Mount Wutai, desiring to freely behold the realm of the Sage.
In the fifth month, he arrived at Huayan Temple to lodge.
He began by drinking tea in the hall, where he saw an elderly monk who appeared humble and unrefined; the monk sat upon the northern bed and asked, "You have come from the south;
do you carry a prayer bead rosary? Bring it here for me to see."
He then personally measured it himself.
While he was looking back, he lost sight of where the monk had been.
At that moment, his spirit became dazed and bewildered, and both doubt and joy arose within him as he said:
"In the past, the monk Sengming entered here and beheld stone mortars and wooden pestles; later, he attained entry into the Holy Temple and was able to meet holy sages.
I wish to dwell here—how joyful that would be!"

Next, from the window of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra hall, he saw the plumage of two auspicious birds, brilliantly colored, flying together above his head; they were seen heading toward the northeast, beating their wings as they departed.
The next day, two tufts of white light entered the room, drifting and lingering for a short while before vanishing.
His fellow monk Fǎděng saw this and was struck with wonder, saying,
"What kind of auspicious omen is this?"
"I vow that you will manifest once more to sever the doubts of sentient beings.
He then beheld the light as before.
Consequently, he went to the Vajra Cave; while gazing toward it and paying his respects, he sat down for a brief rest when he heard the sound of a cow being struck three times. It said:
"Drink some water.
An old man of ancient appearance and imposing form, wearing coarse short garments and dragging straw sandals, with a most unusual head-wrap,
approached him and took his hand, asking, "Where have you come from?"
The old man said,
"I come seeking provisions from beyond the mountains.
[The monk asked,] "Where do you dwell?"
He said, "Seeking provisions for use on Mount Tai.
Turning back to question him, he said:
"Master, why have you come here?
He replied,
"I heard there is a Vajra Cave here, so I have come to join in the merit."
The old man asked,
"Are you weary, Master?
He replied:
"No," he replied.
[The other] asked,
"Since you are not exhausted, why do you sleep so abruptly?"
He replied, "Ordinary people are mired in dullness; how can they be considered strange? He said:
"If the Master is drowsy, might he go and sip some boiled *chuan*?
The old man pointed toward the northeast; seeing a monastery situated some paces away, the old man led the ox forward, and [the Master] followed, treading upon the hoofprints.

Upon reaching the temple gate, he called out "Kuntī" three times; the boy merely opened and closed his eyes. He appeared to be fourteen or fifteen years old, with hair hanging down to his eyebrows, dressed in a coarse tunic.
Qianniu entered the temple and saw that its entire ground was made of lapis lazuli, while the halls, chambers, corridors, and eaves all shone with a golden luster.
The splendor within surpassed anything found in the human realm.
The old man sat perched upon a white-toothed couch; pointing toward a brocade cushion, he bade them take their seats.
A page brought two bowls of tea, and they drank together until finished.
He then lifted a casket of mother-of-pearl containing a full measure of cream and curd, and each was served a spoonful.
He swallowed it and felt as though he had attained some realization; his inner spirit became clear and expansive, and he awakened to his past lives.
The old man asked, "Since you left the household life to become a monk, what have you been occupied with, and what have you been concerned about?"
He replied:
"There is cultivation but no realization; both the Great and Small Vehicles merely touch the surface.
He asked:
He asked, "When you first left the household life, what kind of mind did you seek? He replied,
"I sought the Mahāyāna bodhicitta."
He replied,
"The Master attains it simply by practicing with the initial mind.
He asked again, "How many years have you been ordained?"
"Thirty-one," the old man said. "That your virtue is so pure and refined—
when you reach thirty-eight, will the roots of your merit surely be planted in this ground and flourish!"
Furthermore, descend the mountain slowly and take care to find the path; do not injure your feet.
I am old and decrepit, having come from outside the mountain, and am so exhausted that I wish to lie down and rest.
He requested, saying,
"May I stay for one night?
He replied:
"It is not possible.
Since the Master was accompanied by two companions, and we have not seen him return tonight, how could our grief and anxiety ever cease?
This is because the Master still harbors attachments."
Cajja said: "What attachments do the disciples of Gautama have?
Even though they have companions, they feel no longing or attachment for them."
He asked again,
"Do you carry the three robes?
He replied:
"I have maintained it since receiving the precepts. He said,
"This is the place of sealed adherence."
The monk said:
"There is indeed a sacred teaching on this matter:
if you permit me to stay overnight, I shall mentally relinquish [the robe]."
"If there is a compelling circumstance, the Buddha has indeed granted permission.
[The other] said:
"According to the Hīnayāna, one may not relinquish the robes unless there is an obstacle."
"You should protect [him] with urgency.
The old man brushed his sleeves and adjusted his robes, rising; Zhe also hurriedly followed.
The old man said:
"Listen as I proclaim this verse: 'A single thought of pure mind is Bodhi; it surpasses the construction of stūpas made of the seven treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Though these stūpas may eventually crumble into dust, a single thought of pure mind achieves perfect enlightenment.'"
He bowed his head, listened with rapt attention, and replied:
"Having been granted the proclamation of these secret verses, it is as if I have drunk the essence of *amṛta*.
Now that I am permitted to enter the gateway of wisdom, how could I dare forget your instructions?"
"You may truly be called one who understands words; I shall engrave them in the depths of my heart.
The old man called for Juntie to escort the Master away.
As they were about to depart, he patted him on the back and said:
"Go well," he said,
and bowing once more, he walked shoulder-to-shoulder with the youth until they reached the entrance of the Vajra Cave. He asked the youth,
"What monastery is this, that it has no plaque hanging above its gate?"
The youth pointed to the Vajra Cave and asked in return,
"What cave is this?
He replied:
"The tradition of our predecessors names this the Vajra Cave.
The youth asked, "What characters are beneath 'Vajra'?
Zhiwei reflected for a short while and said:
"Below the Vajra lies Prajñā.
The youth smiled and said, "The one who has just entered is the temple of Prajñā.
Taking the youth’s hand, he bowed and departed.
The youth stared at him with wide eyes, as if wishing to speak.
Zhuo said,
"May I send you something to speak on my behalf, such as a white silk sash and a jade pendant?"
The youth then proclaimed the verses of instruction, saying:

"Absence of anger on the face is the requisite for making offerings; absence of anger in the mouth emits a wondrous fragrance; absence of anger in the heart is a precious treasure; being unstained and undefiled is true permanence."
When the verse ended, in a moment of daze, both the youth and the holy temple vanished, leaving only the mountain forests, earth, and stones visible.
With deep sorrow filling his breast, he sighed incessantly and lamented:
"These final words and remaining discourses are like the lingering echoes of a wind-chime or a bell; they still linger in my ears."

He gazed intently at the place where the mountain elder stood; white clouds rose slowly and billowed up, reaching about a fathom above the ground, transforming into five-colored clouds and rainbows. Upon them sat a Great Sage riding a lion, surrounded by various Bodhisattvas.
After the time it takes to eat a meal, a single bank of white clouds from the east gradually obscured the face of the Bodhisattva, and the multitude of figures vanished along with the clouds.
Suddenly, six monks, including Xiu Zheng, the abbot of Bodhi Temple in Fenzhou, were seen returning together to the front of the cave to pay their respects.
Suddenly, they heard mountain rocks shaking and roaring with a sound like a thunderclap, and the monks fled in all directions.
After a long while, all was silent and nothing could be seen.

Daoru then recounted his encounter; the six men repented and reproached themselves for not having beheld the Sage’s countenance, lamenting that what was but a few feet away seemed as distant as the vast heavens, realizing it must have been due to the obscuring veil of their karmic hindrances.

He eventually retired to this mountain and passed away there. During the Yuanhe era, his disciple Wen-yi composed this posthumous account. **Biography of Puhua of Zhending Prefecture, Tang Dynasty** The monk Puhua was a person of unknown origins. He lived during the Tang dynasty in Zhending Prefecture. His dharma name was Puhua. He did not know where he was from. He wore a robe made of coarse hemp and carried a staff. He would wander through the streets and alleys, shouting, "I am a ghost! I am a ghost! He would also frequently strike people with his staff, saying, "I am a Buddha! I am a Buddha! Once, while walking through the marketplace, he encountered a man who asked him, "What is it that you call 'Buddha'? Puhua struck him with his staff and said, "Do you understand? The man replied, "I do not understand. Puhua said, "If you do not understand, you are a Buddha.

On another occasion, he met a man who asked, "What is it that you call 'a ghost'? Puhua struck him and said, "Do you understand? The man replied, "I do not understand. Puhua said, "If you do not understand, you are a ghost. Whenever he saw someone, he would shout, "I am a Buddha! I am a Buddha! or "I am a ghost! I am a ghost! He would often strike people with his staff, saying, "If you can speak, you are a Buddha; if you cannot speak, you are a ghost. Later, he went to the residence of a high official. The official’s wife asked him, "What is it that you call 'Buddha'? Puhua struck her with his staff and said, "Do you understand? She replied, "I do not understand. Puhua said, "If you do not understand, you are a Buddha. One day, he went to the residence of another official. The official’s wife asked him, "What is it that you call 'ghost'? Puhua struck her with his staff and said, "Do you understand? She replied, "I do not understand. Puhua said, "If you do not understand, you are a ghost. Puhua’s manner was unconventional and his speech was eccentric. He would often shout, "I am a Buddha! I am a Buddha! or "I am a ghost! I am a ghost! He would strike people with his staff, saying, "If you can speak, you are a Buddha; if you cannot speak, you are a ghost. Eventually, he retired to Mount Zhongnan and passed away there. During the Yuanhe era, his disciple Wen-yi compiled this biography. **End of Biography of Puhua of Zhending Prefecture, Tang Dynasty.**
His innate disposition was extraordinary and largely sincere and straightforward; his actions were simple and unrestrained, and his speech was unconventional.

He personally served under Chan Master Jichan of Panshan, who instructed him intimately and in depth, leading him into the innermost sanctum of the Dharma. Yet, despite being cautioned to maintain this realization, he fell into madness and rebellion.
Once, when he met with Master Linji Xuan, he responded to him by braying like a donkey; those attending nearby could not help but laugh.
At times he would dance and sing, or suddenly wail in grief.
Whenever people encountered him, he manifested a thousand transformations and ten thousand shifts, entirely lacking any constant measure.
One day, carrying a coffin on his shoulder, he went through the streets, knocking at every door to announce his departure, saying:
"Puhua will die tomorrow."
At that time, upon examining it, they knew it could not be disparaged.
The people of Zhao followed him in succession out through the eastern gate of the city, proclaiming aloud:
"The burial today does not accord with the *Qingwu*."
After two days had passed, he went out through the southern gate, and the people followed him there as well.
He said again, "Tomorrow will be auspicious.
In this manner, he went out through the western and northern gates and returned; the people grew weary and their resolve slackened.
Once he sat in the wilds and fields, he was as if entering meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).

Among those who have authored treatises in the Chan school, because his words were those of a "first awakened" one, he is categorized among the "scattered sages" (*san sheng*) rather than the "regular members," for his speech does not belong to the formal ranks.

Biography of Dàchuān of Qīxián Monastery in Hánzhōu during the Táng Dynasty. The monk Dàchuān, whose dharma name was Fǎjiǒng, was a native of unknown origin from the Táng period. He lived in profound silence and maintained his integrity with ever-increasing rigor.
His precepts were without flaw, and his speech was never given in vain.
At Qixian Temple in Hanzhou, he practiced the four noble lineages; as his asceticism increased, his spirit flowed like a stream, and his joy overflowed.
Among the people of Mianzhu, regardless of age, all followed him as their spiritual guide.
When his life came to an end, he lay outside the temple; the laypeople prepared a bed and carried him back into the monastery together, diligently performing the funeral rites.
Just as the corpse was about to be lifted, a pair of deer led the way as if acting as attendants.
As soon as he stepped across the threshold of the gate, the temple plaque suddenly fell to the ground; those near and far were struck with wonder and sighed in admiration.
Furthermore, this mountain is numinous and extraordinary, not tolerating those who are coarse or vulgar.
There was once a monk living in deep seclusion who was not reverent or disciplined and committed many transgressions.
A divine being hurled him down the mountain for about seven *li*, yet he was injured only by his toes.
From this time on, there was no one who did not reform themselves and observe the precepts.
At the beginning of the Dali era, the North Mountain transformed into a golden color; upon it were multi-storied pavilions where Bodhisattvas practiced the Way.
In the space of a mere moment, it assumed ten thousand forms and a thousand shapes.
Sūjia resided in this temple for his entire life; as the site was imbued with spiritual power from the very ground, he left behind his shadow for veneration, as if serving a sacred shrine.
Next was Fajing of Mincheng, whose origins are unknown. He practiced the dhūta austerities with great self-discipline and diligence, exhorting the people of Min with words that were firm and upright.
It was heard that within the Liánmén River on Hǎitán Island there was a massive bell. Tradition held that in the past, someone had gone to Guangzhou to solicit funds for the casting of a signal drum.
When his great ship reached this spot, it was suddenly caught in a tempest and sank.

On the day of the full moon each month, the tide comes in greatly; when the water recedes, the *púláo* emerges, allowing a person to pass through its center, with a circumference of about one zhang or more.

During the Dali era, Jing intended to bring forth this bell; he first held a great assembly for vegetarian offerings and the recitation of mantras at Kaiyuan Temple, and sent a young monk to the Dragon Palace to request that the bell be granted to the human world so that it might be struck to signal the transition between dawn and dusk.
The young monk said to the sea deity, "I cherish this to pacify the ocean.
He gave me three small pearls as a token of faith; at that moment, it was as if the young monk had awakened from a dream, and the pearls were in my hand.

Biography of Nanda from the Western Regions during the Tang Dynasty. Regarding the monk Nanda: "Nanda" in the language of China means "Joy. His lineage and the country of his origin are not clearly known.
As a person, he was eccentric and unconventional, alternating between respectfulness and insolence without constancy.
During the Zhongyuan era of the Jianzhong period, he arrived in Min and Shu; at that time, Zhang Weigong Yan was serving as the Governor of Chengdu and welcomed him.

He delighted in saying to himself, "I have attained the Illusion-like Samādhi—entering water without being wetted, casting myself into fire without being burned, able to transform metal and stone, and manifesting transformations without end."

When he first entered Shu, he traveled together with three young nuns; at times he would drink heavily and sing wildly, and at other times he would gather crowds to preach the Dharma. The garrison commander detested this deeply and repeatedly ordered his men to arrest him.
When Xi was captured and brought before him, he said, "I,
a poor monk, have taken refuge within the gates of the Sangha, yet I possess a distinct art of medicine.
He then pointed to the three nuns and said:
"Both of these are excellent at singing and dancing.
The military commander then held them in high regard; he subsequently detained them, providing wine and meat for a banquet, and joined them in drinking and singing throughout the night.

They then borrowed short jackets, trousers, head-wraps, and combs; each of the three nuns applied powder and rouge, and all sat down in a row, casting sidelong glances and exchanging playful smiles, their graceful demeanor transcending the world.
When she was half-drunk from wine, she joyfully said to the nun, "Would you care to perform a dance for the Deputy Magistrate?

Thereupon she stepped forward slowly to dance with him; her trailing silk was like swirling snow, and her rapid movements brought her feet into close contact with his, a performance of unsurpassed excellence.
After a long while, the music ended, yet the dancing did not cease.
Xī (Hui) then exclaimed in derision, "Is this the way women act?
Startled, Xī suddenly rose and seized the sword of a border general; the crowd, believing him to be intoxicated by wine, all fled in alarm.
He then struck off the heads of the three nuns, all of whom fell prostrate upon the ground, their blood flowing for several zhang.
The military commander was greatly alarmed and called his attendants to bind Xi.
Xi laughed and said:
"It was not a matter of carelessness.
Xū raised the three *ni* [measures] which were actually a *zhú* staff of *qióngzhú* bamboo; the blood was merely the wine he had been drinking earlier.
Hǎoxǐ then withdrew to sit and partake in the banquet, while separately ordering someone to cut off his head and nail both ears to a pillar; neither were stained with blood.
He immediately sat upon the mat; as the wine circulated to him, he poured it directly into his severed stump, and his face turned crimson.
Yet his mouth could sing and dance, while his hands clapped in rhythm with the beat.
When the banquet was over and the guests had dispersed, his body would rise of its own accord; he would go to a pillar, retrieve his head, and place it back on, leaving no scars whatsoever.
From time to time, he spoke of people's fortunes and misfortunes, most of which were in the form of riddles that were only understood after the fact.
In Chengdu, there was someone who provided for him for several days; however, Huixi suddenly did not wish to stay, so the host bolted the gate to detain him.

Huixi immediately entered through a crack in the wall; when the man pulled at him, he gradually disappeared until only the corner of his *kāṣāya* remained. After hesitating for a moment, he was no longer to be seen.
The following day, he saw the shadow of a monk in a mural; its form was like the color of the sun, which gradually faded over the next few days.
After seven days had passed, there were only ink traces remaining in the sky.
By the eighth day, the ink traces had vanished.
Someone saw him early on, already within the borders of Pengzhou;
later, his whereabouts remained unknown.
The commentary states:
Is the conduct and appearance of Nanda characterized by the heterodox or the orthodox?
Yet he himself claims to have attained the Illusion-like Samādhi; that this samādhi is shared with King Anala is precisely the Great Samādhi of all Buddhas.
Only as an illusion does one see what is like an illusion; it cannot be divided into objective spheres by means of verbal discourse.
Among the four supernormal powers, there is the power of transformation like an illusion, which is able to transform external phenomena.
Therefore, Nanda alerted the people of Yong and Shu, many of whom revered the ways of ghosts, spirits, and immortals;
were it not for this samādhi, he would have been unable to transform such an incorrigible populace.
Biography of Shi Xuanzong of Mount Zijin in Shouzhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Xuanzong, surnamed Wu, was a native of Yongjia.
In his youth, he left the mundane world; possessed of a broad and magnanimous disposition, he took Changjing as his master at Baoshou Monastery on Yongding Mountain in his native region.
After receiving full ordination, he traveled to various regions to study, eventually arriving at the gate of Chan Master Ciliang in Jiangling, where he was like fine gold being refined in a furnace.

Having resolved his doubts and hesitations, he once again struck his monk’s staff and traveled elsewhere. Upon seeing Mount Zijin, it gladdened his heart, and he remained there to practice meditative contemplation.

Previously, this mountain had been plagued by many fierce tigers; some would devour traveling merchants, while others would injure woodcutters—among those fleeing harsh governance, the weeping of widows was truly pitiable.
Since Zong took up residence there, the sound of barking dogs had ceased and tracks of travelers were cut off; consequently, those entering the mountains from nearby areas no longer felt any dread.
One day, a crowd of monastics gathered when they saw an old man hasten toward the front of the seat, prostrating and kneeling with diligent reverence.
Zong asked, "Who are you? He replied:
“I was originally a tiger, devouring sentient beings here in these mountains.

Because of your Great Master’s transformation, my mind was secretly turned back, and I have been delivered from this karmic body to be reborn in the heavenly realm; thus I have come to express my gratitude.”
During the moments of his turning and pacing, he perceived nothing at all.
In the second year of the Dali era, he took leave of his disciples and passed away suddenly.
He was eighty-six years of age; in the second month, he was interred in a stupa, and a stele stands there to this day.
The Biography of Guangfu of Mount Yangqi in Yuanzhou during the Tang Dynasty. The monk Guangfu, whose secular surname was Zheng, was a native of Nan-yun.
In his youth, he relied upon the great virtuous master Si Hao, a prominent figure in the capital, to receive his dharma instructions.
Upon completing his ordination, he traveled to Mount Song and the two capitals, where he met Chan Master Shenhui and attained a profound understanding of the profound principles of the Way.

He traveled to Mount Yangqi in Yichun to hang up his staff there—within which, peaks and ridges accumulated emerald green and caves entered into the profound, while the sprouts of *lingzhi* fungi grew among the common flora.
He remained seated throughout the day with his eyes closed, sustaining himself on wood-shavings while passing the hours.

At times, there appeared those wearing high crowns and feathered robes, driving cranes and accompanied by phoenixes; at first they would appear and vanish suddenly, but later they would enter his hermitage and converse intimately with him.
Wherever that immortal guest arrived, light clouds and thin mists would follow his footsteps.
He ordered his attendants—the heavenly soldiers and giants—to keep their distance, so that they might converse face-to-face for the duration of several hours.

Thereafter, once his transformation through the Way was perfected, he entered nirvana on the fourth day of the third month in the first year of the Zhenyuan era; it is said that he was ninety-one years of age.
The commentary states:
The paths of the immortals and the Way differ; how could their discourses possibly be the same?
Tong said:

"In the past, there was the True Man Xiao You who was able to discourse on the principles of emptiness; the immortals of Mount Fangzhu built stupas and sincerely revered the Buddhist Way, yet they refrained from shaving their hair and donning monastic robes, being known as 'lay Bodhisattvas'."
Furthermore, the various sages of the Snowy Mountains who seek deliverance through proficiency in the five vidyās are similar [to us].
Nevertheless, their analogous paths must be carefully distinguished.

For instance, among the twenty truths (*satya*) of the Western Regions, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*) share the same names as those in the Śākya system.
"The distinctions among the heavens as they are conceived are truly difficult to differentiate.
Biography of Chan Master Yuanzhen of Mount Wuya in Dengzhou, Tang Dynasty. Chan Master Yuanzhen, whose secular surname was Chen, was a native of Zhongshan.
From a young age, he was alert and awakened, yet devoted to learning; he entered the local schools to study the Five Classics.

Suddenly, he encountered a traveling monk named Youxiao, whose father was an official at the prefectural yamen and possessed a profound aspiration for the Way, so he took in this monk to provide him with offerings and support.
He prostrated himself in reverence before the monks and listened to their discourses on the Way, gaining a profound and spiritual insight.

He abandoned the Confucian classics and delved into the Buddhist sutras; suddenly renouncing all that he loved, he went to Mount Baiti, where he paid homage to Master Zhizhou as his teacher and received instruction.
Later, he encountered Chan Master Heze and attained the Dharma, subsequently retiring to Mount Wuya in Nanyang.
Previously, there were many giant snakes in the mountains, and the mountain cave was inhabited by a venomous dragon; the local people suffered from these threats.
When Zhen arrived here, the two creatures vanished without a trace.
Once, there was a man whose appearance and attire were extraordinary; he bowed and said:

"I have been here for two hundred years. Now, moved by your disinterested transformation and your cultivation free from worldly concerns, we have attained a transcendent ascension through our hidden resonance—could this not be due to the power of your teaching, Master?"
He passed away in the sixth year of the Zhenyuan era at the age of eighty-six; his disciples enshrined his entire body in a stupa.
Biography of Dizang of Huacheng Monastery on Mount Jiuhua in Chizhou, Tang Dynasty. The monk Dizang, whose secular surname was Jin, was a descendant of the royal house of Silla.
Though his heart was compassionate, his countenance was stern; he was naturally gifted with keen intelligence.
Standing seven chi tall, his frame possessed a towering head with exceptionally prominent bone structure, and his physical strength could rival ten men.
He once instructed himself, saying:
"Among the Six Classics within the secular world and the Three Clarities within the realm of arts, it is only the primary truth that accords with the mind.
At that time, he shaved his head and traveled across the sea; leaving his boat behind, he proceeded on foot, shaking his mendicant’s staff as he journeyed in all directions.

While traveling to Chiyang, he encountered Mount Jiuzi; his heart was filled with great joy at the sight of it, so he went straight to its peaks and found a site within a valley that faced south and was spacious and level.
The soil of that land was black loam, and its springs were smooth and sweet; dwelling among the crags and drawing water from the ravines, he passed his days in this simple manner.
Once, while in seclusion, he was stung by a venomous insect, yet he sat upright without a single thought.
Suddenly, a beautiful woman appeared, performed a bow, and presented him with medicine, saying:
"This child was ignorant; I pray you accept this spring-water to atone for my transgression.

Having spoken, she vanished. Looking around his seat, he saw that water was gushing forth from between the rocks. At that time, it was said that the deity of Mount Jiuzi had manifested as a spring to provide for his needs.
During the Tianbao era, Li Bai traveled to this mountain and named it Jiuhua (Nine Flowers).
Local legend holds that the mountain deity is a woman;
its many peaks are often shrouded in clouds and mist, rarely revealing their summits.

Sengzang had long harbored the aspiration to uphold the four great collections of scriptures (*catur-āgama*). He subsequently descended the mountain to Nanling, where a lay devotee transcribed them for him, enabling him to return to the mountain.

At the beginning of the Zhide era, Zhe Guo led several village elders from the foot of the mountain to ascend it. They found themselves in a place of profound seclusion where no one else was present; the clouds and sun were vividly clear, and there dwelt only Sengzang, sitting alone with his eyes closed in a stone chamber.
In his room was a tripod with broken legs; inside the tripod was white earth mixed with a small amount of rice, which he boiled and ate.
The assembly of elders were struck with amazement and sighed, saying, "That the Master practices such asceticism is surely due to the fault of us who dwell beneath the mountain."
Together they constructed the meditation halls, and within a few years, a great monastery was completed.

At the beginning of the Jianzhong era, Lord Zhang Yan governed this region; admiring the lofty character of the Abbot, he petitioned the throne to transfer the former nameplate and establish the temple as such.
When his home country heard of this, they led their followers across the sea to seek him out; as his disciples became numerous, he had no means to provide for them for a year.
Zang then struck the rock and obtained earth, which was bluish-white in color, as soft as flour, and used it to provide food for the assembly.
His followers requested the Dharma to nourish their spirits rather than seeking food to sustain their lives;
they were known in the south as the "Withered Assembly," and there was none who did not revere them.
Beside Longtan there was a quarry of white plaster that was inexhaustible.
In the summer of the nineteenth year of the Zhenyuan era, he suddenly summoned his assembly to bid them farewell; none knew where he had gone.

There was only the sound of the mountain echoing and stones falling, and the striking of the bell became hoarse and died away as if the master had passed into nirvana while seated in the lotus posture.
He was ninety-nine years of age.

His corpse remained sitting within the coffin; when it was opened after three years to be placed in a stupa, his countenance appeared as if he were still alive. When they lifted the bier and moved his limbs, his joints shifted like the rattling of golden chains.
He then erected a small stupa on the Southern Terrace; this was the place where he stored his seat for meditation.
An account of these events by the retired scholar, Right Reminder Fei Guanying, remains extant.
During the Dazhong era, the monk Yingwu also recorded his virtues.
*Biography of Shenxuan of Mount Jinhua in Wuzhou, Tang Dynasty*. Shi Shenxuan’s secular surname was Liu; he was a native of Jianyang.
From childhood, he was grave and quiet, speaking only when questioned.
While traveling as a guest in Wunü, he entered Kaiyuan Temple and resolved to leave the household life.
Not long after, the Governor of his home commandery visited the temple to seek out his teacher; seeing Huixuan’s spirit and countenance were bright and refined, [he was deeply impressed].
The Prefect, who was skilled in physiognomy, looked at him several times and said, "This youth is truly a vessel for transcending the mundane world.
In days to come, he shall receive the profound Dharma; surrounded by a thousand followers, he will surely surpass to the highest fruit—this is no ordinary spirit."
He then recited the *Saptabuddha-koṭi-mantra* without ceasing from dusk until dawn.

Having completed his reception of the precepts, he dwelt in seclusion within a stone cave at the Baijia Rock on the northern side of Mount Jinhuashan; he did not construct a hut but practiced as a *dhūta* in the open air.
Furthermore, there were no beds or couches; however, a divine being emitted purple clouds that spread high above to cover them—viewed from afar, they drifted gently like a solitary pillar pavilion.

A divine personage occasionally came to inquire after his well-being, joining his hands in greeting and saying, "To the east of Mount Chisong Cave, there is a forest and spring of extraordinary beauty; would you not consider residing there?"
Xuān followed the invitation and went to reside there; over several years, many auspicious signs appeared.
In the second year of the Zhenyuan era, he met Chan Master Zhixian, who said to him, "If you continue to recite in this manner, demonic disturbances will surely arise."
To extinguish the enmity of Māra, one must recognize the fundamental nature of the body.

Once the fundamental nature of the body is realized as true, there is neither Māra nor Buddha; one attains sudden and expansive awakening, and both principle and phenomena are perfected, such that the efficacy of divine mantras is doubled.

In the eighth year of the Yuanhe era, Fan Yang, the Censor-in-Chief, took notice of this and dispatched an envoy bearing incense, felt rugs, and utensils as offerings for Xuan; these were all redistributed to the assembly present there.
Next, Wang Zhong, the Secretariat Drafter,
requested that he receive the Bodhisattva precepts for the assembly at Dayun Temple.
In the twelfth year, Meng Jian, the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices from Pingchang, personally invited him from Kuaiji, but he did not go.
In the eighth month, he suddenly returned to his former mountain, and no one could fathom the reason.
Suddenly, he announced his passing; he was seventy-six years of age.
His disciples erected a stupa for him there.
One day, Yuan was at the north of Mount Jinhua, where it was cold and lacked sunlight.
A divine being asked him,
"What do you require, Master?"
He said, "I am on the northern slope of the mountain, suffering from the biting cold. The spirit said,
"It is but a minor matter."
At night, he heard a clamorous sound, and at dawn the next morning, he saw that a small peak had shifted.
Biography of Daoxing of Kaiyuan Temple in Lizhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Daoxing, surnamed Yang, was a native of Guiyang.
From birth, his spiritual faculties were sharp and keen, and his physical frame was as pure as ice and snow.

At the tender age of twelve, he vowed his heart to the Way and studied at the Prajñā Monastery on Mount Nanyue; he sought the ultimate instructions at Zhongling and attained silent realization of the Dharma, which he named "Svatantra Samādhi."
Consequently, he wore sandals made of woven hemp to sustain his remaining life.
To the southwest of Liyang, he felled timber to build a dwelling, occupying a space no larger than a square zhang; tigers and leopards often lay hidden among his bedding and couch.
Later, someone brought timber and provisions to construct a hall and dwelling; before even ten days had passed, everything was completely finished.
Upon inspecting it, no one was to be seen; he then realized that spirits and deities had provided the materials and exerted their labor.
The Prefect earnestly invited him to reside at Kaiyuan Temple in the provincial seat.
Not long after, he passed away in the fifteenth year of the Yuanhe era at the age of sixty-nine; his śarīra were cremated and a stupa was erected there.
The Biography of Shi Huai-kong of Mount Anfeng in Xuzhou during the Tang Dynasty. Shi Huai-kong, surnamed Liang, was a native of Langzhou.
In her youth, she entered the monastic order at Kōshōzan Kōfukuin in her native province.
After receiving the precepts, she traveled to various regions to pursue her studies, where she attained a clear and thorough understanding of the Chan teachings of Daichi.
Later, he arrived at Mount Anfeng in Pengcheng and hung up his staff to dwell there in silent contemplation. Within a few years, he established a great monastery.
Once, a monk appeared, traveling through the air, circling the walls incessantly.
At times he stepped upon lotus flowers, and at other times he walked upon the ground;
all people gazed upon him with reverence. After several days, he took his leave of the air and said, "I shall return to rely upon you again in three or five years."
Having finished speaking, he vanished from sight.
Hui-kong entered nirvana in the first year of the Xingyuan era at the age of eighty-eight.
It was only in the second month of the first year of the Changqing era that his remains were finally enshrined in a stupa.

Biography of Yuanguan of Huilin Monastery in the Capital of Luoyang during the Tang Dynasty The monk Yuanguan was a native of unknown origin. He resided in a house in Luoyang and was by nature simple and unpretentious.

At times he applied himself diligently to Buddhist studies, yet at other times he took pleasure in managing his livelihood; having acquired profits from his fields and gardens, he was colloquially known as the "Yi Dun of the Empty Gate" (the Buddhist world).
Furthermore, his conduct was utterly extraordinary, and he was proficient in musical theory. Toward the end of the Dali era, he became a bosom friend with Li Yuan.

When Li Yuan’s father, Li Cheng, was serving as the Imperial Protector and fell into the hands of the rebels at the end of the Tianbao era, Li Yuan subsequently donated his family estate to Huelin Temple north of Luoyang—which had been Cheng’s private villa—to serve as inexhaustible public funds for the monastery.
He was provided with only a single vessel of food daily, partaking of meals alongside the monastic community for three years.
Yuan was fond of alchemy and dietetics; suddenly, he made plans to travel to the mountains of Shu, such as Qingcheng and Emei, to seek medicinal elixirs.
Liu Guan wished to travel to Chang'an by way of the Xiyu Valley, while Li Yu intended to enter the Gorges from Jingzhou;
they contended over these two routes for half a year without reaching a decision.
Li Yu said:
"I have already ceased serving kings and lords; I do not wish to travel the roads between the two capitals.
Guan said, "In one's conduct there should be no fixed insistence; I beg to follow your command."
He then traveled up the Gorges of Jing, passing through Nanpu, where he moored his boat. He saw several women wearing silk sashes and jade ornaments, carrying jars to draw water.
Observing them, he lowered his head and wept, saying:
"The reason I did not wish to pass through this place was that I feared encountering these women."
Li said, "Since coming from the upper gorges, these followers have been numerous; why do you alone weep?
Guan replied:
"As for that pregnant woman, Lady Wang, she is the one in whom I have entrusted my body.
Three years have already passed, yet she has not yet given birth, solely because of my failure to arrive."
"Now that I have seen this, my destiny has found its destination; this is what the Śākya teachings call 'cyclic existence.
I request that you employ mantras and spells to ensure his swift rebirth, and meanwhile, please delay your departure for a short while to bury me in the mountain valley."
When her family bathes their child, she will also look forward to your visit.
If you should happen to glance at her and share a smile, it shall be a sign that you have recognized her.
Twelve years hence, on the night of the mid-autumn moon, we shall meet specifically outside the Tianzhu Temple in Qiantang; this is the appointed time for our meeting.
Li, repenting of this one act, reached this realization through contemplation; his grief was so profound that he nearly fainted.
He summoned a pregnant woman and informed her of the matter; the woman rejoiced and returned home.
Shortly thereafter, his kinsmen all assembled at the riverside to offer him dried fish and turbid wine.
Li went to bestow upon him the consecrated water.
Guan then performed his ablutions and refreshed his clothing and gear.
When Guan was viewed as dead, a pregnant woman gave birth.
Li went to visit the newborn on the third day; as the infant was wrapped in swaddling clothes and brought into the light, it indeed broke into a smile.
Li wept and informed Wang Shi of the matter, whereupon Wang Shi provided a lavish burial for Guan.
The next day, Li turned his oars and returned to Huilin Temple; only after questioning his disciples did he learn that [the Master] had already prepared for death.
Li constantly recalled their appointment at Hangzhou.

When the appointed time arrived, he went to Tianzhu Mountain Temple. That night, as the moon shone with brilliant clarity, he suddenly heard a cowherd singing the "Zhuzhi" song by the side of Ge Hong’s well. Riding a cow and striking its horn, with two topknots and a short tunic, the boy slowly approached the front of the temple; it was Guanzhong.
Li Qu bowed and said,
"I wonder how you are, sir?
He replied:
“Master Li is a man of true faith.
My path and yours diverge; be careful not to draw near to me.
Your worldly karmic ties are not yet exhausted; simply continue to practice diligently without falling back, and you shall meet me again.”
Li Wuyou was unable to offer any words in response; gazing at him, he was moved to tears.
Guan then sang the "Zhuzhi" song, riding off into the distance on his steed; the lyrics were poignant and the melody lofty, such that no one knew their meaning.
He sighed and said:
"Truly, this is a monk who has attained the Way!
Though separated by but a few inches, the paths of the sage and the ordinary person are distinct; indeed, such must be the case!"

Initially, when Yuan’s father was killed by bandits, he was only eight years old; he was captured by the raiders and wandered between the north and south, passing from one household to another for six or seven years before returning to his close relatives.
When Emperor Daizong heard of this, he appointed him as a clerk in the administration of He Prefecture.
Yuan subsequently abstained from alcohol and meat, refrained from marriage, and did not employ servants; he constantly resided in a single room at Huelin Temple, taking his meals with the monks.
First, he ordered his burial plot in the wilderness to prepare for his final rites, and from time to time he would go there to sleep among them.
As for honor and disgrace, right and wrong, he regarded them all with complete equanimity.
At that time, Li Gongdeyu, the Chancellor, submitted a memorial recommending him, whereupon he was appointed as an Imperial Censor (Jianyi Dafu).
However, Yuan, who was already over eighty years old at the time, submitted a petition refusing the appointment and did not rise to take office.
He passed away after two years—this was in the second year of the Changqing era.
The commentary states:
As for the claim that Yuanguan was already in a womb before he died, one would surely not believe it upon hearing it.
Why is this? Because it contradicts the teachings of all the sages.
I have heard that among the women of noble families in Min, many permit their daughters to say, "I shall come immediately," when they are about to marry.
At the end of his life, someone marked his thighs with vermilion; on that very day, a son was born into his household, whose body bore red characters reading "Come at once.
Instances of this kind were numerous.
Zhuangzi’s statement that “a scholar of narrow views cannot be discussed with regarding the Dao,

for he is bound by his teachings” may perhaps refer to the heterodox doctrines of India which claim there is a future Buddha, or to some other assembly where [the Buddha] once spoke, such that they perceive our own school as being self-authorized.
If this is so, one must not yet dogmatically cling to the teachings already practiced.

As for the contemplation that leads to the realization of such profound heights, it is like the many kinds of inconceivable matters found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*; it is something that thought, mind, and speech cannot pursue even from a distance of a thousand li.
The Biography of Fazang of Mount Lu’s Five Elders Peak in Jiangzhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Fazang, whose secular surname was Zhou, was a native of Nankang.
From his youth, he was bright and talented; beginning his studies of historical records, he attained a profound mastery of medical prescriptions, rivaling the marvelous skill of Zhi Faxun.
There was a monk of Youmen who lay ill, on the verge of death. Daocang took his pulse and prescribed a remedy; after two nights, he recovered.
This monk had frequently engaged in discussions on the profound mysteries (*xuan*), and from that time forward, he conceived the intention to transcend the mundane world.

Having reached an advanced age, he respectfully took leave of his kin and went to Baoji Monastery on Mount Pingtian in his native prefecture, where he received instruction under Master Yuan and received the precepts.
Later, he traveled to visit Chan Master Daji; their words and teachings were like a stone cast into water.

He descended northward with carefree ease to Mount Lu and climbed Wulao Peak; captivated by its spiritual wonders, he stayed alone in a cold forest, gathering acorns and chestnuts and scooping water from mountain streams to sustain his physical life for several years.
Two immortals arrived riding upon clouds; they engaged in conversation throughout the day, sometimes staying overnight, sometimes not returning for a month, and at other times arriving day after day.
When others saw him, they spoke of him from the sidelines as being inconsistent;
yet when the assembly of monks gathered, he left no trace at all.
On another day, he took his leave of the Tripitaka Master, saying:
"Return now to the mountains; you, Master, should dwell there in peace.
Thereupon, his Way became fragrant, and lay patrons collectively established a monastery for him.
He passed away during the Baoli era at the age of eighty-two.
It is recorded that on the fourth day of the third month of that year, [the relics] were enshrined in the stupa.
The commentary asks:
When [the relics] were concealed on Mount Wulao, who were the two immortals who came to engage in discussion throughout the entire day?
Tong said, "In the past,
Liu Xiang compiled the *Lie xian zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Transcendents), stating:
'Are such individuals to be found within the Buddhist scriptures?'"
Furthermore, the disciples of the three Perfected Men—Pei, Zhou, and Tongbo—each studied the Buddha-dharma to some extent; could these not be considered those who have come to inquire about the Way?
This is similar to the response of the grasshopper to the *caochong* (grass cricket) mentioned in the *Shijing*.
The Biography of Shi Jiankong of Xiangshan Monastery in Luoyang, Tang China. Shi Jiankong’s secular surname was Qi, and he was a native of Wu Commandery.
Having suffered from poverty since my youth, although I have been diligent in my studies, I possess little power of memory.
In my prime, I composed poetry that was not particularly ornate or flowery.
I have long been beset by hardship while traveling between the regions of Wu and Chu for already four or five years.
In attending upon lords and dukes, the benefit obtained was meager.
When his cash reached a full string, illness inevitably arose; only when his funds were exhausted did he recover.
At the beginning of the Yuanhe era, while traveling in Qiantang, he encountered a period of famine and scarcity, and thus proposed seeking a meal at the Tianzhu Monastery.
Upon reaching the west of Gushan Temple, he was so famished that he could not proceed; he leaned over the stream and wept, chanting mournfully several times.
Suddenly, a Buddhist monk appeared, sitting by the water’s edge.
Looking into the air and smiling, he said, "Dharma Master, you scholar—have you had enough of the flavors of your travels?"
Kong said, "I have already had my fill of traveling and its flavors.
How can your address of me as 'Dharma Master' be so utterly misplaced?"
It was because when Kō was not yet a monk, his name was Junbō.
A foreign monk said,
"Do you not remember lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* at Tōtoku-ji Temple?"
Kong said, "I have been in my physical body for forty-five years now, wandering between the regions of Wu and Chu, never having crossed the Jiaokou Pass.
So how can there be talk of Luoyang?"
The monk said,
"You must be so consumed by the fire of hunger that you have no leisure to recall past events.
He then reached into his bag and took out a jujube fruit as large as a fist, saying:

"This is produced in our country; those who eat it possess superior wisdom that knows the affairs of the past and future, while those with inferior wisdom know only the affairs of their previous lives."
Extremely hungry from fasting, he ate jujubes and drank from a spring.
Suddenly, he let out a yawn and sighed, leaning his head on a stone to sleep; after a short while, he awoke and remembered preaching the sutras at Tongde Temple as if it were only yesterday.
His tears fell even more profusely as he asked the monks,
"Where is Master Zhen?
They replied:
“Because my single-minded application had not yet reached its ultimate goal, I became a monk in Shu once again.
Now, however, I have severed all攀缘 (pān-yuan, clinging/dependencies). Where is the Venerable Shen now?”
He replied,
"My previous vow is not yet fulfilled.
[The other asked,] "Where is Master Wù?"
He replied,
"Do you not remember how, in jest before the stone image at Mount Xiangshan, I made a great vow:
'If I do not realize unexcelled bodhi, I shall certainly become a valiant and noble minister'?"
"I heard yesterday that you have already attained the rank of Great General.
At that time, among us five traveling monks, I alone attained liberation; you alone remain a man of frost and hunger."
Kong Qi said, "For some forty years I have taken but one meal a day; for over thirty years I have worn but a single coarse garment. I have decisively severed the roots of all worldly affairs."
"How unexpected that your merit is incomplete!
Why do you sit here in hunger and cold?
The monk replied:
"By extensively expounding heterodox views from this lion throne, you cause those who study emptiness to give rise to doubt and confusion.
The pearl of their precepts has been marred, and a faint trace of impurity remains; just as a muddled sound can never produce a clear resonance."
"Their physical statures are hunched and their shadows are bent;
such is the natural way of karmic retribution. Kong asked, "What should be done about this?"
The monk said,
"Regarding what has occurred today, I have no further plan.
As for matters concerning future lives, I shall serve as a warning to you, my son."
He then reached into his alms-bowl bag and took out a mirror, both back and face of which were brilliantly translucent. Addressing Kōng, he said:

"If you wish to know the distinction between noble and base, the span of long and short life, the rise and fall of the Buddha-dharma, and the flourishing or decline of my Way, you should examine this mirror."
After looking into the mirror for a long time, Kōran said in farewell, “I have now thoroughly understood the matter of karmic retribution and the principles of prosperity and decline.
The monk gathered the mirror into his bag and departed; after walking some ten paces, he suddenly vanished without a trace.
In the evening of that month, Kōng entered the Lingyin Temple to renounce worldly life and receive full ordination.
Thereafter, he traveled among famous mountains, increasingly intensifying his ascetic discipline.
In the first year of the Dàhé era, he went to Luoyang, where at the Tiānzhū Temple in Lóngmén he met Liù Chéng of Hé-dōng, to whom he personally recounted the details of his origins.
Tao Cheng heard the discourse on emptiness; he found that all matters were impermanent and was greatly struck by its marvel.
Daokong said:
"I have lived in this world for seventy-seven years and have been a monk for thirty-two years. With my almsbowl, I shall still remain in the world for nine more years."
"When I depart from this world, will the Buddha-dharma decline?
When Zhencheng interrogated him about this, he remained silent and offered no reply.
He then asked for Zhencheng’s brush and inkstone, inscribed several lines upon the northern wall of the scripture repository, and departed.
He said:

"To raise one grain of sand against the sands of the Ganges; to set a snare for a rabbit while a dog snatches it away; for oxen and tigers to clash with horns and fangs—none of these can extinguish the blossoms of the precious sandalwood tree."
The commentary states:
"One who knows his past lives by eating a jujube from a Brahman monk is like one who understands the languages of various nations by consuming medicinal herbs from the Snowy Mountains.
One who discerns good and ill fortune by examining a mirror is like one who foretells events by observing the patterns on the palm of Tuo Cheng."
Eating dates while facing a mirror—how could this be a mere coincidence?
It was no ordinary encounter.
Master Kōng inscribed a prophecy in response to seal off the inquiries of Liù Chéng; its fulfillment was realized during the suppression of the Teachings in the Huìchāng era.

At that time, Emperor Wuzong compelled over 207,000 monks and nuns to return to secular life and demolished more than 47,000 temples and hermitages; thus it is said, "The flourishing of one sand grain brings the decline of sands as numerous as the Ganges; the rabbit is in the snare, yet the dog still snaps at it," expressing the extreme severity of the persecution.
In the year Yi-chou, the Dharma was destroyed; in Bing-yin, he passed away.
The Buddha-dharma is likened to the sandalwood tree: its flowers and fragrance shall ultimately never cease. Thus it is said.
If he were not an extraordinary person, how could his ability to conceal the past and examine the future be so remarkable?
The Biography of Daoxing of Mount Luofu in Guangzhou, Tang Dynasty. The monk Daoxing, surnamed Mei, was a native of Kuaiji.
His father was an official in the Yuezhou administration.
Xing, though young, was knowledgeable in the classics and had already attained a refined and outstanding level of scholarship.

Once, he encountered a monk on his almsround; Xing engaged him in conversation regarding the Way and found himself quite adept at Chan contemplation, whereupon he requested permission to leave the household life.
He went to Zhiyou at Baoshou Monastery on Mount Siming, where he received instruction and pursued his cultivation, gathering firewood and drawing water.
Later, while traveling to Mount Nanyue, he heard of the spiritual influence of Daji in Jiangxi and went there to attend upon him.
While contemplating the nurturing of the sacred embryo, he beheld Mount Luofu’s wonders: it rises three thousand *zhang* high, possessing seventy stone chambers and seventy-two long streams.
Immortals, celestial birds, jade trees, and vermilion grasses grow upon its peaks, half of which extend into the sea.
He dwelt in a stone grotto, remaining silent and settled in dhyāna.
Yet, mountain spirits and water monsters would often cry out in alarm; however, as he went to look at them, he regarded them with utter indifference.
An old man appeared, his features upright and handsome, his robes and cap elegant and refined;

he prostrated himself with his forehead to the ground and said, "I have resided within this place for barely two hundred years. Now, because of your presence, Master, I have been moved by a profound spiritual resonance beyond my own power; I have wandered freely, escaped from suffering, and shall return to the human realm to experience joy."
His responses to various things were mostly of this kind.
He passed away from illness in the ninth year of the Bōreki era at the age of ninety-five.
On the eighteenth day of the ninth month of that year, he was interred in a stupa.
The Biography of Shi Puman of Luzhou during the Tang Dynasty. Shi Puman was a man of unknown origins from the region between Fen and Jin.

Throughout his life in that area, he acted according to his spontaneous impulses, disregarding monastic conventions; at times he would sing and at other times weep, with no one able to fathom his intent.

He refuted worldly matters through his words, and his past deeds were invariably corroborated by evidence; thus, people of the time regarded him as one who was both powerful and disciplined, like Wan-hui.
Sometimes he entered among the Xianbei and Hu peoples to exhort them to cultivate goodness, leading some even to abandon hunting and fishing.
At the beginning of the Jiànzhōng era, he composed several poems in a Buddhist temple in Lùzhōu and then vanished.
What was recorded says:
"This water connects with the Jīng River; its twin crimson hues fill the valley floor."
"The blue ox leads the red tiger; this shall again be called the Year of Great Peace.
After he inscribed these words, no one could understand their meaning.
Later, when Zhu Ci was instigated by the rebels of Jingyuan and the Imperial Carriage took refuge in Fengtian, [the prophecy was fulfilled].
At that time, the empire was conscripting troops while rebels occupied the region of Guanzhong; as they besieged and pressed him in successive battles, people only then began to understand.
This "water" (shui) refers to "Ci" (the name of Li Shi);
the Jing River represents the onset of the rebellion by the troops arriving from Jingzhou.
The two vermilion ones are Cizhi and Taosheng;
as for the "Blue Ox," it refers to the first year of Xingyuan, the year of Yi-chou—where Yi represents wood and is blue, and Chou represents the ox—in that year the era name was changed to Zhenyuan;
then, reaching the second year, Bing-yin—where Bing represents fire and is red.
The Tiger is the sign of the Year of the Tiger. Since the rebels were finally pacified at this time, it was called the "Restoration of the Taiping Era.

Regarding the Biography of Shi Xiexie of Jiangling Prefecture during the Tang Dynasty: The monk Shi Xiexie, also known as Qing, did not associate with others; he would simply say "Xiexie" himself, and thus he was so named.
During the reign of Emperor Dezong, he was traveling in Zhugong, where his clothing was tattered and his appearance was extremely simple and foolish; however, he was skilled at singing the "Hemanzi.
He acted with unrestrained license, having no fixed decorum.
Once he encountered a drunken police officer (*wǔbó*) on the road who insulted him and forced him to sing.
Xie then raised his voice and struck a melodic tune, with the lyrics all exposing the former private and malicious deeds of the officer—matters never before heard by anyone.
The head bailiff was filled with shame and alarm, while those listening by the roadside recognized him as a holy monk and prostrated themselves in repentance for their transgressions.
At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era, he frequently entered the marketplaces, where crowds of youths followed and pursued him; thus, among the people of Chu, he became the source of amusement.
His ultimate end was not known thereafter.
Next there was the monk Hengkuang, who roamed about without restraint;
whenever he fasted, he would consume nothing but several liters of sesame oil.
If he saw a large vessel filled with offerings, he would rejoice.

At Jingzhu, a family specially invited him to drink sesame oil; on that same day, he was also at a vegetarian feast in Hunan, where he manifested multiple bodies to receive offerings, earning him the nickname "The Master of Oil-Eating."
The commentary asks:
"Does the sound of *xie* correspond to the *shang* or the *yu* pitch?
Tong replied:
"In the compilation of the *Chuánjiā*, there are two methods:
first, transcribing the text without providing phonetic glosses; second, transmitting the oral instructions for the tonal registers.
What I have obtained here is the transcription of the text."
If the *Chuci* (Songs of Chu) uses the sound *shēngyú*, it is pronounced as *sūgè*; if the dialects of Shandong use the word *shǎo*, it is pronounced as *xiěxié*.

These matters concern the region between the Jing and Chu rivers; its two pronunciations were heard from those who came to instruct me. The name "Xiē" is identical to the natural calls of birds and beasts.

Biography of the Monk Yishi of Wu Commandery during the Tang Dynasty. Regarding the venerable monk Śramaṇa Yishi of Jianfu Monastery, who was known for his realization of wisdom: it is unknown where he was from.
His appearance was like that of a madman, and his speech was incoherent and disordered.
At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era, he wandered through the gardens of Wu begging; he often displayed prescient knowledge of future events, which led people to regard him with suspicion.

In the marketplace, there were several rooms belonging to a commoner’s house; whenever the Master of Righteousness took up his axe to cut away its eaves, the man would forbid him, but he would not stop.
That man, who had long known of his divine and extraordinary nature, bowed in respect and said to him:
"I, your disciple, rely on this for my livelihood; do not destroy my house."
Looking back, he asked,
"Do you regret it?
and threw down his axe before departing.
During a night fire, the blaze spread extensively, leaving only a few rooms of the eaves he had cut off remaining.

He took pleasure in staying in abandoned temples; regardless of winter or summer, he would constantly collect discarded banners, canopies, and wooden Buddha statues to use entirely as firewood and charcoal.

Furthermore, he would roast carp over a smoldering fire; as the fish leaped about profusely and ash drifted everywhere, he would clap his hands and laugh loudly, eating them without even using a spoon or chopsticks.
The face was covered in grime and he did not wash it; whenever he washed it, it would immediately become overcast and rain. The people of Wu took this as a sign for weather forecasting.
When he was about to die, he drank dozens of *hu* of ash-water, then sat facing north reciting the Buddha’s name. As the officials and commoners watched him, seven days passed before he died.
At that time, during the height of summer, his complexion did not change and his limbs did not decay.
The common people carried him out to the outskirts of the city to cremate him.
Furthermore, there was a monk at An Guo Temple in Jingzhao whose deeds were extraordinary; he burned a wooden Buddha on a plot of land where crops had already ripened.
What he says regarding human affairs is never uttered in vain;
he is likewise a monk whose character is unfathomable.
Furthermore, there is Śramaṇa Zhèngzhì of Yǒngshòu Monastery in the capital, whose family origins are not well known.
During the Zhenyuan era, many miraculous events occurred at the temples in the capital, yet the multitude remained unaware of them.
At times, he would be tilling the fields by day at Zhangdu Hermitage and return to the temple by night.
His hermitage was located at Lanyuan in Jinzhou, Han Province, some seven hundred li from the capital.

He was then known as Master Zhi—this being Changzu An, the Duke Fayun—who could travel vast distances in the space of a single instant; the Daoists call this "contracting the earth's veins" (*suodimai*) to traverse great distances.
If he performs spiritual transformations regarding the objects of form (*rūpa*), though things are distant, they appear near.

Next was an old monk of Jianfu Temple who devoted himself exclusively to recitation and upholding the scriptures, rarely failing in his practice; he could speak of events before their signs appeared, as if witnessing them with his own eyes.
At the beginning of the Dàhé era, Prime Minister Wei Gōng Chùhòu was fond of the Empty Gate (Buddhism) and would separately summon monks of renowned virtue for meals every month.
When the old monk saw that Wei had newly ascended to the position of high official, he remarked, "How extraordinary!
The Prime Minister has found such an excellent place for parinirvāṇa."
No one understood [the meaning of his words].

Later, while he was in audience before Emperor Wenzong, he suffered a sudden seizure; he collapsed on the palace steps, and by the time he was supported and carried out of the hall, his breath had already ceased.
This was precisely verified by the old monk’s words; he died within the inner palace, which is why it was said that his "good place for extinction" was the Kaicheng era.
His final end thereafter remains unknown.
The Biography of Śrīguṇabhadra of Mount Yunxiu in Tangzhou, Tang Dynasty. Śramaṇa Śrīguṇabhadra, surnamed Han, was a native of Xunyang.
In his youth, he was pure and serene, never mingling with other children.

His father served as a subordinate official in Qian’an and had already turned his heart toward the teachings of Śākyamuni; he would often arrange Buddhist images within the office quarters, summoning monks to chant hymns and raise their voices, so that the music of the Dharma resounded together.
Upon seeing this, Jing was filled with joy on his face; he followed the monk without parting and sought to take monastic ordination.
His parents had no means to dissuade him, so he secretly went to Donglin Temple to study under the Vinaya Master Zengsu.
Later, after lecturing on the meaning of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, he traveled south to Yuzhang to attend upon Chan Master Daji.
Subsequently, he resided at Mount Xiwei in Huai’an.
This mountain had previously been infested with fierce beasts in great numbers, which frequently caused harm.
Since Huijian took up residence there, the calamity of tigers subsided, and he was praised by those both far and near.
Suddenly, a man wearing a flat black cap appeared, paid his respects most reverently toward the Dharma seat, and vanished in an instant.
