Seven days later, a person wearing a crown and ceremonial robes, appearing quite extraordinary, ascended into the air before the abbot’s quarters and declared:
“This Great Master is truly a treasure of the Dharma.”
"Having opened the eyes and the celestial vision of humanity, he has come to inform me of this.
Upon hearing and seeing this, his disciples knew that the Master’s realization was profound.
In the fourth year of the Huichang era, he entered nirvana; on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, his remains were enshrined in a stupa.
Whenever one attains the Way, the Earth Deity reports it to the Sky Deity, and so on, successively up to the Peak of Existence; this is how it is witnessed.

Biography of Qingguan of Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai during the Tang Dynasty. The monk Qingguan of Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai during the Tang Dynasty, whose secular name was Mingzhong, was a native of Linhai and surnamed Qu.

At his birth, there were web-like membranes connecting the fingers and toes of his hands and feet; this is what the Buddhist sutras refer to as the mark of the webbed hands and feet (*jāla-pāṇi-pāda-lakṣaṇa*).
When he reached childhood, his spirit was preeminent and extraordinary, and he thus conceived the aspiration to transcend the mundane world.
He then went to Guoqing Temple and placed himself under the tutelage of Vinaya Master Yuanzhang, attending to him with his alms-bowl and water-pitcher.
Neither his parents nor anyone else could dissuade him; he was like a garuḍa bird tearing through tens of thousands of layers of encircling nets.

At the age of eighteen, he received the full ordination according to the Dharma; this was truly because his roots of goodness were deeply planted and his awakening was innate. He thoroughly mastered the texts of the Tiantai school and clearly understood the Three Contemplations (*trividha-śamatha-vipaśyanā*); moreover, having attained profound meditative concentration, his spiritual wonders and responsive manifestations were such that no one could fathom them.
Having read extensively across the hundred schools of thought, he became thoroughly proficient in the Three Teachings.
He was skilled at composing prose and excelled in poetry and calligraphy.
Whenever local governors or imperial envoys arrived, they all sought audience with him, drawn by his reputation; upon meeting him, they found him to be as dignified and solemn as a strict sovereign.
Upon seeing him, they were struck with awe and submission; they would simply approach his low stool and staff to wait upon this noble gentleman.
Whenever he bestowed wealth or treasures, he dedicated them entirely to the permanent endowment of the Sangha, leaving nothing for private accumulation.
Someone asked:
"The expenditures of those of high rank all go toward private gifts; why do they not use them for themselves?
He replied:
"I regret that I have not yet been able to give away my head or eyes, let alone worldly wealth.

At the beginning of the Dazhong era, Buddhist temples throughout the empire were being restored. Guàn entered the capital to request a great bell for his temple to be struck, and he also requested the imperial plaque to be hung there; the calligraphy for the inscription was written by Liú Gōngquán, the Academician of the Jíxiányuàn.
Liu also composed a preface for a poem sent off [the monk] as he returned east.
Liu further requested that the Tripitaka be brought back to the temple.

During the year of Guiyou in the Dazhong era, the region south of the Yangtze River suffered successive famines, and corpses lay scattered everywhere; the Monastery consequently distributed its grain stores to provide relief.
Furthermore, as the mountain monk was passing through the wilderness beyond the mundane world, he entered into meditative concentration within his room and said to his disciple:
"If you do not die, when the grain and millet have ripened, you should summon me out with a *qing*."
Just as he had said, it was not until the following year that he arose from his meditative concentration.
Once, when people from south of the stream invited him to observe the vegetarian feast, it was more than twenty li from the temple.
That night, the mountain streams overflowed, making it impossible for anyone to cross; everyone assumed that Daoxuan would not come.
Yet, he arrived in an instant, and his robes were neither soaked nor damp. His spiritual efficacy was thus evident, and all marveled at him.
People from near and far came to pay their respects daily in such numbers that the clamor became tiresome; he therefore fled to a hermitage on Mount Cuiping to dwell in solitude.
Subsequently, when the assembly at Mount Tiantai requested him to serve as the *Sengzheng* (Chief Administrator of Monks), he feigned madness and remained in obscurity.
The Provincial Governor Du Xiong subsequently memorialized Emperor Zhaozong, who granted him purple robes; when Guan heard of this, he appeared sorrowful and unhappy.
Later, he passed away without illness.
The Biography of Xiyun of Mount Huangbo in Hongzhou during the Tang Dynasty. The monk Xiyun was a native of Min.
When he reached the age for formal instruction, his local school recognized his exceptional intelligence and acumen.
He then severed his attachments and entered the monastery on Mount Huangbo in Gaoyang to become a monk.
By the time he had grown to maturity, his physical stature was only about one chi shorter than that of Wang Shang; a fleshy protuberance rose upon his forehead, which was known as a "flesh pearl."
Yet he was unconventional and unrestrained, such that no one could easily fathom him.
He then traveled toward various regions and entered Tiantai Mountain, where he happened to meet a monk and traveled with him, conversing and laughing with complete composure.
I stole a glance at him; his eyes flickered from time to time, shining brilliantly as they pierced me.
As he walked alongside me, he blocked a great mountain torrent on the road, which surged and overflowed all around. Thus, he cast aside his hat, leaned on his staff, and came to a halt.
The monk was supervising the transport across when [the master] forcefully urged him, saying, "If you, Master, wish to cross, cross by yourself!
Having said this, the monk rolled up his robes and stepped upon the waves as if treading on level ground; he remained entirely dry and had already reached the other shore.
Looking back, he beckoned with his hand,
saying, "Come across.
He then brandished his halberd and shouted:
"Alas! You self-realized man, had I known beforehand that you would surely cut off my shin-bone!
The monk sighed and said, "Truly a vessel for the Mahāyāna Dharma; I am not his equal."
"Even if he could harm me, it would only bring him disgrace.
After a short while, he was nowhere to be seen.
Daoyun was dazed and lost in confusion.
When he traveled briefly to the capital and was begging for alms at his family’s gate, he heard an old woman behind some trees say,
"Are you not utterly insatiable?
Daoyun replied:
"The host does not trouble the guest; how could there be any lack of satiety?
The old woman summoned him inside, and after providing him with food, she said:
“I, whose body is burdened by the five obstacles, have come to receive the grace of your instruction, National Teacher Zhong.
I urge you, Master, to go seek out the Chan Master of Baiyang Mountain; he is truly a towering and magnificent vessel of the Great Vehicle.”

Yunian experienced both [the master's] faults, yet their prophetic recognition was identical; he then returned to Hongjing to see Master Hai, through whom he fully realized the path of the mind, and his reputation grew even more eminent.

He followed his master’s command and resided at the Huangbo Hermitage; the Chancellor of the Shengping era, Pei Xu, held him in high esteem and paid him a personal visit, presenting him with this poem:
“You once transmitted the seal of the enlightened mind; A sphere upon your brow, a seven-foot frame.”
Hanging my staff for ten years, I dwelt by the waters of Shu; today, floating my bowl, I cross the banks of Zhang.
A thousand dragon-elephants follow your lofty steps; from ten thousand miles away, fragrant flowers form a cause for supreme merit.
He wished to serve his teacher as a disciple, yet did not know to whom the Dharma should be entrusted!
Thus, Prime Minister Pei obtained the Dharma and emerged through the gate of its transmission.

He passed away at his residence temple during the Dazhong era; by imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Duanjie, his stupa was named Guangye, and his recorded sayings have circulated in the world.

The Fourth Part of the Sixth Section on "Responsive Manifestations," compiled by the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Zanning and others by Imperial Decree. **Biographies of Eighteen Individuals, with Three Additional Entries.** **Biography of Shenying of Fahua Monastery at Mount Wutai, Tang Dynasty** Śramaṇa Shenying was of unknown surname and origin, though he was a native of Cangzhou. He resided at Fahua Monastery on Mount Wutai during the Tang dynasty. His spiritual power was such that he could cause the mountain peaks to tremble and the earth to quake. Once, while traveling through the mountains, he encountered a fierce tiger. He merely raised his hand and pointed it toward the beast; the tiger immediately retreated and did not harm him. Later, while crossing a river, he saw a large fish leaping from the water. He reached out and grasped its head, and the fish followed him as he walked along the bank. When he arrived at the monastery, he placed the fish in a pond, where it grew to a length of several *zhang*. It remained there for many years before eventually disappearing. In another instance, when he was residing at the monastery, a great storm arose. A massive tree fell upon the temple hall, threatening to crush it. The monks were terrified and fled in disorder. Shenying alone remained undisturbed, sitting calmly as if nothing had happened. The tree subsequently split apart and fell away from the building. Furthermore, when he was once ill, he dreamed of a deity who bestowed upon him a medicinal potion. Upon consuming it, his ailment was instantly cured. Such accounts of his miraculous responses are numerous and cannot be fully recorded here. He passed away at the age of eighty-four. His remains were interred within the monastery grounds. *Biographies of the Remaining Seventeen Individuals follow.* [End of Volume]The purple-robed śramaṇa Zanning and others, by imperial decree, have compiled this work.
