Awakened to the Way through past affinities, he followed a teacher from his youth; he recited the scriptures with diligent application, never flagging day or night.
When he reached the age for receiving full ordination according to the Dharma, he subsequently took up his staff and wandered like a drifting gourd, seeking out wise teachers.
Early on, he was well-versed in profound dialogues and also excelled at expounding the sutras. Subsequently, he visited Chan Master Shenhui, who said to Ying:
"You have a karmic affinity with Mount Wutai; you should go there at once to pay homage to Mañjuśrī and visit the sacred sites."
Having received these instructions, he arrived at the mountain in the middle of the sixth month of the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era to pay his respects, staying temporarily in the monastic kitchen.

One day, after finishing his meal, he went for a stroll in the western grove and suddenly saw a courtyard inscribed with the characters "Fahua. Daoying then entered it and beheld a stupa of Prabhūtaratna, resplendent and magnificent, exactly as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The four gates are made of jade and stone, their merits consisting of exquisite brilliance; the craftsmanship of the divine artisans is rarely fathomed.
Behind them stands the "Protector of the State Benevolent Kings Tower," upon which are images of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra carved from jade and stone.

In front are three gates spanning thirteen bays; on both sides of the inner gate are the corridors of the palace and the site of the dharma-hall, which serve as the ceremonial retinues for Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.

Outside the three gates, the layout resembles the ten monasteries of Mount Wutai, appearing as if situated far beyond the mundane world; the view is vast and expansive, leaving one’s spirit and mind in a state of ethereal wonder.
Upon leaving the examination hall, he again saw a multitude of monks, none of whom were those he had previously encountered, and many of whom appeared strange and uncanny.

Hesitating and unable to reach a decision, he stepped out the door and walked east for about thirty paces; suddenly, he heard the sound of a door closing with a metallic clang. Turning his head to look back, he saw that there was not a single thing there.
Ying then wept sorrowfully and said,
"This Great Sage has surely come to awaken me!
There must be a karmic affinity between us for this place."
He then established a hermitage at the site where the faint traces of the Many Treasures Stupa were found and settled there.
He then made this vow:
"I shall establish a residence for the abbot based upon this transformed temple."
"Day after day and month after month, offerings of faith have been as numerous as a forest, and those who seek refuge are many.
Consequently, he summoned craftsmen, declaring that he would by no means pay those who demanded high prices."
He then traveled a thousand *li* from Yizhou to procure jade and stone for the creation of this merit-making work; it is exquisitely refined and lustrous, its craftsmanship rivaled by nothing seen.
The murals are the handiwork of Wu Daozi, a friend of the Prince’s household; his mastery of the six principles of painting is peerless and held in high esteem by the world.
After the construction of this monastery was completed from beginning to end, it was accordingly named Fahua (Lotus).
Ying presided over the abbotship, bringing order to the community as if by precise tailoring.
Later, he passed away without illness after summoning his disciples to entrust them with his final instructions; he was seventy-five years of age.
The stupa and pagoda still exist today.
Biography of Shi Niu Yun of Huayan Monastery on Mount Wutai during the Tang Dynasty. Shi Niu Yun’s secular surname was Zhao, and he was a native of Yanmen.
In his childhood years, he appeared as if lacking spiritual capacity; sent to the local school, he did not know a single character all day long.
He saw only monks and nuns, and would join his palms with an expression of awe and reverence.
At the tender age of twelve, his parents sent him to the Shanzhu Ge courtyard of Huayan Temple on Mount Wutai to enter the monastic order, where he received Jingjue as his preceptor.
He was frequently tasked with carrying firewood and drawing water; at that time, the assembly looked down upon him for his simple and dull nature, often mocking him with derisive remarks.
After reaching the age for full ordination, it became increasingly difficult for him to recite and study the scriptures.
When he was thirty-six years old, he said:
"I have heard that Mañjuśrī constantly manifests his form upon this terrace."
"I shall now go barefoot; if I should encounter Mañjuśrī, I seek only wisdom so that I may study and recite the sutras and the Dharma.
At that time, braving the cold snow, his resolve remained unyielding. Upon reaching the summit of the Eastern Terrace, he saw an old man sitting by a fire.
Yun asked,
"In such snowy cold as this, from where have you come?
The old man replied:
"I have come down from the mountain," Yun said, "By which path did you come? Why are there no traces of shoes?
He replied:
"I have come through the snow," [Yun] said.
The old man, however, asked Yun:
"What wish do you harbor that you have violated the snow to arrive barefoot? Is it not painful?"
Yun said, "Although I am a monk,
I regret my own dullness and inability to recite the sutras and dharmas.
Having come here wishing to see Mañjuśrī, I simply beg for the karmic reward of intelligence."
The old man said,
"How marvelous!
He spoke again:
"Mañjuśrī is not to be seen here; where else do you intend to go?
Yun said, "I wish to ascend to the Northern Terrace."
The old man said,
"My thought is likewise.
He asked:
"Please, Master, go on ahead.
Yun then traveled across the summit of the terrace, took his leave of the old man, and departed toward the west.
It was not until dusk that he reached the northern terrace, where he again saw the old man sitting by a lit fire; he was greatly astonished.
He asked, "We parted at the Eastern Terrace just now; why have you arrived first?
The old man replied:
"The Master did not know the shortcut, which is why he arrived late.
Although Yun received these words, his mind remained hesitant: "Could it be that this old man is none other than Mañjuśrī?"
Yun then bowed at his feet in prostration.
The old man said, "I am but a worldly person; you should not pay me such homage."
He continued to offer salutations out of mere desire, his feelings remaining unshakable.
After a long while, the old man said, "Cease your salutations.
Wait until I enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and observe what kind of karma you performed in your previous life that has rendered you so dull-witted."
The old man closed his eyes, then suddenly opened his face with a smile and said to Yun, "In your previous life you were an ox;
because you carried the Tripitaka, you have now become a monk, though you are dull-witted."
"Go to the side of the dragon hall and fetch a mattock; I will use it to excise the clotted flesh from your heart, and you will immediately become clear-headed.
Yun then obtained the mattock and handed it over.
The old man said, "Just close your eyes;
wait until I instruct you to open them, then open them. He then closed his eyes.

Next, it was as if a pickaxe were being struck against his heart, yet his body felt no pain, and his mind suddenly became clear and expansive, like standing in a dark room under a bright lamp, or like the full moon hanging in the vast night sky.
When the clouds parted, Yun saw an old man appear in the form of Mañjuśrī, who said to him:
"From now on, you shall recite the sutras and dharmas; they shall pass through your ears and never be forgotten."
"Furthermore, I have a great karmic connection with the East Courtyard of the Huayan Monastery; do not let your resolve waver.
Yun then performed acts of compassion and wept, prostrating himself at the Bodhisattva’s feet. Before his head had even been raised, the Bodhisattva was no longer to be seen.
After descending the mountain following the clouds, his four limbs were uninjured; as for the various scriptures, whatever he glanced at with his eyes, he would immediately recite from memory.
In the fifth month of the summer of the following year, he circumambulated the Yuyewa Stupa, walking in meditation and reciting sutras.

At the beginning of the second watch, a straight beam of light was seen extending from the summit of the northern terrace to the base of the auspicious stupa; it remained for a long time without dispersing, and within that radiance appeared a jeweled pavilion with a golden plaque in front inscribed with the characters "Shanzhu" (Sustained Abiding).
Yunyi Bodhisattva, recollecting the words of his prophecy, constructed a pavilion based on what appeared within the light;
thus, the practice of the Way was implemented, and all people held it in high esteem.
In the twenty-third year of the Kaiyuan era, he passed away without illness at the age of sixty-three by secular reckoning and forty-four years of *dharma*-age (*varṣa*).

His name was Yunming (Cloud Name), lacking the character for "above" (the surname). Because he had received a prediction from Mañjuśrī identifying his original and manifest traces as being that of an ox, he was thus known by that title at the time.
Biography of Daoyi of Qingliang Temple on Mount Wutai during the Tang Dynasty. Daoyi, the Śramaṇa Daoyi, was a native of Quzhou in Jiangdong.

During the Kaiyuan era, he traveled to Mount Tai and resided at the congee hall of Qingliang Temple. While serving as the *diànzuò* (chief cook), he was summoned for communal labor to transport firewood; carrying heavy loads up the steep heights, he showed considerable signs of distress.
Daoyi exchanged a pair of bamboo sandals for a carrying pole and,
donning the three robes of a monk,
traveled northeast for about five li. There, at the foot of Mount Laṅkā, he met an elderly monk of ancient and austere appearance who was leading a young boy named Jueyi.
The old monk walked ahead, and the youth called out, "Let us go to the temple on the east side to drink tea. They followed him into the temple and paid their respects throughout all the courtyards.
There they saw a great three-story pavilion with nine bays on each level, its entirety shimmering like gold, dazzling to the eyes.
The old monk ordered Yi to return early to his quarters, saying, "It is cold on the mountain; it will be difficult for you to stay.

Yi assented, took his leave, and departed from the temple. After walking about a hundred paces, he looked back and saw only mountains and forests; he then realized that the monastery had been a manifestation of transformation.
He returned to Chang’an.

In the first year of the Dali era, he reported these matters in detail to Emperor Baoying Yuansheng Wenwu, who issued an imperial decree to establish Jingeshi Temple and ordered ten military governors to provide the necessary resources for its construction.
He then summoned the master builder Gai Zao and a monk named Cunda to oversee the construction of the timber and earthworks for the building of a single Golden Pavilion temple.
Cunda was originally a monk from the Joyful Magpie Cloister at Nālandā Monastery in the Western Regions.
After the temple was completed, the Emperor issued an edict bestowing upon Amoghavajra the title "Tripiṭaka Master.
The ultimate end of Yì cannot be determined.
Biography of Fǎzhào of Zhúlín Monastery on Mount Wútaí of the Táng Dynasty. Shì Fǎzhào: It is unknown where he was from.
In the second year of the Dali era, he resided at Yunfeng Temple in Hengzhou, practicing diligently without slackening.
Within the rice bowl during the morning gruel in the Sangha hall, he suddenly beheld auspicious clouds of five colors, within which appeared a mountain temple.

Fifty *li* or more to the northeast of the monastery, there is a mountain; at its foot is a stream, and to the north of the stream is a stone gate. Five *li* inside from this gate lies a monastery, with a golden plaque inscribed with the words: "The Great Sage’s Bamboo Grove Monastery."
Although he had witnessed these things clearly with his own eyes, his heart remained filled with despondency and distress.

On another day during a mealtime, within five-colored clouds inside his alms bowl, there appeared the various temples of the Five Terraces; all were golden lands, devoid of mountains, forests, or impurities, consisting entirely of ponds, terraces, and pavilions adorned with myriad jewels, wherein Mañjuśrī and ten thousand holy beings resided.
Furthermore, he manifested the pure lands of various Buddhas, which vanished only after his meal was finished; his mind remained in doubt and undecided.
Returning to the monastery, he asked the monks: "Has anyone among you ever traveled to Mount Wutai?"

At that time, there were two masters, Jiayan and Tanhui, who claimed they had previously been there; their accounts matched exactly everything seen within the bowl, yet they still had not received news of Mount Tai.

In the summer of the fourth year, at Lake East Temple (Hudong Si) in Hengzhou, there was a lofty pavilion and terrace where a ninety-day *pañca-mahāyāga* Buddha-recitation retreat (*nianfo daochang*) was established.

At the hour of Wei on the second day of the sixth month, he saw from afar auspicious clouds covering the terrace and temple; within the clouds were various multi-storied pavilions, and inside the pavilions were several Indian monks, each about one zhang tall, holding *khakkhara* staffs and walking along the path.
Gao Heng of Hengzhou reported that Guo Xian saw Amitābha Buddha together with Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and ten thousand bodhisattvas all present at this assembly.
Their bodies were immense; those who beheld them all wept profusely until their blood ran dry as they paid their respects, and the vision only vanished at the hour of You (5–7 p.m.).

Later that evening, while outside the meditation hall, Daozhao encountered an old man who said to him, "Master, you previously made a vow to go to the Golden World to pay homage to the Great Sage; why do you not go now?"
Zhao looked at him with surprise and replied, "The times are difficult and the roads are perilous; how could one possibly go there?
The old man said:
"Simply depart at once; there shall certainly be no obstacles on the road.
Having spoken, he vanished.
Startled, Daozhao entered the monastery and made a renewed vow of sincerity:
"I have made a full summer’s commitment to travel forward; whether it be a mass of fire or a block of ice, I shall never retreat.

On the thirteenth day of the eighth month, several companions from Nanyue arrived of their own accord; as there were indeed no obstacles, on the fifth day of the fourth month of the fifth year, we reached Wutai County and saw from afar several streaks of white light to the south of Foguang Monastery.
On the sixth day, he arrived at Foguang Temple; indeed, it was exactly as he had seen in the bowl, without the slightest discrepancy.
At the fourth watch that night, he saw a beam of light descending from the northern mountain and shining down. Startled, he entered the hall and asked the assembly, "What auspicious omen is this?"
"Wherein lie good fortune and misfortune?
A monk replied:
"This inconceivable light of the Great Sage always responds to those with whom it has a karmic affinity."
Having heard this, Zhào immediately assumed his dignified demeanor and followed the light until he reached a mountain some fifty *li* to the northeast of the monastery.

At the foot of the mountain was a stream, and to the north of the stream stood a stone gate. There he saw two youths dressed in green, appearing to be eight or nine years of age, with handsome and upright features, standing at the entrance of the gate; one was named Sudhana and the other was called Nanda.
They met with joy, exchanged greetings and performed salutations, and were led through the gate. After traveling five li toward the north, they saw a golden gate-tower.
Gradually approaching the gate, they found it was a monastery.
In front of the temple was a great golden plaque inscribed with the words "Great Sage Zhulin Temple," exactly as he had seen it within the bowl.

It spanned approximately twenty *li* in circumference and contained one hundred and twenty monasteries, all adorned with precious stupas. The ground was composed entirely of pure gold, and flowing channels and flowering trees filled the space.

Zhao entered the monastery and reached the lecture hall, where he saw Mañjuśrī to the west and Samantabhadra to the east, each occupying a lion throne; the sound of their preaching the Dharma was clearly audible.
Mañjuśrī was surrounded by more than ten thousand bodhisattvas on his left and right, and Samantabhadra was likewise encircled by innumerable bodhisattvas.
The light reached the two sages, who rose to pay their respects and asked:

"In this final age, ordinary beings are far removed from the time of the Sage; their wisdom has grown increasingly inferior and their defilements and obstructions are even deeper, such that the Buddha-nature has no means of manifesting."
“The Buddha-dharma is vast and profound; I do not yet know which dharma-gate is most essential for practice.
I only pray that the Great Sage will sever the net of my doubts!
Mañjuśrī replied:
"You are now mindful of the Buddha; this is precisely the right time.
Among all gates of practice, none surpasses mindfulness of the Buddha. To make offerings to the Triple Gem and to cultivate both merit and wisdom—these two gates are the most direct and essential."

Why is this so? Because in past kalpas, by virtue of contemplating the Buddha, by virtue of recollecting the Buddha, and by virtue of making offerings, I have now attained all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
Therefore, all dharmas—the profound meditative concentration of the Prajñāpāramitā, and even the Buddhas themselves—all arise from the mindfulness of the Buddha.
Thus, know that the mindfulness of the Buddha is the sovereign of all dharmas; you should constantly mindfully recollect the Unsurpassed Dharma King without ceasing.
Zhao asked again,
"How should one practice mindfulness?
Mañjuśrī replied:

"To the west of this world is Amitābha Buddha; the power of that Buddha’s vows is inconceivable. You should maintain mindfulness of him without interruption, and after the end of your life, you will certainly be reborn there, never to fall back."
When these words had been spoken, the two great sages each extended their golden hands, stroked the crown of his head, and conferred upon him this prediction:
"Since you have already brought the Buddha to mind, you shall before long realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"If sons and daughters of good family who wish to attain Buddhahood swiftly have no practice superior to the recollection of the Buddha, they will be able to quickly realize unsurpassed Bodhi.
Having spoken thus, the two great sages addressed each other with verses (gāthās).
Having heard this, Ālokabuddhi was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; the net of his doubts was entirely cleared away.
He prostrated himself once more, and having prostrated, he joined his palms.
Mañjuśrī said:
"You may go to the courtyards of the various Bodhisattvas and pay them homage in succession.
Having received these instructions, he paid his respects in order until he reached a garden of seven-jeweled fruits; the fruit was just ripe, as large as a bowl, and he took one and ate it.
Having finished eating, his body and mind were at ease; he approached the Great Sage, paid his respects, and took his leave.
Upon returning, he saw two youths in green robes who escorted him outside the gate.
After paying his respects, he raised his head and found they had vanished; his grief and emotion redoubled.
Thereupon, a stone inscription was erected, which remains to this day.
Again, on the eighth day of the fourth month, [the image] was installed beneath the western tower of Huayan Temple.

By the thirteenth day, Baozhao, together with more than fifty monks, traveled to the Vajra Cave; arriving at the site where Wuzhuo had beheld the Great Sage, they reverently prostrated themselves while reciting the names of the thirty-five Buddhas.

After Zhao Li had recited [the mantra] only ten times, he suddenly saw that place become vast, magnificent, and pure, with a palace made of lapis lazuli where Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, ten thousand bodhisattvas, and Buddhapāli were all dwelling together in one location.
Having perceived this, he rejoiced within himself and returned to the monastery with the assembly.

That night, during the third watch, he suddenly saw five holy lamps on the slope of the eastern mountain of the monastery, located above the western pavilion of the Huayan (Avataṃsaka) Hall; they were approximately one foot square in size.
Zhao recited the incantation, saying, "I pray that these hundred lamps be divided and returned to one side. Immediately, they were divided as he wished.
He further commanded, "Divide them into a thousand torches. As soon as he finished speaking, they were divided into a thousand, arranged in rows facing one another, covering half the mountain.

Furthermore, he went alone once more to the Vajra Cave, vowing to see the Great Sage. At the end of the third watch, he arrived and saw a monk from India who identified himself as Buddhapālī; he led him into the sacred temple, as related in the *Juejiu zhuan*.

By the beginning of the twelfth month, he entered the Nianfo (Buddha-recitation) practice hall at Huayan Temple’s Huayan Cloister; he abstained from grain for a fixed period, vowing to be reborn in the Pure Land.
When the first watch of the seventh day arrived, as he was mindfully recollecting the Buddha, he again saw a Brahma monk enter the ritual arena and said to him:
"Why do you not speak of the realm of Mount Tai that you have seen?"
Having finished speaking, he vanished.
Daozhao suspected this monk and likewise intended not to speak of it.

At the hour of the monkey (15:00–17:00) the following day, while he was engaged in recitation with right mindfulness, he again saw a Brahman monk about eighty years of age, who spoke to Daozhao as follows:
"Master, regarding the spiritual wonders you have witnessed on Mount Tai, why do you not circulate them?
Why not reveal them universally to all sentient beings, so that by seeing and hearing them, they may resolve to attain Bodhicitta and obtain great benefit and joy?"
Zhao said, "It is not that I have no intention to reveal the holy path; rather, fearing that doubt and slander might arise, I have therefore remained silent.
The monk said:

“Even the Great Sage Mañjuśrī, who currently resides on this mountain, still incurs the censure of people; how much more so regarding the realms you have perceived? They merely serve as the conditions for a ‘poisonous drum’ that causes sentient beings who see or hear them to resolve upon Bodhicitta.”
Upon hearing these words, Zhao recorded them according to his recollection.

At that time, the monk Huìcóng of Jiangdong, together with more than thirty people including Chónghuī and Míngqián of Huáyán Temple, followed Zhao to the site of the Vajra Cave in the first month of the sixth year of the Dàlì era. There, they personally visited the Prajñā Hall and erected stone markers to indicate the location.

At that time, the assembly gazed upon him with sincere hearts; their feelings of sorrow and joy were not yet spent when they suddenly heard the sound of a bell. Its tone was elegant and clear, with distinct rhythmic intervals.

When the multitude all heard it, their astonishment and wonder grew even greater. Verifying that what they had witnessed was no illusion, they inscribed it upon the walls of their dwellings so that all might see and hear it, thereby collectively generating the superior resolve and together aspiring for the wisdom of the Buddha.

Thereafter, Baozhao, following his vision, established a monastery at the site where he had inscribed the plaque for Zhulin Temple; it was magnificent and exquisite in its adornment, and was thus named Zhulin.

Furthermore, on the thirteenth day of the ninth month in the twelfth year of the Dali era, Zhao and eight of his disciples beheld white light several times at Dongtai; subsequently, extraordinary clouds gathered in dense masses.

The clouds parted, revealing five-colored light emanating from his entire body; within this light was a red circular halo. Mañjuśrī was seen by all riding a blue-maned lion. Then, a fine snow began to fall, and five-colored circular halos spread throughout the mountains and valleys.
His disciples who shared his vision were Chunei, Wiusu, Guijeong, Jiwon, the śrāmaṇera Wuiyeong, and the upāsaka Zhang Xijun, among others.
After this illumination, he made his mind firm and steadfast, practicing refinement without neglect until the end of his life was unknown.
This is recorded in the "Account of Sheng Temple" by Wang Shizhan, a military official of Jangzhou.
The commentary states:
The Buddha accomplishes the three bodies and necessarily dwells in the three lands, because he manifests the adornments of the primary and secondary environments.
Bodhisattvas have not yet attained the name of "lands," but are merely said to "dwell" [in them].
By cultivating the causes for purifying Buddha-lands, one is born accordingly into the family of Buddhas; thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* contains the "Chapter on the Abodes of Bodhisattvas.
The sūtra states:
"Only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land," which means that those below do not usurp the status of those above.

If the *Aṣṭākṣara-dhāraṇī-sūtra* states, "By the power of Mañjuśrī’s great vows, his realm is identical to that of the Buddha," then since the realm is pure, the teaching of the Dharma is also pure; thus, the meaning of the three lands is identical.
Question:
"In various sūtras, it is said that the Buddha dwelt in places such as Rājagṛha; could these not be considered his dwelling places? Response:
"This meaning involves both identity and distinction; alternatively, it may be that what is attained above also encompasses what is below.

Furthermore, just as the Tuṣita palace is the pure realm of those in their final birth (*caramabhavika*), Mount Potalaka, Mount Qingliang, Mount Cīti, and others are all lands manifested by the pure consciousness of Bodhisattvas."
If this is so, then "Pure Land" and "place of residence" are identical in meaning and differ only in name.

For example, when Fazhao entered the Holy Monastery in the Bamboo Grove, he beheld the pure realm of Mañjuśrī; whereas seeing an old man or a youth upon a mountain peak constitutes seeing a sage within an impure land.

Biography of Changyu of Bimoyan on Mount Qingliang of the Tang Dynasty. Changyu of Bimoyan on Mount Qingliang of the Tang Dynasty was the Dharma name of Shi Changyu. His secular surname was Yin, and he was a native of Fanyang. He left the household life at Anji Temple in northern Yan.
His character was open and unencumbered, and his appearance was serene and extraordinary. He concealed himself among forests and springs, withdrawing from fame and profit.

In the fourth year of the Dazhong era, he took up his monk’s staff and departed from Yan; traveling alone through the northern snows, across a thousand *li* of freezing cold, he proceeded directly to Mount Wufeng. There he visited the Bodhisattva Hall of Huayan Monastery and gazed upon the majestic countenance of Mañjuśrī. He offered his right middle finger as an oblation, moistening it with fragrant oil and burning it with star-like flames. A light ascended for half a day, yet the Bodhisattva’s serene expression remained perfectly intact.
Subsequently, he traveled extensively through sacred sites for two full years, during which time the auspicious omens he beheld were beyond reckoning.
Later, he arrived at Xitai, where he encountered an ancient holy site called Bimokayan, the place where Mañjuśrī subdued the dragon.

At the moment they prostrated themselves in greeting, they suddenly beheld light clouds and golden radiance, so brilliant it dazzled the eyes; gradually these separated to reveal battlements, appearing in form like a city—everyone exclaimed, "This is the Golden World!"
When the transformation was complete, he again asked about that place. The monk said:

"This ground was once occupied by an ancient virtuous one whom the state honored as Great Master Jinguangzhao. His integrity was solitary and lofty, and his spiritual wonders were unfathomable; his deeds are recorded in official chronicles and maps, and all people look up to him."

Moved by a profound interplay of sorrow and joy, he remained there for a long time without ceasing. He then began to thatch a hut on this site to cleanse his thoughts and clarify his spirit. After entering *samādhi* for forty-nine days, birds scattered flowers like rain and people gathered in fragrant clouds; they raised their sleeves and adjusted their robes, seeking refuge in him as if at a bustling market.
He then founded Buddhist temples and monastic dwellings, remaining on the mountain peak for seventeen years without descending.

Day by day, he devoted himself to the study and recitation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in its nine assemblies, the *Pañcavimśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, and other teachings, never wasting a single moment.

The awakened power of the sages penetrates in secret, and the Way transcends the realm of the ordinary. When matters such as ritual greetings arise, others may observe them but cannot fathom their source.
The gentleman turns toward it and the commoner returns to it; by maintaining constant mindfulness, one becomes like a sage.

By the end of Emperor Yi’s reign, he encountered a change in the old regulations; at times he clapped his hands and laughed loudly, and at other times he struck stones with strange words, resembling the "Sea Record" of Liu Qing and acting like the feigned madness of the traveler from Chu.

When calamity broke out in the Central Plains and bandits galloped forth in every direction, the palace was plundered by barbarians and the imperial carriage was covered in dust; reflecting upon the Master’s words, they seemed to fit perfectly like two halves of a tally.
At that time, Emperor Wuhuang of Hedong had long admired his true virtue and sent a letter to him from the mountains.
In the fourth month of the summer of the first year of the Wende era, he commanded Ma Sisu, the Regional Inspector of Xianzhou, to convey his intentions and extend an invitation.
Yu replied: "As for the honors and insults of this floating world, how could they trouble me?"
He resolutely rejected the summons from afar, remaining firm and unshakable.
On the eighteenth day of the seventh month of that year, he called his disciples and said:
"You should examine and guard the foundation of your precepts; dwell well in the remainder of your lives, for I must now take my final leave of you."
Having finished speaking, he passed away with solemn dignity, like a cicada shedding its shell. He was seventy-two years of secular age and fifty-one years of monastic seniority.
His disciples, including Taiwen and others, were overcome with grief and choked with sobs.
On the eighteenth day of the fourth month in the first year of the Longji era, his body was cremated, and dozens of *śarīra* relics were obtained.
Master Wen, out of steadfast filial devotion, erected a stupa to enshrine them; he entered and exited it while mourning, and offered himself at the Imperial Treasury.

Emperor Wu bestowed honorary gifts and funeral offerings of exceptional rank, honoring the martial and civil achievements of his ancestors; furthermore, the governors and magistrates of Lan, Xian, and other prefectures were required by precedent to deduct a portion of their clear stipends to assist in establishing stupas and pagodas as meritorious causes for the deceased.
On the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month, the foundation pit was sealed and the remains interred.
Biography of Shi Yong’an of Yong’an, Chengdu Prefecture, Tang Dynasty. Shi Yong’an was a native of Hongya County in Meizhou.

His physical stature was diminutive and his complexion dark and sallow; his speech and tone were coarse and vulgar, yet his discernment and capacity were broad and expansive, generally beyond measure.

In the third month of the eighth year of the Dazhong era, he went to Chengdu, saying that he had come to pay his respects to the provincial governor, Lord Bai Minzhong, to request the imperial grant of a temple nameplate.
Because his feet were lame, he was carried on a shoulder-litter to arrive.
No one had ever seen him enter a latrine or urinate while returning; therefore, people often called him the "Master Without Outflows" (Wulou Shi).
He was placed within Seongsu Temple for ten days; he informed the Chief Administrator, who dispatched five or six monks to guard him day and night in shifts while keeping watch over him.
Their internal and external dietary habits are roughly the same as those of ordinary people, yet they lack the intention to undress or relieve themselves.
When one examines the accumulation of their ten periods [of activity], it is entirely impossible to know where they move about or perform their bodily functions.
When the Minister of Works presented the memorial to the Duke, the Master took his leave and returned to Meijun.
The official Lu Qiu met him and thought he was merely a young novice;
others said, "This master is already over eighty years old!"
The commentary states:
It is incorrect for people of Shu to call Master An a "Master Without Outflows" (An-leou-shi).
One is termed "without outflows" because, having severed the afflictions so that they no longer increase, one is forever free from their seeds and habitual tendencies.
Now, when the remnants of food and drink return to the nine orifices, Master An merely stops two apertures from flowing;
thus, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there is no "portion of internal affliction."
However, the sequence of their stages and the manner in which they endure [the food] are difficult to discern; they consume it as usual—by what cause does it not flow from the two orifices?

Observing that the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (Treatise on the Compendium of Higher Knowledge) mentions two types of sustenance: "sustenance based on pure reliance" and "sustenance based on manifest reliance," these correspond respectively to Arhats, Bodhisattvas, and Buddhas.
If this is so, then Master An was a manifestation who relied upon and dwelt within food—though he ate, he did not eat; how could impurities arise?
One must surely rectify the name in order to summon its true essence.
Biography of Shi Huiwen of Lingshi Temple in Quzhou during the Tang Dynasty Shi Huiwen was a native of Xian’an.

He frequently exhorted donors that meritorious deeds were paramount, often saying: "As long as one has not yet attained the rank of a sage, one will continue to transmigrate through the five realms of existence; what else can one rely upon but merit?"
Once, while attempting to cast a sixteen-foot golden image at the Xi River, the local administration would not grant permission;
how then could the bronze be procured? He replied, "I await a great donor."
Before long, a husband and wife from Qingxi County arrived with a bronze mirror as a dowry to offer as a gift. Hearing this, he made a vow, saying:
"If this mirror is cast before the heart of the Buddha, it shall be the ultimate expression of the resolve of this couple."
When the mold was removed and the image revealed, it indeed reflected the very heart-mind of the Buddha.
Furthermore, he once traveled to Yuzhang to preach and convert others, obtaining several *yi* of gold, which he suddenly lost when encountering bandits who plundered him.
The situation becoming urgent, he threw the gold into the water and said, "I fear it might damage the field of merit of a noble person; please retrieve it yourself.
Having heard this, Śrāmaṇa went away. The bandits swam through the water seeking it, but could not find it.
Upon hearing that [the official] had arrived at the prefecture, the gold was already mysteriously present within his courtyard.
When he employed laborers and craftsmen, he did not avoid public censure; seeing that he had acquired much wealth, he personally carried fish, strings of meat, and pig shoulders to feed the workers.
Furthermore, when tigers or leopards were encountered on mountain paths, he would sometimes strike them on the head with his staff and say:
"Do not harm people; since I am performing meritorious deeds, why do you not enter into this karmic connection?"
The next day, a tiger carried a wild boar to the place where Fawen was, dropped it before him, and departed with its tail tucked between its legs.
All his undertakings were thus successful, and those who converted to his faith flowed in like a stream; such extraordinary occurrences were frequent.
Biography of Wulou of the Lower Monastery in Lingwu, Shuofang, Tang China. The monk Wulou, surnamed Jin, was the third son of the King of Silla.

The Prince of the Land, as the eldest son by his primary consort, was about to be established as the heir apparent; however, out of youthful admiration for the cession of the throne by King Yan-ling, he wished instead to become a son of the Dharma of Śākyamuni.
He then fled to join a maritime vessel and reached the land of China—intending to travel through the five regions of India and pay homage at the eight stupas of the Buddha.

Having crossed the desert and passed west of Khotan, he arrived at the ruins of the Pamir Mountains and entered a great monastery; the bhikṣus therein were all monks of unfathomable spiritual caliber.
When asked about his intention for traveling to India, he had not yet displayed any extraordinary marks of resolve.
The monk said, "The ancient records contain no mention of such a person; you may not depart on your own initiative."
"There is a dragon pond here that you may go to convert.
Only if there is a sign of success should you proceed further.

Louyi requested to ascend the bank of the pond; there he saw only a single *huchuang* (a low wooden seat), upon which he sat down. As night fell, thunder and lightning broke out simultaneously. The monster spat forth billowing vapors and manifested all manner of transformations, dazzling and unstable.
Liu kept his eyes closed and remained motionless, like a towering tree standing erect; how could a mere breeze possibly shake it?
After a long time, a giant serpent raised its head over his knees. Moved by the utmost compassion, Liu granted it the Three Refuges, whereupon the serpent departed.
He again assumed the form of an old man and came to express his gratitude, saying:
"Having received deliverance from you, Master, it is right that I do not remain long.
Three days hence, I shall cast off this suffering of scales and shells and take birth in a superior realm."
"To the south of here is a large rock; it is the place where my disciple cast off his body. You may also expect to find his remains there by seeking them out in that secluded spot.
Later, he saw a tall and majestic figure, stiff and upright, lying upon the rock.
The monks of the temple all silently consented, and he further said:
"If you must go to India, here is a sacred image of Avalokiteśvara whose prayers are never answered in vain; you may offer your petition to it."
"An auspicious omen has been obtained; you may go without hesitation.

Lou then stood before the image and entered into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). In this manner, forty-nine days passed, yet his body remained afflicted with swelling, and he never leaned on anything for support.
Shortly thereafter, a mouse about the size of a pellet gnawed his left shin, causing a thin yellow pus to flow out that could fill several pecks before he recovered.

When the period of his vow had ended and he received the response [of his success], the assembly of monks said to him, "Observing the Master’s cultivation of merit, it is fitting that you remain in the land of Tang;
with your mind intent on transforming sentient beings, the benefit you bring will be vast."
"My feet are weary from traveling afar; my learning has been limited to what I have heard and seen, and it cannot be forcibly strengthened.
Is this what you, Master, know?
Suspecting that these were the words of a sage and that they would certainly not be uttered in vain, he thus turned back.
As he was about to depart, he said to his attendant Lou:
"When you encounter the 'Lan' [mountain], stop there.
On the road back, there was a mountain named Helan; following the previous record, he entered its range, reached the White Grass Valley (Bai Cao Gu), and settled there in a thatched hut.
Before long, the military rebellions of An Lushan and Shi Siming caused the two capitals to fall into chaos. Emperor Xuanzong fled to Shu, while Emperor Suzong trained his troops at Lingwu.
The Emperor frequently dreamed of a golden-colored person reciting the name of the Buddha Baosheng before him.
The following day, he questioned those around him about the events in his dream. One person replied:
"There is a śramaṇa whose conduct is extraordinary who dwells on the northern mountain; he constantly recites this Buddha’s name."

Emperor Suzong then issued a summons for him to appear, but he did not rise to comply; Emperor Suzong ordered Guo Ziyi, the Vice Commander-in-Chief of Shuofang and Director of the Secretariat, to go in person to persuade him, and only after midnight did he finally come.
The Emperor looked at him and said,
"Truly a man from within a dream.
When the Jie barbarians were finally pacified and the imperial carriage returned, he was placed in an inner monastery to receive offerings.
Truly, as the monkey finds the golden chain light and the bird loathes the carved cage, he repeatedly submitted petitions, wishing to return to his former seclusion.

The Emperor, holding him in high esteem, delayed the response to his edict; thus, before he could fulfill his desire to retire to the mountains, it was suddenly announced that he had manifested his passing.
One day, a pair of feet suddenly manifested upon the right leaf of the inner gate, their soles hovering several feet above the ground.

The gatekeeper reported this to the Emperor, who personally visited the site in his palanquin and obtained a posthumous petition requesting that he be buried beneath his former hermitage in the mountains.
Immediately, this was granted; the funeral affairs were provided by the government.
Thereupon, the door panels were removed and set aside, and offerings were prepared. An imperial messenger was dispatched to supervise the proceedings, and the funeral procession escorted the remains.
Previously, when Xuanshou Leixing was converting the site, it was largely due to Huaiyuan County; consequently, an administrative office was established there, which was called the Lower Temple.

When the remains arrived, the divine seat could not be moved at will, so the assembly deliberated on relocating them. They constructed a separate hall to enshrine them, which was in the third year of the Shangyuan era.

To this day, his true body remains upright and serene, never having undergone decay or change; the door leaf of the inner palace chamber where he lay is still preserved as a relic from that time when the auspicious omen manifested.

Biography of Bao Da of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou, Tang Dynasty. As for the Venerable Bao Da, it is unknown where he was from; he took refuge in this famous mountain and was renowned for his lofty spiritual reputation, being styled the Dharma Master Kṣatriya.
He made the recitation of secret mantras his constant practice.
Within the monastery were sand-casting beds for making seals and mirrors for reflecting the Buddha.
Formerly, when he was in Zhejiang, the surging waves and massive billows caused truly profound destruction.
When the tide surged greatly, it violently splashed against the various mountains on the present-day lake.
Da took pity on the lands of mulberry trees and hemp that had all been transformed into a river, and so he recited mantras to halt the calamities caused by the spirit of the waves.
One night, a great man appeared amidst the surging waves of the Yangtze River, wearing a dark cap and crimson robes, accompanied by a vast retinue.
He said to Da, "I am Wu Yuan of Wu; I am the one who has come to avenge my father and wipe away his disgrace—it is none other than I."
"The Master’s compassionate heart is for the sake of all beings; we, your disciples, have already received your instructions!
Having finished speaking, he vanished.
The next day, the monks of the monastery asked in wonder:
"Who was it that caused the clamor of carriages and horses last night?
When he related the matter in detail,
it was clear that such instances of spiritual resonance with the divine principle are numerous.

From that time on, the sands on the western bank increased year after year, once again providing a source of profit for the common people; he was widely praised and esteemed by his contemporaries, and his transformative influence spread extensively.
Later, nothing further was known of his end.
The commentary asks:
What is meant by "imprinting the sand bed"?
The general reply states:

"When a man of the Way dwells in the mountains, it is certainly not because he treasures fine vessels; one might suspect he has merely fashioned a sitting platform from the sands of the river through skillful construction.
What is it that reflects the Buddha-mirror?"
Tong said:
"It is simply the Mirror Lamp.
Because Lu Hongjian traveled extensively on this mountain during the Zhenyuan era, he composed a record describing Master Da’s frugality and his methods for clarifying the mind."

The Biography of Master Yinfeng of Mount Beitaishan in Daizhou during the Tang Dynasty. Translated by the nameless Monk Zhijiu. Master Yinfeng’s secular surname was Deng, and he was a native of Shaowu in Jianzhou.
In my youth, I was foolish and headstrong, disregarding the commands of my parents as I left home to receive the Dharma.

Later, while traveling to observe various regions, I met Chan Master Nanquan of Chiyang. He had me take up a wash-basin; our interaction was harmonious, and I was approved by Master Yuan. Ultimately, I recognized myself as a successor to Chan Master Ma.
Feng Yuan stated that during the Yuanhe era he traveled to Mount Wutai; his route led through Huaisi, where Wu Yuanji had mobilized troops and defied imperial authority.
When the government army encountered the rebels, they engaged in combat, but victory or defeat had not yet been decided.
Feng said, "I shall go to resolve this slaughter.

He then cast his alms-bowl into the air and followed it, gliding slowly through the sky. As he passed between the two military arrays, the warriors, each beholding the monk soaring through the air, unconsciously withdrew their spears from their scabbards.

After he had traveled extensively to visit all the sacred sites, he suddenly stood upside down before the Vajra Cave and died; his body remained perfectly upright, as straight as if it were planted there.

At that time, those present deliberated that he should be carried to the cremation ground before the sacred cave, yet he remained as immovable as a mountain despite their combined efforts. Those from far and near who witnessed this were struck with wonder and marveled at such a rare marvel.
Feng had a younger sister who was a nun; she entered Mount Wutai and, with eyes narrowed in anger, rebuked him, saying:
"In the past, you, elder brother, did not follow the laws and precepts; even in death, you shall continue to delude people."

At that time, the assembly already knew that although she was their own flesh and blood, how could they dare harbor any duplicity? They requested that she be measured according to the constant standard; as they lightly pushed her with their hands, she fell down with a crash.
He was subsequently cremated, and his relics were collected and enshrined in a stupa; he was given the name Deng Yinfeng. He left behind a verse which said:

"I play for you this single-stringed lute; The pine and cypress remain ever green, undaunted by the cold. Gold and ore may be mixed together, yet their natures are distinct; I leave it to you to test them before your eyes."
The commentary states:
"A stiffened corpse and one who piles up his feet are identical in their physical state;
yet to stand and suddenly vanish, or to sit and pass away, is the cultivation of samādhi."

This man supports the heavens with his head and treads upon the azure void; he acts contrary to the constant order of things and is difficult to comprehend, truly a person whose depths cannot be fathomed.
For such an inversion of the natural order, he is a peerless figure throughout all antiquity.
The way his younger sister, the nun, took [the robes] was like Qu Ping’s being reviled by the female slave.
The power of illusion is such that its skillful means (*upāya*) are great indeed.
Someone said:
"Regarding the campaign against Huaixi, why does the *Book of Tang* not record how Hu Fucheng was liberated from the battle array by Yinfeng’s flying staff?
Tong replied,
"What is transmitted in the minor histories may well capture the actual facts."
"Therefore, can the five schools that produced commentaries on the single classic *Chunqiu* be considered identical?

Furthermore, there was the monk Shi Wangming of Kaishua Temple in Hanzhou; having previously entered the temple and witnessed auspicious responses appearing one after another, he vowed to sacrifice his body, making asceticism his lifelong commitment.

Suddenly, while he was burning incense within the hall, he immediately beheld the ground and the buildings all turning the color of lapis lazuli. A bodhisattva descended into the courtyard riding upon a five-colored cloud and said:
"Your resolve is most steadfast; you shall certainly attain the Way. I have come to bear witness for you."
Wangming prostrated himself with his head to the ground, but after a short while, he was nowhere to be seen.
When the monks of the monastery arrived, they said, "The entire courtyard has turned the color of lapis lazuli.
They sighed in wonder without end.
That monk further applied himself diligently to ascetic practices.

Furthermore, there was a monk named Wangming in Dengzhou who was already advanced in years; he wandered between the regions of Rang and Deng, consuming two pheasants or pigeons daily, which both monastics and laypeople alike condemned.
The old monk never shrank from such things.
Once, while he was partaking of a meal of delicacies, a poor man came seeking food; the monk gave him two of his legs to eat.
When the meal was finished and the old monk had rinsed his mouth, a pair of doves emerged from his mouth—one was able to fly away, while the other crawled on the ground.
The poor man was astonished and amazed; he also spat out his rice, and the pigeon’s two feet were restored.
That monk had not actually eaten the bird.
From then on, the multitude revered him, calling him "The Monk of the Southern Capital who [Rescued] the Pigeon."
Someone remarked in praise:

"In the past, when the Venerable Master Xiang of Qingcheng Mountain drank wine and ate meat, he would then spit it out; the chicken, mutton, and beef all transformed back into their original forms, flew and crowed, and entered into pits and burrows—it was exactly the same."

The Biography of the Venerable Wuming, Former Abbot of Liangshan Temple in Xingyuan Prefecture, Tang Dynasty. As for the Śramaṇa Wuming, it is unknown where he was from. He resided some several dozen *li* west of Baoci City on a place called Zhongliangshan—where several peaks turn inward and support one another, their emerald-green hues coalescing with the sky, situated in the midst of them.
His conduct was ultimately eccentric and his speech was unconventional; those who saw him constantly were not startled, yet those who encountered him for the first time found him strange.

Ordinarily he was extremely fond of wine and meat, and his coarse behavior was practiced openly. Furthermore, he presided over various affairs and often exercised moderation; even the monks feared him, and they called him the "Elder" (Upādhyāya).
At that time, the entire assembly of monks all followed and imitated [the others], yet he alone remained fearless.
An elder monk, observing this, sighed and said:
"If one has not yet dwelled in the Ground of Pure Mind, how can they dare to act in such a contrary manner?"
"Practicing in reverse is not within the realm of ordinary people.
As the world says, 'Gold is tested by fire'; wait for me to test it one day, at one time.
During the Kaicheng era, he suddenly made large pancakes and summoned his disciples, saying:
"Come with you all to wander in the Śītavana forest.
This refers to the many tombs in the mountains and wilds outside the city where people discard their corpses; hence the expression.

The Elder sat upon the ground, unwrapped a flatbread that encased a putrid corpse, and began to devour it with his mouth; his air of such dexterity and gusto was quite remarkable, while the fellow-monks who were traveling with him all covered their noses, spat on the ground, and fled.
The Elder cried out loudly,
"If you can feed yourselves with this flesh, only then may you feed upon the flesh of others.
From then on, the monastics were awakened and transformed into those of refined austerity.
People from both near and far turned to him with faith.
At that time, Liu Zhongying, the Right Vice President of the Secretariat, while serving in the Liangzhou administration, personally went to pay his respects and honor him.
When he passed away, it was said he was approximately eighty or ninety years old.
The true image remains at the mountain temple;
to this day, those between Liang, Yi, and the Three Fu regions refer to him only as the "Elder of Xingyuan.
His wondrous traces and extraordinary deeds are not few, though they have not yet been fully detailed.
The commentary states:
At first, the Elder merely taught according to the Dharma; later, the people all emulated him.
He did not realize that one who has attained the fruit of realization transforms beings through opposition, ultimately performing the work of a Buddha to warn against latent evils before they arise.

Therefore, if one returns to the actual substance of the matter, it refers to what is stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*: "Because the bodhisattvas of great majesty manifest the power of food to abide.
If one were to falsely claim to have attained the fruit and proceed by way of such analogy, how would that differ from a jackal attempting to mimic the roar of a lion?
Biography of Shi Wenshuang of Chongfu Monastery in Taiyuan, Tang Dynasty. Shi Wenshuang’s family name and place of origin are unknown.
Early on, he untied the silken cords of worldly dust and tore asunder the net of craving to seek the Way from his teacher.
By nature he did not sleep; even when exhausted to the utmost, he would simply sit in the lotus posture. This was the practice of the long-sitting dhūta asceticism.
Later, while he was dwelling alone among the hills and mounds, a heavy rain fell for ten days. Having no attendants by his side, a snake entered his sleeve and coiled itself there.

At that time, someone invited him to a vegetarian feast; when the appointed hour arrived, the monk did not go. When the host came again to invite him, he saw the snake and cried out in terror; only then did the snake slowly descend.
He firmly ordered [his servant] to go and bring food; however, Daoshuang declined it, saying that he had already passed midday and would not eat until the end of the night.

On the following day, there was a wolf that thrice opened its mouth wide and leaped forward with the intent to bite and devour him. Daoshuang took pity on it as it was tormented by the fires of hunger and thought to himself:
"I, a foul sack, have no stinginess; I shall give you one meal, so that you may quickly attain a firm and solid body."
"You have accepted my gift; let us together return to the assembly of the good.
After a short while, the wolf lowered its ears and withdrew.
On the day of his death, bells and chimes resounded in the air, continuing for a long time before finally subsiding.
The disciples and fellow villagers gathered to escort him to his funeral bier.

On that day, dozens of banners covered the front of the procession as they led the way; an extraordinary fragrance permeated everywhere, causing the entire assembly to lament with grief as if they had lost their own parents.

The Biography of Benjing of Baofu Monastery in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty. Regarding the monk Benjing of Baofu Monastery in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty, it is not clearly known where he was from.
His spiritual aura was lofty and resolute, inspiring a sense of solemn reverence in all who beheld him.
As the Min Ridge region abounded in masters of the Chan school, he traveled there to study under them one after another.

Hearing that Mount Huotong in Changxi County contained many grottoes and palaces of the immortals—the very place where, according to the scriptures, the Bodhisattva Tianguan resided with his disciples to preach the *Huayan* Dharma of the Ocean of Nature—he proceeded there.
Woodcutters frequently heard celestial music, extraordinary fragrances, and auspicious signs from birds and beasts;
yet, as the mountains do not tolerate the vulgar or the wicked, they were often driven out.
Jing entered the mountains and built a thatched hut. There was a stone cave there known as the "Poisonous Grotto."
Sengjing lived by the side of a cave; the dragon emerged with its body arched and coiled, manifesting transformations without constancy. Jing then summoned it and tamed it.

Furthermore, fierce tigers roamed the roads to cause harm, such that woodcutters dared not venture deep into the forest. Jing stroked their heads and admonished them earnestly; they lowered their ears and departed.
Once, during a clear night, nine men wearing caps, hoods, trousers, and tunics claimed they wished to stay overnight; he took them all inside the hermitage.
When they took their leave the following morning, they all transformed together into cranes and departed, crying out melodiously in the air.
Jingwang did not know its end.

Biography of Fajiang of Faju Monastery in Chengdu Prefecture, Tang Dynasty. The monk Shi Fajiang of Xianshan Monastery was a native of Jiangdong. He traveled to the Min and Shu regions and resided at Faju Monastery—the monastery which had been built by Prince Xiu of the Sui dynasty.
Within the temple was a śarīra stūpa planted by Emperor Wen during the Renshou era.
Jiang harbored a heart of compassion and often anticipated their arrivals with great accuracy, his words never erring in the slightest.
Once, while in his quarters, he said to his disciples:
"Outside there are more than ten thousand people, all wearing caps and with their limbs contorted; they are begging me for salvation.
Go quickly outside the temple and seek them out."
Seeing no one there, the disciple wondered why his master’s words were so confused and contradictory.
While he was standing about hesitantly, several dozen people arrived carrying bamboo baskets on their shoulders filled with snail shells.
Jiang said, "Is this it?"
He ordered that money be taken to ransom it, and it was cast into the water.
Furthermore, Daxingshan Temple in Chang’an was originally the Shaivai Temple of the Sui dynasty; during the Tianxian era of the Tang, it was destroyed by fire, leaving only its foundations.

During the Mingqing era, there was a Daoist named Li Rong of Dongming Guan; he was originally from Baxi and, being a man of refined tastes, frequently vied with Buddhist monks to determine their relative superiority.
Rong came to Xuandu Guan and, leading the Daoist priests, pointed to the ashes and mocked him, saying:
"How could the Way ever be good?
How could what you speak of ever flourish?"
"The Tathāgata has been consumed by fire until nothing remains, leaving behind only a community of monks.

Among the monks were those who felt indignation at the disparagement and mockery of their own school; they urgently raised funds and encouraged others to rebuild and expand the structure even more than it was before.
Regarding these twelve mu of land, although the offerings for this transformative project have daily filled thousands and tens of thousands, the calculation shows it cannot yet be completed.
The assembly of monks scratch their heads and hesitate, not knowing by what means it may be successfully accomplished.
Suddenly, there was a monk whose robes were coarse and tattered and whose appearance was haggard; carrying a worn-out sack, he entered the site and said, "Complete the Buddha hall quickly."
He stepped aside and looked;
it was gold, weighing one thousand *liang* per plow-handle.
The people of the time marveled at this, and from then on his offerings increased daily, so that the temple was quickly completed.
Biography of the Monk Luo of Mount Chalongs in Jiulong, Pengzhou, Tang Dynasty. Regarding the monk Shi Luoseng: he was one who attained the stage of fruition at Shengsi Temple in Shu.
Once, while he was lying ill on Mount Wutai, the monks assembled there were all unaware of his condition; yet they attended upon him with never a moment of negligence.
When nearly ninety days had passed, his illness was cured. As he was about to depart, he said:
"I am deeply grateful for the care you provided during my suffering. That I have now recovered is entirely due to the power of your teachers."
"I reside on Mount Chalung in Jiulong County, beyond the Sword Mountains.
On another day, when I travel abroad, do not forget to visit me.
Later in life, he arrived in Shu and traveled among the various peaks, inquiring everywhere of the elderly woodcutters, yet none had ever heard the name of this mountain.
He then sighed and said, "Alas!
Is this not the delusion of sick Chan?
As he was about to turn back, he encountered a mountain boy who said:
"This is that man who gathered sand at the crag," he said, leading the way forward.

Suddenly, they beheld a temple and pagoda standing solemnly in the void, with corridors and galleries surrounding them in dignified order. Indeed, they encountered the one who had previously been ill there, who came to the gate to greet them and recount their past history.
As the sun was about to set, he said to him:
"This temple cannot be reached except by one who has attained the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows.
You have met me here due to our past karmic affinity."
"To say that you must spend the night here is not acceptable.
If you can be diligent in your cultivation and realization, how could it be difficult to reach this point?
He then ordered his former servant to escort the Master back.
The monk looked back and saw only steep, precipitous cliffs and a wilderness of pine and cypress trees; this was during the Kaicheng era.

At that time, National Teacher Wudada Zhixuan, while compiling his biography, encountered the monk Kesu, who was exceptionally skilled in geomancy. He commissioned Kesu to select a site for his future burial plot, and Kesu identified the front peak of Jingdan.
The mountain resembles the shape of battlements; though it rises and falls in height, its center is level as a grindstone.
Suddenly, an elderly local resident said, "According to ancient tradition, this is called Mount Chalongsan."

Biography of Qici of Fenghua County, Mingzhou, Tang Dynasty. Regarding the monk Qici of Fenghua County, Mingzhou, during the Tang Dynasty: his clan and lineage are not clearly known; some say he was a native of Siming.
His physical form was misshapen and bloated; he had a furrowed brow and a protruding belly. His speech was inconsistent, and he slept wherever he happened to be.

He would often enter the marketplace carrying a cloth bag slung over a staff; whenever he saw something, he would beg for it. Even when it came to vinegar, sauce, fish, or pickles, as soon as they reached his mouth, he would take a small portion and put it into his bag. Thus, he was known as Master Pùdài (Bag) of Chángtīng (Long Beach).
Once he lay down in the snow, yet there was no snow upon his body; people marveled at this as a marvel.
A verse says:
"Maitreya is truly Maitreya, yet the people of the age do not recognize him."
Regarding such phrases as these, people say they are the traces left by Maitreya.
Furthermore, while standing upon a great bridge, someone asked:
"What are you doing here, Preceptor?"
He replied,
"I am looking for someone here.
He frequently went to people to beg for a drink, and at those shops, goods would be sold.
Within his bag were one hundred and one items—requisites for his person.
To indicate good or bad fortune to others, he would invariably manifest signs and portents.
During a period of extreme drought, he would drag his high-toothed wooden clogs and sleep on a city bridge with his knees propped up.
During the floods, he would tie on wet straw sandals;
people took this as proof of his nature.
He passed away at Fengchuan during the Tianfu era, and the local villages buried him together.
Later, someone from another province was seen carrying a cloth bag just like this master.
Throughout the regions of Jiang and Zhejiang, many paintings of his image were produced.
Biography of Shi Zhiqiao of Kaiyuan Temple in Ye-du, Tang Dynasty. Shi Zhiqiao’s origins are unknown.

He was brilliant and outstanding in his youth, and as he grew older, he applied himself diligently to the study of Buddhist learning; regarding all the sutras and śāstras, he attained a profound spiritual insight upon hearing them but once.
When he expounded and proclaimed these teachings, his voice and eloquence were clear and resonant.
Every time he ascended the lecture platform, he considered himself peerless; his only concern was that there were few listeners.
Fearing that while the water was passed from vessel to vessel until no vessel remained empty, he alone would be left without it, he felt he would thus fail the Buddha’s intent.
He then carried his book-cases and traveled extensively across famous mountains to consult with the wise.

Finally, he arrived at Mount Heng Monastery, where he rested for over a month. Once, while in a quiet chamber of the monastery, he was alone reflecting upon the meaning of the commentaries; he then reproached himself, saying:
"Does the principle I have understood not deviate from the intention of the Sage?"
While lost in deep reflection, he suddenly raised his head and saw an old monk entering while shaking his mendicant’s staff.
The monk asked, "What sutras and śāstras are you reading?
What principles and meanings are you investigating?"
He harbored doubts, wondering whether this was within the sacred peaks or among the chariot tracks of the plains; that an Arhat might mingle with the common folk—how could such a thing be fathomed?
He then recounted his own past causes and conditions, subsequently feeling deep remorse and self-reproach.
He further said, "If I may receive the guidance of a worthy master, I am willing to endure this bitterness; I shall clench my teeth and tie my tongue, never again to preach or explain.
The old monk laughed and said:
"Your Master’s wisdom is most extensive; how could he not know this principle?
Even a Great Sage cannot save those with whom he has no karmic affinity, much less one at the initial stage of the path.
Your Master simply lacks the affinity with sentient beings."
Jian asked,
"Will it always be like this for the rest of one's life?
The old monk said:
"I shall try to establish a karmic connection with you," he said.
He then asked Sengqie, "How much wealth and provisions do you have now?
Sengqie replied:
"Traveling from north to south, I have torn my robes to wrap my feet and already traversed ten thousand li; all that I brought with me has been exhausted.
I now see that you possess and maintain only nine-strip robes."
The old monk said,
"This alone will suffice!
You must certainly sell it, and with the proceeds from the exchange, prepare them all as millet cakes and oil-based delicacies."

Fajie followed these instructions and prepared enough food for several dozen people. They then went together into the open fields, where they scattered the cakes and grain, burned incense, and knelt for a long time, reciting a mantra:
"May those who eat my offerings today become my dharma-relatives in future lives; I shall instruct them so that they may attain Bodhi."
When he had finished speaking, crows and birds descended in a chaotic swarm to peck and gather [the remains], while the number of earthworms, ants, flies,
and gnats upon the ground could not be counted. The old monk said, "Twenty years from now, you may return to establish a Dharma seat."
"For now, let us travel about; it is not yet appropriate to engage in formal exposition.
Having spoken thus, he departed.

From this point on, Sengyou applied himself with diligence to the power of the Path, studying and refining it without weariness. His understanding of its meaning and flavor became increasingly profound, and his resolve was set upon transmitting it to others.

In the twentieth year, he returned to Hebei and propagated his teachings extensively in Ye; the assembly of listeners numbered over a thousand people, all of whom were twenty years of age or younger, with no more than two or three among them being elderly.
The commentary states:
The final stage of the intermediate state is fixed and difficult to alter; what one cultivates in this life will inevitably bring about its corresponding fruit in the next.

Now, Zhiyi followed the instructions of a different monk to wait for his disciples twenty years later, exactly as he had said. This being so, he cultivated the fruit of his future birth while still alive; therefore, his words cannot be considered false.
The poem says:
"Waiting for the Yellow River to become clear—how long is a human life?
One who knows those who enjoy eternal longevity will find that the river has often been seen to be clear.

Biography of Master Ning of Fengxiang Prefecture, Tang Dynasty. Master Ning of Fengxiang Prefecture was a native of Qiyang; his personal name has been lost, and he was known at the time only by his surname.
He traveled back and forth without a fixed residence, appearing and disappearing like an ordinary monk.

In the first year after Emperor Zhaozong ascended the throne, while staying in a mountain temple, he suddenly met his end; yet he lay peacefully with his body still warm, as if merely in a deep sleep.
The monks surrounded him on all sides, not daring to perform the funeral rites.
After three days, he revived;
the crowd rushed forward in astonishment to inquire after him.
He replied:
"I was summoned by the authorities of the underworld. When I first saw an official, he said:
'The monk's life span remains, yet you have no provision for sustenance.'"
He then summoned his officials and instructed them to conduct an inspection and verification.
The officials replied,
"There are only three *shí* of dried lotus leaves."
He then ordered that [the man's name] be recorded in the register.
Furthermore, he commanded another person to lead him on a tour through the grounds.
They entered a gate and saw several halls, each with a signboard.
Thereupon, he proceeded on foot to a hall inscribed with the name "Li Kuei-yung.
Through a window, he observed a black dragon with one eye missing, standing upright upon an iron pillar and bound by chains.

Next, there was a hall labeled "Zhu Quanzhong," who was a tiger with a green hide and white markings; he was shackled as before, and in front of him was the chaotic remains of human flesh and blood he had devoured.
The next was inscribed as Wang Jian; he lay upon a bed of yellow gold with a white rabbit beside him.
The next was inscribed as Li Maozhen; he wore the full regalia of a crown and robes like a sovereign, with several maidservants attending him on his left and right.
Next, the name Yang Xingmi was inscribed. Because the windows were low and dark, he could not see clearly.
He asked his messenger, "What are these various strange forms?"
He replied,
"This is the one who will become the future king.
Several palaces in the adjacent quarters appeared dark and gloomy from afar, such that even the messengers could not enter them.
He led him away back to his own office, the Hall of the Judicial Official, and said to the messenger:
"Escort the Master back safely; simply recite the *Gongde Jing* (Sutra of Merit) many times."
Ning asked: "Which is the *Sūtra on Merit*?
He replied:
"It is indeed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*!
The power of this scripture to deliver beings from the underworld is beyond compare.
When he regained consciousness, he looked around for a long time and then recounted what had occurred.
Those who heard this were struck with alarm and subsequently reported it to the authorities.
Later, the Governor of Qí found Fǎhóng’s behavior eccentric and preposterous, and did not believe him at all.
Subsequently, Wù Mào Zhēn was indeed enfeoffed as the Prince of Qín.
Li Kuei-yung slaughtered people with reckless cruelty and was known as the "One-Eyed Dragon.
When the House of Chu usurped the mandate of the T'ang, they were ruthless and pitiless in their destruction; soaring on wings to choose their prey, what are they if not tigers?
Wang Jian of Shu was born in the Year of the Rabbit; he fortified his position by obstructing others to consolidate his own power.
In the Dingmao year of the Tianyou era, he usurped a false title and used gold to ornament his bed—all of which corresponded perfectly [with the omens].
From that time on, whenever he fasted, Ning consumed nothing but lotus leaf soup.
As for all other foods and delicacies, he would not eat them if they did not suit his palate.
People from Qin and Long often invited Ning to enter the underworld to predict good or bad fortune in advance; his predictions never missed the mark.
Once, when invited to a vegetarian feast, he vied with others to provide a pure pond with fresh lotuses; he was known as "The Monk Who Enters the Netherworld" and passed away under Mount Qi.
The commentary states:
"The account of entering the netherworld is much like a dream."

King Mu was about to hold a joyous banquet with the *huán rén* (transformed beings), while Duke Mu of Qin obtained a celestial pheasant; its form remained in the human realm while its spirit roamed the upper realms. Once the former words were uttered, the subsequent events were bound to follow.
Thus we know that the six seasonal signs and eight omens are indeed not empty claims.
Master Ning’s entry into the netherworld was no different from the later Tang official Ma Xun seeing a celestial decree descend, appointing the Prince of Lu as the Son of Heaven.
The objects, images, and inscriptions seen by Ning within the hall ultimately corresponded to his description.
To call it a dream would mean that the dream was verified;
to call it a divine excursion would mean that the excursion was not erroneous.
One should understand that waking and dreaming are one and the same, differing only in their clarity or obscurity;
as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Just as when one awakens from a dream, in all instances there is only consciousness."
There was once the kingdom of Gomang, where the people slept so much that they would wake only once every fifty days; they took their dreams to be real and their waking state to be illusory.
If this were so, then whatever one does while awake would be a premonition of a dream, and one would seek reality within the truth of the dream.
Is it not as if the reversal of dream and awakening are one and the same?
Master Ning was no deluded man; had he truly overthrown the Liang dynasty and replaced the mandate of Tang, the two Lis, along with Wang and Yang, would all have been able to rival the Son of Heaven.
As for those who gaze from afar at these various palaces, could they not be the remnants of those who once partitioned the realm and contended as rival warlords?
The lotus leaves upon which they feed are the same as those of the Sui monk Faqing.

Therefore, in records such as the *Youming lu* (Records of the Netherworld), the accounts of Kang He’s virtue and Li Shanlong’s return from the underworld after entering it all prove to be verified by the facts.
As the Sūtra says:
"It is just like a person in a dream who perceives all manner of things, yet possesses a body that does not leave its original place. This is precisely what is meant.
