Written by the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Zanning by Imperial Decree, Part Five:

Chapter on Resonance and Response, Section Six, Part Five. Thirteen Main Biographies, with Five Additional Entries. Biography of Rumen of Lingshu Monastery in Shaoyang Prefecture, Later Tang. Shi Rumen was a native of Min.
When he first met Master Dao’an, he subsequently spread his teachings extensively beyond the Ling Mountains; indeed, his miraculous traces were numerous.
As a person, he was broad-minded, sincere, and earnest; he spoke little except for good reason, deeply pitied those who were deluded and ignorant, and led them by example with fervent exhortation.

The Liu family resided specifically in Fanyu; whenever they invited Huiming to enter their quarters for consultation, he frequently anticipated their arrival, and his predictions were consistently verified.

The rulers of Guangzhou for generations maintained a close relationship with him, visiting him periodically to pay their respects; whenever they encountered doubts that could not be resolved, they would go directly to consult him.

Min also felt no resentment or jealousy; he would prompt him to dictate verses, all of which were precise and accurate. At that time, people called this "begging for blessings," yet Min privately titled himself "Great Master Zhisheng."
Initially, Min served as his attendant with such great devotion that he fully met [the Master’s] expectations; thus, the Master addressed him by the title "Soyu" (The One Who Leads).
One day, while following him up the mountain ridge, [the Master] sent him away and secretly ordered him to descend the mountain. Looking back, he saw Min entering the earth.
The ascetic hid himself among the grass to conceal his form; after waiting for a long time, he emerged and went to meet him, asking, "Where has the Master gone?
He replied:
"I have an old acquaintance with the Mountain King; I have come to invite him for conversation.
At such times, the deceased would emerge from the hole in the ground.
He then issued a strict admonition, saying:
"It would not be appropriate for me to speak of this externally, lest it leak out my private affairs.
Later, he passed away in his quarters, and his body remained intact without dispersing.
The government provided for his funeral and stupa; this is what is now known as the True Body Stupa of Master Lingshu. Is it not so?
The commentary states:
If the sacred tree encounters great peace, its lifespan will surely be long and enduring, exceeding the ordinary limits of human life.
It seems this is yet another instance of what we have heard as an extraordinary account.
Biography of Shi Quan-zai of Mount Tiantai during the Later Tang Dynasty Shi Quan-zai was surnamed Shen and was a native of Qiantang.

From the time he was held in his mother’s arms, he took no pleasure in meat or blood. His mother repeatedly witnessed auspicious omens and encouraged him to go to Great Master Fa-ji of Mount Jing to shave his head and don the dyed robes of the monastic life.

Furthermore, he practiced meditative contemplation, standing tall and lofty, untainted by the dust and winds of the mundane world; he admired the twelve dhūtas to adorn his conduct, and thus the saying went: "He was one who governed the Way."

Upon traveling to various regions to seek instruction and receiving the certification of Chan Master Shishuang, who secretly provided him with protection and guidance, he entered the Dark Cliff (Anyan) of Mount Tiantai to fulfill his lifelong resolve. This cliff stood in opposition to the place where Hanshanzi had hidden himself; both were sites where mischievous spirits and forest monsters gathered in great numbers.
Zai had resided there for over twenty years; the malevolent birds changed their cries, and the mountain spirits yielded their caves.

Whenever he entered or departed on his rounds, ghosts and spirits performed services for him: some swept his path, some attended by his side, some drew water for him, and others gathered fruit for him. People occasionally saw them, yet Zai never spoke of it.
In the fifth year of the Tiancheng era of the Later Tang dynasty, a fellow practitioner from Mount Jing went to welcome him back to reside at Zhenguoyuan Monastery;
he eventually passed away there after having become a monk at that very institution. Biography of Shi Huaijun of Badong during the Jin Dynasty: Shi Huaijun was a man of unknown origins.
As a monk, he was both simple-minded and eccentric; yet he could foresee events before they had even manifested, his responses being as miraculous as those of a deity.
During the Qianning era, he arrived in Badong without warning.

Xu Jun was also capable of the "sage-script" (cāosèng), his calligraphic style being natural and spontaneous; whether on temple or monastery walls, shopfronts, inscriptions, Buddhist sutras, Daoist texts, or even popular songs and vulgar verses, there was nothing he did not bring forth from the tip of his brush.
When he conversed with others, they would say nothing more than "A-wei.
The villagers treated him as a divine sage.

Prefect Yu was concerned that he was deluding the masses, so he imprisoned him and interrogated him. [The Master] then submitted a petition in verse to explain his situation; his intent lay in traveling between the western and eastern regions of Minchuan, yet because the phrasing and diction were elegant and ornate, the provincial governor found it extraordinary and released him.
Furthermore, upon examining its purport, it seems likely that it originated from within the sea; could it not be of the same lineage as the "Cup-Crossing" (Beidu) masters?

Whenever travelers pass by, they invariably moor their boats to pay their respects—seeking divinations regarding the auspiciousness or misfortune of the upper and lower gorges, and the success or failure of their commercial ventures and material pursuits.
The guest earnestly entreated him, requesting only three or five lines of writing, yet he did not speak clearly; the matter was subtle and its verification profound.
At that time, Zhou Chongbin, a high-ranking military officer from Jingnan, went to visit him and received this written message:
"Submit this for investigation at the Imperial Capital."
Thereafter, when he came to present tribute, because the Imperial Preceptor was conducting a southern campaign, he was consequently imprisoned at Nanfu and ultimately executed.
When the deputy commander Sun Daoneng visited him, he wrote these words:
"Deliver this to Zhulin Temple."
He passed away that year, and his funeral was conducted at the site of the former Zhulin Monastery.
When Huangfu Xuan served as the Prefectural Governor, he commissioned a painting depicting a man with a wooden yoke around his neck and a woman standing beside him.
Soon after, he took a girl from a commoner’s family; having been accused of this, his person was secured and he was imprisoned in the government office.

There was one named Mu Zhaosi, of Persian descent, who had been fond of medicinal arts since childhood. He accompanied his father to visit [the official], whereupon [Mu] painted a Daoist riding on clouds and holding a gourd vessel, with the inscription: “A decree from High Official Gao to the Court Investigator. Later, because Mu’s medical skills proved effective, Gao Conghui, Prince of Nanping, ordered him to abandon the Daoist path and follow Confucianism, appointing him by imperial edict as Acting Court Investigator for the Prefecture.
When the Imperial Preceptor was about to launch a campaign against Jingzhou, Shen Jun composed a poem to present to the Prince of Nanping, saying:
"As my horse's head gradually enters the road to Yangzhou, my kinsmen must surely gaze upon me with clear eyes."
That year, Gao Shi surrendered his sincerity to Huaihai, whereupon the heavy siege was lifted.
Many other extraordinary traces of his are of this kind.
Once, he inscribed a verse upon a banana leaf in front of his courtyard, saying:
"Today I have repaid my karmic debt; the prefectures and counties need no further investigation.
This was seen many times as he traveled back and forth, yet people took no notice at all.
Suddenly, he was killed by someone, his body and head separated; the Regional Inspector performed the cremation for him.
Biography of Xingzun of Kuangguo Monastery in Langzhou, Jin Dynasty. Shi Xingzun was the second son of Wang Shenzhi, the Prince of Min of Fuzhou.
After Zhuangzong of the Later Tang ascended the throne, [Huichao] entered Luoyang to present local products and remained there in the capital guesthouse.
Toward the end of the Tongguang era, as Mingzong was about to take power and military chaos ensued, he shaved his head and beard, changed his clothes for those of a monk, and fled to Ba and Shu.
By the Kaiyun era of the Jin dynasty, his appearance was that of a man over seventy years old, yet his vigor did not decline.
Whenever asked about his age or the number of years since his ordination, he would invariably remain silent.
He resided at Kuangguo Chan Monastery in Langzhong; the monastery’s incumbent maintained the monastic discipline, though no one knew whether he himself strictly observed it or not.

There was a son of the Li family whose household had been invited to a vegetarian feast. In the midst of eating and drinking, he suddenly rose, went out the door, and cried out in a clamorous manner as if to demand something.
He said to Li:
"Tonight there will be a fire, starting from the southeast and reaching the northwest street; let all your neighbors prepare for it."
That evening, as expected, everything was reduced to ashes without a trace remaining.
When the assembly gathered to ask the reason for this, he said:
"Yesterday, a woman dressed in red passed by carrying a torch; I regretted that I could not catch up with her."
Furthermore, at the residence of Zhao, the Magistrate of Law, he pointed to beneath a peach tree and said, "There is this much money," without specifying the amount.
Zhao then summoned men to excavate it; just as the baskets and shovels were being raised, a guest happened to arrive, and the treasure was taken by the household servants.
In the midst of the clamor, everything was transformed into green mud; each person scrambled to obtain over a hundred pieces, which were later used for plastering walls.
Instances of such wall collapses occurred frequently.
Whenever Zun passed by the tombs of others, he would know whether their families would meet with good or ill fortune.

As for his observations regarding the winds, birds, and beasts, he would predict disasters and blessings based on what he heard or saw; these predictions invariably proved accurate. Consequently, throughout the villages and districts, both near and far, everyone used his prophetic utterances as common talk.
He finally passed away at Yushan in Jin’an, where his monastic followers performed his cremation.
Biography of the Nameless Monk of Xiangzhou during the Jin Dynasty. The monk Shi Wangming was a man of unknown origins. He did not know where he was from.
He traveled in all directions seeking the Way, undaunted by hardships.
He vowed to tour and visit every famous mountain and sacred site.
During the Tianfu era, he arrived at a Chan monastery in Xiangzhou, where he hung up his staff and lived with a monk who was upright and law-abiding, observing the ninety-day retreat together.
That man was composed and dignified, yet his speech was often eccentric and provocative; he called himself by the name Faben (Fa-ben).
Whether morning or evening, we dwelt together, our hearts in profound accord, as if bound by a long-standing covenant.
The *Fǎběn* states:
"As for my practice of the Way while living as a renunciant, it was at Zhúlín Monastery on the western mountains of Yèdū—there is a stone pillar in front of the monastery.
Should you have leisure time in the future, I hope you will certainly visit me."
The monk, recollecting their previous agreement, went to seek him out.
Upon reaching a village at the foot of the mountain, he stayed overnight in an araṇya (hermitage) and asked the resident monk,
"How far is it from here to Zhulin Monastery?"
The monk then pointed distantly toward the side of a solitary peak, saying, "That place is it.

According to ancient tradition, it was a site where sages and worthies once resided; now, however, only its name remains, so there are no monastic cells or pure dwellings established for the Buddha or the Sangha."

The community was suspicious of this; at dawn the next day they went there, and upon seeing the bamboo grove, they indeed found a stone pillar within it, yet they were utterly bewildered and could not discern its boundaries.
The monk recalled the words his Master had spoken at their parting:
"Simply knock upon that pillar, and you shall see him.

He then struck the pillar several times with a small staff. Immediately, wind and clouds rose up on all sides, such that he could not see anything within a few feet. After a brief moment, the obstruction cleared, and pavilions and towers rose up before him; he found himself standing beneath the triple gate.
He hesitated for a moment; the Dharma had originally emerged from within him, and upon seeing it, he was filled with great joy.

He inquired about old matters from the Nanzhong region and discussed the local customs of Xiang and Deng. Thereupon, [the Master] led him through the double gates and ascended the secret hall, where he took charge of the venerable elders as if assuming the responsibility of the administrative head.
After repeated inquiries, Faben said, "In my youth, while we were both observing the *zhizu* retreat in Xiangyang, I once made an appointment to visit you; thus, I have come to your mountain gate."
The venerable elder said, "Excellent.
You may invite him out after the meal; there is no seat for him here."
This means there was no designated seating order for ordinary monks.
When the meal was finished, Faben escorted him to the triple gate to bid him farewell.
Shortly thereafter, heaven and earth grew dark, and he did not know which direction to take.
Shortly thereafter, it was found right beside a cluster of bamboo and stone pillars, while the rest could not be seen.
The monk came forth to recount these events, yet no one knew what had become of that other monk.
The commentary asks:
"Who was this monk who entered the bamboo grove?
Tong replied:
"One who has encountered an immortal is himself an immortal; how could the visit to a sacred temple tolerate the impurities of the mundane?
On one hand, it reveals that the sacred temple exists within the human realm; on the other, it shows that the sacred monks participate among the ranks of the monastic community."
Do not disparage the Triple Gem, for the ordinary and the holy are intermingled.
This transmission has been newly recounted by several individuals, yet such accounts have been heard in various places since ancient times.

For instance, during the Wuping era of the Northern Qi dynasty, the monk Yuantong once attended a lecture where he saw a sick monk; when the summer retreat ended and the monk’s illness was cured, they agreed to meet at Drum Mountain’s Zhulin Monastery in Ye, and the details of this account are largely the same.
"This must be the former and latter sites where he reached the holy temple.

The Biography of the Mad Monk of Gaocheng County in Luoyang, Han: Regarding the biography of the mad monk, known as Master Cao: During the Kaiyun era of the Jin dynasty, he traveled throughout the towns and villages begging for stone, ore, and lime. Day and night, he drove his loads into the two mountains of Da-liu and Xiao-liu, saying to travelers and local elders:
"I am building a palace."
However, no one could fathom it; everyone said, "He is a madman—what basis is there for this?
Thus they transported several thousand *shí* [of grain] and sealed the door very securely.
Thereafter, the local people did not expect that this monk would ever leave his traces again.
Toward the beginning of the Qianyou era, when the Han Founder had entered the present Eastern Capital and ascended the throne, he passed away before a year had elapsed.
At that time, an imperial decree was issued to select Rui-ling for burial beneath Mount Daliu;
those who calculated the matter remarked, "There are several million bricks and tiles, which can be molded and fired within this mountain."
"How can there be any charcoal from ore here?
Suddenly, a village headman said, "Originally, there was a monk who stored several thousand stones of ash in this place; according to the measurements, it should be sufficient."
Upon investigating the matter, he found that the mountain range had been completely cleared, with not a single thing left behind; thus it was proven that this monk was no madman.
Furthermore, there was the Venerable Master Cao of Zhenzhou, a native of Hengyang.

They do not dwell in fixed residences, their speech is confused and contentious, they wear tattered tunics and worn-out sandals, with soiled faces and darkened complexions; they are known as a class of people who are wind-crazed and dissolute.
The people of Qi and Zhao all find them unfathomable, yet they hold them in high esteem.
Sometimes he was summoned for a meal; having finished eating, he would depart in silence, his demeanor appearing as if he were angry though not intoxicated!
An Zhongrong, the regional commander stationed there for several years, incited the military officials and local citizens to petition the imperial court to erect a Stele of Virtuous Governance.
On the day the stele was about to be erected, its form stood firm and imposing.
Master Cao pointed at it and laughed heartily, saying, "It cannot stand; it cannot stand."
Everyone looked at one another with pale faces as the officials drove them away, yet they continued to chant without ceasing their voices.

When Zhongrong secretly conceived rebellious thoughts, groomed his horses, and sharpened his weapons, he was on the verge of committing treason; the court suppressed and destroyed him, and the stele was subsequently demolished.
Whatever he pointed out or refuted was like an echo responding to a sound.
His final end remains unknown.

The Biography of the Monk Jian of Jingzhong Monastery during the Later Zhou and Western Shu: Regarding the monk Jian of Daci Monastery whose name was lost, his secular name was also Jian, and his surname was Wang; he was a native of Jingzhao.
From his youth, he was observant and wise, and his speech and demeanor were far superior to those of his peers.
In the eleventh year of the Dazhong era, when Du Shenquan presided over the examination on statecraft, Feng Juan, the Director of the Secretariat, was also a fellow candidate of that same year.
During the Qianfu era, when the rebels of Chao were rampant, he followed the current to escape the chaos.

Arriving at Zhugong, he sought refuge with Cheng Rui, the Regional Commander; when Rui’s campaign against Huaihai proved unsuccessful, [the monk] subsequently shaved his head and entered the monastic order.
When Lei Man occupied Jingzhou, Zhao Ning of Xiangzhou defeated him.
Emperor Zhu of Liang dispatched Gao Jichang to exterminate him, and Jiangling subsequently came under the control of the Gao clan.
He remained in seclusion between Kuí and Xià to avoid the turmoil of the times.
In the third year of the Tóngguāng era of the Later Táng dynasty, he entered Shǔ to seek out Fēng Juān, only to find that the latter had already passed away.

He subsequently resided at Jìngzhòng Monastery; his beard and hair were white, yet his complexion was ruddy and radiant, and he moved about with such carefree ease that people could not fathom whether his demeanor was genuine or feigned.

There was a scholar-official from Huayang named Wang Chuhou—who had failed the examinations in Wushu during the year of Yimao (the second year of the Xiande era of the Zhou dynasty)—who entered the temple to write out his sorrows among the pines and bamboo, where he discovered this sealed letter.
Jian said,
"Could this not be Wang Chuhou?
Chuhou was startled and said:
"We have never been intimate; why do you call us so suddenly?
Jian replied, "I simply recognized them."
He then stated that he was originally born during the early Dahe era of Emperor Wenzong of the Tang dynasty, and that more than one hundred and thirty years had passed until the present.
Chu Hou asked: "What is the state of my own physical form?"
"The affairs of your son will reach their culmination next year.
From this point forward, the events shall become clear.
His intention was to say that Shu was about to perish, and he instructed him not to disclose this.
When he sought him again the following day, his voice and traces had vanished into obscurity.
One day, however, he returned to knock at the gate and said, "I have gone for a time to pay homage at Mount Emei; I shall return after observing the summer retreat at Heishui."
He secured the document on his desk and picked up a scroll to examine it; it was Chu Hou’s essay for the prefectural examination, which read:
"To examine the true from the false is not a matter of writing by candlelight."
"How much you have deceived me!
He then reached into his breast, drew out the draft of the poem, and showed it to him, saying, "Is this not the actual original from the examination?
Chu Hou was struck with unceasing astonishment and said:
"I had recently made some minor revisions after my examination to remedy the errors of haste committed by candlelight.
From where did you obtain this original copy?
Jian replied:
"It is not merely this one rhapsody; everything you have composed throughout your life is stored here.

The next day, he visited him and led Chuhou into the northern corner of the temple. Together they paid their respects at the shrine of the late Grand Marshal, Duke of Bin, Du Cong, and sat beneath the western corridor. Suddenly, several officials of various appearances emerged from the main hall in a single file, descended the steps, and performed two prostrations.
Jian said, "The new official is here; you may pay your respects in the courtyard.
Chuhou rose in a state of trepidation.
Jian said, "These people will serve as your subordinates; why should you fear them?
Do you not know that Mount Tai has appointed you as the Lord of Fate?"

"Since you still bear the ambition of your youth and have not yet fulfilled your former aspirations, I request that you wait until after you have passed the imperial examinations to carry out this plan.

He further examined the register of official stipends and saw that the number of candidates for the upcoming spring examination list had already been fixed, and that you were included among them; this was a case of being secretly ordained and openly received.
"To assume the name of one in the human world while consuming the stipends of the netherworld—this is for the yang to bestow and the yin to receive.
Chu Hou was struck with terror and did not know how to respond;
he could only ask, "Who will be the names of those who pass the imperial examination next year?"
He unrolled his paper and took up his brush, immediately writing a short letter and giving it to him, warning him:
"Conceal this with the utmost secrecy.
Should it leak out, disaster will follow before you can even turn your heel."
After a short while, the officials dispersed.
Jian took Xiu’s hand and exited the temple; they departed as darkness fell.
When the spring examinations concluded, Jian came to Chu Hou’s residence and left a note that read: [The remainder of the note is omitted per instructions.]
"I shall return briefly to my humble cottage; there will be no further meeting between us.
Later, when he went to the monks' hall of the monastery to inquire after him, the master had already departed elsewhere.

He then tore open the short-sealed letter and read it; it contained only these four lines: "Zhou Cheng and Tong Cheng, the two Wangs have different names; one of them is King; a hundred days shall be the term."
When the notice was posted, it was verified that there were eight scholars.
As for the two Wangs—Wang Chuhou and Wang Shenyen—the latter was one of them.
Disliking the "one-hundred-day deadline," Wang Chuhou associated only with his fellow graduates, hosting grand banquets where they indulged in pleasures to their heart's content.
Consequently, no further disturbances arose, and he passed away suddenly that very night.
Those of his own age all dreamed that Chu Hou was walking through the palace courtyard wearing a blue robe and holding a magnolia-wood tablet, escorted by an imperial retinue.
When they verified the honor of his appointment to office, it lasted for only one hundred and twenty days.

Examining closely, Jian was born during the early Taihe era of Emperor Wenzong; he attained full physical maturity during the Dazhong era of Emperor Xuanzong, by which time Wang Chuhou had already met him at over one hundred and thirty years of age.
Next, there was an anonymous monk at the Daci Temple in the capital city of Shu who constantly recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* with such a pleasing voice that people delighted in hearing him.
When it was time for his almsround, he would take only as much as was necessary to sustain himself.
Suffering from a slight ailment in his body, he was shown a prescription for medicine.
The monk then took up his staff and entered Mount Daimian in Qingcheng to gather herbs.
As he followed the stream and crossed perilous terrain, clouds and mist suddenly rose on all sides, and he lost his way, not knowing where he was headed.
After a short while, he saw an old man. The monk bowed to him, exchanged pleasantries regarding the weather, and asked, "What brings you here?
The monk replied, "I have come to gather some medicinal herbs."
The old man said, "My cottage is not far away; would it be possible for you to briefly employ your supernatural powers to travel there?
The monk replied:
"Having lost my way and become disoriented, I wish to follow you, Master.
After a short while, the clouds dispersed, and he saw a house that was dark and imposing.
Upon approaching it, the old man said:
"Let us first inform the master of the manor.
Upon entering the gate, the monk beheld the scene; everything was extraordinary and beyond ordinary description.
He asked:
"Have you broken your fast?
He replied,
"I have not yet eaten."
As he burned incense, he felt an extraordinary sense of distress and requested that the monk recite the scripture he was studying.
The monk chanted the sutra with a resonant voice, encouraging him to complete the entire section.
The offerings of food provided were all the same as those found before Daci Temple.

When the fast was concluded, a servant in green robes carried a bamboo vessel and offered it with fragrant herbs; he then gave five strings of cash to the master as expenses for purchasing sesame cakes.
The old man joined his palms and saw him out.
Someone asked, saying,
"This is Master Sun Simiao.
He had already been at the temple for over a month.
When the money was brought into the temple, it turned out to be gold coins.
Upon hearing this, the Wang family collected the gold coins and provided the monk with five hundred strings of cash instead.
The monk distributed these as alms, thereby knowing that the immortal would always reside on famous mountains.
Next, there was a petition from Luomu County in Jiazhou stating:
"The Mountain Man Sun has rented a donkey and failed to pay for it; we request that he be summoned.
When the young boy was questioned, he said:
"This is Sun Simiao.
The magistrate was struck with wonder and gave him money to pay the debt in his stead.
As the man was leaving the county road, he saw Master Sun taking two hundred coins and handing them to him, saying:
"I have been waiting for you here all along; why do you find this so strange?
The monk who obtained the gold coins did not know its ultimate destination.
Biography of Shi Jian of Huguang Monastery in Hangzhou, Zhou Dynasty. Shi Jian, whose secular surname was Zhao, was a native of Danchun.

He did not follow the precepts and models of conduct, remaining complacent in his unrestrained behavior; he wore tattered robes yet recited many verses and hymns, delighting in making prophetic predictions regarding calamities and blessings throughout the regions of Hangzhou and Yue.
Even those who initially lacked faith found their experiences to be as consistent as matching tally-sticks.
Regarding the mountain scriptures and geomancy, Yi Xing and Jing Chun each separately attained the essential gateways; Yi Xing often remarked:
"In the past, Dao Bian of Mount Tai obtained the arts concerning the examination of tombs; apart from this, there is nothing else of value."
He delighted in relocating mountains and examining burial sites for others; his predictions regarding auspiciousness and misfortune were always as he had said.
He had no fixed dwelling and frequently visited the homes of the noble families; whenever he claimed he was hungry, he would immediately seek a meal of chicken.
Furthermore, he obtained fine wine and drank several cups before departing.

Initially, he did not offer any words of thanks; however, he was highly skilled at calligraphy—inscribing large characters on nameplates and temple gateways—and when he wrote them, he would prophesy their fortune or misfortune, with the results being verified after a long or short period.
He first resided at a monastery beside West Lake in Hangzhou and passed away without illness.
Later, a traveler from Changsha saw him in the marketplace; they walked hand in hand and conversed about old times, after which the traveler sent word to the abbot of Chongshou Monastery:
"You previously owed me such-and-such an amount of money; I now release you."
"I slept on a straw mat beneath my bed; there was a piece of meat wrapped in paper that must have rotted, so I discarded it.
Following these words, the monk of the monastery inspected the spot and indeed saw it; he subsequently painted a portrait of the figure and made offerings to it.
Jian Zeng once said, "The Spired House shall later be consumed by fire.
When the Southern Pagoda of the Prefecture was scorched by a celestial fire in the year of Wu-wu, his words proved to be without error.
The Biography of Monk Wang Lohan of Qianfu Temple in Mingzhou, Song Dynasty. Monk Wang Lohan was a monk of unfathomable character.
He was extremely fond of pork and spoke with the wildness of a madman; later, many of his words were found to have been prophetic.
Once, while he was drying his clothes, a thief intended to snatch them away, but [the Master] lowered his head and feigned sleep.
There was a man who would approach him to beg for alms, and [Huiyuan] never showed even the slightest hint of parsimony.

In the sixth month of the first year of the Kaibao era, he suddenly passed away while sitting in meditation. Three days later, when his body was being lacquered and wrapped in cloth, a sudden sound of bubbling and gurgling was heard between his two cheeks; everyone said it was because they were festering and rotting.
One night, he sent his dream to several people, saying:
"The lacquer has clouded my consciousness; how can it be opened?
The next day, he summoned a lacquerer to peel it away. The flesh was red and white, and round grains of *śarīra* fell out; these were collected and venerated.
To this day, his physical body remains preserved at this temple.
At that time, the Chief Preceptor Zanning composed a stele inscription to record these wonders.
The King of the Southern Han, the Qian clan, privately changed the name [of the temple] to "Venerable Honored One of Secret Cultivation and Divine Transformation."

Biography of Zonghe of Yanshou Monastery in Tanzhou, Song Dynasty. Zonghe, whose secular surname was Dao, was a native of Minyue. He traveled across the mountains and along the Xiang River in search of a spiritual teacher.
As a monk, he stood out in his integrity and was free from desire; though he lived among a community all day long, he did nothing but smile.
The people of the southern state of Chu held him in great faith and esteem.

Later, while he was residing at Juyanshou Monastery, the former Counselor-in-Attendance, Lord Jia Ci—who was serving as the military governor—heard of him and went to pay his respects; however, no conversation took place between them.
The common people discussed it, saying, "How could one who has attained the Way fall within the scope of ordinary measurement?
Nevertheless, Jia firmly requested to go and serve as the abbot of Wenshu Temple.
On that day, he ascended the seat and briefly expounded upon the essentials of Chan before dispersing the assembly.
The following day, he addressed the multitude, saying:
"I have a matter to attend to and shall depart for a short time; you worthy ones should not detain me."
His attire was like that of a wandering monk; having crossed the Pengchui River, he arrived before the Huangzhou Post Station and stood upright until his death.
People from near and far rushed to witness the ceremony.

At that time, the postal official of the horse-stable (mā-pù shǐ-chén) oversaw the funeral arrangements and constructed a stūpa at the place where [the Master] passed away; this was in the second year of the Kaibao era (969), which is likely the site now known as Zhen-shen-yuan (Hall of the True Body).
Furthermore, there was Shi Daoyin of Dà'ān Temple in Miánchí; it is unknown where he was from.
He traveled between the regions of Miánchí, Chán, and Jiàn, saying of himself:
"When those who have left the household life observe frugality, they rarely trouble others."
"To share one's path with the beasts of burden means there is no room for right or wrong to fill one's ears.
He once kept a black dog; whether entering or leaving, rising or lying down, they never forgot each other nor were they ever parted.
Every time he ate, he would take his iron bowl to the fire to cook; once the gruel was ready, he would eat it together with his dog.
Whether moving ahead or following behind, his conduct and movements were so extraordinary that no one could fathom them.
Once the monk passed away, even his dog perished with him.
Now, at Da'an Temple, an image of him has been sculpted, yet both his physical body and this likeness remain preserved from the Kaiyuan era.
The people of Luoyang hold him in deep reverence, and the shrine is filled with incense and flowers.
The lineage of Master Dian-Dian of Lingjiu Mountain Temple in Dayi County, Yongzhou, Song Dynasty. Regarding the monk Master Dian-Dian: it is unknown where he was from.
During the Guangzheng era of the Meng clan’s reign, he lived in seclusion at Dayishan Temple south of Yangnan, frequently frequenting the wine shops.
Although he had taken up the monastic life, his conduct was always like that of a madman.
Whenever he encountered others, he would invariably point them out while speaking; thus, he was known by the name "Muzhi" (Pointing Eye).

There were those who had taken a vow to eat only vegetarian food, yet wine and meat were never absent from his table; he took this as his constant practice, and even the common folk did not find it distasteful.
As the sun set, he purchased yellow and white hemp paper, brushes, and ink, and placed them in his sleeves before returning home.
After traveling several li, he was so deeply immersed in his state that he reached home only when darkness had fallen.
The room where he lived had an outer door but no four walls.
Once inside, he would close the door so that no one could enter.

Initially, a young novice monk from the neighboring monastery tiptoed in to observe him; he saw [Huiyuan] holding a candle and sitting with legs spread wide, with paper and brush set before him. He was scolding someone and writing large characters, the meaning of which the novice could not understand.
Often, with a sudden exclamation, he would act with decisive resolve.

After a long time, as he gazed intently at the boundary between light and darkness, there appeared to his eyes a shimmering array of figures like officials of a court; their tunics and robes were not of the garments worn in this world.
Onlookers were struck with fear and withdrew.
When questioned about the matter the following morning, he responded with anger and gave no answer.
After several years had passed, the people of Yang and Ze all regarded him as a divine anomaly; his ultimate end was thereafter unknown.
The commentary says:

Master Dian was able to interrogate ghosts, yet he possessed no particularly lofty purity; in establishing norms to inspire the goodness of sentient beings, was he not the same as the ancients who adjudicated matters in the underworld?
Tong said:
"What is produced resides in the mind. If it does not arise from the power of the True Path, it is the same as the Way of the Five Pecks of Rice.
If it does not originate from the conscious application of talismans and prohibitions, it merely moves spirits and deities to inspire faith and be driven by one's will."
Therefore, the *Śīla-sūtra* states:
"If it is necessary to manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to inspire and transform those to be saved, one displays the power of psychic travel (*ṛddhipāda*).
In the *Vyavahāra-śāstra*, it is said that Bodhisattvas take delight in the playful transformations of supernatural powers.
Furthermore, this may be one who is at the stage of practicing the pratyekabuddha path; thus the treatise says:
"The Pratyekabuddha, relying upon various villages and towns, begs for alms and delivers others through his own person."
"He does not manifest various supernatural powers through verbal expressions, so as to cause those who slander him to turn toward the path.
Biography of Xingman of the Zhiyi Chan Monastery on Mount Tiantai during the Song Dynasty. Xingman was a native of Nanpu in Wan Prefecture.
Having reached the age of maturity while still a youth, his nature was bright and clever; he was devoted to his kin and sought to become a son of the Buddha.

As soon as he had completed receiving the precepts, he heard that the path of Chan flourished between the two lakes and that the gate of Shishuang was filled with many eminent scholars; he therefore went there to seek instruction.
When the various Chan masters passed away one after another, Faman went to Yuzhang to observe the various Dharma assemblies;

having found a state of peace and stability there, he subsequently heard of the sacred traces at Tiantai. Thereupon, he packed his belongings and traveled there, settling at Zhiyi’s Monastery at the foot of Mount Huading, where he took charge of the monks’ tea stove.
Seeing people, he was always cheerful and pleasant; for several decades, he never showed a single look of anger.
He slept on a simple earthen bed, leaving the space beneath it empty, and warmed himself by burning refuse.
Every day when he removed his clothes to go to bed, the fleas and lice swarmed about and bit him; yet, once he had been fed and cared for as usual, he would put his clothes back on as before.
If someone were to secretly feel beneath his garments, not a single flea or louse would be found there.
Previously, outside the chamber railing there was a great pine tree, upon whose horizontal branches a small tree grew as an epiphyte.
Whenever Man came out to sit, that parasitic tree would invariably sway and lean toward him; at the time, people said that this tree was performing a prostration for the *chátóu* (tea master).
Those who did not believe him would wait specifically for the moment he emerged from his bowl, at which point they would become agitated.
Once he had left, however, he would stand tall and upright, remaining utterly unmoved.
Although he ate with the assembly, he took only a small portion and ceased.
Within forty years, no one had ever seen him urinate or defecate.
During the Kaibao era, he informed others in advance, saying, "I am about to depart.
He instructed the assembly of monks to recite the name of Mañjuśrī for his assistance; then, sitting in silence, he passed away through transformation. He was approximately eighty years of age.

Fayuan composed many verses to chant the Way. Regarding the transmission of Fayuan of Maizhai Monastery in Weifu during the Song dynasty: Master Fayuan, whose secular surname was Hao, was a native of Yuan County in Zhending. He was known as the Monk Li Tongxuan. Due to the karmic conditions planted in previous lives, he emerged from the mundane world without hindrance.
In the second year of the Changxing era of the Later Tang dynasty, he entered Guanyin Monastery in his native prefecture.
He applied himself diligently to recitation and study; the Master shaved his head for him, and after an interval of one year, he received the full precepts.
Later, he took up his staff and carried his satchel, traveling to pay homage in various directions.
Upon reaching Shao Mountain, he hung up his alms-bowl and stayed there to study the Tripitaka.
In the third year of the Kaiyun era of the Jin dynasty, he returned to his native land and resided at T'ien-wang-yüan (Tianwang Monastery).
In the following year, the Khitans invaded the capital. The Khitan King, Ye-lü De-guang, returned to Changshan Luancheng and died there.

Prince Yongkang Wugu succeeded him as the ruler of the foreign state. At that time, while the army was returning from Zhenzhou to the north, the chieftains Madaha and Ye-lü Xiali were left to guard Xiaping (i.e., Changshan), where all the officials and soldiers of the Jin remained.

The Han generals were deliberating on a plan to expel the barbarian invaders, but before their strategy was finalized, the streets and alleys were split between the two sides; those among the barbarians who were of Han descent were the first to be attacked, and everyone, young and old alike, was slaughtered.
At T'ien-wang-yüan, eight monks were executed, and Yuán was among their number—at that time, those seen being put to death were especially numerous.
Initially, as Yuán extended his neck to receive two blows of the blade, it was as if striking wood or stone;
Yuán cried out, "I beg for one more stroke!"
Consequently, his body and head were separated.

When evening came, Yuan suddenly beheld the late-day sun as if in a dream; he also had a slight realization that he had been executed. Thinking to himself that he was already dead, he perceived the sun and moon even within the darkness.
He hesitated for a moment and raised one arm to test by touching his head; he then realized it was as it had always been.
Suspecting this again and again, he did not dare to move it, fearing it might fall apart.

Furthermore, it was said that because it had been bound together with congealed blood, when he pressed upon it heavily, there were traces around his neck, appearing like a seam about the thickness of a thread, which remained thus for the rest of his life.
At that time, as the city had already expelled the barbarian tribes and things had somewhat settled, bystanders helped him up, and he returned to his monastery the following morning.
Just as the monks of the monastery were about to eat their congee, they saw Yuan and, taking him for a ghostly apparition, all fled in panic.

After some time, having ascertained the truth, they exclaimed with joy that he had returned from the dead; people from far and near came to pay their respects, marveling at such a rare and extraordinary occurrence.
The people of Changshan vied with one another to present offerings and alms to him.
Thereafter, Huayan wandered through various regions, having no fixed dwelling place.
During the Xiande era of the Zhou dynasty, he stayed at the Maozhai Monastery in Cheng’an County, Daming Prefecture, where he diligently searched for the Tripitaka teachings.
In the sixth year of the Kaibao era, he suddenly said to the assembly:
"Human life is illusory; how can it endure for long?
When things reach their limit, they undergo transformation; there is ultimately no small difference between birth-and-death and nirvana."
Before many days had passed, he passed away.
Both the monastic and lay communities mourned him as if they had lost a close kinsman.
On the day his body was escorted for cremation, they were moved to find śarīra relics like grains of millet or sorghum.
At seventy-four years of age, his dharma-ordination year was fifty-one.
At that time, Fan Lu-gong Zhi personally inquired about Yuan’s origins and treated him with great gravity.
Upon further questioning regarding his conduct, he learned that Yuan had already read through the Tripitaka twice.
Furthermore, there was the miner-monk of Lenggqasī Monastery in Fuzhou, the son of a soldier stationed at Haitan.
Initially, when his mother was pregnant with him, she remained in a state of profound stillness and took no pleasure in meat or pungent foods.
Upon his birth, he was precocious and extraordinary, refusing to eat fish or meat.
When he reached the age of eight, he took pleasure in eating wild vegetables; if anyone was seen weeding or tilling the soil, he would immediately say that they were killing living beings.
Whenever he saw meat or fish being cooked in a household kitchen, he would take handfuls of sand and ash and throw them into the cauldrons, valuing their not being eaten.
He said of himself:
"The pagoda at Kaiyuan Temple was built by me during the Sui dynasty."
He frequently spoke of events before they had even occurred, and later they all proved to be perfectly accurate.

[The Emperor] then requested him to leave the household life; consequently, he donned the dharma robes. A fragrance issued from the crown of his head like that of burning aloeswood and sandalwood, and he was thus titled "Holy Monk" (Shengseng).

At that time, the Imperial Censor Huangfu Zheng was acting as the Acting Governor (liuhou). He invited [the Master] into the official residence and prepared several hundred meat-filled dumplings (*rouduizi*), with only one being vegetarian. Dishes and vessels were set out in an intricate array, all displayed before him, with the intention of testing who among them was ordinary and who was a sage.
When Min took his place at the banquet, he directly picked up a plain dish and ate from it, while the remainder of the dishes he merely brushed aside with his hand as he composed his work.
At that time, all of Huangfu’s subordinates were struck with awe and admiration.
Whenever he went out into the streets and alleys, crowds would surround him.
He himself declared, "My life shall end at thirteen; I am destined to enter extinction.
When that time arrived, he indeed passed away.

He was subsequently cremated before the temple, while the men and women of the entire city wept in mourning. Following the rites of a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin), a stupa was erected over his remains.

Furthermore, during the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, there was a man named Li Tongxuan in the northeast of Taiyuan who claimed to be a descendant of the Tang imperial lineage, though it is unknown which royal house his progenitors belonged to.
He held official rank and noble insignia as light as straw, cherishing instead the forests and springs; his every movement was beyond measure.

He stood over seven chi tall, with a complexion of a purplish hue. His eyebrows extended past his eyes, his beard and whiskers were as if painted, and his hair was deep blue-black and curled in spirals. His lips were red and lustrous, and his teeth were closely set.
He wore a crown of birch bark and was dressed in robes of coarse cloth with wide sleeves.

His waist was not bound by a girdle, and his feet did not tread upon shoes; thus, though it was winter, he suffered no affliction from chapped skin, and though it was summer, he was not invaded by filth or sweat.
He was free and self-possessed, unencumbered by any constraints;

yet he was erudite in matters of both antiquity and the present, penetrating the essence of both Confucianism and Buddhism, such that his eloquence and expression resounded like the striking of a great bell.
Yet his heart remained inclined toward the *Avataṃsaka*, and he never ceased to dwell upon it.
Whenever he examined the commentaries and exegeses of various schools, which were so voluminous and prolix that students spent their entire lives without making any progress, he felt constrained.

In the spring of the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era, carrying a copy of the new *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and leaning on a staff, he traveled from Dingxiang to the southwestern part of Yungxian in the Bingzhou region. Arriving at the home of Gao Shanu in Daxian Village, Tongying Township, he stayed in a detached room to compose a treatise. There he expounded the *Avataṃsaka*, remaining within the confines of his courtyard for nearly three years.
Gao’s neighbors found this strange and could not fathom it.
Every day he consumed ten dates and one *baiye* (cypress leaf) cake, requiring nothing else.
Later, he moved to the side of an ancient Buddha hall at the Ma family residence in Nan Gu, where he built a small earthen hut to rest in seclusion.
The Gao family’s offering of jujube cakes also arrived.

Once, he took his treatises and scriptures to the Mian family estate—which was Guange Village—and encountered a tiger along the way. Daohuan saw it, patted its back, and the tiger placed the scriptures and treatises it was carrying onto its back and carried them to an earthen grotto; the tiger then departed with its ears drooping.

Originally, there was no spring at that site for drawing water. During a violent storm, an old pine tree over a hundred feet tall was uprooted, forming a pond approximately ten feet deep. Its water was fragrant and sweet; to this day, it is called the Elder’s Spring (Chángzhě-quán).
The villagers often sought rain by invoking him during periods of excessive heat, and his prayers were frequently answered.
Furthermore, when he composed his treatises, there was no oil or candles in the room.

Every night, as he held his pen to his mouth, two white rays of light several feet long would emerge from his temples, illuminating everything with brilliant clarity; this became his constant practice.

From the moment he arrived at the earthen grotto, two women suddenly appeared, dressed in coarse cloth with white cloth head-wraps; they were of elegant appearance and refined countenance. They placed a tray of food before the grotto, and Xuan ate it alone.
In total, five years passed, during which the provision of paper and ink was never lacking; yet when the treatise was completed, he had already passed away.
The treatise he composed consists of forty fascicles, which comprehensively summarizes the textual meanings of eighty fascicles of sutras.

Next is the *Deciding Doubts* (*Jueyi lun*) in four fascicles, which summarizes the profound essentials of cause and effect across the ten assemblies and enumerates the dharma-gates of the fifty-three stages.
One day, while his fellow villagers were gathered for a drinking feast, Huian came to them and said, "May you all dwell in well-being; I am now departing!"
The villagers were startled and marveled, thinking he had gone elsewhere; they said,
"He has reached his end."
All wept with grief and longing as they escorted him to the earthen shrine, saying, "Departure and dwelling are but constants.

As the villagers descended the slope, they looked back at the site; it was shrouded in dark clouds and mist. At the hour of the rat (midnight), he sat upright and passed away within the shrine. A white light issued from the crown of his head, piercing upward through the vast void. This occurred on the twenty-eighth day of the late spring in the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era.
His age at death was ninety-six.
At dawn, several people went up the mountain and found that his meditation cell was filled with snakes and vipers, such that they could not advance.
They called out to him together, whereupon the snakes and vipers dispersed in all directions.
The elders and the young, moved by shared remembrance, halted their carriage to welcome him north of Mount Dàshān; they constructed a city of stone and interred him there.
This is the Śrāvastī Aranya on Mount Fángshān, where the divine blessings reside.
On the day of the funeral, two spotted deer, a pair of white cranes, and various other birds and beasts appeared as if in a state of mournful longing.

In the sixth month of the ninth year of the Dali era, a monk named Guangchao arrived at the hermitage to collect two copies of the treatises. He summoned a scribe to transcribe them on the mountain, intending to bring them into the Fen River region for circulation; from this point on, these treatises flourished.
During the Zhizhong era of the Dazhong period, the monk Zhi-ning of Min-yue was about to add commentaries beneath the text of the treatise, completing one hundred and twenty fascicles.
There were seven fascicles of synoptic exegesis for the treatise that were not included within the annotations; these have also been transcribed and appended at the beginning.

In the year Dingmao of the Qiande era of the Song dynasty, the Min monk Huìyán reorganized and systematized [the material], establishing the title *Huayan jing helun* (A Combined Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra), which circulated in the world and was highly esteemed by all.

Tong replied:

"This refers to the identity of mind and phenomena; such identity is equanimous and unimpeded.

While spurious sutras may be incinerated, the *Li lun* (Treatise of Li) is difficult to burn away, for it is not within the realm of those who are merely minor sages.

When the cinnabar is perfected and transmuted through repeated cycles, one ascends to immortality upon its ingestion;
when the wisdom-forging is complete, its efficacy is verified by the fruits of realization.

If, however, one’s name is not yet inscribed in the registers of the sages and one’s power does not accord with the King of Sutras, how can one lightly lift this body to transcend the mundane world? It would merely dazzle the physical eye and cause the monkey-like mind to be filled with agitation.
Those known as the followers of the Śākya clan differ in their status, high and low;

they may also be compared to a herd of elephants—whose tusks can gore and strike, whose trunks are skilled at contracting and extending, whose strength repels nine oxen, and who gallop past four horses.

On another shore of Lake Anavatapta, on the leeward side of Mount Gandhamādana, there are elephants that spread their two wings to fly and employ the skillful means of their seven limbs; they surpass the elephants of the oceanic mountains a hundredfold, being peerless in their excellence, and are named Airāvata—the dragons among elephants.
Truly, it must be understood that the śramaṇa possesses the power of spiritual resonance; this is precisely what is meant by such a statement!
As for "that which can resonate" and "that which is resonated with," it refers to the arrival of the power of cultivation, whereby celestial deities necessarily attend and serve him;
as for "that which can penetrate" and "that which is penetrated," it refers to his ability to manifest supernatural transformations (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) and reveal them to others.
When the subject and object both achieve resonance and penetration, then there is no ultimate fruit of the Three Vehicles that does not resonate and penetrate.

Formerly, Huijiao of the Liang dynasty composed biographies and established the category of "Numinous Marvels" (*shenyi*); this was intended solely to encompass those sages and worthies who have reached the ultimate stage.
Alternatively, as for the successive portents and their hierarchical gradations, there were naturally some deficiencies that could not be fully encompassed.

When Master Xuán arrived, he did not follow these precedents but instead reformed them into the *Gantong* (Resonance and Penetration), taking its name from the phrase "resonating and thereby penetrating. Here, "penetration" refers to the nature of wisdom (*jñāna-svabhāva*), while "resonance" refers to cultivation; the fruit is indeed penetration.

Examining this principle, its scope is vast and encompasses all things; it is just like Ban Gu’s expansion of the "Nine Schools" (jiu liu) and his transformation of the "Shu" (Annals) into "Zhi" (Monographs).
Furthermore, is it not the case that the sages' re-drawing of the hexagrams was superior to their initial drawing of them?
If so, then if they had not previously observed what is above and examined what is below, how could there have been subsequent transformation and penetration?
This was not due to Master Xuan’s personal ability; rather, it was possible because he relied on the transformative principles established by Jiaxiang.
To trace its origin: when the chamber is still, a pure whiteness arises; when the mind is still, spiritual powers manifest.
Compared to what the Confucians and the Mysterious School (Daoists) can achieve, how does my Way measure up?
It induces the arousal of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), which manifests with sovereign ease;
the Dharma is free from clamor, and all manifold conditions are utterly extinguished.
Where the gateways of wisdom open, the six supernormal powers arise from this;
when the marks of movement cease, the five eyes shine forth by means of this.
By what means did Maudgalyāyana manifest his fame as the foremost?
When Aniruddha gazes upon things, he possesses this vision of half a head;
Mount Meru enters a mustard seed, and the waters of the great ocean are swallowed at the tip of a hair.
At such a time of inconceivability, the mind and mouth of the ordinary person are both lost.
The realm of the Buddhas is one and the same, regardless of where their supernormal powers arise.
Furthermore, within my teaching, faith, understanding, cultivation, and realization serve as the standards:
when it comes to translating scriptures and transmitting the Dharma, they give rise to faith;
Explaining the meaning and practicing meditation constitute awakening and understanding;
clarifying the Vinaya and protecting the Dharma constitute cultivation and practice;
and spiritual wonders and responsive resonance constitute the realization of the fruit.
Who would say that in the Semblance and Final Dharma ages there are no practices or fruits?
This is also spoken from the perspective of the majority:
it is just like the carving of a staff at Mount Dandan, which signaled Hou Jing’s return to the West.
Heshang Tulu pointed toward heaven, foreknowing that Wenxiang would face south as sovereign;
Master Guang entered the practice of the *Anle* (Peaceful Bliss) Samādhi, and his disciples realized the gateway to samādhi;
on the banks of the Si River, Śākyamuni manifested nineteen types of physical forms.
The Venerable Wanhui traveled back and forth over more than five thousand li.

In various regions he had further alternative names; in this land, his miraculous feats were observed so extensively that it was difficult to confine him to a fixed state or to examine him for a constant form.
He arose from the ocean of vows, and his essence was originally but Zhiji.
Born from his own mind, he divided his substance;
originally a monk of Kang, he beheld the Bodhisattva’s welcoming rebirth;
with brilliant refinement, he was like the Prince of Xiang who came to receive alms in the state of Qin.
His lifespan remained unfathomable and his manifestations were without fixed pattern:

at times he propagated the transformation in several dynasties, and at times he attained a life-span of three hundred years; he caused the hearth-altar to collapse, or turned back [the Emperor] by obtaining the imperial flute;
he admonished the mountain deity with jade tablets, and peacefully rescued the Prime Minister of Tang; or he filtered [the water].
The Dragon Child arrived, sometimes carrying away the bones as he marched and entering the gates of the Holy Temple to seek out Zhuge Liang;
at times divine light issued from his mouth, or a monstrous creature sank into the river. Fenggan recognized him as Mañjuśrī, and Wuxiang spared him from his life as a bandit.
He dreamed of escorting a stupa across the sea, and divided his body within a kiln cave.
In meditative seclusion, he sometimes emitted light from his *ūrṇā-kośa*, or caused a princess to be born;
at times he obtained shimmering pearls, or tamed a fierce tiger; he recorded the names of ministers, or moved the nests of magpies.
His lifespan exceeded a hundred years, and he remained hidden on Mount Wutai. At other times he wrote in cursive script as a prophecy, or sought out an audience to hear his teachings.
Some concealed their forms yet left behind their shadows; some were born as soon as they saw their mothers;
some inscribed extraordinary words, while others spoke to roaring beasts. They recorded the passing of Lord Wei and were startled by Zhang Du’s nocturnal return.
Some crossed a stream without wetting their robes, while others constantly ate filth without discharging it; some even died standing on their heads.
Some would directly vomit up their pigeons; some had their bodies and heads separated yet remained joined together;
some sat in meditation until death for half a year and then rose again.
If enlightened by the Wheel of Dharma, they mostly assumed the form of śramaṇas.
Suppose they were manifested through miraculous traces, appearing in the guise of the old men Hanshan and Shide;
their sores were loathsome and their scabies were detestable.
At times they acted contrary to the constant flow of worldly norms, and at times they spoke with boastful exaggeration to those of inferior sort.
All these are difficult to fathom; who would say they are easy to understand?
They are merely the means by which one takes through opposition to achieve compliance, and the intent of using inverted authority to harmonize with the Way.
Someone said:
"Is this doctrine of spiritual resonance not somewhat strange?
He replied,

If one merely pursues the strange aspects of human nature, one becomes a person who deviates from the norm and turns their back on the Way!
Such strangeness cannot be fathomed by the mind, nor can its limits be proclaimed by the mouth.
This causes both immortals, spirits, and ghosts to regard it as strange—immortals become strange through their refinement and cultivation, while ghosts are strange by their very nature.
Why is it that the "strangeness" within the Buddha-dharma is different from this?
Passing through many lifetimes and kalpas, one practices in reliance upon the True Dharma; thus, the functioning within the stage of the outflow-free fruit manifests spontaneously.
To know this as strange is indeed the true strangeness—for what is called "strange" by ordinary people is called "penetration" by the sages.
Being moved by resonance, one attains penetration; thus, this chapter is titled accordingly.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"By means of the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one takes the medicine of wisdom."
"Once he has attained its power, he will then transform sentient beings.
