Compiled by Imperial Decree by the *Sāṃghika* Dharma Master Tōnghuì of Tiānshòu Monastery in the Left Ward of the Song Dynasty, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Zànníng, et al. Section Seven:

On the Relinquishment of the Body (*Yíshēn piān*). The Seventh Section on the Relinquishment of the Body contains twenty-two primary biographies and two supplementary accounts. **Biography of the Monk Sēngzàng of Fénzhōu, Tang Dynasty.** The monk Sēngzàng was a native of Xīhé.
From his tender youth, he transcended the mundane; his spirit was flourishing and his mind pure. He truly followed the path of integrity and goodness, dutifully occupying a low station.
Upon receiving the precepts and the teachings of the good, he closely guarded his sense faculties and their objects.
Whenever he saw a temple, he would invariably pay his respects; upon encountering one of great virtue, he would observe the full rites of propriety.
However, whenever he met a monk or a layperson, he would bow low and run past them, as if avoiding a high official or a magistrate.
When it came to communal affairs, he acted as an equal to the lay attendants, humbling himself even more than a servant or slave.
Upon seeing the old clothes of others, he would secretly wash and rinse them, then separately perform the mending and stitching.

When it came to the sweltering heat, he would strip off his clothes and enter the thickets, enduring the biting and sucking of mosquitoes, gadflies, horseflies, and leeches; though blood flowed like dregs of mustard seed, he bore it until his body was drenched in sweat.
He constantly recited the name of Amitābha Buddha; even those skilled in calculation could not determine the total number of times he did so.
With firm resolve and a tranquil mind, he never for a moment faltered.
When he became aware that his life was coming to an end, he said to those attending him:
"I am fortunate," the mountain monk said, "to have the devas and humans come one after another to welcome me.
Zang spoke again:

"I closed my eyes and heard that I was proceeding to the Pure Land; it was only after gathering the assembly of superior beings and scattering flowers that I returned here—this was precisely when I relinquished my life-span."
He joined his palms in prayer, recited the Buddha’s name, and passed away in peace.
This is the Biography of Chan Master Zhengshou of Hanshan Guang Temple in Tang China. As for Chan Master Zhengshou, it is unknown where he was from.
His deportment was dignified and upright, and his integrity and resolve were lofty and firm. Carrying his mendicant’s staff and trailing his alms-bag, he paid visits to various masters.

Nevertheless, as karmic conditions met and affinities converged, he found his true refuge at the gate of Chan Master Kuo of the South Pagoda, where he decisively unraveled the web of doubt and cultivated his practice in secret for his own spiritual benefit.
Later, Shoudu remained silent and lived in seclusion at Suibu Mountain Temple, where no one recognized him.

At that time, Prince Chongfu of Qiao—the second son of Emperor Zhongzong—was slandered by Empress Wei, the Dowager, at the beginning of the Shenlong era, for allegedly committing the crime of "heavy lubrication" (collaborating in illicit acts) with the brothers Zhang Yizhi and others.
He was transferred to the post of Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Junzhou—where he was placed under strict guard and forbidden from attending to official duties.
When Empress Wei presided over the court, additional soldiers were stationed to provide protection.
Upon the execution of the Wei clan and the accession of Emperor Ruizong, he was transferred to the post of Regional Inspector of Jizhou.

Although he had not yet set out on his journey, he suddenly felt a sense of unease and joylessness; thus, he turned his heart toward Master Cao and commissioned the construction of a *stūpa* for the *saṃskāra-kāya*, raising it to a height of seventy feet, which was exceedingly magnificent and grand.
At that time, Master Zao’s illness had become critical and grave. Prince Qiao sent a messenger to ask the master, "Who will succeed you in following your lofty footsteps?
Zao replied, "This poor monk has Zhengshou remaining."
The king asked the monks,
"Who is truly long-lived?
Some replied:
"The Master has a disciple named Shan Guang who dwells in the mountains, his traces hidden and his brilliance obscured.
The King sent an envoy to summon him there. Daoshou said to Master Cao, "I am delighted that Your Majesty has become my patron.
His stupa is already completed; I wish to perform a preliminary trial for him—may I do so?"
Hao said, "Excellent;
perform it for me as a trial.

At that time, Huishou adjusted his robes, joined his palms, and entered the stupa. Composing his countenance and closing his eyes, he sat in the full lotus posture and immediately entered parinirvāṇa. His entire body remained intact without dispersing, and he was thereafter known as the Master Who Tested the Stupa.
Upon hearing this, Prince Qiao sighed in admiration all day long, saying,
"Even a disciple such as I would act thus!
He then separately deliberated on a new plan and commissioned the construction of a monastery for Master Daozao.
The commentary states:
"Those who excel others must first seize their hearts; Master Shou was foremost in his sincerity.

Indeed, those who go straight forward will surely be able to come directly back. Unbound by the accumulation of karma and unconfined by the cage, having shed the tether and opened the coop, one attains freedom from birth and death.
Since he is free, he has already attained the stage of fruition!
From the perspective of conventional truth, Master Shou is the "blue" that surpasses the "green" (the student excelling his teacher).
That he can maintain his resolve and rectify his conduct, emerging ahead of his master and advancing a thousand li in a single day—is this not precisely what that means?
The Biography of Wuran of the Shanzhu Ge Cloister on Mount Wutai during the Tang Dynasty. Regarding the monk Wuran: his clan and native place are not clearly known.

He received his formal training at Mount Zhongtiao, where he lectured on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, *Hetuvidyā* (Logic), and the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*; those who were proficient followed him.
He constantly reflected:

"The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that when describing the dwelling places of the bodhisattvas, it mentions the Golden World in the northeast; since ancient times, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and ten thousand holy beings have resided therein, expounding the Dharma, sometimes manifesting as old men and sometimes as youths."

I have recently heard that Buddhapāli came from the Western Regions—tireless across the shifting sands and uncomplaining over the snow-capped peaks as he sought out sacred traces—and during the reign of Emperor Gaozong, he reached Mount Tai at Siangliang Ridge to offer prayers and prostrations; there he beheld an old man, who was none other than Mañjuśrī.

Although Li had met him in person, his doubts were not yet resolved; he was thus instructed to go to the Western Regions to retrieve the scriptures, proceed to the Vajra Cave, enter the realm of Mañjuśrī, and never return from there until this day.
"If the ancient worthies were thus, how could I possibly lack the karmic affinity?
Thus, Yan departed from that place and traveled everywhere to seek out renowned masters.
Whenever he encountered followers of the Chan school, he investigated the nature of reality and principle to the utmost.
Having occasionally attended Dharma assemblies and explored their profound mysteries,
he arrived at the Shan-zhu Pavilion of Mount Tai in the seventh year of the Zhenyuan era.
At that time, the monk Zhiyun was serving as the first *dujianjiao shousengzhang* (General Superintendent and Head Monastic Official) for the ten monasteries of Mount Tai.
He then suspended his staff and settled his mind there, vowing never to leave the mountains.
He often reflected that the realm where Mañjuśrī transforms beings is not something an ordinary person can overcome; how, then, could he afford to be indolent?
In winter he gathered firewood to provide for the community; in summer he traveled on foot; through spring and autumn he never stayed in one place, doing so for over twenty years.

In total, he visited the various terraces more than seventy times. There he beheld manifestations such as golden bridges, jeweled stupas, bells and chimes, and circular halos, the limits of which could not be fathomed.
He further said:
"Does a mouse living among the pines and cypresses know that there are fine cypress trees within the hall?
To say that there is something even superior to these various auspicious signs—my obtaining a small portion of it would not yet be sufficient."
Finally, at the eastern side of the central terrace, he suddenly saw a temple with the plaque "Fusheng" (Born of Blessings). Inside were several myriads of Indian monks.
Tanyen prostrated from head to foot before them, and they exchanged greetings of mutual comfort. Seeing that Mañjuśrī was also a monk, he said to Tanyen: "You have a karmic affinity with this place;
you must take charge of the assembly and not let it go to waste. It would be a pity to have the aspiration alone without the practice."
When he had finished speaking, the transformed temple and its assembly of monks vanished, leaving nothing to be seen.
Fayingran sighed and said,
"Beholding such spiritual wonders, how could this be in vain!"
"What permanence or solidity can there be in this fragile and precarious body?
He then followed these words by extensively increasing his offerings and almsgiving, providing for one million monks at each assembly, and burning off a finger as a mark of his commitment.
Gradually reaching five million in number, offerings arrived from both far and near like the waters of the ocean flowing into a reservoir.
When the provision of ten million had been completed, his ten fingers were entirely consumed by the flames.
During the Kaicheng era, he addressed the great assembly, saying:
"I have a slight karmic affinity with this mountain; I have traveled seventy-two times to various sacred sites that no one else has reached, and I have visited them all."
Furthermore, had I not departed from this mountain, my profound vow would have been fulfilled; what greater fortune could there be!

Alas, I am now aged and infirm, seventy-four years of age and fifty-five years since my ordination. While I still draw this final breath, I wish to burn a single incense stick atop the summit of the Central Terrace to bid farewell to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the ten thousand Bodhisattvas.
"Or if my death brings me peace, who would willingly take my place?

Furthermore, all of you are disciples of the Bodhisattva and members of the Dragon King's retinue; having planted the seeds of goodness, you have come to dwell on this mountain. You have been diligent day and night, restraining the three karmas, and have made a solemn pact to meet together at the three assemblies of the Dragon Flower."
"At this time, as you descend the mountain, may there be no obstacles.
Joining his palms, he said, "Farewell," and departed.
At first, the assembly did not understand his meaning and all said, "May you return early."

Ran simply carried his flask and staff and burned only famous incense; he then ordered Zhao Hua of the Ji clan to bring two ends of waxed cloth, a bundle of coarse hemp, and one *dou* of fragrant liquid. From dawn until dusk atop the central terrace, he prostrated and burned incense without ceasing for even a moment, abstaining entirely from food and drink, reciting the Buddha’s name with such devotion that his voice never faltered.

By the time it was already deep into the night, Lady Zhao wondered at the reason for this; she climbed the steep heights and saw that the Dyeing Master had not moved from his former spot, but was instead becoming even more focused and diligent.
The Dyeing Master said to Zhao, "I have a secret vow; you must provide me with supporting conditions and must not obstruct me."
"I shall take waxed cloth, hemp, and oil to wrap around my body, so that at the hour of midnight, I may offer this burning of my body as an offering to all the Buddhas."
"If I attain the Way, I shall deliver you.
Zhao Shi remonstrated with him, urging him earnestly to desist, but he would not stop.
He then wrapped his body in cloth, donned hempen garments, doused them with oil, and set fire to the crown of his head, saying:
"I must have my ashes and bones scattered so that no extraordinary signs remain.
Zhao Shi followed his command exactly without the slightest deviation; she began the cremation from the crown of his head, and it was only when she reached his feet that the body collapsed.
Lady Zhao sighed and said, "In the past I heard of the Medicine King who burned his body; now I see this venerable one before me—how marvelous!
How tragic!"
Later, his disciples collected his true remains and erected a stupa on the southern slope of Mount Brahmarṣi, which remains there to this day.
Biography of Shi Dinglan of Fugan Temple in Chengdu Prefecture, Tang Dynasty. Shi Dinglan, surnamed Yang, was a native of Chengdu.

Originally belonging to the class of violent butchers and wine-sellers in the marketplace, Heaven bestowed this nature upon me; repenting of my past transgressions, I vowed to join the Six Harmonies and spread transformation throughout the Three Shu regions.
At that time, all turned to him with faith and built a monastery, naming it Shengshou (Holy Longevity).
The circumstances for its founding had not yet been revealed; thus, it was concealed among the common laborers.
Her parents had died young, leaving her with no means to perform funeral rites for them.

Whenever she encountered the anniversary of their deaths, Lan would weep until she was choked with grief; she would then strip naked and enter Mount Qingcheng, allowing mosquitoes, gnats, fleas, and flies to bite and suck at her skin and body, saying, "I sacrifice my internal wealth to repay their labors."
"In Shu there are black and white moles, shaped like grains of millet, which bite people's mouths and flesh, yet they are rarely seen.

Next, they would draw blood to transcribe scriptures; later, they would roast their arms; and finally, they would pluck out their ears, gouge out their eyes, and feed them to birds of prey and fierce beasts."
Thereafter, as he walked, he could not avoid stumbling against objects unless assisted by a guide.
Later, a strange man appeared, holding up an object like a pearl between his palms; it vanished into the hollow of his eye, yet for a moment his vision remained as it had been before.
A voice from the underworld announced:
"The Heavenly King of the South has returned the master's eyeballs.
People near and far were struck with terror.
He often said to others:
"I have heard that in the *Śīla-samvara-sūtra* there is what is called the 'Unsurpassed Gift. I vow to practice it diligently, so as to swiftly attain the supreme fruit."

In the third year of the Dazhong era, Emperor Xuanzong issued an imperial decree for him to enter the palace for offerings; out of reverence for his spiritual responses, the Emperor treated him with exceptional courtesy.
His disciple Yuanheng attended to him at his side, constantly performing services.
In the second month of the sixth year, he further vowed to set his shoulders and upper arms ablaze.
Although the Emperor repeatedly exhorted him, urging that he was advanced in years and should instead focus on long-term cultivation, Hui-lan did not obey the imperial decree;
he subsequently set himself on fire and passed away.

There were those who requested that his name be changed and a stupa be erected for him; by imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Juexing (Awakened Nature), and his stupa was named Wuzhen (Realization of Truth).
In the capital of Shu, it is simply called the Dinglan Stupa Monastery, and its incense offerings and lamps have continued without interruption to this day.
Biography of Hongxiu of Jianfu Monastery on Mount Huangbo in Fuzhou, Tang Dynasty. Transmitted by Jingxian. The monk Hongxiu was a man of unknown origins.
His divine countenance was preeminent and his profound mechanisms were subtly operative; residing at Huangbo Mountain Temple in Min, he gathered a multitude of monastics.
Beyond his formal teachings, he was dignified and full of joy.
He constantly said:
"Past debts must be repaid; once they are fully repaid, what cause for worry or fear is there?
Both things and self will be at ease."
No one understood his intent.

During the period of the Guangming era, when the rebels of Chao were rampant, Huixiu went outside the monastery, removed his inner robe, and placed it upon a stone sounding block beneath a pine tree, saying:
"I swear not to defile this pure ground."
He remained composed, extending his neck to await the blade; yet when the blade fell, there was no blood. The bandit was struck with astonishment and prostrated himself in repentance.
His disciple Jingxian performed the cremation of the master’s remains and collected seven śarīra relics, which he enshrined in a casket as precious treasures.
There was a person of deep faith who attempted to exchange them for beans at the same rate, but he could not catch up; he then went to consult a diviner, who interpreted the omen, saying:
"Matters of life and death, or nobility and meanness—none of these can be distinguished within my hexagram."
"To be worn out and to lose it, to lose peace and to lose it—how could anyone have known this would happen?
Subsequently, he obtained [the relic] and placed it within a stupa; he divided it into seven grains and sealed them inside a lapis lazuli vessel, which shone with a brilliant luster.
At that time, Sengqinghuo composed a prose work and verses to commemorate his virtues.
Biography of Shi Quanhuo of Yantou Monastery in Ezhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Quanhuo’s secular surname was Ke; he was a native of Quanzhou.
From his youth, he was exceptionally gifted; his capacity and temperament were vast and profound, yet he was simple and unpretentious.
He took Master Qingyuan Yi as his teacher.
Traveling to Chang’an, he visited Ximing Monastery, where Master Zhao conferred the full ordination upon him.

He immediately went to Baoshou Temple on the Left Street to study the sutras and vinaya, resolving their essential principles; as he was about to begin his teaching career, he struck his mendicant’s staff and headed south to Wuling Deshan.
The medicine and the disease corresponded perfectly, leaving no further doubt or obstruction.
Later, he settled in the vicinity of Dongting; the place was called Wolong, where he built a dwelling and took up residence.
His followers followed him like shadows.
He later resided on Mount Tangnian; there was a jagged stone cliff on the mountain, and he established a monastery there, naming it Yantou (Cliff Head).
In all his practices and applications, he pared away the superfluous and grasped the essential. Sitting upright and motionless, he allowed the multitude to surround him at will, saying:
"Why do you not reflect upon this?

How many affairs are there within a household! Yet, those who have truly realized the sign of transcendence amidst circumstances of both adversity and favor—since Huo Zhi began his career, the Central Plains have been embroiled in many troubles, with feudal lords rising up like pillars and mad rebels coming to plunder; everyone else has fled in avoidance, yet Huo alone remained composed and at ease."
The bandits rebuked him for not providing provisions and, in a fit of rage, ordered him to be struck with blades; yet he showed no sign of fear.
This occurred on the eighth day of the fourth month of summer in the year Dingwei of the Guangqi era.
His disciples enshrined him for burial; after the interment, his remains were collected and cremated, yielding seventy-seven *śarīra* relics.
Emperor Xizong bestowed upon him the posthumous title Qingyan (Pure and Austere), and the stupa was named Chuchen (Transcending the World).

Regarding the funeral arrangements, the lay patrons, the brothers Tian Yong and others, provided the funds for the construction. Shi Xuantai of Nanyue composed an inscription to commemorate his virtues.
His teachings were lofty and formidable; at that time he was known as the "Yantou Way," and it was said that few could grasp its profound meaning.
The commentary says:
Why did the two masters, Xiu and Huo, not seek to avoid their peril when faced with it?
Tong said:
"What is difficult for ordinary beings is easy for Bodhisattvas.
Having undergone successive births and repeatedly cast them off, why lament?
In the past, An Shigao repeatedly paid back his debts, departing from them as if brushing away dust."
Once the burden of karma is lightened, the suffering associated with the physical body ceases, and one merely exchanges it for a solid, adamantine body.

Even among the immortals, those who meet their end by the blade are said to have attained "sword-liberation" (jiànjiè); how much more so for those who have correctly cultivated and realized the fruits of the path?
"By the principle of relative dependence, one must not fail to act; otherwise, one will ultimately be a cause for shame.

Biography of Yuanhui of Fayongwang Temple in Jiaxing, Wu Commandery, Tang Dynasty. Shi Yuanhui’s secular surname was Lu; he was a descendant of Lu Ji, the Interior Historian of Pingyuan during the Jin dynasty.
His father was Dan, a Wénlínlang and Yúnqíwèi serving as the Judicial Official of Wēnzhōu; Huì was his second son.
From childhood he was precocious and intelligent, and as he grew up, he became refined and gentle; fearing the fate of a withered tortoise, he aspired to be like a slender wild goose.
In the second year of the Kaicheng era, he took leave of his parents and became a disciple under Qingjin at Fakkongwang Temple.
In the first year of the Huichang era, he went to Hengyang to receive the full precepts and began his formal study of the Vinaya.
He entered Mount Wutai to pay his respects and continued to observe various auspicious omens.

In the second year, he returned to Jiahe for a period of rest and resided at Jianxing Monastery. There, he resolved to maintain the "Three White Dharmas" and recited the five classes of Maṇḍala scriptures, burning incense-sticks upon his own arm.
In the fifth year [of the Kaiyuan era], he was subject to the general purge of monastics and temporarily concealed himself as a layman.
At the beginning of the Dazhong era, he returned to the Dharma-gate.
In the seventh year, he reconstructed Fawang Monastery.
Furthermore, he burned incense upon his arm as an offering to the Buddha’s tooth relic at Ba’en Mountain.
He then proceeded to Mount Tiantai and crossed the Stone Bridge; his purpose was clearly directed, and he encountered no significant anxieties or perils.
During the Xiántóng era, he accompanied the finger-bone śarīra of the Buddha as it was being sent to Chóngzhēn Temple in Fèngxiáng.
He then set fire to his left thumb while reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* aloud; within less than a month, the finger grew back as it had been before.
In the third year of the Qianning era, he happened to fall ill.
On the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month, he entered nirvana at Zunseng Monastery; his reported age was seventy-eight, and his years as a monk were fifty-eight.
The disciples Duan, Su, and others reverently enshrined his seat and buried it between the regions of Wu and Kuaiji, referring to him as the "Three-White Bhikṣu.
As for his prostrations, recitations, and upholding of the teachings, they were beyond counting, as recorded in the separate register.
The commentary states:
When the thumb is incinerated until the fire is spent and the ashes fly away, how can bone and flesh subsequently arise from the remains of the charred carbon, restored as before in no long time?
This is like a lotus flower growing in fire; they are of the same kind, yet differ in their manifestations.
What are the "three whites"? He replied:
"There are two kinds of practice:
first, the physical matter, which consists of white rice, water, and white salt;
second, the principle, which consists of the body not touching [objects] everywhere, the mouth reciting the true sutras, and the mind not following false conditions."
"These three were clearly virtuous and not of black karma;
is this why they enjoy such fame?
The Biography of Master Shucao of Puzhao Temple in Jingzhao, Tang Dynasty. Regarding the monk Shucao: one day he arrived at Puzhao Temple within the Pingkang Ward of Jingzhao.

He often carried a bundle of straw mats and sat or slept beneath the two corridors, taking no pleasure in staying in rooms or quarters; some say this was the practice of a *dhūta*.

That evening, he consequently set his body ablaze with bundles of hemp. By dawn, there was nothing but ashes and embers; moreover, no skeletal remains were left, and the foul odor of the filth had almost entirely vanished, nor was there any sound of fire spreading or of people crying out in alarm.
Calculating his youth, it was impossible that he could have burned this entire body;
yet, since nothing remained, it was evident that he had ignited the fire of samādhi to burn himself.
The multitude all offered praise, and many people came to observe the ceremony.

The lay devotees of the capital subsequently molded his ashes into the form of a monk and placed it beside the Buddha hall; he was popularly known as Master "Straw-Bundle," and his prayers were frequently answered.
The commentary states:

In the *Womb Sutra* (*Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*), it is said that when a Bodhisattva, through meditative concentration, restrains the mind and enters the *tejodhātu-samādhi*, deluded sentient beings claim that the Bodhisattva has been consumed by the fires of the kalpa; this refers to that very instance.
The bhikṣu has not yet reached this state; there is nothing here to delude people.
If he were able to burn a massive carcass with a small amount of straw, then he could be believed!
Therefore, the Book says:
"The people must not deceive one another with falsehoods and illusions.
How lamentable!
The Biography of Xingming of the Hermitage on Mount Nanyue during the Tang Dynasty. Shi Xingming, whose secular surname was Lu, was a native of Changzhou in Wu Commandery.
In his youth, he followed a teacher in his native region; later, he traveled afar to seek the Way. Yet, he was upright and dignified, living in carefree independence with a spirit of lofty disdain.

Initially, he visited Mount Wutai and Mount Emei, where he paid homage to the two world-transcending Bodhisattvas, Suvarṇavarṇa and Rūpyavarṇa, both of whom manifested before him in accordance with his mind.
From there, he ascended Mount Tiantai, climbed Mount Luofu, entered Mount Heng, and traveled through Zizhong.
This occurred during the late Tang dynasty, when the regions around Xiang were fragmented; they vied for territory over mere paces without ceasing, and there was not a single peaceful year.
Thereupon, he settled at the foot of Mount Zhurong with the intention of remaining there for the rest of his life.
He stayed at the Seven Treasures Terrace and formed a close bond of friendship with Xuantai and Buna.
Regarding their respective temperaments—whether they were fond of or averse to things—Xuantai likewise never opposed them, nor did he weigh their preferences against his own.
He once said to his dharma friends:
"I do not wish to follow Sengya by being burned in a wooden tower, nor do I desire to become like Qu Yuan, who was buried within the belly of a fish."
"I vow that in the end I shall cast away my body; should one not strive to emulate Prince Sattva, who attained the fruit of sainthood after many kalpas?
He spoke these words repeatedly, yet [the king] did not believe him at all.
Suddenly, amidst the thickets, he cast himself before a roaring tiger; they vied with one another to devour him until, in a brief moment, his flesh was exhausted.
At that time, Master Tai collected his remaining bones and cremated them, obtaining śarīras.
He then gathered flowers and drew water, composing a text to offer as a sacrifice.

In his words, he clarified that [the deceased] was courageous and capable of renouncing internal wealth, thereby shattering the dharma of stinginess and perfecting the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). Through the three spheres—those not yet relinquished, those already relinquished, and those to be relinquished—all being suddenly empty, he attained the great fruit as easily as if picking up a blade of grass from the ground.
The commentary states:
The Buddha commanded the bhikṣus to bestow food upon sentient beings; this brings benefit and harmony in both worlds, and the resulting karmic fruit is not slight.
If you, O Illustrious One, fulfill the great perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), you will distance yourself from stinginess and greed.
One achieves great valor and attains fearlessness;
one achieves the emptiness of the three wheels, which is the merit of the unconditioned;
and one achieves the mind that renounces with difficulty, thereby purifying the Buddha-lands.

To cast away one’s body—how vast is its benefit! Is this not what is meant by saying that a skillful rewarder achieves great encouragement with little expense? This is precisely it! Her father engaged in trade, exchanging goods for profit;
her mother once dreamed of a person dressed in magnificent attire who claimed to be seeking lodging for the night, and she subsequently conceived.
From birth he possessed extraordinary qualities, being unlike his peers as a child.
Whenever he heard the sound of bells and chanting, he would concentrate his mind and listen intently.
At the age of twelve, he dreamed of a magnificent golden man who led him into a secluded hermitage.
At dawn the following day, he informed his parents of his intention to leave the household life to become a monk.
Before they had granted their permission, he wept and refused to eat.
His parents, moved by his natural sincerity and unable to suppress their feelings of compassion, finally yielded to his wishes.
He immediately retired to the Caotang Monastery to study under his teacher, reciting the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* and the *Bodhisattva Precepts* until dawn without sleep.
After nearly one year, he had abandoned his original texts and attained thorough mastery through oral recitation.
At the age of seventeen, he was permitted to attend the lecture series on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, gaining a general understanding of its major principles.

By the time he reached his early twenties, he had perfected the highest grade of ordination; he upheld the monastic rules and precepts with such integrity that there was never any deficiency in his conduct.
At the age of twenty-three, his mastery of literary meaning was thorough; he received the transmission of the *Shengji* from Dharma Master Zonggan at Chongfu Monastery.
He further studied *Hetuvidyā* (Logic) and *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only), expounding them without deficiency, such that several of his disciples emerged as exceptionally brilliant scholars.
Dashi Biancai of Chongfu Temple was his most eminent disciple.

In the second year of the Tianyou era, when the Li clan had seized control of Hedong, Emperor Wu invited him to reside at the Jingtu Cloister of Dajian Temple, where he provided him with the four requisites of monastic life.

He devoted himself exclusively to studying the teachings of the Tripiṭaka and cultivated meritorious karma for rebirth in the higher realms. He established five successive assemblies of the Great Unrestricted Fast (Amogha-pūjā).
On one occasion, he offered his own body as food to wolves and tigers; when he entered the mountain valleys, the beasts would sniff near him and then flee.
Furthermore, he lived naked among the thickets and forests, feeding on mosquitoes and gadflies.
He then traveled to Xianyan Yuesi Temple to cultivate the Way and settle his spirit.
Having completed a full reading of the Great Tripitaka, he established a vegetarian feast and burned off one finger as an act of merit and celebration.
In that monastery there was a sacred image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, for which seven lamps were perpetually lit and offerings of incense and flowers were presented.
Later, he was invited by several students to descend to the city, where he propagated the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra; its exposition continued without interruption throughout the four seasons.
Every month, they established bathing rites by the rivers and marshes to feed aquatic creatures;
using their own offerings (*dakṣiṇā*), they immediately ransomed feathers and down—submerging themselves in the profound and ascending toward the lofty—to fulfill the nature of life.
He sometimes provided food for those in prison, or bestowed relief upon the poor and destitute; he also donated banners and canopies to the Jingming and Jincang pagodas.

In the second year of the Changxing era of the Later Tang dynasty, the assembly requested that a Three-College Academy be established behind Dajian Guosi Temple to provide for the listeners from the four quarters.
At that time, he also lectured on the new translation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, transmitting it to Dharma Master Jihui of Chongfu Temple.

Consequently, for three years he did not step outside the temple gates; for every single character of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* he performed one prostration, and for every character of the *Mahābuddhanāmasaṃgīti Sūtra*, totaling one hundred and twenty fascicles, he likewise performed a prostration.
He further refined one finger, so that in total all five fingers were thus treated.
At that time, the Jin Gaozu was in seclusion at Jinyang and held him in the highest esteem.

Upon his ascension to the throne, whenever [the Master] entered the capital of Luoyang for audience, the Emperor invariably invited him into the inner palace for leisurely conversation and bestowed upon him very generous gifts.
The Emperor bestowed upon him purple robes and a posthumous title, but he firmly declined them before finally accepting.

Having heard rumors that the Dharma Gate Monastery in Fengxiang possessed the true body of a finger bone of the Buddha, he took leave of the Emperor and traveled to Qiyang to pay his respects; beholding its extraordinary wonder, he further burned one of his own fingers as an offering.
Chen’s two hands were reduced to only two fingers.
Continuing at Tiantzhusi, he studied the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* under Master Chulun.

After only a few days, he fell slightly ill; on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month, at the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.), he passed away while resting his head upon his arm. He was sixty-three years of age and forty-four years since his ordination.
In his daily life, he wore only coarse cloth and did not store away surplus garments.
He performed the six-period prostrations to the Buddha without ever failing even once.

When news of his passing reached the region of Longdi, both the monastic and lay communities (the "black" and "white" assemblies) assembled with full ceremonial decorum to escort him to the cremation site, where several hundred grains of śarīra were obtained.
The disciples returned the sacred relics to Taiyuan; by imperial decree of the Jin dynasty, they were enshrined on the western mountains of Jin Water, where the small stupa remains to this day.
The verse states:
When Master Chen relinquished his life, how could it have surpassed his own diligent perseverance?
Having cast off superficial glory, how could it surpass its own profound understanding?
If this were so, it could not be designated by a single name.
It is like the *campaka* flower: its color is yellow and beautiful, yet true gold puts its hue to shame.
When its fragrance wafts far and wide, even the ox-head sandalwood feels abashed by its scent.
That many names arise from a single substance—is this not the "Dust of the Public" (Chen Gong)!

Biography of Dao Yu of Pingtian Monastery on Mount Tiantai during the Jin Dynasty. Dao Yu, whose secular surname was from the kingdom of Silla, was a man of that land; his ancestral clan name is not clearly recorded.
Since the year of Renzi in the Jingfu era of the Tang dynasty, he traveled to Tiantai, where he lingered and hung up his monk’s staff within the assembly hall of Pingtian Temple.
He received others with loving-kindness, yet he ultimately never abandoned the dialect of the islanders.

He constantly carried a single almsbowl to receive food; having finished eating, he would practice brief walking meditation and remain in constant sitting posture, never letting his side touch the mat.
At midday, he swept the halls and corridors and attended to the monastery’s permanent assets.
When he obtained leftover or surplus food—even if its appearance was poor or its aroma had changed—he would collect it in a vessel and eat it himself during his mealtime.

He provided the monastic community with supplies for bathing and boiled tea. Whenever he encountered wriggling insects within firewood, he would set it aside in a remote location; his commitment to protecting living beings was exceptionally earnest.
All that he wore were garments of coarse cloth, so heavy they were difficult to carry.

At the beginning of summer and the end of autumn, at midday, they would expose their chests, backs, thighs, and calves, saying they were feeding mosquitoes, gnats, horseflies, leeches, and various other insects; these would bite and sting them until blood flowed upon the ground.
He practiced in this manner for over forty years without ever neglecting it for even a moment.
Whenever he met with guests, he would say nothing more than the two syllables "yi yi," as he was entirely unable to understand the Chinese language.
Yet he understood people's intentions without fail.
His topknot was white with age, and his eyebrows were likewise gray.
From his body issued *śarīra* relics of a deep blue-red hue, like pearl-like grains; whenever anyone sought them, they obtained them at will.

On the tenth day of the tenth month in the third year of the Tiānfú era of the Jìn dynasty, the year Wùxū (938 CE), he passed away in the Sanghārāma. It is estimated that he was over eighty years of age.
The monks carried him up the mountain and cremated him; from the ashes, they recovered śarīras in numbers beyond counting.
Some even obtained giant bones.

In the second year of the Qingtai era of the Later Tang dynasty, he once traveled to Shiliang; upon his return, he stayed overnight in the hall with Yù. It was a spring evening, and they were warming themselves by burning firewood logs, making a constant crackling sound that did not cease throughout the night.
It is said that whenever there was a great vegetarian feast (dazhai) for making offerings to the arhats, Sengyu would not eat.
When people saw him being welcomed during the procession for the arhats, they asked:
"Why do you not go inside the hall to receive the offerings?"
He would say aloud, "I-i go," or "Feed the insects.
At times, when a pack of tigers smelled him, they would circle around and depart.
Biography of Jingchao of Xiangji Hermitage on Mount Lu in Jiangzhou during the Jin Dynasty: Shi Jingchao was a man of unknown origins.
He had long maintained the precepts as if guarding a life-preserving float;
his nature was upright and sincere, and he would not speak with sycophancy.
When he traveled abroad on foot and sought out excellent locations for his dwelling, upon reaching Mount Lu, he conceived the intention to settle there and cease his wandering.
He devoted himself exclusively to reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*, making it his constant practice.
Many people of the Nine Rivers looked up to him with admiration.

He once performed prostrations for each character while venerating the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; having completed two full recitations in this manner, he burned one of his fingers as an offering of light to celebrate the completion of his veneration of the scripture.
Next, he prostrated before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as before.

From within his skin, śarīras emerged in a shimmering array—lofty, round, and lustrous. Whenever there were seekers, they gathered them by the hundreds and thousands from his seat, the floor, and the ground.
He passed away in his hermitage during the Tianfu era.
His tomb and stupa now stand upon Mount Lu; visitors pay their respects there, sighing in admiration and lamentation.
The colophon says:
To speak of "casting off the body" necessarily implies the total abandonment of one's entire physical frame, as was the case with Prince Sattva.
Now, using a finger as a lamp and holding a wick upon an arm—how does this compare to that precedent? Is it not a matter of exceeding good fortune?
Tong said,
"To cauterize one's fingers or sever one's arm is an ascetic practice for the relinquishment of the body.
How much more difficult is this to accomplish during the Age of Dharma Decline!"
"This is like maintaining a small measure of integrity; he may be included among the 'Biographies of Exemplary Administrators' (*xunli zhuan*).
The Biography of Shi Zhitong from the *Fengxiang Fu Famen Si Zhi* of the Jin Dynasty: Shi Zhitong’s secular surname was Zhang; he was the son of a prominent family from Youfufeng.

Had I known earlier that he would transcend the world and be able to devote himself to the Pure Gate, I would have selected a renowned master for him to serve as his teacher, so that he might attain the highest grade of rebirth; thus, throughout the lecture halls of all regions, he would have applied himself with thorough diligence.
During the final years of the Later Tang dynasty, warfare followed one after another, from which time the imperial carriage had already toured to the east.
While traveling briefly in Luoyang, he encountered the Tripiṭaka Master Vajra, who was practicing the teachings of Yoga; he paid his respects and studied under him.
He then wished to ascend Mount Tiantai and Mount Luofu, and so took his leave.
The Tripitaka Master said,
"I have come here seeking to translate scriptures because the Central Plains are currently embroiled in many affairs."
The Prince deliberated on the southern expedition, asking, "How can we proceed when the roads are blocked? Tong replied,
"If we cross the Celestial Moat by water, what can they do to us?"

The Tripitaka Master said, "If you go to the regions of Wu and Kuaiji, you may entrust these Sanskrit manuscripts to them; perhaps through favorable conditions they will be transmitted and translated.
Daotong replied:
"I have received your command.
In the fourth year of the Tianfu era, the year of Jihai, the Heavenly King bestowed an edict upon the Wuyue Kingdom; he then boarded a sea vessel and reached the region of Zhejiang.

At that time, the Wenmu Emperor of the Qian family, in accordance with the protocols of the imperial court, prepared ceremonial regalia and musical troupes to welcome [the relics] into the palace courtyard for veneration. They were enshrined within the Zhenshen Pagoda Temple, where they were provided with abundant offerings and generous gifts.
He was invited to travel to Mount Tiantai.
Thereupon, he ascended Mount Chicheng and climbed to the summit of Mount Huading; subsequently, he hung his staff at the Dharma-seat of the Venerable Zhiyi.

Upon reading the *Record of Miraculous Auspiciousness in the Western Pure Land*, he transformed his conduct and turned his mind, vowing to be reborn in that land; henceforth, he never sat with his back to the west.
In the mountains there is a "Waving Hand Stone. Formerly, Zhiyi dreamed that upon this stone was a monk standing by the sea, raising his hand as if beckoning him.
When Zhiyi entered Tiantai, he saw that monk, whose name was Dingguang; his earlobes were so prominent they rose above his crown—he was a divine monk of unfathomable mystery.
They met one another, and [the Emperor] asked Huiyi,
"Do you still remember my invitation?
Huiyi replied:
“Yes. This rock rises steeply, and looking down, there is no ground beneath.
One may ascend it and cast oneself off, vowing to be swiftly reborn in the Pure Land.

He threw himself from his body and fell into the midst of a large tree; its branches were supple and its trunk was yielding, as if someone had caught him, so that he suffered not the slightest injury.
He then struck the gourd again and threw it, which fell onto thick, lush grass at the foot of a cliff; it sustained a slight wound, but after a long time, he revived.

The assembly of monks believed he had been devoured by wild beasts or tigers; however, seeing that his body was still bloated and swollen, they carried him back to the original site of the Dharma hall.

Initially, when he first departed, he did not inform the assembly, so they dispatched people along various routes to search for him. Upon reaching Luoxi, there was a village diviner whose prognostications were frequently accurate, so someone went to consult him.

The deity said, "That monk is in the southwest, currently protected by the Golden Armor Deity so that he does not die; when I arrived there, my vital energy was exhausted, and it is truly difficult to approach him."
All these events accorded perfectly with the divine words.

Later, he went to Fahua Mountain in Yuezhou to silently cultivate pure karma. As he was about to pass away, a white substance grew on the floor of the room where he stayed, appearing like a coating of powdered pigment.

Not long after, he passed away while seated upon his meditation couch. When his body was moved for cremation, five-colored smoke covered the crown of his head, and a wondrous fragrance was smelled by all throughout Mount Fahua.
The commentary states:
In the past, Bakula possessed five instances of non-death; now, Master Tong possesses two instances of non-death.
In the past, Fachong threw himself from the Thousand-Fathom Incense Burner Peak and did not perish; Tong’s case is likewise.
Was it not because the non-deva dragon carried him on its wings that not even a single hair was harmed?
And why was he able to prolong his life, maintaining his physical form and mind until they were severed?
It was merely to enable him to further cultivate the practices for the Pure Land.
The Biography of Shi Daozhou of Yongfu Monastery in Lingwu, Shuofang, Jin. Shi Daozhou, surnamed Guan, was a native of Huile in Shuofang.

From his childhood, he was intelligent and refined, possessing proper decorum in the Confucian schools; although he recited the *Shijing* and *Shujing*, he delighted in hearing the Buddhist scriptures and resolved to leave the household life at the Peacock King Temple (Kongquewang Yuan) of Longxing Monastery.
Thereupon, he attained the pearl of the precepts and gradually perfected the moon of his mind; his chanting and hymns were so resonant they were worth hearing.
He then led lay devotees to establish Yongxing Temple, completing the work without seeking to be its master.

He took leave of the Generalissimo Han Gongzhu and entered the White Grass Valley of Mount Helan, where he established a retreat for recitation and contemplation; moved by his devotion, a dried-up spring surged forth once more, and a numinous serpent swam within its waters—thereupon, he ascended the Dharma Platform to preach and lecture.

Monastics and laypeople gathered like swarms of bees, and offerings of alms accumulated like mountains; the resonance of their hymns and chants could arrest the drifting clouds, while the transformation of the wild and fierce was like that of the *chīxiāo* bird changing its cry.
He then drew blood to paint an image of the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara.
Whenever a period of extreme drought occurred, he would abstain from food and close his eyes, vowing that only after rain had been brought forth would he consider filling his belly.

In the second year of the Zhonghe era, hearing that the region around the capital was in turmoil, he severed his left arm at the base of the stupa in the Nianding Yuan south of the city and burned it as an offering to the Great Compassionate One (Avalokiteśvara), praying: "I vow that weapons shall be laid aside, and that peace shall soon prevail throughout the Central Plains and the northern frontiers."
Having finished speaking, a sudden clap of thunder and a fierce wind were followed by a torrential downpour.
On another occasion, he cut off his left ear to pray for rain for the people, and again fasted for seven days to petition for snow; in both instances, his wishes were fulfilled.
As for the frontier tribes, there were none who did not stand in awe and reverence.

On the sixth day of the second month in the year of Xinchou, the sixth year of Tianfu, before midnight had passed, he sat in the full lotus posture; having finished his final instructions to his disciples, he passed away, having reached the age of seventy-eight.
The remains did not decompose, as if he were still in meditative absorption; consequently, they were enshrined in lacquered silk.

The Biographies of Twenty-One Monks, with Three Additional Figures Included. Biography of Xingjian of the Sui Dynasty. The monk Xingjian was of unknown origin. He constantly practiced meditative contemplation (*dhyāna-vipaśyanā*) and maintained the most rigorous integrity. Once, while traveling eastward, his path led him to Mount Tai. As the sun was setting, he entered a temple on the mountain to seek lodging for the night.
The magistrate issued an order, saying:
"There is no separate lodging here; it can only be under the corridors of the shrine hall.
However, those who come to stay as guests will inevitably meet with the calamity of a violent death."
"Let my teacher deliberate upon it.
Fu Jian said,
"Do not worry."
Having no choice but to comply, he spread out a mat beneath the eaves.
As Sengjian sat upright in meditation reciting the sutras, after about one watch of the night, he heard the sound of a ring of ghosts within the house.
After a short while, the spirit emerged; his robes and cap were most magnificent, and his retinue was resplendent.
He joined his palms toward Sengjian, who said, "I have heard that many who stay here die; could it be that you, O Dānapati, are harming them?"
The deity said, "The one who encountered death arrived specifically here; hearing the voice of your disciple, he died of his own accord. It was not that I killed him.
May you, Master, have no cause for concern."
Jiangu invited him to sit and they conversed for about the duration of a meal. Then he asked him:
"It is commonly said that Mount Tai governs the ghosts; is this indeed so?"
The spirit said,
“It is true that this disciple has meager merit.
Do you wish to see those who have passed away?”
Jian said, "There are two fellow monks who have already died; I wish to see them.
The spirit asked for their names, and he replied:
"One person has already been born among humans;
the other is undergoing retribution in hell and cannot be summoned here. You must go to him, and you shall see him.
Upon hearing this, King Jian was greatly delighted. He rose and went out, and before long he arrived at a certain place where he saw the flames of hell burning with intense ferocity.

The messenger led Sengqian into the inner courtyard of the wall, where he saw from afar a person amidst the flames crying out, unable to speak; his form had been transformed beyond recognition, and the stench of scorched flesh and blood was heart-rending.
Jian could not bear to watch this for long; moved by compassion, he sought an opportunity to escape.
Suddenly, beneath the eaves of the temple hall, he found himself sitting with the deity as before.
Jian asked:
"If I wish to save my fellow student, is there a principle by which this may be achieved?
The spirit said, "It can be done;
if you can transcribe the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he will surely be able to escape."
Soon after, as dawn approached, the deity took leave of the monk and entered the hall.
At daybreak, the temple official saw that Sengjian was not dead and marveled at this strange occurrence.
After Sengjian departed, he hurriedly reported his previous vow; once the copying and painting of the sutras were complete, he brought them with him and stayed overnight at the temple.
The deity emerged as before; he joyfully prostrated himself, inquired about the purpose of the visit, and informed him of the matter.
The deity said, "I, your disciple, already know."
The Master was copying a scripture when he had only just written the title; the man had already escaped and was now born among humans.
However, this place is impure and unsuitable for housing a scripture; I pray that you, Master, will take it back and deposit it within the temple.
Having spoken thus, at the break of dawn he took his leave and departed; this was during the Daye era.
Sengjian’s dwelling place was not constant, and no one knew his ultimate end.

Biography of Shi Chongzheng of Chongfu Monastery in Taoyuan Prefecture, Tang Dynasty. Shi Chongzheng, surnamed Hou, was a native of this very prefecture.
