Whenever a great flood occurred, the temple buildings were all submerged, yet his monastery suffered no harm, as if there had been no inundation at all.
All such extraordinary manifestations were like this.
The Biography of Shao Kang of the Pure Land Practice Center at Mount Wolong in Muzhou during the Tang Dynasty. Shao Kang, whose secular surname was Zhou, was a native of Xindu Mountain in Jingyun.
Lady Mulu dreamed that she traveled to Dinghu Peak, where she encountered a jade maiden who presented her with a blue lotus and said:
"This flower is auspicious; I entrust it to you. You shall later give birth to a noble son; you must cherish and protect it!"
On the day he was born, a blue light filled the room and a fragrance like that of a lotus pervaded it.

By the time he reached the age of infancy, his eyes were azure and his lips were vermilion; he possessed one of the marks of a Buddha—his teeth—and he constantly sat upright with a smile upon his face.
At that time, a man from the village who was skilled in physiognomy observed him and said:
"This child possesses the talent of a high minister or a sovereign; had he spoken, I would not have known this.
When he was only seven years old, his mother carried him into Lingshan Temple to pay homage to the sacred countenance on the Buddha's birthday. His mother asked Kang:
"Do you recognize me?
he suddenly spoke, saying,
"Śākyamuni Buddha."
Upon hearing this, everyone marveled at it—for he had been mute since birth.
Consequently, his parents allowed him to leave the household life.
At the age of fifteen, he had already completed five sections of the sūtras; he received the full precepts at Jiexiang Temple in Yuezhou and subsequently went to Yi Temple to study the Vinaya.
After five summers, he went to Longxing Temple in Shangyuan to study the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era, while at the hall of Baima Temple in the capital Luoyang, he saw an object emitting light; upon investigating what scripture or dharma it was, he discovered it was Shan Dao’s "Text for Guiding Others toward the Western Land."
Kang saw this and was filled with joy; he made a vow, saying:
"If I am destined for the Pure Land, may this light reappear upon these scrolls!
No sooner had his oath ended than the scrolls indeed flashed again, within which appeared countless transformed Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
He then went to the Shadow Hall of Shandao in Chang’an and prayed there.
He beheld the true image of Shandao transform into the body of a Buddha, who said to Kang:
"If you follow my instructions to benefit and bring joy to sentient beings, we shall be reborn together in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing."

Seng-kang, as if he had attained some realization, traveled south to Guoyuan Temple in Jiangling, where he encountered a Dharma Master who said to him, "If you wish to transform others, go directly to Xinding; your karmic affinity lies there."
Having finished speaking, he vanished; there remained only a fragrant light that drifted toward the west.

Upon arriving at Muxun, he entered the city to beg for alms and obtained some money. He would coax small children who were able to recite "Amituofo" even once, giving them one coin for each recitation.
After more than a month had passed, children began to emulate him; he would give money to those who recited the Buddha’s name most frequently.
For one year, whenever any man or woman saw Kang, they would say, “Amitābha Buddha.”

He subsequently established a Pure Land practice center at Mount Wulong, constructing a three-tiered altar. He gathered followers to perform ritual practices at midnight, chanting twenty-four hymns of praise to extol the Pure Land.
Whenever he encountered a day of fasting, people would gather in clouds; those converted numbered about three thousand.

When he ascended the seat, he would have his male and female disciples gaze at the face of Kang. They would then chant "Amitābha Buddha" in a loud voice; the Buddhas would emerge from his mouth, ten in succession like a string of pearls.
He would then declare: "If you behold these Buddha-bodies, you shall immediately attain rebirth."
In the tenth month of the twenty-first year of the Zhenyuan era, he addressed the assembly with final instructions, exhorting them only to diligently cultivate the Pure Land.
Having finished speaking, he sat in the full lotus posture; his body emitted a brilliant light, and he passed away.
The color of the sky suddenly changed, a violent wind arose from all directions, and a hundred birds wailed in grief.
Mount Oryong (Ulong-san) also turned white at once.
Today, the tomb and stupa remain on Taesiron in the eastern part of the prefecture; as many years have passed, only the square stone remains.

The soil beside the stone is traditionally said to cure illnesses; whenever the people of the prefecture suffer from various ailments, they all burn incense and take some of the earth, and most are cured after taking it accordingly.
The four corners of the stone appear like the ruts of a carriage wheel.

In the third year of the Qianyou era of the Han dynasty, Chan Master Deshao of Mount Tiantai rebuilt the stupa; it remains lofty and spacious to this day, and is popularly known as the "Later Shandao."
The commentary states:

The verses and hymns composed by Kang all conform to the melodies of Zheng and Wei; they are crafted in transformed styles that are neither sorrowful nor joyful, neither resentful nor angry, thereby attaining the tonal resonance of the Middle Way.
It is like a skilled physician who coats bitter medicine with molasses and honey to entice an infant to take it into its mouth.
Were it not for the exercise of great authority and the assumption of provisional forms, how could one employ such skillful means (*upāya*) to achieve the Infinite?
When he chanted the name of the Buddha, the form of the Buddha emerged from his mouth; Shandao likewise performed such Buddhist services, so this was no small matter!

The Biography of Fazheng of Kaiyuan Temple in Jiangzhou of the Tang Dynasty. The Biography of Fazheng of Kaiyuan Temple in Jiangling of the Tang Dynasty. Shi Fazheng, whose personal name was Huizong, was a man of unknown origins.
He broadened his mind and carefully cultivated his conduct.

He presided over the three karmas as the master of time and supervised the six sense faculties as the censor; every day he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* twenty-one times, maintaining reverent diligence without ever succumbing to indolence.
At the beginning of the Changqing era, he fell ill and passed away suddenly.
It is said that he was instantly transported to the realm of darkness and led before the King, who asked him:
"Master, throughout your life, what fields of merit did you cultivate?"
"What virtuous fruits have you obtained?
He answered simply, "Reciting the sutras.
The King then invited him to the upper hall, had him ascend the embroidered throne, and requested that he recite the scriptures seven times.
From the King downward, all the attendants joined their palms; those below the steps who were being interrogated, flogged, beaten, or pleading for mercy became as silent as if no sound existed.
When the recitation was finished, the King sent one person to escort Zhengling back to the human world. Descending the steps, the King bowed to see him off, saying:
"May you, Venerable One, live another thirty years in this world and never cease your recitation and upholding of the Dharma."

Following the official for several li, they came to a massive pit; he was ordered to lean over and look down, whereupon the official pushed him in, as if falling from the void, yet he suddenly revived and rose up.
Initially, when he was about to die, only his face did not grow cold; he recounted this event, and there were many who changed their minds and turned toward goodness.
In the following year, having reached over eighty years of age, he passed away at the monastery where he resided.
Next was Shi Huizong of Gong’an County in Jingzhou; his secular surname was Cai.
Initially, he entered the monastic order in a casual manner and possessed no particular skills.

Suddenly, he was afflicted by a *gǔ* (poisonous insect) infection, until his body became as skeletal as a bone. Consequently, through the intensity of his suffering, he resolved his mind toward the Dharma and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* while awaiting his end.
Upon reaching his fiftieth year, he dreamed that someone ordered him to open his mouth and drew out more than ten strands of hair from his throat.
That same night, he again dreamed of vomiting a long earthworm over a cubit in length; because of this, he was finally cured—this occurred at the beginning of the Changqing era.
The monk Xingjian of Mount Jing witnessed this event.
As for Huiyong, his final destination remains unknown.
Biography of Shousu of Daxingshan Monastery in Jingzhao, Tang Dynasty: Shi Shousu was by nature lofty and transcendent, differing from the common crowd.
Residing at Xingshan Monastery in the capital, he always made the recitation and upholding of scriptures his primary duty.
His quarters were secluded and remote; in the courtyard stood four green paulownia trees, all of which had been planted by his own hand when he was still a layman.
During the Yuanhe era, many high-ranking officials and ministers frequented this monastery.
In midsummer, the green paulownia trees would suddenly begin to exude a sap that was quite messy, staining people's clothes like dripping grease and being impossible to wash out.
At that time, Zheng Yin, the Chancellor of the State, was once staying with several Secretaries and Ministers to escape the summer heat.
Finding the dripping sound of the water tiresome, he said to Bao Su, "Would it be acceptable if I, your disciple, were to cut down this tree for you and each of us planted a pine in its place?"
At dusk, he cursed him with a solemn oath, saying:
"I have cultivated you for over twenty years; yet because of the dripping sweat you shed, you are loathed by others, just as one cannot rest beneath a wicked tree."
"If it continues like this next year, I shall certainly burn myself as fuel.
From that time on, he vanished from sight!
Having previously vowed never to leave the monastery, he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* thirty-seven thousand times.
Every night, young marmots would come to disturb him gently, coming to listen to the sutras.
At mealtime, crows and magpies would take food from his palm.
When other monks tried to lure them with food, the entire flock would fly away in a startled clamor.
At the beginning of the Changqing era, a monk named Xuanyou inscribed this verse for the monastery:
"Thirty springs have passed since the thirty thousand Lotus Sūtras were recited; for half my life, I have not trodden the dust of the monastery gate."
At that time, these were considered excellent verses.
Regarding Sū’s life until his death, nothing further can be known in detail.
The colophon states:
One who pricks the lacquer tree constantly suffers from its scarcity of sap; because it is cherished, it is difficult to obtain.
One who cuts down the bitter melon tree suffers from its abundance of bitterness; because it is loathed, it is easy to find. Alas!
That the green paulownia tree shed sap was something rarely heard of in the world;
yet when Master Su rebuked it, it ceased its activity the following year.
How can there be a disciple who has left the household life who does not surpass these insentient trees?
Since it cannot prevent lacquer from being stained by external objects, nor can it enhance the flavor of the Wei sauce for one's food,
if one simply accepts the admonitions and rebukes of teachers and friends, one will ensure that they remain pure and untainted.
The *Analects* says:
"If you have committed a transgression, do not hesitate to correct it.
According to our fundamental teaching, one repents of offenses and attains purity, which is no different from being as one was originally.
Consider this.

The Biography of Master Huayan of Youzhou during the Tang Dynasty. Regarding the biography of the Śramaṇa Master Huayan of Youzhou during the Tang Dynasty: the Śramaṇa Master Huayan’s name and lineage are unknown.

He resided north of the city of Youzhou and constantly maintained the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as his practice for purification; at that time, he was popularly known by this name, which was simply taken from the title of the scripture to serve as his invocation.
When he recited [the scriptures], the entire city heard him as clearly as if they were beneath his courtyard eaves.

During the Wansui Tongtian era, when Zhang Renyuan, the Duke of Han, served as the Governor-General of Youzhou, he heard the sound of the sutras at night, with every line and phrase distinct and orderly.
When he rose at dawn, he said to his wife, "Last night, the Daoist chanting in the city north of the palace seemed as if it were right in front of the official residence; did you hear it?"
The lady asked,
"How distant is this land that it can be heard of?
Zhangjun replied:
"If you do not believe this, you may each dispatch a young servant on horseback to go and verify it.
Indeed, there was no discrepancy.
Zhang Jun invited him to enter the city; upon meeting him, he said to Zhang Jun:
He asked, "Is there no vow that has not yet been fulfilled?
He replied, "I have recently made five hundred monastic robes; having offered them as alms to the Arhats, I have departed."
Huayan said, "Do not go elsewhere;
simply deliver it to the monks at Zhulin Temple on Mount Mian, west of the prefecture.
When the messenger arrived with incense and clothing to enter the Buddha niche, the mountain had already vanished, and though they searched for Zhulin Temple, there was no trace of it to be found.
Having thus delved deeply and ascended a high mountain, he encountered an old man who asked him, "Just follow me.
Suddenly, the clouds parted to reveal a monastery; its scenery was unlike anything found in the mundane world.
After entering the monastery and distributing the *kāṣāyas*, two persons were missing.
The elderly master said, "You may take back two portions: one for Zhang Renyuan and one for Master Huayan."
From this point on, it was known that Master Huayan had come from Zhulin Shengsi Temple; he was invited to stay for one night, yet by the time he departed, a year had already passed.
Having engaged in his ministry for a long time, when his life ended, he passed away while sitting upright, and his physical body did not decay.
Many people from Fanyang went there to offer prayers, and at times there were signs of response.
The pagoda was subsequently destroyed due to the turmoil of war.
The commentary states:
"How can a single recitation reach the ears of everyone, both near and far?
Tong replied:
"As for those nearby, it is because they wish to uphold the sutra; this is due to the power of its wholesome merit."
"At a distance, he expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet each being hears and understands it according to their own kind.
It can be known for certain that this man is a member of the monastic community of a holy temple!
The Biography of Wenzhao of Baiti Mountain in Hedong Prefecture, Tang Dynasty. Shi Wenzhao was a person of unknown origins. He resided at Baiti Mountain in Hedong Prefecture during the Tang dynasty.
I am but a person of simple nature and slow wit; yet, upon seeing a Buddhist image, I feel joy and serenity.
Once, I went to Baiti Temple and, having paid homage to the painted portrait of Dharma Master Tanyan, I left the household life.
He devoted himself to reciting various sutras, yet he knew not how to interpret or elucidate them; he was constantly frustrated by the dullness and turbidity of his innate nature.
Suddenly, while dozing, he saw the Dharma Master Tanyan, who was one zhang in height, with eyes that radiated light in all directions. The Master said to Zhao:
"As for what you desire, how could I possibly bring it about?"

"I possess a single scroll of the *Ciming jing* (Scripture of Clear Intelligence). If you seek it from him, he will surely preserve it with care; you shall obtain its spiritual resonance as easily as picking up a blade of grass from the ground!
He then drew it from his sleeve and presented it to him—it was the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
I took up the reading immediately; after seven recitations, I was suddenly startled awake, yet the scripture remained vividly before my eyes.
Thereafter, my understanding flowed without obstruction, as if I had practiced it for a long time.
The modulations of my throat and tongue—curving, rising, and sinking—followed rhythmic variations that were unlike any ordinary chant.
From then on, his intelligence grew daily more refined and his eloquence was ever-present in his speech; at the time, people said that Guanyin had taken up residence within his person.
He would further say:
"My teacher is the National Preceptor of the Zhou and Sui dynasties."
"In all the commentaries and exegeses I have compiled, they were invariably bestowed through divine inspiration during my dreams; thus, I have no cause for shame in relying upon them as my resources.
This concludes the Biography of Fazhao of Shanfu Prefecture, Tang Dynasty. Regarding the monk Fazhao: it is unknown where he was from.
In his conduct he was often impulsive, and his travels were not consistent.
In the first year of the Changqing era, he entered an inn to seek shelter from the rain; as time passed, the mud became increasingly deep, and when it was past noon, he failed to obtain almsfood.
He then shouted for his servant boy to buy pork, boiled several pieces of *hupi* cakes, and consumed this coarse meal with such lack of shame that he was as if no one else were present.
The guests all reviled and cursed him, and some of the youths wished to beat him.
Yet Sengzhao made no response at all.
When night fell, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; though there was originally no oil or candle, the entire room was filled with light, and a wondrous fragrance pervaded it.
In total, twenty-one guests came to prostrate and apologize for their transgressions, each offering him clothing and other items.
Yet Zhao sat there as if seeing nothing at all.
Afterwards, his final destination remained unknown.

Biography of Huipu of Qingzhu Chan Monastery in Guangji County, Qizhou, Tang Dynasty The monk Huipu, surnamed Song, was a native of Qishui in the same prefecture. His secular surname was Song, and he was originally from Qishui in the local commandery. He was a man of the Qishui district.
Xingdi was broad-minded and clear-sighted, possessing a sharp and outstanding intellect; having received the precepts (śīla), he maintained his conduct with the purity of ice and snow.
In the twelfth year of the Yuanhe era, finding that Mount Guangji was both beautiful and spiritually potent, he wished to take up residence there.
He first conceived the plan to recite the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*; after many years had passed, he finally mastered all forty-two fascicles.
Those who heard of this sighed in admiration, saying:
"This great scripture in four volumes—how could it be studied through mere rote memorization? It is surely beyond the reach of ordinary estimation!"

Some, suspecting that his words were merely a superficial recitation of the sections, attempted to test him by citing the titles of chapters out of order; yet he was never faltering, nor did he omit anything, nor did he speak too slowly, and all were subdued.
Pu likewise did not observe the precepts; he personally engaged in slash-and-burn agriculture, seeking only to satisfy his basic needs.
Wearing garments of grass and coarse cloth, he passed the festivals of Fu and La while the sound of the sutras never ceased day or night.
Thus he spent thirty years [there], and among the local people and scholars, there were none who did not honor him; they expanded and renovated the temple buildings.

In the winter of the third year of the Dazhong era, without prior illness, he gathered the assembly to announce his departure from them, then sat in the full lotus posture until his end, appearing as solemn as one in deep contemplation.
The disciples wrapped the remains in fragrant clay and enshrined them within a stupa on a mountain peak, naming it "Nirvana.
To this day, the offerings of incense and lamps have never ceased.
*Biography of the Itinerant Monk from Tang China in the Present Day at Dongjing*, by an anonymous author: During the Changqing era, a monk from afar arrived; his appearance was coarse and violent.
Seeing a temple attendant within the monastery, he rebuked him, saying:
"Take this money and buy wine for me!
When the temple monks saw this, they were incensed that he did not restrain or discipline him, feeling that he was bringing disgrace upon their monastic quarters; how could they endure such a thing?

He then seized the jar and struck it against a cypress tree outside the monastery; the jar shattered with a metallic clang, yet the wine remained solidified and would not flow, adhering to the tree like green jade. It could not be dispersed by shaking and emitted no odor when smelled.
The temple monks were startled and asked the guest, "What are you doing?

The guest replied, "I regularly recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. I must first drink a cup of this substance so that my chanting is clear and resonant; I have made this my habit, for it cannot be done otherwise."
"Venerable sir, do not be offended.
While the temple monk hesitated, his expression grew somber.
The guest then took his vessel to the tree and filled it; the wine fell entirely into the vessel, leaving not a single drop behind—spectators gathered like a wall around them.
Suddenly he began to weep aloud; in an instant, his vessel became worn and he grew intoxicated with joy.
One did not know where this monk went or returned.
This is the biography of Shi Lingyou of Da Wen Guo Temple in the Capital of the Tang Dynasty. Shi Lingyou was a man of unknown origins.
He was reclusive, pure, and upright, and he applied himself with great diligence to his recitations and studies.
Once, he suddenly died of illness and vanished into the underworld.
When he was led before the King of the Netherworld, the King asked, "What karma have you cultivated?"
He replied, “I have long maintained the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, for many years already!
The King pressed his palms together and repeatedly exclaimed, “Excellent! Excellent! and requested that he recite it.
He pouted his lips and moved his tongue, making the paragraphs and sections distinct.
When he had finished reciting, the King said,
"It is not yet perfect."
Why is this? It is because one section of the text is missing.
Why has the thread that strings the flowers been severed?
Although the Master’s lifespan has come to an end, he shall be released to return to the human realm for ten years, with the intent of exhorting all people to receive and uphold this scripture.
Its true original text is located upon a stone stele at Zhongli Temple in Haozhou.
After this had been done, he revived seven days later.

Youyou subsequently memorialized the Emperor, requesting an imperial edict to have a true copy of this sutra transcribed and its punctuation added; this is what follows the passage "There is no dharma that can be preached; this is called preaching the Dharma."
The commentary states:
In the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, when it reads "the fifth day of summer," one does not dare to lightly add [a missing character];
the same principle applies to Buddhism—one must not recklessly concoct [falsities].
Tong said, "It is no hardship that Lingyou obtained the stone scriptures from Zhongli Temple; they correspond perfectly.
However, if Daoming were to add or interpolate them, it would cause people to harbor doubts and suspicions, inevitably inviting falsehood."
He hastily altered his practice, claiming he had received a divine revelation; one must be cautioned against such things!
This is the biography of Shi Weigong of Lingqiu at Faxing Monastery in Jingzhou during the Tang dynasty. Shi Weigong was a person whose origins are unknown.
When he was young, he left secular life at Faxing Temple; his tastes were lowly, and he frequently associated with friends who did not follow the Dharma.
Although he deviated from the monastic conduct, he remained diligent in reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, rarely removing it from his lips.
Drunkards and gamblers flocked to his door; his conduct was full of falsehood and deceit, and he possessed no sense of shame.
Later, he fell ill and died.
There was another in the same monastery named Lingkui whose behavior was similar; they were known as the "two pests of the monastery."

Ling Kui went out briefly; about one *li* from the monastery, he encountered six or seven young men who were exceptionally handsome, dressed in fresh and clean garments, each holding musical instruments of the Kucha style.
They asked Ling Kui, "Where is the Venerable Weigong?"
Jiū immediately told him the location, suspecting that the temple was performing incense offerings and music for the Buddha.
At dawn, he returned to the temple; hearing the sound of the bell, he cried out, "Gong has passed away!"
What was seen was merely a celestial vision.
It was because he had relied on the power of the sutras that he would surely be reborn in a Pure Land; [the author] also used this account to encourage Lingkui.
Lingkui was moved to realization and humbled himself, becoming highly esteemed by the monastic community, and ultimately achieved a state of sublime transcendence.
The Biography of Shi Suīduān of Dèrùn Monastery in Míngzhōu during the Táng Dynasty. Shi Suīduān, surnamed Zhāng, is unknown as to where he came from; he came to Dèrùn Monastery seeking a teacher.
As a person, he was honest, upright, pure, and refined, and did not engage in frivolous socializing.
When his teacher bestowed upon him the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he could recite it as if it were something he had mastered long ago; everyone marveled at this in astonishment.
Reaching his later years, he remained diligent without slackening—reciting constantly for twelve hours without ceasing.
In the second year of the Xiantong era, he suddenly sat in the full lotus posture and passed away; in an instant, seven stalks of blue lotuses emerged from his mouth.
People from far and near rushed to attend the ceremony;
the villagers united in their efforts to construct a sarcophagus and interred him at the foot of Mount Dongshan.
Over twenty years later, his tomb repeatedly emitted a radiant light. When it was opened for inspection, his physical form remained as if he were alive.
The multitude welcomed him back to the temple and adorned his remains with lacquer and hemp cloth;
it is now known as the Zhen-shen (True Body) Hall, which still exists there.

As for this temple, it was originally the study hall of Kan Ze, the Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince and Marquis of Duxiang during the Wu dynasty; it was later donated to become a *saṃghārāma*, and its plaque was inscribed with the character from his name. This is the present-day Puji Temple.
The commentary states:
"To claim that at the end of his life he produced an *udumbara* flower from his mouth—is this possible?
We have heard that when a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, this flower grows upon the path above the sea. How could such a thing exist now in this age of the Dharma’s decline?"
Tong said, "When one responds out of being moved by another person, one cannot be constrained by the times.
It is like the qilin, which is not a creature native to the Middle Kingdom, yet it appears when moved by an enlightened king; the principle is the same."
Biography of Shenzhi of Baoshou Monastery in Zhuji, Yuezhou, Tang Dynasty. The monk Shenzhi was a native of Yiwu in Wuzhou; his secular surname was Li.
The ancestors of the Li clan were the descendants of Mu, a minister of the Yellow Emperor.
During the Han dynasty, there was Li Gui, who served as the Chancellor of Lu Commandery; because he resided in Yanzhou due to his official post, his descendants subsequently became people of Lu.
His ancestors were all farmers, and they had followed a tradition of simple and unadorned living.
From his youth, Zhi possessed upright integrity; earnestly desiring to renounce the household life, he went to Yunmen Temple to take Wei Xiao as his teacher.
At the age of twelve, he practiced eating only once a day;
he maintained the *Mahākaruṇā-hṛdaya-mantra* and received full ordination in accordance with the Dharma, applying himself with rigorous diligence.

Shortly thereafter, during the Huichang suppression of Buddhism, although his physical appearance and attire were altered, his vow to remain a monk remained firm; that at such times he was neither worn down nor defiled was evident then and there.
In the first year of the Dazhong era, he returned to the Way.
He traveled through Jiyang and stayed in a meditation chamber, remarking:
"The fish of the imperial court have hidden away in the marshes; this is only fitting!"
"This place is my marsh and forest.
He would constantly consecrate water with mantras from his cup to cure a hundred ailments; those who drank it were mostly healed.
The common people followed him in succession, providing for him daily in countless numbers, and they called him the Venerable Dabeji (Great Compassionate).
During the Dazhong era, he entered the capital of Jingzhao. At that time, Prime Minister Pei Xu of Shengping had previously dreamed that Zhi would come; when they finally met, he was filled with joy.
The Prime Minister’s daughter was possessed by a spirit, but Zhi recited incantations for her, and she recovered within seven days.

He then submitted a petition requesting that the temple be granted the official title "Dazhong Shengshou," and was further bestowed with one bell from the Left Shen-ce Army, an embroidered banner of the Empress Dowager, and five thousand scrolls of the Tripitaka.
Lord Pei composed the inscription for the temple’s plaque.
Zhi passed away at Dongbaishan in the twelfth month of the Bingwu year of the Guangqi era; he was sixty-eight years of age and forty-eight years of Dharma ordination.
He moved his seat to Nanshan in Jiyang and entered a stupa there.

Regarding Shi Congshen, who followed [the lineage] of Congshen at Chanzhi Temple in Yangzhou during the Liang dynasty: his clan and family name are unknown. In his youth, he entered Chanzhi Temple in Jiangdu, where he left the household life and recited several tens of thousands of words of scripture.
That monastery was the former palace of Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty.
In the fifth year of the Xiantong era, he received full ordination at Fengfu Monastery on Mount Yantai.
He had extensively studied under masters of the Vinaya and the sutras, having been thoroughly immersed in their teachings.
Later, he combined his three robes into five patched garments and traveled to visit all the famous mountains and scenic wonders without exception.
At the end of his travels, he returned to the Huaidian region and was appointed as the head of the monastic community.
For five or six years, he maintained the strictest discipline in all matters.
He constantly recited the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, never failing his daily count.

On the eighteenth day of the third month in the second year of the Zhenming era, he fell ill; by the hour of Wuming on the nineteenth, his breath grew faint and he passed away, his countenance remaining as usual.

Upon cremation, thirty śarīra relics were obtained; they were firm, lustrous, and passed through forging without loss. Biography of Hongchu of Dayun Monastery in Wenzhou during the Liang Dynasty. Hongchu, whose courtesy name was Fangwai and whose secular surname was Tang, was a native of Yongjia.
From birth, his appearance was extraordinary, setting him apart from other children.
By the time he had merely reached the age of childhood, his character and capacity were vast and expansive.
Outside of Chu, all his brothers had left secular life to enter the monasteries of Yue; consequently, he prayed to his parents, wishing to follow them as well.

The net was so loose that the fish escaped; the cage was opened and the crane flew away. *Du* grass grew upon the orchid isle, and fresh silk was dyed with vermilion. They exhorted and corrected one another, and their recitation and study became ever more proficient.
At the age of twenty-three, he finally attained the unconditioned state of the highest grade.
Upon returning to his native commandery, the regional governor Zhu Bao, who was aware of his reputation and integrity, greeted him with increasingly respectful courtesy.

During the Dàshùn era of the Táng dynasty, there was a dilapidated and overgrown site of the abandoned Dàyún Monastery to the south of the city. [The Master] submitted a memorial to Emperor Zhāozōng, expressing his desire to rebuild it from the foundations.
The Emperor granted his request.
Thereupon, the various artisans all set to work, with King Chu personally presiding over them.
They applied their skills and measured their achievements so that nothing deviated from the original plan;
meanwhile, the recitation of scriptures and the crafting of ritual images proceeded without interfering with one another’s order.

In the early years of the Qiánhua era, King Wǔsù of the Qián clan established a *kaidù* ordination platform at Longxīng Temple in Hángzhōu. He summoned Chǔzú to serve as a member of the ordination assembly. Consequently, he petitioned Emperor Taizǔ of Liáng to grant him purple robes and a title; however, Chǔzú firmly declined, saying that the Emperor would not listen, and he ultimately did not don them. He remarked of himself, "My virtue is meager; how could I wear these robes, which are the honor bestowed by the destiny of the Dharma-gate?"
At that time, the poet Zheng Shuo traveled south and visited Dharma Master Hongjing, where he happened upon him at Chu’s residence.
Having come to know of his noble conduct, Zheng composed a poem to present to Chu, saying:
"The purple robes on the rack remain unworn; The golden characters on the desk he gazes upon for long."
Chu Kuan was compassionate; people never saw a trace of anger on his face.
His spirit was clear and refined; his chin was full and fleshy, and his belly was pendulous.
His eyes did not glance askance, and when he looked back, he would invariably turn his whole body.
In his worldly speech, he did not let his tongue wander frivolously.
He lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* approximately fifty times.
One day, within the lecture hall in Chu, lotus flowers suddenly sprang forth, with double-layered stalks and overlapping petals, their fragrance rich and pervasive.
On the fifth day of the sixth month in the third year of the Changxing era (the Renchen year), he passed away without illness.
He was seventy-five years of secular age and fifty-two years of monastic seniority (*dharma-varṣa*).
Both the clergy and the laity mourned him with deep affection.
In that year, he moved the stupa to the right ridge of Ciyun.
Aside from his exegesis and lecturing, he practiced the Way and recited sutras late into the night.
On the eve of his passing, the lamp light suddenly dimmed and the sound of the sutra recitation grew faint; he addressed his disciples, saying:
"Raúl, prepare my carriage; I shall depart.
Within the couch upon which he lay was a white snake, as thick as his arm, which had always shared his bed; he strictly instructed his young attendants not to disturb him by surprise.

Shengchang compiled the *Commentary on the Sutra of Rebirth Above* and drew blood to transcribe a copy of the *Lotus Sutra*; to this day, the people of Yongjia regard him as a rare jewel among the treasures of the Sangha.
Biography of Hongju of Xiaosong Mountain in Wenzhou during the Later Tang Dynasty. The monk Hongju, surnamed Tang, was a native of Yongjia.
He left home early at Longgong Monastery in Yuezhou.
At first, he recited the entire *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Having received full ordination, he traveled on foot to Chang’an to study the Vinaya.

While he was reading the stele of Huadu Monastery, a candidate for the imperial examination happened to overhear him. Seeing that Seng’u’s eyes followed the text as he recited it with great fluency, the candidate marveled at this and, realizing he could recite the inscription from memory, requested that Seng’u repeat it for him.
When a Confucian scholar covered his text, he found not a single error.
They then went together to Chongsheng Temple, where the same was true; moreover, he possessed a powerful memory, for which he was highly esteemed by his peers.
He said that he was returning to his hometown and requested to receive the formal reliance (*niśraya*) of the two assemblies.
As for his refined conduct, throughout his life he had never once scolded even a cat or a dog, let alone anyone else.

However, while he practiced the Way and recited the sutras day and night, there were spirits who protected him—some lighting candles for him, others adding incense on his behalf; all of them were ghostly beings.
In the third year of the Tiānchéng era, the year Wùzǐ (928 CE), following a period of flooding, a great drought ensued, and the people suffered from successive famines.
When a bandit entered his house, Jǔ treated him as a guest; he personally prepared gruel and rice to feed him, saying, "Depart slowly;
the mountains are deep and there is no one here."
"You all are merely being beset by a celestial calamity.
The thieves bowed and departed.
Among the disciples, some wished to attack them while they were unprepared, but Ju said:
"You are no longer my disciples; I shall abandon you and enter the deep mountains forever!
At these words, his sons abandoned their intention to carry him lightly.
In the gui-si year of the Changxing era, he passed away peacefully and without illness, sitting upright in the full lotus position.
At the third watch, he knocked on the door of his niche three times. His disciples wept as they opened it, and he said:
"I tell you all, change me into new clothes; the superior beings of the Buddha-lands find my vestments impure."
His funeral rites were completed, and for seven days his head remained warm.
At that time, there were three large dogs in the monastery—capable of fierce biting—who, on the day the stupa was moved, became tame and affectionate toward the people.
At that time, deer and wild boars roamed together with birds in the mountains; the dogs were not fierce or aggressive, and the beasts did not flee in alarm.
After the burial, a tiger circled the tomb, howling and crying out.
Such was the nature of his emotional resonance with things.
He had a younger brother named Hongchu, who also possessed noble conduct and was highly esteemed by their contemporaries.
Later, there was Shi Daoxian, whose biography appears in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Dao in Fengxiang Prefecture* of the Later Tang; it is unknown where he was from.

He maintained the practice of reciting the *Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra* as his daily routine; eventually, he received the Yoga initiation, whereby the efficacy of his vidyā-mantra practice produced increasingly numerous signs of spiritual response.
Once, he dreamed at night that the Buddha was leading him, Xianxing, and they walked step by step upon thick clouds as if treading upon solid ground.
They traveled for many hundreds of li without his ever knowing the distance, and [the Buddha] pointed them out, saying:
"This is the kingdom of Magadha; this is the kingdom of Campā; these are the kingdoms of South India, West India, Kaśmīra, and so forth."
As he traveled, he took notes, his joy and exultation beyond measure.
Upon waking, he had intuitively mastered the Sanskrit phonology of the Five Indias and the Siddham script.

At that time, monks from the Western Regions arrived at Qixia; various Hu monks from north of the Pamir Mountains often falsely claimed to be people from the Five Indias. When they approached, Prajñācandra would first dismiss them by engaging them in conversation.
"From which country do you come?
Whether from the northern Rong tribes or the southern Brahmans, none dared to deceive him.
Both the monastics and the laity along the Longdi Pass received his secret treasury of teachings and hailed him as an Ācārya.

By the end of the Changxing era, Emperor Mingzong passed away, and Liu Conghou was established as emperor. Qingtai of Fengxiang did not submit to his authority; Emperor Conghou dispatched Wang Sitong to lead an army against him, whereupon Qingtai fortified the city walls to defend himself.
Qingtai asked Xian, "It is extremely perilous;
what should be done? He replied:
"Summon Dou Bala; we can then anticipate victory or defeat.
Qingtai went out to mount the city walls and address the troops. Dou Ba, clad in armor and grasping a spear, came before the horse, assuming the posture of one ready for combat.
Having leaped over, he cast off his armor, threw away his spear,
and fled. Xian said,
"This is surely an omen that the enemy will surrender."
It was indeed as he had said.
Qingtai then led his troops eastward and summoned Xian to accompany him.
Upon entering Luoyang, he ascended the imperial throne and changed the era name to Qingtai.
The worthy replied, "The reign title is inauspicious; why is that?
'Water' [shui] reveals 'stone' [shi]."

In the second year, the Emperor issued an edict to transfer the Jin High Ancestor of Bingzhou to the position of Tianping Commander; he then fortified his position with troops, secretly allied with the Qidan, and launched a long march into Luoyang. Qingtai set himself on fire and perished, which indeed fulfilled the omen of "Shi appearing."
Before the Jin troops arrived, Fotudeng passed away in Luoyang; those who now transmit the Great Teaching in the two capitals are all his great-grandsons or further descendants!
As for Dou Bala, he was a native of Qifu and his family was wealthy.
Carrying a vessel on his back to sell water, his speech was incoherent; he did nothing but run about wildly with his hair disheveled and his robes cast off, much like Li Shunxing.
Whenever he encountered ox-carts or donkey-carts, he would invariably clap his hands and laugh.
Upon his death, they cremated him; amidst the mass of flames, he was entirely transformed into golden butterflies that flew away.
Some gathered them in their hands or fanned them with their robes as they carried them back home to offer them worship.

Biography of Shi Ruoxu of Mount Lu in Jiangzhou of the Han Dynasty The monk Shi Ruoxu, whose name is lost, lived in seclusion on Mount Lu. For several years he maintained his practice of reciting the sutras, never leaving his stone chamber.
The Prince of Jiangnan, Lady Li, held his Way in high esteem and repeatedly summoned him, yet he ultimately did not descend to comply.
He spoke only thus: "This old monk is incapable; how could I possibly merit the King’s devotion?"
"If we call out to one another again, he will flee into the deep mountains!
Regarding clothing and goods, they would yield to him; however, when it came to incense, they accepted it from him.

He passed away while seated in meditation during the height of summer in the Zhongwu era of the Qianhuo period; his body did not decay, and people of Pencheng now make offerings to his physical likeness.
Furthermore, Shi Wangming of Tanzhou constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and never uttered any other words.
Ma Xianzong, the Prince Wenzhao of Changsha, treated him with exceptional honor and respect, summoning him to the Tiance Fu Xiangxi Yuan to provide for his sustenance.
However, the account he told was so strange and extraordinary as to be startling.
One day, he summoned the monks in charge of the Buddha hall and ordered them to quickly fold up the Buddha images and move them to the two side corridors.
The monks all considered him to have gone mad and looked at one another with smiles.
His movements were exceedingly frantic and hurried.
In a moment, he entered the main hall of the temple, took his seat upon the Buddha’s throne, and suddenly passed away.
The monastics and laypeople throughout the entire province vied with one another to pay him homage and burn incense; this was during the Qianguyu era of the Later Han.

Biography of Xingtao of Dasha Temple in Kuaiji Commandery, Zhou Dynasty: Shi Xingtao, surnamed Chen, was a native of Changcheng in Huzhou. He resided at Dasha Temple in Kuaiji Commandery during the Zhou dynasty. His biography follows.
His father’s name was Liang, and his mother was surnamed Tao; her heart of doting affection for him was unlike that she held for her other sons.
Yet, in his quick-wittedness and sharp intelligence, he stood out preeminently among the other children.
His parents encountered many obstacles to his resolve to leave the household life, yet in the end they were unable to restrain him.
In the second year of the Tiānyòu era of the Táng dynasty, he followed Master Guāngyuǎn to receive the tonsure and the precepts.
At the age of twelve, he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, completing the entire volume in fifteen days.
Next, he finished the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, just as Dao’an had requested the scriptures in the morning and returned the original texts by evening.

He subsequently received the full precepts at Longxing Temple in Yuhang and proceeded to Shuanglin Temple in Jinhua, where he studied the *Nanshan Lüchao* under Master Zhixin. He remained there for an extended period, devotedly internalizing the teachings, until his contemporaries honored him with their respect and deference.
Whenever it was time for his regular meal, he would place unhusked rice and vegetables in a small cauldron and eat them after boiling them together; beyond this, he strictly avoided any rich flavors.
With a mind of profound understanding, he unraveled complex principles as easily as splitting wood, never showing any sign of difficulty.
He once said to others:
"When one's preference for something is so intense, one sees no other object as worthy of such preference."
"My passion is that it is joyful and without excess.
During the Tiānchéng era of the Later Táng dynasty, he resided in Yuè; finding delight in the mountains and waters of Ruòyè, he perused the Mahāyāna Tripitaka and wore garments of hempen cloth.

He recruited both monastics and laypeople to establish a scripture-recitation hall in the northwest corner of the temple; he constructed pavilions, towers, and halls until it flourished as a separate cloister, providing for monks from all quarters without ever suffering from want.

In the seventh month of autumn in the year of Renzi during the third year of the Xiande era, he manifested illness and passed away at this monastery; his age was sixty-two, and his dharma-ordination years were forty-four.

Tao’s character was upright and just; he neither flattered others to their faces nor harbored secret hatreds behind their backs. His feet never hurried to the doors of the wealthy and powerful, his bags held no surplus goods, his rooms were never bolted shut, and his speech was free from idle chatter.

He also perused various books and extensively explored the sūtras and śāstras; lamenting that Guo Yi’s *Yinyi* was sparse and incomplete, and that Huilin’s *Yinyi* had not been transmitted, he subsequently composed approximately five hundred fascicles of the *Dazangjing Yinsu*, which are currently in circulation among the monasteries throughout Jiangzhe and its vicinity.

However, its brevity makes it inappropriate to be called a "commentary" (shū)—if one were to call it a "commentary," it could elucidate an entire Tripitaka, surpassing even the hundred volumes of Ci'en by several times over.
His upright integrity and adherence to the Vinaya were truly lofty and eminent by ancient standards.

Biography of Shi Shouzhen of Kaibao Temple in Eastern Capital, Song: The śrāmaṇera Miga Daoyin, Shi Shouzhen, was a native of Wan’nan in Yongxing. His lineage was transmitted from [the tradition of] Kaibao Temple in Eastern Capital, Song. Shouzhen was a man of Yongxing’s Wan’nan.
His secular surname was Ji, a lineage descending from Emperor Xin of the Han dynasty.

His ancestors and parents had long maintained upright conduct and auspicious virtue; for generations, their filial piety had filled the villages and neighborhoods. Thus, his fellow villagers praised his filiality and came to call him Ji Dīnglán—Zhēn was indeed a descendant of this very line!

When the Huang rebels violated the laws of state and Emperor Xizong was forced into exile, the imperial carriage fled westward to escape their onslaught; as Xian and Hao fell to the enemy, he consequently moved his residence to Shu.

Upon reaching the age for capping, he happened to visit Shengshou Temple and saw the Venerable Xujin’s conduct transcending the mundane; his speech surpassed ordinary standards. Thereupon, [the young man] untied his sash and removed his cap, and facing north, served him as a disciple.
Once the sevenfold prostrations were completed, he first visited Master Conglang to study the *Awakening of Faith*;
next, he relied on Master Xingguang to receive the transmission of the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*;
and finally, he paid his respects to Ācārya Yanmi to be granted the Yoga teachings. In each case, he attained the essential points and fully grasped their ultimate purpose.
Having personally attained clear realization of all dharmas, he expounded the sublime scriptures for nearly forty years without the slightest negligence.
He was bestowed with the title "Zhaoxin" (Luminous Faith).

He lectured on the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* more than seventy times in total; in all cases, he transmitted the lamp by means of the lamp and poured from vessel into vessel, leaving behind approximately twenty successors of the Dharma.
He opened the initiation mandala five times, ordaining over three thousand monastics, nuns, officials, and commoners; he opened the water and land mandala twenty times.

He regularly established the cycle of Mañjuśrī’s Five Topknots teachings at the fifth watch of the night, and by the second watch of the night, he established the cycle of the Western Amitāyus teachings, reciting the name of the Honored One Amitābha and practicing the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection, vowing to be reborn in the Pure Land.
One day, he said to his disciple Yuanyu:
"Did the Tathāgata not say, 'I cannot guarantee that my exhalation will be followed by my inhalation'?
My life is fortunate, yet you are already advanced in years. Now, wishing to conform to worldly custom, I intend to pre-construct two stupas; would this be permissible?"
Upon meeting [the Elder Guangdu], he bowed his head in greeting and replied:
"The Elder Guangdu has for many years requested that a stupa be built on the ground to the right of his monastery!
Now that the Great Master has directed his intention toward it and the Elder has offered his excellence, the conditions and causes coincide in profound harmony; how could this be allowed to stop?"
Thereupon, craftsmen were gathered to undertake the construction; from the tenth month of that year until the first month of the following year, the carving was refined and the painting completed.

On the ninth day of the eighth month of the autumn in the fourth year of the Kaibao era, he commanded the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name. When the chanting had continued for some time, he ordered it to cease, and he suddenly passed into parinirvāṇa. His secular age was seventy-eight, and his monastic seniority fifty-three.
On the twenty-first day of that month, he was cremated and interred beside the Jidu (Jñānaprasthāna) Monastery outside the Beiyongtai Gate.
The obtained śarīras were lustrous and smooth, and each person took them to offer worship.
Next was the śrāmaṇera Miga, a native of the kingdom of Khotan, who specialized in reciting the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* without ever ceasing.
During the Shengli era, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, invited him to ascend to heaven to recite and uphold the scripture. Śakra said:
"I am constantly harassed by the asuras; therefore, I have humbled myself to invite you here. I pray that you will recite and proclaim the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to ward off those enemies."
He then ascended the seat and recited this sutra with a clear voice.
At that time, the host of asura armies, upon hearing the sutra, manifested their divine powers and vanished all at once.

Furthermore, the śrāmaṇera Doyin constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. During the early years of the Baoli era, while returning home at night after having gone elsewhere, he encountered a fierce tiger on the road; suddenly, it met him as it was roaring and leaping before him.
Knowing he could not escape, Yin closed his eyes and sat down, silently reciting this sutra alone while vowing in his heart for protection. The tiger then crouched in the grass to guard him.
At daybreak, as villagers passed by, they saw the tiger; it remained crouched where it was, with saliva dripping onto the ground.
After receiving [the transmission], he maintained his recitations and further increased his lofty conduct.
The treatise states:
"The essentials for entering the Path take the three types of wisdom as their gate."
If you wish to attain hearing-and-retention (*śrutadhāraṇī*), do not exceed the practice of reading and reciting. Why is this?
It begins solely by relying on the source; once the source is established, the Way arises.

Next, one must relinquish the conventional expressions; for if these expressions are retained, the moon will be lost. This is like pointing toward the cassia reflection in the sky while still clutching the horsewhip on one's back.
To remain thus obstructed and fettered is to distance oneself further from the Way.
Thus, when a new impulse arises and traces may suddenly shift, one must ensure that there is broad vision and extensive learning.
Furthermore, to set aside the written word and sing out with lofty voices—this depends upon one's rank and position, and such a person is first designated as a "Dharma Master."
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"To receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, transcribe, and practice according to the Dharma"— this is it.

To begin with, when the scriptures and commentaries first reached Zhendan (China) and were translated during the Han court: in the north, Zhu Falan was the first to proclaim his reputation for directness and analytical exposition; in the south, only Kang Senghui raised the melodic strains of the *qǔyùn* to facilitate understanding through intonation.
Lan is born of the Yuezhi, while Hui belongs to the Kangju clan.
With these two families situated on either side, we must discern right from wrong; let us not act like foxes on the ice, nor inquire about the path by the watchtower.
Tong said:
"The monks of Western India maintain various traditions, and their practices differ:
some adhere strictly to what they heard directly from the Buddha, making them even more difficult to reform."
Some claim that our own school permits many divergent branches;
some are direct and plain;
others are skillful in their melodic singing.

Consequently, as lineages of transmission have been handed down, each school vies for mastery, asserting "this is right and that is wrong," or "I am correct and others are in error. Thus they remain in contradiction throughout the year, with no end in sight.

Therefore, when one performs a single period of beautiful chanting or recites three sections of a gāthā, it can move horses and chariots so that they refuse to advance, and stir the collective listening of both humans and devas; such is the efficacy of these modulated sounds.

As for Pan-te’s few phrases and Bo-gu’s brief verses—where he merely stirs his lips to dispel sorrow and employs clever turns of speech to raise his tongue—even these have led some to ascend to the rank of a "Middle Sage" or to evoke spiritual responses; this is simply proof of the power inherent in sound.
To summarize this in a single word: whatever moves the dragon deities and enables them to produce wholesome states in beings is the correct pronunciation for recitation.
Someone asked:
“I have often heard that the speech of the Ābhāsvara Heaven is the Brahma-voice (brahmasvara).”
"I do not yet know what constitutes the Brahma-voice;
please describe its appearance so that I may see it.
Tong replied:
"The various dhāraṇīs are the Sanskrit language;
the sounds of the *bhaiṣajya* (chanting) are the Sanskrit phonology.

His remains were interred within the monastery grounds, and a stupa was erected over them.
