They all vowed to become slaves of the monastery, tending the bells and sweeping the grounds.
The Imperial Commissioners (Cāifǎngshǐ) Wáng Zhìyīn and Hèlán Wù jointly recorded auspicious omens and presented them for imperial report.

Emperor Ruizong’s latent aspirations were in accord with these dreams, and by imperial decree, the signboard reading “Jianguo” (Founding State) was changed to “Xiangguo” (State Chancellor)—this being because the various Emperors had ascended the dragon throne from the position of Prince Consort (Xiangwang).

An imperial edict was further issued to the Venerable Minggan of Fo-shou-ji Monastery to jointly oversee the meritorious works, ensuring that the local prefectures and offices were not unduly disturbed.

Jia Zeng, Secretariat Drafter; Cui Zhao, Palace Attendant; Lu Yi, Assistant to the Director of the Imperial Secretariat; and Cen Xi, Palace Attendant and Chief Councilor, all contributed their emoluments to establish these karmic conditions—some initiating the original resolve, while others provided the power of external protection.

While serving as a high official under the Xuanzong Emperor, he transmitted his spiritual essence to the Prince of Lu. Upon the Emperor’s accession to the throne, on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, the Retired Emperor personally inscribed the temple’s plaque. By imperial decree, the Venerable Tandi, along with two disciples and one court official, were sent to deliver the edict, the ceremonial banners and flowers, and the temple plaque; they arrived to receive them and hoisted them in the temple.

Yun Dao transformed the Liang Garden through his teachings and brought glory to the tree of fortune; yet, with a hundred-year lifespan being finite and the four elements constantly shifting, he passed away in a separate courtyard of the monastery.
He was buried in the eastern suburbs of the present capital, where the monastery’s manor, stupa, and pavilion remain.
At that time, he was hailed as the founding patriarch of temple construction.
After Yun passed away, in the fourth year of the Tiānbǎo era, a great pavilion was built called Páiyún.
During the Zhìdé era of Emperor Sùzōng, the East Pagoda was constructed; it was named Pǔmǎn and its construction was completed in the tenth year of the Dàlì era of Emperor Dàizōng.
Some say that the monk who built the stupa was able to manifest multiple bodies to travel and convert others, making his spiritual rank unfathomable;
Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti were painted and sculpted by the court artist Wu Daozi.

Furthermore, in the fourteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, when Emperor Xuanzong returned from his eastern tour of Mount Tai, he issued an imperial decree for Cheng Dao to travel to the kingdom of Khotan to copy the likeness of the Heavenly King (Indra), which was then painted upon the temple walls.

The monk Zhiyan solicited contributions from the public to paint the *Three Vehicles’ Stages of Entry into the Path* on the northern wall of the West Storehouse; all praised it as a masterpiece of extraordinary excellence.
The current halls and buildings were all constructed after the fire of the Dàshùn era and were subsequently renovated by Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty.
The wall paintings by Gao Yi, a court attendant for imperial edicts (Hanlin Dazhao), were at that time universally acclaimed for the excellence of their brushwork and ink technique.

Biography of Huiyan from Huayan Temple in Hangzhou, Tang Dynasty: Huiyan, whose secular surname was Chu, was originally a native of Henan. He served under Huichang and Shouru. [End of] Biography of Huiyan from Huayan Temple in Hangzhou, Tang Dynasty.
While eating vegetables in Qiantang, he settled his family there.

He observed that Tan Ying possessed brilliant virtue; from birth, he was naturally liberated and profoundly realized the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), thereby honoring the fundamental source of goodness.
From his first thought until his renunciation of the household, he took Huichang as his teacher.
Master Chang’s virtue was complete and all his resources were sufficient; advanced in years and revered for his conduct, he had long served as a model for others.
Furthermore, he observed that [his disciples] did not depart from benevolence for even a single moment, and he told his disciples:
"The unsurpassed Way has purity as its foundation.
If one can employ their mind for even a single thought-moment, I have never seen anyone among them who lacks sufficient learning."
"It has been a long time since there has been a true monk in the region south of the Yangtze;
perhaps this youth shall serve as the Dharma drum to let both the distant and the near hear [the truth].
Such was the manner in which he was already distinguished by the discernment of a master of realization.

In his native district there was the ancient Huayan Temple; as it occupied land surrounded by mulberry trees, it was situated near the ancestral graves of Master Xuánlǐ. During the period when the Sui dynasty lacked vigor, the monastic buildings fell into ruin; as its fame shifted like a valley stream, its traces were likewise occasionally abandoned.
During the early Tang dynasty, it was reconstructed by recruiting faithful patrons.
In the *Wénmíng* era, an imperial edict permitted the restoration of its original scale and dimensions, while also relocating its foundation.
With mountains behind and water before, his movements traversed these scenic wonders.
At first, he received full ordination under Tianzhu; next, as a *Senglü*, he resided at Yixianju; and later, with venerable virtue, he presided over Huayan.
The three monasteries followed one another in bringing all beings equally to the Way; for the Way is omnipresent, yet it manifests through the shifting of its teachings.

I, Lan, have long taken it as my duty to compassionately rescue and aid all creatures, and thus I proposed that the flowing stream by the lake in front of the monastery be designated as a sanctuary for the release of living beings.
At that time, the Prefect Yuan Congli, encouraged by this, entered deeply into the gate of compassion and prohibited [hunting] within six *li*.
The Magistrate Yang Minyan, moved by a dream, further expanded the prohibition to ten *li*.
Thus, with their necks arched and tails flicking, they bobbed up and down, gasping for breath, unaware of any harm and able to fulfill their natural instincts.

Lan further considered the scriptures and images to be paramount; consequently, he had four images painted in the hall, with Maitreya as the foremost, and cast three hundred and fifty gilded bronze statues, with Amitābha as the foremost;
he also transcribed over two thousand fascicles of sutras, with the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* written in gold letters as the foremost.
By virtue of such merits, which resulted in rewards manifest in this very life—the Emperor posthumously conferred upon his father the title of Prefect of Hezhou;
and Wuliang, the Right Attendant-at-Horse and Duke of Shu, was his elder brother.

During the days he was engaged in his studies, the Dragon appeared at Linhu Lake; everyone went there to witness it, yet Master Shu remained composed and did not leave his desk. Such was his dignified bearing.
In the early years of Emperor Minghuang’s reign, Master Shu served as a lecturer to the Emperor, who held him in high esteem.

Upon returning home to visit his mother, she was already one hundred and ten years old, and his brothers were all advanced in age; thus, in the place where he attended to her morning and evening needs, he did nothing but preach the Dharma.
He passed away at the temple he had built at Linping in the twenty-second year of the Kaiyuan era, having been ill for some time; he was eighty-four years of age.
The monks Mingliao, Da jue, Puxian, Shenman, and Huai sun all participated in his dharma lineage and enshrined the dharma-relics within the foundations beneath Xili Cave.
Xu Anzhen, Vice Minister of Works, composed a stele inscription to extol his virtues.
Furthermore, Shi Shouru of Aitong Temple in Min was diligent in exhorting and converting others; the people of Yue Shang flocked to him like a gathering of ants.
He established a secluded hermitage to provide relief for the masses, prioritizing altruism.

In the tenth year of the Kaiyuan era, he constructed a bathhouse at the temple; however, as the terrain was steep and high while the clear spring flowed below, a well-sweep was useless. Fetching water required a long walk, which ultimately proved laborious.
His thoughts did not reach this point, and thus he had no way to alter his plans.

Suddenly, one night, the lower stream was completely drained; some twenty paces from where the bathhouse was to be built, a clear spring burst forth. People of the time called this a miraculous work of the unseen, saying that the spring had been moved there by divine power.
The people of the Seven Min regions all placed their faith in him, until he finally passed away in a side room of the Wenshi (Warm Room) Monastery.
Biography of Xuanlang of Qingtai Temple in Dongyang, Tang Dynasty: Shi Xuanlang, whose courtesy name was Huiming, was surnamed Fu.
His ancestors were from Puyang Commandery and belonged to the lineage of Lord Zheng, the Governor of Jiangxia.

During the era of the Cao Wei dynasty, they sought refuge in the region east of the Yangtze River; he was the sixth-generation descendant of the Great Master Xi of the Liang dynasty and subsequently became a native of Wushang.
When her mother, Lady Ge, was first pregnant, she dreamed that she was riding a sheep-cart, flying through the air and treading upon the void, after which she felt her body grow heavy.
From that time forward, she could not bear even the scent of pungent vegetables or blood.
Even when she was nearly ready for childbirth, it was as if she were still in a deep sleep.
After awakening, his mind became light and his body peaceful; he did not cry like an infant, but instead smiled with a gentle, open expression.
At the age of nine, he left home to become a monk; when his teacher taught him the scriptures, he could master seven pages a day.
On the nineteenth day of the intercalary fifth month in the first year of the Ruyi era, by imperial decree he was ordained and assigned to Qingtai Temple.
Upon reaching the age of twenty, he traveled far to seek out Master An of Guangzhou, where he received the full precepts.
Having first studied the disciplinary codes (*vinaya*),
he further read extensively through the sūtras and śāstras, investigating their points of agreement and divergence, with a particular focus on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
He often lamented that although ancient masters had composed commentaries and sub-commentaries, their judgments were not entirely fair or impartial.

In the past, while at Miaoxi Temple in Kuaiji, I discussed the secret essentials with Chan Master Yinzong; although we mutually acknowledged each other’s views, the fundamental principles were not fully exhausted.
Hearing that the Tiantai school could clear away the stagnations of the assembly and lead one toward the single principle, I therefore went to Dhyāna Master Huikai of Tiangong Temple in Dongyang.
Wei inherited the lineage from Zhivi of Kuozhou—at that time, it was commonly said that Wei was the reincarnation of Xu Ling and a high disciple of Master Guanding.
Lang attached himself to him and did not mind poverty or hardship.

He mastered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Mohe zhiguan*, the *Chanmen zhang*, and other such works; regarding the scriptural traces of every school, his investigations reached the highest degree of precision.

Later, following Master Sengcong, he re-cultivated the method of contemplation (*guanfa*). He was extensively proficient in Confucian texts and simultaneously well-versed in the principles of Daoism, such that there was nothing he did not survey.
Although he was conversant with various philosophical views, he uniquely took "cessation and contemplation" (*zhiguan*) as the path for entering the Way and the domain for settling the mind.

Although the various sages have successively contemplated this, they take the compassionate wisdom of Avalokiteśvara as their practice and excellent ford; they let their minds roam within the Ten Vehicles, aligning themselves with the profound stillness of the Three Contemplations, benefiting all beings through the Fourfold Accommodation, and realizing the universal pervasiveness of the Six Identities.
Although his mind had reached beyond the realm of material things and his body grew weary of the human world, he cast aside his former dwelling and resolved to reside among the forest thickets.
He practiced the eighteen kinds of dhūtas and the twelve ascetic observances, secluding himself in the cliffs of Zuo Xi; consequently, he took this as his title.
He sat alone in a single room for over thirty autumns, wearing garments of hemp and flax and subsisting on coarse vegetables.

Having a vow to be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, he understood that this must be supported by meritorious deeds; thus, he constructed the walls of his hall and painted images of Avalokiteśvara and Piṇḍola-bharadvāja.

Thereupon, he burned incense and concentrated his mind, whereupon five-colored divine light immediately manifested; both monastics and laypeople beheld it together and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Thereafter, sometimes monkeys would come to hold his alms bowl, and at other times flying birds would settle to listen to his preaching of the sutras.

At that time, a blind dog came to the mountain gate, howling loudly and rolling on the ground. Daolang took pity on it and, with refined incense and sincere devotion, performed a repentance ritual for the dog; before ten days had passed, both of its eyes were suddenly restored to sight.
In the sixteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, the Prefectural Governor Wang Shangke invited Lang to leave the mountains and reside temporarily below the city.
Lang declined on the grounds of illness and returned to his original dwelling.
Thereafter, he taught others without weariness and gave lectures regardless of whether a large assembly was present.
He wore a single *uttarāsaṅga* for over forty years and never changed his single *niṣīdana* throughout his life.
In eating, he did not indulge in rich flavors; in his dwelling, he necessarily occupied a humble room.
He would not light a single candle unless for the purpose of seeking out the scriptures;
he would not take a single step unless for the purpose of beholding the countenance of a Sage.

His subtle conduct and cultivation of the mind were such that he strictly adhered to the regulations of the Vinaya; consequently, śramaṇas from distant regions and elders from neighboring territories flocked to his residence until it was filled to capacity, gathering there of their own accord like winter sunshine or summer shade.
As the temple buildings were in a state of decay, he instructed the monk Lingbing to construct new halls, shrines, and images, and to build two successive brick stupas.
For the painting work, he did not use ox-hide glue, but instead prepared all the materials with fragrant liquid.
The teachings of Tiantai flourished so greatly; how could this not have been due to this?
One day, he turned to his disciples and said:
"My various affairs are now concluded, and my years are drawing to a close!"
On the nineteenth day of the ninth month in the thirteenth year of the Tianbao era, he passed away from a slight illness at the age of eighty-two, having spent sixty-one summer retreats as a monk.
He established a stūpa at the site of the rock cave; during his lifetime, he constantly composed the *Fahua jing kewen* (Outline of the Lotus Sutra) in two fascicles.

His disciples to whom he transmitted the Dharma were: Daobin of Longqiu Temple in Quzhou; Huicong of Jing’an Temple; Fayuan of Fahua Temple in Yuezhou; Shen’ung; Shouzhen of Foye Temple in Changzhou; Daozun of Ba’en Temple in Suzhou; Daoyuan of Dabao Temple in Mingzhou; and Qingbian of Kaiyuan Temple in Wuzhou.
"At the age of seven, I aspired to the Way and sought a teacher with all my heart;
in less than three years, I had mastered more than half of it!
One who practices this Way is called Zuoxi."
"Furthermore, his transmission of the Dharma is designated as that of the Fifth Patriarch!
The śramaṇa Shenxiong of Yushan has produced a true eulogy!
The lineage verse says:
Observing the period prior to the Tang dynasty, those seeking ordination were permitted to choose for themselves a master of renowned virtue.

In recent times, however, official ordinations have been conducted by assigning candidates according to their order of arrival; this has been managed by established administrative offices, so that the candidate no longer acts of their own accord.
Is it not precisely this that Lang seeks in his pursuit of the precepts?
In this way, teacher and disciple refine one another, giving rise to both affection and righteousness;
were they instead to wait until the moment of crisis to request such instruction, it would be as futile as chasing a wild horse across the plains.

Biography of Huiming of Fuchuan Temple in Huzhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Huiming’s secular surname was Chen; he was a descendant of Chen Shi, the Grand Marshal of Taichou during the Han dynasty, and his family had resided in Yingchuan for generations.

When the Yongjia Emperor fled south, [Zhi]zu served as a secretary to the Minister of Education. His great-grandfather, Zhongwen, assisted in the founding of the Chen dynasty and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Danyang.
Zu himself served as the Magistrate of both Shuangxi and Gushu counties.
His father served as the Magistrate of Lanling, and thus he was a native of Lanling.

From the very day his mother conceived him, he observed the precepts of the Buddha: his feet refused to tread upon the grounds of a kitchen garden, and his mouth would not taste from vessels containing raw meat.
In a divine dream, he had a vague vision as if hearing the sound of the Dharma.
Shortly thereafter, he was born; when he gradually reached the age of childhood, he finally prayed to renounce secular life, and his parents both consented.
When he received full ordination, it was the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era.
He studied the Vinaya-piṭaka and once said to others:
"In ancient times, when punishments first became excessive, Bocheng Zishu withdrew from the world."
"Although I have not abandoned the monastic precepts, how vexing it is that contentious debates are so rampant!
If only the method of 'mind-sealing mind' were reached—how sublime it would be!
Thereupon, he traveled west to Fangyan, where his spiritual ground was suddenly opened.
During the Tianbao era, he made a vow to reside at Mount Qingliang; however, as the Huai and Bi rivers were blocked by military forces, he immediately turned his steps back.

There, he encountered a Zen practitioner with whom he traveled to Wanling, where he established three *aranya*s (monasteries) at Upper Shimen. When large tigers came to cause disturbance, he treated them as if they were barking dogs.
At that time, during a severe famine, whenever a band of robbers intended to arrive, they would invariably shout out to give advance notice; such instances occurred repeatedly.
Previously, the people of this district were fond of hunting with arrows and nets, but after he transformed them through his enlightened teachings, they all burned their snares, nets, and weapons.
In the fifth year of the Tiānbǎo era, he settled at the Yūpō Dōcháng.
There was a Master Yù—of the lineage of Sīzōng of Bái-tǔ—who, though his traces were near and his conduct subtle, was unrecognized by the world. Upon first meeting him, [Master Yù] said:
"The Bodhisattva who transmits the teachings of the Southern Patriarch—why have you come so late?"
On another day, they ascended the peak of Yubi together and saw a mountain to the southeast that stood out with its lush, azure majesty.
Addressing Master Yu, he said, "I have long shared a karmic affinity with this mountain."
In the eighth year of the Tiānbǎo era, there was an official decree.

The regional governor, Wéi Nánjīn, recommended him for his lofty conduct; a formal petition, signed by both monastics and laypeople, requested that he be enrolled in the Ninghuà Monastery within the prefecture.

Ming firmly declined and instead registered as a disciple of Fuchuan—this being the very peak he had gazed upon from Yubi in the past and the site of the former residence of Wu Jun of the Liang dynasty. The local Gazetteer states:
"To the south of the Green Mountain, two ancient Buddha statues were unearthed; their date of origin remains unknown."
At the place where the image was obtained, a miraculous spring gushed forth, and for this reason it was named "Buddha Creek.
Beside the spring is an ancient shrine to the King of Wu; the local customs involve licentious sacrifices, with offerings of livestock being made in excess.
Thereupon, they moored for the night near the temple; suddenly, thunder and rain arrived in torrents, felling trees and blowing away roof tiles.
After a short while, the rain ceased and the moon emerged, and they beheld a man whose retinue and guards were most magnificent.

Ming said, "Householder, you were a worthy man while alive and have become a luminous spirit after death. Why do you allow the common people to be constantly offered as blood sacrifices? Do you not realize that this matter brings calamity upon your own karma?"
The deity said, "This was not my original intent; it was done by others.
After he had performed repentance and prostrations repeatedly, the deity consequently conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon him.
The deity joyfully said, "If you, Master,
wish to relocate the temple, I, your disciple, am willing to relinquish this site to be forever offered as a Zen monastery.
Subsequently, the temple was indeed moved to the side of the shrine, where they discovered an inscription on the bottom of a bronze basin containing the two characters "Huiming" (Wisdom-Brightness).

In the first month of the first year of the Jiànzhōng era, he manifested illness; on that day, the water in the courtyard turned the color of spring dye, mountain rain darkened the daylight, and fierce tigers circled the walls before departing with mournful howls.
On the twelfth day, he suddenly passed away at the age of eighty-four and with fifty-one years of monastic seniority.
On the twelfth day of the second month, a stupa was erected for him on the western mountain of the monastery.
His Dharma-transmitting disciples were Huixie, Huimin, and Ruizhi—three who were like Śāriputra or Śroṇakoṭiviṃśa.
Among his Bodhisattva-precept disciples, the Regional Inspector Lu Youping, Yan Zhenqing, Guduwensu, Du Wei, and Pei Qing were profoundly steeped in the flavor of Chan.
Bi Zhou composed the inscription for his stupa.
Biography of Ziyu of Dayun Temple in Huzhou during the Tang Dynasty: The monk Ziyu, whose courtesy name was Zhenying, was surnamed Shen and was a native of Deqing in Wuxing.
His ancestors had lost their state to Chen, and thus they took that as their clan name; he was a descendant of the Lurid Princes mentioned in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Yu was born with such innate intelligence and wisdom that he required no formal instruction from a teacher.

Before his hair had even reached the age of total youth, he took leave of his parents to leave the household life. During the year of the Great Pardon (Ruyi nian), when people were granted ordination, he tore his robes and shaved his head, casting aside worldly affairs, and received the precepts at Dafuxian Temple in the capital city of Luoyang.
He prayed with such earnest devotion that he could not even find time for a brief rest.

On the evening of the third day, he beheld a divine being standing solemnly before his eyes; appearing and disappearing in an instant, sometimes identical and sometimes different—could this not be the fruit of his utmost sincerity?
Thus, he kindled the lamp of the Tathāgata and wore the seal of the Bodhisattva.

Having realized the holy truth, he returned to the Great Cloud Dharma-assembly; that he firmly grasped the handle of the Vinaya and brought the monastic administration into orderly operation was indeed most fitting!
Yu’s conduct has always been pure and profound; he is without blame and without fame.

He causes the scholars of the world to have those who follow external paths and those who are icchantikas—whose minds are like whirling winds and whose words gush forth like springs, disturbing my holy teaching and undermining my wondrous gate—but Yu meets them with composure and entices them with skillful means, so that none fail to bow their heads, humble their countenances, and receive his instructions!

He constantly performed the ritual of paying homage to the names of fifteen thousand Buddhas, combined with the Compassionate Repentance, circling the altar once every day and night, or perhaps once every two or three days.
At night, nine holy monks would descend to the place where he was performing the repentance; they would walk the path together with him and then depart with a snap of their fingers.
Sometimes, when there was no lamp or candle at night, he would mentally and verbally recite this mantra; a circular light would then illuminate the room, as if he were sitting within the moon.
Such occurrences happened frequently.
Depressed that the entire district lacked a stupa or temple, Sengyu resolutely conceived the plan to construct one.
With a single chant, they harmonized in unison, thereby completing the sacred hall.
Over his lifetime, he transcribed the Tripitaka three times, totaling sixteen thousand fascicles.

At the beginning of the Tianbao era, Dharma Master Zu of Lin’an died; after three nights had passed and he was about to enter hell, he saw in the underworld that Huǐ had led him before the King of Hell, who said to him:
"This man can lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; Your Majesty should grant him clemency.
The King said, "I have only heard that Master Yanlun can lecture; why do I not hear this master's name?"
When he had thus pleaded three times and the king could not bring himself to humble him, the king consequently pardoned him.
It so happened that a villager had given him a cow that was naturally barren; yet it subsequently yielded milk. Such was the nature of his spiritual resonance.
In the autumn of the eleventh year, he passed away while sitting in dhyāna.

In the spring of the twelfth year, when they were about to open his spirit-casket and cremate him, his countenance remained unchanged, as if he were still alive. Although the growth of a beard at Shaolin and the cultivation of hair at Qichun are remarkable, how could these alone be considered extraordinary?
Yao Dan, Acting Censor-in-Chief and Great Master of Judicial Review; Yao Ji, Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial; and Prefect Yang Huicai, all joined him in placing their faith in him.
Biography of Shi Weishi of Xiangshan Monastery in Cixi, Mingzhou, Tang Dynasty: Shi Weishi, whose secular surname was Tang, was a native of Fuyang.

As for this man, he purified his conduct through ascetic practice (*dhūta*) and cultivated his mind through meditative observation (*dhyāna*). He dwelt in serene stillness, sitting for long periods without sleep.
Initially, his mother suppressed his aspiration, not permitting him to shave his head and don the robes of a renunciant.
Soon after, the cage opened and the birds flew away; from the caves on the bank, springs gushed forth. He emulated Sudhana’s travels for universal study and shared Kashyapa’s disciplined practice.
During the Tianbao era, he went to Mount Ruoshu in Mingzhou, where at night he heard a spiritual voice announce:
"This is a sacred site of the Sage Dapeng; it is truly a famous mountain!"

The following day, he ascended the mountain; its grottoes were deep and winding, and its rocky cliffs rose sheer like chiseling. Abounding in such exquisite and extraordinary features, it was truly a sacred realm.
There was a great footprint of the Buddha; when he inquired of an old hermit of the mountain, he replied, "This auspicious sign first appeared during the Kaiyuan era."
He subsequently resolved to dwell there, with the intention of making it his lifelong home.
At that time, the sea pirate Yuan Chao had gathered like swarms of bees and ants, dividing his forces to plunder and slaughter the innocent.
Upon reaching Mount Xiangshan, the multitude all fled in haste.
Shi alone remained at his seat with eyes closed; he first blocked the entrance of the cave with a large rock.
As there were approximately two or three hundred bandits, he further hauled a massive stone over two zhang wide to press down the mouth of the cavern.
Shishi actually let out a cry and raised him up with his palms; the bandits bowed in prostration to thank him and departed.
The people of the town held him in high esteem and subsequently established a vihāra for him, which was completed in less than two years.

In the eighth year of the Dali era, the Prefect Pei Jing petitioned for the imperial authorization to inscribe the plaque for Xiangshan, and by imperial decree, seven monks were ordained and their names enrolled there.
In the winter of the second year of the Zhenyuan era, he manifested illness and passed away at the temple, attaining parinirvāṇa while sitting in the full lotus posture.
He was sixty-two years old in the spring and autumn [reckoning], having completed thirty-one years of Dharma ordination (*varṣa*).
Biography of Zengren of Longxing Monastery in Lingwu, Shuofang, Tang China. The monk Zengren, whose secular surname was Shi, was a native of Chenliu in Peiguo.
In the year he reached the age for official registration, he entered the local school.
He cast his eyes upon the records and scrolls of the hundred schools until they entered his spirit.
His mastery of the arts and literature was already refined; yet, when he followed the ranks of the census officials to take the examinations, he did not succeed on several attempts.
At the beginning of the Huichang era, he traveled briefly along the frontier walls and visited the ancient Helan Mountains, where he found a pure site within the White Grass Valley.
Thereupon, he resolved to attain bodhicitta, immediately cast off his scholar’s cap, and returned directly to the teachings of Śākyamuni.
He then cleared the weeds and tied together thatch to build a hut, redoubling his diligent efforts.
Members of the Qiang and Hu tribes vied with one another to arrive and offer him butter and milk.

In the fifth year, the regional inspector Li Yanzuo, admiring his integrity, constructed a separate cloister at Longxing Temple and named it "White Grass" (Bai Cao)—a name taken from the original site where he first began his spiritual cultivation.
He endured having his blood drawn to transcribe various sutras.
In the seventh year of the Dazhong era, Lord Li, concerned that he was becoming emaciated, went in person to exhort him, saying:
"Why do you, Master, seek to benefit only yourself by practicing the conduct of the Hīnayāna?"
"Why do you not cherish your innate nature and uphold the teachings?
The benefit [thereof] would be vast indeed!
Because his stubborn attachments were so rigid, he subsequently composed the "Treatise on the Destruction and Injury of the Three Teachings" to manifest his intent.
The Commander examined it and esteemed it all the more highly.

In the ninth year, while reading the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, he investigated the forty-two arms down to the "Fearless Hand" (*abhaya-hasta*). Feeling doubt, he established a ritual altar and prayed for ten days; then, from the midst of the air, its true seal manifested, with both fists clearly visible to the eye.
He then commanded an artist to paint this arm.

When some people mocked and slandered him, he endured it and once again made a fervent and sincere plea; the artist washed his brush in a bronze bowl, whereupon a single flower of jewel-nature suddenly appeared, its stem, calyx, stamens, and petals all vividly clear, leaving those who saw it in utter amazement.
On the tenth day of the seventh month in the twelfth year of the Xiantong era, he entered parinirvāṇa at Baicao Temple at the age of fifty-nine.
On the seventeenth day of the tenth month, his remains were enshrined to the south of Shuiguan, and a stupa was erected there.
Initially, Ren pricked his own blood to transcribe the scriptures, totaling two hundred and eighty-three fascicles.
He also painted a statue of Vairocana; the pavilion was thirty-five chi high, and the gate was one zhang and six chi wide.
He produced three hanging scrolls illustrating the *Mahākaruṇā-puṇya* and personally authored the six-fascicle *Mahākaruṇā-śāstra*, both of which he stored away in various chests.

As the *campaka* flower spreads its fragrance far when caught by the wind, and as the *śarabha* roars loudly upon encountering a beast, students gathered in a circle and invited him to establish his seat at the Shoushan Monastery in Anlu.
Thus, a crowd of over four hundred people gathered in a circle, holding ritual implements to listen to Ghoṣa’s exposition and casting lots in anticipation of Guptadatta’s deliverance.
This greatly benefited those with various capacities, and many attained the Way.
During the Taika era, he said to the assembly:
"I am not yet weary of my travels among mountains and waters; let none of you detain me.
At Mount Tiantai’s Mount Chicheng, Daoyou once stayed."
"At Huading and Shiliang, Zhiyi once subdued the Māras!
I shall go there to visit them.

Starting from Xiangyang, he traveled by winding paths through Wozhou and Tianmu to enter the western gate of Tiantai, where he reached a level plain. In the valley, there was a peak named Dasha, known as "Pingtian" (Level Field). This was it.
Beholding its four surrounding peaks, lush and verdant, there are stone gates to the east and west, with three wells and a dragon pool.
Entering the stone bridge to the east, one reaches the Sacred Temple; this is where the Venerable Daoyou of Green Robes once thatched a hut to dwell.
Before long, he saw a tigress nursing her cubs, staring fixedly at Hui'an.

Hui'an pressed down on the tiger's head with his staff and said, "I have heard that this mountain is the dwelling place of immortals and the retreat of arhats. I now wish to stay here to practice dhyāna; may you, donor, not disturb me."
After spending the night there, he took his son and departed.

On the twenty-seventh day of the tenth month of the seventh year of the Daiwa era (the *kichi-ushi* year), he constructed a meditation hall (*jōshitsu*), accompanied by a single attendant boy who provided only water and firewood.
In the spring of the eighth year, meditation companions gathered like spokes converging at a hub; through their collective effort, they completed this monastery, naming it Pingtian.
During the Kaicheng era, it truly became a great site of practice.
In the seventh month of the third year of the Huichang era, he announced to the assembly that he would enter nirvana; he was seventy-four years of age.
He ordained the disciple Quanliang, whose secular surname was Chen; having realized the Way of the Master, he was one of those who possessed the "feathers of a phoenix"—a singular talent indeed!
It is said that because [Hui]yuan entered nirvana during the Shangyuan era, his physical body remains incorruptible.

Huida relocated the stupa to the front of this mountain, where this temple was established with a Hall of Five Hundred Arhats. The Regional Inspector Quan Yi of Yongjia painted images of five hundred arhats; whenever they were invited for a ceremony, he would invariably spend the night at Shiqiao Bridge burning incense, and with banners, canopies, conchs, and cymbals, lead them into the hall, where a fragrant breeze would escort them there.
The momentum of the banners and standards bent forward, yet they stopped as soon as they entered the gate.
To the inner side of the stone bridge lies the Shiliang Sheng Temple.
Just as the Buddhist chants began, the fragrance of incense started to drift forth.

First there was a golden bird soaring through the air; subsequently, by the trees and rocks of the grove, one beheld a Brahman monk—sometimes walking, sometimes sitting, sometimes making the gesture of beckoning, or appearing in the form of reclining in mid-air—undergoing a thousand transformations and ten thousand shifts in the space of a single breath.
The Qian family, Kings of Hannan in the Han region, have provided offerings for many years, during which auspicious signs have been exceedingly frequent.

In the third year of Taiping Xingguo of the present Emperor, Zan Ning, the Chief Rectifier of Monks for the Two Zhe Circuits, was summoned to the Zifu Hall and questioned regarding the dimensions and measurements of the Stone Bridge. He reported everything truthfully, and the Emperor sighed in admiration for a long time.

In the eighth year, Daozhe of Futian Temple personally petitioned for a vow to sever his own wrist as an act of ascetic refinement, requesting that this temple be reconstructed. Thereupon, the Inner Palace Attendant of the High Rank, Wei Shaoqin, and Zhang Chenggui were commissioned to reform its architectural regulations, making it appear as if it had been manifested from a celestial palace.
The portrait hall of Master An now stands to the right of the temple.

Regarding the lineage of Weize of Fengci Temple in the Tang capital: Shi Weize was one whose will transcended the mundane and whose spirit dwelt beyond the phenomenal world; whenever he undertook any virtuous endeavor, others followed him like waves following the tide.
It is commonly said:
"An image is a powerful condition for generating goodness; it must not fail to be established in abundance.
At the first stage of contemplation, one is as if facing a stern sovereign."
Next, when the mind is undisturbed, the gate of contemplation will naturally form in the middle stage;
finally, when one reaches the state of suchness and vast openness, how could samādhi not manifest before one?
"Therefore, when we exhort and transform the deluded common people, should we not take this as our primary introduction?
Consequently, whether carved or molded, the images appeared in dense profusion.
He constantly engaged in spiritual cultivation, and within the capital city, he was especially encouraged and supported.

During the Yuanhe era, Empress Dowager Guo of Emperor Xianzong, for the sake of posthumous merit for her mother, the Princess of Qi, commissioned the construction of the Fengci Vihāra; she then sought out and selected those of renowned virtue, and [the Master] was chosen among them to reside there.

Not long after, he heard that there was the Stūpa of King Aśoka at Mount Mù in Siming. During the Eastern Jin dynasty, Liu Sahe had sought its manifestation, so he went there specifically to pay homage.
He then conceived the idea of using the powder of the seven precious gems and, by means of molds and glue, casting and carving a replica that was an exact likeness.
He personally carried [the image] back from Yongdong to offer it for veneration at Cisi Temple; the people of the capital all looked up to him with devotion and faith.

Biography of Mingzhun of Chanding Temple in Chang’an, Tang Dynasty: As for the Śramaṇa Mingzhun, his clan and lineage are not clearly known. His place of birth was originally the Lingxu Daochang on Mount Tiantai, where he left the household life and traveled to various regions.

Upon arriving at the capital, he visited the ancient divine monk Zhiyuan at Beishan in Fanyang, who had carved scriptures into stone and cast them in iron to await the descent of Maitreya, thereby eliminating the perils of water and fire.

Furthermore, at Changshou Monastery in Eastern Luoyang, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was transcribed; at Shengshan Monastery, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was transcribed; and at Yue Monastery on Mount Song, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* was transcribed. All were engraved upon durable stone, intended to ensure their imperishability.

In the first month of spring in the year Wuyin of the Zhenyuan era, Zhun happened to see the temple monk Caishan quarrying stone; the stones were all stubborn and coarse, leading him to realize that the artisan lacked sincerity and the mountain spirit was withholding its bounty.
At that time, Zhen addressed the spirits of the underworld through a ritual manual, requesting them to attend to their duties.
Suddenly, while in meditative absorption, he saw several scrolls containing immeasurable stones; amidst the profound darkness, as if by some divine carving, they were all inscribed with characters.

At that time, the Regional Commander, Duke Cui of Boling, exhorted the various aides of the幕府 (mufu) to each write one chapter; from the "Preface" to the "Exhortation to Resolve," there were twenty-eight in total.
The circular corridors stood tall, and the work was completed in less than a year.
Those who transformed others according to the Dharma were all of this sort.
This was during the eighth month of the first year of the Yuanhe era.
His final whereabouts are not recorded.
The Biography of Youxuan of Baoli Temple in Hongzhou during the Tang Dynasty. The monk Youxuan, whose secular surname was Liu, was a native of Youzhou.

Having long cherished the aspiration to transcend the mundane world, he fulfilled his former resolve upon reaching the age of twenty. He went to Master Xian of Bingzhou to realize the profound accord of the Dharma.

In the second year of the Yuanhe era, he struck his mendicant’s staff and traveled to the region south of the Yangtze River, arriving at Dayun Temple in Kuaiji, where he saw monks of the three studies who had halted their practice of the *śīla-cakra* (the wheel of food) and were entirely lacking in material provisions.
As his profound words elicited responsive echoes, lay patrons provided him with abundant offerings.
Before long, he moved to the ancient Miaoxi Temple on Guishan in the heart of Lake Hong.
In the ninth year, while Meng Jian of Pingchang was stationed as governor in Yue, he visited the master to inquire about the Way; subsequently, a great monastery compound was established.
In the twelfth year, he ascended Mount Nanyue again and took up residence on its summit.

In the thirteenth year, Shang You, the Governor of Yuzhang, held his Way in high esteem and invited him to reside at Dongming Temple—a site established during the reign of Emperor An of the Eastern Jin dynasty—which was then crowded with a large number of monks.
During the Bōreki era, he submitted a petition to change the name to Seifuku-ji and established a *kaidan* (ordination platform) there; subsequently, by imperial decree, it was renamed Dōsō-ji.
All the statues and images within were the result of En’s spiritual guidance and transformation.
In the first year of the Taika era, Imperial Censor Shen Fu further increased his faith and devotion.
Hyeon constructed a five-story Buddha pavilion separately to the south of the monastery; when the work was completed, he said to his disciples:
"Meritorious deeds are inexhaustible, yet one's life has its appointed end."
"There may be things left incomplete; let later generations provide what is necessary.
After my death, you may take my body, lacquer it, wrap it in cloth, and place it beneath the pavilion.
Having finished speaking, he passed away. His disciples specially erected a stupa beside him.
Biography of Shi Zhīyùn of Mount Wutai during the Tang Dynasty Shi Zhīyùn was a native of Zhongshan.

Having bid farewell to his parents from childhood, he came to the Shanzhu Pavilion on Mount Wutai, where he took Master Xiànlín as his teacher. After reciting the scriptures with full mastery, he received the tonsure and ordination.
His countenance was clear and noble, and his temperament stood high and firm; regarding worldly wealth and resources, he had few desires and was easily contented.
Coarse food sufficed for his belly, and rough clothing served to ward off the cold; yet if he possessed even a single inch of silk, he never failed to use it to relieve the poor and the sick.
He traveled extensively to visit and study at various monasteries, participating in numerous lecture assemblies.
He transmitted the two scriptures of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, exhausting their origins and fully realizing their principles.
Later, he hung his staff upon a high peak, retiring to a secluded life to quiet his mind.
During the Yuanhe era, he was appointed by the assembly as the Chief Inspector and Guardian Abbot of Mount Wutai.
Although Huīyùn repeatedly declined the appointment due to the frequent political migrations of the time, his refusal was not granted, and he consequently ascended to this office.
Later, when a year of famine arrived, the temple buildings fell into desolation.

There was Huayan Temple, the place where the Great Sage had once dwelt in truth; although many pilgrims visited, offerings were sparse, and the courtyards and halls were in a state of neglect. Consequently, the community requested that he serve as the Chief Overseer of Offerings for Huayan Temple.
At that time, virtue was not solitary, for there appeared Fazhao, Wuzhuo, and Chengguan.

When Master Guan was composing his *Commentary on the Avatamsaka Sutra*, a vast multitude gathered like clouds; they requested Huaiyun to serve as the presiding lecturer, providing daily sustenance for a thousand monks.
For more than ten years, there has been no shortage of food;
everyone says, "There is inexhaustible storehouse of rice and flour," and over the long years, it has become quite abundant.

There was a monk from a neighboring monastery named Yìyuán—who was also a preeminent scholar of his time—who remarked that since Zhìyùn had long been aware of the temple's permanent assets, his private disparaging remarks were not born of an impartial mind, but were those of a greedy person.
At night, a divine being informed Yuan:
"The Elder Monk is counted among the number of the thousand Buddhas; you have uttered light words against him.
If you do not repent, you shall fall into the evil realms."
Yuan then went to the monastery at dawn to strike his feet in repentance and apology; such was the evidence of this.
When Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty implemented the suppression of Buddhism, Huīyùn fled into the mountain valleys, yet he did not abandon the transformative realm of Mañjuśrī.

Before a full year had passed, Emperor Xuanzong ascended the throne and issued an imperial edict for fifty monks to be ordained at the various temples of Mount Wutai; he also provided offerings of robes and vestments, and the mountain gate was reopened.
Yun served as the head monk of ten monasteries and concurrently as the Director of Construction and Master of Offerings for the Mountain Gate.
In the seventh year of the Dazhong era, he traveled with Huanhai to the Imperial Terrace, where the fourfold assembly established an unconditioned feast (mochae) with exquisite and sublime offerings.
After one month, he addressed the great assembly, saying:
"I wish to let this frail body rest for a while and to quiet my mind and withdraw from the world.
As for assisting in the various affairs of the community, I am no longer capable; I entrust these matters to the wise and talented, that they may continue my legacy."
He then sat upright in a purified chamber and passed away at the age of seventy-seven, having been in the monastic order for fifty-eight years.
The commentary states:
"In the Sangha, these are the administrative offices; they are like the main rope of a net, like the ridgepole of a house!"

From the establishment of the orthodox doctrine by Yao Qin, the capital was recognized during the Wei dynasty; under Northern Qi, the ten administrative divisions were established with assigned personnel, and during the Tang dynasty, the offices of the Monastic Registrar (Senglü) were appointed.
These differ from what is commonly heard: it was during the Zhenyuan era that Zhiyun first began to be enfeoffed as the "Monk-Chief" (Sengzhang) of Mount Wutai!
It is also like the fish, salt, and clams, which the *qiwang* (prayer-offering official) is charged to guard.
The Biography of Wen-zhi of Mount Lühou in Kuaiji during the Tang Dynasty. Wen-zhi, whose secular surname was Zhu, was a distant descendant of Shang-qiu and a native of Xujiang in Quzhou.
Shushi became a monk with the dharma name Weikuan; he was thoroughly versed in many versions of the sutras and śāstras.

Weikuan was summoned by imperial decree to Chang’an, where he resided at Daxingshan Temple. By further imperial decree, he was invited into the Inner Court (Neidaochang), where he was also requested to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
Zhi followed him into the inner quarters.
At the age of fifteen, he could recite such sutras as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and the *Vimalakīrti*.
At twenty-three, he received full ordination; in seven days, he completed the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra, and after two summer retreats, he lectured on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
At twenty-seven, he lectured on the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Over the course of forty years, he mastered the various great sūtras and śāstras; later, he joined with the two meditation masters Beici and Yuji to inquire about the essentials of the mind.
Having become widely learned and proficient, he returned to Fale Temple in Jiaxi to lead a group of disciples.
At that time, a tiger would come to listen to the Dharma, and Zhi would stroke its head before it departed.
Later, when he went to Yongjia, following Zhong Shiliang’s purge of Buddhist establishments, he hid on Mount Dafurong in Lecheng County, practicing only the art of fetal breathing (*tai-xi*).

During the Dazhong era, he was invited repeatedly by Wei, the Prefectural Governor, but would not come. The Governor insisted that he be placed upon a couch and carried out to Kaiyuan Temple in the prefecture, where he resided.

Offerings poured in from all sides; with these funds, he reconstructed the Great Buddha Hall, as well as the lecture hall, corridors, and sacred images, and commissioned the copying of the entire Tripitaka, leaving nothing incomplete.
The Vice Commissioner for Integrity of Yuezhou, Shen Erqing, ordered him to reside at Lühoushan Monastery—the former site where Chan Master Benningben had propagated the Dharma.
Zhi lived there, occupying nothing more than a thatched hut.
On the fourteenth day of the tenth month in the second year of the Xiantong era, he informed the assembly that he was bidding them farewell.
On the fifteenth day, he sat upright and passed away; he was eighty-four years of age and had sixty-two years of monastic seniority.
He was interred at Yungu, where a stupa was erected.
Duan Shi, the Prefectural Governor of Yuezhou, composed the biographical record for him.
Biography of Shi Zongliang of Guo Ning Temple in Mingzhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Zongliang, surnamed Feng, was a native of Fenghua.
He lived beside Mount Yue (Moon Mountain) and was later called the "Moon Monk.

During the Kaicheng era, Liang shaved his head and received the Dharma; he then devoted himself to the Vinaya, adhering strictly to the four modes of deportment without leaving any conduct unexamined.
He said, "My birth was ill-timed; coinciding with the hardships of the Huichang persecution, I went into hiding in deep mountain crags and cave dwellings on my home mountain.

During the Dazhong era, when the state was restored and Guo Ning Temple was rebuilt, those of pure and lofty character were summoned to register their names, and I, Liang, was included among those appointed as abbot."
Li Pin, the Governor of Jianzhou, wrote the inscription for the temple’s stele, stating:
"Those whose minds were pure and whose conduct was untainted numbered twenty-eight, by whom the vacancies were filled."
"The abbot was Guangzhu, while the Vinaya monk was Zongliang and the Chan monk was Quanyou.

Regarding the state-sponsored Tripitaka library, he redoubled his efforts in transcribing the scriptures; he personally sought out authentic original texts, selected the finest paper and ink, and gathered offerings and donations to construct the triple-gate, the library hall, and various merit-earning corridors—all of which were accomplished through the power of Zongliang.
In his later years, he devoted himself exclusively to meditative stillness and did not step outside the temple gates.
The scholar Fang Gan presented him with a poem that said:
"A single pool of autumn water, its bottom always visible; a thousand-foot pine by the stream, its branches never growing."
"How much do those who study the Buddha through the Gate of Emptiness know? Only you, Master, have completely shaved away the flowers of the mind.
He passed away at this temple at the age of eighty.

Hui-liang was constantly accompanied by several dozen śramaṇas, including Guan-shuang, Qi-wu, and Bu-yin; they were all men of pure and extraordinary character who delighted in taking turns composing literary gatherings and forming friendships beneath the forest trees.
He composed the "Stele of Yuelinsi" and approximately three hundred poems; his hymns and praises circulated widely during his era.
Furthermore, he applied himself with keen resolve and ever-deepening devotion toward the two fields of merit: that of the Buddha and that of the Sangha.
Sheng Luo Yin of Jiangdong admired and yearned for Sengliang;
Sun He of Le’an held him in the highest esteem and, in his *Record of Talented and Famous Men of the Siming Prefecture*, listed various scholars and eminent gentlemen before stating exclusively:
"The Buddhist master Sengliang was widely emulated by leading literary figures."
Biography of Fanhui of Kaiyuan Temple in Yuezhou during the Tang Dynasty. The monk Fanhui, whose courtesy name was Defu and whose secular surname was Li, [was a native of] Yuezhou.
His capacity and magnanimity were vast and expansive, and his aspirations and conduct were refined and disciplined.
Since he first received the Dharma, there has not been even the slightest deficiency.
Having mastered the gradual teachings, he reached their most subtle and profound depths.

The school of the *Sifenlü xiangbu shu* (Commentary on the Dharmaguptaka-vinaya) flourished into a profound treasury; those of initial capacity who requested instruction all reached the most profound depths.
In the intervals between his lectures and exhortations, he oversaw the administrative affairs of the monastery.

This monastery was founded during the Liang dynasty; though four hundred years have elapsed, its pavilions and galleries still stand loftily, yet their bracket-capitals and beams have become dilapidated.
Now that it is being renovated, the methods employed are systematic and the construction is flawlessly executed; it has been made exceptionally magnificent—how marvelous!
How magnificent!
Furthermore, the *Huguo jing* pavilion and all the other buildings have been entirely renovated.

Next is the temple’s gate pavilion—which was originally commenced by the late Master Tanli in the fourth year of the Chang’an era—but as it had fallen into ruin, it has now been reconstructed and covered over once again, matching its original design.

Furthermore, during the Yonghui era, the Venerable Master Kang Senghui lamented that the hall and seat where his manifested body resided were too low and cramped; he therefore recruited people to reform the old regulations, which took place during the Xiantong era.
Upon his single word that he would rest there, the lay devotees responded with enthusiastic acclaim.
Later, he passed away at the monastery where he resided; this is the present-day Dàshàn Monastery (Guangshansi).
Biography of Shi Zhiguang of Kāiyuán Monastery in Yā State, Tang Dynasty: Shi Zhiguang was surnamed Cui. His place of origin is unknown.
His vessel of virtue was naturally complete and his roots of the Way were uniquely firm; his transformative influence was grand and elegant, manifesting extraordinary traces.
Whenever any sick person approached him, he would take a piece of bamboo as a staff, point it at the site of their pain, or strike it once, and there was none who did not recover instantly.
As for those with lameness, they would rise; those with crippled legs, they would run. What need is there to mention other minor ailments!

At the beginning of the Qianning era, when the Wang family first established control over Chengdu, the former Governor of Ya Commandery, whose name was not recorded, resigned from his post and traveled east to visit [the new rulers], bringing Guang along with him.
The ruler of Shu, Lady Wang, had long been aware of his extraordinary arts and addressed him solely as "Holy Master.
Previously, during the Xiantong era, the kings of the Southern Man tribes, Jang and Tancho, came to besiege the city; Chengdu was on the verge of falling.
At that time, the Heavenly King manifested in the form of a śramaṇa, approximately five *zhang* in height, with eyes emitting streams of light; the barbarian troops immediately retreated.
Consequently, the people of Shu erected a five-*zhang* image of a monk at Baoli Temple north of the city.
Later, when the official Niu Shangruyü slandered him, military conflict and fires followed one after another; he feared nothing more than the collapse of the Vaiśravaṇa Hall.
Wang Shi then said to Guang, "The Master’s extraordinary arts and moral influence move people's hearts. Taking advantage of this, could you not restore the Hall of the Heavenly King?"

Formerly, when Director of the Imperial Secretariat Wu Xinglu was dreaming, he was commanded [by a deity] to "restore my image. Just as he was beginning the construction, the imperial decree suddenly arrived.
He requested that his spiritual power be used to bring it to completion.
He followed his instructions and moved to the foot of the Heavenly King’s pavilion, occupying a single corner with nothing but a small couch.
The following day, the sick crowded his door, and he collected between two hundred thousand and three hundred thousand coins in daily offerings.
Furthermore, he spoke to encourage others to provide timber, and within ten days it was all transported and piled up, which he entrusted to three officials for management.

Initially, when Guang was at his home temple in Yajun, he resided in half a room within the Kadi shrine hall; with a low door and a thatched mat for bedding, he did not permit women to even reach the doorway.
He possessed only a single bamboo alms-bowl.
At every vegetarian feast, he would receive twenty cash in offerings, which he invariably cast into the bowl.
Once it was full, he would place it in the Buddha Hall, strike the bell to assemble the community, and distribute the contents equally between himself and others.

On ordinary days when invited to a layperson's home for a meal, he likewise maintained a broad-minded disposition, accepting only twenty coins, some clean rice, vegetables, and bean soup; beyond this, he would not allow a single other item. Even when offered much more as a religious gift (*dakṣiṇā*), he would not accept it, and having finished eating, he would depart without any words of thanks or farewell.
Thereafter, his divine efficacy increased further; whenever he encountered the sick, a single pinch or a single shout would cause them to rise.
At times, he would have paper money burned, or have food and drink gathered and scattered.
If he encountered anyone suffering from severe pain or affliction, he would tear paper, dip it in water, and apply it to the afflicted area, which would also effect a cure.

In the first year of the Guanghua era, while the construction of the Hall of Heavenly Kings was nearing completion, he followed the banks of the River God’s pond and chanted incantations over food to feed the fish.
After a night had passed, some ten billion fish, each two chi or more in length, all floated to the surface of the water and died.
I waded through the flowing stream and rescued ten thousand fish, who were reborn together in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Biography of Fazang of Baotai Monastery in Fuzhou, Tang Dynasty. Shi Fazang’s clan and lineage are unknown. By nature he was upright and principled, and he delighted in practicing charity toward others.

Once, at Weichuan, he converted the masses to build a monastery; its Buddha hall and monks' quarters were all magnificent and beautiful, adorned with carved floral patterns, such that the region of Fuzhou hailed it as a grand sight.
Zang suddenly fell gravely ill and passed away.
He arrived at a secluded hermitage adorned with the seven treasures, such as had never existed in the world.
Outside the gate stood a monk of extraordinary appearance and countenance, who spoke out, saying:

“Fazang, although you have built this monastery and it will not fail to yield its wholesome reward, how can you avoid the transgression of misappropriating the property of the Triple Gem? How shall you wash away this stain?”
He revealed his hidden head, and the monk said,
"If you simply transcribe the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and constantly practice its recitation and upholding, will your sins not be extinguished?"
"It may even prolong one's lifespan.
Having finished speaking, he revived.
He personally transcribed the sutra and recited it orally at midnight.
It is said that he passed away at the age of one hundred and ten;
the people of Diaoyin have held him in deep faith and reverence to this day.
The Biography of Haiyun of Mount Wutai during the Tang Dynasty. Shoujie Shi Haiyun’s clan and native place are unknown.
Coming to visit these sacred sites, he began at the side of Nantai; there, he selected a steep and precipitous peak and a secluded forest valley to dwell in solitude.
His asceticism and devotion to the Way were so rigorous and austere that they were difficult to emulate.
Those who followed him were few and not numerous.
When he entered parinirvāṇa, his disciples observed the precepts, washed and swept the relics, and erected a stupa over them.
It was formerly transmitted that Yun was an emanation body of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Menren Shoujie was the son of Gao Lishi; he followed Master Mojian with such diligence that he never retreated.
Yun showed him the way, saying:

"In the capital there is a Chan master named Wolun. Although he is said to be reclusive and obscure, he is in fact propagating the seal of the Sixth Patriarch, which is difficult for anyone of his time to fathom."
"The method of transformation and guidance is like that of the cuckoo bird, which feeds its seven offspring equally.
You must go quickly and follow him.
When he saw Hui-lun, before long after they had begun their discussion, [Hui-yuan] said:
"Your teacher Haiyun has entered parinirvāṇa.
Upon hearing these words, his grief was as bitter as salt and wormwood; he immediately set out for the destination, just as he had been told.
Thereupon, they followed one another’s footsteps and succeeded to their traces, and the flourishing transformation continued from generation to generation.
When the time came for him to manifest his parinirvāṇa, sorrowful clouds gathered and darkened the sky; ghosts and spirits wailed in lamentation, and a stupa remains there to this day.
The commentary asks:
Is Haiyun the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) of Samantabhadra, or not?
Tong replied:
"The Bodhisattva descends to transform beings, not constrained by fixed characteristics; if he should appear as a bhikṣu, he immediately manifests and preaches the Dharma.
If this is so, why would he disturb Mañjuśrī’s realm, causing the distinction between the principal and the attendant to be lost?
Tong said,
"If it were as you ask, one would be no different from an ordinary person!
How could a sage seek after 'mine'?"
Biography of Faxing of Foguang Monastery on Mount Wutai during the Tang Dynasty. The monk Faxing was a native of Luojing.
At the age of seven, he left the household life and did not associate with worldly customs.
He attended to the master’s handkerchief and basin, never shrinking from toil or hardship.
He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, completing the entire volume within a single year.
Furthermore, he recited the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* for no more than ninety days.
Regarding the precepts and monastic protocols, he maintained them strictly without transgression.
Seeking out sacred sites, he took pleasure in dwelling among forests and springs, and was registered as a monk at Foguang Temple.
His integrity was solitary and eminent; whatever benefits he bestowed upon sentient beings, he did not personally take charge of.
He entrusted his disciples to cultivate merit on his behalf, constructing a three-story, seven-bay Great Pavilion for Maitreya, ninety-five feet in height.
The seventy-two honored images and the eight great dragon kings were all magnificently adorned.
The assembly at Mount Tai, with diverse tongues but one voice, requested that he serve as the abbot of the mountain monastery.
This was because he had unified and governed [the community], establishing standards and regulations so that all were harmonious and free from contention.
In the first month of spring in the second year of the Daiwa era, a voice was heard in the air saying:

Among these, there is not one that lacks some form of composition.
Although I have not yet had the opportunity to examine Master Jiang’s *Ruiying Chao*, I have heard from various sources that his words are likewise beneficial for the times.

If one does not preserve what is useful and instead alters the virtuous principles and elegant chapters of the ancients, how is this different from destroying old dykes because they are no longer needed—surely there will be a flood?
Biography of Gwangseo of Jingongwon on Mount Jujang: Śramaṇa Gwangseo’s secular surname was Han; he was a native of Geumcheong-ri in Yingzhou.
In his youth, he studied the Confucian classics and harbored the ambition to assist the state and govern the people.
Repeatedly, a divine being appeared in his dreams to admonish him, saying:
"You possess a great karmic affinity with the Buddha-dharma."
He then went to Zhenrong Monastery to join Fawei, attending to his staff and water jar and performing the duties of a devoted disciple.

After receiving full ordination, he recited the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* until he had thoroughly mastered it; whenever he reached the passage, "Rely on the meaning, not on the words," he would explain it to his preceptor and request further instruction. Fawei promptly granted his permission, whereupon he traveled to Sanxue Monastery in Taiyuan. Through both cold and heat, he studied with diligent perseverance, repeatedly refining his understanding of the *Huayan* and *Dabanruoboluomi* sutras.
He then gave lectures on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Sūtra of Rebirth Above* at two assemblies. Suddenly, he said to his fellow practitioners:

"I recall that in years past, I often reflected upon 'relying on the meaning. Recently, while residing at the Academy, I have now lectured on these two sutras. By exhausting the principles and realizing the nature, and by knowing the fruit through verifying the cause, have I not been able to practice without merely relying on the teachings, thereby avoiding a背离 (contravention) of the practice of the four reliances?"

Shortly thereafter, he took his leave of Jinshui and returned to his former mountain. Carrying the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* upon his head, he circumambulated the Bodhisattva Hall, performing prostrations to the Buddha while turning clockwise six times each day and night.
At that time, it had been three years since the High Ancestor of Jin had assumed the mandate.
His reputation reached the imperial inner chambers, and he was subsequently granted purple robes.
The following year, he was conferred the title Tongwu (Penetrating Enlightenment).
The monastic officials and the assembly earnestly entreated him to preside over the ritual platform, but he declined their leave-taking, refusing to comply.

The officials said to him, "Your Master’s conduct and understanding surpass those of ordinary men; yet you alone seek to perfect yourself. If this fine jade remains uncut, it will surely cause others to weep with blood."
Reluctantly accepting his request, he spent two or three years teaching others, yet Xuanjian persistently sought to be excused from his duties.
Coinciding with the succession of a new, minor king, the monastery was left without a presiding master; the assembly unanimously proposed:
"Who else but Daoyu?"
He replied, "This mountain is a place where guests from all four seas travel; how is it that you have not stepped outside the monastery gates for years?
As the one in charge of offerings, what do you require?"

Although he was thus spared from following [the command], from that time forward, the offerings and provisions were delivered in abundance; for eighteen years, more than one million monks were supported.

One night, clouds and mist arose together, and sleet and snow fell in profusion. Across the bay, a single white ribbon-like stream appeared, about three or four feet wide, which then suddenly vanished.
At the dead of night on the following day, his discarded training robe suddenly returned to its original place; was this perhaps the escorting of the dark spirit?
In the tenth month of the seventh year of the Xiande era, the year of Gengshen (960 CE), he manifested illness and said to his sons:
"The Dragon-like One grew weary of great suffering; the Phoenix-like One sighed at the flowing river. All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; such is the law of arising and ceasing."
Having finished speaking, he passed away like a cicada shedding its shell.
His secular age was sixty-six, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇerī-vassa) was forty-six.
He was cremated at the foot of the Eastern Peak; his sacred relics were collected and enshrined within a stupa, where the śarīra were offered to the faithful according to their circumstances.
Biography of Yanjun of the Guanyin Chan Monastery in Dongjing, Song Dynasty. The monk Yanjun, whose secular surname was Lian, was a native of Xingtai.
From the time of his birth, he was surrounded by a profusion of divine wonders; casting off his bonds with resolute spirit, he vowed to enter the Gate of Emptiness.
From the moment he received the pearl of the precepts, he maintained its perfect luster throughout his life.
Thereupon, taking up his bowl and staff, he declared his intention to travel everywhere in search of the truth; he ascended Mount Heng and Mount Lu, and climbed the peaks of Min and Shu.
Once, having reached Fenglin, he suddenly encountered a deep valley where he beheld a district of radiant brilliance, with the seven treasures spread out in profusion across the plain.
At that time, his companions looked at one another and said,
"How marvelous! Can it be picked up as easily as stooping to gather something?"
Jun replied, "The ancients,
while hoeing their gardens, treated gold as if it were mere rubble.
If you wish to harbor it, you will only hasten your own misfortune."
"I have been waiting for you in my fields where the *guǎn* grass covers my head; I require this to provide for the Sangha of the four directions.
Having finished speaking, he departed and went to pay his respects to the Master of Mount Toudi in Shuzhou, asking him, "Where did you stay when you arrived yesterday?"
Jùn said, "In the Immovable Dharma Hall. He asked:
"If it is said that there is no movement, by what means has one arrived here? He replied,
"Arriving here— how could this be movement?"
He said, "It turns out that originally there was no place to lodge.
However, the Master of the Mountain silently granted his permission.
When I was about to return to Zhao, my route passed through Chenliu and reached present-day Dongjing.

There I encountered the Imperial Protector of Liang, the Duke of Longxi, who was the elder brother of Shi Zhi—the former Regional Inspector of Heyang and posthumously titled Minister of the Secretariat. Although he held a high-ranking official position, he was a fervent believer in the Buddhist school; he engaged in elegant discourse on the profound mysteries, much like Liu Yimin’s devotion to Jia Yuan.
They consulted together regarding the donation of their residences to establish a temple for the Benevolent One.
Huijun did not refuse or resist, seeking instead to settle his body and nature.
Once the meditation hall was completed, he carried on the ancestral tradition; yearning for the Way and exhausting the mysteries of the profound, his halls and chambers became fully filled.

During the periods when the two emperors, Gaozu and Shizong of the Zhou dynasty, were in seclusion, they formed friendships with the scholar-official Jun as commoners; whenever they ascended to the abbot’s quarters, they invariably performed the ritual of kneeling.

Upon their accession to the throne, they extended generous favors to him, and even when he reached the highest ranks of the court, the emperors would always bow their heads to the ground upon seeing him, engaging in lofty discourse and abstract discussion as if they had arrived at a mountain of precious jewels.

In the third month of the Bingyin year, during the era of the Qianzhen Emperor, he manifested illness. As his condition grew critical, his disciples sought physicians and offered medicine, but he closed his eyes, clenched his lips, and refused to eat. After delivering his final instructions to his disciples, he assumed a serene expression with solemn dignity, joined his palms to bid farewell to the assembly, and passed away.
He reached the age of eighty-five and had spent sixty-five summer retreats.
Initially, when he was favored by imperial grace and granted a purple *kāṣāya*, he accepted it but did not wear it;
when he was bestowed the title of "Preceptor of Pure Precepts," he held it but did not use it.

As he was leaning on his staff and appeared emaciated and frail, the Founder of Zhou issued an edict to his attendants not to allow the Great Master to eat a full meal, but rather to have him take *khādanīya* (solid food) only after midday.
His excellence was honored yet difficult to emulate;

his compassionate gentleness enveloped all things, extending from his own person outward to the wider world—truly a single family within three courtyards. In the two halls to the east and west, the assembly never numbered fewer than several hundred.
Over the course of fifty years, he provided for a total of hundreds of thousands of monks.
Among the Chan monasteries in the capital, his was ranked foremost.
On the eighth day of the fourth month of that year, he was buried at Fengtai Village on the eastern outskirts, where a white pagoda stands today.
At the various temples in the capital of the Sun Deity (Rājagṛha), each led forth banners and streamers, while conch shells were blown and gongs struck in succession for two or three *li*.
The number of monastics and laypeople escorting the funeral procession reached ten thousand.
Wang Zhe, the Director of Edicts, composed the inscription to manifest and honor his virtue.
Biography of Shi Congyan of Baotan Monastery in the Western Capital of the Song Dynasty: Shi Congyan, surnamed Mi, was a native of Yan.

From his earliest years, he was known for his circumspection, and as soon as he reached the age of understanding, he was noted for his respectful demeanor. Possessing a noble and upright character, he maintained a broad and open disposition.
When he reached the age of fifteen, his parents granted him permission to leave the household life at Huijiao Chan Monastery in the Bingzhou region.

After receiving the precepts, he traveled along the Yangtze River rowing his boat and discussed the transformation of the sea into a *kūn* fish; his contemporaries stood in awe of him, all of whom came to revere him as their master.
Thus, he set his mind upon the ancestral teachings, seeking to polish his jade-like virtue at the hands of others.

Thus, departing northward from the icy heavens and gazing south toward the cassia seas, he gave no thought to the foul miasmas but only longed for the monastic groves; having the good fortune to encounter Zen Master Longya Mountain and resolve his doubts, he flourished as a realized adept.
In the Bingshen year of the Later Tang Qingtai era, he returned to travel among Mount Song and Mount Shao.

As the capital region began to settle and public sentiment became harmonious, Huayan established a Chan monastery and invited a multitude of monastics to gather there, providing them with offerings and support.

On the third day of the eighth month in the second year of the Kaibō era, he manifested illness and passed away.
In the fourth year, the Xinwei year, his temporary burial site was changed to a permanent one, and he was interred within the multi-storied pagoda.
Biography of Changjue of Pujing Monastery in Dongjing, Song Dynasty. Shakyamuni Changjue, surnamed Li, was a native of Chenliu.
