Thereafter, I cultivated my conduct and put my words into practice; although the Tripitaka remained beyond the reach of my mind, I made the study of the mind my primary pursuit for reaching ultimate realization.
He entered Mount Wutai once more to pay homage at the sacred sites of Miaoji.

Later, in the third year of the Tiānchéng era of the Later Táng dynasty, he first established a small Chan monastery to the right of Lìjǐng Gate in the Eastern Capital, which was granted the imperial plaque name Pǔjìng.
Furthermore, on the third and eighth days of every month, he would arrange for the monks throughout the capital to perform their ritual ablutions.

Whenever the fragrant water was being drawn or the supply of firewood and charcoal ran short, Daohui would invariably order small huts to be demolished and the rafters and beams removed to assist in the cooking fires!

There were princes and kings who looked up to him with reverence and submitted petitions recommending him for the purple robe; he resolutely declined and would not accept it, devoting himself solely to the urgent task of benefiting others through his practice as his own responsibility.
On the third day of the twelfth month in the fourth year of the Kaibao era, he fell ill, yet remained light, at ease, and undisturbed.
On the eleventh day, he informed the assembly and passed away while lying on his right side.
He was seventy-six years of age and had fifty-six years of seniority as a monk (*saṃgha-vassa*).
After his cremation, the *śarīra* relics were collected; they were of five colors, magnificent and beyond counting.

I once resided in the capital and frequently visited this monastery. There, I read the preface to the poem "Presented to Jue" by the Minister of State Tao Gu of Beihai, which was written for Zhang Zhongxun of Xiangdong. It states:

"From the Tiansheng era of the Later Tang through the Qianyou era of the Han, every third and eighth day of both the waxing and waning moons, the great assembly of the capital was bathed. Over many years, the expenditure amounted to one million three hundred and sixty thousand coins, totaling ten million strings of cash."
Although this charitable offering was accomplished through collective effort, it is truly the power of the Master’s public transformation and guidance. Alas!

Beneath these great fires lies the ancient fiefdom of Chenliu; since the time of the Zhou and Qin dynasties, it has been a land of warfare, yet its population is vast and its local customs remain keen and vigorous. Here, boats and carriages converge, and merchants and wealth are gathered in abundance.
In the past, King Hui of Liang was a worthy feudal lord who once said to Mencius,
"How can I benefit my state?
This clearly demonstrates that the transformative influence of ritual and yielding is superior to the mind that craves profit!
Moreover, Liang was but a thousand li from Lu, yet even there the ways differed; how much more so at a distance of one hundred and eight thousand li?
Although King Liang and Mencius were contemporaries, their minds might have differed; how much more so in the case of the Venerable Gautama?
In the past, although Mengzi was entrusted with this culture before it had perished, he was unable to propagate the Way of the White King;

now, when the Venerable Master lived even further removed from the Sage, he was ultimately able to practice the teachings of the Dharma King. Had it not been for his inner purity of the three karmas and outer clarity regarding the six sense objects, using the conduct of supreme impartiality to transform others—how could anyone have received the transformation through a mind of supreme impartiality?
Tao Hongjin further stated:

"Since Mount Ling shrouded the first basket of earth and the ocean of Dharma silted up and flowed away, the jade-like radiance grew dim and subtle words ceased, while the golden staff broke and heterodox views arose."
Only those of the highest caliber contemplate the equality of form and emptiness, wherein both self and objects are extinguished.
A single meal of hemp and wheat is shared equally with the joy of dhyāna;
a single robe, regardless of heat or cold, merely serves to cover the withered body.

"Successively, both kings and ministers wished to present a memorial requesting that the title 'Great Master' (Dashi) be conferred upon him, and they entreated that he be permitted to wear a square-cut robe dyed purple; however, [the Master] firmly declined each time," and so forth.
Zhang Zhongxun presented Jue with a begging bowl, a staff, and straw sandals, composing a five-character verse for each item and carving them upon a small stele.
Such was the manner in which eminent figures and great scholars distinguished themselves.
Biography of Shi Yong’an of Ba’en Temple in Hangzhou during the Song Dynasty. Shi Yong’an, surnamed Weng, was a native of Yongjia in Wenzhou.
In his youth, he was pure and profound, with inner brilliance that accorded with principle.

He encountered the Great Master Hui-zheng of the same commandery, who was like a phoenix crying out from the Yueqiao Mountains or jade polished in the Lan-tian fields; he had mastered the *Wenxin* and immersed himself in the depths of profound learning. Because [Hui-zheng] had emerged from the school of Sun He, the Shiyi (Supplementary Official) of Le'an, [the young man] harbored a heart of admiration and went to pay his respects, requesting ordination.

However, his character was lofty and independent, making it difficult for him to find companions; thus, he treated worldly affairs with indifference, following along as smoothly as a ring. This was likely because, having attained early wisdom, he sought out a master.

During the Tiānchéng era, while accompanying [his teacher] on a journey to Hangzhou, he suddenly conceived the intention to follow twelve *dhūta* practitioners. He secretly fled, intending to ascend the Mínglǐng mountains to seek instruction in the Chan school.
As the frontier regions were beset by hardship and turmoil, he turned back and built a hermitage on Mount Tiantai.
Later, upon encountering the Dharma assembly of Master Shao, his many doubts were suddenly dispelled; he returned once more to pay his respects.
He rebuked him, saying:
"By abandoning filial piety and support, you have hastened your own guilt. Now that these traces of your conduct remain here, do you have any plan to remedy your prior transgressions?
Dao'an knelt and replied:
"From the beginning there has been nothing; please accept this as a sufficient response.
Zhengken nodded in agreement.
The King of Hannan, the Qian family, summoned him to reside at Ba'en Temple and conferred upon him the title "Chan Master."

He then took the *Huayan Lilun* as the essential compendium for the assembly and, intending to harmonize it with the sutras, solicited donors to carve woodblocks so that it might be printed and disseminated.
Whenever he received offerings from patrons, he rarely heard of him hoarding them; instead, he dedicated them to the two fields of merit.
At the end of the *kāthā* year of the Kaiyuan era, he burned it, yet the tongue remained.
Though it was repeatedly cast into the fire and forged until its color became like glowing charcoal, it would become soft and pliant upon cooling; it is now enshrined within the Puxian Daochang.
It is said that he was sixty-four years old and had been ordained for forty-four years.
[Biography of Shi Yanshou of Yongming Temple in Qiantang, Song Dynasty] Shi Yanshou, whose secular surname was Wang, was originally a native of Qiantang.

During the time when the two provinces of Zhejiang were independent states, he served as an official in charge of collecting military supplies. During the period when Master Cuiyan Zan was flourishing his teachings, Shoushe abandoned his wife and children, shaved his head to don the dyed robes, and ascended to receive the full precepts.
He once practiced meditative concentration for ninety days on Tianzhu Peak at Mount Tai; there was a bird, similar to a *chian* (a small gull), which nested within the folds of his robe.

Having thus received the definitive resolution of his views from Master Shao, he retired to Mount Xuedou; apart from instructing others, he sat before the waterfall chanting sutras in silent meditation.
For clothing he used no silk or cotton down, wearing only a cloth tunic to endure the year;
for food he took no rich flavors, subsisting on wild vegetables that cut short his midday meal.
King Qian of Hanning held him in the highest esteem and respect, requesting that he perform the Fangdeng Repentance ritual and redeem various creatures for their release.
He was universally loving, compassionate, and gentle; even when others treated him improperly or interfered with him, his countenance remained unmoved.
He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* approximately thirteen thousand times.
He frequently encouraged faithful people to construct stupas and images.

He personally maintained no stores or accumulations and was deeply devoted to the Way of Poetry. He authored several tens of millions of words in records such as the *Wanshan tonggui* (The Ten Thousand Goodnesses Return to One Source) and the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source).
When the King of Goryeo read his records, he dispatched an envoy to present him with a cassock woven with golden thread, a rosary of purple crystal, and a golden ritual pitcher.
He passed away at his residence temple in the eighth year of the Kaibao era, the year of Yihai (1035), at the age of seventy-two and with thirty-seven years of ordination seniority.
He was buried at Daci Mountain, where a pavilion was erected to commemorate him.
Biography of Shi Yizhuang of Tiangong Monastery in the Western Capital during the Song Dynasty. Shi Yizhuang, surnamed Zhang, was a native of Huatai.
Upon reaching the age when one is freed from the cares of childhood and the time for attending a tutor, his spiritual brilliance became manifest and worldly distractions were suddenly cast aside.
He then joined the ranks of the Sudhana at Kaiyuan Temple in this prefecture and ascended to receive the precepts of moral virtue.

Because he delighted in traveling to distant regions, he began his studies at the capital of Luoyang, where he listened to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. His insight surpassed that of others, and as he propagated the teachings to instruct sentient beings, the assembly requested that he reside in the Jiuyao Cloister.
He did not diminish his lawful sustenance, but used it to assist those coming and going.
His compassion benefited all living beings, without interruption from beginning to end.

At the beginning of the Jianlong era, Shen Gong, the Attendant Gentleman of the Left, submitted a memorial requesting that he be granted purple robes; subsequently, more than thirty monks and nuns came to receive instruction under him.
Zhuang was by nature earnest and diligent; for fifty years he advanced in his lectures with constant vigilance, performing the rites of repentance twice daily without ceasing until old age.
He passed away suddenly in the eighth month of the Wuyin year of the Taiping Xingguo era. His secular age was seventy-eight, and his monastic seniority was fifty-nine.
In the second month of the following year, the stupa was relocated to the west of Bodhi Monastery at Longmen.
Biography of Shì Pǔshèng of Guǎ’ài Monastery in the Western Capital of the Song Dynasty: Shì Pǔshèng, surnamed Zhāng, was a native of Lùzé in Shēn Prefecture.
In his youth, his passions were frivolous and shallow; however, he suddenly resolved to head for Huayan Temple on Mount Wutai to serve as a disciple under Master Chao-hua.
Someone asked him, "Why have you crossed mountains and traversed regions to seek ordination?"
"In that Raoyang, are there not surely temples and master craftsmen?
Sheng replied,
"By attaching oneself to a divine steed, one can travel a thousand li in a single day."

"I know that the auspicious signs in the wondrous and pure lands are often obstructed by perverse conditions; yet you have caused me, a mere ordinary person, to swiftly attain the realization of fruition—is this not truly so?
Hearing these words, the assembly said, "A child who acts on impulse possesses such lofty insight; none among us can equal him."
Sheng said, "I am not one of those who lie upon metal and leather armor, finding no weariness in death; my wish is merely to enter the gate of compassion and contemplate benefiting all beings.
Upon receiving full ordination, he traveled south to Lu Prefecture, where he lectured on the *Sūtra of the Rebirth Above*.
Having heard that Great Master Chongfa was transmitting the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* and its teachings were flourishing in the capital of Luoyang, he went there to study under him.
Of all the commentaries and sub-commentaries, numbering in the hundreds, he could recognize them immediately upon seeing them.
Within a few years, he became thoroughly proficient and comprehensive in his mastery.

Regarding the *Chao* (Excerpts) by Zhongshan Zhenbian, which was the version transmitted by his predecessor, he observed that it contained many errors and omissions; thus, he spoke out boldly, saying:
"The details and brevity are uneven, and the analytical interpretations are not appropriate."
He then revised the work by deleting much and supplementing little, producing four fascicles that circulated in the world.
Emperor Taizu Shende bestowed upon him purple robes and conferred the title of Master Xuanchao.

On the fourth day of the seventh month in the autumn of the fourth year of the Taiping Xingguo era, he manifested illness and passed away at Jingtu Monastery; he had reached the age of sixty-three and had spent forty-three summer retreats in meditation.
The disciples collected the śarīra relics and buried them on the western mound of Longmen Mountain at Baoying Monastery, where they erected a stupa to commemorate them.

Biography of Shi Lü of Kaibao Monastery in Eastern Capital (Kaifeng), Song Dynasty. Shi Lü was a native of Fanyang; his surname was Jia. He was a descendant of the late Prime Minister, the Duke of Wei, and there is a biography of him in the *Tang Shu*.
From a young age, he was weak in physical strength yet upright and prudent; he did not engage in combative skills with other children.
When he reached the age of fifteen, he shaved his head at Minzhong Temple and took Zhen She as his preceptor.
Yan Su solemnly exhorted him, yet the conduct he followed did not step beyond the boundaries of conventional propriety.

From the Liang dynasty down to the Great Zhou court, the emperors and high ministers of that interval all held him in profound veneration.

From the time of Yuele’s later generations, the monasteries flourished and remained strictly in accordance with established regulations.

One day he said to his disciple Shuji:

He passed away on the twenty-third day of the first month in the second year of the Qiandé era. He was eighty-one years of age and had held the rank of *dharmagupta* for sixty-two years.
In the third month of the fifth year of the Tàipíng Xīngguó era, he was reinterred at the site of Jùnyí in Běibù; the jinshi scholar Jiǎ Shǒulián composed the inscription for his stupa.
The Treatise says:
When the Buddha appeared in the world, his teachings were translated during that time; the essential point lies in cause and effect, and what is ultimately deduced concerns demerit and merit.
As for demerit, it is the stairway leading down to the three miserable realms.
Blessing (*puṇya*) is the stairway for ascending to the ranks of the sages.
The stairway is the same, yet there is a distinction between those above and those below.
This chapter on "Fate" (*ming*) is titled "Promoting Blessing" because it seeks to benefit others.
Just as the rising and falling of a scale, or the light and darkness within a room, it is known that these two states cannot exist simultaneously.
This is also analogous to the saying: "Fragrant and putrid herbs are not stored together in the same vessel; Yao and Jie do not rule over the same country."
In the sphere of ordinary beings, it is said only that their transgressions are many;
among the ranks of the noble ones, one hears only that their merit is profound.
Because they accord with their nature, [virtue] is easily created; because they oppose their inclinations, [transgression] is difficult to cultivate.
Cultivation has many gateways and practice has numerous paths.
Generally speaking, with respect to the *dānapāramitā*, it brings about the "Infinite Deliverance" (*apratigha*).
It begins with the "meritorious conduct of humans and devas," such as giving food and drink, building bridges, and providing public wells.
Next is the "conduct of a Wheel-turning King," which consists of middling and lower grades of goodness.
As for the higher grade of the ten wholesome actions, it constitutes the "meritorious conduct of Brahmā. These are:
first, constructing a stūpa; second, repairing old temples; and third, requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Next is the "meritorious practice of the Two Vehicles' purity," which is identical to the three grades of goodness, differing only in that the power of its self-benefiting function is stronger.
Next is the "meritorious practice of the ultimate stage," which accomplishes the two adornments and adorns the marks and signs.
By being unimpeded regarding the three spheres and seeing that the essence of all phenomena is empty, one gains extraordinary benefit that extends to the end of the future.
Such being the case, how vast is this merit!
How great!
Thus we know that for a sage, it is easy to bring about blessings. Why is this so?
This is because they are pure.
Ordinary persons are the opposite, for they are easily defiled by external influences.
Therefore, even the merit of threading a needle is performed by the Buddha; knowing this, one should not feel weary of such merit.

Maudgalyāyana kindled fires, Mahākāśyapa trod upon mud, Ajita offered necklaces and precious jewels, and Trapuṣa distributed the bedding and requisites of the Saṃgha. All these were deeds performed by great beings;

they were the skillful means of the Sages, intended so that through their transgressions people would not grow weary of eliminating them, and through their merits they would never tire of acquiring them.

Moreover, since the teachings were transmitted beyond the mountain ranges and the Dharma spread throughout the Central Plains, as the years have passed, practice has gradually become superficial. Therefore, when the monastic community seeks to cultivate merit, they follow the gate of ritual observance; following the example of the former sages who ceased their transgressions, they perform the methods of repentance.
Now, in practicing the "Ritual Repentance," one should quiet the mind and contemplate the heart;

when the mind gives rise to nothing and that which arises has no place to abide, at such a time, both favorable and adverse conditions are without marks—this is the ground where transgressions are extinguished and blessings arise.

As it happened, Huisui was lecturing and providing instruction; through his detailed guidance, Sengcheng attained the essential meaning.
He then transcribed the entirety of the Dharma teachings of the One Vehicle and returned to the East.
Fearing that others might ask from whom he had heard them or by whom they were authenticated,
and wishing to prevent doubt or error, he composed this work to serve as a supporting testimony for the provincial governors.
At that time, Lu Chun, the Prefectural Governor of Taizhou, issued a judgment stating:

"The Acharya Saichō, though his physical form belongs to a foreign land, is in nature truly of the same source; he was uniquely endowed with innate wisdom and possesses profound understanding upon encountering any category of phenomena."

He transmitted the teachings of Tiantai from afar and further encountered the eminent master Sui, a true dragon-elephant among men; together they unified the myriad practices within the single mind and realized the diverse paths through the three contemplations, personally inheriting the secret mysteries whose principles transcend all names and words.
Fearing that disciples from other regions might yet fail to believe and accept this, he requested a seal of authentication; how could it not be permitted to serve as a basis for trust?

Hui-cheng sailed across the sea to the kingdom, bringing the teachings of the Dharma. He designated a mountain as Tiantai and named a temple Guoqing; like the wind blowing and lightning flashing, these teachings spread widely.
The Japanese monk Yōson (Yōson) was his ancestral teacher;
later, he passed away at the temple where he resided.
Biography of Jinping of Mount Xinyin in Huai’an Prefecture, Tang Dynasty: Shi Jinping, surnamed Wu, was a native of Jingzhao.
He left home at an early age at Mingfu Monastery on Yonganshan, where his demeanor was upright and elegant.
He thoroughly investigated all the Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras;
his exegesis and commentaries were so refined that they brought joy to those who heard them.
Moses Chan-guan encountered Master Heze Shenhui at Luoyang and attained awakening; he then remarked:
"How profound it is! For one who does not know from without, how difficult is that which is known!"
Later, he traveled to Tangzhou and settled at Mount Xiyin.
The Regional Inspector Zheng Wenjian invited him into the city to propagate the fundamental tenets of his school.
He passed away at the age of eighty-one; in the third month of the fourteenth year of the Dali era, he was enshrined in a stupa.
Biography of Dao-yin of the Two Sages Monastery on South Mountain in Ningzhou, Tang Dynasty. The monk Dao-yin, surnamed Wang, was a native of Pengyuan.
His bearing was lofty and his temperament broad and serene.
Having early on cast off worldly toil, he vowed to follow the path of profound stillness.
Following the guidance of his teachers, he subsequently aspired to travel afar and attained the sudden illumination of the essentials of the mind under Master Heze.
Upon his return to his native land, his reputation spread far and wide; those who aspired to his Dharma were as numerous as the crowds at the marketplace of Huayin.
Without being summoned, followers arrived in great numbers, and through abundant offerings, a magnificent vihāra was established.

On the final day of the third month in the thirteenth year of the Dali era, he entrusted his final instructions to his fourfold assembly; sitting cross-legged at midnight, he passed away at the age of seventy-two and with thirty-five years of ordination.
The disciple Bianzhen erected a stupa to enshrine them.
Today, the entire bodies of both the Master and his disciple remain incorruptible.

Commentators maintain that because their attainment of the Way was authentic, their physical vessels were likewise so; they are like an alchemical crucible: when the elixir is perfected, the crucible itself is transmuted into gold.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, it is said:
"All bodhisattvas achieve the patience that is like space; they attain a body that does not come because there is no going, and they attain a body that is not born because there is no extinction."
"He has attained a body that does not aggregate, because it is without dispersion or destruction.
Is this not what is meant by the "hidden master"?
This is the biography of Dao Wu of Taoshan in Wenzhou during the Tang Dynasty. Regarding the monk Dao Wu: it is unknown where he was from.
His aspirations were lofty and his conduct unrestrained; his discernment and capacity were beyond measure.
In his later years, he resided at a monastery on the side of Mount Tao in Yongjia, which was the very place where he lived in seclusion and composed the *Zhen'gao*.
During the Dali era, Emperor Daizong established this vihāra for Tao Zhenjun. He meditated here with unwavering diligence, and people looked up to him with deep reverence.
One night, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture; his flesh remained intact without decay, as if he had entered samādhi. It was decided that he should not be cremated or buried.
Five years later, he suddenly raised his right hand in a gesture resembling the transmission of incense.

The local officials and common people marveled at this, and they reported the matter to the throne. By imperial decree, he was granted a purple *kāṣāya* robe and posthumously titled Great Master Shixiang (Real Aspect).
To this day, within the stupa, the people of the prefecture offer prayers, with banners and flowers piled up in abundance.
The commentary states:
Generally, among those who entered nirvana, the raising of a finger was intended to indicate the number of those who had attained the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
In the past, Guṇavarman raised two fingers when he passed away; did this signify that he had already realized the second fruit of the path?
Subsequently, when Dharmakṣema was about to pass away, he bent three fingers.
Huìjǐng, however, clenched two fingers in his fist and pulled them back until they were bent.
Now, as we meet here with fingers extended, are we not all alike?

This is the Biography of Huanxi of the Tang Dynasty’s Capital Region. Regarding the biography of Huanxi of the Tang Dynasty’s Capital Region: Shi Huanxi was a man of unknown origins. He did not hold any official rank.
By nature he was free from constraints, compassionate, patient, broad-minded, and gentle; people never saw him display a look of anger, and thus he was given this name.
Observing the splendor of the state, he arrived at the capital; whether among the nobility and officials or the common people, all extended invitations to him, and he rarely refused them.
His speech was unconventional and his deeds difficult to fathom.
Emperor Dezong heard of him and held him in high esteem.

In the twelfth year of the Zhenyuan era, by imperial decree, a *śīla-maṇḍala* (ordination platform) was established at Yongtai Temple to ordain monks; at that time, Huixi and the Baotang Chan school were specially ordered to receive their precepts, which brought great honor to the monastic community.
On the nineteenth day of the sixth month of that year, he passed away at this very temple.
There was also a monk named Shi Wuce from Yunmen Temple in Kuaiji; he was a foreigner whose place of birth—whether north or south of the Pamir Mountains—is unknown.
Whether Hu or Fan, how could they be distinguished?
He traveled east across the desert during the Zhenguan period, staying wherever he found spiritual inspiration and passing the seasons there.
Later, he settled at Yunmen Temple by Yuexi to cultivate the Way.
However, he was well-attuned to human nature and was thus titled "The Benevolent and Wise" (Lìzhì) by the Indian monks;
tradition holds that he was the reincarnation of the Daoist practitioner Kāṅ Bǎoyuè, a conclusion surely reached through the verification of past events.
Meeting with a man of renowned virtue, they conversed until the end of the night.
Jiaoran of Wuxing inscribed on the wall of the side chamber:
"Of the myriad mountains of Yue, Yunmen is peerless; the Western monk’s ancient countenance is truly named 'Moon'."

"Returning from walking the path after sweeping the stones in the Qingchao, he sleeps beneath the forest trees in meditation, gazing at the pine-snow. The state of his lofty transcendence is thus described in the "Zhòu Cí" (Eulogy on Zhòu). From his youth, he bore extraordinary talent; his nature was in harmony with the Way. Having first cast off worldly fetters, he gradually entered the monastic life.
He received full ordination at the Lingyin Precept Platform under the Vinaya Master Shouzhi, where he listened to the path of the *vinaya* and applied himself with particular diligence.
Within his collected works, he composed verses that expressed his inner sentiments, truly reaching the subtlest depths.
His writings were so elegant and refined that he was hailed at the time as a magnificent vessel of the Buddhist tradition.
Later, he traveled extensively to visit famous mountains, and there were few dharma assemblies where he did not attend as a listener.
Nevertheless, he pursued various disciplines concurrently, reaching the pinnacle of excellence in both secular histories and classical scriptures.

Throughout all my travels, whether in the capital where high ministers and officials treated me with profound respect, or in various provinces where local governors held me in esteem, it was invariably the case that they first entreated me with verses to lead me into the wisdom of the Buddha; the original intent behind my mission of transformation lay precisely herein.

In his middle years, he visited various Chan patriarchs and attained a thorough understanding of the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground. He formed a spiritual friendship with Yuán Hào of Wǔqiū Mountain and Língchè of Kuàijī;
thus, a contemporary proverb went: "Zhòu of Xiá is capable and refined."

At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era, he resided at the East Creek Hermitage (Dongxi Caotang), wishing to cease his poetic pursuits as they were not in accord with the intent of the Chan path; he thus admonished himself, saying:

"Even if one possessed the broad learning of Confucius or the vast erudition of Xu Chen, to spend one's entire day before others boasting of the Way and flaunting its principles would only serve to disturb my true nature."
How could this compare to the solitary pine and a fragment of cloud, facing each other at the meditation seat, where the Way is harmonized without words and nature is shared in ultimate stillness?
I shall enter Mount Zhu and become a companion to the pine and the clouds.
The *Shishi* (Poetic Styles) he authored and his various other writings were all set aside and not recorded.
Looking at his brush and inkstone, he said:
"I have exhausted myself with your service, and you have wearied me with your dullness; for several decades, I have gained nothing at all."
How much more so for you, who are but an external object—what burden could you possibly place upon a person?
Since you abide without mind and depart without self, I shall release you to each return to its original nature, allowing things to be simply things, unrelated to me; would this not be joyful?
He then ordered his disciples to expel him.

In the fifth year, in the fifth month, Li Hong, the former Vice Minister of the Imperial Chancellery, arrived from north of the River having incurred reprimand; he was transferred once more to serve as the Governor of Hu. When they first met, not a single word had been exchanged, yet they felt as if their spirits had merged in a moment of clarity.
I have long known that you are proficient in Buddhist principles, and thus I requested further instruction from you.
First I inquired about the source of the school, and next I asked about the mind-seal; you smiled before responding.
On another day, when the subject of the *Shishi* (Poetic Styles) was mentioned, you explained in detail your long-held aspirations.
The Duke said, "Not so.
He firmly ordered his disciples to retrieve the original draft; upon reading it once, he sighed and remarked:

"In my youth, I once read Shen Yue’s *Píngzǎo*, Huìxiū’s *Hànlin*, and Yù Xìn’s *Shīzhēn*; the arguments of these three masters were by no means equal to this. Why then do you cling to the narrow views of the Hīnayāna and use your former aspirations as an excuse?"

He then recommended Wu Jide, a literary talent from the district who was the descendant of the Liang dynasty Court Attendant Wu Jun; his writing possessed a family tradition, and I held him in high esteem.

During the day, he considered Lu Hongjian his most intimate friend; meanwhile, the Chancellor Yu Gongdi and Yan Luyong Zhenqing commissioned him to assist in compiling more than twenty volumes of the *Yunhai*.
He composed the *Wuzazhu* (Five Miscellaneous Writings) fascicle, employing a style that was remarkably ingenious and daring; he truly did not disgrace his distant lineage of the Xies of Jiangnan.
By day he purified his will and loftily transcended his mind; worldly fame and meager profit were things he could not be enticed by.
He occupied himself solely with the forests and mountains, associating only with practitioners of the Way; thus, throughout his life, he never showed a trace of indolence.
He also established "dark" vegetarian rites (*mingzhai*), following the ancient custom of burning incense on the face, as an offering of food for the spirits and deities.
During the day, he resided at Xingguo Temple in the prefecture and conceived the intention to donate his own clothing and purse to it.
Once there was a military official named Shen Jiao, a native of Deqing, who was returning from the prefecture by night on horseback when he reached Luotuo Bridge; the moonlight was as bright as day.
Seeing several men dressed in magnificent robes and caps, Zhao asked them in wonder,
"How have you come to this place?
They replied:
"The Master Ran is performing a secret retreat at Xingguo Temple to the east of the Shrine of King Xiang; we shall wait for him there.
The next day, Zhao went back to check, and it was indeed a ghost.

Furthermore, when Chang Cheng, Jiu Xu, Qian Pei, and Xing Yi were on official travel and moored their boats south of Mount Lü, they saw several hundred people carrying food vessels and bundles of silk, passing by with cheerful conversation and laughter. They wondered if these might not be the very ones [the Master had described].
When asked the reason for this, he replied, "I have come to attend the vegetarian feast hosted by Master Ran.
At that time, Yan Lugu was serving as the regional governor; having been an old acquaintance, he held him in even greater esteem and respect.
In the first year of the Zhenyuan era, he passed away at Mount Shan Temple.
His collected works consist of ten volumes, with a preface to the collection written by Yu Di.

In the first month of the eighth year of the Zhenyuan era, an imperial edict ordered that his literary collection be transcribed and entered into the Imperial Library; the entire realm celebrated this honor.
Observing his writings, they are tireless and never wearying; they accord with the laws of composition in their clarity and vigor, marking him as a great talent of his generation.

During the day, Zhousheng often associated with Wei Yingwu, Lu Youping, Wu Jide, Li E, Huangfu Zeng, Liang Su, Cui Zixiang, Xue Feng, Lü Wei, and Yang Kui—some in official positions and others in plain clothes—and they would invariably engage in lofty chanting and take delight in the Way.
Since the Way is identical in its essence, we have thus established this friendship from the outset.

Therefore, I have composed the *Biographies of Confucian and Buddhist Friends* (*Rushi jiaoyou zhuan*) and the *Classified Collection of Buddhist Scriptures* (*Neidian leiju*), totaling forty fascicles, as well as the *Hao’nuzi* in ten fascicles; these were widely circulated among the nobility of the time.

In the fourth year of the Yuanhe era, the Prefect Fan Chuanzheng and the monk Lingche of Kuaiji passed by the old monastery together; visiting the Shadow Hall, they mourned for a long time, leaving this inscription:
“Daoan has already returned to the land of nothingness; Huiyuan comes now to visit his former thatched hall.”
"I, too, was among those who entered his gate at that time; let us together chant these fine verses while burning incense.
Thus, there have been a succession of later worthies who have admired his enduring virtue.
Furthermore, there was the monk Fulin of Dashi Mountain in Huangzhou during the Tang dynasty. His secular surname was Yuan, and he was a native of Jingzhou.
His father served as a judicial official in Xiangyang and had long revered the teachings of Śākyamuni.

Lín had been fond of the Buddhist gate since childhood and constantly maintained his integrity and conduct; knowing early on that he must sever worldly attachments, he received the tonsure under Master Qiánzhù at Xuánjìng Monastery.
After completing the full ordination, he personally paid homage to the Patriarch Hézé, whereupon he attained realization of the true mind.
Later, he went to Huangbo, where he cleared away the thatch to establish a dwelling; it eventually became a large monastery where he gathered monastics from all quarters for meditation.
When Huilin passed away at the age of eighty-two, he was interred in a stupa in the fourth month of the second year of the Xingyuan era.
The Biography of Huai Kong of Mount Ding’an in Anlu, Tang Dynasty. Śramaṇa Huai Kong’s secular surname was Shang; he was a native of Heyang.
The son of a wealthy family, though young, was already dignified and solemn.
He took leave of his relatives and entered the monastic life at Guangfu Monastery on Mount Dabu in his home province.
Master Daming, intuitively perceiving that Zhikong’s character and capacity were extraordinary and unconventional, instructed him in the recitation of various scriptures.
After receiving the Dharma, he surveyed the capital region.
It happened that the Chan Master Beixiu was propagating his teachings there, so he went to him to resolve his doubts.
Later, while traveling to Ding’an Mountain in Anlu, he suddenly encountered an old man who urged him to subdue this valley, saying, "I shall receive great benefit from this."
He then tied up some thatch and settled there; it turned out that the man who had come before was none other than the local tutelary deity.
Shortly thereafter, as villagers were entering the mountains to hunt tigers, they saw the monk sitting alone in the air and rejoiced, saying to him:
"This place is infested with many violent tigers, and our villages are not at peace. We pray that the Venerable One will show us a method for pacifying these calamities."
Kong said: "The tiger is also a sentient being; if you slaughter and harm it, it will surely come to retaliate.
When will this cycle of mutual retribution ever come to an end?"
The old monk said, "For the sake of you all, I can skillfully perform a rite to ward it off.
The villager replied, "I am a fool of little knowledge; I only follow whatever instructions are given."
Kong said, "Return to your homes and,
with one mind, establish a *bodhimaṇḍa* and arrange a great assembly.
Kong himself attended the dharma gathering in advance.
When evening came on the day of his arrival, a tiger was lying prostrate before the hermitage with its eyes closed.
Hui-k’ung said:
“Alas, you evil creature! One retribution has not yet been extinguished when you further increase your past calamities by devouring fellow human beings.”
"Heaven has not yet executed you, but once dead, you shall surely fall into hell.
How I pity you!
Having been thus rebuked, the tiger suddenly lingered for a moment and then departed.

The next day, when the vegetarian feast was concluded and he ascended the mountain, the tiger was in front of the hermitage leading its seven cubs; it took the remains of the meal and threw them to them, and each ate its fill.
He performed repentance rites for them, and the seven tigers subsequently all passed away.
The common people were all delighted and said,
"By following our Master and residing here, our customs have become free from pestilence, and for years the grain has ripened in abundance.
They performed their prostrations and withdrew.

At that time, Grand Master Zhang Liao was serving as the Governor of the province; he dispatched an official of his administration, Murong Xing, to invite [Cai] into the province, but [Cai] declined on the grounds of illness and did not rise from his seat.
He then led a group of craftsmen to construct a meditation hall for him.
When his life was complete, he manifested illness and passed away at the age of eighty-three.
On the sixteenth day of the third month in the third year of the Zhenyuan era, he was cremated, and his relics were collected and enshrined in a stupa.
Biography of Shi Huiyan of Liuzhou during the Tang Dynasty. Shi Huiyan, surnamed Miao, was a native of Xiangyang.
His father served as the Magistrate of Judicial Affairs in Dongping.
When Tan’yan was young, he entered Kaiyuan Temple; hearing the sutras, he was filled with joy and sought ordination from Dharma Master Bianzhang.
Master Zhang lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* daily, and Tan’yan constantly followed him to listen, entering into a state of spiritual absorption.
Having mastered the profound meaning, he was further able to lecture and discourse upon it.

One day, he joined a group of companions to travel beneath Mount Hua; intending to ascend Maonü Peak to behold the Immortal’s Palm, his route led through Luoyang, where he visited the Patriarch Heze and attained a comprehensive realization of the Great View.
Having entered Mount Nanyue, he subsequently resided in Liyang; many who attained the Way did so in Jiangnan.
He passed away in the twelfth year of the Zhenyuan era at the age of seventy-nine.

Biography of Xingjue of Guochang Monastery in Jingzhou, Tang Dynasty. The śramaṇa Xingjue, whose secular surname was Liu, was a native of Julu. His complexion was as white as jade. He resided at Guochang Monastery in Jingzhou during the Tang dynasty.
From his youth, he was brilliant and quick-witted, remaining steadfast in his principles; harboring the aspiration to leave the household life, he could not be dissuaded by his parents' entreaties.
Early on, he entered the Yongtai Monastery of his own region, where he received instruction and received the precepts.

Later, while in the capital at Luoyang, he encountered Master Huihui, through whom he attained awakening to the profound principles of the Dharma; he then resolved his mind upon the Way and rectified his conduct.
Wandering through various regions, he came upon an ancient temple in Jiangling, where the halls and buildings were in ruins and all was silent and deserted.
Jue removed his travel bag and hung up his monk’s staff.
The next day, he encountered woodcutters who were struck with wonder and said, "This is Guochang Temple; it has been abandoned for three cycles.

Thus one knows that human affairs arise from mutual causes and the Way follows the convergence of conditions. Scholars arrived, local residents came, and what had been desolate became a flourishing temple.
At that time, the Minister Cui invited him to enter the city, but he declined and did not go.
Offerings and alms arrived in succession, whereby his transformative influence flourished.
He passed away in the fifteenth year of the Zhenyuan era at the age of ninety-two.

This was a poem composed by Sun Wo, the former Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, during his banishment to the south; the details of this matter are recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of Nanyue*.
The commentary states:

Cao Yi lived in the southern region of Mount Yue during his prime; it was already possible for him then, but it remains unknown whether he would have been able to endure the hardships of old age while residing in the remote north.
If he were indeed capable of this, he would be a superior practitioner of the highest capacity.

The Biography of Shi Huimu of Mingxin Monastery in Yuezhou during the Tang Dynasty. Shi Huimu’s secular surname was Zhu; he was a native of Shijiyang, a family that had long been among the prominent clans of the region.

Having been bathed in the tender years of childhood within a family of strict and clear precepts, he was instructed in the Confucian classics until he had grown into a distinguished and outstanding talent.
Intending to follow the ranks of the census officials, he visited Chan Master Chizhen of Juezhi Temple—later posthumously titled Daguān—to subtly offer him a critique.
Mu attained awakening through this.
The following year, he received the tonsure and traveled to Hongjing to pay homage to Master Guanyin, whereupon his mind was suddenly in accord with the Dharma.

In the seventh year of the Xiantong era, he returned to his native village; there, Magistrate Wei led those of sincere faith to establish Qizhen Monastery, attracting Zen practitioners from all quarters who came from afar.

The Intendant of Integrity, Pei Yanlu, summoned Muzhi; when the Jing-sha Hermitage at Jian-shui was completed, he returned it to him as its title plaque. Subsequently, Muzhi resided there, abiding peacefully yet remaining capable of moving on.
At the request of Qi Zhao, an official in Yuncheng Prefecture, he resided at Mount Yusi; he passed away before long.
He was eighty-eight years of age and forty-five years since his ordination. Thus it is recorded.
The third day of the seventh month in the fifth year of Qianning.

The Anonymous Monk from Nanwaya in Youzhou of the Tang Dynasty. The biography of the anonymous monk from Nanwaya in Youzhou of the Tang Dynasty: The Chan practitioner Shi Wangming of Mount Zhurong was exceptionally austere in his conduct; he lived alone among the kilns and hearths south of the city of Yan.
During the Tianyou era, harvests failed in You and Ji, and corpses lay scattered along the roads.
While returning from his alms-round, he heard the wailing of an infant in the ruts of a carriage track; moved by compassion, he took it back with him—it was a girl abandoned by starving people.
She sought cow’s milk to nourish her.
When she was seven or eight years old, he brought her into the city to seek fine silks to clothe her.

By the time she reached the age of maturity, her appearance was so radiant and beautiful that she seemed almost beyond the mundane world; yet, though some mocked and rebuked him for this, the monk never wavered in his resolve.
It happened that Liu Ren-gong, the commander of Yan, was out hunting deer and chasing rabbits when he entered directly into the monks' quarters at the kiln site.
A soldier saw a woman standing beside a monk and reported it to the commander; Liu went there in person to see her and asked for the reason, to which they all answered truthfully.
Liu said, "I, your disciple, wish to collect them; would that be permissible?
The monk replied:
“Very well. Having early proven himself free of stinginess, he personally assisted [the woman] onto his horse.
Upon returning to the residence, Yuan Zhen was found to be a maiden; Liu Yi took pity on her and did not allow her to be ranked among the lower positions.
The Emperor continued to hold that monk in high esteem, regarding him as one who had attained the fruit of the stages of realization.
He constructed a separate vihāra for him to reside in, and Liu went to visit him once every ten days.
When the monk passed away from illness, his disciples entered to deliver the news; the woman was sitting alone at the time, and upon hearing it, she died of grief and lamentation.
Liu built a stupa for the monk as a memorial.

Furthermore, there was an unnamed Chan practitioner on Mount Zhurong who was upright and outspoken by nature; he did not concern himself with formal decorum, yet whenever he expounded the Dharma, he skillfully highlighted the essential tenets of the school, drawing both monastics and laypeople to him like a bustling market.
Once, while drinking wine, he encountered poison; at that moment, he vomited and purged, and his decaying clothes fell away as if stones had split apart, yet there was no pain within his body.
Each time, a snake and a tiger would appear to guard him.
Upon the conclusion of the cremation, a single bone fragment remained, as large as the soundbox of a lute.

The monastic community built a fire and cremated it again; while burning, its color was identical to the nature of the flames, but when the fire was extinguished and the ashes had cooled, the color was white like snow. Is this not the attainment of a "solid śarīra" (relic) from a portion of the entire body?
To this day, his words and phrases are transmitted within the mountains, and a stupa has been erected for him; he is known as the Daoist of Mount Zhurong.
Biography of Xi Yin of Kaiyuan Temple in Hongzhou during the Tang Dynasty: Shi Xi Yin of Bao'an was styled Juchieng and surnamed Xu.
From his youth, he was upright and rigorous, possessing innate spiritual insight.
At the age when one wears the *xī* (a hairpin for children), he developed a fervent desire to transcend the mundane world; his parents could not dissuade him from this intent.
After shaving his hair and returning to the Dharma, he applied himself diligently to his studies, penetrating deeply into the inner sanctum of the *vinaya*.
Furthermore, regarding his refined and elegant sentiments, they were not acquired through artificial cultivation but arose spontaneously from his natural disposition.
During the Guangming era, he fled from the rebels of Chao and entered Mount Lu at Zigui Peak; this was truly a noble retirement.

Nevertheless, on many occasions during the blossoming spring and the moonlit night, or at the setting sun and the lofty autumn, he would compose couplets with refined phrasing and compile them into a collection; these works were often forceful, vigorous, and clear-sounding, becoming widely circulated among the people.
Clad in tattered hempen robes, those who did not recognize him would call him a mountain hermit or a rustic, thinking him utterly incapable.
Yet, having attained the essential meaning of Guizong’s Chan, he propagated it together with others, never being stingy with the Dharma.

In his daily life, he engaged in poetic exchanges with Guànxiū, Chùmò, and Xiūmù; Shèn Yán, Cáo Sōng, Zhāng Níng, and Chén Chāngfú were all retired scholars who served as his companions in the art of versification.
Hiding himself, he became a beacon to which scholars from all quarters flocked; he was as serene and untroubled as water.
Later, when bandits had somewhat subsided, he entered the regions of Jing and Chu, ascending Mount Zhurong, where he roamed with carefree and haughty ease.
In the third year of the Guanghua era, he traveled to Panyu and gained the recognition of the Grand Marshal Xu Yanruo.
In the second year of the Tongguang era, he met by chance with Wei Zhongfu of Julu at Hongjing, and they became close friends through their shared devotion to literature and the Way.
He passed away during the Tiānchéng era of the Later Táng dynasty.

His disciple Yìngzhī took approximately one hundred poems by Yǐnzhī and presented them to Zhòngfǔ, who composed a preface for the collection; the version currently in circulation is titled the Guìfēng jí (Collection from the Camphor Peak).
Next was Shi Ba’an of Lingguang Temple in Jiahe; his secular surname was Xia, and he was a native of Changshu in Gusu.
His spirit and bearing were refined and eminent, and his character and conduct were virtuous and balanced.
In his prime, he was entangled in domestic affairs, yet he vowed to cast them off like discarded sandals.

After receiving full ordination, he devoted himself exclusively to the gateway of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Having thoroughly mastered the essential instructions, he did not wear even a thread of silk; he relied solely on alms for sustenance and slept upon straw mats.

In the past, when Dao’an traveled to Mount Wutai, he lamented that those from the south were unaware of its wonders; he subsequently led both monastics and laypeople to construct a replica of Mount Wutai’s layout at Lingguang Temple, which remains preserved to this day.
When his affairs were concluded, he passed away without illness.
He had lived for one hundred and eighteen years and held the Dharma-ordination for seventy-eight years.
Because his body did not decay, his disciples applied lacquer to it and enshrined it for veneration in a separate hall.
When the monasteries were destroyed during the Huichang persecution, he was subsequently burned to death.
Biography of Master Jin of Xuanweng Monastery in Hedong, Tang Dynasty: Master Jin, whose secular surname was Wang, was a native of Pingyao in Xihe; his birthplace was Zhukeng Village.
From childhood he was tall and imposing, yet by nature simple and blunt.
His actions were eccentric and unlike those of ordinary people;
he left home to become a monk on Mount Songyan.
His subsequent physical form was one zhang in height and one circumference in girth at the waist; his words regarding matters were often remarkably accurate, and he remained present after death.
The local people made offerings and sacrifices to him, and their prayers were all fulfilled according to their wishes.
From the West River to the Jihu region, all held him in high esteem.
*Biography of Shi Wuzuo of Mount Siming in Liang*. Shi Wuzuo, whose courtesy name was Bubing and whose surname was Sima, was a native of Gusu.
His father was Chen, a District Magistrate of Wanchou County;

his mother was Lady Dai. When she first became pregnant, she dreamed of a strange śramaṇa who called himself surnamed Xu and claimed to be the abbot of Liu-shui Temple. He wished to lodge there for the summer retreat, and having finished speaking, he sat cross-legged.
That night, his father dreamed that a single character was written upon a platter; it greatly pleased him, and he said to himself, "This child may advance to become a Son of Heaven.
At dawn, each recounted their dreams, and the mother said, "I believe the one in my womb must be a śramaṇa."
The mother said, "If a son is born,
I shall release him into the flowing waters so that he may leave the household life.
When the child was born, he was indeed remarkably intelligent and lovely, and moreover, he loathed the smell of meat and pungent odors.
By the time he reached the age of four, his mother personally instructed him in recitation; his intelligence was like gold being easily refined, and he retained everything in memory without omission.

His father wished for him to pursue the studies required for the examination of young scholars, yet as [the boy] gradually displayed a gentle and harmonious demeanor, he constantly manifested a desire to transcend the mundane world.
Shortly thereafter, the father stole a glance at the daughter of the Yao family; finding her both beautiful and graceful in appearance, he desired to take her as his own with great intensity.
His mother strictly forbade this, saying:
"If she were to renounce this son and leave the household to become a nun, it would alleviate your desire to take her."
The father then granted her request and sent her into the Liushi Temple.

Hardly more than a month had passed when Lady Yao’s marriage broke up; at that time, it was said that this girl was a *kalyāṇamitra*, having served as the superior condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for her renunciation.
At the age of twenty, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Subsequently, he lectured on and mastered the *Shanbu lüchao* (Excerpts from the Vinaya with Deletions and Additions), the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, and the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*.
He diligently investigated the religious systems of the One Vehicle and the Five Vehicles.
There were no writings of Confucius or Laozi that he did not peruse.
Later, he studied the profound teachings (xuanxue) under Chan Master Xuefeng Cun, penetrating deeply into the inner sanctum.

Upon reaching San’gu Mountain in Luling, a lay patron established Yunting Monastery, and in Yuzhang, Nanping Monastery was founded; he was invited to serve as the abbot of both, yet in each case, he shook out his robes and departed.
The former jinshi Tang Bing composed a stele for the Tripitaka, recounting the reasons why Master Gong declined the invitation.
He resided at Hongjing for ten years, yet he had not even set eyes upon the face of Master Hong, the Zhong family patriarch.
He then traveled to Kuaiji and Siming, where he formed the intention to spend the remainder of his life there.
Qian, the Prince Wusu of Wu-Yue, held him in high esteem and summoned him to emerge from Siming; however, he returned to the mountains on the pretext of illness, effectively declining the call.
He composed a poem expressing his intent and presented it to the King, but the King would not retain him either.
The poem says:
"The nature of the cloud-swallowing crane is solitary; how can it endure the gates of fame and profit?
"Though I have entered the kingdom out of gratitude for your kindness, I decline on account of illness and shall return to the mountains.

At that time, Sun He of Le'an in Fenghua was living in retirement, leading a life of carefree indifference and refusing to associate with the monastic community; he would only receive Fazhao, conversing with him all day long.
The Jinshi (Metropolitan Graduate) Yang Yan also admired the pursuit of life as a recluse beyond the forest.
He died in Siming during the Kaiping era of the Liang dynasty at the age of fifty-six.
Initially, he excelled in cursive and clerical scripts; his calligraphy was vigorous and robust, and many people copied his works to establish their own models.

He composed several dozen texts of liturgical repentance for various rites, annotated Da’an’s "Text on the Six Periods of Bowing to the Buddha" in one scroll, and also wrote poems and songs; all of these circulated throughout his time.
He refrained from entering nunneries, did not visit official gates, did not compose name-cards (*meishishi*), and did not pursue worldly profit; he styled himself the "Recluse of Ease" (*Xiaoyaozi*).

This is the biography of Guanhui of Dongchan Monastery in Chengdu Prefecture during the Liang Dynasty. Biography of Guanhui of Dongchan Monastery in Chengdu Prefecture during the Liang Dynasty: Chumu, Tanyu, and Shi Guanhui: Guanhui’s courtesy name was Deyin. His secular surname was Jiang, and he was a native of Denggao in Lanxi, Jinhua.
At the age of seven, his parents, who were naturally fond of him, sent him to the Chan Master Yuanzheng of He'an Temple in his home county to leave the household life as a novice attendant.
Each day he would recite one thousand characters of the Lotus Sutra from memory.
Whatever he heard even briefly, he never forgot it from his mind.

He lived in seclusion with Chu Mo, both having shaved their heads and donned the dyed robes; they resided in neighboring courtyards, discussing poetry across the fence and taking turns chanting to seek rhyming couplets. When monks saw them, they were all struck with wonder and amazement.

After receiving full ordination, his reputation for poetic talent resounded throughout the age; he then traveled to Yuzhang to transmit the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*, both of which were profound and subtle in meaning, and he was diligent in his exegesis and instruction.
The Prefect of this commandery, Wang Cao, treated him with even greater respect and esteem.
His successor, the Prefect Jiang Gui, opened and purified a repentance and precept platform, appointing Xiu to serve as the platform supervisor.

At the beginning of the Qianning era, he traveled with his aspirations to visit the Wuyue King Qian, the Wuhusu; he subsequently presented five chapters of poetry, each consisting of eight lines, which greatly pleased the King, who bestowed upon him generous gifts.
The King established his merit in eliminating the false, and the court honored him as a meritorious official.

He then separately erected a hall and a stele to record the names of the generals and officers who had exerted their strength together to pacify the Yue; he subsequently inscribed his poem of repose on the back of the stele, demonstrating such high esteem.
He excelled at minor calligraphy and attained mastery of the six laws of painting;
he was particularly adept at ink wash, and his depictions of forms were worthy of admiration.
At the request of Mr. Qiang’s pharmacy on Zhong'an Bridge, he produced a set of Arhats, saying:
"Whenever I paint a statue, I must first pray for a dream of its true likeness before I complete it.
Thus, his style differed from that of ordinary practitioners.
From then on, he traveled through Yí and Shè, where his way met with that of the Venerable Lán of Táng'ān Temple.

Later, he thought of ascending Mount Nanyue and traveling north to pay his respects to Cheng Rui, the military governor of Jingzhou. Initially, Cheng treated him with great courtesy and provided him lodging at Longxing Temple.
At that time, the Palace Secretary Wu Rong was there on a term of exile; they met and engaged in frequent discussions on both the Way and poetry.
In the third year of the Qianning era, Rong composed the preface to the *Xiuzuo ji* (Collection of Works on Rest and Activity).
Shortly thereafter, he was falsely accused by the military governor of Jingzhou, and Xiu was demoted to Gongan.
Amidst his deep frustration, he inscribed a verse upon his inkstone, saying:
"Only upon entering the casket does the body find peace.

His disciples urged the Master to enter Shu; at that time, the Wang family was plotting to usurp the throne and was summoning worthy scholars from all quarters. Upon meeting him, they were greatly delighted; he was treated with great courtesy and received lavish gifts and rewards, being bestowed with the title of Chan Yue Da Shi (Great Master Chan Yue).
The Ruler of Shu often called him "The Monk Who Comes for a Purpose.
At that time, Wei Ai cited this auspicious title.
What he excelled at was song and chant; his satirical verses were subtle and profound, yet they remained rooted in edification.
In character and refinement, he was not inferior to the two Lis—Li Bai and Li He.
He passed away at his residence in the second year of the Qiánhuà era of the Liáng dynasty at the age of eighty-one.

The ruler of Shu, filled with grief and compassion, provided official funerals for all of them; the pagoda was named Bailian (White Lotus) and erected as a stupa outside the North Gate of Chengdu during the Qiandé era of the pseudo-Shu dynasty—specifically the third year of Liang’s Qiànhuà era, the Guiyou year.
Xiu was capable of the "sage-like calligraphy" (caosheng).
His disciple Tanyu compiled the Master’s collected works in the guiyou year, placing the preface by the Imperial Secretary Wu at the beginning, with Yu himself providing the postscript.
Wei Zhuang once presented him with a poem that said:
"Is it because of poverty that we are often kept apart? It must be that you simply dislike wine that you do not come to visit.
Furthermore, he was on very good terms with Mr. Guangcheng Du Guangting, who was a fellow townsman.
He ceased writing calligraphy; those who prized it transmitted his works, calling them the "Jiang Style.
He once beheld the true likeness of [the Buddha], which was stout and short, and the Shu Chancellor Wang Xi composed a eulogy for it.
Tanyu’s study of the precepts was refined and subtle, and his seal script was bold and vigorous; he compiled a revised edition of Xu Shen’s *Shuowen Jiezi*, which circulated in Shu.
He also had a collection of poetry, which followed the style of Master Ya.

Biography of National Teacher Guo of Shuangxi Monastery on Mount Lu during the Liang Dynasty. Regarding the Venerable Guo of Shuangxi Monastery on Mount Lu during the Liang Dynasty: it is unknown where he was from.
His vessel was refined and pure, and his conduct was earnest, lofty, and transcendent; dwelling alone like a solitary clod of earth, he soared far above the confines of the physical form.
His studies were vast and extensive, yet he desired to cease his solitary journey; finding the beauty and uniqueness of Mount Lu, he vowed to live in seclusion to fulfill his aspirations.
He built a thatched hut and irrigated a garden to plant vegetables, leaving them for the mountain dwellers to gather as they pleased.
When someone asked him the reason for this, he replied,
"I planted these without intention, and I relinquish them without intention."
Examining this insight and knowledge, one truly reaches the highest stream of the Way.
The Vinaya Master Xiumu constantly inclined his mind toward honoring [the Master], presenting a poem to the Duke which said:
"Entering the gate, all is empty and still; you are truly a child who has left the home."
"Those with practice do not see ghosts; those without mind are called deluded.
Later, he passed away in his quarters and was buried at the foot of Mount Ssanggye, where a small stupa was erected.
Now, when one addresses him by the character "Guo," is this his name or his clan?
I have not yet ascertained this in detail.
Biography of Shi Zhixuan of Quanzhou during the Liang Dynasty. Shi Zhixuan was a native of Quanzhou.
In his prime, he aspired to the Dharma and emulated the character of the monk Yijing.
Vowing to live lightly or die, he desired to travel to the Western Regions to pay homage at the Eight Stūpas and seek out sutras and dharmas not yet transmitted to this land.

Toward the end of the Tang dynasty, he joined companions to cross the shifting sands; in every country he reached, he contemplated the past, sought out masters, pursued the extraordinary, and sought out wonders, collecting Sanskrit manuscripts and seeking śarīra relics.

In the fifth month of the first year of the Kaiping era, he arrived at present-day Dongjing (Luoyang), bringing with him the bones of a Pratyekabuddha and palm-leaf manuscripts of the sutras and vinaya written in Sanskrit.
He set out in the prime of his life, but by the time of his return, he was already advanced in years.

Emperor Taizu of the Liang dynasty, having recently overthrown the mandate of the Tang, was greatly pleased upon hearing that Xuan had returned. He bestowed gifts and provisions upon him, requesting that he translate [the scriptures] to take back to Jiaye.
At that time, however, the land was embroiled in the turmoil of war, and there was no leisure for such tasks.
Biography of Qi Ji of Longxing Temple in Jiangling Prefecture under the Liang Dynasty. Shi Qi Ji, surnamed Hu, was a native of Yiyang.
He maintained a lofty and brilliant integrity, yet his physical appearance was humble and unassuming.

From childhood, he renounced worldly life at Daopei Mountain Temple; he was exceptionally intelligent and surpassed his peers, receiving the full precepts and training in the monastic discipline (*vinaya*).
By nature he was devoted to poetic composition, his temperament being refined and serene.
Once, a Chan practitioner came from Deshan to describe its underlying principles; unconsciously, [Huangbo] found his spirit wandering through the vast and boundless realm.
He then went in person to pay his respects and inquire after their well-being; once he attained awakening and understanding, all traces of [dualistic] signs vanished.
Thus, at the various Chan monasteries—such as Yaoshan, Lumen, and Huguo—who among them did he not seek instruction from?
Regarding fame and profit, he viewed them all as being like floating clouds.
During the Dharma assembly at Shishuang, he was requested to oversee the monastic affairs.
When the Liang dynasty overthrew the Tang mandate, the empire fell into turmoil.

At that time, Gao Jichang, by imperial command of the Liang Emperor, attacked and expelled Lei Man from Zhugong; he was subsequently appointed as the Acting Governor (Liuhou) of Jingzhou and soon thereafter formally received the regional command (Jiedu).

When Emperor Jun lost his grip on power and Zhuangzong of Hedong entered Luoyang from Weifuzhou, the Gao family subsequently carved out a territory for themselves. They sought out men of integrity and reputation from all quarters, obtaining Yi Feng of Qi and Ji of the Southern Peak, regarding them as proof of the initial efficacy of their "casting gold" policy.

In the first year of Longde (Xinsi), during the month of Zhongli, he was appointed to reside in the Pure Court of Longxing Monastery; he was provided with a monthly stipend and commissioned as the Sangzheng, though this was not to his liking.

On a leisurely day and a tranquil night, amidst many matters of literary composition, I have thus written the "Fifteen Chapters of Questions Unasked at Zhugong" to express my intent and to comply with the command of the Illustrious One.
He had a goiter on his neck, which earned him the nickname "Poetry Sack.
Content with his humble circumstances, he wrapped himself in tattered rags and bound his knees with hempen cloth.

Delighting in mountains and rivers, he was too indolent to pay court to princes and lords; this led to the familiar verse: "Never once have I taken a single word to easily seek audience with the feudal lords."
He exchanged poems with the recluse Zheng Gu of Mount Hua.
Upon his death, the *Bailian ji* (White Lotus Collection) circulated in the world; he styled himself the Śramaṇa of Mount Heng.
Biography of Wuji of Guangfu Monastery in Lingzhou during the Later Tang Dynasty. Shi Wuji, surnamed Shi, was a native of Shuofang.
During the reign of Emperor Xuanzong, the Buddha-dharma flourished once more.

In the ninth year of the Dazhong era, at the age of thirteen, he resolved to leave the household life and became a disciple of Master Fakong at Baicao Monastery. He maintained his discipline with profound integrity, brushing away the dust of worldly clamor.
In the third year of the Xiantong era, he went to the capital as a guest and received the precepts and ordination at Ximing Monastery.
Regarding the hundred arts, he was willing to explore them all.
I admire Dinglin’s mastery of painting and Dai Andao’s skill with the *qin*. As for myself, in addition to my studies and exegesis, I have practiced both arts concurrently.
Previously, Tang Hengfu once served as the military governor of Shuofang; later, we met in the capital, where he treated me with the courtesy due to a family monk.
Thus it was known that his words and deeds were mutually exalted, and he was further able to lead others through his preaching.
He presented himself to the Merit Commissioners of the two streets, requesting to be attached to Ximing Monastery.

Shortly thereafter, Emperor Yizong went to Famen Monastery in Fengxiang to welcome the True Body (the Buddha’s relic). Zhang Siguang, the Right Assistant Commissioner for Propagation, submitted a memorial appointing [Hengfu] to serve as a chant leader (*zandao*). This greatly pleased the Emperor's heart, and he bestowed lavish rewards and favors upon him.
During the Guangqi era, he transmitted the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-jvalita-prabhāsa-āveśa-sarva-graha-nakṣatra-maṅgala-maṇḍala-dharmaparyāya* and returned to his native prefecture.

When the Prefectural Commander, Duke Han, heard that he was capable of dispelling calamities within his administrative division, he established an altar at the football field and performed the rites with great success, receiving many spiritual responses.
During the Jingfu era, when Grand Marshal Duke Han established Guangfu Temple, he petitioned for [the Master] to serve as its abbot.
He governed all according to the monastic rules and precepts; those seeking ordination along the borderlands invariably requested him to act as their spiritual father.
In the year of Bingzi during the Qiànhuà era of the Liáng dynasty, Hàn Gōng Shū, the Chancellor of the Central Secretariat, submitted a memorial to bestow upon him the master title of Hóngyuǎn.
On the first day of the fourth month in the third year of the Tóngguāng era of the Later Táng (the year of Yǐyǒu), he passed away while seated in his chamber.
His tendons and bones remained as if alive, and his spiritual presence seemed still present; when people of both the frontier tribes and the Han observed this rite, they sighed in admiration, saying:
"In the past, during the Zhide era, the eminent monk Biancai of Longxing Temple in our prefecture passed away while seated in meditation, and his body was subsequently lacquered and clothed."
In the first year of the Qianning era, the provincial governor submitted a memorial, and by imperial decree, he was posthumously titled "Nengjue" (Able Awakening).
Is it not fitting that the traces of this master should be honored at a different time for the same service?
The Grand Chancellor, Duke Han, ordered artisans to apply lacquer to the monument.
During the reign of Emperor Zhuangzong, Xue Zhaoji, an official of the military administration, composed an inscription to commemorate his virtues, stating:

"The Biography of Shi Yongguang of Guo Ning Temple in Mingzhou during the Later Tang. Shi Yongguang, whose courtesy name was Dengfeng, was surnamed Wu and was a native of Yongjia. He was a descendant of Wu Jing, a former Vice Director of the Left in the Court of History under the Tang dynasty.
In his youth, he left home to receive the tonsure at Taoshan Temple.
He lived in strict seclusion, never mingling with ordinary people.
He delighted in asserting his own superiority and treated his fellow monastics with disdain.
He frequently composed poems in archaic styles that were pedantic and lacked flavor; yet whenever he produced a clever line, he would show signs of self-satisfaction.
He was skilled in cursive and clerical scripts. Upon hearing that Lu Xisheng had been exiled to Yuzhang, Guang went there to pay him a visit.
Lu Tianjing was composed yet possessed an air of pride; while residing upon his boat, he repeatedly sent his calling-card to seek an audience, but Lu would not grant him an interview.

One day, Lu devised a clever stratagem to pay his respects; after conversing with him several times, he earnestly entreated him for instruction in the cursive script, whereupon Lu bestowed upon him the secret instructions for the "Five-Fingered Finger-Pressing" method.
His calligraphic style was seen to be preeminent and robust; his turning of the wrist and revolving of the brush were beyond the comprehension of ordinary people.
He subsequently traveled westward, where Emperor Zhaozong summoned him to write before the imperial couch and bestowed upon him a purple square-cut robe.
Later, he went to pay his respects to the military commander of Hua, Han Jian, who bestowed upon him the title Guangli.
From Hua, he returned to his native village and visited the King of Wusu, the Qian clan, who received him with the courtesy due to a guest.
However, his character was rigid and extreme, which did not satisfy the King’s wishes; he subsequently retired to Yongdong, where he spent the remainder of his life.
He left behind a collection of literary works, which is highly esteemed by those who appreciate true art.
Among his calligraphy disciples were Conggui and the monk-administrator of Wenzhou, Zhicong, both of whom mastered the secret precepts of the brush.

There were court scholars who presented songs and poems in his honor, including fifty families such as the Palace Secretary (Nèihan) Rong of Wu and Luo Jiangdong Yin; these alone formed a single collection.
At that time, the Governor of Siming, Yang Quan, having long admired Guang’s lofty reclusion, personally presided over the funeral rites and issued the orders for the burial.

Three years later, in accordance with the custom of the Western Regions, his body was cremated; when the coffin was opened, the remains appeared as if he were still alive, with his beard, hair, and nails all having grown long.
His relics were collected through cremation, and a small stupa was erected for them during the Changxing era of the Later Tang dynasty.
Biography of Shi Zixin of Xuanzhou during the Jin Dynasty Shi Zixin, whose secular surname was Sun, was a native of Linzi.
